speechtext:
That m-ay be, but it is not according to the dignity or the duty of the Government to leave a province without representation for such a long time. It may be that it is difficult for the right hon. the Prime Minister to make a choice. However, I do not see why some one has not been called upon to fill the vacancy during t'he last six or seven weeks. The -Government ha-s six or seven supporters on the other side of the House from that province every one of whom, I am- sure, would be
willing to accept uie responsibilities of omce. It is impossible to believe that every one of these six or seven representatives of the people from the province of New Brunswick is so modest that he will not accept any office -at th-e hands of the Prime Minister. Is it, that the sweets of office have turned -sour and that nobody wants to taste them? The people of New Brunswick are- anxious that something should be done, and, while the Prime Minister -continues' to lead the destinies of the nation, New Brunswick should be given its fair share of representation as well as assuming its responsibility for the administration of affairs. In- the years gone by -and up to the present time- the province of New Brunswick has been represented by men of great talent, high position and enjoying a large measure of public esteem. We have had a long succession of able representatives from Confederation down to recent times. We had, first, Sir Leonard Tilley, and then we had the present right hon. the Minister of- Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), who, as Minister of Finance, represented the province of New Brunswick in the councils of the nation not only with dignity to himself but with satisfaction and honour to his province. We consider him yet the great -genius of finance on the other side of the -House although he has not lpen given by this Government the position which would enable him to exercise that talent. We are anxious that we -should be represented in this Government no matter what the difficulties may be. One more cannot add much more to its weakness while it may -add something to its -strength.
Before I proceed any further, as my voice is now raised on behalf of the province of New Brunswick and perhaps the last to be heard from that province in this debate, let me say that I do not wish to resume my seat without making reference to the visit of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales who first -set foot in Canada within the province which I have the honour to represent. It was in the city of St. John that His Royal Highness, our future King, who, in the years to come will succeed not only to the throne of his father but to that of his ancestors, every -one of whom from Queen Victoria to George V has added lustre to the British Empire, first met the people of Canada. Let me -say here to the House and the country that the people of New Brunswick received His Royal Highness with the same enthusiasm as has been manifested in the larger cities of Montreal,

Quebec and Toronto, and that thousands ot citizens and thousands of returned soldiers went from the northern and other parts of the province, travelling hundreds of miles in order to be present at the reception of the Prince of Wales, their future King. They have gone back to their homes enthusiastic over his appearance and the development on his part of the true spirit of democracy which characterized the conduct of His Royal Highness not only at St. John but at Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa.
We were promised last session that a tariff commission would he appointed consisting of some of the responsible ministers who, together with experts, would travel through the country and acquire all -the knowledge possible in order to be ready at an early date to take up the question of tariff reform. Two months have passed but no step has been taken that I know of yet with the object of forming that commission although many other commissions of different kinds have been appointed since. It has always been my chief aim to see the tariff reduced on the necessaries of life and reduced more particularly on behalf of the larpiers. The farming industry is the chief industry of Canada. We stated last session that further reductions should take place more particularly on food and on the necessaries of life. We saw no effective reduction of duties in the last tariff presented by the Minister of Finance. It is true the Conservative papers of the country have busied themselves since the close of the last session pointing out to the country that an amount of $17,000,000 has been taken off the tariff by the abolition of the 7| and 5 per cent duties imposed by this Government themselves at the opening of the war. Only a couple of days ago we found the Ottawa Journal calling attention to the question of the tariff and emphasizing the fact that when in June the Government brought down the Budget, $17,000,000 was taken off the tariff at one fell swoop thus giving the West lower duties on agricultural implements than reciprocity would have given.
Let me say for the edification of the peo-[DOT]ple that the reduction of seventeen millions of dollars referred to has been effected by removing duties imposed by the Conservative 'Government in excess of the tariff that existed when the Liberal party were in power. After war was declared the Conservatives added special war duties of 7j and 5 per cent to the general and Brit-

ish preferential tariff rates respectively upon, with certain exceptions, all imports. When the war closed, and at the persistent request of the Liberal Opposition, the Government saw fit to remove those duties [DOT]which had not resulted in any great good to Canada. For my part, I always regarded the five per cent special tax on imports coming from Great Britain as evidencing a disappointing lack of loyalty to the manufacturers and workmen of that country, for it meant the imposition of $5 uipon every $100 worth of goods coming from 'Great Britain before they could be landed in Canada. The newspaper in question also refers to the small reduction on farming implements made by the Government as a greater benefit than the reciprocity agreement would have been to the people of Canada. How can that be argued when under the reciprocity agreement the farmers of Canada, particularly those in the West, would not only have got free access to the markets of the United States for their wheat, but virtually for all their other grains, potatoes and live stock? They could have sold their live stock at better prices in the country to the south than they could realize in Canada and could have imported, free of duty, such animals as they needed to improve the stock maintained on Canadian soil. As to the duties on farming implements Canadian farmers would undoubtedly have derived a much greater benefit under the terms of the reciprocity pact than under the legislation of last session. Since 1913, however, the Canadian manufacturers have been given a free market in the United States and have been able to successfully compete in. that market with their American rivals. Therefore, the necessity for the maintenance of the duty on the more important farming implements should have disappeared at once.
The people of Canada have now to consider the question of trade with the nations with Which they have been at war. No doubt there will be great reluctance in the minds of our people to do any trade at all with Germany. Certain restrictions have been imposed upon Germany by the allied nations. I do not say those restrictions are too severe in view of Germany's conduct, but the question must be considered that the compensation to be exacted from Germany depends upon the possibility of her making payment in the future. We have not yet received any payments from that country, and if we deprive her of the power to trade with other countries we can

never expect that she will be in a position to pay any compensation. Canadian financiers may have to seriously consider the possibilities of trade between Canada and Germany. It must be remembered that Canada had commercial dealings of some importance before the war with the German Empire. In the period from 1909 to 1914 the exports of Canada to Germany were valued at 8,398,000 marks. In 1911 those figures had trebled, and in 1913 our exports amounted to 64,100,000 marks, nearly seven and a half times the figures of 1909. On the other hand German imports to Canada had only reached the sum of 60,500,000 marks, giving a trade balance in favour of Canada of 4,000,000 -marks. There is this fact to be considered in connection with our trade with Germany before the war; unfortunately, the bulk of Canada's purchases were in the form of manufactured goods, while our exports consisted chiefly of raw material. That is quite contrary to what should have happened, and something we should be careful to guard against in future if trading with Germany is again resumed. Canada should only buy from Germany those manufactured goods which we cannot produce economically at home, and export to that country no raw material that we can profitably utilize here. As to the future trade relations between Germany and her Allies, the latter have been careful to provide for certain economic clauses which I consider are in harmony with my own principles as an old member of this House, and my desire to see this country move towards the goal of free trade with all reasonable rapidity. There are certain other provisions which tend towards freedom of trade between the allied and enemy nations, under the terms of which the enemy nations cannot impose a greater duty on goods imported from allied countries than are exacted on goods imported from friendly or neutral nations.
Let me take the liberty of citing to you, Mr. Speaker, two or three clauses of Part 10 in regard to commercial relations, from which you will observe that the principle of freedom of trade between the nations of the world is dealt with in such a way as. in my opinion, should convince us that the greater freedom of trade we have with the other nations of the world the sooner will Canada take its place among those nations. Article 264 reads:
Germany undertakes that goods the produce or manufacture of any one of the Allied or Associated States imported into German territory, from whatsoever place arriving, shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges (including internal charges) than those to
which the like goods the produce or manufacture of any other such State or of any other foreign country are subject.
Germany will not maintain or impose any prohibition or restriction on the importation into German territory of any goods the produce or manufacture of the territories of any one of the Allied or Associated States, from whatsoever place arriving, which shall not equally extend to the Importation of the like goods the produce or manufacture of any other such State or of any other foreign country.
The principle of freedom of trade has been enunciated by the representatives of the Allied nations, of whom my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, was one, and as he accepted that principle I hope he will endeavour to put it into practice.
Profiteering and unrest are still with us. In the United States prompt measures have been taken to stop profiteering and alleviate the sufferings of the masses. We have seen that the labour element is not without consideration for the position of the country. They have said that they wanted an increase of wages only because of the increase in the prices of the necessaries of life. Only a few days ago the Labour leaders in the United States who had been threatening to call a strike, demonstrated their intelligence by their manly behaviour, when they told the President that they would give him three months to reduce the cost of living, and if he succeeded in doing so there would be no strike and they would continue at the same rate of wages as they are earning to-day. It is not reasonable to always blame the labouring man if he is not satisfied with his fate. The labourer to-day wants a rate of pay that will enable him to support his wife and children and educate the latter to the best extent possible; and it is the duty of every Government to see that the necessaries of life are kept down jto such a figure that the mass of the people may be able to live in peace and contentment. I admire the attitude of the labour element in the United States, and I believe that that attitude expresses the feelings of our own labour element.
The term democracy is often used. I say there is only one democracy that will give the people happiness, and that is Christian democracy. The returned soldier has perhaps not been able to receive at the hands of the people everything that was promised him, and we cannot expect him to enjoy life and to feel that we have been grateful to him until in addition to the showers of sentiment thrown upon his head, substantial means are afforded him to give his wife and family the life to which they are entitled. [DOT] Under a Christian democracy dif-

ferent races and creeds will be able to live together in peace and harmony-and I am thinking more particularly of Canada-and will be able to enjoy the sweetness of life in fraternal fellowship. I hope that this great Dominion of ours will be able to enjoy this Christian democracy and that we will hear no more of the French race and the English race, nor of Catholics or Protestants, but that we will regard one another as Canadians. The expression of harmony between the two races and creeds is one of the great virtues of British sentiment, and we all know that the British flag is symbolical of fair play and sympathy for minorities and for races and creeds of all kinds.
In such a democracy the profiteer will have no contentment, and if he does not disgorge his millions made at the expense of the poor, he will be forced to go to Germany or Russia if he wishes to continue his nefarious practices. Fortunately we have at last a Commission with some power to deal with profiteers, and that Commission is sitting to-day in Montreal. May I be permitted to say that. I hope the Commission may take the same drastic action as the Commission which the United States has appointed, which is empowered to impose a fine of five thousand dollars and a year's imprisonment upon profiteers of food.
It would be well for the Board of Commerce, now sitting in 'Montreal, to look into the conditions respecting the profits on [DOT]clothing, including boots and shoes-more particularly the clothing, boots and shoes used by the masses of the people.
I wish to refer again to the fact that New Brunswick is in the unusual position of being without representation in the Cabinet. If New Brunswick had had a representative in the Cabinet during the past couple of weeks I should likely have conferred with him some days ago on a recent incident in my province. Much has been said about the arrest of defaulters and deserters. I shall not enter into a discussion of that question to-day; I wish simply to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to something which happened a few days ago in the county of Kent in my province. An officer who had been looking for defaulters lost his life and the verdict of the coroners' jury was to the effect that it was not known whether the officer's death was the result of an accident, or whether it was at the hand of a criminal. The evidence given at the inquiry leads to the conclusion that the death of the officer was due to an accident, pMr. Turgeon.]
the firearm which he was carrying having exploded and killed him almost instantly. I shall not give my version or judgment of the matter, but I wish to point out the seriousness of the situation. Here are men going round in search of human beings with firearms in their hands-using them, I might say, indiscriminately.
When conscription was put into effect thirteen hundred volunteers from the county of Gloucester had gone to the field of battle, and if during a few months no more enlisted it was because, in a county whose chief industries are agriculture and the fisheries, there were no more to leave; all the others were required at home. Of the thirteen hundred and more volunteers who went overseas, 1,150 were French-Acaddans. No blemish rests upon the name of the Acadians of the Maritime Provinces. I deemed it my duty from time to time during the course of the war to call upon my constituents to go to the front-all who could possibly leave their fathers and mothers. They responded nobly to my call; yet to-day the county is scoured by officers simply because one or two or a few of these young men, most likely in ignorance of the law and of their responsibilities and duties under it, did not come forward. As has been said to-day and on other occasions in this House, the military service law was such that every young man in the back districts could not be expected to be familiar with it; many of them, therefore, remained at home and worked on the farm for their fathers and mothers. But now these men are being sought after, eight or nine months after the commencement of the negotiations for peace, when everybody is rejoicing in the hope of the enjoyment of priciples of democracy and justice to whose triumph we have looked forward as the result of the successful conclusion of the war. Houses have been opened and entered in the middle of the night; disastrous results have attended the intrusion of these officers into homes. I call upon the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) in the absence of the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn), to make a thorough investigation into this whole matter, and in the meantime to stop chasing about for more defaulters in the county of Kent. I hope that these few remarks, made without any previous preparation or consideration, will have their effect, and that the Prime Minister will look into the case which I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to add my

congratulations to those which have already "been so worthily bestowed upon the mover and the seconder of the Address? May I also, speaking for the people of the county of Frontenac, express their appreciation of the honour which has been conferred upon the Dominion of Canada by the visit of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales to this country and their pleasure at the cordial reception which he has received in every part of Canada which he has so far visited.
It is not my intention, Sir, to occupy more than four or five minutes of the time of the House. I would not occupy even that length of time were it not that I think it my duty to place some facts on Hansard in order that the hon. member for Antigon-ish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) may correct in some particulars the essay which he read to the House yesterday.
I wish first to allude to the expressions which have fallen from the lips of certain hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to the losses which we have sustained on this side on the occasion of certain members leaving this side or leaving the Government. Up to the present time we have not noticed any very great decrease in our assets on this side, and I venture to say that hon. gentlemen opposite will not notice any appreciable increase in the assets on their side because of the movements of certain gentlemen who have seats in this House. The sympathy, however, comes from a source which at once commands our respect, because no persons could speak with fuller hearts about the loss of adherents to a party than those gentlemen who sit opposite and who have passed through the trying times of the last two or three years.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Turgeon) has made a plea for the defaulters-those who failed to do their duty in the time of war- and he apparently deprecates going after these persons in a way that will be effective. If we went after them With feather dusters or with ice cream cones, how would he expect us to induce them to come forward? The fact of the matter is that certain persons failed to do their duty; they violated the laws of this country, and it is no more than simple justice that they should be punished for their delinquency. I think it is due to the men who came forward and voluntarily offered their services that those who failed to do their duty should be brought to a realization of their responsibility and of the wrong which they committed. I appreciate what has been done by the constituents of my hon. friend. He has 5
very much to be proud of, and I rejoice with him in the number of voluntary enlistments from his county, but in my judgment that should not excuse those who failed to respond to the call. They should be made to realize, whether they come from Gloucester county, Frontenac county, or any other part of the Dominion, that they failed in their responsibility as citizens of this country at a time of crisis, and they should not be allowed to go scot-free.
The hon. gentleman also alluded to the removing of some $17,000,000 of duties by the Finance Minister last session. Hon. gentlemen opposite, including my hon. friend, have seen fit at various times to advocate a reduction- of duty, and it therefore does seem rather strange that when the duty is taken off they should not be satisfied-my hon. friend said that the removing of that amount of duty last session was of no great good to Canada. He also spoke of the increase of 7J per cent. I think I am right in saying that when that increase was made my hon. friend made no protest, nor did those who sat with him on the other side of the House. It was generally accepted as the proper thing to do.
In regard to his observations concerning the removal of the duty on agricultural implements, the record of the Liberal party in that respect is such a peculiar one that I should think hon. gentlemen opposite would never refer to the duty on implements. For eighteen years they had denounced the duty on agricultural implements, and had promised the farmers of this country that if they were returned to power they would give them free agricultural implements; yet when they were returned to power, their fifteen years of office was characterized by an absolute betrayal of the people to whom they had made promises. When they did undertake to do anything with regard to the duty on agricultural implements, after being in office for a number of years, down to 1907, they made a reduction of 2| per cent.	They reduced the duty
from 20 to 17* per cent, but at the same time raised the valuation for duty purposes. The valuation of a binder, for instance, wag raised from $80-the valuation when the duty was 20 per pent-to $100, so while they were trying to make the farmer believe that he was getting a reduction in the duty of 2J per cent, in reality they made him pay $17.50 on a binder, where, under the 20 per cent duty he paid



only $16. These are 'the gentlemen who today, out of office, appeal to 'the farmers as the farmers' friends. I make the assertion, which oan< be substantiated by fact upon fact, that the Borden Administration has done more for the farmers of Canada since it came into office than the Liberal party did during the fifteen years it occupied the treasury benches. I do not propose to follow that matter any further.

In what respect, as a matter of principle, does he differ from the man who made his millions before the war started? How did this other acquire his millions if it was not out of the sweat and misery, of the white slaves who worked for less than adequate wages in order that he might become rich? There is very little condemnation for that man; yet, I say that, as a matter of principle, the only difference between the two is the difference of opportunity. Men took advantage of the war. I do not believe they are one particle worse than the. men who took advantage of the situation previous to the war to make use of the labour of thousands and hundreds of thousands of people up and down this country and to give them a wage by which they could scarcely provide the necessaries of life.
You tell me that the big problem of Canada is the high cost of living. When did it become a problem? Is there anything new about it? The only thing new about it, and the only thing that makes it a problem, is the fact that it is pinching people whom it did not pinch before. There has always been a cost of living problem in this country for the man whose wages were not sufficient to enable him to buy the necessaries of life. It did not require a great war for him to have a high cost of living problem on his hands. The high cost of living problem to-day is due, in so far as the prices of foodstuffs are concerned, to the relation of supply and demand, to the scarcity of the necessities of life and for the foodstuffs required for the people to live upon. What has brought about that scarcity? In the first place you have had 50,000,000 or 60,000,000 men, who formerly were engaged in production of one kind or another, destroying things for the last four or five years. You could not have anything else but scarcity. Let me go a little farther back to the time when there was a problem in this country. I refer to a time not within the last eight or ten years but to' a time antecedent to that. We will go back to 1896 if you like, and we will recall the golden days when the Liberal party was in power. Was there no problem then? I will tell you what the problem was then. The problem then was that the people living in the cities and towns were buying their eggs for 12J to 15 cents a dozen and their butter for from 20 to 25 cents a pound. The fact of the matter was that the farmer was selling his produce in very nianv cases at less than it cost him

to produce. That did not constitute a prohlsm at that time but that was the beginning and the basis of the problem of the high cost of living to-day. That is what drove people off the farms; they were not making one-quarter of one per cent on their investment and they went to the cities and towns. You need not take my word for that. Take the statistics, take the last census and you will find that the migration from the farms throughout Ontario and the older provinces went on steadily during the whole fifteen years that the Liberals were in power. I have stated the reason why they left the country, forsook rural life and went to the cities and towns. They went because young men realized that they could make a better living by going to the cities and towns than they could possibly make by remaining on the farm. They are up against the problem in the country of not having sufficient labour with the result _ that you have lessened production, scarcity and a greater demand for food than there is food to satisfy that demand. Beyond any question you must have higher prices for the various articles of food khan formerly.
Inhere has been a great deal of criticism in the press, and a good deal of unfair criticism by people who live in the cities, of the profits that are being made by the farmers. I have lived in a country constituency and amongst farmers all my life. I think I understand country conditions in the province of Ontario as well as any man. I have looked very carefully into the conditions under which farming operations are carried on and I have come to the conclusion that the prices that the farmers of the ' county of Frontenac and the adjoining counties are receiving for what they have to sell are not a cent higher than those which they should receive if they are to continue their business upon their faims. I do not care what it is that you mention, the farmer is entitled to every cent he is getting and he is getting none too much for what he produces and has to sell.
You say:	Get more men on the farm;
get greater production. Very good; I agree with that. Every farmer will agree with that. But we are up against conditions today in Canada which cannot be laid to this Government or to any party; they are conditions arising out of the war. Prices were paid for shells and munitions that attracted young men from the country to the city. Why not? If they could get $6 or $7 a day making shells, is it reasonable to suppose that they would not go to the towns and the cities to receive such an attractive wage?

They could not make any such money at home. They took advantage of the offer and they went to the towns and cities where they could get higher wages and shorter hours of work. The prices paid for shells were very high but the urgency was great. There was an immediate demand for them. If I fall into the lake and I am struggling to save myself and calling for somebody to help me, I am not going to quibble with him about the price he has to pay for the, rope which he is going to throw to me. I say: Throw it in, no matter what it costs. That was the position we w'ere in with regard to our troops in France. They were facing troops that were equipped with everything necessary to carry on the war and they were restricted in the matter of shells and munitions. They must have shells at once and it did not make any difference what these shells cost. Any man who had a boy over at the western front and who knew that that hoy was handicapped by a lack of the necessary equipment and munitions to fight the enemy would not stop to quibble about the price paid for those munitions.
Those were the conditions which have unbalanced things in this country. A great many people throughout Canada are making a living by stirring up unrest. Some of them sit in this House; they are taking advantage of the position they occupy in order to exaggerate every little thing that can he brought up in order to stir up any person or any section of people against the present Government. I think the Government will live through it. I think the people of this country, when they have an opportunity of calmly considering these various matters, will size them up pretty nearly right and will also size up pretty nearly right the men who have the honour and privilege of occupying seats in this House. They will determine whether a man in this House is honestly and sincerely endeavouring to solve the problems we have to face in this country or is taking advantage of every little opportunity to make capital for his political party. I believe the people have sufficient intelligence to size up the men of this House and the men outside of this House who are agitating in various parts of the country.	.
The prevailing unrest is attributed to -the returned soldier. I believe Sir Arthur Currie spoke correctly when he said at Toronto that the unrest in Canada was not caused by the returned soldier who went overseas and fought for his country at $1.10 a day, but by the men in this country who remained in perfect safety at
home and pulled down from $5 to $6 and $7 a day. I believe Sir Arthur Currie was absolutely right in that statement.
In conclusion, I have this to say to the leader of the Opposition and those who sit with him: If they think they are capable of fooling the farmers of this country again as they did in 1896, they have another big think coming. I assure hon. gentlemen opposite that they cannot do it again.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Yes, let us discuss it for a~ moment. The reciprocity pact of 1911 was different in some respects from the platform which was worked out at the last Grit convention held in this city in the month of August. If I remember rightly the great concern of the thousand or more people who attended that convention was about the farmer. He was the man to whom my friends opposite were appealing, he was the one for whom they were expressing great concern. What was proposed by the reciprocity pact of 1911 ? Hon. gentlemen opposite proposed by that pact to force the farmers of Canada to compete against the world, and they left the manufacturers absolutely untouched with the slight exception of the change that was proposed in regard to agricultural implements. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite if that is not a fact? If I am making any misstatement I will pause for a moment and allow my hon. friends to mention any other manufactures that were touched by the pact in question. I ask, were hon. gentlemen opposite concerned then about the price of clothing, boots, or anything else the people had to buy? No, with the exception of the implement manufacturer they left the manufacturer untouched just as they left him untouched in 1907. Just as in that year they said to the manufacturers, who were showing -some concern because of the promises the Liberals had made to wipe out pro-

tection. " Do not be a bit alarmed; we have devised a way by which we can fool the farmers to the limit and yet actually give you fellow's more protection than you are now receiving." " How are you going to do that?" That was simply A, B, C to any person worthy of being called a Grit. The Grit understands political economy along that line; he is 100 per cent perfect where it comes to a question of that kind. "We will simply cut down the duty on binders from 20 to 17^ per cent. We will feature that in big headlines in the Globe and the other Grit papers in the country. The farmers will see that and they will say, "There you are. They are getting after these bloated manufacturers. Look at what they have done. They have cut the duty down from 20 to I7j per cent." " Well, what then?" " We will simply raise the valuation on a binder, which is now $80, to a $100, and the farmer will never get on to that. You fellows will know all about it, and the duty will really be $17.50, whereas it was formerly $16." That is what they did in 1907. The farmers fell far that, so hon. gentlemen opposite said: "We will try it again in 1911. We are afraid to tackle these manufacturers except when we are in the House. We can swear at the manufacturers a little there as far as the rules of Parliament will allow us, but we won't interfere with them." When a big deputation of manufacturers came down to learn the plans of the ' 'Government Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: " I assure you, gentlemen, we have been very, very careful not to do anything to hurt the manufacturers!." 'He used the word "very" twice, in order to carry conviction to the minds of these disturbed manufacturers. Sir Wilfrid said: " We propose to enact this reciprocity pact, but don't worry. We are not going to touch manufactured articles at all; we know you would not stand for it. But the farmer will stand for it, and we will take the duty off every blessed thing that he has to raise. We will make him compete with every other country on the face of Gad's earth in what he has to sell, but he will still pay through the nose-as we have always been telling him he had to under the tariff that we have -for what he has to buy." That is the history of 1911. Now hon. gentlemen opposite are playing the fiddle1 to a new tune. They have come forward with a certain platform and they pledge themselves to do this and do that. I notice there was a great hush-at least I presume there was a great hush, for I was not there-and a great solemnity throughout that great gathering, [Mr. Edwards. 1
when they were preparing the resolution with regard to agricultural implements and cutting those duties off. They did not simply content themselves with passing a resolution, but with eyes lifted to the heavens and hands clasped-I suppose in prayer for success in their future political endeavours-they said "We, the Liberal party of the Dominion of Canada, pledge ourselves to carry this out and to cut these duties off if you will put us into power." I do not know that my friends opposite accompanied their pledge with prayer in 1896, but they made their pledge at that time just as strong as they could make it without prayer. I repeat the statement to hon. gentlemen opposite: You cannot put that over again; you can have all the conventions in the city of Ottawa that you like, and you can call the faithful-that is, all those who were against conscription, because any one who favoured conscription need not apply-you can call the faithful into conventions; you can deliberate on these resolutions and say what you are going to do, but the facts of history are staring you in the face. There is the past to be reckoned with, there is that great record confronting you; there is that great apostacy, there is that great betrayal; there is that great going-back on the pledges and the promises that you had made for eighteen long years. You declared when you were in Opposition that you were ready to wade in blood if necessary-because you were going to cut off the head of protection and trample on its body 

you were ready to wade in blood if necessary to wipe out the protection on manufactured articles and give the farmer a chance. And when you got the opportunity you left the manufacturers absolutely alone; the only man you touched was the farmer. You told the farmers of Canada at that time: "We do not care what the climatic conditions of this country are, you will compete with the world." I say, Sir, to-day, as I have said before, that the policy of the Liberal party, or of 'any other party in this country, in that respect, is absolutely illogical, and it is unfair to the farmers of Canada to compel them to compete with the world in the things they produce.
The tariff, Mr. Speaker, gives us a means of equalizing conditions to a certain extent. We have got to take into consideration to-day not the distance we are from this or that country, but the length of time it takes to bring the goods of any country to Canada. Is it fair that the farmer of Ontario or of Quebec or of any other part of Canada, who has spent thousands of

dollars in putting up expensive barns and stables to house his stock during our rigorous winter, should be told that he must compete on equal terms with the farmers of the Argentine, who have to spend not one dollar on expensive buildings, for ' their *stock are in the open the year round, and whose cost of labour is probably not one-tenth of what it is here? That is, in effect, what any person is saying to the farmers of Canada in general when he announces that he is going to adopt a free trade policy and force them to compete on equal terms with farmers in other countries, who, instead of having the most rigorous climatic conditions to contend with, possess every advantage so far as climate is concerned.
I say it is absolutely unfair, and if hon. gentlemen opposite think the farmers of this country have not thought these things out for themselves and determined the kind of policy they want, then I believe my hon. friends opposite will have to give this matter a great deal more consideration in the future than they apparently have in the past. When I rose I had no intention of doing any more than performing what I consider to be a duty on my part, Mr. Speaker-that of placing some facts on Hansard which would enable the hon. member for Antigon-ish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) to make the necessary corrections in that very beautiful essay which he read to the House yesterday. Although he is not in his seat I trust he will take advantage of the fact that my remarks will be found in [Hansard to make the necessary corrections before he sends out his essay to his constituents.

speechtext:
Well, I accept the statement of the Prime Minister. But even if it was submitted to the British Parliament, it would have been binding without submission to or ratification by that body. I am not fully conversant with the questions that were discussed at the Peace Conference; I had not the opportunity afforded to the Prime Minister and his colleagues of being present and of obtaining full information with regard to the matters which were considered. I am not, therefore, in a position to submit any amendments to the Peace Treaty, and I shall not do so. It may not be perfect. It may not contain all the conditions that France would like it to contain. But the task of framing the conditions of peace was a very difficult one. The Premier of France has said that it was harder to make peace than to make war. There were many difficult problems to settle. Many nations were represented at the Conference; each nation had its own needs, its own desires, its own aspirations. After all, I think we may congratulate the world upon the fact that the Treaty has been entered into and that it has brought an end to the horrors of war which have prevailed for more than four years.
The Peace Treaty has been supplemented by the agreement which I have mentioned, entered into between Great Britain, the United States and France. The President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Great Britain have assured France that their countries will always be ready to go to her assistance if she is again threatened with attack by Germany. This supplementary agreement may protect France for many years from any attack by Germany.

A concomitant of the Peace Treaty is the Covenant of the League of Nations. This Covenant is not binding upon Canada unless it is accepted by the Canadian Parliament. The League of Nations Covenant has been designed for a great purpose- that of avoiding wars in the future. But it may not serve this purpose. I had hoped that the Covenant would contain a provision for general disarmament, but I see no such provision in it. In fact, the nation which was most insistent upon the formation of this League is actually increasing its armaments, and other countries are doing the same. Indeed, we are increasing ours, because at the last session of Parliament legislation was adopted providing for the doubling of our military force. But the main purpose of the League seems to be that of avoiding future wars, and if it achieves that purpose-and I hope it will- it will be a good thing for the world. .
But we must admit that under some of the provisions of this covenant we are assuming very heavy obligations. The Prime Minister says that if we ratify the Peace Treaty and the Covenant of the League of Nations our status will not be changed. It may seem at first sight that our status will not be changed. The Prime Minister says also that an Imperial Conference will be convened in the near future and that these questions will then be discussed. But if we become a member of the League of Nations; if we accept the Covenant and all the obligations which it involves, our status must change; we shall not be free, as we have been in the past, to take part or not to take part in any war, as we see fit. Our action will not be vol- * untary; we shall have to fulfil our obligations under the Covenant. It is true that we can get out of the League, but in order to- do tbait we would have to give two years' notice, and even then we could not discontinue our membership in it unless we had fulfilled all our obligations. I shall defer expressing my considered opinion upon this matter until we come to deal fully with the Peace Treaty. But when the Imperial Conference meets I hope that our Prime Minister will insist upon preserving our autonomy. He will still be Prime Minister, I suppose-unless we have an election in the meantime-and I hope that his views will not change; that he will not consent to any change in our relationship with the Mother Country which would cause our autonomy to be diminished in any way. There has been a movement in England and even in this country, to een-
. SEPTEMBER 8, 1919
tralize the Government of the Empire in London and to diminish the prerogatives of the British Dominions. I hope that the Prime Minister is not of that school. He may have shown himself at times to be a great Imperialist, hut he has assured us that he is for Canadian autonomy and I am willing to trust him until the next Imperial Conference.
During the last few years we have been accustomed to Government by Orders in Council, and I could not help thinking that it was strange that we should be asked to meet in Parliament to ratify a Treaty the ratification of which was not absolutely necessary. Orders in Council dealing with very important matters have been passed during the last few years, even when Parliament was sititng. The Government would not trust the Canadian Parliament in connection with purely Canadian matters; yet Parliament is now asked to discuss Imperial matters-matters which have already been settled before being submitted to this House.
Mr. Speaker, I have some further remarks to make, and I move the adjournment of the debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antingonish and Guysborough) :
speechtext:
I have the honour of having been a member of the House for fifteen years and this is the first occasion on which I have risen to a question of privilege. During my absence from the House on Friday afternoon the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), in referring to myself, made the following statement:
Where did that hon. member obtain his knowledge of shipping? In his part of the country there is a firm known as the Carmichael Shipping Company, and II believe the hon. gentleman has a very direct and personal interest in the prosperity of it. That firm before the war was receiving freight rates on deals and lumber of thirty-five shillings a standard,

and during the latter part of the war it received as high as three hundred and fifty to three hundred and "eighty shillings a standard. Now, Mr. Speaker, there are pirates in this country as well as profiteers.
I wish to say that this statement is untrue and has not the slightest foundation in fact. I do not say that the hon. member deliberately made a false statement, because I have no doubt that this story was told him by some malicious person. Whoever told it to him must have had some knowledge of the deal trade, because the hon. member is about correct in regard to the rates. The firm in question carried no deals since the war broke out. They owned only one steamer which was commandeered by the Admiralty early in the war. She was placed on duty in the most dangerous part of the coast of Europe, carrying goods to the army -at Saloniki. She made five trips to Saloniki and on the sixth when bound for an Italian -port was torpeoded by an enemy submarine andisnow at the bottom of the Mediterranean. Her captain : nd chief engineer were confined for nineteen months in a German prison and during that time their wages were paid by the firm that owned the vessel. This was the only steamer owned by the firm and there could be no question of profiteering, for the Admiralty paid monthly freight at what was known as the blue-book rate, which was less than one-third of the commercial rate current at the time. I would not have troubled the House with this explanation but for the fact that the statement of the hon. member involves to some extent the reputation of an in-portant business firm that has borne an honourable name in the province of Nova Scotia for over a hundred years.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden)

made his very important and illuminating speech on this Treaty a few days ago, I had the honour of moving the adjournment of the debate which we are now resuming. This question is one of the most important, if not the most important, that this Parliament has ever dealt with. It is more important perhaps than anything we have ever discussed because it is of wider international scope than anything that I at least have taken part in the discussion of in this House. It took a long time to draft and formulate this Treaty. The active operations on which this Treaty is based commenced on the 12th day of January, as we are told by those who know about it, and from that time until the 28th day of June, the ablest men, I suppose the world can produce, were busily engaged in discussing this Treaty and forging it into the shape in which it is before the House to-day. In discussing it, Sir, we require to bring to bear upon it the best talents we possess in this Parliament. I believe that the time at our disposal, or the time that will be given to the discussion of this Treaty will not by any means be sufficient to enable hon. gentlemen in this House to fully comprehend the meaning, scope and far-reaching effect of this document. However, we have to deal with it. It requires the best judgment and talent that any lawyers we have in this House can bring to bear upon it as well as the ability and talents of any international lawyers that we have here and those who are versed in the history of treaties, in the universal history of the world, and in negotiations between nations. All these talents and all this knowledge will come into play if	we wish to ' effectively, properly
and intelligently deal with this question.
I do not suppose, Mr. Speaker, that we have a great many men of that class- in this .House, speaking with all due respect. We have men in this House who have had largely to deal with the various matters of life, who have not specialized on any one of these subjects, and for that reason we are able to bring to bear on this question only such knowledge as we have gained in the different walks of life in which we endeavour to make our living.
We cannot too often refer to the position which Canada has occupied in connection with this war. It may be possible that sometime we are apt in the hurly burly and haste of life to be willing to get away quickly from all thoughts of the war and think no more about the part we took in it as a Parliament, or the part that our sons and daughters took in it both in Canada
and overseas. That should not be. Our connection with this war, its effect upon this country and its effect upon the world are landmarks in the history of the world that should not be forgotten. It has brought Canada to a proud position in connection with the affairs of the world that we should not forget and that we should take care to refer to whenever the proper occasion presents itself. We have an example of this among the great men of the neighbouring republic. They always take care, and properly so, to refer to the milestones in the history of that great country and such references enable them to keep in mind the facts of which they have reason to be proud. In like manner, I am sure, that, in the days to come, now and forever while we live as a nation, we shall always he proud to keep fresh in our memories the honour of those who have won for us the proud position which Canada today occupies in connection with this war and with the peace which we are now about to consummate, if it is not consummated already.
We are, of course, two parties in this House-perhaps three now-at all events we are two parties. In most things we differ, in most things there is a controversy between us, but in connection with this treaty I do not think it is a party question and as far as I and hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are concerned, we shall give this important document fair and honest consideration, bringing to the notice of the Canadian people its salient points and the points that should receive careful attention. I do not think that any person in this House, or any Liberal in this country proposes to take any party advantage of this situation.
I regret exceedingly that the Prime Minister is not able to be in his seat to-day. He is slightly indisposed, which we all regret, and I am sure we all join in the hope that his illness will prove to be very slight and that he will soon be back in his place. I would be pleased indeed if he were present to-day so that he might hear for himself any references which I may make to the very able speech which he delivered in the House a few days ago. He was asked on that occasion by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) what would happen if we did not ratify this treaty. Among other things which the right hon. gentleman said that a change of Government would result as an effect or product of the refusal of the House to>
ratify this treaty. I do not think

that the right hon. gentleman should have taken that position. I do not think that it was a proper position for him to take. If the right hon. gentleman was looking for reasons why his Government should go out of office, it would not be necessary for him to cross the Atlantic to find them. The' country is full of reasons, any one of which could be taken as a good and sufficient reason why the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues should come to the conclusion that the day has arrived when they should pass the reins of Government over to, we hope,- more capable hands.
But the right hon. gentleman has thought proper to say that if ratification were not [DOT] given to this Treaty it would be a good and sufficient cause for the resignation of the Government and for the Governor General to look for other advisers. This conclusion, Sir, was not, in my judgment, logical or well-founded. The causing of the war was not brought about by the Government of Canada. Therefore, it had no responsibility for the starting of the trouble which was the basis for this Treaty. The Canadian Government did not make this peace, it is not in any way responsible for the making of it-except that the representatives of Canada were at the Peace Conference looking on and helping by way of looking on, and perhaps advancing a slight suggestion .here or there. But this Treaty cannot be said to be the product of the brain of the Canadian Government, and whether it is right or wrong, whether it is a good Treaty or not, it would be, I think, highly improper and an insane deduction for the Canadian people to say that this Government should be turned out of power because the King and his counsellors thought proper to put His Majesty's signature to this document. I repeat the Canadian Government is not responsible for the Treaty, and the failure on the part of this Parliament to ratify it is not in any -way, as I understand it, a reason why the Canadian Government should go out of power. I can only understand the position taken by the Prime Minister in one way, and that is he is anxious to make a party question out of the matter, a question that is entirely free from partisan politics as far as we on this side of the House understand it.
It is important to us, Mr. Speaker, to see whether or not the status of Canada having regard to the past, the present, and the future, is in any way affected by this bargain. We are proud, Sir, of the position which we have held in the past, we are

proud of the position which we occupy now, and we hope that we shall continue to conduct the affairs of this country and our relations with the Mother Country and the Empire in such a way that ourselves and our children will have reason to be satisfied, contented and happy, and so that we may look forward with confidence to the future.
Now, Sir, in the past such statesmen as Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald, Hon. George Brown, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper, Bart., Sir Oliver Mowat, Hon. Edward Blake, Sir John S. D. Thompson, and Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, were proud of the position this country has occupied ever since Confederation. Sir John Macdonald, for example, was perfectly satisfied with the status of Canada and her .relations with the Empire and her usefulness to it, without the Dominion being committed to taking part in any outside wars at all. That, Sir, as I understand it,' was the position always taken by that great Canadian statesman, who, with perhaps the single exception of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, filled a bigger place in the hearts and minds of our people than any other Canadian statesman. We occupied an important position in our relations with the rest of the Empire before we ever participated in European or foreign wars. It is true that we have moved forward. We first took part in the South African War. From that we grew and developed into participating in the war which is novf closed and with which we have to deal more especially to-day. On both occasions we acted upon our own initiative, on. both occasions we acted entirely upon the absolute free will of the Canadian people as expressed by this Parliament. I submit, Sir, that a decision* of that kind-the exercising of our own will in that way in respect to the directions that' we may give to our sons and our daughters as to the attitude they may take in connection with any European or foreign wars being in the hands of our own. Parliament, it is the most satisfactory condition in whicn we can find ourselves.
One of the questions which this House has to consider is, are we, by implication or otherwise, giving our assent to a document which materially changes our position in that respect? Henceforth, is it going t->
be by the free will of the Canadian Parliament, the free will of the Canadian people, that we shall take any part in troubles between other nations, or are we going to be bound simply to do what we are called upon

to do and what we must do-or at all events what we are in honour bound to do-under the terms of this document? I submit, Sir, that it is the intention of this Treaty, it is the intenion of the signatories who represented Canada when this document was signed, if I properly gather the effect of their \york-it is their intention that henceforth any action we snail take shall not be the free will of the Canadian people, but tnat it will be a compliance with the terms of the Treaty, whatever those may be. Those terms are to be from time to time interpreted by a Council which will sit in Geneva, which w'ill deal with certain facts and make certain findings, and on which Council we are not likely to be represented. I think I am safe in saying that on that Council we shall not be represented at all as far as Canada is concerned. I presume that the British Empire will be represented, but there is no certainty that this Dominion will have representatives upon that Council. Therefore, Mr, Speaker, the condition of things shall be that henceforth and forever the action or part which Canada shall take in any foreign wars will be decided by that Council,'a memo, of their decision will be sent to us, and we will simply be called upon to perform the will and wish of that Council whether we like it or not. I jlo not agree myself with the idea of Canada signing this document as a separate and distinct nation, because despite whatever we may say, or whatever ambitions we may attempt to put forward in the line of being a nation we are not a nation in the true sense of the term. We are part of a great Empire of which we are proud, and we are nothing else. I fully agree with the representatives of Canada who took every possible part in the deliberations, as far as the Empire was concerned, that the Canadian plenipotentiaries should sit in the Council as the plenipotentiaries of the Empire, and that whatever conclusions should be reached should be conclusions on behalf of the whole Empire.
I am not to be understood, Mr. Speaker, as saying that I do not attach any importr ance to Canada being represented on those Councils-I do say that we cannot be too strongly represented on those bodies-but at the same time I maintain that it is not a strength but a weakness for us to put ourselves to one side, to separate ourselves from the rest of the Empire, and attempt to become a separate nation, or a separate part of the Empire as far as those obligations are concerned.'
That, Sir, is the position which I take as far as those deliberations are concerned, and I submit that as jong as we are not a nation, and cannot under international law be regarded as a nation, that it' is better, ir. any negotiations that may take place, for us to maintain to the full the proud position which we occupy as a part and parcel of the British Empire.
I said that we were not a nation in the sense of being able to deal exclusively with other nations; wre are not. I wish to quote in that regard an authority on international law. Although a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, I do not profess that anything I might say on the point would be regarded as authoritative, and therefore I quote from Halleck, a recognized authority on international law. At pages 70 and 71 of the first volume it is laid down as follows:
The sovereignty of a State has reference to its political character, rather than to the nature of its territorial possessions. The territory of some States is in one compact body, like Belgium and Mexico, while the territory of other States, like that of Great Britain, consists of detached parts situate in every quarter of the habitable globe. Under the general appellation of State are included all the possessions of a nation, wheresoever situated, so that a colony, however distant, is, in the eye of international law, as much a part of the State which establishes it as is a city or a province belonging to its most ancient territory. By a sovereign State is meant a community, or number of persons, permanently organized under a sovereign government of their own; and by a sovereign government is meant a government, however constituted, which exercises the power of making and enforcing the law within a community, and is not itself subject to any superior government.
I want hon. gentlemen to note particularly that essential to a nation, that it must have a parliament which can make laws and which is not subject to any superior government.
These two factors, one positive, the other hegative-the exercise of power and the absence of superior control-compose the notion of sovereignty, and are essential to it.
As a colony, a possession or a dependency constitutes only a part of the State, it cannot in itself be regarded, in international law, as a distinct political organization. Hence, any public or private corporation, created by, and deriving its authority from, a. State, cannot of itself constitute a separate and independent sovereignty.
According to that authority I do not think it can be questioned that it is useless for us to say that we are an independent nation. We comply with all of this definition. The Parliament of Great Britain created this confederation, and that parliament in , many respects still has control over any legislation of ours. If hon

gentlemen choose to look at section 56 of the British North America Act, they will find that any legislation we may pass may be Vetoed at any time within two years by the King in Council. If it were only by the King it might be said: Well, we have to recognize the authority of the King. But it is not by the King alone that Canadian legislation can be vetoed at any time within two years; it is by the King in Council. Therefore members of the British House of Commons, and possibly members of the House of Lords, can get together and advise the King that our legislation should not be approved. Consequently we are not an independent nation because our legislation is at all points subject to the control of members of the British House of Commons as they may be from time to time advisers of His Majesty. Therefore we come within the definition given by this authority, that we are not an independent parliament, and that our legislation is not absolutely within our own control.
If hon. gentlemen will look at section 132 of the British North America Act I think they will agree that it is easily dedu-cible from that section that it was never the intention that we would ever in the making of treaties have to deal with any foreign country. That section says:
The Parliament and Government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper few performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the Empire and such foreign countries.
I think it is perfectly clear, Sir, that the intention of the framers of the Act of Confederation was that treaties would be made between the Empire and foreign nations, in which treaties we would be involved and in respect of, which certain duties would fall upon us not as a separate part, but as an integral part of the body politic of the great empire to which we belong. [DOT]
Therefore, I submit, Sir, that our professing to make a treaty or to call ourselves a nation, and as a nation to become a member of the League of Nations, is absolutely impossible and cannot be carried out, and that in attempting to do so this Parliament and thio Government have undertaken responsibilities which they are not in a position to carry out. We are not in a position to declare war, we are not in a position to declare peace. How can any nation be said to be a member of this League of Nations, which league has largely to do with the imposition of conditions which will prevent war or which will bring about peace? We are not in a position to do any of those

things, and therefore, Sir, I think we are attempting to do what is not within our power.
I purpose to refer to only a very few of the articles of this very lengthy and very important treaty. Article VIII provides:
The members of the League recognize that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest poipt consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations. The Council, taking account of the geographical situation and circumstances of each State, shall formulate plans for such reduction for the consideration and action of the several governments.
Such plans shall be subject to reconsideration and revision at least every ten years.
After these plans shall have been adopted by the several Governments, the limits of armaments therein fixed shall not be exceeded without the concurrence of the Council. .
The Members of the League agree that the manufacture by private enterprise of munitions' and implements of war is open to grave objections. The Council shall advise how the evil effects attendant upon such manufacture can be prevented, due regard being had to the necessities of those Members of the League which are not able to manufacture the munitions and implements of war necessary for their safety.	,
The Members of the League undertake to interchange full and frank information as to the scale of their armaments, their military, naval and air programmes and the condition of such of their industries as are adaptable to war-like purposes.
Mr. Speaker,- that Article involves maintenance by Canada of a standing army, a navy and an air force, and we are binding ourselves, with the other parties to the League, to lay before those other powers from year to year full information with regard to our various war materials, our war implements, our war preparations, and so on. I submit that that is not desirable. It is not the wish of the Canadian people that they should be forced into a condition of this kind; that they should be required to maintain a standing army, a navy and an air force. We are willing and we have always been willing to take our part side by side with the Mother Country whenever that was neces'sary; we have always been willing to stand by the flag. But I do not think it is consistent with the feeling of the Canadian people that they should be called upon, for instance, to enter into some petty quarrel between any of the new kingdoms of republics that are being formed in Europe, or to intervene in some trouble that may exist between Mexico and any of the minor republics of South America. Under this Article, when this Council, in which we have no representation, calls upon us to do so, we are bound to take a part in such

quarrels as I have mentioned. I submit that we can only do consistently and constitute nally what we agree to do under and by virtue of the machinery provided by and for the British Empire, of which we are a component part.
Of course, this agreement is already ratified. I do not think it is good politics or very high statesmanship-nor do I think it is necessary-to tell the people and Parliament that we must ratify this Treaty. The Treaty is already ratified; we are not called upon to ratify it. My authority for this assertion may be questioned, but if hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to read the speech made by the Right Hon. Lloyd George when he introduced the Bill concerning the Treaty, they will find that Lloyd George told the members of the Imperial Parliament simply that they were to pass a Bill enabling the Government to furnish the necessary means and money and appoint the necessary officers to carry out the provisions of the Treaty. The purport of his speech was that he was introducing a .measure to provide the necessary funds and the necessary power to implement the Treaty. He says, in distinct English-any person can see it in the English Hansard-that the Treaty itself does not require ratification. I am indebted to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) for a copy of the English Hansard in which the Right Hon. Lloyd George's speech may be found. I quote:
The Prime Minister (!Mr. Lloyd George) (whose rising was the subject of a general ovation, members standing and cheering) : I have to lay on the Table of the House, and to ask the leave of the House to introduce two Bills to enforce the most momentous document to which the British Empire has ever affixed its seal. There are two Bills which I shall have to ask the leave of the House to introduce. It is unnecessary to obtain the ratification of Parliament to a Treaty, except in one or two particulars. The ratification is for the Crown, but there are certain provisions in the Treaty of Peace, signed last Saturday, which it is necessary to obtain an Act of Parliament in order to enforce.
There were two treaties, one the Peace Treaty, which we are dealing with here; the other an agreement, which may or may not come before us, entered into between Great Britain, United States and France. In that agreement there was a specific provision that its ratification by the Parliaments of the countries concerned was necessary. Bills respecting both these Treaties were introduced at the same time by the Right Hon. Lloyd George, and he specifically said that the Peace Treaty proper
had already been signed by the King and did not require ratification.
There is no authority or justification for saying that our ratifying or not ratifying the Peace Treaty will have any general effect upon it or interfere with it one way or the other.

speechtext:
Did Mr. Lloyd
George ask this Government to submit the Treaty to the Canadian Parliament for ratification?	[DOT]
