speechtext: ' There is nothing in his speech about it. I have read the whole of his speech.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Has not the
statement been made in this House that we are asked by Mr. Lloyd George to ratify the Treaty?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I very closely followed' the remarks of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and as I understood him he did not mention Lloyd George. He said- Hansard will show that he said it-that we made a promise-I think that was the language of the Prime Minister-we promised or undertook that this Treaty would be submitted to the Canadian Parliament. At all events, that was the effect of the Prime Minister's statement. I understand that to mean that our representatives promised the King or his advisers that this Treaty would be submitted to the Canadian Parliament, and that they are now carrying out that promise. Our ratification of the Treaty does not involve any international negotiations, does not have any international effect, does not change it in the slightest degree. I suppose our representatives said to themselves. It is better; it is better politics, to submit this Treaty to the Canadian Parliament; it may please the Canadian people; it may tickle the fancy of members of Parliament to be asked to deliberate upon it. That is all it means. The Treaty is absolutely obligatory upon us now; whatever we may say. about it will not change the situation in the slightest degree. Indeed, we have already signed it. I may be wrong in my assertion, but I do not think the plenipotentiaries from Ottawa received their power from us; I think they received their commissions from the King; I think they were appointed on the other side of the water. In that way, although hailing and saying that they were from Canada, they were simply plenipotentiaries of and directly representing His Majesty the King, and as such they signed the Treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It is quite true the plenipotentiaries were plenipotentiaries named by the King, but upon an Order in Council of the Government of Canada recommending such nomination.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Anything else would be inconceivable to me. I could not conceive that His Majesty in Council would undertake to name representatives from any self-governing colony like Canada without consulting the Government of that colony in regard to the matter, and it was only a matter of propriety and politeness and well-sustained practice that the King in Council would ask this Government to suggest who should be the plenipotentiaries for Canada at this conference. That is all it was, and once that was done, they were no more Canadian plenipotentiaries than Lloyd George himself or the Right Hon. Mr. Balfour, or any other representatives of the British Empire. They were all in the high and honourable position of representing the Empire,and as such high and honourable representatives they signed the Treaty, and that is the end of the matter. That they are laying the Treaty before us now does not make the slightest difference one way or the other.
Speaking, however, entirely for myself and having nothing to support me but mv own opinion, I believe that the position might be different as regards the League of Nations. By what is known in law as the doctrine of estoppel, if we want to insist upon our rights as a member of the League of Nations, other powers might be estopped from denying our ability to become a part of that league if any advantage were to accrue to Canada from it. We might say to them: You cannot now deprive us of any benefit we might derive from being a member of the League of Nations, because you have accepted us and as a matter of * law this doctrine of estoppel might apply. But beyond the fact that other nations might be estopped from refusing to grant us the status of a nation, because they have recognized us as such, I do not think that by signing the League of Nations covenant and calling ourselves a nation, we derive any advantage or by any means change our constitution.
There is, however, another point in which our position in connection with the League of Nations differs from our position in connection with the general treaty. I think that by signing the League as a separate nation we would be in honour bound to recognize the decision of that General Council which is to meet at Geneva and which is

to allocate to the different powers the parts they have to take in any war.
4 p.m. If we reserve to ourselves the right to say whether or not we shall recognize that Council, we shall be very much as we were before, following the lead of the Mother Country and taking such part in the wars of the future as the honour, standing and importance of this country may demand and require. If we reserve to ourselves the right of staying just where we were before so far as that Council is concerned I do not think we shall be in any very different position from what we would be in if our plenipotentiaries had not signed as representing a separate nation. As far as I understand the matter, that is the position.	.
As regards section 10, we are undertaking for all time to come to be policemen, so to speak, along the lines dividing any countries in the world who are parties to this League. We are binding ourselves to go down to South America at any time that there may be trouble between any of the score of small republics there, which almost every month are to be found in a revolution of some kind or another. By this covenant we are binding ourselves that, if we are asked by this Council to go down and take part in those fights we shall obey its behest.
There is in section 16 another extraordinary condition of things, namely, that we put ourselves in the position of possibly being in arms against the Mother Country. It is quite possible that some trouble might arise, say, for instance, between Great Britain and the little republic of Uruguay. I mention Uruguay because some years ago we had with that republic some trouble which was very effectively aired in this House, and we were obliged to send a Canadian commissioner down there to try to settle the trouble which ultimately was settled. Supposing another such trouble arises and Great Britain finds it necessary to send a warship there and to declare war upon Uruguay, what is our position? We undertake to say that if Great Britain goes to war without consulting and getting the consent of the whole League of Nations, and if she asserts her right by the power of her warship, we shall cut off further relations of any kind by trade or otherwise with the British people and furnish whatever means we can to fight Great Britain in her trouble with Uruguay. Hon. gentlemen may smile, but that is the position.
In section 16 we say that we shall refuse to have any intercourse with any member of

the League that goes to war or raises any trouble without our consent or the consent of the whole League. We undertake to be a separate member of that League. Our plenipotentiaries undertook to say that they signed that Covenant separately and apart from Great Britain, and we cannot blow hot and blow cold. We cannot say one minute that we are a nation and apart by ourselves and then when obligations arise that may embarrass us, take shelter under the wings of the Mother Country, and say: We are not a nation; we were only playing that; we did not mean it, and we will not take any part in this affair at all. It is for us to consider carefully those three articles, 8, 10 and 16 which, to my mind, are the most important as regards the League of Nations. I ask hon. gentlemen who are responsible for their position in this House, whether or not we should carefully consider them and get the fullest possible explanation from hon. gentlemen of the Government, particularly from the plenipotentiaries who represented us at Paris, as to what effect those three articles have upon Canada.
I wish to refer to the Bill that was introduced by .the Prime Minister of Great Britain when this Treaty was under consideration. The language of that Bill will indicate that nothing was done in connection with ratification; and except for the necessary change to make our Bill a Canadian instead of an English Bill, there is not one particle of difference .between this one and the Bill which was given its third reading there. I shall read the English Bill, which is not very long:
Whereas, at Versailles, on the twenty-eighth day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen, a Treaty of Peace (including a protocol annexed thereto), a copy of which has been laid before each House of Parliament, was signed on behalf of His Majesty, and it is expedient that His Majesty should have power to do all such things as may be proper and expedient for giving .effect to the said Treaty ;
Be it therefore enacted by the King's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:-
1. (1) His Majesty may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such Orders in Council, and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the said Treaty, and for giving effect to any of ths provisions of the said Treaty.
(2) Any Order in Council made under this Act may provide for the imposition by summary process or otherwise of penalties in respect of breaches of the provisions thereof, and shall be laid before Parliament as soon as may be after it is made and Shall have effect as if enacted in this Act, but may he varied or revoked by a
subsequent Order in Council and shall not be deemed to be a statutory rule within the meaning of section one of the Rules Publication Act, 1893.
(3) Any expenses incurred in carrying out the said Treaty shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by Parliament.
2. This Act may be cited as the Treaty of Peace Act. 1919.
That is the whole of the Act, and hon. gentlemen who have obtained a copy of our own Act will find that it is practically the same, word for word. There is not a word about ratification of the Treaty in the English Act and not a word about it in our own Act. We are therefore admitting, at any rate by implication and by our actions, that the Treaty is already ratified, and we are simply passing an enabling Act to provide for such actions as may be necessary in connection with the operation of the Treaty.
There are many other things that should be said on the subject, but I realize that there are several members who will no doubt wish to express their views in connection with the Treaty. The time at' our disposal for its discussion is limited and for this reason I do not think that I should speak much longer. Let me say in conclusion that so far as party feeling in connection with this question is concerned, there was never in this House from the beginning of the war up to the present day anything but the greatest unanimity in doing whatever was necessary to carry on the war successfully. We all remember very well our meeting in the old House on the 19th day 6f August, 1914. You will recall, Sir, that on that occasion our great chieftain the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the declaration that whatever would be necessary or whatever could be done by the Liberal party or by himself and those who followed him would be done until Victory was won, and truth, justice, and liberty were fully assured. That, Mr. Speaker, was the position which was taken by him at that time as a Liberal, and it was also the position that was taken by the great leader of the Liberal party in the Old Land. The words of the Right Hon. Mr. Herbert Asquith when he was Prime Minister have frequently been quoted and it will do no harm to have them repeated in Hansard. Mr. Asquith, speaking in regard to the objects for which we entered tthe war, made this memorable statement:
We shall never sheathe the sword which we have not lightly drawn*until Belgium recovers in full measure all land more than all that she has sacrificed, until Prance is adequately secured against the menace of oppression, until



the rights of the smaller nationalities of Europe are placed upon an unassailable foundation, and until the military domination of Prussia is wholly and finally destroyed.
That was the position taken by the great Liberal leader of Grekt Britain, and it is no stronger than the position taken by the equally great Liberal leader of Canada. Now, Sir, some people may think that we had differences about the war. True, there were differences of opinion as to the way in which the war should be carried on, but there was never any difference as to whether Canada should do her best and utmost to win the fight, and I am sure it is the privilege of independent thinking men to have their own. views as to how such matters should be conducted. Invariably men fail to see things in exactly the same light and there were some differences as to how the war should be managed; but that Canada should participate was a question on which there was absolutely but one heart, one soul, one mind, and one purpose from start to finish; a common determination to stand by the Mother Country with every man, with every dollar and with every resource. That being the case, all of us, Liberal or Conservative, irrespective of our political affiliations, can. equally rejoice to-day in the happy condition in which we find ourselves as regards the consummaton of the agreement that brings this awful conflict to a peaceful and satisfactory end.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret exceedingly that there are a few things in connection with the eloquent address of the leader of the Opposition with which I must differ-
. not with his closing sentiments, but with some of the constitutional aspects of the question. Although possibly it may not be pleasing to the hon. member that I should disagree with him, I will at least give him the added knowledge and credit that in his constitutional arguments he agrees absolutely with the most conservative representative of the Government of Great Britain, and the representative of the most conservative people in Great Britain; that they are better able to look after this matter than are the people of Canada. It might be nice for the leader of the Opposition to know that so far as that is concerned he has the assistance in his argument of one of the most eminent men in Great Britain. As regards the ratification of this Treaty, there' is no statement in connection with the matter which the hon. member has read that shows that the
	,
Treaty has been ratified at all. Up to date, so far as I have heard, there has been no ratification of the Treaty by Great Britain. It certainly had not been ratified on the date on which this Bill passed in the House of Commons, because it was after that I left Great Britain; and- it is not ratified yet. One of the principal arguments in regard to the matter of ratification was as to whether the British Dominions would have the power to advise the King, because the House of Commons of Great Britain has not had the privilege that the House of Commons of Canada has, for this is the first occasion within the confines of the British Empire on which any Parliament has been asked to approve a Treaty. Great Britain has never done so; Canada has the advantage, at least from a democratic standpoint, of being the first Government which has ever submitted a question of this kind to the Parliament of its country.
This Treaty is going to be ratified, when it is ratified, by the King of England on behalf of the United Kingdom of Great Britain. It is going to be ratified by him on the advice of their government. When it is ratified on behalf of Canada it is going to be ratified by the King of the British Empire upon the advice of the Government of Canada. The promise that was referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) was not a promise by Lloyd: George to the Government of Canada but it was a promise to this Parliament last session made by the Prime Minister of Canada that before ratifying this Treaty he would submit it to this Parliament and' that for the first time in the history of the-world it would be given an opportunity of expressing its opinion on such a matter.. There is no question in the motion of ratifying the Treaty. It is a motion to approve as a whole or disapprove of the Treaty. I am not going to discuss this afternoon the details of this Treaty. This Parliament has a perfect right to discuss these details if it sees fit but it only can accomplish anything by either approving or disapproving of the Treaty as a whole, and that is the motion that is brought before us to-day.. We are not here to deal with one or two little things in the Treaty but we are here to deal with it as a whole and it is for Parliament to either approve of it or disapprove of it. '
There have been those, I am told, in Canada who say that there should be no change in the constitution of Canada without a vote of the people. I agree with that in one respect; I believe that there should

be no change for the worse in the constitution of Canada without the consent of the people. But any one who has taken the former point of view has studied to very little effect the constitution of the British Empire, or the constitution of that portion of it that we have the pleasure of living in. The constitution of the British Empire has gone on improving from day to day, from year to year, slowly, no doubt, but to-day we have an example of the most radical change in the constitution of this portion of the empire in the submission to Parliament of this treaty which the Government, under the British constitution, might have ratified by Order in Council as soon as they had a copy of the Treaty presented to them in Ottawa. That would have been a constitutional way of doing it but instead of doing that we have submitted it to Parliament, That is a radical change in constitution but it is a change which I think the members of this House will, approve of and I have no doubt the people of Canada also will approve of that kind of radical change in the constitution.
There are people no doubt who think that the statesmen of Great Britain can legislate for Canada better than we ourselves can. Possibly they can but that has not been the feeling of most Canadians in the past. The feeling has been that matters that affect the interest of Canada, whether for better or worse, should be looked after by the people of Canada. The people of Canada have the idea that they prefer not to revert to the old Crown Colony conditions but to look after their welfare themselves.
The powers that were given by the King to the plenipotentiaries were not powers to act for the British Empire as a whole, but powers to sign treaties for the Dominion of Canada. The question has been asked as to what difference it would make whether we ratified or did not ratify this Treaty. I regret to see that the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) has misunderstood the position in regard to that matter, but the answer was given that this motion was submitted to Parliament and if the motion did not carry, the Government, having submitted it as a Government motion, would be defeated and would resign. That is the natural consequence. They did not submit the Treaty; they submitted a motion and if that motion is defeated the constitutional course would be for the Government to resign. I hope the Government will not make another amendment to the constitution and endeavour to hold on to office for any further length of time if this Parliament thinks they 61 '
are not carrying out their duty in submitting this motion.
In connection with the Treaty, there are certain matters that may possibly be of interest. When people, the representatives of Canada, have been away for seven or eight months dealing with matters of such transcendent importance, whether the recital is dreary or not, I think that some information as to what they have been doing should be laid before the House.
The Parliament of Canada will recognize the fact that Canada, in going into this war, occupied an absolutely different position from almost all the other allied and associated powers. Canada had no special interest to serve. No attack had been made on Canada, and no special objection had been raised by the people of Canada to the conduct of Germany up to that time. Canada entered this war for various reasons, one of which would be for the purpose, as an integral part of the British Empire, of assisting the Empire. Another object was the purpose of seeing that democratic institutions were kept alive. For these two reasons, among others, the people of Canada went into the war, but in so far as this war was concerned there was no particular right of theirs attacked and she had no interest peculiar to herself to serve. In that respect the people of Canada differed from almost all. the other nations and from a number of the British dominions which had German colonies close to them and which had material interests which were endangered. We were in the war because we thought it was our duty, and when we went to the Peace Conference we went there on a different basis from most of the other nations which had special interests to defend. Canada was interested in the fact that she had taken part in the war and she was interested in seeing that there should be a good treaty made, in that respect there being no difference between her and the other nations. But, in so far as the actual Treaty was concerned, aside from the League of Nations and the labour provisions, Canada had no special interest in connection with this Treaty except to see that the best possible treaty was made. In that respect the delegates from Canada and from the other British dominions gave every possible assistance. The first question that arose after the delegates left here in November last and during their two months' stay in the city of London was as to, representation of the Dominions at the Peace Conference. The claim was made by the Prime Minister of Canada, on behalf of Canada, and the

claim was made by other Dominions, that having taken part in the war, having spent their hundreds of millions of dollars, and having sacrificed their hundreds of thousands of lives, they had a right to be present when the Treaty of Peace was negotiated. If it was going to affect their interests in any respect, as it afterwards did in respect to these two matters which I have mentioned, they insisted that they had a right to participate.
There was a long discussion in regard to that and I would say in my opinion there was an absolute impossibility that it ever would have been granted if those delegates had not been there during those two months fighting for the rights of Canada and of the other British Dominions to be represented, and to at least express their opinions so far as circumstances might render it necessary to express them. We do not claim that we negotiated this Peace Treaty. We do not claim that it is the result of the efforts of the people of Canada or the peoples of the other British Dominions; the Peace Treaty is very largely the result of the efforts that were made by the representatives of the five Great Powers, and any one who was present will recognize the fact that these five Great Powers were doing the bulk of the work and the bulk of the deciding. I do say, however, that so far as the British Dominions were concerned the circumstances were such that their representatives occupied perhaps a much more important position than the representatives of any of the smaller nations or powers that were there, the reason for that being that the British Parliament was in session at the time, and it was absolutely impossible for British Ministers to be there. The five British delegates were not able to be present, only three members of the British Government were able to attend continually in regard to these matters, and it was absolutely essential, a great portion of the time being taken up with other matters, and it was a great assistance to them, that the chief Ministers from the various British Dominions, with some practical experience at least, should be there to work. And undoubtedly they did work. In conjunction with the permanent officials of the British Government in respect to all these matters, they worked hard six months, for the purpose of assisting in the formation of & treaty that would be to the advantage of Great Britain, to the advantage of the British Empire, and, ,so far as possible, a fair and honourable treaty for the world at large. That work was performed in connection 
with what I may call the Peace Treaty proper.

speechtext:
That very considerable work was performed by the delegates from Canada and elsewhere, is demonstrated by the voluminous book which has been published. The manner in which this work was done, and it probably could not have been carried out otherwise, was that probably hundreds of committees, largely international committees composed of representatives of all the allied delegates, sat for the purpose of going into various matters and made reports. Each of these international committees had sub-committees. France had sub-committees, Great Britain had sub-committees, also Italy, Japan and United States. Each of these sub-committees worked and prepared and presented reports upon the various items which are included in the Peace Treaty. I happen to have a trunk full of documents, the preparation of which was necessary, to say nothing of several other loads that were destroyed. These were compiled in connection with reports made upon points that were finally crystallized into the Treaty. These reports were gone over from time to time, referred back to committee, and finally in completed form

presented to the Council of the five Great Powers for the purpose of being finally passed. Nothing was ever considered there except objections that had been raised and dealt with previously, and over-ruled in the international committees, and were submitted to the Council for final arbitration. In that way it was possible to carry out the enormous amount of work that was performed by the representatives of the various countries during that time. As it happened, the formal meetings of the Peace Conference were not at all meetings for discussion, bus meetings for the purpose of registering the decrees that were practically completed before they got to the Conference, except upon- one notable occasion when the Prime Minister of Canada held the Conference up for a few minutes for the purpose of getting a motion passed in connection with the rights of Canada. Upon the larger questions no discussion took place among the delegates assembled at the general Peace Conference, everything practically having been agreed upon before the questions were submitted for the final registration of the Conference.
As to the work of the Canadian delegates, apart from that of the delegates of the other British Dominions, I do not wish to enter into details further than to say that Sir Robert Borden, on behalf of Canada, -wrote and circulated a memorandum in regard to the League of Nations which exercised very considerable influence upon the final arrangements in that regard.
The leader of the Opposition contends that we can take no part in the League of Nations. Let me say that Mr. Clemen-ceau, President Woodrow Wilson, and Mr. Lloyd George disagree absolutely with the hon. gentleman in that contention-. I quote the following:
The question having been raised as to the meaning of Article IV of the League of Nations Covenant, we have been requested by Sir Robert Borden to state whether we concur in his view, that upon the true construction of the first and second paragraphs of that Article, representatives of the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire may be selected or named as members of the Council. We have no hesitation in expressing our entire concurrence in this view. If there were any doubt it would toe entirely removed by the fact that the Articles of the Covenant are not subject to a narrow of technical construction.
(Signed) G. Clemenceau, Woodrow Wilson D. Lloyd George.
Dated at the Quai d'Orsay,
Paris, the sixth day of
May, 1919.
So far as that is concerned, I am quite-satisfied, Mr. Speaker, to leave it, as those gentlemen will probably all be present at the first meeting of the League of Nations,-and if Sir Robert Borden happens to be there with their letter, there will probably be very little discussion as to the true meaning of this clause.
The only other point in connection with the Treaty is the Labour Convention. Possibly thousands of people agree with the leader of the Opposition that this and the League of Nations Covenant might better have been dealt with separately and disassociated from the Treaty of Peace proper. I am not prepared to argue that there is not a great deal to be said in support of that contention; but the fact of the matter is that it was absolutely impossible to negotiate the Treaty unless the League of Nations Covenant and the Labour Convention were associated therewith, and the delegation would have broken up absolutely' without accomplishing what they were attempting to do. It was only by the association of the three documents that they were able to get the final unanimous consent of the Allied and Associated Powers to what was done during those six months. If there had not been a League of Nations to come into existence for the purpose of guaranteeing some of the important considerations of the Treaty, it would have been necessary to continue' to occupy Germany with a big standing army for the next thirty years until all the regulations were carried out. That was the reason why these three " documents were joined together, and it was the only reason why a great many of the representatives consented to associate themselves either in the League of Nations or in the Labour Convention. But those who were there on behalf of the Dominion of Canada took the position that if it was absolutely necessary for the making of an honourable peace that there should be a League of Nations and a Labour -Convention. They thought, with the labour conditions in Canada so far superior to the labour conditions in many other countries, that it was proper for them to join in any international union that was absolutely essential for securing the peace of the world.
In connection with this labour question, I may say, Mr. Speaker, that for the first time in my life while I was over-seas I assumed the duties of the Minister of Labour in his absence and took a special interest in this matter. I did this the first day that I saw the report of the Inter-

national Labour Convention, which was prepared for the purpose of being submitted, without change, to the Peace Conference. I found that so far as that Convention was concerned the' gentleman who drafted it thoroughly agreed with the leader of the Opposition-they thought that the delegates of the British Government could better look after the labour interests of the Dominion of Canada than we could; and it contained a special clause to the effect that a member with its self-governing Dominions should only have certain representation upon that governing body, and under no circumstances could there be any other. So far as I was concerned, Mr. Speaker, although I would have been willing to sacrifice many things in connection with the matter, I said that that was not in the interests of the Dominion of Canada, and that the fight would be kept up until the last minute before I would ever consent to a document of that kind under which the labour men of Canada, who were so proud of their International Union, would have to go to the city of Washington on a footing inferior to that of the negroes of Liberia. I kept up the fight, and Sir Robert Borden kept up the fight and made it stronger perhaps, and finally, only the day before the Peace Treaty was presented to the Germans, those clauses were struck out and the Dominions received exactly the same recognition in regard to that International Labour Convention that was accorded to any of the thirty-two Allied and Associated Powers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having detained the House long enough in regard to this matter, I would in closing just like to say what a vote does mean as to whether we approve or disapprove of this Treaty. I cannot go so far as to answer the question, what would be the result of not approving the Treaty, further'than it was answered the other day, because the result depends upon other people. But we know some things that might happen. If the Government of * Great 'Britain advised the [DOT] King to ratify this Treaty, for the British Empire, regardless of whether or not it was thrown out by this Parliament, then it would be for the people and the Government of Canada to decide what should be done next. If the Government of Great Britain decided to ratify it on behalf of the United Kingdom and leave out Canada, then the question remains, whether Canada is still, technically, at war with Germany. To such a question the most abstruse study would have to be given by the Government and the Parliament of Canada. Therefore I think that in the in-

terests of the Dominion of Canada and in the interests of the British Empire it is not well to raise a question of that kind. If the leader of the Opposition still thinks the Treaty is already ratified, then there is no reason for raising the question. We, who think it is not ratified do not desire to raise the question. The Government desire to take the position that the Dominion has up to date done everything it could for the purpose of assisting and keeping within the British Commonwealth, and we have no desire to raise any question of that .kind at this stage of our history. Neither is there any object in raising such a question when, as the hon. leader of the Opposition has stated, there is no political interest in connection with it. We will have lots of opportunities to quarrel in the future-human nature is not going to change materially, even though we have a League of Nations-and the political feelings of the people will remain very similar to what they have been in the past. But I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that the members of this House, as representing the Dominion, should upon this one occasion set aside all personal bickerings or political differences in connection with this matter and unitedly say that, as a whole, it is better for the Dominion that they should approve of this Treaty as the eve of a horrible war and the dawn of what we hope and pray is an honourable and lasting peace.
Hon. HENRI SEVERIN BELAND (Beauce); Mr. Speaker, in conformity with the wish expresssed so eloquently by my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sifton) I want to assure you that my intention in rising to speak this afternoon is not to approach the subject before the House in a party spirit or in a spirit of hostility.
The subject is such as to impose upon all members of this House the necessity of forgetting their party affiliations m whatever observations they deem it proper to offer. It is in that frame of mind that I venture to present to the House a few remarks, which, I hope, will not be prolonged.
The Peace Treaty bf 1919 Is certainly the most momentous event in the history of the world. It throws in the shade, as it were, treaties like that of Westphalia and Utrecht, the Congress of Vienna, the Treaty of Paris of 1763, and the Congress of Berlin. For Canada this Treaty is full of possibilities and of far-reaching consequences and it is incumbent upon all the members of the House to give to it a few moments

at least of their earnest, honest, and undivided attention.
The Treaty is a striking evidence of the fact that the war which for four years devastated humanity has, so far as the Allied nations are concerned, reached a victorious and a happy conclusion. Canada, which of its own volition, in the full independence of its Parliament, took such a conspicuous part in the war and contributed so much to the downfall of imperialistic Germany and of the powers associated with Germany, has every reason to rejoice in the result achieved. The provisions of the Treaty point out in an unmistakable manner that the instigators of the war have received at the hands of the Conference of Versailles the treatment they deserve. As one who for over four years was the constant witness and in many cases the victim of Prussian methods and of pan-German aspirations, a perusal of a large number of the clauses of the Treaty affords me deep satisfaction.
The plea so repeatedly made that the war had been imposed on Germany, that theirs had been a war of defence, was with the object of galvanizing at first the attacking power, and later the power of the German nation to resist and endure. This plea, of course, is false and deceptive. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, before I deal more fully with the Treaty itself, to refer to one or two events that developed during the early period of the war in connection with the pretended disclosure of certain documents by Germany -in Belgium. The particular event to which I want to refer has not been given as much publicity in the press of the Allied nations as it has, I assume, in the press of Germany.	_
On many occasions, as the House is undoubtedly aware, the extreme Socialists have in the Reichstag -attempted 'to secure from the German Government a straight declaration of renunciation to the territory of Belgium and -to the political and military subjection of that country, 'but they failed always to secure a satisfactory answer. The German press, obviously inspired by the military authorities, carried on a campaign the chief argument in connection with which was that Belgium had failed before the war to observe certain responsibilities -and obligations imposed upon her by the Treaty of 1839. A few months after the occupation of Brussels, the semi-official organ of the German Government, The Nord Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung published what purported to be a secret understanding between the military -authorities of England and the military authorities of Belgium in connection with the landing
of troops on the Belgian coast. The publication of this document, as one would surmise, -excited -a good deal of sentiment in Germany and in Belgium, as I was able to find out then and later. In this connection, however, the Germans failed to bring out prominently before their people a stipulation which appeared in the margin of this document to the effect that the landing of English troops in Belgium -should not take place before the German troops had invaded Belgium. A similar arrangement, for all w-e know, might bav-e been entered into by Belgium with Germany. The only logical conclusion of it all is that Belgium was determined to protect her neutrality, against all comers with all and by all honourable means.
But there is more than that. The Nord Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, with an evident desire to justify the invasion of Belgium on the first of August, 1914, added a semi-official declaration to the -effect that the document to which I have referred was known to the competent authority in Germany before the war. One can readily see that it is here attempted to give a reason and a justification for the invasion of Belgium. But let us go one step further and witness the sitting of the Reichstag which took place on the fourth of August, 1914, when the then German Imperial Chancellor, Bethmann-Hollweg, made, in substance, the following declaration; "Our troops"-meaning the German troops-"are at the present m-om-ent on the territory of Belgium; it is against the rights of peoples; it is against international law; but necessity knows no law, and Germany undertakes *to restore Belgium to her independence and to recompense her for all damages caused to her civilian population or to her property as soon as Germany shall have attained her military ends."
If we take this declaration in conjunction with the statement of the German semiofficial organ that the famous document was known to the competent authorities before the war, we have sufficient indication that the German Chancellor did not consider that Belgium had failed in the least degree in the discharge of her international obligations. The varying, incomplete, unsatisfactory and in many cases, nebulous statements made during the long years of the war by the successive chancellors of Germany, Baron Von Bethmann-Hcllweg, Von Michaelis and Hertling, reveal only too clearly the well-considered intention of the German Government at all times to annex Belgium in toto or par-

tially had the fortunes of war been favourable to them.
Their treatment of Poland is also marked with an ill-design of exercising their peculiar gifts of domination over that country. From the day that the German Emperor proclaimed the Kingdom of Poland, (I think in the month of December, 1916), one would have believed that all the Polish prisoners in Germany would have secured their release. But the corridors and cells of the prisons of Berlin continued to be flooded, so to speak, with prisoners of Polish nationality, and those prisoners were gradually, by processes which I do not care to describe, converted into labourers for the munition factories, each of those prisoners thus releasing a German soldier for the front. Those who refused to work in the German factories were tendered another bait; they were asked to join the Royal Polish army, created for the purpose, as it was claimed, of protecting the independence of Poland, but that army, as the House knows, was under the high command of German generals. In Courland, Lithuania, Esthonia and Livonia skilful canvassing of the population by the creatures of the German Government was devised to bring over them the rule of the Hohenzollern sceptre.
It is in a retrospective glance of the mind, when all these machinations appear anew, that the various clauses of the Treaty, severe arid drastic as they might appear, seem only too just. The lust of conquest, and the desire for domination have received a decisive check. The acquisitions of territory by Germany, in the East, the West, and the South, achieved in some , cases in violation of solemn treaties, and in all cases in complete disregard and utter disdain of the laws' of humanity, have been reversed against their authors. To the Conference of Versailles, that is, to an imposing array of victorious nations assembled for the purpose, has devolved the task of rectification and settlement in a general sense. The task is now done.
We are now asked, not as a sovereign nation-we are not and we could not he considered as a sovereign nation-but as a British dependency, to give our approval to the provisions of the Treaty of Peace, this Treaty which deals not only with matters pertaining solely to the settlement of the war, but with matters bearing upon social subjects and also having relation, as in the case of the Covenant, to the autonomy of some of the nations.
It may be that some reservation should be made here. The Minister of Public 
AVorks (Mr. Sifton) has in his remarks referred extensively to labour, and for my part I have no objection to offer to the provisions of the Treaty that deal with labour. It is eminently proper that a whole chapter should be devoted to the organization of labour and to the principles whiclj apply to its diversified aspects. This particular feature of the Treaty 5 p.,m. is highly commendable, and the nine methods and principles enumerated in section 2 of that chapter will and may well be considered as the Nine Commandments of labour. Taken all in all, and even with the imperfections pointed out by some critics, chapter 13 ot the Treaty dealing'with labour is as perfect a document as could be devised and may well be regarded as a sure foundation on which satisfactory industrial relations will in future be established.
The chapters which deal with the delimitation of the boundaries of Germany and other European, Asiatic, and African nations; with the limitation of armaments, naval and military of Germany; with transportation by land and sea, and commercial problems; with reparation, by financial and economic means; with the. general subject of colonies and the mandatory system- these chapters, although open to much criticism and likely to give rise to friction in the future, ought to be unreservedly endorsed by this Parliament, if the action of this Parliament were in any degree necessary to give them' any validity which they would not otherwise have.
A feature of the Treaty of Peace, and one which is very important and which -calls for special attention, is the Covenant of the League of Nations. The Peace Conference has been persuaded into accepting this proposal, conceived and laid before it by the President of the United States, Mr. Woodrow Wilson. Constituted by no less than twenty-seven different powers, it has for its object and task to administer justice in the world, and, in doing so, to endeavour to maintain peace. What more noble role could be assigned to a body of powerful nations, especially after the iniquities and atrocities committed without number, and the bitter sufferings and mournings accumulated during the fifty-two months of the war! This League of Nations is devised to give that peaceful era for which the world longs. There is on the part of the desolate and devastated world to-day an ardent thirst for peace and rest, a thirst which is a thousand times more ardent than was felt after the Napoleonic wars.

The Covenant of the League of Nations forms an integral part of the Treaty. It is its first chapter. Whether it is subscribed to by a sufficient number of nations to give it efficacy, a number of nations powerful enough to enforce its decisions, remains to be seen, and the future only can tell. But' at this moment the League of Nations fills with hope the hearts and the souls of many millions of people who have been torn from their homes and daily occupation and hurled into war for the sole purpose of vindicating certain principles heretofore considered essential and fundamental by civilized nations. So far as I am concerned, I wish God speed to the League of Nations.
But one cannot fail to recognize the fact that, for the first time in the history of Canada, Canadian representatives have attached their names as signatories to a Treaty of Peace. We have here the spectacle of twenty-eight sovereign powers, of which nine are kingdoms or empires and nineteen are republics, affixing their signatures to a document, and together with them appear 'the signatures of five dependent nations, all of them bearing allegiance to the same Sovereign power, England. These dependent nations are: Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and India. Are we, representatives of the Canadian people, given to understand that we are asked to approve of the Treaty because the political status of Canada in the world has undergone a change? Are we to understand that if the Canadian Parliament should refuse to ratify the action of our delegates, the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. A. L. Sifton) and the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. C. J. Doherty), who signed for Canada, the signatures given on behalf of the British Empire by Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Barnes, Mr. Bonar Law, Mr. Balfour, and Lord Milner, would be questioned or impaired? My impression, nay, my conviction, is that no consequence of any importance to Canada, nationally or internationally, would result from our abstention, any more than if India's approval failed to be given. The clock of the world would continue to strike the hours and half hours as before. We are assured, however, by the Government, and by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister in particular, that we have gained in political status, and what the new status of Canada will be is to be decided at a conference which is shortly to be held. Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that Canada is gradually assuming more and more international obligations without any corresponding international status. A fever of imperialism, the main symptom of which is a blind desire
to centralize in London the administration of Canadian affairs, is haunting the mind of some of our public men. In the interests of the solidarity and the permanence of the British Empire, and of the happiness and prosperity of its component parts, it is the duty of the Canadian Parliament to resist this tendency. Imperial Federation is considered by some as a forward step politically, but I have no hesitation in saying that in my humble opinion it is a retrograde movement. Pending some more definite information from the Prime Minister we are bound to come to the conclusion that Canada, as a result of the establishment of the League of Nations, has assumed obligations and responsibilities of tremendous dimensions without corresponding political advantages. Not being a Sovereign State, Canada could very well have left it to the representatives of Great Britain to enter the League of Nations. In such an event, ipso facto Canada, as an integral part of the British Empire, would have been a member of the League and would have shared in its benefits without being exposed to most difficult and dangerous situations politically and militarily. Let no hon. gentleman construe my words as the expression of a sentiment of selfishness and egotism. I lay claim to being as true a Canadian as anyone of those who from the housetops make pretentious declarations of their Canadian-ism. Had Canada been a sovereign nation like Belgium, Portugal, or the United States, my advice would have been to join the League of Nations. Mr. Wilson, in his speech delivered the day before yesterday, said that the League of Nations was impossible without the concurrence of the United States. That is perfectly true, and we can agree with the President of the United States in this contention. But if Canada were not a member of the League of Nations the British Empire would remain in the League, with whose proper existence nothing done toy this .country could interfere. But Canada is not a sovereign state. It has, I confess, many of the features that distinguish independent nations; but the domain of its political action has its limitations and restrictions, and those limitations and restrictions are numerous and important. I may be told that there are precious compensations ; there are precious privileges; there are precious powers that are granted Canada by the British North America Act. That I admit. By the British North America Act in particular, and by subsequent legislation adopted by th.e Canadian Parliament, the Canadian Parliament alone

lias the power to dispose of the Canadian militia either in this country or out of it. Without any interference, without any coercion from outside, it has been exercised on many occasions, and on no occasion with more glory and more brilliant results than during the last five years. But if this Parliament approves without a single reservation that part of the Peace Treaty which is called the Covenant of the League of Nations it ties its hands. It surrenders to a council of nine men sitting in Geneva the right to dispose of Canadian troops to quell any eventual disorder in any of the five continents, or to carry on any war, great or small, on the surface of the earth. Everyone remembers the Siberian expedition, and confesses that it was unpopular. It was a great blunder politically and militarily. But there Was a redeeming feature about the Siberian expedition in the fact that it was entered into by the independent, or at any rate the seemingly independent, action of the Canadian Government.

speechtext:
It is true Parliament was noE consulted. It was one of the numerous mistakes that were made by the Government. Can any one picture to himself what the result would be if, after the League of Nations is duly constituted, a council of nine men in Geneva should order 5,000 Canadian soldiers to the Antipodes? The dissatisfaction, I venture to say, in Canada would be so great as to border on revolution. My contention is that it is not making for the consolidation of the British Empire but rather for its disintegration.
But there is more than that, Mr. Speaker. The various clauses of the covenant vest in the Council of Nine the most extensive powers. Let us see how_ this Council of Nine will be composed or 'constituted. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) in. his eloquent remarks a few minutes ago, pointed out that there was nothing in the Covenant of the League of Nations that prevented Canada from being represented on the Council of Nine. Technically we must agree with the minister, but how is the Council to be constituted ? It will be constituted of nine men, five of whom will be representatives of one of the five big powers-Great Britain, the United States, France, Italy, Japan.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I see the hon. gentleman has made a mistake; it is the British Empire, not Great Britain.

speechtext:
Yes, I should have said the British Empire, because it carries out my view more effectively. The British Empire is exactly what I had in mind. That is the reason why, in the selection of the four other members, the 27 other sovereign and independent nations will never select another member from the British Empire. The British Empire is already represented, ipso facto as France, the United States, Italy and Japan are. Would any one for one moment contend that the 27 other nations, having to select four members, will resort to the selection of one member from the British Empire? No; the four other members will be selected from the other nations from amongst themselves and Canada will not be represented on the Council of Nine.
We have the Council of !Nine. Now, I will go one step further than my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in reference to this particular feature that I want to draw the attention of the House to. Let us suppose that a dispute arises between England and Italy over a strip of territory in Africa and that war is threatened. The final decision being in the Council of Nine, such decision is binding on all the members of the League if it is unanimous, but in an instance like this the two parties to the dispute have no vote; the decision rests with seven members of the Council. Let us suppose that the decision of the seven not interested in the dispute is against England and in favour of Italy, and that England, in spite of the decision, chooses to resort to war; will any one kindly tell me what exactly the position of Canada then will be? Will Canada, bound by the signatures of those gentlemen who were there feel under an obligation to side with Italy against the mother country? That is a question. I may be told that these are remote possibilities. I admit they are remote possibilities, but they only illustrate the futility, if not the absurdity of the contention that Canada of its own status becomes a real member of the League of Nations. The Minister of Public Works, in answer to a question by my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) said that all the five big powers objected to Canada joining the League of Nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I do not mean that Great Britain objected; they were making a fight for us.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I had anticipated, Mr. Speaker, that we would have this admis-

sion on the floor of the House. It is very important. I myself believe that England would rather hot have Canada join the League of Nations. Great Britain is satisfied that whenever her interests, or the interests of the British Empire are threatened, she . can count upon the hearty and generous cooperation of this leading dominion of hers -Canada. I understand, though I do not approve of the sentiments of pride

of personal pride-which must have expanded the breasts of the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister when they returned to Canada. Having landed here with this Covenant of the League of Nations, they seemed to say to every one who cast his eyes in their direction "We are it; we are responsible for this marvellous feat." On many occasions ' we have said and repeated that Canada enjoyed almost complete autonomy. That was true in many respects and may it remain true.
I surmise-and I think I am right in surmising-that the representatives of Canada at the conference at Versailles made serious and persistent objections to some proposals. We have been unable so far to detect what those objections were. But one of the proposals to which they must have objected very persistently was that of making the Covenant of the League of Nations a part of the Treaty of Peace. They have been overruled if they have objected. We all know how, steadfast, how persistent and how persevering was the President of the United States in this opinion of his that the Covenant of the League of Nations should be one and the same document with the Treaty of Peace proper.
The next proposal to which, I presume, they must have objected or taken exception to is undoubtedly that embodied in Article X and part of Article XVI of the Covenant. I see my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works smiling. It is a smile of approbation. These articles fail to establish any distinction between sovereign powers and dependent nations in regard to contributions in armed forces to carry out in any part of the world the decisions of the Council of Nine.
I assume that our delegates then realized that by those clauses Canada surrendered the right of Parliament to decide the question of sending troops out of Canada. Our delegates have signed the Treaty, and unless this Parliament attaches a reservation to it we are committed completely, and, as long as we remain members of the League
of Nations, irrevocably. A reservation, Mr. Speaker, does not necessarily imply blame of our delegates, does not necessarily imply blame of the Government. A reservation does not affect the existence of the League. A reservation does not mean that we intend to shirk any responsibility or any duty. We have only to take as an illustration what has happened during the last four or five years; and in spite of the fact that our endorsation affords no validity to the Peace Treaty, and the Covenant of the League, which is a part of the Treaty, if the Government insists upon having the opinion of the House in an academic resolution I submit that with such a reservation Parliament should approve of the Treaty.
I submit equally, Mr. Speaker, that we should approve of the Treaty of Poland which, I understand, is going to be submitted equally for our endorsation, although our representatives did not sign it.

speechtext: They did.

speechtext:
They did sign it? Then I do not understand a remark that was made by the leader of the Government in the Senate the other day in reply to a question put to him by the Hon. Mr. Dan-durand. Referring to the Treaty of Poland, Mr. Dandurand said:
Although it does not seem to have been signed by the representatives of Canada.
Hon. Sir James Lougheed: No, by the representatives of the British Empire; and the British Empire has been treated in the Treaty as being made up of Great Britain and the overseas dominions.
Perhaps I do not rightly construe the words of Sir James Lougheed, but it is immaterial. There is before me a copy of the Treaty and I notice that in the preamble to it the British Empire is designated as in the other Treaty. I was under the impression, though it was so designated, that the representatives of Canada had not been asked to sign it. I say that we should approve of the Treaty of Poland. We cannot read this remarkable document without feeling deeply gratified at seeing this unhappy nation at last restored to her independence.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
We all rejoice in it. The mistakes the sufferings, the injustices, and the cruelties of a long era, are blotted out and Poland is conveyed to the table of nations, as it were, to start to write history in common with all the free nations of the world. But before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I beg the privilege of

requesting all my colleagues, and for that matter all Canadians, to devotea little attention to one clause in the Treaty of Poland, and I ibeg them to read that clause carefully. It is clause 9 which 'provides for the protection of all minorities, racial, religious, linguistic. It sets forth that in towns and districts where a considerable proportion of Polish nationals of other than Polish speech are residents, adequate facilities are provided for insuring that in the primary schools the instruction shall be given to the children of such Polish nationals through the medium of their own language.

Hear, hear.
Mr. iBELAND:	It also provides that all
public funds under the State, municipal, or other budget, for educational, religious or , charitable purposes, be equitably distributed.
