subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
complete to this extent: that individuals and states may quarrel; 'but it is incomplete to this extent: that as between States there has not been in the past a court to which states could appeal, -coupled with the power to enforce the verdict of that court. True, there has been arbitration, but 'arbitration has been only partially successful because there has been nothing to compel the parties, to carry out the verdict of the court of arbitration. The League of Nations comes before us now with a court for the trial of cases and with an agreement to provide the necessary power to enforce the verdicts of the court.
In the past iwe have experienced many unscientific methods for dealing with common ailments. Well-meaning people have sought to deal with the question of the liquor traffic, the 'question of venereal disease, without taking into consideration the factors of human nature, without calling science to their aid, without dealing with these matters logically. Some attempts have been made to put an end to war. The most common proposal to end war is not to prepare for war. We have followed out that policy-which is still strongly advocated-but it has not kept war away from us. On the other hand, we have had our wars; we have gone into most of them ill-prepared, and we have had to pay, in the lives of our young men and in a tremendous expenditure of money, to -a larger extent than would have been necessary had we been prepared. So that it would seem to be of no particular advantage to be unprepared.
The proposal which we have before us may not end war, but it is a logical and reasonable proposal whereby war may be made more difficult, if not altogether avoidable. Consider for a moment the history of the social state. The development of the man who went out and took vengeance with a club brings him into the community. There private war is forbidden; his quarrels must go to the head of his clan for settlement. Then comes the formation of the state, made up of these communities. Private war is again forbidden, but war still remains as between states. What is more logical and more reasonable than that states should now join together for the purpose of forbidding war between themselves, at the same time providing that court to which they may resort and that force or power which is necessary to enforce the verdicts of the court? That is what we are face to face with in the League of Nations-
(Mr. Griesbach.]
a court to which quarrels may be carried, and that power to enforce the verdicts of the court which has been lacking in our previous arbitration treaties.
Now, there are two points for consideration: first, will this League prevent all war, and, second, ought we to participate?
I can see at once the war to enforce the verdicts of the court. If the League is a failure, we shall be back to where we were before.
Then, ought we to participate? We have participated in this war, and it logically follows that if we would secure the peace which we struggled for, we should now participate in this League in order to ensure the carrying out the terms of the Treaty. Without the League there will not be fulfilment of the Treaty, and, as I said a moment ago, the blood and treasure which has been shed will be largely in vain.
What are our obligations? Our obligations are, according to our strength, to march with the free and liberal nations of the world to the suppression or the punishment of the outlaw nation. I do not fear that obligation, because, in the first place, we shall probably march in a just cause; and, in the second pltfce, we shall have the previous deliberation and discussion through our representation in the League which is essential to the waging of a just war. In the past there has not been, so far as we are concerned, that previous discussion, that previous consideration in connection with wars in which we have par- * ticipated. That is a state of affairs which ought not and cannot continue; it is a state of affairs which is dealt with by this League-. We are given a representation; we are given an interest; we are given the opportunity of discussion and of deciding upon the justness and wisdom of the proposal which is made which brings us into a war.
We enter this League as a sovereign State. The Prime Minister very eloquently put that aspect of the case before us in the speech which he made the other day. from which I should like to quote in this connection. He said:
That in this, the greatest of all wars, in which the world's liberty, the world's justice, in short the world's future destiny were at stake, Canada had led the democracies of 'both the American continents. Her resolve had given inspiration, her sacrifices had -been conspicuous, her effort was unabated to the end. The same indomitable spirit which made her capable of that effort and sacrifice made her equally incapable of accepting at the Peace Conference, in the League of Nations, or elsewhere a status inferior to that acoorded to nations less ad-

vaneed in their development, less amply endowed in wealth, resources and population, no more complete in their sovereignty and far less conspicuous in their sacrifice.
That, in my judgment, supplies the most complete argument in favour of our belief that we ought to enter-that, as a matter of fact, we have entered-this League of Nations as a sovereign State.
It is true that many of the incidents and attributes of sovereignty are absent from our status. 'That is so because of the peculiar relations which exist between ourselves and the rest of the Empire. The League of Nations and the world1 must take us as they find us; they must have regard for the conditions under which we live. They must accept us and realize that we are a nation and a company of nations with a common Sovereign and a common flag, and that we have no desire to alter that, and that, I think, is the spirit of the League.
Throughout the drafting of this document there is the evidence of British statesmanship. It has studied vagueness in order that it will be capable of that evolution which has brought the British constitution to the point where it now is, and the League recognizes and the world must recognize that the great Empire to which we belong is still in process of evolution and that that evolution must continue. This document makes us a world power in law and promotes us from the condition of a colony or dependency to that of sovereign status. It confers upon us rights and obligations which startle us with their magnitude and far-reaching consequences. But after all we are asked to do only a formal thing, namely, to make legal that which already exists in fact. By the solidarity and determination of our people in waging this war to a triumphant conclusion, by the splendid efficiency and unquenchable courage of our troops in the field, we have won our place in the world, and no document which we may be called upon to sign, can add to or take from the place that is ours, for it is written in the hearts and minds of our people and upon the bloodiest fields of France and Flanders.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight oclock.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the magnificent speech delivered this afternoon has fairly well covered the ground for us. If I were possessed of the information which the
Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) has and which he did not give to us, and if I knew what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) knows, and has not so far told us, I am sure my remarks would be quite interesting. The speech from the Throne which was delivered on the first of September contains the statement that our participation in the war " has involved heavy burdens and vast sacrifices which the people have borne with an unflinching spirit;" and, further, that "the labours of reconstruction may be difficult and even painful." These words were uttered in view of the subject now under consideration. The ratification of the Treaty by the Dominion Parliament has no importance whatever for us except for the fact that we, the representatives of the Canadian people, are asked to approve in a direct way what already the British Crown and the Canadian delegates have duly signed, in the name of the British Empire. I am not satisfied with the manner in which we are asked to deal with such an important question as that which we are now considering. We, as" a young people having to meet the financial obligations that have arisen during the war and having borne great sacrifices in men, are not only called upon to-day to carry a heavy burden and bear a vast sacrifice but are also asked to endorse without delay the Peace Treaty, including section 10 which reads:
The members of the League undertake to-respect and observe as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all the members of the League. In case of any such aggression or in case of feny threat or danger of such aggression, the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
I believe this is too strong an obligation on the part of the Canadian people, for it pledges them to the world for the future. For my .part I do not wish to undertake more than we can do. At present there is no one in Canada who can say what would become of this country, with our two billion dollars of debts, with the great unrest in the different parts of Canada, the strikes, the high cost of living, the interest due on war loans, the pensions to disabled soldiers, and the pensions to widows. I say in all sincerity that before plunging into unforeseen undertakings in future wars in Europe we should carefully weigh the circumstances and be circumspect in our actions. If in the name of humanity we were again called upon to send an expedition to fight the Bol-sheviki in Russia, would we be ready at this moment to do so? What would you, Mr. Speaker, think of being called

upon to join an army for service in Armenia or Serbia, for instance, during the coming winter? The British Crown has pledged Canada, with the consent of its delegates, and now whether or not we ratify the Treaty and the Covenant of the League of Nations, the League will carry on its business as though we were not a nation. The Crown has already done for us what it expected us to do in regard to the League of Nations and the covenants of the Treaty. I learn from the papers that Germany is aiding the "Beds" to give Poland trouble, and is still helping the Russian army; that Boumania makes a threat to pass the Bed menace on and says it will not oppo.se the Bolsheviki if the Allies disregard her claims. What does all this mean to the Canadian people? It means that more men will be sent to the battlefield; it means more money out of the treasury and it means that there will be more widows and orphans. It means more sacrifice. I am of the o.pinion that this country at the opening of the present session was entitled to a balance sheet well prepared by the Department of Finance, and that a balance should have been struck showing where we stand financially. Before pledging ourselves deeper in enormous expense in connection with future wars in Europe or Asia we should put ourselves in a better position at home. Reconstruction and re-establishment at the present hour are matters that should particularly occupy our attention. We owe not only a debt of gratitude to our soldiers; we owe them our support and help. We owe a living to the widows and orphans whose position the war has made extremely difficult. In the speech from the Throne there is not a word of praise to the soldiers or widows. Great Britain and the Allies called upon the Canadian people for help during the war and we responded beyond their expectations. Surely, then, we can be trusted in future, whenever in our judgment our action is necessary, to do all we can when called upon to defend the weak from the strong, and prove ourselves again, as we have done in the past, true and loyal to the Mother Country. Why a written guarantee on the part of the people of Canada when the Treaty has already been ratified? Have we not a better proof than any written guarantee in the 400,000 soldiers who voluntarily enlisted to help the Motherland? Have we not a better proof in the number of widows and orphans we have at home? Have we not a better proof in the large number of Canadian women who crossed the ocean to take care of the wound-
ed soldiers? These facts, to my mind, are a better pledge to the League of Nations of Canada's righteousness than our ratification of this Treaty. Let the Mother Country trust us, for we are still the same young and vigorous people who did not lose the opportunity of showing our readiness to join a good cause when called upon to do so. Mr. Speaker, allow me to read in French a statement made lately in Europe as regards the result of the war and what we should do:
(Translation). Humanity is paying the price of the unprecedented effort that it has just put forth. Having struggled 'beyond its strength, it now needs rest, that It may relax its musales, soothe its nerves, recover possession of its will to live, by turning away from visions of death.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I agree that in discussing the question which we are privileged, to debate to-night, opinions should not necessarily be shadowed by the position in which members sit in the House. However, as the debate proceeds it is increasingly evident that those who are not in favour of the Treaty axe on one side of the House and those who are more enthusiastic for it are on the other. Perhaps this is a result of our political way of doing things in Canada, but whether that is so or not and in any event, I am sure that we have heard nothing here this afternoon or to-night which transgresses the courteous course of the debates which have characterized this House, and I shall try not to offend. At the same time, in regard to opinions expressed on the opposite side, it seems to me that we might divide them- not to speak offensively-into those who are pessimistic about the result of the Treaty and our joining in it, and those, on the other hand, who seem to be anti-imperialistic, as they would like to call themselves, but whose position I regard rather as one of standoffishness. In the first group of these I think we must put the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) who is gallantly and unselfishly occupying his vicarious and somewhat delicate position in a manner which should gain for him the gratitude of his own followers and which, I assure him, has the admiration of members on this side. He is the leader of those who might be called the pessimistic school. He minimizes everything. His speech to-day throughout minimized the efforts of the Canadian statesmen who were plenipotentiaries in Europe; he minimized the position of Canada. He might be called- I see he has just come in-the leader of the

Little Canadian party, if there is such a thing. He seems to idealize or embody that feeling which is of the shrinking, shivering kind, typified in people who do not like to see Canada emerge from the position which it has hitherto held, do not like to see Canada make progress, and are afraid that any step made in a new direction may land her in trouble and tribulation. I venture to say, however, that the people of Canada are mot of that build. We have built ourselves up from something very small and tottering, a small nationhood at the beginning but gradually growing. And I am surprised, as indeed we must all be surprised at this new attitude of my hon. friend the leader- of the Opposition and some of his followers, because he was not taught thus in the last few years of political life in this country. There is one man in Canada whom we all admired to a great extent, and that is the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I admired and followed him until he failed us in a great crisis in which it [DOT]was impossible to continue under his leadership.
If Sir Wilfrid Laurier did one thing more than another to accentuate his leadership of the Canadian people, it was to teach them to realize that they had become a nation, and when he used that expression on art important occasion it created an enthusiastic feeling on the part of the people of Canada, a feeling which had never before entered their breasts. Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke of the nation. He spoike of the twentieth century being Canada's century, and he continued with all the ability and acumen that he possessed to urge his fellow- _ citizens towards greater and bigger things. Yet, we find his supposed followers coming into the House to-day and taking an entirely opposite position. Hot one cheerful word, not one word of optimism has 'been uttered that I can recollect but rather have we heard words of fear and pessimism. Is this really the feeling of those who are on the other side, is it really the feeling of many in Canada; or is it just the old fashioned way we have got into of presenting acute political differences and accentuating party ideas? If these ideas are not held so strongly as is indicated, there is still hope for us.
Canada, I contend, is a nation, not because somebody says so but .because it has gradually emerged into a position of strength and vitality and is being recognized by the world as a nation. I do not care for the British North America Act-
Mr. iMOWAT:	Wait until I say it and
then I will give you a chance for applause. I do not care for the British North America Act because it deals with legal matters, questions of jurisdiction and extent of jurisdiction. Section 56 provides that within two years an Act of this Dominion may be annulled and not ratified. Seldom has anything of that kind occurred; in fact scarcely within our memory has an Act been annulled, We are not bound by the clauses of the British North America Act which is our charter, when we begin to have national aspirations. I venture to say that.no Parliament in the United Kingdom would fail, on the slightest reason being presented, to modify the British North America Act if it was found to be coercive or restrictive of our national ideals. We are too closely in touch in spirit with British statesmen and the British people component of the British Parliament to have an obstacle like that thrown in our way.
Canada has asserted its claim to nationhood for many years. In 1878 the right to set up its 'own tariff walls; it was felt in 1878 to/be a grievous thing towards the tradesmen in England. There was exasperation expressed. The opinion was expressed by prominent lawyers that the fixing of tariffs, which is one of the greatest causes of war and differences between nations, was not competent to Canada because she wa3 a colony. Canada held to her lines rightly or wrongly on the matter of free trade and protection or anything of that sort, and contended for the right of the Government and the majority in this Parliament to pass restrictive high-tariff legislation. Then the feeling in Great Britain subsided. They said: "All right, if you are going in for nationhood, we are not going to put anything in your way." We had that tariff for many years.
Again, in 1893, the Liberal party came to the conclusion that we should have a preference in favour of British goods as against those of foreign countries, and when they came into power in 1896 they did enact a preferential tariff which brought about a feeling of codiality between the Mother Country and ourselves that has prevailed to the present day. Mr. Kipling, who was looked upon as the greatest poet in so far as national affairs and aspirations are concerned, wrote some verses which were accepted in the Old Country and this as significant of the change which had taken place in the status of Canada. They ran thus:

speechtext:
Oh, oh. 7



A nation spoke to a nation ;
A queen sent word to a throne;
Daughter am I in my mother's house,
But mistress in my own.
Mine the gates to open;
Mine the gates to close ;
But I abide by my mother's house

What was said by Kipling-"a nation spoke to a nation"-was accepted by ns. That is many years ago, and it is altogether too late now for ns to he arguing or debating in this House upon the question or to attempt to change the flow of Canadian thought so as to minimize our position in the world.
But none of these things was entirely sufficient to put us in the position we are in now-neither the enactment of the high tariff nor the change in the tariff, nor the mere calling of this country a nation. None of these was sufficient to bring us to a full realization of all that we really are. But to-day, fortunately, we have the sturdy action of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) at this very Peace Conference which we are discussing. We know the difficulties he had and they were natural difficulties. No one wonders at other countries feeling that the Mother Country was thoroughly competent to legislate for the whole Empire and the Mother Country itself may have had doubts as to the propriety of our entering as a full-fledged nation. They might have anticipated difficulties with other countries as a result of sponsoring the claim of the right hon. the Prime Minister that we should be recognized as a nation. But he had his way and when it was known that we were recognized by the world as a nation there was nothing that could have thrilled the people of Canada more or. caused them to look forward with greater confidence and hope to the future than the struggle which he made.
Then, besides the pessimists and the minimizers, and the Little Canadians whose views have been expressed through their representatives to-day, there are those who want to stand off from any closer relations with the Empire. Many on this side do not understand that attitude but we are quite ready to listen in order to appreciate if possible what is said in that connection. I was surprised, I must say, to find my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers), whose speech gave great pleasure on this side of the House, setting a bad example by calling Canada a colony. I am unable to appreciate why it is that anybody wishes to minimize the position of Canada instead of giving her the position

which her importance merits. The word "colony" was also used by the Leader of the Opposition.
That may be effective in debate but I venture to say again that it does not express the real feeling of the people of Canada at the present time. We have the strength of a nation, we have the robust and virile people to make a nation, we have all the natural resources which a rich and powerful nation should have. And if we are to be a nation when we have a population of eighty millions why should we not be a nation now, why not so arrange and adapt things that we will be ready with a population of eight millions for the time when we become a nation of eighty millions? There is no time like the present.
I also suspect my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe)-although I did not have the pleasure of hearing his remarks, I read his speech-of having what I might call a scunner towards closer relations with the Empire. But we must remember that we form part of the British Empire, and that Empire is not a state but a nation. There is this difference between a nation and a state: nationality means the getting together, by accident, conquest, or other reason, of people of the same ideas who wish to live together, to understand each other, and to be left alone. That constitutes nationality, but a state is something more than that. It is having all these feelings, or perhaps not having them, but having the machinery or organization to get the peoples together. Now surely, belonging as we do to the British Empire, there is no one in this House or this country who does not deem it important that we should be as close as we can to the different component parts of that Empire. The British Empire may be likened to a wheel or rather the hub of a wheel with many different coloured spokes running out, if I may use as illustration the vari-coloured advertisement which we all see in the streets. And when we speak of an Englishspeaking 'Canadian or a French-speaking Canadian, or an immigrant Canadian, a Maori, an Australian, a Boer, or a New Zealander, they are all from the same hub. But remember, as we get nearer to the hub of that wheel we are all ourselves drawn closer together. That is my idea of what the component parts of the British Empire are to-day. It is my belief that there is nothing to-day in the world in the way of nationality or government that has done more for the world than the British Empire, with

its sense of justice, with its vigour, and with its ability to improve the countries which it peacefully incorporates. There is nothing which has contributed more to civilization than the British Empire. Of course, we are all proud of the British Empire, and proud of belonging to it and for that reason we should endeavour ^.0 strengthen it wherever we can.
I hope that my hon. friends opposite who have this feeling about shrinking against what they call centralizing things in London will not take that position with regard to this Treaty. Why, what is going on is the very reverse of centralizing in London. When we are asked to approve of this Treaty, not to ratify it, but approve of it, we are doing it independently. As was said to-day before, we are the first Parliament or legislators in the British Empire that has discussed the matter, and there is no centralizing in London unless we are prepared to give that centralization. My idea of Canada is that it is the biggest, the richest, and the greatest component nation of the British Empire, and with proper feeling there is no reason why all, no matter what may be the nationality of this country, should not go on and help towards that result. We must needs refrain from saying exasperating things of each other and try to understand each other's point of view. There is no reason why we should not think of Canada in the words of a robust Canadian, Charles Mair. I do not know whether he is living yet, but he was alive a few years ago and was liviing near Calgary. It is Charles Mair who gave us this ideal:
Hake Canada a home of generous life Of ample freedom, slowly won.
Of modest maid and faithful wife.
Of honest love 'twixt sire and son.
First feel throughout the throbbing land A nation's pulse, a nation's pride.
The independent life. Then stand Erect, unbound, at Britain's side.
I think we might all agree upon the sentiments in those verses.
Now, to deal with the question of the Constitution before I finish. It does not seem to me that we can settle this question or bring this debate to any good conclusion by carping or being too critical of the constitutional elements which surround the question. We cannot settle the question of the nationality of Canada by taking a detached sentence from Halleck's International Law, as was attempted here to-day, in order to prove a point-it cannot be done. Halleck had not this particular state of affairs in his mind. I doubt if he had Canada in his mind; he was thinking more of the 74
European nations. We are beyond the ordinary international law, or constitutional law, as it is generally understood in Europe. We cannot be so circumscribed by it. The British constitution is an extraordinary erection in that it has come on bit by bit, liberty upon liberty, line upon line. Nobody can tell you how it has been made, but it suits our purpose. It is in no way like the' American constitution where you have a formal agreement entered into and which requires specially voted amendments. We govern well and satisfy the people of the British Empire because of the elasticity of our Constitution, and we hope nothing will be done to restrict it or make it less elastic. It is not a written constitution; it has been built up by word of mouth and by the sane, proper and patriotic action of the Parliaments which go to make up the British Empire.
This League of Nations is not a new thing. It is not a new proposition that we have to discuss, except that it has new features. Leagues of nations have been made before. In 1815 there was the Treaty of Vienna which provided for the internationalization of the River Danube by an agreement between the powers. In 1856 there was the Treaty, or the Declaration, of Paris, made after the Crimean War, in which the practices of maritime warfare were discussed and settled' upon between the different nations meeting at the time. Then there is the Red Cross Agreement of Geneva, made in 1864, for the treatment of the wounded; and in 1874 the Treaty of Agreement of Brussels, by which the methods of warfare on land were discussed and which were mainly, as I understand it, the basis, of the subsequent Hague convention. But, the trouble with all these agreements and treaties was that there was no enforcing power, and history having taught us the fact that agreements without the enforcing power were futile and scarcely worth the paper they were written on-barring the Red Cross Treaty which, with the excep tion of one country, has been carried out by the nations of the world-not being able to enforce these treaties they lacked an essential quality when they were entered into. So we come to the present League of Nations which means simply that the civilized nations of the world shall do the policing of the world. If there is an invasion of the integrity or the territory of one of the nations composing it, we must go to her rescue-we bind ourselves to do it. Such a thing was never incorporated in

any previous treaty, but we are bound to do that because we are turning ourselves for the good of the world into international policemen. Let me give a very ordinary illustration: In every well-constituted town there is a police force which has certain regions and certain beats, and on the whistle of one constable or roundsman, the others will come to his aid if he is being attacked, and no police force is worth anything unless there is this co-operation and instant rushing to help the belaboured man. What would Canada be able to say if, as a result of the action of this Parliament, we should stand aloof and say: " We do not want to get mixed up in any European country's affairs, which do not concern us at all; this is our beat and we do not want to go outside to help anybody else; we are afraid of the results that might follow"? So by this Treaty, the most important in the history o,f the world, the civilized nations have agreed to do the policing of the world, and it would ill become Canada churlishly or shrinkingly or fearingly to excuse herself from participating in a work which must, it seems to me, redound to the good of the world. The Treaty contains an enforcing clause. My hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, asked: Does the approving of the Treaty take away our liberty of choice as to entering into a European war? Yes, it does. And I thank Heaven that it does, because if we were left without the obligation which we have voluntarily taken upon ourselves, and if, owing to the politics of the times, any nation could divorce itself from the general action of the associated nations, then the League of Nations would not be worth the paper it is written on. Of course we are bound together, and we will he proud to do our small part in enforcing generally upon recalcitrant nations that peace which will redound to the good of the world.
We say, perhaps: We do not want to mix ourselves up in foreign affairs. But has it never occurred to some, Mr. Speaker, that Canada may need protection of such a league in a very few yeare to come? It wias declared here to-day, when the Minister of Public Works was interrogated as to who said 'this ot that, that it would be improper to mention names. I think it was a wise declaration on his part, and therefore I am not going to mention names-what is the use? But as anybody with any sense must see, there are elements at work which may leave us open to attacks from well constituted maritime powers which may become

dissatisfied. It may be that we will be the first country to need the protective force of thite clause 10 of the League of Nations, and it would be a pitiable thing if we were to discard it simply because we have a shrinking dislike to enter into European troubles.
Here for the first time we have real internationalism, not mere pious agreements which have no force-not Hague conventions which anybody may break, and which nations did break in the late war-but we have internationalism reduced to a definite and Obligatory basis. Let us see hoiw it is going to work, this agreement between the best nations of the world to do certain things and to refrain from doing certain other things. I say it would be a pity to send this Treaty back with a stab of disapproval. It must not be forgotten that we are going to be a respected nation in the League. We sent over five hundred thousand men, most of them voluntarily, to a war which they believed had to be fought for the sake of humanity. Do you suppose that has not had its effect upon the peoples of the world? We know it has, and we have had many a tribute of admiration and praise that we, so far from the battleground, and with our extensive territory stretching from the Yukon to the Atlantic coast, could send men from every quarter of our Dominion to enter into this war. It was a glorious thing to do, and oiir Allies have acknowledged the value of our contribution to the victory which crowned our united efforts. We won the respect of the world, and let us not now be laggard in doing our share for the success of the world's greatest Treaty-a Treaty which may become the greatest boon that mankind has ever experienced.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in availing myself of this opportunity of discussing the Treaty of Peace, it seems hardly needful for me to say that I fully recognize and appreciate not only the vastness of the problems involved, but also the far-reaching consequences which they will ultimately have on the future of Canada. Laying aside for the time being the reservations and the criticisms which a perusal of this document may suggest to one, I feel prompted at the very outset of my remarks to recall the magnitude of the task of those whose mission was to draft this Treaty, to pacify a world which had, during four years of war, suffered the greatest carnage known in history. I could not better illustrate the thought which I wish to convey, Mr. Speaker, than by citing

the word of a great French writer and statesman: That during the seven months which preceded, the signing of this Treaty it was as if humanity had been placed on the dissecting table so as to better discover the mystery of its new organism and of its new life, to detect and to stamp out from its very soul the venom which had poisoned it in the past and nearly brought it to its downfall. This was the lofty purpose which the representatives of the great powers had in view, and to what extent their efforts were crowned with success a study of the document which is now the subject of this debate can alone enlighten us.
A Treaty, Sir, which has for its object the re-modelling of a whole world, when presented for ratification to this Parliament -though I strongly hold, as others have done before me, that this ratification is alike dangerous and unnecessary-should not at least have prompted the Government to pursue the course which they had intended to pursue-to snatch from any individual member of this House the time and opportunity to study this Treaty with the care and attention which the interests of this country demand. Such hasty action, Sir, as it was intended to impose upon us was not justified, in my opinion, on any ground of reasoning, and furthermore, may I add, it was in direct contradiction of the attitude which had been taken by the governments of France, of Great Britain and of the United States where the statesmen seem to respect more clearly the privileges and the rights of Parliament than the genr tlemen who for the time being are occupying the treasury benches of this House.
Wishing, Mr. Speaker, to curtail my remarks as much as possible, I will endeavour as briefly and as clearly as I can to lay before the House the general conclusions which I have reached and which will explain the vote I intend to cast on this most important matter. It is a fact that this Treaty has been severely criticised and in some quarters unmercifully assailed by men of outstanding character and reputation in all the allied countries. Let us not be surprised at this divergence of view on the part of men who are not responsible for the framing of this instrument, when we recall that the Treaty itself is but the result of a compromise between those who had the responsibility of drafting it.
Bearing this thought in mind, what do we find in this Treaty? We find features which will assuredly have the hearty support of the interested people. We find clauses which do not live up to our expectations;
we find others, again, which seem to shatter the very hopes of those who have sacrificed so much, by endangering the safety and future freedom of action of the countries which they indirectly affect.
iSir, what appeals to me most strongly in this Treaty is that in it are to be found, though modified and amended, the principles which prompted and inspired the famous fourteen articles of President Wilson, which at the time of their pronouncement on the 8th of January, 1918, stirred the Allied world, and commanded its hearty and enthusiastic support. What are these principles? Could they not, when considered in their last analysis, be reduced to the following three political axioms:
1.	That each part of the final settlement should be based on justice, under reserve of dispositions the most proper to guarantee permanent peace.
2.	That no territorial settlement should be made that does not comply with the interests and advantages of the populations involved in the said settlement.
3.	That each well-defined nationality should see its aspirations realized in the fullest measure.
Mr. Speaker, looking over this Treaty from cover to cover, though we may perceive that these axioms were not always rigorously adhered to, can we not proclaim that it is through the instrumentality of these principles that new nations have come to life, endowed with the blessings of freedom, at last delivered from the yoke of oppression? Unfortunately, Sir, we cannot close our eyes to the fact that great as has been the advance in the right direction, there are still many flaws in this Treaty, regrettable omissions which we may hope soon to see remedied and adjusted. I am frank to admit that for myself I should have liked at this moment, when we are witnessing the births of nations, the resurrection of Poland, the transfer of Alsace-Lorraine to its rightful owners, to see also the final settlement of the Irish question. I only hope and pray that the bitterness engendered through centuries of struggle in that country may soon disappear through the influence of freedom, generously accorded to her people.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the three considerations which the study of this Treaty from its larger aspect have suggested to me.
I now come to the last and most important point which I wish to raise, as many others have done who preceded me. Is it necessary for this Parliament to ratify this Treaty? What would be the consequence of our ratification or of our .abstaining from ratify-

mg the Treaty? In what direction lies the surest safeguard of Canadian interests, which we are here to protect? These questions have been raised and fully discussed in the course of, this debate. I unhesitatingly range myself with those who have argued, to my mind so well and so conclusively, that ratification by this Parliament is unnecessary and that whatever may be our action in this House, the Treaty will remain unaffected. No amount of sophistry, from whatever quarter it is launched, can, in my opinion, effectively veil this truth: that in the authority within the British Empire to which belongs exclusively the right to declare war in the name of the Empire-the King and his constitutional advisers-is alone vested the power to make peace for that Empire. What, therefore, are the motives that have prompted this Government to such hasty action-to the calling of a special session to ratify a Treaty that needs no ratification by us? It is in the Covenant of the League of Nations, and especially in Article X, that we may find a reason for their action.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to he understood as being opposed to the principle of the League of Nations. I strongly believe that permanent peace cannot be hoped for without the closest co-operation between the democratic nations of the world. These nations are called upon to protect and to defend two principles: the principle of justice inherent in the aspirations of their people, and the principle, too often forgotten, of mutual respect among all nationalities. In the defence of these principles, and to better assure that peace and justice may in the future triumph in the world, we are now erecting a new organism representing alike nationalities and democracies-an organism which is embodied in the Covenant of the League of Nations. But, Sir, could we not have attained this same high purpose through other means than by those which bind this country in the future to abide by the decision of a Council in which we shall not be represented-a decision which may be so far-reaching in its consequences as to have the effect of dragging us into a war, of conscripting our young manhood and our wealth for the purpose of protecting the territorial integrity of other nations, and this without giving to our Parliament the right to deliberate and to decide on the merits of the case?
The Government, by forcing us to ratify a Treaty though no good can be derived from such action and though no necessity is apparent for it, are only taking advan-

tage of the reluctance that a member may have to reject it on general grounds, in order that they may better pursue their old policy of imperialism in disguise-always ready to raise an altar to Canadian autonomy, but never failing to undermine in action what they so highly praise and proclaim in words.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the situation as it presents itself to me. It is grave and critical, endangering, as it does our future freedom of action. By the adoption of Article X we are stripping this Parliament of its most valued prerogative; we are placing the Canadian people at the beck and call of a Council not responsible to the nation for its actions. By one stroke of the pen we are mortgaging our freedom, receiving practically nothing in return.
Our prospects under this arrangement are not bright. Let us at least comfort ourselves with the hope that the prophecy of President Poincare of France may yet be realized, when he said that "real and permanent peace will not emerge from any single instrument of peace, but will be the outcome of a never-ceasing and collective effort on the part of the allied and associated powers."
Mr. FRANK B. STACEY (Fraser Valley): Mr. Speaker, as I recall the words of the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) in his opening remarks this afternoon, with regard to what should he the characteristics and qualifications of those who take part in this debate, I assure you that it is with the greatest hesitation that I rise to offer any observations whatever upon the subject which is occupying the attention of this House.
When Parliament assembled a week ago I had no intention of making any remarks upon this subject. I mistakenly assumed that the language of the document which we are now considering would be couched in legal and technical phraseology and that an ordinary man would have difficulty in understanding it and should, perhaps be silent when the time for discussion came.
But I found that what is, to my mind, the very heart of the document was capable of interpretation by an ordinary layman or workingman like myself. While I do not presume to discuss the question from the standpoint of its constitutionality, I purpose offering some observations as to the Treaty, especially that part of it called the Covenant of the League of Nations, as it appeals to the ordinary man, to the .man in the street, to the man who is not versed in the technicalities of legal inspection and

discussion, But as it is, I believe, regarded by the great majority of ordinary men and women who are interested in knowing something about the real, practical meaning of this Covenant of the League of Nations. I shall not pretend nor attempt to speak respecting the Treaty of Peace itself.
It strikes me-and I believe it appeals in this way to hundreds of thousands of our citizens-that after five years of agony, heartaches, carnage and immeasurable destruction, the allied nations conceived an idea, that grew into a plan, which was finally formulated into a document, which gives greater promise and 'hope of a lasting peace in this world than has ever before been seen or known by men in the long and chequered history of humanity. The preamble itself is a remarkable and striking statement, a tribute alike to the high spirit of the signatories, and, under the circumstances, to their magnanimity as victors.
I shall presume to offer a few remarks on the article that has been referred to so frequently, not only this evening, but on previous occasions, namely, Article 10. As I have intimated, I have not had a legal training. I do not pretend to read into this Treaty possible difficulties; I do not pretend to be able to discuss the constitutional difficulties which may arise, which are possibly real and genuine and which this nation may have to face in the future. But I remember this, that objection has1 been taken to Article 10 by hon. gentlemen opposite because its .provisions may involve us in conflicts in some far-away section of Europe, or in some distant portion of South America. We must not forget to-day that the world is very small, so small that Jules Verne's book has long since been thrown into the bonfire, and it is quite possible that there are within this Chamber hon. gentlemen who themselves may voyage around the world in less than eight days. All those manifestations and conditions which obtained a generation ago are changed. If distance is to be measured by time, the Atlantic ocean is not any larger than some of our great Canadian lakes used to be. Why should not Canada have a place in the League of Nations? During half a century or more we have grown out of a national infancy and childhood and youth into a young manhood; we have been under the protection of the great Mother Country, and there is, I am sure, no disposition on the part of any one to-day to 9 p.m. break with England. She has, in *a sense, led us by the hand until now, reaching the stage of manhood, we
are, I trust, prepared to take our place beside her, shoulder to shoulder, in every great plan which looks towards the peace, prosperity and happiness of the world. Hon. members opposite have to-day been searching the pages o.f history to ascertain some precedent for the action that is now proposed to be taken. As I see it, we are not reviewing history, we are making history; we are not following precedents, we are establishing precedents. And, why should we not, as a self-governing nation, be prepared, at this stage in our history, to assume our place and take our full measure of responsibility at this critical time in the history of the world?
In my province, which province by the way sent more than 10 per cent of her total population to the front, there were, during the course of the war-I regret to say this, but I want to be honest-a few men who apparently did not realize the duties of citizenship. True they claimed and desired all the privileges of citizenship in my province; they claimed the right to the franchise; they sought the protection of the British navy and also, the protection of the allied forces, including the protection of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. But for one reason or another they did not enlist. Sometimes they had a fluttering around the heart; sometimes they thought they had a flatfoot, and occasionally we found them obsessed with the idea that they needed a change of climate. For the benefit of their health or for the advantage of their pocket, they concluded that a trip across the line to the 'south would be of advantage to them, and so they went. At any late, they failed to join up, and we had in our province a few men who, while they desired all the privileges of citizenship, refused to assume the responsibilities of citizenship.
I fear lest there may be some spirit akin to the foregoing in the action of those gentlemen here or elsewhere who would like to have the full protection afforded this country by the ratification of the Treaty of Peace, including the League of Nations and including Article X-who would like to have all the advantages and all the privileges, without assuming the responsibilities and obligations which are embodied in that article. It was very aptly pointed out by the hon. member for Megan-tic (Mr. Pacaud), if I mistake not, that this proposition is the application of the idea and principle of co-operation-national co-operation. This is true. I cannot conceive of the Canadian Parliament or the

Canadian people refusing to approve of the Treaty of Peace, especially with regard to this Covenant of the League of Nations. The preamble, I may say, is a marvellous introduction to a state paper that will take its place by the side of any state paper in the annals of human history. I shall read two or three sentences:
In order to promote international co-operation and to achieve international peace and security -by the acceptance of obligations not to resort to war.
I call attention to the three succeeding clauses:
By the prescription of open, just and honourable relations between nations; by the firm establishment of the understandings of international law as the actual rule of conduct among governments; and by the maintenance of justice and the scrupulous respect of all Treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another.
As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, these three last clauses that I have read contain the very reasons which led 32,000 of our young men five years ago to rush to Val-cartier. These three clauses give the reason why, a little later in the dark and awful days of the four years that followed, over half a million more of their brothers and sisters went to their aid. The reason is found in this preamble. There is no additional reason to be ascertained; it lies here and here alone. But the words of this preamble are words and only words. They are great words; they will be historic words, and will ever be read as an expression of high statesmanship and of splendid ideas.; but they are words only. The essence, the acid test of this preamble, is found in Article X. You cannot make use of the preamble legitimately, reasonably, logically, without also accepting Article X. 1 believe in my heart, Sir, that it would be an example of the very personification of audacity for any man or any Parliament to say: "We refuse to approve of Article X," and then have the nerve to proceed to approve of the remaining two hundred pages. In the days of. the future should the storm break over our heads or over the head of some other small nation, we are united in our aim to speedily bring the struggle to an end and protect the weaker nation. I claim that there is a greater probability, amounting almost to a certainty, of actual peace than could possibly be secured without the provisions of Article X. And should the storm break and troubles come, then we are prepared to do our share. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that Article X of this Covenant means in 
substance, in commonplace phraseology stripped of all legal technicalities, that we believe in peace and want peace. It means that we want peace ourselves and want peace for all nations of the world; and because we want it and because we bate war, we are willing to co-operate with other nations in keeping the world's peace so far as may be humanly possible. Is it not reasonable and sane, iand comparatively sure, that with these provisions and with these ideas there is greater probability of peace than if we and all others refused to say "We shall bind ourselves together in the joint interests of humanity." Moreover, is it not a laudable aim for any young nation just entering upon its maturity to ally itself with the very highest civilization of the globe in its determination to be, in a very broad sense, the safeguard and advocate of the peace and prosperity and liberty of the world?
There is one view of this question that has not been presented to this House. It may not, strictly speaking, be involved in the letter of the Treaty, indeed, I am willing to admit, that it is not; but it appears to me to be a question of very great and serious import. And not only in my humbly judgment but, I believe, in the judgment of the great bulk of the citizens of Canada the question is agitating their minds: They are thinking and speaking about the matter which I am going to venture to introduce to this- House now.
I shall assume that this Parliament will ratify the Treaty of Peace; I shall assume that otir country is entering upon a new era, upon a new and larger life. She has won by the valour of her sons upon the battle field and by the statesmanship of her legislators in the councils of the nations a very high place in the world's record of great deeds. The world over the magic word Canada" upon the shoulder straps of every Canadian soldier from the humblest private to General Sir Arthur Currie, has been both the pride of the wearer and the admiration, if not indeed the envy, of every observer. With these facts and results behind us, and with a future that one can hardly overestimate ahead of us, and entering now upon a larger national life my problem is: How shall we the Canadian people so relate ourselves to the new conditions and to the new national life to ensure that our country will become not merely great in population or in wealth, but in all those higher attributes of mind and spirit which alone are the assured factors in national prosperity? This, Sir, is the question that has been in my mind and

which is in the minds, I have reason to believe, of our best citizens and I believe also, although not expressed as yet, in the minds of the members of this House.
Where is the Canadian citizen who has not been thrilled, who has not even been moved to tears at the recital of deeds of unparalleled heroism by our soldiers overseas? And of equal courage and matchless devotion of our daughters as they have taken their places in ministering to the needs of those who have been wounded? How can we, I repeat, in view of all these things, so relate ourselves to the future that we shall be equal to the increased responsibilities and obligations which are resting upon us as a nation? If there is any phrase or single sentence that better embodies or suggests the answer to my query than another, it is this: The character and the development of our Canadian citizenship. I am well aware of the fact that this is neither the time nor the place to discuss that question at length, but I shall venture to give a few moments to it because of the reasons I have assigned.
If I might express in the most general terms my appreciation of the character and the qualities suggested in the term " Canadian citizenship " I would do it by referring to four main factors which contribute to such a true and desirable Canadian citizenship. First, in our homes we shall be compelled through youthful inquiries in the future to lay greater emphasis upon patriotic principles and the relation of the family to national life than we found it necessary to do prior to 1914.
Then there is the Canadian press. I suppose that in referring to it I am treading upon sacred ground-or otherwise.. I cannot help but feel that, notwithstanding the very efficient service rendered by the Canadian press to Canadian ideals and to the true spirit of Canadian citizenship, there is one thing that I would fain see changed and changed for the better. I do not think that the cynical spirit sometimes continued almost to exaggeration by the press is conducive to the development of the highest type of Canadian citizenship and ideals. I come to another factor that enters vitally into the character and development of our Canadian citizenship and that. Sir, is found in our school system. We are coming to a day of change. The best citizens behind our public schools realize . that mistakes have been made in the past and that some change is necessary. Throughout this land there is an idea that the day is not far distant when the passing of an examination
will not be regarded as the be-all and end-all of our public school life. Greater attention must be given to the expression of the individual as a factor in our national life. But speaking of our educational work as a great factor in our national life, I place special emphasis upon the opportunities and obligations of our Canadian colleges.
I do riot now refer to the technical institution which furnishes our country with experts either industrial, economic, professional or scientific. I have in mind the college of liberal arts whether for ladies exclusively or the university course for both sexes leading to the Bachelor's degree. These institutions are in the main turning out not professors or scientific or economic experts but citizens who will take their place in the ordinary ranks of domestic or commercial life, but who, by reason of their extraordinary educational advantages, should be more than ordinary citizens. That is to say, the main objective of the college of liberal arts should not be scholarship but citizenship. The latter must become the goal, the former, a means of reaching it. Our country's future will be largely determined by the ideals of citizenship inspiring our people. The great opportunity and business of the college and university is to project upon society broadminded, or rather spacious-minded, men and women, well-balanced and sane, who will become big citizens. Our country's supreme need to-day, to-morrow and for all time, is not so much bright scholars as big citizens. We need more bigger, broader, better citizens, and the college system or curriculum which fails to produce the goods must either be changed or ultimately go to the scrap heap. The citizen does not exist for the college, but the college for the citizen. Education is of real value only as it qualifies for, and results in, good citizenship. Many a good citizen has never had a college life, but a good citizen is always a truly educated man, nevertheless. Perhaps I can best explain my meaning by the following illustration:	A
few weeks ago I ran across a man in my province who, from the standpoint of the schools, would be called an uneducated man. In fact, Sir, he himself claimed to be an uneducated man and deplored the fact most sincerely and heartily. But I found that he could give me the name and the characteristics of every plant that grew in that district. He could tell me the names and describe the uses of all the trees in that section of the country. If a bird flew by or alighted upon a tree he could

tell me its name and give me all its characteristics. If he saw the footprint of an animal on the ground he could tell me its name and describe its habits-in fact, he was a reliable authority on the entire flora and fauna of that district, and yet he claimed to be an uneducated man. As I said, from the standpoint of the schools, he was uneducated. He knew little of mathematics, less of literature, I doubt if he could spell the word "philosophy," and he thought he knew nothing of science. Moreover, Sir, he was a good citizen, inasmuch as he took his part in the great war faithfully and well. And last June, when the whole of the West between the Bed river and the Pacific was threatened with an incipient Soviet revolution resulting in some of its leaders being imprisoned and not, as the hon. the leader of the Opposition described the other day as being driven to prison because they were labour leaders-far from it, and let me say that the records of the courts have vindicated the position I took here last June and take here to-night-during that unsettled month this man acted as a steadying force in the community. He counselled against rocking the boat. He was a sort of moral and social anchor during the troublous times of last June. He counselled quietness, and steadiness, while some so-called scholars counselled otherwise. That man, Sir, was a good citizen, and from the standpoint of Canadian citizenship well-educated, although from the viewpoint of the schools, he would not perhaps, in the past at least, be so designated. My argument comes to this point: that our university life must so shape itself to meet the demands of the coming generation that the great aim of every college of liberal art in this Dominion, from ocean to ocean, would be nothing less than to turn out the very highest type of Canadian citizenship that can be produced within its walls. This man to whom I refer, I think, illustrated better than any one I have ever met the thought that was given expression to by John Milton two hundred and fifty years ago, and I doubt if his definition has ever been excelled, when he said:
I call therefore a complete and generous education that which enables a man to perform justly, skilfully, and magnanimously, all the offices, public and private, both in peace and war.
Now, I come to discuss, for a few moments only, another factor, another great force, in the creation of a right ideal of Canadian citizenship. I have briefly

touched upon the home, more briefly upon the press, and perhaps at greater length upon the college. But, Sir, there is still another factor which plays a most important part in the development of that type of citizenship which will enable us as a people and as a nation to take our place and maintain it in the days to come through the new relations that are put upon us. I refer, Sir, to the influence, and the power, and the work of the church. The college man says a good citizen must be an educated citizen. I agree with him, I accept his statement. The church-man will say a good citizen must be a Christian citizen. I do not deny the statement, I am inclined to agree with him. iBut, Sir, I believe this country has come to realize that notwithstanding all they have done in the past the churches of this land must lay more stress, more time, and more energy, upon those means which tend towards the development of a high ideal of Christian citizenship. That church, individual or denominational, will take its place in the Canadian life which, in the largest degree promotes a true and strong citizenship, and not very much longer will there attach to the cloth as such any special recognition or any inherent authority in the social world.
The churches of our realm have done a grand work for the Empire during the past four or five years; but they have a greater work to do from ocean to ocean in seeking upon all occasions to inject into the minds of their people the paramount importance of Canadian citizenship. I said a few moments ago that the college existed for the citizen, and not the citizen for the college. I go further and say that the church exists for the citizen, and not the citizen for the church. That church will take its place and do its work that sets before its people the highest type of true Canadian citizenship. It is not the cut or the colour of the leader's garb that to-day has or to-morrow will have any influence along the line of real leadership. It is not what is below a man's collar that makes for citizenship, but what is above it. What is above it is of prime importance; what is below vit is of very minor importance.
The ratification of this Treaty of Peace, including the Covenant of the League, of Nations, Mr. Speaker, will take place, I believe. That means that we are entering upon a new era with a new and a larger life. Our responsibilities are great, our obligations are heavy, but our resources are

almost boundless. With faith in our future and with confidence in one another and with a sincere purpose to give the very-best that is in us to our country and to posterity, I believe that we can and will not only take our place but maintain that position in the world's great League of Nations.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 9.40 p.m.
Tuesday, September 9, 1919.
