speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the following proposed motion of Sir Robert Borden, adjourned from September 8:
That it'is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany (and the Protocol annexed thereto), which was signed at Versailles on the twenty-eighth day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen, a copy of which has been laid before Parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiaries therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members dn this side of the House have been crittieised for having requested la short delay for ithe purpose of acquainting themselves with the provisions of the Peace Treaty before giving their decision on the most important resolution now submitted to them. May I say that I do not offer any apology for the oourse I have followed and fox having refused to be a mere registering machine to record the will of any man, even the distinguished Prime Minister of this country. Nor should any criticism of the provisions, or some of the provisions, of the Treaty, be branded as party politics. The real danger to Canada lies in the action of those seemingly irresponsible persons who are ready to approve without knowing, or to promise without acquainting themselves with what they are promising. If what the Right Hon. the Prime Minister has suggested is right, and that our adoption of the proposed resolution is necessary to the validity and the coming into force of the Peace Treaty, this would perhaps be the most important session of Parliament held since Confederation. We would be called upon to take a decision tbait might effect the lives, happiness, fortunes, and security of the sons Of Canada for many years to come. Surely, therefore, it is our imperative duty to inform ourselves thoroughly as to what we are about to do and to give this matter a mast careful scrutiny.
I may say, however, that in my humble opinion the resolution now before the House will not influence one iota the proceedings with regard to the Treaty or its coming into force, and that under our constitution we shall be bound by its provisions.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, in view of the answer given the other day by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister to my hon. friend

the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) that I am not living in the past, but that I am a Canadian of 1919, claiming for my country all the rights she is entitled to and desirous to see her go forward and occupy amongst the nations of the world the place she deserves. But the mere assertion of an illusion or a dream as being a fact does not make it so. I have no hesitation in stating that the Treaty will be binding upon us regardless of the resolution now before this House. The Government press is deceiving its readers by asserting that we are called upon to ratify the Peace Treaty. I have here a sample of that deception taken from the Toronto Times:
The British and New Zealand Governments have ratified the Peace Treaty; the other selfgoverning: dominions are proceeding to do so. When Sir Robert Borden moves for ratification at Ottawa, Mr. Fielding raises objections. He wants to know what difference it will make if Parliament refuses to act. In so doing he sneers at Canada's new national status which the Prime Minister rescued from the Peace Conference.
That, Sir, is a mistake. Parliament is not called upon to ratify the Treaty. I see that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) is nodding his assent to my contention, but in case there should be any further misapprehension on the point I will take the liberty of quoting constitutional authorities to bear me out. My first authority is Todd's Parliamentary Government in England under the heading of "The Right of making Treaties:"
It is a peculiar function of sovereignty to make treaties, leagues, and alliances with foreign states or princes; and by the law of nations it is essential to the validity of a treaty that it be made by the sovereign power, for then it binds the whole community.
In the British Empire this sovereign power is vested exclusively in the crown, acting under the advice of its responsible ministers.
Whatever engagements or contracts the sovereign enters into, no other power within the kingdom can legally delay, resist or annul; although the king's ministers are responsible to Parliament for their participation in the conclusion of any treaty derogatory to tile honour and interests of the nation.
And further:
The constitutional power appertaining to Parliament in respect to treaties is limited. It doe* not require their formal sanction or ratification by Parliament, as a condition of their validity.
And further:
But while Parliament may refuse to agree to measures submitted to them for the purpose of giving effect to any treaty, they have no power to change or modify, in any way, a treaty itself.
My other authority is Anson's Law and Custom of the Constitution. He states:
['Mr. E. Lapointe.]
When a treaty is concluded it is signed and sealed in duplicate by the ministers representing their respective countries with their- own seals. If the treaty contains, as is usual, a clause providing that it shall be ratified and ratifications exchanged at some future date and specified place, then until ratification neither side is bound by it. If there is no such clause, the treaty takes effect in accordance with the terms therein contained. The power to ratify or reject is vested in different parts of the Sovereign power, according to the constitution of different countries, in a popular assembly, as the Cortes in Portugal; in a second chamber, as the Senate in the United States; in the Executive, as the Crown in England.
It would appear that the Government of Great Britain did not want this House or my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to be under any misapprehension as to that. Mr. Lloyd George did not move a resolution in the British House of Commons ratifying or approving the Peace Treaty; all he did was to introduce -a Bill, similar to that which has been introduced here, to give effect to some provisions of the Treaty for the appointment of officers and other purposes. He even took the trouble to say that the Treaty did not require any ratification. On introducing the Bill he spoke as follows :
There are two Bills which I shall have to ask the leave of the House to introduce. It is unnecessary to obtain the ratification of Parliament to the Treaty except in one or two particulars.
And the leader of the Government in the House of Lords also took the trouble to state the position in these words:
My Lords, this Bill to which I have the honour to ask Tour Lordships to give a second reading is not, for the reasons which I explained ' the other day, a Bill ratifying the Treaty of Peace that has been concluded between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany, but it is a Bill giving power for the execution of the Treaty in certain respects for which Parliamentary sanction is required.
Will any hon. gentleman say that the Canadian Parliament has more power with regard to the ratifying of treaties- than the Parliament of the Mother Country? If it has, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is right in saying that we have made an important step forward. Indeed, we have gone so fast that the citizens of the United Kingdom cannot keep pace with us and are not aware of our rapid advance.
But let us not delude onrselves, Mr. Speaker. We have absolutely no right to change, alter, or modify this Treaty in any way. We cannot change one line of it; we cannot dot one "i", we cannot cross one "t"; and whatever we may presume to do we shall nevertheless be bound by its provisions. The fact that the representatives

of Canada added their signatures to those of the British representatives does not change our constitutional position. It will he noticed that the first lines of the Treaty describe who are the parties to it. Twenty-iseven powers-not thirty-two-are mentioned on the part of the Allies, of which five are described as the principal Allied and Associated powers, being the United. States of America, the British Empire, France, Italy, and Japan. The other twenty-two powers are then enumerated, and they do not include Canada. Obviously Canada is there as part of the British Empire and has no separate entity.
Then, on page 2 and following pages are given the names of the representatives of the various powers or high contracting parties, as follows:
The President of The United States of America, by:
The Honourable Woodrow Wilson, President of The United States ;
The Honourable Robert Lansing;
The Honourable Henry White ;
The Honourable Edward M. House;
General Tasker H. Bliss.
Then, the second one is:
His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the seas, Emperor of India, by:
The Right Honourable David Lloyd George;
The Right Honourable Andrew Bonar Law;
The Right Honourable Viscount Milner;
The Right Honourable Arthur James Balfour ;
The Right Honourable George Nicoll Barnes.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that it is clearly and unmistakably stated that His Majesty is so represented for all purposes by these gentlemen; he is not represented in a restricted way. Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Bonar Law and the other British plenipotentiaries are not described as representing His Majesty for the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; they represent him for the British Empire at large. Then follow the words:	.
And for the Dominion of Canada, by:
The Honourable Charles Joseph Doherty;
The Honourable Arthur Lewis Sifton.
For the Commonwealth of Australia, by:
The Right Honourable William Morris Hughes;
The Right Honourable Sir Joseph Cook.
For the Union of South Africa, by:
General the Right Honourable Louis Botha;
Lieutenant General the Right Honourable Jan Christian Smuts.
For the Dominion of New Zealand, by:
The Right Honourable William Ferguson Massey.
For India, by:
The Right Honourable Edwin Samuel Montagu ;
Major-General His Highness Maharaja Sir Ganga Singh Bahadur.
So that whatever step we have taken towards nationhood by signing the Treaty has also been taken by India-and nobody in this House will suggest that India has approached the stage of nationhood; she does not even enjoy responsible government.
I am glad, indeed, that we had representatives at the Peace Conference. I do not share the opinion of those who claim that we had. no business to be there. My criticism is rather in the opposite direction; my complaint is that our representatives were not there on a basis of perfect equality with those of the Mother Country.
The Prime Minister said the other day, in his speech on the resolution which is now before us, that Canada had been consulted prior to. the Peace Conference, through the *medium of the Imperial War Cabinet, with regard to the conditions of peace which should be imposed upon Germany. I accept this statement, though there is evidence to qualify it. On November 5, 1918, representatives of the Allied Governments gathered at Versailles for the purpose of dictating the terms of peace to be complied with by Germany prior to an armistice. On that occasion they issued the following declaration:
The Allied Governments have given careful consideration to the correspondence -which has passed between the President of the United States and the German Government. Subject to the qualifications which follow, they declare their willingness to make terms with the Government of Germany on the terms of Peace laid down in the President's address to Congress of January, 191'8, and the principles of settlement enumerated In his subsequent addresses.
These were the " Fourteen Points " of President Wilson. That declaration was sent to Germany and Germany asked for an armistice, which was granted under those conditions. That declaration having been made, there remained, as President Wilson said to Congress, only the " interpretation and application " of the specified terms. The Prime Minister of Australia, Mr. W. M. Hughes, was in London before Mr. Lloyd George left for Versailles. Everybody understood that the object of the conference was to arrange the terms of an armistice. Mr. Hughes had no idea that terms of peace were to be discussed; no intimation to that effect was given to him. Three days after the meeting, in an address to the Australasian Club in London, he entered a vigorous protest against what had been done. He spoke as follows:
In the settlement of the Terms of Peace the Dominions have not been consulted. They have *been informed of those terms, as indeed, has every other citizen throughout the Empire, but

have had no share in shaping them. I am1 not going to say more on that point than to express regret that the Dominions have not had an opportunity of stating their views before the terms of Peace were decided. It may be said that the Dominions will have an opportunity of expressing their opinions at the Peace Conference. It may be that this will he so, hut it is .perfectly clear that the deliberations of the delegates at the Peace Conference will he limited by the terms of Peace already settled. Beyond this they cannot go. They can neither take from nor add to these.
He followed liis speech by a letter in the London Times, in which he said:
I have remained here at my Government's request for the purpose of setting forth its views -with which, I need hardly say, I agree-before any terms of peace were definitely settled. But no opportunity has been given me to do this. I was not even informed that the peace terms were being discussed at the Versailles Conference, which I had presumed was engaged in settling the terms of the armistice with Germany as it had done in the case of Austria. The first intimation I received that the terms of peace had been discussed at Versailles was conveyed in the document which notified me that they had been definitely settled.
Mr. Bonar Law was asked in the House oi Commons whether the Dominions had been requested to attend the Conference, and he dodged the question by saying that all the Dominions could not have been represented. When asked why Mr. Hughes, who was in England at the time, had not been invited to attend, he replied:	" I really do not
think we can go into details." This shows conclusively that this Dominion, as well as the other sister nations of the Empire, had not been consulted in a very extensive way with regard to the conditions of peace which were to be required of Germany.
Indeed, it was quite proper that Canada should be invited to the Peace Conference. The glorious part she played in the war and the sacrifices made by her heroic soldiers entitled her to at least an honourable and courteous recognition. But as part of the British Empire, Canada, as well as India- having regard to the constitutional relations existing, as 'between the Dominions and the Mother Country-was and is bound by the signature of the representatives ol the British Empire and the ratification oi the Crown. The Treaty is made between the British Empire and the other powers, and whether we approve of it or not, it binds the whole of the British Empire, including the Dominion of Canada.
A proclamation .by this Parliament that we refuse to be bound by this Treaty and to acknowledge the right of the British representatives to sign this Treaty for us would be tantamount to a declaration of independence and a formal separation from [Mr .E. Lapointe.]
the Empire. It is useless and idle for hon. gentlemen to wax eloquent about our achievement towards full and complete nationhood, as the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) did last session, and as I fully expect he will do to-day, and to become intoxicated with the flavour of his own magnifying words.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
A necessary attribute of full sovereignty from the, standpoint of international law is the independence of . a state of every other state in the matter of its international rights	as well as in the
matter of its domestic policies. The Prime Minister described our membership in the League of Nations as a further manifestation of our new status. May I say again, that we share that honour with India, which I am sure does not claim to have reached nationhood as the result of such membership. But even there we are made members of the League by no act of our own, but by the high contracting parties, of which Canada is not one except as part of the British Empire. We were contracted into the League of Nations.
But the fact that we are designated in the League of Nations as a separate entity creates nevertheless an anomalous and equivocal situation. We are going to have separate representatives in the assembly of the League. We have even the right to be represented on the Council by one of the four representatives of the small nations, if the assembly chooses to elect or appoint one Canadian representative as one of those four delegates on the Council. I expect, however, that this is not likely to occur and that the British Empire, having permanent representation on the Council of the League, the other nations will not appoint a representative of Canada as one of the four representatives of the small nations. According to the Covenant, whenever a dispute is submitted to the League, the nations that are parties to the dispute do not vote. If a dispute intervenes between Great Britain-I mean between the United Kingdom-and, for instance, the United

States, will Canada, as a separate member of the League, have the right to vote, or shall we be considered as a party to the dispute by reason of the fact that we are part of the British Empire? I should like the President of the Council who, I expect, is going to speak this afternoon, to answer this question. But Mr. Woodrow Wilson has already ariswered the question from his point of view, and I should, indeed, like to know whether his point of view coincides with that of our representative in the League. Mr. Wilson, in the course of a conference between himself and a committee of the United States Senate, made this declaration which is taken from page 4284 of the Congressional Record "of the present month:
Senator Brandegee:	Supposing there were a
dispute between- the United States and that portion of the British Empire known as the United Kingdom-England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales-as to some right of one of our ships to enter an English port, for instance, and that dispute should come before the Council, and, upon the request of Great Britain, it should be removed to the assembly. The article I have just read provides for a report concurred in " exclusive in each case of the representatives of the parties to the dispute."
The President:	Yes.
Senator Brandegee : Now, all the self-governing, colonies of England, or at least five of them, have a vote in the assembly, and the British Empire also has a vote. I assume in the case of the dispute which I have supposed ,of course, the United States would be excluded from voting, as being a party to the dispute; and I assume the British Empire would be excluded, but I am not sure.
The President:	Yes, sir; that is what I assume.
Senator Brandegee: Do you assume also that Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and India would be excluded?
The President:	They are parts of the British
Empire.
Senator Brandegee:	They are parts of the
British Empire, but are they parties to the dispute which I have supposed to have arisen between us and England?
The President:	1 admit. Senator, that that
is a complicated question; but my judgment about it is quite clear. I think I can give one instead of three answers.
Senator Brandegee:	Yes.
The President:	Disputes can arise only
through the Government which have international representation. In other words, diplomatically speaking, there is only one " British Empire." The parts of it are but pieces of the whole. The dispute, therefore, in the case you have supposed, would be between the United States as a diplomatic unit and .the British Empire as a diplomatic unit. That is the only ground upon which the two nations could deal with one another, whether by way of dispute or agreement. Therefore, I have assumed and confidently assume that the representatives of all parts of the British Empire would be excluded.
Senator Knox:	But the fact that you give
representation to Canada and Australia and New
Zealand and other autonomous self-governing British colonies rather contradicts the idea, does it not, that they are one Government?
The President:	I think not, sir, because in
making up the constitution of the Council, it was provided, to speak with technical accuracy, that the five principal allied or associated governments should each have one representative in the League; and in the opening paragraph of the Treaty itself those powers are enumerated, and among others is the British Empire. "The Empire of Great Britain," I think, is the technical term. Therefore, their unity is established by their representation in the Council.
I should like my hon. friend to say if he concurs in this expression of opinion of Mr. Wilson, one of the fathers of the League. We are facing an unavoidable dilemma. If the opinion of President Wilson is correct, we are not enjoying a full and separate membership in the League; we are a mere addition to the voting power of the British Empire when questions in which the Empire has no concern are discussed and decided upon. On the other hand, if that opinion is erroneous, if we are for all purposes separate and distinct members of the League what would be our position in case of a conflict ' between Great Britain and another member of the League, in which the executive of the League should decide against Great Britain and a war ensue? Article 16 of the Covenant of the League of Nations reads as follows:
Should any member of the League resort to war in disregard of its covenants under Articles 12, 13 or 15, it shall ipso facto be deemed to have committed an act of war against all other members of the League, which hereby undertake Immediately to subject It to the severance of all trade or financial relations, the prohibition of all intercourse between their nationals and the nationals of the covenant-breaking state, and the prevention of all financial commercial or personal intercourse between the nationals of the covenant-breaking state and the nationals of any other state, whether a member of the League or not.
It shall be the duty of the Council in such case to recommend to the several governments concerned what effective military, naval or air force the members of the League shall severally contribute to the armed forces to be used to protect the covenant of the League.
The consequence therefore would be, il we are to be considered as a separate entity in the League, that we would have to keep our pledge, redeem out obligations, and *side with the other members of the League against Great Britain, and thereby cease to remain in the Empire, ot else we would disregard and break our pledges under the Treaty and take sides with Great Britain. We would have to violate either the Treaty or the constitution of Canada; either the one or the other. All this is the consequence of our present constitutional relations; it is the inescapable logic of our



international situation. Most assuredly the position is anomalous and abnormal. The right hon. the Prime Minister fully recognizes that. He emphatically states that a change must be made. Let me quote his very words (Hansard, September 2, 1919, p. 23):
The future relationship of the nations of the Empire must he determined in accordance with the will of the Mother Country and each Dominion in a constitutional conference to be summoned in the not distant future. Undoubtedly it will be based upon equality of nationhood. Each nation must preserve unimpaired its absolute autonomy, but it must likewise have its voice as to those external relations which involve the issue of peace or of war. So that the Britannic Commonwealth is in itself a community or league of nations which may serve as an exemplar to that world-wide League of Nations which was founded in Paris on the 28th of last June.
So the Prime Minister of Canada commits himself in emphatic words to the claim of full equality of nationhood at this proposed conference. It will indeed mean a radical change, and I sincerely hope that this aim is possible of attainment. The party with which I am associated has always taken and held advanced ground on this most important question, but I desire to say to the Prime Minister and his colleagues that if I would favour an association of the various nations of the Empire on the basis of full equality, I am strongly opposed, and I believe the people of Canada
4 p.m. are opposed, to all schemes of centralization by which Canadian policies would be framed and decided upon outside of Canada by any body of men in which Canada would have only one representative out of twelve. Canada will never agree to be ruled or governed from any place other than Ottawa. Canada is a nation, wants to be a nation, and she never, never, will become a province.
The right hon. the Prime Minister spoke in laudatory terms of the Imperial War Cabinet. He may be assured that any such representation or voice as Canada had in that body will not satisfy the Canadian people. His words of last year that the Imperial War Cabinet was a cabinet of governments were grandiloquent words, and nothing else. There is no such thing as a cabinet of governments. There cannot be a cabinet unless there is also a parliament to which such cabinet is directly responsible. Even in Great Britain the functions of that cabinet were not understood or defined. I find in the Hansard of the British House of Commons the following illuminating question and answer:

P. E. Morrell, M.P.: If the Imperial War Cabinet is executive what is its relation to the War Cabinet of five?
Mr. Bonar Law:	It is difficult and not very
advisable to define the relation.
I quite understand that answer.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Very diplomatic.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Any such body as the Imperial War Cabinet will not satisfy the aspirations of the people of Canada. I hope, Sir, that in any schemes which may be contemplated the truly Canadian position will be adopted and maintained. A famous French statesman was once asked his advice as to the best constitution for France. "It is France itself," was his answer. I believe it would be well to apply the same principle to Canada, and say that the best constitution for Canada is Canada. Our national peace and harmony proceed, from natural laws which must toe ascertained by the application of scientific methods. Greatest among those laws is that of descent and heredity, which it is useless to try to supersede. Consequences invariably proceed tfrom antecedents.
I also desire to tell the Government that any proposed changes should be submitted to Parliament before Canadian representatives agree to such changes. For the Canadian ministers to go to London, agree to a proposition and come back to this Parliament with a cut-and-dried arrangement is not treating the Parliament of Canada fairly. We must be consulted before, not after. When the pact of Confederation was entered into-and at that time it was a great constitutional change in this country -the first step was the introduction and the adoption of a resolution by the Parliament of United Canada. And. Sir, such precedent niurt be followed in any other constitutional changes that may be devised for this country. I also submit that no important changes should be effected without a referendum to the people of Canada which is the supreme master of its destinies. I was Surprised yesterday to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifbon) say that it is all very well to submit a change to the people of Canada when that change is in the wrong direction but that is not necessary when the change is in the right direction. That is good Conservative, Tory doctrine. Let me remind my honv friend that all arbitrary rulers, all privileged classes, all selfish interests, have always contended that they were working in the

right direction. With all deference to my hon. Mend, it is not the Minister of Public Works or bis colleagues who should judge o.r decide what is best for the people of Canada. lit is for the people of Canada themselves to say. I have said that the question should be decided by .a referendum and not by a general election because in a general election there are so many other questions and considerations >as to becloud the issue. We cannot-we must not- gamble with the .future destinies of our country.
I shall now say a few words about the Peace Treaty itself. It has been stated in the papers and it has been stated in speeches from the other side of the House that this involves a constitutional change, a remarkable step. I have taken the trouble to inquire what that ohange iis and how that step has been taken. Holding the vieiw I do and being .convinced that anything I may say, or even any vote I may give on the resolution, would have no effect whatever on the validity or binding power of the Treaty, I shall not attempt to enter very extensively into the discussion of what I consider to be Tather an. academic resolution. This Treaty was obviously a compromise between various interests and although some features of 'the agreement are objectionable, I am free to state that in a general way the statesmen who participated in its preparation deserve a good deal of credit. Germany has been made to pay a severe penalty for her brutal and criminal actions. Militarism is hopelessly broken. She i.s left without a general staff, without conscription, without universal military training, with a strictly limited amount of light artillery, with no. air service, no fleet, no domestic basis in the way of raw material for armament manufacture and with her whole western border fifty kilometers east of 'the Rhine unfortified and demilitarized. New natibns are created preserving generally, if not invariably, national aspirations and racial lines. A very unfortunate exception is made in the case of Shantung which in many respects constitutes a rank injustice.
Principles of natural law and morality in dealing with racial and national minorities in each country are enunciated and sanctioned by the great powers of the world. May I be permitted to quote Article VIII of the Treaty with Poland which embodies the general principles asserted in the Peace Treaty?
Polish Nationals who belong to racial, religious or linguistic minorities shall enjoy the
si
same treatment and security in law and in fact as the other Polish Nationals. In particular they shall have an equal right to establish, manage and control at their own expense charitable, religious and social institutions, schools and other educational establishments, with the right to use their own language and to exercise their religion freely therein.
Article IX was quoted yesterday by my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland). This is not to he wondered at. Poland has agreed to that most willingly because Poland Oaiew what coercion meant in these matters. As was pointed out in an article in the Montreal Gazette this morning, the three powerful governments of three great empires adopted a policy of one flag, one school, and one language for their Polish provinces. The governments have gone, the flags have gone, the Polish language remains. It has outlived the Hohenzollerns, the Hapsburgs, and the Romanoffs. I would advise some of the public men of Canada to read this clause, think it over carefully and forever banish from their ' minds the Prussian idea of proscribing anywhere in this country the language of its discoverers and first settlers. Surely the laws of morality and natural justice must apply equally to the victorious nations as to the countries which they have created.
Finally, and this is from my point of view the most important part of the Treaty, there is the creation of a League of Nations. In principle there is no stronger admirer or partisan of the establishment of such a league than I am. The war that has been fought was a war to end all wars and wars cannot be ended unless the old system is changed. The fact that the Turkish State, a disgrace to civilization, had to be1 maintained to ensure what was called the balance of power, is to my mind a sufficient reason to discredit the old system. When the great project of a League of Nations was launched, the democracy of the world rallied to its support. But I am afraid that the true Mends of the League are not satisfied with the body which is created by the Peace Treaty and the various articles of the Covenant which shall govern its functions. Certain statesmen in sympathy with the old order, the most distinguished of whom is Mr. Clemenoeau, the Prime Minister, never concealed their hostility to the new proposal and I fear that their influence was felt in such a strong manner that what is called the League of Nations in the Treaty does not differ much from the old balance of power.

The first object of the League of Nations in the minds of its first advocates was to abolish militarism and to secure general disarmament. Nobody thought that this meant disarmament for Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and Turkey, and a race for armaments between the members of the League. Yet no one will deny that this is the present condition of things.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Wait a minute. The United States propose to increase their military strength four times what it was prior to the war-who- says " not at all and proceed also to the building up of a powerful navy. Great Britain is considering a new scheme of naval power, and Admiral Jellicoe has left on a pilgrimage to the various British Dominions to offer them free and generous advice as to what they should do in the matter of organizing and maintaining a navy, or contributing to the Imperial navy. May I suggest that when the noble lord reaches this country he should be granted a most cordial welcome, but at the same time made to understand that it would be more appropriate for him to wait until he is called upon to do so by the people of Canada before offering his advice? In the meantime, our own peaceful country has doubled the number of men who compose the permanent militia. Indeed, the nations which are members of the League do not display much confidence in their own creature as to maintaining the peace of the world. I sincerely hope that militarism will be crushed not only in Germany, but everywhere. I am glad the League, will see to it that no military force shall be maintained except what is absolutely necessary for police protection.
Another condition which is essential to the success of the League is that it must be a League of all the nations and not an alliance of some nations as against the others. Even Germany must be admitted to membership in the League. Lord Robert Cecil, the strongest friend and supporter of the League in England, has just written a very important article advocating general disarmament and admission of the enemy countries to the League as the two necessary conditions to its ultimate success.
As to the famous Article X of the Covenant, I admit that my objections to that article are not, perhaps, so strong as they were before I studied the various provisions of the Covenant and before I read the explanation given by President Wilson a few days ago to [Mr. E. Lapointe. I
the United States senators. But I would like to know whether Mr. Wilson's interpretation of the articles of the Covenant coincides with the opinion of our own Government as to the meaning of that clause. The President, as reported at page 4284 of the Congressional Record, says:
In order to answer that question I must go a little hit afield. In the first place, I understand that article to mean that no nation is at liberty to invade the territorial integrity of another. That does not mean to invade for purposes of warfare, but to impair the territorial integrity of another nation. Its territorial integrity is not destroyed by armed intervention ; it is destroyed by the retention of territory, by taking territory away from' it; that impairs its territorial integrity. I understand the Covenant to mean that that is in no case permissible by the action of a single nation against another; that there is only one permissible method and that is, if territorial arrangements are unsatisfactory, that they should be brought to the attention ot the world through the League and that then the League should exercise such rights as it may be able to exercise for a readjustment of boundaries.	-
I believe that territorial aggression, in the sense of territorial capture, is, by the wording of the Act, made illegitimate.
Senator Brandegee:	The words are not
" territorial aggression," but " external aggression."
The President:	But it says the preservation
of its territorial integrity against internal aggression.
Senator Brandegee:	Suppose the external
aggressor, having gotten within the territory of the aggressee, stays there?
The President:	Then that impairs the territorial integrity.
Senator Brandegee: Certainly ; and then on a call by the council for us to perform our international contract under article 10, if Congress does not favour performing it you think we would not be subject to criticism by the othej members,of the League?
The President:	Oh, we might be subject to
criticism; but I think Congress would be at liberty to form its own judgment as to the circumstances
Senator Brandegee: I agree with you entirely, and under our constitution Congress would have to do so.
The President:	Yes; that is understood by
all.
As to what each member of the League would be obliged to do, that would be following a recommendation by the Council of the League, and here are Mr. Wilson's words, and I would ask my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) to say also whether his own opinion coincides with Mr. Wilson's interpretation. I am now quoting from page 4271 of the Congressional Record:
Article 10 is in no respect of doubtful meaning when read in the light of the Covenant as a whole. The Council of the League can only '[DOT]advise upon" the means by which the obligations of that great article are to be given effect to. Unless the United States is a party to the policy or action in question, her own affirmative

vote in the Council is necessary .before any advice can be given, for a unanimous vote of the council is required. If she is a party, the trouble is hers anyhow. And the unanimous vote of the council is only advice in any case. Each government is free to reject it if it pleases. Nothing could have been made more clear to the conference than the right of our Congress under our Constitution to exercise its independent judgment in all matters of peace and war. No attempt was made to question or limit that right.
I would like the Government of thi& country to give us the same interpretation of Article X of the Covenant as the President of the United States has given to the United States Senate.
Another question which was rather difficult was that concerning our right to withdraw from the League. The Covenant gives that right to all members of the League, provided they have fulfilled their international obligations and given two years' notice of withdrawal. I was afraid that it would be the Council of the League that would judge as to whether a member asking for withdrawal had fulfilled its international obligations, but here again President Wilson gives another interpretation. Here is what he has to say:
The United States was by no means the only Government interested in the explicit adoption of this provision, and there is no doubt in the mind of any authoritative student of international law that such matters as immigration, tariffs, and naturalization are incontestably domestic questions with which no international body could deal without express authority to do so. No enumeration of domestic questions was undertaken because to undertake it, even by sample, would have involved the danger of seeming to exclude those not mentioned.
The right of any sovereign State to withdraw had been taken for granted, but no objection was made to making it explicit. Indeed, so soon as the views expressed at the White House Conference were laid before the commission it was at once conceded that it was best not to leave the answer to so important a question to inference. No proposal was made to set up any tribunal to pass judgment upon the question whether a withdrawing nation had in fact fulfilled " all its international obligations and all its obligations under the covenant." It was recognized that that question must be left to be resolved by the conscience of the nation proposing to withdraw.
Here again I would like to know whether this is the interpretation given by the representatives of Canada.
Sir, we must make sure that the supreme power of the Parliament of Canada will be asserted and maintained. We have been told very often that our soldiers fought to keep Canada free. We must see to it that our public men do not undo their work and bind Canada in any dangerous way. I would certainly favour an amendment or reservation clearly stating that our approval of the Treaty .shall in no way impair or take away the rights and privileges of the Parliament of Canada. At least, our responsible ministers should make this clear and give their interpretation of the Covenant, so that no danger will lie ahead of us. It must be made perfectly clear that no Canadian soldiers can ever be ordered to fight any where except by the authority of this Parliament. The lives of Canadian citizens must never be sacrificed except by *the will of the Canadian people expressed through their representatives in this House.
In conclusion, &ir, let me join those who have already spoken in expressing the hope that this Treaty will establish permanent peace in the world. I sincerely trust that iwhen this Treaty comes into force the bugle shall sound the truce of God to the whole world forever.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Council): Mr. Speaker, we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the address of my hon. friend the member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe), but I am quite sure the House could not but contrast the viewpoint presented by my hon. friend with that presented yesterday by the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie)-two views of Canada's status about as far apart as possible.
My hon. friend in opening spoke of the importance of the question now before us and suggested that this session was the most momentous since Confederation. With the exception of the session of 1914, when Canada decided to throw her whole energy into the world struggle, I think what my hon. friend has said is true-that the question now before this House is the most important this country. has been called upon to consider.
My hon. friend spoke of the time required for consideration of the Treaty, and I agree with him that the matters dealt with in it are of so great moment, not only to Canada, but to all other portions of the British Empire and to the world, that every deliberative assembly owes it to itself, to the country which it represents, and to posterity, to give the gravest consideration to the problems presented. I regret, however, that the consideration which my hon. friend has given to those problems has not enabled him to accomplish some things which I think might have been of real benefit to the House. In the first place, it apparently has not enabled him to appreciate the resolution now under consideration. My hon. friend is an exceedingly able

lawyer and he spent some time in arguing that the ratification of the Treaty was an executive act of the Crown, and that therefore action by this Parliament was of no moment. There is no resolution before this House for the ratification of the Treaty. Let me read the resolution so that we may have the issue clearly before us. It is in this form:
That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany (and the Protocol annexed thereto), which was signed at Versailles on the twenty-eighth day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen, a copy of which has been laid before Parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiaries therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.
There is not a word about ratification in that resolution. (My hon. friend need not quote constitutional authorities to show that it is not the function of Parliament to ratify treaties. Ratification is an executive Act by the head of . the State-in this case by the 'Sovereign. The Sovereign ratifies upon the advice of his constiutional advisers. But the view of the Government of Canada is, that while they had the right by executive act to advise His Majesty to ratify this Treaty with respect to 'Canada, yet having regard to the importance of this Treaty and its 'bearing upon the future history ol Canada, it was the duty of the Government to submit it to this Parliament and ask their approval before they took the responsibility of advising ratification. It is well, Mr. Speaker, that we should keep clear the issue that is before us.
My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) suggested yesterday, and it has also been suggested by other hon. members, that any action of ours is of no effect, that the Treaty is already in force so far as Canada is concerned by virtue of its ratification by Great Britain. That, again, is an entire misunderstanding of the situation. The Treaty has not been ratified by Great Britain. The British Parliament has passed the Act referred to, which, in giving power to the British Government to execute the Treaty, is, in effect, an approval of the Treaty by the British Parliament. But the British Parliament has not ratified it.

Will the minister
make clear to this House what is the difference, so far as the action of our plenipotentiaries is concerned, between our approving what they did and our ratifying what they did?

speechtext:
I will try to answer my hon. frieend's question by stating the difference between " signing " and " ratification." Signing and ratification are two entirely different executive acts. One finally settles the terms of the Treaty-and once the Treaty is signed it cannot be amended; it is quite true that an " i " cannot be dotted or a "t " crossed, any more than one party to an agreement can dot an " i " or cross a " t '' or change the agreement in any way after it is signed, without the consent of the other party.
It is not anomalous that this Treaty should be brought before the House and that the House should not be in a position to amend it. When the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) brought down the reciprocity agreement some few years ago-an understanding arrived at in the form of correspondence between two Governments-this Parliament could not dot an " i " or cross a " t "-could not change the agreement in any way-without the consent of the other party to it. Was that any reason why the Parliament of Canada should not pass upon it? No, in that case Parliament was given an opportunity to pass upon the agreement.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I will come to that in time; let me first answer the leader of the Opposition. I point out these two distinct things: the executive act of signing, which settles the terms of the Treaty, and the executive act of ratification, which gives it legal effect. It does not become binding or effective until ratified. And what is the

reason? Take the case of United States as an illustration: the assent of the Senate of the United States is necessary before the Treaty can be ratified. As has been pointed out, in some other countries the assent of some governing body is necessary before the Treaty can be ratified. But between the date of signing and the date of ratification any nation has the legal right to refuse to proceed further with the treaty. In that case the Treaty fails for want of ratification.
As the leader of the Opposition has raised the question, let me give him one or two authorities on the subject. Yesterday he quoted from Halleok's International Law; I can do no better than submit a paragraph on this point from Halleck, for my hon. friend's information. I quote:
The question how far, under the positive law of nations, ratification by the State in whose name the treaty is made, by its duly authorized minister or diplomatic agent, furnished with full power, is essential to the validity of the treaty, was at one time the subject of much doubt and discussion. But it is now the settled usage to require such ratification, even where this pre-requisite is not reserved by the express terms of the treaty itself. The municipal constitution of the State determines in whom the power of ratification resides. By the constitution of the United States of America, treaties are negotiated and concluded under the authority of the President, but the advice and consent of the Senate is essential to enable him to pledge the national faith, by making a treaty the supreme law of the land.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks that he is informing me, I may assure him that I am thoroughly familiar with those terms.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is familiar with the terms I do not see why he asked what was the difference between ratification and approval.
On the question why there is a difference between signing and ratification, I quote from Oppenheim's International Law, second edition:
The rationale for the institution of ratification is another argument for the contention that the conclusion of the Treaty by the representatives is to be distinguished from the confirmation given by the respective States through ratification. The reason is that States want to have ai) opportunity of re-examining not the single stipulations, but the whole effect of the Treaty upon their interests. These interests may be of various kinds. They may undergo a change immediately after the signing of the Treaty by the representatives. They may appear to public opinion in a different light from that in which they appear to the governments, so that the latter want to reconsider the matter. Another reason is that treaties on many important matters, are, according to the Constitutional Law of most States, not valid without some kind
of consent of Parliaments. Governments must, therefore, have an opportunity of withdrawing from a Treaty in case Parliaments refuse their recognition. These two reasons have made, and still make, the institution of ratification a necessity for International Law.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the situation is this: The Treaty has been signed; its terms are settled and concluded. It has not been ratified, and before His Majesty does ratify it, this Parliament is asked to express an opinion on the question whether it should be approved or not.

speechtext:
I thought I had made it clear in my earlier remarks that the Government, before recommending that His Majesty ratify, requested the approval of this Parliament as a basis for the Act.
A good deal of criticism has been made in this House and in the country with respect to the Government passing Orders

in Council. All the Orders passed since Union - Government was formed would not have one tithe as great an effect upon Canada and her future history as the passing of an Order in Council approving of this Treaty in order that it might be ratified by His Majesty. It was the bounden duty of the Government of Canada, having regard to the gravity of the issue involved, to submit this Treaty to Parliament and to ask its approval before the act of ratification took place.
Ahow pie to direct attention to the terms of the Treaty itself. The Treaty provides that it shall not come into effect until ratified. It expressly provides that it due- not go into effect until ratified by three great powers, and one of the urgent reasons for prompt action by this House is because His Majesty will not ratify the Treaty until the Parliaments of the Dominions have passed upon it, and His Majesty is exceedingly anxious that the British ratification should be deposited at the earliest possible date. The Treaty goes into effect with reference to the three great powers, and Germany, when this first certificate of ratification, is deposited. It goes into effect with reference to the other powers when they deposit their respective certificates of ratification; it does not affect any of the other powers until they make their deposit. 'Some hon. gentleman has suggested, that, the war was over when the Treaty was signed. Such is not the case. On page 8 of the Treaty it is expressly provided :
From the coming- into force of the present treaty the state of war will terminate.
Not only has the Treaty not yet been ratified, but the war with Germany will not be legally terminated until the Treaty is ratified by three of the great powers. My hon. friends have asked why this Treaty should be aubmitted to Parliament, and have suggested that there is no necessity for such a course being taken. On a number of occasions the Government of the day have submitted treaties to Parliament for approval. On two or three occasions at least that has been done, and I have copies of the Acts here. In other cases, treaties have been submitted for the purpose of securing the necessary legislation to carry them into effect. The Washington Treaty of 1888 was approved by this House before ratification. It did not finally go into effect because of the failure of the United States to ratify the Treaty. The Treaty with reference to pelagic sealing was not submitted to the House for approval before the Act

was passed, but the then Government oi Sir Wilfrid Laurier passed an Order in Council approving of the ratification of the Treaty by His Majesty. That Order in Council was transmitted to England, and His Majesty approved and ratified the Treaty with the advice, consent and approval of his Canadian advisers. Then, when the treaty was ratified, the necessary legislation was passed. We are, in this case, adopting the proper constitutional course. The difference is that we are going further than, any Government has gone up to this time by submitting the broad question of approval to the House for ratification-

that is, that Her Majesty should act on the advice of her Canadian ministers. -but I say that Canada is not always to remain a colony.	.
My hon. friend referred yesterday to Canada, as h colony.
Light as our dependence may be on the Mother Country, that dependence is not to remain for ever. If we were to admit that, if we were to say that we were always to remain in a dependent condition we would, be the scorn of the world, and it would be scorn well deserved.
The fact is, Canada's status has been improving during all this period. Our rights of self-government have been steadily enlarged from year to year.
My hon. friend from Kaanouraska (Mr. Lapointe) speaks of submitting changes in the constitution to a vote. He is too keen a student of the British constitution not to know that the most important changes in the constitution have not been by any sudden act, by any decision on some particular matter that involved a great change. There is one view-I do not know whether any hon. friend entertains it or not-and that is that 'Canada should cut the tie that binds her to Great Britain and become an independent nation. I do not know whether my hon. friend means that or not when he speaks of our representative not being on an equality with the representatives of Great Britain. If he does mean that, then I beg to express my complete dissent from that position. The other view was the view presented yes-5 p.m. terday by the leader of the Opposition, practically relegating Canada back to her colonial status. Neither the one view nor the other represents sound Canadianism, the patriotic sentiments of the people of this country. The people of this country are determined, on the one hand, to maintain their connection with the Motherland; they are determined, on the other hand, to exercise the powers of a nation within the Empire.
My hon. friend has referred to the Constitutional Conference which the Prime Minister mentioned. That Constitutional Conference was decided on at the Imperial War Conference in the year 1917. The terms of the resolution deciding on that Conference have been submitted to this House on a number of occasions.
The resolution was submitted to this House in 1917, wheniSir Wilfrid Laurier was here leading the Liberal party, and, as far as I can recall the facts, he offered no objection whatever to the terms of this resolution. I do not think there is any serious objection to its terms on the part of our citizens. It indicates the basis along which our constitutional development should proceed. That was before the election and it was before the people. I never heard any criticism from any source of the resolution then adopted, or of the principles laid down in that resolution. Let me just draw my hon. friend's attention to it:
The Imperial War Conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the Empire is too important and intricate a subject to be dealt with during the %var, and that it should form the subject of a special Imperial Conference to be summoned as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities.
They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such readjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations of an Imperial Commonwealth, and of India as an important portion of the same, should recognize the right of the Dominions and India to an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of common Imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action, founded on consultation, as the several Governments may determine.
My hon. friend wants to know what is the basis of the constitutional conference to be 'held following the war. The basis set out in this resolution which has been before this Parliament for two or three years. My hon. friend need not be in doubt as to the ideas or policy of the Government in so far !as this matter is concerned. ' Then my hon. friend questioned somewhat the status of Canada at the Peace Conference. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition questioned it from another angle. The leader of the Opposition stated that we had not the rights of sovereignty. Technically that may be the fact under the British North America Act. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens, while speaking last session, questioned our position at the conference and while he did not compare our position to that of the United States, he recited an imaginary dialogue between Lloyd George and President Wilson, in which a comparison was drawn between our position and that of the United States. He asked if the state of New York requested representation at the conference, would the state of New York get representation? What was the situation in reference to the war? In the United States they have one Government that raised troops, that levied taxation, that waged war upon an enemy. His Majesty has at least five governments that exercise these sovereign functions. There is no comparison whatever between the situations of the two. It was with the free

will of the Canadian Parliament and with the sanction of the people that the Government of Canada raised the troops and levied the necessary taxation to send them across the sea to take part in this war. His Majesty acted on the advice of his advisers in Great Britain in raising troops in Great Britain and in dispatching them across the sea to take part in the war. His Majesty acted on the advice of his Canadian advisers in raising troops in Canada, and in sending them across the sea to take part in this war. It was the same with Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. For the purpose of waging war against Germany there was not only one government in the British Empire, there were at least five governments, His Majesty was the King of all, and all acknowledging allegiance to him.

Commander in Chief of 'the British .armies in the field. It reads as follows:
For matters of military operations the Canadian forces in the Field have been placed by the Canadian Government under the Commander in Chief, British armies in France. For matters of organization and administration, the Canadian Government still retains its full responsibility regarding its Forces. Matters of organization and administration frequently have a direct bearing on military operations and discipline, and vice versa, and it is, therefore, considered that where they have such bearing these matters should be made the subject of conference between the Canadian authorities and the G.H.Q.

perhaps a lack of appreciation on my part but I cannot understand the difficulty which my hon. friends experience judged by some of the questions they are putting.
What is the situation? What is the constitutional position? The British Empire is composed of five or six nations with one Sovereign. When that Sovereign is at wai .all these nations are at war, but the part that any one nation takes in that war is determined by its own parliament exercising its own sovereign power.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Hear, hear. . .Mr. FIELDING: It has been so in the past.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Heretofore, it has been so.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I am not questioning the fact that that has been our status up to date. What I say is tiba-t the power which we have exercised in determining our part in the war entitles us to some voice in the terms of peace, and that is what we have secured at the Peace Conference. I do not claim that the Government of Canada has improved the status of the Dominion during this war, but what I say is that the troops of Canada at Ypres, Courcelette, Vimy Ridge, Passehendaele, Arras, Amiens, and Cambrai made such a place for Canada in the Empire and in Europe that any government here would have been false to its duty if it did not seek to maintain that place at the Peace Conference. I can understand men who did not want Canada to go into the war, who thought that this was not Canada's concern at all, that she should limit her operations to this country and to this continent-I can understand them saying we should not have been at the Peace Conference, I can understand them saying we should keep out of the League' of Nations; but I am absolutely at a loss to understand the men who agreed that Canada's sons should go forth to help defeat Germany and bring peace to the world saying that Canada should not take any part in deciding what the peace terms should be. What was Canada's position at the Peace Conference? My hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) has said in reference to Canada's position that her delegates were not on an equality with the delegates from Great Britain. I do not know just what mj hon. friend had in view when he made that statement, unless he meant that we should have been there as an independent power. If he did not mean that, I do not know just what be did mean.
Now, let us look and see just what the status of Canada's representatives was. In the first place, the Prime Ministers of the Dominions were on the panel from which the British Empire delegation was chosen. In that respect, they were sharers in the representation of the whole Empire at the Peace Conference, in the five delegates that represented the British Empire. In addition, Canada had the same representation, the same status, and the same rights as the smaller powers at the Conference. What I would say to my hon. friend is this: It is true Canada did not have the same position as Great Britain, because she had not the strength, the population, the power, of the Mother Land, but she had a better status than any other small nation in the group of nations that took part in the Peace Conference. She had her own representatives and she was entitled to share in the Empire representation as well. Now my hon. friend (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) has raised the question about the signatures to the Treaty, and he asked: Would not Canada be bound by the signatures of the representatives of the Empire mentioned in the Treaty? My hon. friend read the first five names in the Treaty and then he says the names of the Canadian representatives and other Dominions follow but they were unnecessary. Another hon. gentleman, I do not remember who it was, said it was obvious it pleased the Canadian representatives. It looked very well to have the Canadian names in and, therefore, those names appeared in the Peace Treaty. What is the situation, Mr. Speaker? The Treaty is made by His Majesty, the head of the state, with the heads of the other states. The state in that sense consists of the whole Empire. It consists of the United Kingdom, it consists of all the dependencies, as well as the self-governing dominions, and India. Those British plenipotentiaries signed for all the Empire, except those. specially mentioned who were expressly authorized to sign for their respective countries. My hon. friend looks incredulous. Well, let me give him the proof.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Very much so.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I am prepared to help clear up the misgivings of Doubting Thomases, if I can.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I hope you will.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I have before me the
Order in-Council of the 10th April, 1919, which provides for the appointment of the

Canadian plenipotentiaries, at least which recommends the names to His Majesty for appointment as plenipotentiaries. I will not detain the House to read the document in full but I shall read the most important portions. It says:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on report from the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, stating that it is expedient in connection with the Peace Conference to invest fit persons with full powers to treat on the part of His Majesty the King in respect to the Dominion of Canada with persons similarly empowered on the part of other States, is pleased to order and doth order that His Majesty the King he humbly moved to issue letters patent to each of the following named persons (then come the names of the Prime Minister, Sir George Foster, Mr. Sifton, and Mr. Doherty) naming and appointing him as commissioner and plenipotentiary in respect of the Dominion of Canada, with full power and authority, as from the first day of January, 1919, to conclude with such plenipotentiaries as may be vested with similar power and authority on the part of any powers or states, any treaties, conventions, or agreements, in connection with the said Peace Conference, and to sign for and in the name of His Majesty the King in respect to the Dominion of Canada everything so agreed upon and concluded and to transact all such other matters as may appertain thereto.
Upon that recommendation of the Governor General in Council in Canada His Majesty the King did issue an authority to those ministers to attend the Peace Conference, not on behalf of Great Britain but on behalf of Canada, to conclude terms of peace at that Conference, and I think it is perhaps only right that one should put upon record the terms of that power because it shows clearly the status of the Canadian representatives at the Peace Conference.
George, by the Grace of God, of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, King, Defender of the Faith, Emperor of India, etc., etc., etc. To all and singular to whom these Presents shall come. Greeting!
Whereas for the better treating of and arranging certain matters which are now in discussion, or which may come in discussion between Us and other Powers and States in connection with the forthcoming Peace Congress.
We have judged it expedient to invest a fit person with Full Power, to conduct the said discussion on Our Part in respect of Our Dominion of Canada:	Know ye, therefore, that
We, reposing especial Trust and Confidence in the wisdom, Loyalty, Diligence, and Circum-speetion, of our Right Trusty and WelUbeloved Councillor Sir Robert Baird Borden, Knight Grand Cross of Our Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George, one of our Counsel learned in the law, etc., etc., Member of the Parliament of Canada, Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, have named, made, constituted and appointed, as We do by these Pres-
ents name, make, constitute and appoint him, Our Undoubted Commissioner, Procurator, and Plenipotentiary, in respect of Our Dominion of Canada; Giving to him all manner of Power and Authority to treat, adjust, and conclude with such Ministers, Commissioners, or Plenipotentiaries, as may be vested with similar Power and Authority on the part of any Powers or States as aforesaid any Treaties, Conventions, or Agreements that may tend to the attainment of the above-mentioned end, and to sign for Us and in Our Name in respect of Our Dominion of Canada everything so agreed upon and concluded, and to do and transact all such other matters as may appertain thereto, in as ample manner and form, and with equal force and efficacy as We Ourselves could do, if per-sonnaliy present, engaging and Promising, upon 'Our Royal Word, that whatever things shall be so transacted and concluded by Our said Commissioner, Procurator, and Plenipotentiary in respect of our Dominion of Canada, shall, subject if nfecessary to Our Approval and Ratification, be agreed to, acknowledged and accepted 'by Us in the fullest manner, and that we will never suffer either in the whole or in part any person whatsoever to infringe the same-
Mark those words. My hon. friends say that the British ministers could have signed for Canada. I say the British ministers could not have signed for Canada, in the face of this power given to Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues.
-we will never suffer in whole or in part any person whatsoever to infringe the same, or act contrary thereto, as far as it lies in Our power.
In witness whereof We have caused the Great Seal of Our United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland to be affixed to these Presents, which We have signed with Our Royal Hand.
Given at Our Court of St. James, the first day of January, in the Tear of Our Bord, One Thousand Nine Hundred and Nineteen and in the Ninth Year of Our Reign.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister a question? By what process was this Order-in-Council transmitted to His Majesty the King? Was it through His Excellency the Governor General direct to the King, or through the British Government?
