subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I cannot answer my hon. friend's question at the present time, for I have not the information. It was transmitted while the Prime Minister and his colleagues were over in England. But my recollection is that the Prime Minister stated when presenting the Treaty to the House that he took steps to see that the issue of the authority to the plenipotentiaries was directly connected with and based upon the Order in Council.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
The Order in Council was addressed to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the right hon.

Sir Robert Borden stated in his speech last week, which statement will be found at page 22 of Hansard. The question which now arises is: Whether it was at the direct request of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom that this authority was issued by the King in favour of Sir Robert Borden.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: That is the question.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I have no doubt whatever that the Prime Minister of Great Britain absolutely concurred in this action. It was all taken with his full approval after the understanding was arrived at with reference to the representation of the Dominions.
I am at a loss to understand the objection of my hon. friends. Do they think the Prime Minister of Canada should not have had that authority?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: He should have had authority.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Then if the Prime Minister should have. had the authority, what is the object of criticising and finding fault with our representation at the Conference?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: We are not criticising; we are putting questions to get light on the subject.	.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: We are merely asking for information.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It has been repeatedly pointed out that our constitutional relations within the Empire are in a state of transition. The whole object of the Constitutional Conference is to put those relations on a more satisfactory Basis, if we can. It is not possible to say one day that the situation is so and so, and the next day that it is so and so; it is a gradual process, an evolution from the position of a colony to that of a sister nation of equal status with 'the Mother Country, and when this Constitutional Conference is held I feel confident it will accord us that position.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: We have not got that position to-day, then?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: We have it in fact, and the British Government recognize that we are entitled to it, but the machinery for giving effect to it has not yet been fully worked out.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: A waste of time.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
That machinery has to
be worked out. In the meantime there are bound to be anomalies. We have a definite
goal in view, and we are seeking to attain that goal as speedily as it is possible to work out the machinery for giving effect to it.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend allow me a question? What would be the practical difference between the status of a sister nation and the status of an autonomous colony?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It depends on the position that is accorded. Calling a thing a certain name does not necessarily make it what you name it; it is what it really is that counts.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: You want to ascertain what step Canada has made.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Just in the same way,
when Sir Wilfrid Laurier returned from the Queen's Diamond Jubilee in 1897, he declared that Canada was a nation. A great many people disputed that proposition. Part of the argument yesterday of my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (iMr. McKenzie) was against that position. One might argue that Canada was not a nation at that time; but she was attaining that status; and the assertion of that status by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the concession of that status toy the Government of Great Britain, has made possible the subsequent develop-' ment. So to-day, when this Government says the status of Canada must be equal to that of Great Britain and the other Dominions in the Britannic League of Nations, if you choose to call it, the recognition of that status by the Government of Great Britain puts us in a position where all that is necessary now is to complete the working out of the machinery in order that we may enjoy that status; and that is the object of the Constitutional Conference which is to be called.
Yesterday my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition quoted from the British North America Act the section which authorizes Canada to carry out any Treaty affecting Canada made between the Empire and any foreign Power. Under the British North America Act Canada now has the constitutional right to carry out this Treaty and all that is involved in it and implied toy it. The British North America Act, Section 132, reads .as follows:
The Parliament and Government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising under Treaties between the Empire and such foreign countries.

I believe that Canada under this Treaty, particularly under the Covenant of the League of Nations and the Labour Convention, holds a higher national status than she has enjoyed in 'the past. I also believe the action of the Imperial Government in passing the Act authorizing His Majesty to take all action necessary to carry the Treaty into effect, and the ratification of the Treaty, will be a recognition of Canada's improved status by the Imperial Government, which has the legal authority las well as the constitutional right to' do so.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Does that apply to India also?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I am not concerned in
discussing the 'position of India at this time; I am concerned only in discussing the position of Canada. So I say upon all these fa'cts the position of Canada is wonderfully advanced over the old position. We are recognized now as a nation of equal status with the Mother Country and other Dominions. The Constitutional Conference must work out the details. They are not easy to work out and will be fraught with the greatest difficulty. No one should minimize the difficulties of the situation. There is no parallel far an Empire like this of self-governing nations seeking to work together. It is the greatest experiment in democratic Government that the world has ever seen. But I believe a solution will be found. I have confidence in the Anglo-Saxon genius for government, I have equal confidence in the genius for government of our friends of French Canadian birth and race, for they have shown great capacity in that direction. Sir George Cartier showed wonderful capacity and vision in the work he did in helping to bring about Confederation.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier showed an equal capacity for government in the work which he did in connection with our constitutional development. So I hope that in the working out of these problems we shall have the aid of men of both races in this country- just as I am sure we shall have the aid of men of both races in South Africa

in order that we may arrive at a solution that will ,be practicable and under which the Empire, consisting of several nations owing allegiance to a common sovereign, may continue to work together in pursuit of the great ideals which they hold in common.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to tire the minister, but if he will permit me I will put one more question before he proceeds to the discussion of another point. Can he

tell the House why Newfoundland was not represented at Versailles, and what difference there is between her status and that *of Canada and the other Dominions?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Did I understand my hon. friend to say that the British Empire ivas composed of five nations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I said at least five.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend name those nations?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: The United Kingdom is one, Canada is another, Australia a third, New Zealand a fourth and South Africa a fifth.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: What about India?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I will not discuss the constitutional position of India. A discussion of that matter would only becloud the real issue; no object can be gained by entering into it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I must remind hon. members that the House is not in Committee. Many of the questions which have been asked are not even relevant to the subject matter of the speech which is beirig delivered by the hon. minister and I must request that the rules governing debate be more strictly adhered to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Great Britain, having agreed to refer the matter to arbitration, having referred it to arbitration and having agreed to carry out the award, would be the one to refuse to carry out the award. I think we are absolutely safe in counting on that.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: That is not an answer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says: "That is not an answer." Let me take the case if Great Britain refused to carry out the'award. Under article 16, the Council of the League would have to recommend what action should be taken. It is an unthinkable proposition that they would recommend Canada to take action against Great Britain, but nevertheless, I will take my hon. friend's case. If the Council of the League decided that Canada was one of the nations that should make a military contribution, theh Canada immediately becomes entitled to membership in the Council and to take part in its deliberations; she then becomes a country of special interest and entitled to sit as a member of the League:
Any member of the League not represented on the Council shall be invited to send a representative to sit as a member at any meeting of the Council during "the consideration of matters specially affecting the interests of that member of the League.
Canada becomes entitled to have a representative present, and the Council cannot act unless the members are unanimous.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: In that case, would not Canada be considered as a part of the British Empire?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Let me read the clause
again. This is the second last paragraph of article 4 on page 10 of the Treaty:
Any member of the League not represented on the Council shall be Invited to send a representative to sit as a member at any meeting of the Council during the consideration of matters specially affecting the interests of that member of the League.
The Council cannot act except unanimously.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Does the minister contend that every time Canada receives a recommendation of the League to do something, she will have the right to be represented on the Council?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Certainly, it is clearly so stated.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: As a full member having a vote?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: As a full member having a vote.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
The minister cannot
show that in the Covenant.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It states so.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It does not state that the member will have a vote. On the contrary, it is stated in some other place that a party to a dispute is excluded from the vote.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: This is not a party to the dispute; it is a party called on to take action. Canada becomes a party of particular interest and entitled to representation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Not if they call upon her to take aotion against Great Britain. If they ioall upon her to take action, she thereby becomes entitled to sit on the Council as a member, and that Council cannot act except by unanimous consent of the members, and Canada could not be called upon *to take action unless she herself consented to do so. So the case my hon. friend has presented is impossible under the conditions governing the action in the League.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Does the minister contend that when this member is invited on the Council, it is in any other capacity than that of making* representations to the Council?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: She becomes a full member for the purpose of that discussion.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I cannot construe the
clause in that way.

speechtext:
That
means that Canada shall never be called upon to take action unless she agrees to it. Is that the answer of my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: She cannot be conipelled to take action unless she agrees to it, so far as action under that clause is concerned.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: It is interesting to have that on Hansard.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
It is interesting to have
that declaration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
That is the view I would reach from reading the Covenant. After reaching that conclusion from perusing the Covenant, I had the opportunity last night -probably many hon. members also had it- of seeing the official explanation issued by the Government of Great Britain in reference to the terms of the Covenant of the League. It was published as a parliamentary paper, and I was particularly inter-

ested to see that the position I ba/ve taken was supported toy the explanation in this parliamentary paj^er, as appears from the following extract:
It is the duty of the Council, with the help of its n\ilitary, naval and all advisers, to recommend what effective force each member of the League shall supply; for this purpose, each member from which a contribution is required has the right to attend the Council, with power of veto, during the consideration of its particular case. The several contingents will therefore be settled by agreement, as is indeed necessary if the spirit of the Covenant is to be preserved, and if joint action is to be efficacious.
The situation mentioned cannot arise under the conditions and terms of the Covenant; and, therefore, the fears he has expressed he may dispel. The Canadian ministers have not put Canada into a difficult or impossible position. I had intended discussing some other phases of the Treaty, but as I intend to conclude by six o'clock, I shall not discuss them.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Go on.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I intend to conclude by
six o'clock, but I want to point out again that the object of the Treaty is to insure peace and to prevent war by providing means for settlement of justiciable cause by a judicial tribunal, or of matters suitable for arbitration by arbitration, and, in some cases, by conciliation, and by requiring that the members of the League shall not take action for definite periods, three months, or nine months, as the case may be, in order that there may be full opportunity for conciliation. In that respect the Covenant of the League of Nations represents the best hope of our humanity, which has suffered through this war as our humanity has never before suffered, to free our race from the cause and ravages of war. It represents the best hope of the best men of all the nations, and I think it is a proud position for the Parliament, the people and the public men , of Canada to have some part, though small, in expressing their approval of and participation in this momentous document which we earnestly hope will prevent the repetition of the crimes and horrors from which our humanity has suffered during this war.
Let me say this word in conclusion. The League of Nations is to aid in preserving the	peace of	the world.
There is another momentous agreement contained in this Peace Treaty, namely, the Covenant dealing with labour organization. Next to world-peace the most important thing for our humanity now is industrial peace among the nations of the
9i _
world. I wish I had time to discuss the labour clauses of the Treaty, but I have not. I wish I had time to discuss the features of the new organization in which Canada is also a party-not without the strenuous effort of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works and his colleagues. To hon. member who thinks that our ministers need not have gone to the Peace Conference, who say that it was sufficient if Canada were represented by Great Britain, I say: How would representatives oi Great Britain represent at that Conference the industrial conditions of Canada? How would the employers of Great Britain represent the employers of Canada? How would the workingmen of Great Britain represent the workingmen of Canada? If the Prime Minister and his colleagues had1 done nothing else, in view of the magnitude of the industrial problems facing us these days, the fact that they secured representation for Canada in this international labour organization, entitling us to send our Canadian representatives to participate in its deliberations, their trip to the old country was well worth while and will be of lasting benefit to Canada. We trust the other treaties will soon be signed, that peace not only with Germany, but with all the other nations at war may soon come, and I say to my hon. friends on both sides of the House: Canada-having taken such a magnificent part in this- war, Canada's position having been so splendidly maintained at -the Peace Conference by the Prirpe Minister and his colleagues, are we not big enough to forget party and prejudice at this time and give the meed of praise to the statesmen of Canada who stood for Canada's interests among the nations of the world? Canada is great in-her territory, in the character of her people, in her institutions, in her free democratic government. This Treaty will affect Canada not only to-day with her eight millions of people; it will affect- Canada when she has from twenty-five to fifty millions, when Canada is not only one of the greatest powers on the Pacific, but one of the great powers of the world; it is a Treaty which we hope may mean an adjustment of international conditions gradually worked out through its provisions that will avoid war, not only for a generation, perhaps, but for a century to -come. If the Government of Canada, when such a momentous document was being settled, affecting our future for generations, had failed to take their part and see that Canada's interests were not prejudiced, but her rights conserved, they

would have wholly failed to- do their duty to the people of Canada. They have maintained at the Peace Conference the splendid position which the troops of Canada won for her in the field of battle.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with a considerable hesitancy, not only on account of the very great importance of the matter itself, though several speeches have been made already and have led me to comprehend the matter better than I had done before, but also on account of the remarkable speech which -was delivered this afternoon by the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Kowell). As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have not the habit.of agreeing with the minister, but I can say in all sincerity that I admired very greatly his talent and eloquence and also the agility with which he skipped around the troubles, difficulties and intricacies of the problem that he was dealing with.
As the minister said, this is a question which is far beyond the realm of political warfare, a question which is far above the common, ordinary grounds of our partisan struggles and .strifes. I have no intention of discussing it in the spirit of the politician, no intention of approaching it in the capacity of a partisan. The few remarks that I shall address to the House to-night will be presented by a Canadian who wishes to speak as a Canadian, and I feel confident, Mr. Speaker, that- my remarks will be received by the House in the same spirit as that in which they are made.
In 1914, when the whole civilized world was under the impression that the era of warfare had ceased, that our degree of civilization had reached such a point that- it would be impossible to have wars as we had them in the past., the -universe was -startled to hear that the German and Austrian empires had thrown down the gauntlet to the rest of the world and had proclaimed the gospel that now might was to be right. Never, I believe, shall we forget the scenes of horror that took place during the invasion of Belgium and Northern France. We still hear the rumbling of the German guns through Belgium. We still see the flames of destruction as they 'burned in the cities of Liege, Namur, Dinant and Louvain. For a while the whole civilized world thought that with the Golgotha

erected by Germany Christian civilization would disappear and we should go back to the age of paganism. But much has happened in the years that have elapsed. You remember as -well as I do the news that used to come from Europe depicting the carnage and the horror of it all. Luckily the war ended, and in 1919 in the city of Versailles, a city which was made famous by the great French king, the Grand Old Man of France, Mr. Clemenceau, got up, and facing the German delegates *who represented. the old regime in Germany said: "The hour of reckoning has co-me" and the German delegates were forced to sign the Peace Treaty that we have now- before us for consideration.
This document, I believe, has to be divided into two portions for intelligent consideration. First, it is the document which brought about peace; therefore, it contains the provisions of the Peace Treaty itself. Not only did the statesmen who met in Paris want to put a stop to the state of war that had existed but they also desired to maintain a state of peace, to maintain throughout the world such a condition of things that war as we have seen it for four and a half years would be impossible. The second portion of the Peace Treaty, and which has been inserted for the purpose of safeguarding peace throughout the - world, is known as the Covenant of the League of Nations. This Peace Treaty, and this Covenant of the League of Nations, have, in my judgment to be considered from two aspects. They have to be considered first as regards the entire world and they have to be considered as regards the Dominion of Canada.
The remarks I shall address to the House will be very incomplete, and the conclusions I draw will be very imperfect. I would like to have been able to offer something better for your consideration, but unfortunately the delay which has been granted to us by the Government has been very short and we have had but a very few days to peruse this very important and bulky document. When I examined this Treaty, when I drew certain conclusions from its contents, I took into consideration the very great troubles and difficulties that were met, .1 have no doubt, not only by our Canadian delegates but 'by all the delegates who were in Paris. These troubles and difficulties arose by reason of the existence of conflicting interests between the Allied and Associated Powers. They also arose on -account of the spirit of revenge in many countries after the war

was finished. They also existed on account of that traditionalism which exists in Europe and which influences the minds of many statesmen. They also arose on account of the very great difference between the political ideals existing in the Old World -which -is Europe and in the New World which is America, including the United States and Canada.
Moreover, the Canadian delegates must have experienced very great trouble and that trouble must have arisen from the fact that our national status is altogether misunderstood and misapprehended by the statesmen of other countries. Not only do the people of the United States misunderstand altogether our standing in the British Empire but in Europe-in France, in Italy and in every country-it is absolutely impossible for them to understand our position within the British Empire because their colonial system is altogether different from ours.
It is after paying due regard to all these elements of trouble that I will offer certain considerations on the Peace Treaty.
This Peace Treaty, considered as an instrument to bring about peace is very severe, but if the members of this House remember how Germany conducted the war, and consider the conditions which were imposed by victorious Germany on Russia and Rou-mania, still more the conditions ithat would have been imposed, according to the statements and declarations of the leading men of Germany on the Allied countries if this war had terminated with a German victory; and moreover, if we bear in mind the behaviour of the German plenipotentiaries at Versailles, we must come to the con-elusion that the Germans were entitled to absolutely no favour and could expect none.
But, Mr. Speaker, while we had a right to impose upon Germany a treaty which was severe, I say there is a great danger -a danger which has been avoided to a certain extent but not altogether removed -of imposing on Germany a treaty which would be considered absolutely unjust and tyrannical. I do not say that the Treaty is such, but that if you consider certain clauses of it you may think those clauses might bring about a certain condition of things and a certain condition of mind in Germany that will cause trouble in the near future. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I am wrong; I hope that my apprehensions are unfounded. When I read through the Treaty I found certain provisions that I would have liked to see somewhat modified and made less severe. Mr. Speaker, there
have been in the past examples of very unjust treaties, and they show that a people that have been crushed, and unjustly crushed, always rise, and that very soon, to take their revenge. I might point out to the members of this House as an historical antecedent what happended when Napoleon I, after the battle of Eylau, saw Prussia lying prostrate at his feet. In those days Louisa, Queen of Prussia, went and asked an interview with the French Emperor, and in that interview, which has been described by all historians, the Queen begged from the French Emperor that certain privileges be left to the Prussian people. Napoleon thought that his victory was definite, that his triumph was final, and he refused to grant to the Queen of Prussia anything that she had asked. Napoleon left the room where that interview had taken place. He journeyed to Potsdam where Frederick the Great lies, and took away the. sword that the great Prussian had carried throughout all his battles. Mr. Speaker, the Prussian people were not crushed for long. A few years afterwards a Prussian army was lined up agajnst the French army on the Plains of Waterloo, and Napoleon learned that a people cannot be crushed, they can only be humiliated, and that a fair peace is far preferable to one that is unjust and too . harsh.
Mr. Speaker, let us come closer to our own era. Let us remember the Peace of 1870. In those days the President of the French Republic, Mr. Thiers, asked from Prince Bismarck certain conditions for France. Bismarck refused, to grant his request. Bismarck thought that France had fallen never to rise again; and to-day the sons of Bismarck have had to go to Versailles to accept from President Clemenceau a peace that was imposed by the victorious Allies, among whom France had one of the first places.	I do not offer
these remarks, Mr. Speaker, in the view that the peace as concluded between the allied powers and Germany was unjust, but I simply say that some of its provisions appear to be very severe and to offer a danger for the future. In contrast, and recalling the results of the generous peace let the members of this House remember what happened when England defeated the Transvaal armies. Botha met Lord Kitchener. England, represented by the Commander in Chief of her armies, offered very generous conditions to her fallen foe, and a few' years afterwards when the recent great con-

flict broke out Louis Botha was behind the Empire's forces to help along the victory.
In the present Peace Treaty the provisions that I refer to are, first, that which calls upon the Kaiser to be handed over to the Allied powers by Holland, to be tried by an international tribunal. I would be the last man in this Chamber to offer any justification for the conduct and behaviour of the German Kaiser; but I say that a trial of the German Kaiser would offer certain dangers. A trial in London or Paris would make of a man who is now fallen and altogether ignored by the rest of the world a martyr, would make him a great rallying personality for the German people, and would offer a great danger to the world's peace. The Treaty is also very severe as respects the economic dependence of Germany upon the Allied countries. I do not wish to enter into a discussion of this clause in great detail, but simply to say this: According to the actual relations which exist between all countries of the world, the ruin of one has an effect upon all the others. Should Germany be impoverished, should Germany be ruined, all the other countries of the world would feel the effects of her ruin. Moreover the Treaty contains provisions for reparation in regard to damages done by Germany, and I say that if the Allied powers do not ' allow Germany to revive her trade and to again take the position as a trading country which she occupied before the war, it would be absolutely impossible for her to pay the reparation damages that have been asked of her by the provisions of the Treaty. Tlie last point to which I would call your attention, Mr. Speaker-, is the clause in the Treaty that keeps Germany out of the League of Nations. As pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamour-aska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe), a league of nations to be complete and to attain its object must comprise every nation in the world. I hope, therefore, it will be possible for the Allied countries to include Germany very soon in the League of Nations so as to ensure that Germany will not be in a position to enter into alliances with other countries and to create in the face of the new League of Nations alliances in Europe and in Asia that will threaten the future peac^e of the world.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the provisions in the Peace Treaty that I consider may be too severe. I am not in a position to criticise the Treaty. The statesmen who were at Paris and Versailles and drafted the Treaty knew the conditions much better than I do.

I hopb they were justified in inserting those clauses, and I hope the terms imposed will not, as I fear they will, jeopardize the future peace of the world.
I think that the Treaty contains certain clauses which should not be there at all, and among them I would mention the clause that hands over to Japan the district of Shantung. It seems to me that the weakness of China should have been her protection among the Allied powers, and that they should have prevented Japan from robbing -because it is nothing but robbery-that district from China.
Other clauses that I would like to see in the Treaty are missing. Of clauses that I would have read with great pleasure the first I would mention is one giving something to Canada out of this war. We iiave he-ard members of the Government and their supporters tell us the wonderful achievements of our army over in Europe.
I approve, of every word that these ministers and members have said. But if Canada has done wonderful things during the war, at the Peace Conference our representatives should have obtained something for this country, -as every other country has benefited to a greater or less extent. If the Treaties are perused it will be found that Greece is to be given something, as are France and Italy; if the drafts of the other treaties are examined it will be found that every country in Europe is obtaining something, and even countries in Africa. Canada gets nothing. I am Soi'ry that our delegates, the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) did not see that Canada at least obtained an indemnity. Our financial condition is very poor, we need the money, and after having fought as " we did I think we should have been granted a substantial indemnity. Probably I shall be answered that in accordance with the provisions of the Peace Treaty Canada will get her share of the indemnity to be exacted from Germany when it is allotted to the different countries. But that share will be so very small that it will practically amount to nothing, whereas we should have been given something substantial. Another clause that I should like to have seen in the Peace Treaty is giving to Ireland the right that has beep given to several other nationalities in Europe-the right of self-determination. Last year I spoke on this question in the absence of the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). He has since returned from the Peace Conference, but, unfortunately, although in this Cabinet ha

represents the Irish population of Canada, and has been very busy sitting on all sorts of commissions, apparently he has forgotten to raise his voice in favour of Ireland. It is said, Mr. Speaker, that the Irish question could not be settled by the Peace Conference because there exists in Ireland an English Protestant minority, and that that minority-the Ulster minority-cannot be coerced. I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice when he follows me in this debate, if he does, to tell me what difference exists between the Irish problem and the problem which he solved in Bohemia. In Bohemia there are a. very great number of German people, and those people were forced to stay in the new State formed by the Allies. The hon. Minister of Justice had no hesitation in concurring in that arrangement. That being so, I would like him to explain why he refuses a similar solution of the Irish question. Not only has that principle been applied in Bohemia, it has been applied in Roumania and in the settlement of the former Austrian provinces which are now given over to the Jugo-iSlav IState and to Italy. In a word, Mr. Speaker, everywhere in Europe there is no hesitation amongst the Allied Powers to form new States and to coerce small minorities; but when it comes to Ireland the Canadian delegates and the other delegates of the British Empire, together with the delegates of the other nations, decide to leave the Irish question alone and not to heal the wounds which the Irish people have suffered from for more than two centuries.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, the Treaty can be considered as an instrument to maintain peace throughout the world, and for that purpose it contains the Covenant of the League of Nations. The idea of a League of Nations is not new. Leagues have been formed in earlier times, but unfortunately those leagues were not successful because they were founded either on a selfish basis or on very undemocratic principles. We had in the old days the Hanseatic League. Afterwards we had tjhe Pacte de Famille formed among the Bourbon Kings. Then we had the Holy Alliance. All these alliances and leagues have disappeared. At the Peace Conference President Wilson was the sponsor of a new League of Nations. I hope that this new League will assure to the world a new era of peace. The principle of the League of Nations will be approved, I believe, by every member of this House. But while the principle is worthy of approval, I think we have a right to examine with great care the details of the organization of the League to see if fMr. Cannon. 1
really the object for which it was formed will be realized. As I said a few moments ago, the League should be completed by the inclusion of Germany and Austria, and when it includes every nation in the world, then I think it will be in a position to maintain peace. But as the League of Nations is now constituted Germany and Austria are excluded. Other countries have been invited to joint the League, but I notice with great surprise that one country situated on the American continent has not been invited- I refer to Mexico. Why should Mexico be excluded?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Oh! oh !

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Why should Mexico be
excluded if the United States are acting in good faith and wish to secure the peace of the world? Is Mexico excluded simply because the United States have designs on that country and want to act there free from control of the League of Nations?
Some members , on the other side laugh, but I think that is a question which deserves the serious consideration of this House.
As I have said, I am in favour of a League of Nations .if it is a means of ensuring the peace of the world. But a League of Nations which would be simply a new alliance formed on the basis of the [DOT]old European system of continental alliances or " balance of power " should not be approved by Canada or by any other country which is desirous of having peace. When Germany formed the alliance with Austria and Italy, known as the Triple Alliance, she wanted to dominate the world. For four years and a half the Allied countries have fought Germany in order to preserve the world from German domination. England, United States, Japan or France have no more right to dominate the world than Germany had.
The League of Nations, in its constitution, involves certain dangers to the freedom of the component parts of the League and to the autonomy of our own country.
In order to understand the question it is necessary that hon. members go back to the history of other days and examine the status of Canada at different periods as recorded by our different constitutions since we came under the British regime. I do not wish to enter into full details or particulars. I simply wish to remind the House that in 1763, when the Treaty of Paris was signed, Canada was a Crown colony. In those days the British Government was the supreme master of everything that was done in Canada; the people of Canada at

that time had absolutely no. control over the action of the Government as represented by the Governor . himself. A few years after England took possession of this, country the American revolution started, and the American colonies, which had been threatened by the Mother Country with taxation without representation, declared their independence and refused to let the Imperial Government interfere in what they deemed to be their own local affairs. Facing the American Revolution, the .British statesmen decided that it would be good to improve conditions in Canada so far as government was concerned and give to the Canadian people a larger measure of liberty. The Quebec Act was passed in 1774. Under that Act the administration of the Governor was subject more or less to the control of his advisers who sat in the legislative Council. As we go on we see the gradual evolution of constitutional liberty in Canada. When the French revolution occurred, the statesmen of England, afraid of the spread of revolutionary ideas throughout the world-ideas that were being .propagated by the French revolutionists of that day just as revolutionary ideas are being propagat'ed to-day by the Bolsheviki- thought it was time to give us a still larger measure of liberty and freedom, so we had the Act of 1791 which gave to Upper Canada and to Lower Canada a new constitution. But if we examine the constitution which was granted to Canada at that time we see that it was very much restricted and limited and that the Governor through his executive was altogether independent of the representatives of the people. Under that regime of more or less absolute domination by the central Government we lived until .1840, when Lord Durham in his famous report advised the Imperial Government to bring about a change in the relations existing between the Mother Country and the colonies. The British statesmen of 1840 gave us a new form of government, but it was not responsible government; we were given a constitution which was in very many ways imperfect. Through the efforts of leading Canadian statesmen of that day-men like Baldwin and Lafontaine-we .secured responsible government; we took the last step towards the securing of a Government in this country which was, so to speak, the master of our local affairs and which asserted the right to deal with Canadian problems. United Canada improved its condition in 1867 by co-operating with the 
other provinces in the formation of the Confederation, of which we are all proud.
The British North America Act gives us certain liberties, certain privileges, certain prerogatives. Yet when the President of the Council says that we are an independent nation he may be saying something which is pleasing :to the eaT of every Canadian, but he is saying something which does not fit in exactly with the words of our constitution. The hon. gentleman this afternoon 'made a very clever distinction between what he designated as our legal rights and our constitutional rights. I admire the minister; he is a very clever lawyer, and a lawyer always shows his talents when he is defending a bad case. The hon. gentleman showed this afternoon that he was more than a clever lawyer; the worse the cause the more able he shows himself to be. This distinction between legal right and constitutional right is a distinction which is applicable to England only. The British constitution is not a document; it is not contained in any book. The British constitution is unwritten; it is an assemblage of customs, precedents and' usages. The President of .the Council is perfectly justi-* fled when he says that .there is a distinction .between a legal right and a constitutional right, but F repeat .that that distinction applies only in England, not in Canada; and I will show you why. In Canada our constitution is a written document. We have, so to speak, our charter; we 'have our privileges as a people and as a country.
The British North America Act binds the Government just as it binds every legislature of every province of Canada, just as it binds every citizen of this, country, and there is no cause for making a distinction between a legal right and a constitutional right. We have only the rights which are granted to us by the British North America . Act, and we cannot g<? outside of that Act to find any other privileges, or rights.
When there was a war in Egypt the Imperial authorities made, through the Canadian Government, a demand on the Canadian people for some help in that war. Sir John A. Macdonald was Prime Minister of Canada at that time; he was the leading spirit of the Quebec Conference, which drafted the British North America Act; he was the leading spirit of the National party in Canada; he was the leading spirit of the Tory party in Canada, and^ I do not think that any words uttered by Sir John Macdonald will be disavowed by the supporters of the Government in this House. Sir John

A. Macdonald at that time said that Canada would not take part in any Imperial war unless Canada wanted to, and that not a Canadian soldier should leave our shores without the consent of the Canadian Government as expressed by the representatives of the people. And as a matter of fact in that war in Egypt Canada did not take an official part. Later, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was Prime Minister of this country, a war took place in Africa, and Sir Charles Tupper, who was the leader of the Conservative party at that time, started an agitation throughout Canada asking that Canada should participate in that war. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the then Prime: Minister, said in the House of Commons that Canada would take part in the war, but only of her own free will, and that England had no right to force Canada to send soldiers to Africa; that only the Parliament of Canada had the right to say what should be done in that regard. Moreover, when a law was passed to send soldiers to Africa, if I am not mistaken, a proviso was inserted in the law stating that that should not be a precedent to be'used in the case of future wars of the British Empire.
As regards our trade relations:	Before
the war Canada had negotiated treaties. We had the Franco-Canadian Treaty negotiated by our own representatives; we had the German Treaty, which was denounced by Canada without the Imperial Government taking part in such denunciation. In a word, if I may sum up, the situation as I view it, before the war Canada internationally was bound by whatever the British Empire did as regards foreign policy for Canada is a part of the British Empire, but imperially Canada was absolutely free to do whatever she wanted within the British Empire whenever a war might arise. As regards our trade treaties, we were independent to make treaties wherever and how we wanted, subject always to the powers that were conferred upon our representatives by His Majesty the King of Great Britain.
In 1911, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was the leader of the country at that .time, wanted Canada to take the last step to full nationhood, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) was sent to Washington to negotiate, as the representative of Canada, a trade treaty with the United States. Reciprocity was negotiated through our ministers and our ministers only. Moreover, in that year, Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced into the House of Com-nions his naval policy, a policy that meant that Canada would have a navy under
Canadian control, manned by Canadians, for the defence .of our Canadian coasts. At that time Sir Wilfrid, I think, represented the true spirit of the Canadian people, and Canada wanted to see that her rights as a nation were respected and maintained. The year 1911 brought on a change of Government, and if our status before the war was that which I have just detailed, what was the status of Canada during the war when the present Administration was at the head of our affairs? To-day I listened with great interest to the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) and yesterday to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton), and I was very much surprised to hear Tory members like those who sit in great numbers on the other side cheering the declarations of independence, so far as Canada was concerned, from the Mother Country, when those same Tory members were in 1911 going throughout Canada denouncing Sir Wilfrid Laurier as a traitor because he wanted to have a naval policy that safeguarded our rights as a nation. I am not a "Little Canadian"; I am not a supporter of the old colonial regime; I am not a man who is in favour of accepting the dictates of Downing Street; I am in favour of as great a measure of freedom and liberty for my country as I can obtain. But when I hear the ministers of the present Government tell us that they have secured a new status for my country, I turn my eyes to the past and I say, as the old Latin poet said: "Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes."

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
"I fear the Greeks even whilst bringing gifts." Our liberty, our freedom and our independence would be given to us by a Tory Government. The Prime Minister of this country (Sir Robert Borden), who distinguished himself by his small colonial sentiments in 1911 and in 1913 when he introduced his Bill to give $35,000,000 to the British Empire, would change his mind. I hope he has, but I doubt it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier wanted to safeguard the autonomy of Canada in connection with the naval policy which he introduced in 1911. The Government of today fought that policy, and instead of insisting upon the rights of Canada, as they claim to have insisted recently, they wanted Canada to send to England a bag containing $35,000,000 in gold as the tribute of slaves to their master. Mr. Speaker, I will support the President olf 'the Privy Council and the Minister oi Public Works when they vindicate the

liberty of my country, but I will always ' 'ask from this Government more evidence of good faith than I would ask from any other body because their past record is a very poor evidence of their sincerity.
I do not wish to enter into a discussion as to whether Canada was represented at Versailles as an entity distinct and separate from the British Empire, but I should like to ask the President of the Privy Council this question, and I hope lie will answer it: If Canada bad distinct representation at Versailles, will the King give a distinct ratification for Canada, or will there be only one ratification for the whole British Empire? Moreover, if the representation of Canada at Versailles is different and distinct from that of the British Empire, were our Canadian delegates appointed by the Canadian or the Imperial Government?

speechtext: They were -appointed by the Canadian Government.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
That answer covers only half the truth, and I will prove it. An Order in Council was passed by the Canadian Government recommending that our Canadian delegates be appointed, but that Order in Council h-ad to be sent to the Prime Minister of Great Britain, and it was the Prime Minister of Great Britain who eaw that I-h-e appointments were made. Our delegates were the appointees not of our Canadian Government, not of the Imperial Government, but of the Rt. Hon. David Lloyd Geo-rge.
I am not one of those who say -that Canada should not have been represented at Versailles. I was proud to -see our country represented, and I hope that never again will war be declared or peace b-e made without Canada being consulted. The only criticism which I offer o-f the presence of our delegates -at Versailles -is this: -that if they oocupie-d -seats there, those seats were not big -enough for the country they represented. We should have been in the front row, and our country should -appear in the Peace Treaty, in the same manner as other countries. We should not have been there as a subsection but as a whole' chapter.
The President of the Privy Council told us this -afternoon that Canada was a member of the League of Nations, a member altogether separate from the British Empire.
I hope he is right.

speechtext: If I understood the minister aright, he said that the British Empire was a member of the League of Nations, and that Canada was also a member of that league. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Canada is a member of the League of Nations, but Canada is a part of the British Empire.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I admit that, and I do not think the minister will deny it. Let me ask my hon. friend this question: If Canada is a member of the League of Nations as an entity, and the British Empire is also a member of the League, where will the Canadian delegate sit when h-e represents Canada as a separate entity, and where will he sit when representing Canada as part of the British Empire? I would also draw the minister's attention to the statement made before Congress by President Wilson of the United States. The minister told us this afternoon that he. would not like to interfere in the disputes of American politiciaiis. That is very proper. But we are not talking of disputes of politicians, we are talking about the interpretation given to the Covenant of the League of Nations by the author of that Covenant. My hon. friend from Kamour-aska (Mr. Lapointe) quoted this afternoon from President Wilson's address before Congress (Congressional Record, p. 4285) where the president declared that whenever a question should arise in which the British Empire was interested Canada would not have a vote. That is the interpretation given by the man who drafted the Covenant of the League of Nations, and although I have -a great admiration for the President of the Privy Council I am very much afraid his interpretation would not stand against that of President Wilson.
The President of the Privy Council went further. He said that whenever the inter- . ests of Canada were at stake, Canada would have a place on the Council of tire League of Nations, that the Council could not take any decision without the unanimous consent of all the members of the Council, and he drew the inference that Canada would therefore not be obliged to do anything imposed on her by the Chuncil unless she had consented to it. I disagree altogether, and I would refer my hon. friend to Article 15 of the Covenant of the League of Nations which -says that -the decision of -the Council has to b-e unanimous, but that tha-t unanimity shall -not include -the votes of ith-e interested parties. It says:
If a report by the Council is unanimously agreed ito by the members thereof other than

the representatives of one or more of the parties to the dispute-
I would ask the President of the Privy Council to reconcile his statement of this afternoon with the express wording of Article' 15,
