speechtext:
I do not think we shall make any real gain by attempting to interpret this Treaty by this dialogue. The two things are entirely distinct; they relate to wholly different matters. The clause my hon. friend is dealing with deals with a dispute between two nations referred to the Council for investigation, and subsequently possibly for decision. That is not the case I was dealing with. I was dealing with a case under the other clause where the League may recommend to a nation that it should take certain action against another nation. If the league is going to recommend to a nation that it should take certain action against another
9 p.m. nation which is violating the Covenant of the League, then quite clearly under the clause I mentioned that other nation is entitled to be present and take part in the discussion as to what ii should do to carry out the? Covenant.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Clause XV covers the
case. It says:
If there should arise between the members of the League any dispute likely to lead to a rupture-they will submit the matter to Council.
Then it goes on to say:
If the Council fails to reach a report which is unanimously agreed to by the members thereof, other than the Representatives of one or more of the parties to the dispute, the Members of the League reserve to themselves the right to take such action'as they shall consider necessary for the maintenance of right and justice.
I hope the Government are right , when they declare, when they assert, that \ve have attained to nationhood. But, on the other hand, I doubt their declaration on account of their past behaviour and of present happenings. President Wilson refused to acknowledge our international status. When he was asked in Congress what would happen to Canada if trouble should arise between England and the United States, President Wilson said that there would be no trouble with Canada because Canada had no diplomatic relations with the United States and therefore Canada had no international status. How can we be a nation in the true sense of the word if we have no international status? Mr. Speaker, we are a nation! The Prime Minister of this country declared to the House on Tuesday last that we were a nation and he was proud to say it and I was proud to listen to him saying it. But, on the other hand if the members of the House consult Hansard they will see that the Premier told us that to obtain a French copy of the Treaty he had to do it through- Lord Milner, Colonial Secretary in the British Government, and that we, a nation, who had to sign this treaty, that we, a nation that had the right to all the privileges of such a status, could only obtain one . copy although we had asked for 500! If we were a nation and we wanted copies of the Treaty, we should not ask Lord Milner, who is evidently very badly disposed, but we ought to do it directly and write or cable to Paris.
* The Prime Minister in his speech announces that very soon there is to be a meeting in London, and at that meeting the future relations of the self-governing dominions with the Mother Country will be regulated. If the Government is sincere, and if the Prime Minister actually secures our new status at that meeting in London I pledge myself to support him, but be will have to stand by the position which he took in 1918, with all its consequences, and he will have to insist, first of all, that the title of King of England be changed and that in future the King be no more known as the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the Overseas Dominions, but as His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom and Ireland, and also His Majesty -the King of Canada. How can the King act for Canada distinctly from the rest of the British Empire,, as the President of the Privy Council contended this afternoon, unless he has the title of King of Canada and acts as such?
If we are really a nation, if we have attained that status of independence which many people in this country desire, we shall also have to change our constitution in such a way that no more shall we be bound to go to war simply by the fact that England has declared war. If the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) speaks in this debate -I admire his talent and I have great respect for his experience-I will ask him if he can seriously contend that Canada is an independent nation, as his colleague said this afternoon, when Canada has not .a word to say when war is declared and has not a word to say as to the conditions of peace? We will have to be consulted before war is entered upon and we will have to be consulted before peace is signed.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: You are afraid to be right,

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I am afraid of being right. Up to the year 1919 not a soldier could leave Canadian soil without the consent of the Canadian Government as expressed by the representatives of the Canadian people meeting in Parliament. For instance, when Great Britain declared war on Germany if the Canadian people had said in Parliament: " We will not send one soldier to

the war," Great Britain could not have forced us to send any. Canada went to war not because the Dominion was only a part of the British Empire but because this country wanted to take part in the conflict in favour of the true democratic principles that ought to Tule the world. But if this Treaty is approved, if Canada becomes a member of the League of Nations, our last particle of freedom and liberty will disappear; and when England as a member of the League of Nations, or rather the British Empire as a member of the League of Nations, starts a war, for instance, with Turkey, the Council of the League will turn to Canada and tell this country: "You have got to take part in this war, not because you are a part of the British. Empire, but because your representatives in Parliament in the year 1919, when they met for a short session of thirty-one days, gave away the liberties that you had secured after years and years of fighting and of combat." That is the situation as I understand it.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I reaffirm again my high admiration for the theories enunciated by the members of this Government. I hope they are right but I am afraid they are wrong; and I say that if we have signed this Treaty, if we become members of the League of Nations, we should do so under the reservation of all our rights as existing to-day and with our complete and full autonomy. As far as I am concerned I will accept this Treaty and the membership of this League only subject to these reservations.
We have been told by the President of the Privy Council that a new era is dawning upon the world. His eloquence has shown us skies lighted up by the rising sun of eternal and permanent peace. The sight and the view is beautiful, I enjoy the spectacle, and I hope it will continue. But if we want to have peace in the rest of the world let us first have peace in our own country. I therefore advise the President of the Privy Council-if he wishes to gild this league and to have linings more beautiful even than those his imagination has described to us to-day-to tell the papers of this country, over which he has a certain influence I understand, to educate the population and the citizens of Canada to' their new duty as a nation; if we are a nation.
As the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) said, the sooner we understand Our responsibilities bf citizenship the sooner we shall have a great, a noble and a united country. We from the province
of Quebec, who during this period which has just closed have suffered direly the insults which were hurled at us under varying circumstances, were pleased a few days ago to see the son of His Majesty, our King, come to our old city of Quebec, where the future of America was decided on the Plains of Abraham in 1759, and there tender to the loyal French Canadian population the royal hand-the hand which has shown to the world that even in warfare the descendants of the Kings of England are always worthy of their forefathers. When the hand of the Prince of Wales was thus extended to the French Canadians I hope, Mr. Speaker, that our compatriots of the English provinces saw the extension of that hand as a sign that social and civil warfare in Canada has come to an end. If we are good enough to be so treated by the heir of the Imperial throne of England I think the loyal population of Ontario can join with us in building our country so that she .may be as big in the future as she ought to be; and it is only on the basis of a true Canadian spirit of equal justice to all that our country will enter this new era announced to us by the Government with internal peace and with external independence and respect.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the patriotic sentiments of the hon. member from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). When I saw him chasing the Minister of Justice in regard to Ireland I could not help but come to the conclusion that the Minister of Justice is possessed of many of the graces that the angels are supposed to have and is more than circumspect as to what places he suddenly rushes into.
I am going to speak only for a short time and I shall devote myself to certain questions that I think arise out of this debate. But, in the first place, I wish to ' say that I am here to vote for the resolution before the House, because I think the Treaty is a good Treaty and we ought to ratify it in the interests of the world at large. In fact, this Treaty is the greatest document that humanity has had up to the present. For one thing, it substitutes arbitration, conciliation and discussion in the open for the intrigue of diplomacy, whether openly avowed or concealed. I believe that its intrigue, deceit and licentiousness have made diplomacy the prostitute that has wrecked the history of the last thousand years, and I am glad to see that secret diplomacy has to come to an end. Great results are bound to come from the new diplomacy-the dis-

cussion and trial of public questions in open court and their settlement by arbitration. But now that we have a League of Nations it will not be arbitration that will rule the world, I hope, but rather public opinion, and certainly public opinion has the right *to rule the world. It seems to me that hereafter public opinion, as expressed by the people in journals and in discussion, and the publicity thus given to the facts, will afford more than anything else security for the welfare of humanity. .Therefore, it is a matter of satisfaction to me that this League of Nations is to be created and that I have the honour and the opportunity as a humble member of this House to vote in favour of the ratification of the Treaty and of all that goes with it in the subsequent legislation that is to be passed to make good that Treaty and the League of Nations.
I also appreciate everything that has been said by the Prime Minister and his colleagues who attended the Conference in regard to the good result that is likely to accrue from the provisions which deal with the problems of labour. That is something that everybody can approve of, and the working people all the w'orld over-and we are all workingmen in this country-will be glad to see that the problems of labour have been placed on an improved basis, and I feel sure that it will be bettor for the world to have some kind of internationalism in regard to these problems. For that reason also I shall give my vote in favour of the proposal, now before the House.
I would not have had much further to say had not the question of the future of Canada and its so-called new status been projected into the discussion, and for a few minutes I wish to refer to this alleged change in the status of Canada which has taken place or is about to take place, and also to the suggestion that Canada Iras in some way become a new nation and that we have entered into a League of Nations within the British Empire. I want to try to clear up this question and to give my views in regard to it-views that may be worthy of consideration not only in this House but outside. This question has been allowed to remain in the background for some time, other matters having been given preference to it, but it is before us now and must be disposed of.
We have been told-and the hon. member (Mr. Cannon), who has just taken his seat, has partly made my speech for me-we have been told that we are now a nation,' and Sir Wilfrid Laurier told us years ago that we had became a nation.

Now, I am a Canadian; this is my country; I have no other country but Canada. For many years as I have sat in this House I have thought time and again of our political status, 'although I have not said much about it. I shall be convinced that wTe are a nation only when I know that we have the sovereignty that goes with a nation. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Cannon) that as long 'as Canada has not the right to make her own constitution-and we have not that right-we are not a nation, and we have not sovereignty. We have not sovereign rights in regard to treaties and in regard to war. We cannot make war; we 'cannot make peace. We cannot send ambassadors to other countries; we cannot receive ambassadors here. We have not sovereignty even in the matter of shipping. We have not sovereignty in the matter of copyright. As the member for Dorchester said, our courts are not the supreme 'and final interpreters of our own law. So that when hon. gentlemen say that we are a nation, I tell them that we shall be a nation only when we shall have assumed full sovereignty; only when we have the rights which are at present denied to us.
We are boasting, of our being a nation within the galaxy of the Britannic nations. But I want to recall to this House the fact that independent of anything we may think or anything we may do the Parliament of Great Britain can to-morrow change the Royal succession as it exists in the present Royal family of England; they can set up another form of government, a democracy or a republic, without consulting us in any respect. So that when we make these professions about our having nationhood and things of that kind, we must remember that we have not nationality, in that what we have can be taken away from us tomorrow by an Act of the Parliament of Great Britain. It may be taken away in a night in connection with a revolution-and this age is an age of revolutions. In the presence of these considerations, therefore, we have to give attention to the subject of our relations with the Empire, to this question of nationality; and in some way we have to try to clear the matter up.
I do not mean to advocate any particular thing in connection with Canada's position,
' as to her sovereignty, as to her nationhood, as to her relations with the Empire. But we have been told in this House that a great constitutional conference is to he called at a very early day to settle the question of the relations which should exist between the various nations within the Empire. I

say that we must first lay down the principle that nothing be undertaken in the way of a constitutional conference without our asserting our absolute right to know how such a conference is to be conducted and without our retaining the right to pass absolutely upon the transactions and conclusions of that conference. Not- for one moment do I wish that we shall be led into something. I happen to be of, the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, when he was in this House, and I have been guided more or less by some of the principles which he laid down. If there was anything that Sir John A. Macdonald was jealous of, it was the maintaining of Canada's right and Canada's autonomy. What the President of the Council quoted here to-day from Sir John A. Macdonald concerning Canada's right to determine her own fiscal policy is my doctrine, as it was his; and I apply it not only to fiscal policy but to everything else, and especially to any great constitutional changes that have to be made.
So I lay it down here that before any more missions are undertaken to London and before there are any more conferences in regard to the constitution and the political future of this country, not only must the lines, to be followed at such a conference, be laid before the people, but nothing must be finally done at any such conference without our. representatives first laying the matter before the Canadian people for their consideration. It will not do for the delegates whom we send to' Great Britain to deal w'ith these matters to come back and say: We have been in conference; we recommend this thing, and if what we recommend is not adopted, we will resign our places in the Government. The air should be cleared with regard to these things; hereafter Canada should be fully considered in connection with these matters.	[DOT]
During the last few years I have been more than worried about these things. I could not speak out when the war was on, but I did not like all these missions to England. I did not like the commitments that were being made. I did not like it when even the heads of the Government here saw fit to go to England and take part in these conferences, the only reason given being that Mr. Lloyd George was very anxious to have representatives of Canada go over there and sit with him. What he ought to be anxious and concerned about is first of all to state why he wants representatives of the Government of Canada to be there. Of course, it may be difficult to do that in time of war, but from this time on, having regard to the official announcement that a great council of the Britannic nations who are supposed to be independent is to be called, everything must be done in the open and done after full discussion. The result of all these transactions and deliberations must be laid before the people of Canada and Canada should not be committed until the people have had the fullest opportunity of discussing them. When I say that, I am standing on the platform of Sir John A. Macdonald and also on the platform of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; and I think I have good reason for taking this position.
If these great changes that, are suggested are to take place, we must also have regard for present conditions as they exist in this country, and for the British North America Act and the federation of Canada which it created. We know out of what questions and discussions the British North America Act aro$e and what problems it, in a measure, endeavoured to solve. If our delegates go to England in the near future to discuss these questions, they must review and acquaint themselves with the questions that were, considered when Confederation was created, and the first people they will have to have regard to are the people of Quebec who entered into that compact and agreement out .of which the Confederation of Canada arose. Furthermore, if we are going into this question of the future of Canada, not only must we pay some regard to the views of Ontario and Quebec and the Maritime Provinces at that iirtie, but in the light of to-day. In going into this great question of recasting the whole organization of the British Empire and especially of Canada, we must pay regard to some of the new divisions in which the people of Canada are constituted. First and foremost, before we enter into or commit ourselves to a great, new departure of this kind, we must consult the people of western Canada, the farming community of Canada and the labour interest of Canada. In fact, every portion of our country must have ample opportunity of discussing these questions in the light of its interests and its views. And so, while I say I am in favour of the ratification of the Treaty and will gladly vote for it, and while I am prepared to discuss these questions of the future of the country-and they may be coming up almost immediately and the Prime Minister may be leaving for England by almost the next boat after this House is closed-I want to

put myself on record here and now on behalf of myself and my fellow countrymen against any attempt to rush this question just now to any immediate settlement. I want the fullest discussion; I want all the facts brought back, and I want the people themselves, whose destinies may be changed by this new proposal, to have an opportunity of discussing it.
Not only do we go into this new discussion as a member of the British Empire, but more and more, when we come to settle the future of Canada, must we have regard to the fact that we are a great power or country or state, it may be, on this North' American continent, and we must have even more regard for this continent than for our European connections and alliances. America to-day is the home and centre of democracy, and when I speak of democracy, I speak of that democracy which was created by Oliver Cromwell, which subsequently was advanced by George Washington and which has been upheld in a marvellous way by Abraham Lincoln and by some of our own statesmen and public men here in Canada. We have given a new meaning to democracy, and it is the democracy of America, as1 exemplified by the United States and Canada, that is the saving grace of the world today. We must have regard, therefore, to the fact that we are on this North American continent, and that Canada is the intercontinent which looks across the Atlantic to Europe and all its problems and which also looks across the Pacific to Asia and all its problems; "and when .we come to make the great decision that we must make-.but, I hope, not make too soon or too rashly-we must have regard for all these things, for all our previous commitments, and must keep all our pledges and promises of the past, and most of all, keep ourselves straight and in line in the ser-ice of democracy.

Does my hon. friend mean that we should have more regard for our relations, say with the United States, than for our relations with the (Mother Country?

I did not say quite that. But I said, when we are considering all these questions of our relations with Europe and our relations .with all other countries, we must recognize what

the Prime Minister said here the other day-and he was not the first to say it- that Canada, in going to the battlefields of Europe, led the democracy of America in that great work, and the United States had to follow us.
Mr. EDWAF.DiS: What did my hon. friend mean when he said that we must have greater regard for our relations with the countries on this continent than for our relations with our Allies?

speechtext: I am not going to be cross-questioned on this matter; I am going to state my views, and I will take the responsibility of my views. What I wish to say is that when we are told that new problems are to be brought before us and that great changes are to take place and that great conferences are to be had, we must have regard for all these things and we must recognize .that we are on this continent-and it is a great fact that we are on it. When I say that I have not a word of criticism to pass on the old land which was the home of my fathers, or of Britain which is the mother of all parliamentary institutions and largely of the liberties of the world. But we must consider and have regard for everything and we must take the right time to consider these questions, and I come now probably to my last argument and to the last statement I wish to make..	*

I object to the word

speechtext:
Then we shall leave the word "mpre" to the dictionary. I am still here.
I want now to come to what I regard also as a matter of the greatest importance, and that is this: While we have been led into this discussion of the new status of Canada and the greater status that she is about to assume, I do not think that the discussion of these questions or the bringing on of a gre at constitutional conference in Europe is the thing to which we at this time ought to give our greatest attention. Now that the war is over, these questions may very well be left to the future, and I do not think this great constitutional conference, soon to be held in England, is the pressing question. The pressing question in Canada to-day is the reconstruction of Canada and

the re-establishment of the men who took part in the vfar, and we can well afford to let stand for a time these questions of the future and these constitutional questions, and I am not discussing them nor proposing them.
I would much prefer to see the time of this House taken up with the discussion of reconstruction in this country. The most, pressing question in Canada to-day is the high cost of living, and it must be dealt with. The next most pressing question, and it is rampant in Toronto to-night and all day yesterday, is the civil re-establishment of our soldiers. Great, questions have also arisen out of the war in regard to our policies on banking and commerce. Many great questions also arise in connection with the the tariff and how this country is going to raise a revenue sufficient to meet its obligations. To my mind these are the pressing questions of the day that must be settled by Parliament, and ought to be settled now. The war has been brought to a successful conclusion, the League of Nations is under way, and when the Treaty has been ratified I am quite willing to let these agreements work out as best they can for the benefit of humanity. With all respect to the various opinions in this House, to my mind Canada can better afford to give most of its time and energy now to the pressing questions I have mentioned. What we want to do is to restore Canada to her ability to produce. More production is what we want, to pull us out of our trouble and danger. While I appreciate what has been done for labour, and the	improved	status it- has
achieved, to my mind there, is just one thing for every Canadian, whether he is a member of this House or not and that is to do all that in him lies to increase our .production so that we can have enough goods of various kinds to export, to give us a trade balance in our favour as against other nations at an early date. Let us reestablish our soldiers'in civil life, and give our attention 'to the other pressing problems of the day, and do whatever we are called upon to do in connection with the League of Nations. And when I have said that, I have said all I have to say to the House to-night. I apologize for taking up the time of the House, but I could not listen in silence to this discussion, and most of all read what has been said by the newspapers and on the platform, in view of the amount of unrest there is not only here but .all over the world. The main 10
thing now is for us not to discuss politics so much as to discuss economics and to give our main attention to the problems that are knocking at our door for attention.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OP THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late
hour, at this stage of the discussion, I shall not trespass upon the patience of the House, as I do not rise to participate at any length in the debate that is now in progress. May. I preface my remarks by reminding the House that owing to the paramount importance of the Treaty of Peace now under consideration, I should deem myself to be recreant to my duty, did I not make a few remarks in our beautiful French language which was on a footing of equality with the English language at the Conference of Versailles, the outcome of which is the Treaty now under discussion.
Mr. Speaker, 1914 and 1919 will remain two outstanding landmarks in the world's history, ranking among the epoch-making events in the annals of the nations.
We had the wars of the Empire, under Napoleon, culminating in his defeat on the Waterloo battlefield and later on, we witnessed with tearful eyes and broken-hearts the frightful catastrophe, the war of 187071, to which the Treaty of Paris put an end, and we are just emerging from that epochal conflict which happily had its triumphant conclusion in the Treaty of Peace at Versailles.
History, the avenger of all wrongs, has recorded the two wars just mentioned, and the pen of the historian is about to describe the one in which we have been engaged, the greatest war ever yet waged, and the supreme effort put forth in the cause of freedom, justice and for the vindication of the rights of humanity.
In 1914 Germany let loose on the world that war, thinking that she could easily win jt, and as for forty years she had been organized as a military machine, who could resist her militarist spirit, her lust .of world conquest? Who could withstand her numberless battalions, ,so well disciplined, and well nigh invincible?
But she had reckoned without heroic Belgium, which was going to throw her whole energy into the world struggle, and almost exhaust her national forces; she had counted without France, which was to be bled almost to death, and suffer untold agonies; she had reckoned without Italy, whose sole wish ivas to continue living in peace; she had counted without Great Britain and its colonies, *which could not



allow the weak to be crushed beneath the heel of the enemy: she had reckoned without the United States, which was going to be swept into the war 'by the vision of all those useless hecatombs of men, women and children, and of a future pregnant with dangers to its own security.
And during four years, humanity stood aghast at the gruesome spectacle of armies such as had never been embattled rushing against each other, of millions of human lives being sacrificed to the god of a merciless war, while the gaunt spectre of starvation was stalking through the land, amidst scenes of slaughter,, spoliation, ruin, shameless holocausts of irreparable treasures lit up by blind barbarian vengeance.
But on the day appointed by Providence, Foch and his valiant armies smashed the Austro-German effort and sounded in clarion notes before an expectant world those memorable words: "Liberty is no longer imperilled; Right and Justice shall not disappear from the earth."
And we had the Treaty of Versailles.
After the effort put forth by Canada in sending to the battle front over five hundred thousand men, in shouldering a debt of over a billion dollars, and at the cost of over sixty thousand of soldiers who had laid down their lives for the defence of the Empire, could Canada look with indifference as a detached spectator, at the conclusion of a Treaty imparting to a wondering world the good tidings which, on Christmas Night, the angels brought to the shepherds in Judea: "On earth i>eace, good will toward men."
Mr. Speaker, rejoicipgs were general, and it was but natural that Canada should as much as, if not more than, any other country, thrill with pleasure' upon hearing that the terrible scourge of war had passed away and that an era of peace, justice, and benevolence was being ushered in for the whole human race.
This Treaty we have now before us, and are invited to ratify it, but here, among several other questions involved, there is a very important one that I wish briefly to touch upon. Heretofore, Canada had been free to take part or abstain from participating in foreign wars, even those wars which could affect the British Empire; yet it had never occurred to any one that there was any danger of our country keeping aloof and looking with indifference upon the fate of arms when Great Britain was being involved in a great world struggle on the issue of which the honour of the Crown and the destiny of its subjects were staked.
[Mr. Gauvre.au. 1
From time immemorial, down to the enactment of that too-famous* Conscription Act which will stamp with indelible disgrace the men who framed it, the more so as one recalls to mind the sordid antipatriotic and almost inhuman grounds acted upon by its promoters in bringing forth and enforcing this measure, I may say that Canada had volunteered her help to Great Britain in her wars. Witness the part taken by Canada in the Nile Expedition, and in old Boer War days in South Africa. And when Germany invaded Belgium, and Great Britain drew the sword in defence of the weak and to save Liberty threatened by the Teutonic hordes, 'Canada without haggling, raised an army of 400,000 men who flocked to the colours and voluntarily went over the top facing death, to help the Allies in this new crusade against modern barbarians.
Why should not this state of things continue? Why erase with one stroke of the pen all that our past history made up of constitutional liberty, and throw us gratuitously, for the sake of the League of Nations, into the vortex of militarism, without reference to our feelings, in order that' Parliament may vote a ratification which will bind us for ever?
But the hand of rampant Imperalism was going once more, after so many fruitless efforts, to drag along the Dominions and to involve them into the wars of the Empire which Canada could with good reason deem unjust and hurtful to her best interests.
Under the cover of the rejoicings and festivities which marked the cessation of hostilities our Imperialists in London and even in Canada availed themselves of the opportunity to hitch us up to the Imperialistic car, and under pretence of claiming that our participation in the war had entitled us to a place under the sun, among the nations, and while inviting us to attend the Conference at Versailles and to sign the Treaty of Peace, they succeeded in masking their thoughts and disguising their projects, and now, by bidding us to ratify the Treaty, and affirming the principle laid down in clause X, they want to bind us forever to the fortunes of that Empire which we have always been ready to defend, without being obligated by a clause of the Treaty, devised for such a purpose.	i
In forecasting the future, I do not wish to act the part of a prophet of evil. Desirable as it may be, I see in that League of Nations a source of trouble, of entangle-

merits and international dangers the more to be apprehended because there are in Europe so many sore and bleeding wounds not yet healed up.	'
To my mind there is in Clause X a preconceived idea. I see behind it an almost machiavelian hand striving to smotheT every feeling of patriotism, spontaneously manifesting itself through material;, help ' proffered in times of stress and struggle such as our Mother Country is liable to go through.
I am quite aware that the Treaty, as soon as it is signed by His Majesty the King, obligates the whole Empire, a part of which we are proud1 to be, but let me tell you, Sir, that Canada would have been better impressed and even more grateful had we been ignored in the ratification of the Treaty, and left free and untrammelled as formerly, voluntarily to clasp hands with the Empire across the seas whenever an opportunity offered.
Our constitution is all of a sudden changed by that Treaty, and from a free country we are being enslaved by a clause which could unexpectedly involve us in unjust or arbitrary conflicts, in wars of spoliation, because history which has recorded those scraps of paper could very well repeat itself, even in quarters' from which it would be the least expected.
I have here a clipping from a remarkable editorial, which offers food for thought, and that appeared in the columns of the Citizen of September 8, under the heading "Canada's National Status." And in order to render full justice to the author of this editorial, let me read it in extenso:
In the circumstances it is folly to talk of Premier 'Borden " wresting a new national status for Canada from the peace conference." What the present peace treaty represents is not a new national status but a surrender of Canadian rights. Hithertofore we have gone to war, when we have done so, voluntarily. Henceforth we shall he compelled to go to war, if we accept the treaty as it stands.
If Canada has attained a new national status, now is the time to demonstrate it. We can do so by objecting to a section of the treaty that takes out of our hands the most important decision in national life-the making of war or peace. To assert that we have gained in nationhood by surrendering this right is surely absurd. As the matter stands now, the United Kingdom enters into an agreement with a great group of other nations to involve Canada and the rest of her overseas dominions with her in war, should occasion arise, and this without any reference to us. If we sign the treaty as it stands, -with Article X. in full force, we bind ourselves to go to war as soon as Britain does, whether we like it or not. And should Italy attack France, for example, we should be involved at once through Britain's obligations, and
>104
compelled to send troops overseas to support France.
The Canadian Parliament is called upon for a most momentous decision. The facts are clearly before it, in the language of the contentious clause and in the ratification of the treaty by Britain without reference to Canada's action. Only by a reservation in the matter of Article X. can Canada's present rights be maintained. If parliament endorses the treaty as it stands we are committed to participation in future European wars without reference to our own feelings in the matter or our ability to live up to our obligations, financial and otherwise.
(Translation) Therefore, I say that once it has ratified this Treaty Canada will cease to be a nation following her own path toward a wonderful destiny. This country will feel as though it were condemned to chain and bail, and for us of the province of Quebec I believe we shall no more he able, as our ancestors used to sing, to say with Sir George Etienne Cartier, whose centenary we were celebrating a few days ago:
Originaire de la France Aujourd'hui sujet d'Albion,
A qui donner la preference De l'une ou l'autre nation?
Mais n'avons-nous pas je vous prie
* Encore de plus puissants liens?
A tous prffdrons la patrie:
Avant tout soyons Canadiens.
I am, ready to vote in favour of any amendment tending to assert our determination to be consulted before being led to participate in future wars in which Canada would not be directly or indirectly concerned.
Hon. Mr. DOHERTY moved the adjournment of the House.

On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) asked if the Government would bring down forthwith copies of the correspondence which may have taken place between the Imperial and Canadian Governments on two branches of the subject now before the House; first, in regard to the representation of Canada at the Peace Conference; second, as to the steps that might be deemed necessary for the ratification or approval of the Treaty. In reference to the first, the Government has no objection to bringing down the correspondence, but it is necessary to secure the agreement of the British Ministry to this course, and we are communicating with them in reference to the matter. I may say, however, for the information of the House, that certain cable communications passed between the Government here and the Prime Minister, after he arrived in England, in reference to Canadian representation, the substance of which was communicated by him to the Imperial Government, and as that consists of our own cables there is no objection to their being brought down. As they are not
IMr. Speaker.]
lengthy, and for the information of the members, I will read the cablegrams. The first is from the Acting Prime Minister, to Sir Robert Borden, and is dated 4th December, 1918:
Council to-day further considered Canadian representation at Peace Conference and is even more strongly of opinion than when you left, that Canada should be represented. Council is of opinion that in view of war efforts of Dominion other nations entitled to representation at Conference should recognize unique character of British Commonwealth composed of group of free nations under one sovereign and that provision should be made for special representation of these nations at Conference, even though it may he necessary that in any final decisions reached they should speak with one voice; that if this is not possible then you should form one of whatever delegation represents British Commonwealth. It surely is not contemplated that each nation at war should have exactly same numerical representation as Great Britain and Prance. Should not representation be to some extent commensurate with war efforts? Would you like Order in Council passed or any other official action taken declaring attitude of Government on question of Canadian representation at Conference? If so, please cable.	'
This was followed by a cable from Sir Robert Borden to the Acting Prime Minister, dated January 2, 1919.
In Cabinet to-day I took up question of re-, presentation of the Dominions and spoke very frankly and firmly as to-Canada's attitude. My proposal which I consider the most satisfactory solution that is practicable and which was accepted by the Cabinet is as follows:-
First, Canada and the other Dominions shall each have the same representation as Belgium and other small allied nations at the Peace Conference.
Second, as it is proposed to admit representatives of Belgium and other small allied nations only when their special interests are under consideration, I urged that some of the representatives of British Empire should be drawn from a panel on which each Dominion Prime Minister shall have a place.
I pointed out that Canada has no special interest such as South Africa. Australia and New Zealand, in respect of additional territory and that the basis of representation accorded to small allied nations would, therefore, be unsatisfactory from Canadian point of view. I emphasized the insistence of Canada on this recognition and I urged that the British Empire has the right to define the constitutional relations between the nations which compose it and their consequent right to distinctive representation. It is anticipated that British Empire will have five representatives entitled to be present at all meetings of Conference. I expressed my strong opinion that it would be most unfortunate if these were all selected from the British. Islands. Probably three will be named and two others selected from the panel for each meeting. The panel will comprise both British and Dominion Ministers. No public announcement can be made until these proposals have been communicated to Allied Governments and accepted. I shall be glad to have' views of Council. My proposal really gives to Dominions fuller representation than that accorded to small allied nations such as Belgium.

To that communication the Government replied as follows:
Council has considered B115- that is the cable of the Prime Minister which I have just read-
-and sees no reason to change view expressed in P35-
that is the cable of the 4th December, 1918, wihich I read.
If Peace Conference in its .composition is to express spirit of democracy f&r which we have been fighting, as Council thinks it should, small allied nations like Belgium which have fought with us throughout war should be entitled to representation throughout whole Conference, even if limited to one member, and if this were agreed proposal that Canada should have same representation as Belgium, and other small allied nations, would be satisfactory, but not otherwise. Canada has had as many casualties as the United States and probably more actual deaths. Canadian people would not appreciate five American delegates throughout the whole Conference and no Canadian entitled to sit [DOT] throughout Conference, nor would they appreciate several representatives from Great Britain and Canada none. There will he great disappointment here if you are not full member of Conference. We fully appreciate that you are doing everything in your power to secure suitable representation for Canada.
There is a cablegram dated January 16, 1919, from the Acting Prime Minister to the Prime Minister:
Announcement as to Canadian representation at Peace Conference most favourably received. Hearty congratulations on' success of your efforts in this regard.
There is one other document which has some bearing on the matter. The first plenary session of the powers being assembled, the Peace Conference adopted a scheme of organization and the rules under which its business should be conducted.
The rules of the Conference are to be found in the second Annex to what is known as Protocol No. 1 of the Preliminary Peace Conference, that is, the formal record of the proceedings of the first Plenary Session. The question of status is dealt with in the first rule set out in this Annex, which reads as follows:

As however fhe Government is anxious to give the House the fullest possible information, I will lay upon the Table a memorandum prepared on behalf of the Prime Ministers' of the Dominions and sent by Sir Robert Borden to the British Empire delegation and to the Prime Minister of Great Britain in reference to the position of the Dominions in connection with the signing of the Peace Treaty. Air. Speaker, at the request of the Prime Minister I would like to make another statement. This has reference to the transfer of Canadian owned ships to Canadian registry.
For a considerable time the Canadian Government have had under consideration the question of securing the transfer to

Canadian registry of Canadian owned ships at present on the United Kingdom registry. Many Canadian owners wish to make this transfer, but in view of the pressing need for tonnage the Minister of Shipping has heretofore refused to sanction, such a course. As a result, however, of representations recently made by the Canadian Government, the Government of the United Kingdom have consented to alter their policy in this respect, and they have agreed to the announcement of the change in the following terms set forth in a telegram from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, dated August 16:
" Subject to adequate safeguards of the maintenance of our present rights in regard to the carriage of government cargo by liners, it is proposed that all ships that were Canadian owned before the war, and any ships transferred to Canadian owners during the war, are now to be transferred to Canadian registry if their owners desire it."
A subsequent telegram from the Colonial . Secretary, dated August 19, explains that the above proposal concerning transfer >to Canadian registry is not intended to apply to cases where there has been a special stipulation to the contrary.
This refers to cases of the sale of British owners to Canadian purchasers of ships of British registry. Owing to the great demand it w'as found necessary to retain rigid control of British ships and no British owners were permitted to transfer their ships without definite stipulation that such a transfer should not carry with it any rights other than those of the seller. The purchaser, therefore, in that case would receive the ship subject to the Government right of requisition, and of preventing transfer to another registry.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the following proposed motion of Sir Robert Borden, adjourned from September 9:

That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany (and the Protocol annexed thereto), which was signed at Versailles on the twenty-eighth day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen, a copy of which has been laid before Parliament, and which was signed on behalf of -His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiaries therein named, and that this (House do approve of the same.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I meed hardly 'tell tJhe House that it is not my intention to follow the lines along Which this -dehate has 'proceeded and to d-eail with the constitutional -aspect of this question. It is my intention to discuss wha-t the document we -are considering really i-s as laid upon the table of this House-the Treaty of Peace between Germany on the one -hand and the Allied and Associated Powers on the other.
This Treaty, Mr. Speaker, brings to an end ith-e greatest tragedy that -the world has ever known

a tragedy which on the western front alone involved no fewer than
27,000,000 casualties, 7,000,000 of which are now 'sleeping beneath the sacred soils of France and Belgium; a tragedy which put upon the Allies alone a debt of $150,000,000,000; a tragedy which has dethroned kings, wrecked governments, destroyed our economic system and brought the world to the verge of bankruptcy. That is the condition of things that this Treaty is supposed to end.
Canada has made great sacrifices in this war and this Parliament has 'the right to discuss the terms of the Treaty. This Parliament has a right to know whether the liberties Which- were so well won on the battlefields otf the world have been preserved -by our representatives at the Peace Conference at Versailles. It is to that aspect of the question that I wish to direct the 'attention of the -House for a few moments.	.	*
But before discussing the 'terms of peace, we might well look at the causes of war and see how the terms of this Treaty will apply to what in the past have been the great incentives of military effort. With my limited knowledge of history it appears to me that one of the causes of war in the past has been the military ambition of monarch's or nations. Another cause has been the lust for territory on 'the part of nations, for the purpose of [DOT]colonization or of trade. Another has been the natural desire of peoples to be linked with their own kin and with those of their own tongue. It was from this aspect, I think, that the representatives at the Peace Conference viewed the state of the -world as they found
it. Many wrongs have been done in the past which they felt it was their first duty to rectify. Not -only had -they to deal with the present condition of affairs resulting from this war; they had in mind the untold misery that had been caused -and the unfair treatment that had been -accorded to many nations as the result of previous military conflicts. T-h-es-e they have in certain measure attempted to remedy. Alsace and Lorraine have been returned to France, and Bosnia goes to Serbi-a. West Prussia, Posen and part of East Prussia go to Poland, while Silesia, North Schleswig and the remainder of East Prussia are allowed to settle their own national allegiance by a popular vote of their people. Four new free nations are created which -consist of no less than sixtydive millions of people, fifty millions of whom were five years ago under oppression and bondage. That, I think, is the first result, one of the great results, of this Treaty which we are now asked to ratify.	.
Another result of the Peace Conference which may have a very happy effect upon the world is one which has not so far been mentioned in this debate. I refer to the mandatory policy which has been inaugurated with respect to weak and backward nations. Nations of this kind are to be developed and educated along the lines oi scientific government; they are to be treated like children in a school who are taught to look after themselves-; they will be enabled to obtain all the advantages of western civilization. When we reflect that this principle can be extended to all the backward nations of the earth, we see in the possibilities that may emerge from that policy one of the great blessings which may result from this unhappy war.
Then, the representatives at the Peace Conference have attempted to do away with the conditions brought about by the greed of nations in the past for trade. They have thrown open various countries to freedom of trade; they have put them on an equality so far as freedom for carrying on business in concerned.
Let us now come more particularly to the conditions- of the Treaty. This is a treaty with Germany, who, we must remember, was the great aggressor; who was the cause of the much lamented state of affairs which have prevailed during the last five years. What are the conditions which have been laid down in respect of the ambitious military nation which was the cause of this war? If we look at the military terms which have been imposed upon Germany, we see

that the army of this once great and powerful nation, which was able at the beginning of the war to mobilize between 9,000,000 and
12,000,000 men, has been reduced to 100,000 men and 5,000 officers. That, I think, presages well for peace so far as Germany is concerned. In addition, the demobilization of troops in Germany is restricted to five per cent a year of the total force. It will be remembered that in 1806 France restricted the Prussian military force to. 20,000 men, and Prussia, in order to evade that restriction, said: We will maintain only 20,000 men, but we will train 20,000 new men every year. It will be remembered also that a few years later, at the battle of Waterloo, she was instrumental, to some extent at least, in defeating the French, who had imposed such drastic terms upon her.
In addition to the terms which I have mentioned, the forts of the Baltic and the Rhine are to-: be done away with. The fortifications of the Kiel Canal and of Heligoland are to be destroyed. Conscription has been abolished. The naval terras are almost as drastic. Germany is allowed to keep only six battleships, six light cruisers and twelve torpedo boats; she is permitted to have no submarines and no 'air force. Her fourteen cables are yet to be distributed by some method to be arrived at by the League of Nations. War material must not be imported or exported by Germany. Thus we see the drastic military conditions to which this once powerful military nation has been subjected.
We have surrounded our late enemies with a natural fortification. We have on the west the natural fortifications of the Rhine. Then we have the Alps, and in the near East we have the Danube. On the eastern- flank we have created two nations and made them free and independent: Poland and Czecho-Slovakia.
Thus we have her hemmed in as it were on every side by free and independent peoples. The frontiers of Great Britain will be on the Rhine; those of Egypt and India will be on the Danube, and it is worthy of note by those of us who recall our ancient history that those were the natural boundaries which were used by the great Roman Empire.
Turning to the economic conditions that are imposed, we find that they are equally if not more severe. Germany has to pay an indemnity of $25,000,000,000, and I hope that that is not the total amount, as it does not seem to me that $25,000,000,000 is sufficient indemnity to put upon a nation which

caused the Allies a war debt of $150,000,000,000. I hope that there will be other levies put upon Germany at -a later date. Germany accepts responsibility for all the damage done to the Allies and associated governments. She agrees to reimburse civilian damages. She agrees to replace shipping on a ton for ton basis, this to be drawn from her merchant marine and from her coastal and river shipping. She agrees in addition to build merchant ships for the Allies for years to come and to devote her economic resources to rebuilding the devastated regions of the western front. Germany agrees to return to the most favoured nation treaties without discrimination, while the Allies and Associated Powers are given freedom of transit throughout Germany. Germany loses 3,000 square miles of her industrial territory and 7,000,000 people. She loses 1.000,000 square miles of her colonies and' 12,000,000 people, colonies with which before the war she had a foreign trade of no less than $13,000,000. She loses her markets, her mercantile marine, her raw materials. We take from her three-quarters of her iron and coal and a large share of her phosphates. We take thousands of vessels and hundreds of thousands of animals. We have put upon her an immediate levy of $25,000,000,000. Philip Scheidmann former chancellor of the German Empire, said on May 12, speaking from his place in the House:
This treaty is, in the view of the Imperial German Government, unacceptable, so unacceptable that I am unable to believe that the earth could bear such a document, without a cry issuing from a million throats in all lands.
As regards us, Mr. Speaker, who saw something of the devastation caused by Germany in the western fields of Europe, who saw her violate every law of God and man, this appeal does not fall on very sympathetic ears. We hope that she may be taught through the harsh terms of this Treaty that more than in the biblical sense "the way of the transgressor is hard." We welcome as a just retribution the punishment which is about to be inflicted upon the late Emperor of Germany and those associated with him who 'were responsible for this war.
We must, of course, realize that these economic terms are terms which will be carried out by any nation only when it is compelled to do so, and this brings us to the conditions which are provided for in the enforcement of this Treaty. First and foremost among them, in my humble judgment, is the League of Nations. .Thirty-two nations have agreed to submit all their troubles to arbitration; more than that, they have-

agreed to use their influence to get all other nations to do the same. Who is there in this House or in this country to-day that will believe that if in 1914 we had had such an organization as that, this war would have come upon the world? Personally, I do not believe that if the Treaty which has just been signed between Great Britain, France and the United States had been in existence prior to the war, such a conflict would have come to pass. But above and beyond all this, one of the most important uses of the League of Nations is that it will be an authentic channel by which the views of the leading powers of the earth may be given to the world. That alone is, I think, a ver.y important thing.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken a great deal about Article 10 of this Treaty. The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) yesterday proved, I think, conclusively that the sovereign power of this House was in no way encroached upon by this Article. But I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite-and they say they are all in favour of this League-what use this League would be without Article 10. It appears to me that it would not be worth the paper it is written upon nor the time that it took to write it. The including of that Article gives the League a dynamic power and force which will undoubtedly be a benefit to this country. Hon. gentlemen have to a considerable extent quoted the President of the United States, the author of this League, but I should like to remind them that a few days ago, before the Committee on Foreign Relations at Washington, he stated that Article 10 .implied nothing more than an obligation; that if the United States were going to war, Congress would have to declare it and the Government would have to come to Congress for the means for carrying it on.
Moreover, Articles 16 and 17 give the League power to put economic pressure upon any nation or nations which may violate their agreements. Article 16 says that if any member of the League disregards its covenants and resorts to war, its foreign trade and personal relationships shall be cut off from the rest of the world. We see ' there great possibilities of exercising, so to speak, an economic blockade against any country that refuses to abide by the decisions of the League of Nations. Article 1'7, directly following that, makes provision whereby any countries at war that are outside of the League are to be invited to come in, and if they enjoy the benefits of the League the same restrictions are imposed upon them as are imposed upon members
of the League proper. Let us consider for a moment what this means. Germany, as well as other countries in Central Europe, requires a great deal of raw material to be imported from other nations. Under the present terms of this Treaty she is allowed to buy coal and iron in the market without any discrimination, but we can readily see that if she refuses to abide by the decisions of this League, that privilege may be immediately cut off and all the economic pressure which practically the world can exert may be put in force against her. Germany, in 1913, imported no less than 94,000,000 bushels of wheat, the total world supply in that same year being 4,000,000,000 bushels. The Allies at that time grew no less_than
2.071.000.	000 bushels, or over 50 per cent of the total. That is, there was that much directly under the control of the Allies, or the members of the League of Nations. Germany, after 1870, owed much of her economic progress to the iron which she got in Lorraine. Turning to the iron fields of the world, we find that we 'have taken three-quarters of what she formerly possessed away from her, and in the possession of the Allies alone there is no less than three-quarters of the iron of the world. Copper, which is the next most important basic metal, is held in similar proportions. In 1913 the total production was 1,000,000,060 tons, and of this the Allies held no less than
770.000.	000 tons. The case in regard to coal is similar; of 1,100,000,000 tons, the Allies controlling over 823,000,000 tons, showing that they could impose an almost overwhelming economic blockade.
Of the 22,433,000 bales of cotton available in 1912 the Allies held over 19,500,000 bales. * These figures will indicate the power the League of Nations may exercise without resorting to force of arms. I repeat, Canada may have much to gain by being a member of the League, and no nation need expect to derive from membership in the League benefits of any importance without incurring some obligations.
Another very important part of this Treaty, to my mind, is that comprising the labour clauses. It is perhaps too soon for us to comprehend fully all that they may mean to the world, but if these provisions with regard to labour are carried out by the different members of the Leagile we can readily conceive that they will be a great blessing to humanity. In passing, we in Canada ought to be proud of the part the Prime Minister of this country and his colleagues have taken in drafting these momentous labour clauses. It would take

too long to enumerate all the labour provisions, but the opinion expressed in the Covenant that labour is not merely a commercial commodity, the regulations for securing humane conditions of labour for men, women, and children, the introduction of the 24-hour day weekly rest, the abolition of child labour-these are provisions [DOT] which will do much to alleviate the troubles and the toils of labour.
Mr. Speaker, practically the whole of this debate has centred around Article X. I would ask this House and the country to consider whether Canada has not some duty to perform for the benefit of the world and of humanity. We have passed through .a dark night filled with trouble, tears, and death, and we on this side of the House think that Canada should now step out on the platform with the other nations of the world and do her part in carrying to those nations less prosperous and less blessed than ours the blessing of our free institutions and the civil and religious liberty which we possess. We should do so in the interests not only of Canada herself and the great Empire to which we belong, but also in the interests of humanity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take much time in debating this question, because I think the House is already well informed, and further, in view of the limited time that has been given to the members of this House to get acquainted with the facts it has been somewhat difficult to analyze thoroughly the Treaty and the Covenant.
I should have liked before discussing this question to have had a full report from the hon. gentlemen who represented Canada at the Peace Conference of their activities, of the speeches they delivered and the objections they made at all sittings of the Conference w'here Canada's interests were at stake. I think we are entitled to a full report of their deliberations.
I regret that the Prime Minister showed some little nervousness the other day because a few questions were put to him, with the view of enlightening the House, by the hon. member, for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding). I do not wish to be severe, but it seems to me there is a lack of dignity on the part of the gentleman who occupies the exalted position of Prime Minister of Canada when he threatens to resign from office the moment he is asked a few pertinent questions. You will remember that a year ago when the hon. member for Kingston pressed his motion for the abolition of

titles we were threatened with the resignation of the right hon. the Prime Minister in the midst of the great war. This year, when an hon. member who belonged to the Unionist wing of the Liberal party asked a few pertinent questions of the Prime Minister, we again had the threat of resignation if the Treaty and the Covenant were not approved almost without any discussion. Mr. Speaker, we have not been accustomed in our Canadian Parliament to this mode of procedure. ,

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I regret we are obliged to discuss in haste the very important question before us to-day. I said the very important question; I should have said the most important question that has ever come before the Canadian Parliament since Confederation. I shall endeavour to offer a few observations on this question, speaking for no one but myself.
As regards the war itself, I need not say that I have approved and I still approve of Canada's participation in the great war, both in men and in money. I have given my all in this war, and I have no lesson to receive from any hon. gentlemen as regards my patriotism, my loyalty, and my admiration for British ideals of civilization, freedom and self-government. It was a war between two conflicting ideals-the German ideal, that might should prevail over right, and the British and French and 1 should say Christian ideal, that right should prevail over might. It was the bounden duty of Canada, and the moral duty of every civilized nation in the world, to see that our ideal should prevail, that right should prevail over might. The war has been won, and won, thanks to Divine Providence-for I believe in the intervention of Divine Providence in human affairs.
It has been won thanks to our dead heroes; and let me ,say, Mr. Speaker, that if the silent voices in Flanders Fields could be heard to-day, those young men who are under the sod would say: O Canada ! we did not fight, we did not fall to promote a new imperialism, to implant a new .militarism. We fought for freedom; we fought for justice; we fought for civilization. The war was won, , I repeat again, thanks to the intervention of Divine Providence, thanks to our dead heroes, and to the indomitable spirit of the Allied armies, among which the Canadian army played such a glorious part. Yet, Mr. Speaker, if I approve of Canada's participation in the great war I must sav at once that I cannot approve of the war

policies of the Government. During the last five years we have seen exploitation, extravagance, profiteering, waste, all which is the cause of the discontent that exists in our country. I cannot approve of the war policies of the Government because, all throughout that period, from the inception of the war to this very day, there has been an utter disregard of the constitutional rights of Canada There has been a complete absence of statesmanship-statesmanship that should make for union and not for disunion. There has been an abject surrender of principles 1 to party exigencies. Mr. Speaker, I shall not make any other reference to party politics, but lest my remarks this afternoon should be misunderstood, I say again that I .approve of Canada's participation in the war in regard to both men and money, but disapprove of the war policies of the Government, for they were not in the best interests of the cause. Bygones are bygones. The glamour of war has faded away and the country is now facing grim realities. The Liberal party, to which I have the honour to belong, can well afford to await the verdict of an enlightened electorate voting under a Liberal, a Canadian, a British franchise, when the war policies of the last five years are scrutinized. The war is won, the Peace Treaty signed, the League of Nations is created, and now the Dominion Parliament is asked to ratify or rather to approve of both. The first question which arises is this: By virtue of what powers are we called upon to ratify or to approve of the Treaty and Covenant? To say that we approve but do not ratify is only a fine play of words. If this Parliament approves, without any reservation, the Peace Treaty and the Covenant, Canada is committed to all the consequences of the Treaty and the Covenant. By virtue of what power are we called upon to ratify the Treaty and the Covenant? We are not a Sovereign nation. We have no Treaty making powers, and no one knows it better than my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council. I am fully aware that sometimes in the past Canadian ministers have negotiated in Prance for instance and in Spain, a treaty between France and Canada and between Spain and. Canada. But, Sir, if the Canadian ministers were allowed to negotiate those treaties they did so because they were made plenipotentiaries by the hand and seal of His Majesty the King. I remember the case of the Franco-Canadian Treaty which was signed by my hon. friend who was then Minister of Finance, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and by Mr. Justice Brodeur, who was then Minister of Marine and Fisheries. They affixed their signatures to that treaty not as Canadian ministers but as British plenipotentiaries. In spite of all the pious wishes which have been expressed, and duly so, by the Canadian Parliament, we
3 p.m. have no treaty-making power.
except the power we have of making treaties with the Indian tribes of the north. That is our sole treaty-making power. Mr. Speaker, I am a British citizen wherever the British flag floats; but if I were a British elector in the United Kingdom I would stand by the Treaty of Peace, and by .the Covenant of the League of Nations without much questioning. I would 'perhaps criticise some of the terms of the Treaty, but I would stand by the Treaty and by the Covenant because, legally, as a British elector, I would have a say in the matter. As a Canadian, however, I have no say at all in the foreign affairs in which the United Kingdom is involved. I would stand by the Treaty because it marks the end of the most cruel of all wars, and I would stand by the Covenant because, indeed, it is a noble, it is a generous effort to abolish militarism in the world and to put an end to the reign of the bully in European and in world -politics. Yet, if I were a British elector in the United Kingdom, I think I would offer a few observa-, tions concerning the Treaty. For instance, I would deplore the fact that the representatives of both Great Britain and France have in that Treaty given official recognition to the German Empire as an entity. Mr. Speaker, I do not make this, statement on my own judgment. I base my view on the very able criticism whi'ch was published in England and in France a few days ago and signed by the ex-foreign minister of France, Mr. Hanotaux. Mr. Hanotaux claims that the greatest mistake which was made in the Treaty-and it is its most outstanding one-was the recognition by the Powers of a United German Empire. Those of us who are familiar with modern history know that the United German Empire was the creation of Bismarck, and that Empire was the result of fraud, of theft and of corruption.
I will not delve into history, but, Sir, the Powers, according to Mr. Hanotaux, should have given back to Germany her status of before 1870. Before 1870 there was a German confederation and that confederation was much less formidable than the German Empire, under the sway of Prussian militarists, became. If I were a British

elector I would-as was stated yesterday by our young friend, the distinguished member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), who delivered .a speech worthy of his ability, and worthy of the best traditions of this House-force my representatives at Westminster to settle, first of all, the Irish question before joining the Le-ague. Mr. Speaker, I am not uttering a phrase for the mere pleasure of uttering it; I am stating what is a fact. Why, today, if you read the British press, and notably the London Times, you will see that Lord Northcliffe himself advocates the immediate settlement of the Irish question, without which settlement he claims there can be no Imperial unity. I merely mention the name of Lord Northcliffe; the fact of mentioning his name bears its own lesson, carries its own weight. When a man like Lord Northcliffe, the proprietor of the London Times, has come to the conclusion that there can be no Imperial unity unless the Irish question is settled, it speaks volumes for the temper of the British electorate at the present time. Not only is that the opinion of Lord Northcliffe, but it is the opinion of my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who some years ago spoke in Toronto,at a public meeting, called to discuss a memorandum which had been prepared by a Toronto committee. This memorandum contained the following conclusions:
1.	Canada showed her determination to preserve and strengthen the ties which now bind her to Great Britain and other portions of the British Commonwealth.	*
2.	Effective organization of the Empire must not involve any sacrifice of responsible government in domestic affairs, or the surrender of control over fiscal policy by any portion of the Empire.
3.	But it is an inevitable development of responsible government in the Dominions that they should assume their proportionate share in the defence of the Empire, and should have a voice in determining its relations with other states.
Notice, Mr. Speaker, " a proportionate share in the defence of the Empire and a voice," etc. One does not go without the other.	.
4.	We think, therefore, that as soon as circumstances permit, political leaders throughout the Empire, irrespective of party, should meet to consider the problem.
As my friend the President of the Privy Council was then the hope of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario, he was asked to support the conclusions in this memorandum. He spoke at a large meeting held, if I mistake not, at the University
[Hr. Demieux.]
of Toronto, and there he is reported to have said:
Mr. Rowell declared that the Irish question must be settled first, that the present duty was to save the Empire now and reorganize it after. wards, that a co-operation of free peoples was better than centralization in government.

speechtext:
It was sanctioned by
the King and signed by His Majesty, and therefore I would, in the truly British old-fashioned way, stand by King George and silence King Carson. But enough on this subject. I have spoken as if I were a British elector, which I am not; as a Canadian I have no say in the matter at all. I can only approve of the Treaty of Peace and the Covenant in so far as they do not impair or abridge any of my constitutional rights, and I think this is sound Canadian and sound British doctrine. I may be told, and it is quite true, that anyhow as a British subject I am bound by the Treaty and by the Covenant. This is quite true in a sense, but by ratifying, or approving-the two expressions .are only a play upon words 

the two instruments submitted to us, the Canadian Parliament is committing itself

to prospective agreements of the gravest im-. portance. The Canadian (Parliament is surrendering its control over the military forces and defences of Canada, and such is the meaning of article 10, which can stand a study of the judges of the/Privy Council much better than article 17 of the school regulations of Ontario. It is clear and well worded; it is written in French and in English, and you may discuss it which way you like it has that meaning-that if Canada adopts this Covenant without a reservation as to the constitutional rights of the Canadian Parliament you are surrendering the control of your military forces and of your finances. Article 10 reads as follows:
The Members of the 'League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all (Members of the (League. In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
I quite -agree with what my hon. and gallant friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGib-bon) said a moment ago, that the Covenant would be meaningless and worthless without Article X. Article X is the teeth of the Covenant, and without it the League could not be enforced. But again, Mr. Speaker, I must look upon the whole issue as a Canadian-and call me a little Canadian if you please. The fact remains that iwe are to-day considering this question as members of the Canadian Parliament, and not as members of the Parliament of the United Kingdom. I must lookhipon the whole issue as a Canadian living under a constitution vesting us with limited powers only. I do not fear the encroachments of the United Kingdom in fiscal matters. Our fiscal independence was settled many years ago- and all honour to Sir Alexander Galt, who drafted the noble document which was read yesterday by my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). In military matters we are governed also by and from Ottawa, and not by and from London; and we do not want to be governed by and from Geneva. By approving this Article X without any reservation, we declare that Canada is bound by all the obligations that may be undertaken not only by the United Kingdom but by all the other members of the League. Great as are the powers of this self-governing Dominion, she has no voice in the foreign affairs of the British Empire. Why should we play on words, Mr. Speaker? It is all very well to -speak of Canada as a nation on a footing of equality with the Mother Country.
In one s-en-se it is true; in another sense it is no.t true, unfortunately.
The answer given by such a great statesman as Mr. Asquith, and by an ex-Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. Ha-rcourt, to this question: Shall we, -the Dominions, have any say in the conduct of foreign affairs^settles the point.
