We pointed out to him that the Committee of Imperial Defence is a purely advisory body, and is not and cannot under,any circumstances become a body to decide on policy, which is and must remain the sole prerogative of the Cabinet, subject to the support of the House of Commons.
Could the case be put more squarely and in a more concrete form than it is put there by those two great Liberal English statesmen? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that their answers settle the issue.
I said that Canada was a self-governing Dominion, that she had no voice in the foreign affairs of the British Empire, and that her obligation as regards the war issue was for the defence of her own territories. The questions of peace and war do not came under the purview of her constitution, the Imperial Parliament being supreme in such matters. The right hon. the Prime Minister the other day made this announcement to Canada:
The future relationship of the nations of the Empire must be determined in accordance with the will of the Mother Country and of each Dominion in a Constitutional Conference to be summoned in the not distant future. Undoubtedly it will be based upon equality of nationhood.
Undoubtedly, not certainly-suggesting that there is a doubt.
Bach nation must preserve unimpaired its absolute autonomy,-
That is what we claim, Mr. Speaker.

but it must likewise have its voice as to those external relations which involve the issue of peace or of War.
Mr. Speaker, if this announcement is true-and I believe it is true-the word of the right hon. gentleman is as good as his bond; it involves that an organic change in our constitution is contemplated. Well, Sir, I contend that this Parliament has no mandate to subscribe to this organic change. No Imperial Conference, which is only a consultative body, and no war cabinet, which was evolved during the war for a special purpose, can in such important matters override the Canadian Parliament and the Canadian constitution. Let us not be deceived by fine words; above all, to use the expression of Disraeli, let us not " take a leap in the dark."
The President of the Council waxed eloquent yesterday as he spoke of the future of Canada. I was reminded of a .remark made by a French statesman, M. Salvandy, I think it was, one of the ministers of the days of the French restoration. He had

delivered a very eloquent address before the House of Representatives, and as he was congratulated by one of his friends, he said: "Yes, but I was dancing on razor blades all the time." I may add that there were no safety razors in those days.
My hon. friend was very vague yesterday in all his definitions. He spoke of Canada not as being a nation, hut as being a nation within the Empire, that sounds well, but it is nothing else than a play upon words; it is meaningless from a constitutional point of view. There is no such thing as a nation within the Empire.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is very anxious to get from us his slogan for the next election. In order to get the electors to forget his sins of omission and commission, it would suit its purposes to denounce first, last and always, the disloyalty of those French Quebec members who stand "for a seperate nation", who advocate "independence." But we shall not dance to his tune; we will remain Canadians.
Again, do repeat in English the words of a great French statesman, I say that we are to-day what we were yesterday and to-morrow we shall be in the hands of Providence. Providence will shape the destinies of this nation, not my hon. friend, not the Tory party, not the Liberal party. Providence will shape the destinies of Canada; we are only the instruments of Providence. According to our merits or demerits the destinies of this country will be shaped.
My hon. friend says that we are a nation within the Empire. Have we the attributes of a nation? My hon. friend has studied international law and can answer that question. It is true that we have territory; it is true- that we have population; it is true?-no, it is not true-that we have sovereignty. These are the three .attributes of a nation, according to international law-territory, population, and sovereignty. Territory, as I say, we have-an immense expanse of it from the North Pole to the sixty-fifth parallel and from the Atlantic ocean to the Pacific. But if we wish to add one handful of earth to that territory, we have to go to London and have the British North America Act amended. When the Hudson Bay - territory was purchased through the campaign of George Brown, but by the Macdonald Government, Sir

John A. Macdonald had to go to London in Older to settle the terms; he could not add to the British territory of Canada. Mr. Speaker, there is quite a movement, as we all know, in favour of the West Indies becoming a part of the Canadian confederation. If we wished to take steps to effect a union with these beautiful islands, we would have to ask permission from the British authorities at Westminster.
But have we sovereignty? Can we appoint a consul to represent the interests of our Canadian merchants in any city, town or village south of the boundary line? Can we even appoint a consular agent? A motion was made some years ago, and, I think, passed by the House of Commons, recommending that representations be made to the home Government requesting that Canada be given the right to be represented abroad by consular agents or by consuls in purely mercantile matters. What became of that resolution? Like many speeches delivered by -the President of the Council, it was torn and scattered to the four winds of heaven.
Last session my hon. friend agreed as to the desirability of the appointment of a commissioner to represent Canada in Washington, and we agreed on the name of the man who should be appointed. What has become of the suggestion that such an appointment be made? We have large interests with the great republic to the south of us and the presence of a Canadian commissioner at Washington would greatly assist the business men both of Canada and of United States. Yet no sooner had the suggestion been made by my hon. friend in this House than the question was taken up in the British Parliament. I forget the exact answer that was given by Mr. Bonar Law or Mr. Walter Long, but it was, to say the least, a very frigid answer-and the appointment has not yet been made by Canada. It shows, Mr. Speaker, how little we have to say in connection with foreign affairs; we have not the^power even to appoint a commercial agent to represent us in the city of Washington.
I remember having had many conversations some years ago with the Canadian Commissioner in France, the late Mr. Hector Fabre, and I know of his troubles with the British Consul at Paris. The British Consul, not the Ambassador, mind you, did >no't understand why there was a Canadian office at the Rue de Rome, when he, at the British Consulate, was representing the interests of Great and Greater Britain in Paris. That shows that we have not
many of the attributes of a nation, seeing that we are begrudged the appointment of an agent at Paris, and we are practically told not to dare appoint an agent in the city of Washington. Sovereignty! Have you read, Sir, the speech delivered in the Senate last session by Senator Nicholls, exposing a most scandalous state of affairs as regards the commandeering of Canadian ships? I shall not refer any longer to this question, because I should like to be brief; but my hon. friend wanted to create an impression throughout the country. Ho began by depicting in glowing terms the future of Canada, so as to prepare for a coming election and to get his slogan out of our admissions. He put the alternatives before the House. Is it the status quo? Is it annexation? Is it independence? My hon. friend was in quest of an election cry; but if he wants an answer to that question, I may remind him in all friendliness that the "Canada First" party was started in the great city of Toronto, and that the Annexation Manifesto which was signed in 1849 did not not bear the signatures my hon. friend may think of. The mentioning of this Annexation Manifesto of 1849 comes in apropos, it seems to me, during the course of this discussion. There are hon. gentlemen who think. they are well advised in promoting the cause of centralization and who would like to merge Canadian every-day interests with British every-day interests. Why was the Annexation Manifesto signed and circulated in 1849? We Know that before 1849, indeed long before the year 1840 even, there existed for Canada and all the other British colonies a preferential tariff in Great.Britain, and during the years which elapsed between the year of the rebellion and 1842 or 1843 big business was being done in the old provinces Upper and Lower Canada; our merchants, our exporters were shipping grain and lumber in large quantities to Great Britain, as Canada had a preference in the British market. Then the agitation took place Tn favour of the abolition of the Corn laws- it was the coming of free trade in England. What happened? The moment there was taken away from the colonies, and particularly from Canada, this preference advocated again to-day by some of my hon. friends, one pi whom I see on the other side; the moment this preferential policy was abrogated by Great Britain, a grievance Was at once created amongst the merchants of Canada, and the result was that we had the Annexation Manifesto. The merchants of Canada said: If Great Britain will not

give us a preference, we will annex Canada to the United States of America.
Speaking on that subject, the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) not very long ago used these words which I am about to quote, and I believe that coming from one of the leading lights of the Unionist party, they are a vindication of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). We know how the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was labelled and was dogged by the Torv party in Canada during the campaign of 1911 because, like the Britisher and the good Canadian that he is, he discussed freely with American statesmen commercial interests which concerned both. Canada and the United States. Yet he was denounced in every city, town and hamlet in this great province of Ontario as an annexationist, nay, as a traitor, as disloyal. He was defeated in his own constituency because he had dared to advocate the very policy which, in the words of the President of the Council, saved Canada from annexation in 1849. This is what the President of the Council said:
I wish to point out to you that when this question of trade arose in a crucial form between Canada and Great Britain the Liberal attitude was-" Let the Mother Country do what is best in her own interest, and we will do what we consider best in ours, and that their course would not in the least affect our loyalty." The Conservative attitude was-''Unless you continue to feed us by preference, the connection may not lie as valuable as we otherwise thought it would be."
My hon. friend added:	.
Some of the distinguished leaders of the Conservative party in the city -of Montreal emphasized this view by issuing the famous " annexation manifesto" of 1S4S-49. Lord Elgin was a very wise man. He saw this annexation cry grow out of economic conditions. He thought he saw a method of removing the pressure and offering relief to those who were suffering. He went over to the United States and negotiated the treaty Of reciprocity. The annexation sentiment died, and the Conservatives [DOT] who held annexation views, became just as loyal as their neighbours.
I commend those words to the anti-reciprocity league and to the back and front benches. Sir, let us not involve Canada in the domestic affairs of Great Britain. Let us not entangle Canada in the foreign affairs of Great Britain. Oh, yes, they comprise the ablest men-presidents of universities, newspaper editors, political economists. Remember, Lord Milner is not ito be despised; he is one of the ablest men in the British Empire. Those Imperialists will try to foster their ideas and to implant their principles throughout, the Empire by all sorts of methods and every combination and device possible. They will try to get some weak kneed Liberals to support their plan-indeed, they have secured the services of my hon. friend. By the establishment of Round Table clubs they have reached many young men of Canada. I have been approached myself, as have also many others, with the invitation:	Come along;
we want to help you Canadians. But once you sit around the table it is easy to realize, Sir, that the so-called true Imperialists will only be satisfied if Canada surrenders the rights she possesses. To-day it will be called a Scheme of Imperial Federation; to-morrow it will be termed a Britannic Alliance; another day it will be an Imperial Partnership; another day it will be Sister Nations of the Empire, or, as my hon. friend said yesterday, the Commonwealth of ^he Empire; but the same principle underlies all these combinations 
-it is always Imperial Federation disguised.
The Conservative party and, I might say, Canadians of all parties, have some regard for the opinion of the late Sir Charles Tup-per. He was a good Canadian and a good Britisher, and in 1893, speaking in the city of Winnipeg, he used the following language :
I am perfectly satisfied that a more unwise, a more injudicious, thing could not possibly occur to Canada than to change her Constitution in any radical respect whatever. We have a constitution that has stood the test of more than a quarter of a century and that I would not be willing for any representation in the Imperial Parliament or anything else to change in any material respect We must ever retain the entire complete and independent management of our own affairs.
Mr. Speaker, the great political power of to-morrow in Great Britain will not be the Imperialist party, it will not be the party of Lord Milner, of Walter Long, of Bonar Law, in other words, the jingo party; it will be the Labour party. And what does the labour platfonm contain^ That platform was launched a few months ago by its brilliant leader, Mr. Henderson, who used the following language:
Like them,-the Labour Party-we have no sympathy with the projects of " Imperial Federation," in so far as these imply the subjection to a common Imperial Legislature wielding coercive power, (including dangerous facilities fo>-coercive Imperial taxation and for enforced military service), either of the existing selfgoverning dominions, whose autonomy would be thereby invaded; or of the United Kingdom, whose freedom of democratic self-development would he thereby hampered; or of India and the Colonial Dependencies, which would thereby run the risk of being further exploited for the benefit of a "White Empire." We do not intend, by any such " Imperial Senate " either to bring the plutocracy of Canada and South Africa to the aid of the British aristocracy, or to enable the landlords and financiers of the Mother Country to unite in controlling the growing popular democracies overseas. The absolute autonomy of each self-governing part of the Empire must be maintained intact.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say once more that I approve of the Treaty of Peace, and I approve the principles of the Covenant of the League of Nations. I believe with Viscount Grey: .
Nothing but experience convinced individuals that law was better than anarchy to settle the relations between themselves. And the sanction that maintains law is the application of force with the support of the great majority of individuals behind it. Is it possible that the experience of this war will produce a settled opinion of the same sort to regulate the relations of States with each other and safeguard the world from war, which is in fact anarchy?
I believe in that liberal principle of a League of Nations backed by force in order

to enforce its decisions; but, Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian, subject only to Canadian law, to a Parliament elected by the Canadian people, I approve of the Treaty and the League, provided a reservation is made, that nothing in this act of mine shall impair or abridge the rights, or in other words, the autonomy of Canada.
At the Liberal convention which was held a few weeks ago in Ottawa, I seconded the following resolution, which was moved by a gentleman from Toronto, Mr. Gregory, K.C.:
Resolved, that we are strongly opposed to centralized Imperial control and that no organic change in the Canadian constitution in regard to the relation of Canada to the Empire ought to come into effect until, after being passed by Parliament, it has been ratified by vote of the Canadian people on a referendum.
Mr. Speaker, I stand by the principle of thait resolution. The Prime Minister of Canada has no right to attend, with some of his colleagues, a conference in London and there commit his country 'to any policy of centralization. The Canadian Parliament, representing the Canadian people, is entitled to know and' to pass upon the policy which the Government intends to propound before that new body which is to be created in London.
I know that wiben any hon. gentleman on this side speaks of autonomy or of the constitution, at once he is met with the suggestion that he is overdoing it. If this Parliament was homogeneous; if there were but one race in this country, the Englishspeaking race, I would understand that such a discussion would be unnecessary. But we have in this country a majority and a minority, and I wish to impress upon my friends who belong to the majority that the minority, in whatever country it dwells, is ever jealous o.f its constitutional rights. No one should be surprised, therefore, if when a question of this kind comes before the House those who belong .to the minority are anxious to be enlightened; are anxious that no cause of grievance be created; are anxious that no hasty change should be made. Any change from the minority's point of view implies a risk, and every risk for a minority is a danger.
I am a British citizen. I am proud of my citizenship; I would not exchange it for or traffic it with any other citizenship in the world; yet I am of French origin and of French blood. I appreciate the rights and privileges which I enjoy under the Union Jack. My hon. friend need have no craven fear that any one belonging to the minority, that I know of, would turn
that flag down or 'would exchange his citizenship. The French Canadians are well - aware of the fate that befell the French minority in the United States. When Louisiana was purchased by the United States there was a large French settlement in that state, but if one goes to New Orleans to-diay he will find that if there is a French civil law it is interpreted before the courts in English. In the Louisiana Legislature there is no French language to speak of; the same applies to the courts of the land. So there is no one in our province who would support a movement in favour of annexation.
Oh, if it were only possible for us to understand each other! You, our; friends from the province of Ontario, are often misguided. You misjudge your fellow men from the province of Quebec. Why should some of you attempt to bully them? Why . do you not treat them with more consideration? The minority is always nervous; is always jealous of its rights and privileges, and there ,are causes of misunderstandings which should not exist. Do not always offer the cup of bitterness; offer the milk of human kindness. The war is ended now -gloriously ended from the Canadian point of view, from the British point of view. Our soldiers in the trenches have intermingled and have sung the song of love; why should we in Canada perpetuate the hymn of hate? Why should not the public men in the Government estop-I use the legal expression-the newspapers from abusing those who belong to the minority?
Is our country, or is it not, an asset to the British Empire? Can we be an asset if, instead of being united, we are essentially divided ?
There is tabled before you, Mr. Speaker, the Treaty which was signed by the Great Powers with Poland. You have exemplified in that Treaty the basic principles which should guide Britishers and Christians all over the world-respect of the minority,
, respect of their religious, national and linguistic rights. You, men of the majority on this North American continent, are you afraid of five million people who speak the French language? You are over 110,000,000 speaking the English language; surely John Bull would stand his ground under such circumstances. I appeal again to the public men of this country; I appeal to the ministers of the Crown to put an end at once to that deplorable agitation which has been going on from one end of the *country to the other since the beginning of the war.

Treat us as equals, because we are your equals. If we are to become, as we will, members of the League of Nations, let us first of all, before joining it, resolve to form a more essential League-the League of a United Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion that is before the House and the subject with which it deals are the most important considerations that have been submitted to the Parliament of Canada since Confederation. In discussing this matter I shall endeavour to stick as closely as possible to the subject in hand.
I believe that it is big enough and important enough to call for our best consideration without our turning aside from it in any way to endeavour to make political capital for any party, or to give political bias to any of the things that are embraced in the Treaty.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), who, with his usual eloquence, has occupied about one hour and three-quarters, has debated very few of the features of this great Treaty, and, therefore, he will, perhaps, excuse me if I do' not follow the vagaries in which he has indulged, because I believe, when he reads that speech, he will come to the conclusion that it is not equal to the great occasion on which he spoke, nor does it uphold fully the ability that he has displayed on some former occasions on very much lesser subjects. I shall refer only to some two or three points that the hon. gentleman has made, believing that my time can be better occupied in endeavouring to elucidate in a humble way and from the standpoint of a business man some of the features comprised in the Treaty. The first remark that struck my observation, that I thought was worthy of note, was this, "that Canada had no treaty-making powers." I think those are the words of the hon. gentleman. It is true he uttered them before the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) came into the House, or I fancy his coat tail would have been pulled, and he would have been reminded that in 1911 the member for Shelburne and Queen's, accompanied by the then member for Brant and others, went to Washington and negotiated the reciprocity treaty because they themselves told us so, and throughout that election the reciprociy treaty it was called. Therefore, I think the hon. gentleman went somewhat afield when he said that we had no treaty-making powers. Nor was that the first occasion on which Canada made a treaty. Sir John A. Macdonald, twenty or 
thirty years prior to that, went down to Washington and negotiated what was called the Washington treaty, if my memory serves me correctly. It is true that this Treaty and all other treaties must receive the sanction of the Mother Country, but we had the power of negotiating them and the various matters that were dealt with in those treaties were put in by the Canadians themselves who went to Washington to negotiate them. 1 think I am speaking by the book, and I will call the attention of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) to the fact that treaties have been negotiated before now by members of the Canadian Government.
The hon. gentleman has brought in *several questions which, I say, have no bearing on the discussion, but I think I ought to refer to at least one or two of them. He has brought in the Irish question, and I wish the hon. gentleman would just listen to me for a moment while I show wherein, in his own speech, according to his own showing, he has transgressed his own doctrine. The Irish question, he says, should be settled by the Imperial Government before we, as a part of the British Empire, become a party to this Treaty, because it is a burning question, and he tells us he would settle King Carson right away. He did not tell us what he would do with Ulster, but I gathered from hi? speech that he would trample on the rights of Ulster with both feet, and, King Carson would immediately be dethroned. How does that fit in with his closing remarks when he appealed for tender treatment to minorities? It shows that the hon. gentleman, when he is dealing with the minority in -Quebec, as he calls it, has very tender feelings, but when he- comes to deal with Ulster, which does not see eye to eye with Quebec in religious and other matters, he would put both feet upon its neck and trample it in the dust and dethrone King Carson. A fine piece of strategy on the part of the hon. member for Maisonneuve! A beautifully high, Christian principle which he would extend to the minority in Quebec but which he would deny to the good old country of Ireland! We have enough troubles on this side without indulging in the Irish question, and we have no more right to drag the Irish question into a debate on this Treaty than we have to drag in the treatment of the coloured races by some of the great powers which are also parties to the Treaty. We could soon get *a long way off the Treaty, and I do not purpose being dragged in that direction. But

the hon. member for Maisonneuve ought to be more consistent, and when he appeals for tender treatment towards minorities, let him remember that all minorities do not dwell in Quebec; there are a few in Ireland as- well and we think that they should be treated with the same consideration as the hon. member appeals for in the case of the minority in Quebec, in which case he may be quite right. Although I asked him how he would settle this question, he did not tell us how he would do so. He is not an Irishman-it is true, he has told us so. The British Government has said: If Ireland will decide what will settle this question, we shall be only too pleased to do it, but up to date there has been devised by neither the majority or the minority in Ireland anything that will settle this question. The hon. gentleman says that the King is good enough for him in this respect, and that he would let him settle it. Well, he refused to tell us on what principles he would let the King settle it, and if he were in power in Great Britain to-day, he could no more settle the Irish question than he can the .school question between Ontario and Quebec, not a bit more. He may appeal for minorities and all that, using fine, high-sounding phrases, but when it comes down to hard pan, you cannot make the different elements amongst those very distinctive people in Ireland come together and live together in peace and harmony under one common rule. That has been tried for thirty years, and I, as an Imperialist as I have been called, would be willing to give of my substance and of my time for the next two or three years if I could help to settle what I believe has been a great bone of contention in the British Empire for a long time. But that is nbt a matter that appears in the treaty, and therefore, we should not discuss it. I do not purpose dealing with anything further that the hon. member for Maisonneuve has said. It is true that he has expressed in a few closing sentences some opinions with which I myself agree, and I shall endeavour to point those out as I go along in debating this treaty.
The war has come to an end and this treaty is proposing a basis on which a final settlement shall be made. In that respect the destinies of nations and of the civilised world rest within the four corners of this great agreement. I believe that this marks a new epoch in the history of Canada, in spite of what hon. gentlemen opposite may have said. Never before has a treaty of
any kind between the nations of the earth been committed to this Parliament for its opinion. Never before have we been asked what our view is with regard to a compact into which we have entered. I for one say that this is a step in advance of anything that has ever before existed in this country and that we are privileged-and I hope we shall rise to the height of the privilege that it is-to give the very best of our knowledge and wisdom to the discussion of this great question.
In that respect I agree to a very large extent with what the Opposition has done so far. They have appealed for time and for information, and in my judgment this is so great a question that it should not be rushed through this House in two or three days if it is thought that two or three weeks would be better. We are asked to undertake obligations that are going to bind us and our children and our children's children as far into the future as we can see. We should therefore take every possible precaution to see that our rights and privileges are safeguarded in every respect. While I say that, I know that nothing I can say or that anybody else may say on the floor of this House can change one line of the Treaty. The Treaty is submitted to us simply for approval, or ratification, or adoption, or whatever you like to call it, but we cannot change one word in the Treaty without the permission of all the other powers that are parties to it. My friends opposite, I think, are suffering undue qualms of conscience with regard to what is buried in the signature that is asked. They seem to shrink from the responsibility of adopting or ratifying or approving this Treaty. Many of their fears I think are more or less groundless. We must at times take risks. On great occasions we must come to decisions, and come' to those decisions fairly quickly, and I cannot see anything unreasonable in asking this House to set its approval on this Treaty. Perhaps I may make a homely comparison in order to make the matter more clear to hon. gentleman opposite. This is a most unusual session; the subject under discussion is a most unusual one; and we have some other very unusual conditions in the House. For instance, on the front benches of the Opposition some kind of treaty, or entente cordiale, or combination, has been arrived at between two great political powers, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Shelburne and

Queens (Mr. Fielding), for the joint leadership of the Opposition. I do not know whether it is a treaty-

There -may he a eonvenant between them. It cannot be a League of Nations, but it is a league of two great powers. The question I would ask is: Has this agreement been sumbitted to the Liberal caucus? If so, did they ratify or approve or adopt it, or did they amend it? We have not heard, but we would like to know the terms of this union, because likely they are applicable to the Treaty under discussion. Then you have fears for your autonomy. That is an awful word, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has told us, and he has quoted my views from the naval debate of some years ago. I want to tell you gentlemen opposite that I think your autonomy is in danger right now, because whether this treaty that has been made between these two gentlemen has received the endorsement of the caucus or not we are told by the press that a king will shortly enter this House and will say to these two great powers: "Step to the right.
. Step to the left. Sit back. I am the king and leader of this great party." Why didn't you elect a president? Surely the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) who has announced himself as a great democrat, has overlooked the fact that he is going to.be led by a King, when he might have had a democratic leader.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has told us that he is a great democrat, and I, of course, believe what he says, because he is a man who speaks what he believes and testifies what he does know, and sometimes I think he testifies a little more than he knows. I think I have spent more time than I should have in trying to enlighten my friends opposite on what they are asked to do. They are asked to ratify or approve

of this treaty. I want them to understand that in my view, if this House ratifies the Treaty, we shall be'bound by its provisions and shall have to live up to them. I am inclined to think that we shall have to live up to the obligations in the Treaty whether or not we ratify it. I am rather of the opinion that we shall have to.
The Treaty documents that have been put in the hands of hon. members are so voluminous and contain so very many important clauses that it is impossible for a layman of my calibre to attempt to elucidate any but a very few of the articles contained in the Treaty of Peace and the Covenant of the League of Nations. I have said on a former occasion, that I believe the mixing of the League of Nations with the Treaty of Peace was the greatest tactical mistake that the 'Conference could possibly have committed, and I say that again from the bottom of my heart. There is a difference of opinion with regard to the League of Nations, but there is no difference of opinion with regard to making a good sound treaty of peace with the enemy. I think the Treaty was big enough to be handled by itself, and the other matter would have been taken care of a little later on. However, that has not been done, and I, as a loyal subject of the Emipre, and I trust as a good citizen of the world, am going to back this Treaty and vote for its ratification even though I disagree with many of its provisions. I think some of its provisions are extremely dangerous and unworkable, but I am willing to give the Treaty the benefit of the doubt and defer to those who ought to know better, because I believe that in the long run this may prove to be a blessing to humanity.
The High Contracting Parties to the League of Nations were called together to achieve international peace by a lot of very high-sounding principles, which I cannot do better than read. They agree to achieve international peace and security.
-'by the acceptance of obligations not to resort to war, by the prescription of open, just and honourable relations between nations.
by the firm establishment of the understandings of international law as the actual rule of conduct among Governments, and by the maintenance of justice and a scrupulous respect of all treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another.
These are idealistic, high-sounding phrases and are worthy of the best conception of the most enlightened nations of the world. With these articles I am in full accord. The origiir.l members of the League, etc., are then dealt with. The first serious objection I have to offer is to Article VII,

Clause 1, w-hich provides *that the seat of the League is to be established at Geneva.
I ,am told, and I (have seen in the papers, that this is to be changed, but there is nothing in the documents that are laid before the House to indicate this. If the Minister, who is present, will tell me that this change is to be made I shall be glad to learn the truth of i't, but I should like to know in favour, of what city the change v,ill be made. In my 'Judgment no decision has been arrived at, nor is any one in a position to state what city will receive the honour of being the seat of the League.
I do not think that the League of Nations should have been housed at Geneva. Why do I say that? Geneva is the capital of Switzerland, a country which, during the war, never sent a man to fight, a country which was busy liming its pockets with the gold of its jstruggling neighbours. And I cannot conceive of anything that could have warped the judgment, as I think has been the case, of the powers that assembled to consider the terms of peace to such an extent .as to lead them to place this permanent body in Geneva, when there were such cities as Brussels, the capital of a country that had suffered untold .agonies during the war, and Paris, the heart of the most valiant nation that took .part in the war, the nation that produced the good President Clemenoeau, who in nfy judgment, is the most outstanding and brilliant figure of the whole war. If this Treaty is good we owe a very large degree of its virtue to the "Tiger of France"-Clemenoeau.	I
could not speak too highly in praise of his brilliant action throughout the war and in the negotiations for peace that followed. I believe he has had an immense effect upon what has been done; but unfortunately in some respects he was unable, by either voice, vote or influence, to carry the conference always in the direction it should have taken. I aim not now speaking simply by book or from the four corners of the Treaty, but I have in my hands voluminous articles-far too large to be read to the House <at the present time-which justify the opinion^ I express, iwhich opinions' are largely drawn from these articles.
I think, however, I should be justified in stating that the Covenant of the League of Nations was incorporated in the Treaty largely at the instance of President Wilson and those who were associated with him in the United States and who to-day, it would appear, are the principal kickers against its contents. I deplore this situation, hut we cannot overlook it and I think we are justified in requesting some information as
to what is going to happen if this Treaty is carved up in the way in which the Ottawa Journal, no later than September 5, informed us it would be. This is what I read:
Committee approves shell of Treaty but refuses to accept vital conditions.
This is the Senate Committee of the United States.
Article 10 is repudiated in totality by Foreign Relations Committee of TT.S. Senate-Also claims right to retire from League of Nations.
What follows?
The Senate Foreign Relations Committee late yesteTday finished its work on the Peace Treaty with Germany, and after adopting four reservations to the League of Nations Covenant, ordered the Treaty to be reported to the Senate with about two score amendments previously incorporated.
I would ask the hon. gentleman who is leading the House whether, should these two score amendments be introduced, the Treaty will come back to us in order that we may review and endorse or otherwise deal with the amendments that are injected by the United States Senate?. Can this Treaty be unduly amended after it has been passed? We are told that we cannot amend a word, that we cannot dot an "i' or cross a "t . Is it possible that the United States, which has been the main sponsor of the League of Nations, should now be endeavouring to incorporate such a number of amendments? The report goes on to tell what some of the amendments are, and they are very important to us and should receive our grave consideration. They provide: "for the return of Shantung to China under the amendment of Senator Lodge to substitute China for Japan in the Shantung section;" " for withdrawal of the United States from representation on the numerous international commissions." This amendment was by Senator Fall, Republican, New Mexico, and involved about thirty-five textual changes.-"For limitation of the authority of American representatives on the Reparations Commission to act without direction of their Government except on shipping questions."
They provide, further-and this is what I want Canada to note " for equal voting power in the League Council Assembly of Great Britain and the United States." The United States proposes that it shall have equal voting power with Great Britain and all her Dominions. Now, if, as one or two gentlemen have said to-day, voting and influence should be decided in proportion to what 'has been done to win the war, surely it cannot be seriously contended that our

esteemed brethren to the south, for whom I have the very highest regard, should have as much to say about the Treaty as Great Britain and all her overseas Dominions that were in the war from start to finish and sacrificed' millions as against the United States' hundred of thousands. It is invidious to draw distinctions of this kind, but when the Senate proposes that these things shall be done we cannot afford to ignore altogether what has been done by our neighbours in the United States. There are other important amendments, but time would fail me to deal with them all. However, I ask the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty), who is sitting here and will likely speak later, to tell us what will become of these amendments. Will they come back to this House after we have ratified the Treaty, or will they be rejected by the great Executive Council of the League of Nations? These are important considerations which we cannot afford to overlook. As regards the selection of Geneva as the headquarters of the League of Nations, I think, when we are talking of amendments, that this matter is a proper one for consideration, and the seat of the League, I submit, should be changed to any one of the great cities I have mentioned, such as Brussels, which was the heart of the storm; Paris, vrhich also was almost in the centre of the storm; Home, London, and even, yes, even Washington. These all have infinitely better claims to be the home of the League of Nations than has Geneva; for Switzerland never spent a dollar to help save civilization. I, for one, strongly protest against the selection of Geneva, and I understand that a storm of protest 'has been registered in Great Britain against it. I hear that the seat is to be changed, and in my opinion it cannot be changed too soon. We come next to Article 8:
The Members of the League recognize that the maintenance of Peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest points consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations.
The Council, taking account of the geographical situation and circumstances of each State, shall formulate plans for such reduction for the consideration and action of the several Governments.
*Such plans shall be subject to reconsideration and revisioh at least every ten years.
That, I think, is a wise provision, I have no objection to it, and it seems to be a proceeding along the right lines.
Now I come to deal with clause 10 which has been such a stumbling block to mem-

bers opposite and which seems to be more or less in the mind of every member of the House, and we want to know what it means. I as a business man, want to know what article 10 means, and though I have listened to this discussion, though I have read the speech of the Prime Minister and as many documents as I could possibly digest in the last few weeks in regard to it, I have not as yet reached any decision in my mind as to its meaning, and I think it is up to the Government or somebody else, to tell this House, before the Treaty goes through, what our obligations are in a military and in a naval way under that clause.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I am fully of that
opinion. I am not saying this to injure the Treaty. I said I was going to support it and I want to see it go through. But we as business men, to whom this Treaty is committed, should investigate, should inquire, and should find out what article 10 means. I have told you that it presents one of the most wonderful ideals that the world has ever put down on paper. These ideals of the League of Nations, to preserve the benefits that man has received from the Christian religion, and from civilization ever since the world began down to the present time, are being crystallized in this Treaty and being put where nothing can harm them, but we want to know on what basis they are going to be defended.
The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) in his closing remarks, which 1 think were a great deal wiser than the most of his speech, has just told us that if the League of Nations is any good and has any force it stands finally on the power
that lies behind it

or, in other words,
the amalgamation of the armies and navies that compose the forces at the back of the League of Nations. I think article 10 is worthy of serious debate, and I for one am not speaking with a view of making the slightest political capital for myself or for anybody else. I do not wish any individual, any government, or any cabinet minister, to be held responsible for any view that I hold with regard to article 10, but I say, in my judgment, that if the League of Nations has any backbone in it at all it is finally contained in the five or six lines composing the article referred to. First, you * have moral suasion, then you have diplomatic interference. Later on you have economic pressure, and the exercise of all those arts of civilization

that are apt to bring a recalcitrant nation into line. 'But when all these' have been tried without result, what is the final appeal? It may he said that it is unchristian, it may be said it is the old doctrine, but it is there in the Covenant just as truly as the English language can put it, in my judgment-it is " the big stick." Ii the League of Nations has any value, after it has tried all these expedients to bring the fractious nation into line, it has the expedient of telling them that if they are not open to reason, if they are not open to humanity's appeal, if they do not' have regard for other nations, if they fail to understand all other arguments-then, " If you won't do it, we will make you." That is the good old doctrine that ife as old as the hills, and that is going to stay with us, in my judgment, for all time in spite of our ideals-and I trust that my ideals in that regard are just as advanced as those of other gentlemen who may think I am giving utterance to a very heterodox suggestion. But I believe that, so far as the Scriptures themselves are concerned, they have taught us that when all these other things fail the final remedy is a sudden jerk-up:
"He that being often reproved and hardeneth his neck shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."
And there are many other passages in the Scriptures to the same effect. Now the League of Nations is replete with what I conceive to be pious opinions which are very beautiful, and pious observations which are very valuable, but in the few brief lines in Article 10 lies the crux of the whole situation, and in my judgment it means- and I repeat that I alone am responsible for what I am saying-that every nation that sanctions this Treaty will have to put up a certain amount of force to back it up later when it is required. My hon. friends opposite fear that that will be done without the ratification of Parliament. I cannot say whether it will be done with or without the ratification of Parliament, but if you are a member of the League of Nations as Canadians you will have to put up your share, or pay somebody else to put it up. That is my judgment and reading of Article 10, although that view may be all wrong. Can we escape our obligations? The argument of those gentlemen who shout so loud for Canadian autonomy, and shout so loud for Canadian nationality, and fail to realize that all these bring their obligations. I cannot understand. If ' we are a big enough nation to sign the Treaty we are a big enough nation to put up what is required of us, and we
will have to put up the men and the money that our population and our resources call for as compared with the other thirty-two or forty-two, or whatever number it may be later on, signatories to the League. I see many defects about the League, but I hope it will work out all right. I do not want to see difficulties that I can avoid, but let us consider this supposition: Suppose, for instance, Germany is again the aggressor and France is the object of attack? France's forces have been limited to probably less than 100,000 men-
I do not know the exact figures. Germany's forces have been placed at about 100,000 and they are only proportionately reduced. Suppose that France is again the object of attack. Where is the machinery contained in the League of Nations, or have any of the gentlemen who returned from overseas yet explained that point, to hold back the enemy while the League tells the different nations that compose the combination how quickly and how many men they are to get to the front? These are all questions that we must consider. France would be attacked and Paris would be entered before the United States forces could get over. You cannot get away from the possibility of future wars-they are there. I have here an article which deals very fully with this Treaty, and it makes the statement that Bonar Law, speaking six months after the armistice was signed, stated that there were twenty-three wars at present in progress. Twenty-three wars in progress six months after the armistice was signed! Then the League of Nations has got plenty of work ahead of it, and it is setting off in very stormy times; and if any gentleman on either side of the House thinks that we are in the position of using only moral suasion and reading texts of Scripture to those who threaten civilization, my own view is that they have another guess coming.
We are at the present moment up against the most unsettled conditions that the world has ever known. The Dark Ages of the past thousand or two thousand years contain no record of such atrocities as are at -this moment being committed in Russia and in other countries of Europe. The League of Nations, I hope, will be able to control all these things, but it appears to me that they have got a very big task ahead of them, and that we who are expecting to escape with little or no obligation will find that our modest army, which was raised last session from 5,000 to 10,000, will look very little in the presence of some of

the difficulties which we shall be called upon to settle.	[DOT]
If any one connected with the Government can give me any other interpretation than I have placed on Article X, I will be only too pleased to hear it; but in my judgment it carries most serious obligations. Those obligations I am prepared to assume, but I want hon. members to know that I am signing with my eyes open-that I believe my signing implies my assumption of these obligations. I think the qualms that affected the hon. member for Kamour-aska (Mr. Lapointe) yesterday are very well founded, and that whether or not Canada is a party to undertaking these obligations we cannot renounce them and remain as a constituent part of the League of Nations.
If the League of Nations means anything it means that all the civilized and enlightened Powers of the world are joining together to settle all difficulties with greater and lesser peoples by certain methods laid down within the four corners of that agreement. The principles are explicitly laid down, and probably for a time at least they will be lived up to to the letter; but I fear there is a rude awakening in the near future for many who think we have heard the last shot fired and seen the last battleship launched.
I do not want to he pessimistic, nor do I want to cast any cold water on the League of Nations or any other thing that will bring peace and happiness and unity to this war-stricken world; but I want to say that in my judgment we should not rest pur faith on any broken reed, nor should we believe that once this great Treaty is signed all trouble is ended forever. I have said that the United States is largely responsible for the idea of the League of Nations. I believe it has received a good deal of encouragement in other countries, notably Great Britain; but, if I am credibly informed, a great many of those in Great Britain who have advocated the League of Nations have done so with a view to appealing to the good opinion of the United States rather than in any belief that it was the final settlement of the ills of the whole world. I hold in my hand a document written by one of the most able men in Britain, the Duke of Northumberland. He is a man of affairs; he was involved in the coal strike and had to deal wjth some rather obstreperous individuals He has given here some reflections on the League of Nations, and as a good Britisher, as I profess to be, and believing him to be also an equally good if not better Britisher

than I am, I hope it will not be considered that 1 am endeavouring to do any harm to any feature of the Treaty if I read you a few of his reflections, which were published by him in England last month. This is what he says, in part:
At last the public have been informed what the League of Nations really means. It was certainly time, for if the future system of international relations is to be founded on this principle, the public should have known all about it long before this. It is true that no opinion they may express upon it will affect the question, because there is no intention of submitting the decision to them . This seems somewhat strange, in view of. what we have been told about the value of " open," as distinguished from " secret," diplomacy. Indeed, we are told that the great advantage of the League is that it is democratic ; it will bring all the peoples of the world into touch with the foreign policy of their Governments, but the foundation on which that foreign policy rests is nevertheless a. matter with which Parliament has no concern. If it had been left to the diplomatists to establish this system, the public might have been content to acquiesce, for, with all the faults of the old diplomacy, there is something to be said for the principle that "there is nothing like leather," but when the matter is left in the hands of a body of amateurs the public should be very chary of accepting their conclusions without exhaustive investigation.
Many excellent people-
This is what I wish all those who look upon the Treaty as something ideal to listen to very critically:
Many excellent people have greeted this scheme with enthusiasm, not so much from any conviction of its practical success as from a vague Idea that there is a kind of ethical or religious principle involved In it.

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Is there not?

maintopic: DERATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Yes, there is. I have already said that, and the Duke says that tha,t is the reason people are favourably impressed:
This idea has been fostered by the Church of England; many of its bishops, led by the Archbishop of Canterbury, who was present and spoke at the meeting at the Albert Hall, have given it their enthusiastic support. If their action had merely consisted in showing their approval of any honest effort on the part of a stricken world to establish peace on a secure foundation, no criticism could have been directed against it; hut they have gone much further than that, and their action really amounts to associating the Church with a political expedient. - "At bottom," said the Archbishop, speaking of the League, " it was the fruit of the Christian faith." Now, with all due deference to the Archbishop, this League no more deserves that description than, say, the Roman Empire, which was certainly a far more efficient League and had nothing whatever to do with the Christian faith. The truth is, it is just as much a political device as is any other principle of foreign policy. It is not a whit more Christian than the principle of the balance of power. But, apart from this,

there is apparently, to judge from- the phrases used, a vague notion that it is a means of achieving the Christian ideal. If this can be done by political means, what becomes of the Church's mission?
But, as a matter of fact, this policy is indistinguishable from that of the balance of power; both are based on the principle of combination against an aggressor. The only difference is that one is reasonably effective; the other is not. The fact that the supporters of the League claim, to quote Lord Robert Cecil, that it provides "machinery for the discussion of international labour questions, the improvement of health and hygiene, the protection of native races,'' the removal of abuses such as the sale of opium and of arrifcs and ammunition, etc., is no argument for the League at all. All these results could be obtained perfectly well by improving our diplomatic machinery and holding periodical International Conferences. But it may be said, Why object to the League? It can do no harm-at least it points us to an ideal of brotherhood and closer co-operation between nations. The answer to this question is that the League would be harmless if it rendered us more, instead o>f less prepared for war in the future. Its supporters do not, of course, assert any such exaggerated claim as that it eliminates the danger of war, but they do assert that it will tend to remove the minor causes of conflict by a general improvement in the system of international relations, and that we shall be better prepared for war because we shall receive more notice when a danger arises, and the whole machinery of the League will be brought into play to avert it. But this argument really ignores the danger of a future attempt to dominate the world such as has been made by Germany.
The writer goes on at considerable length, and I would like to read the whole statement if time permitted, but I do not wish to weary the House, and so I shall read but another sentence or two:
The opponents of the League are accused of having no alternative to offer. As a matter of fact, the League has probably sacrificed a finer opportunity for establishing peace on a sure foundation than has existed at any previous period in history. The Entente Powers were, after the Armistice, absolutely supreme- they could have imposed any conditions both on enemies and neutrals. With a definite offensive and defensive alliance between Italy, France, Belgium, Holland and .Denmark; with the British fleet securely established at the mouth of the Baltic and with Constantinople in Our hands ; with a combined, carefully thought out scheme of defence, of a line stretching from tha North Sea to the Swiss frontier; with a definite guarantee of military support from Great Britain ; with Germany deprived of essential requirements for the manufacture, of munitions and materials of war; with the British fleet in a position to blockade every German harbour at a few hours' notice-the western Allies would at least have been secure for the next fifty years or more. Whether they will be so now is problem atical.
These and other arguments as advanced by the Duke of Northumberland are, it appears to me, worthy of the very serious consideration of those who think that the
British nation as a whole is fully in accord with the idea of a League of Nations.
I have dealt somewhat fully with this League of Nations because I believe it is the principal stumbling block in the way of ratification of the Treaty. As I say, in my judgment the Covenant of the League of Nations should have been dealt with separately. The Treaty of Peace with Germany, Austria, Turkey and Bulgaria could have been submitted to us many months ago had it not been for this League of Nations. Probably the Treaty of Peaee would have been signed long ago and then the League of Nations, if it was to be gone into, could have been taken up later, the matter being given full deliberation and due regard being had to all the obligations entailed by the League upon Canada and upon every othe' country which would be a party to it.
Article 21 of the Covenant reads as follows:
Nothing in this Covenant shall be deemed cO affect the validity of international engagements, such as treaties of arbitration or regional under standings like the Monroe doctrine, for securing the maintenance of peace.
That looks to me like a kind of mental reservation placed there for the purpose of appeasing an outcry that was being made by our neighbours to the South. It may be that it was justified, hut I suppose every other nation could have submitted something concerning which they would like to have had special treatment. I do not approve of the mentioning of the Monroe doctrine ahead of any other doctrine that might be mentioned by any of the other signatories to this Treaty.
Here is what Article 26 says about amendments :
Amendments to this Covenant will take effect when ratified by the Members of the League whose Representatives compose the Council and by a majority of the Members of the League whoes Representatives compose the Assemblv.
No such amendment shall bind any Member of the League which signifies its dissent therefrom, but in that case it shall cease to he i Member of the League.
So that if amendments are submitted and adapted, any of the thirty-two powers who do not approve of the .amendments must cease to be members of the League. It looks to me as if it will very .soon be a dwindling League. It is quite passible to contemplate that in the not very distant future, Germany and associated powers, invited somewhat later on to enter the League, may be the main voting force in the League before it is finally destroyed- as I expect it will be, in time.

number of the population of the earth; but when we think of all the destruction that has been caused and all the outrages that have been committed during this war, I, for one, think that punishment of a fitting nature should be meted out to every one of those high in authority who can be proved guilty of such gross outrages on a long-suffering humanity, such as the sinking of the Lusitania, with its innocfent thousands on board, or the deaths that I have referred to*, and the hundreds and thousands that have been killed in air raids who had nothing whatever to do with the war and whose taking off could have no effect whatever on its outcome. In my judgment all these acts call for punishment-not vengeance but punishment of a kind that they who committed these outrages can understand; for there are certain [DOT] classes of punishment that the ordinary German does not understand. Therefore I would hit him in the pocket, because that is the most sensitive part of his constitution. I would hit him also for the brutal outrages that were committed in the name of war necessity, and which were no more necessary and could no more be justified than taking the life of a new-born babe. These acts call for condign punishment. Though I have not mastered all the provisions in the Treaty for the punishment of these people, I trust that the punishment will be good and proper, and that these people will be put in their places.
I close these few imperfect remarks by saying that I look upon the ratification of this Treaty as the most serious step we shall ever be called upon to take as long as we live. I look upon this occasion as the most momentous which the Canadian Parliament has. ever faced. I recognize that the Treaty carries obligations that bind us and our children, and will continue to bind us as long as the Treaty exists and we are members of the League. But, as the Treaty has gone as far as it has, although I have many misgivings as to its final success, I am willing to accept the League and advocate the ratification of this Treaty by this House. Though I recognize it as an experiment, as the most gigantic experiment that the world has ever tried, I heartily wish it Godspeed and every success; and if any act of mine, or any prayers of mine, can help to make this Treaty a success and bring the blessings to the world that are foreshadowed here I would regard it as a glorious privilege. I appeal to my friends opposite not to make

this a party question. I am in accord with a great many of the things that have been said on the other side of the House, but I am going to support the Treaty because I cannot see that there is anything else that we can do. I do not think my hon. friends opposite can .rightly do anything else. I want to see the House stand united on this Treaty, While we may wish to make mental reservations, or even written reservations, it is not permitted for us to do so at .this stage. Therefore, I ask hon. gentlemen to take it on faith, the same as I am doing, and with their voice and vote and work help to make this Treaty the grand success that President Wilson and those associated with him expect it to be, so that the world may rise to a higher and better plane, and Christianity and civilization and the rights of the weak may prevail. I ask you gentlemen not to make any party capital out of so great a question, but when this question comes to a vote, vote on it not simply as a national question but one of international importance that will have the most far-reaching effects on every country in the world.
On motion of Mr. L. J. Papineau, the debate was adjourned.

Moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7, to amend the Adulteration Act (respecting bran and shorts or middlings).
Explain.

The object of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, is to prevent what has become a common practice, moTe particularly on the part of the large milling companies of Canada, namely, the adulteration of bran and shorts or middlings by adding thereto an enormous quantity of both ground and unground weed seeds, which is permissible under existing legislation, although entailing heavy losses annually on those engaged in raising and feeding live stock, and in agriculture generally.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I would like to call the attention o! the Government to a despatch which appeared in yesterday evening's city papers, purporting to be from Australia and having reference to the indemnity to be paid to that Dominion by Germany. The despatch is dated Melbourne, September 1, and is in this form:
Premier Hughes has informed the members of the Australian cabinet that if Germany makes the first indemnity payment toy 1920, Australia's share will toe ten million pounds sterling.
When the indemnity was fully paid, he stated, Australia's share would toe nearly sixty million pounds sterling.
Is the Government in a position to inform the House whether that is a correct statement or not, and if it is, how does Canada's share in regard to indemnity correspond with that which is claimed for Australia?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position, of course, to express any opinion as to whether Mr. Hughes' estimate-as I assume it to be- of the amount of indemnity which Australia may ultimately receive is or is not accurate. I presume that he based his estimate upon such claims as he may have knowledge that the Government of Australia contemplate making, and which he anticipates would be allowed, and likewise upon such reliable knowledge as he may believe himself to he in possession of as to the claims which will be established by the other Allied and Associated Powers, and the consequent portion which might equitably be allotted to-Australia. This is the only method by which I can .see he is able to arrive at the figures mentioned. Of course, as I say, it is quite impossible for me to express any opinion as to the accuracy of his method.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TRANSFER OF CANADIAN OWNED SHIPS TO CANADIAN REGISTRY.
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition



(Mr. McKenzie) yesterday asked me if I could give any information whether ships no.t British, which were under charter to Canadian companies, and which were commandeered by the British Government, will be returned to the former charterers, and I promised to inquire and make answer to-day. The question doubtless refers 'to ships owned in Great Britain and registered there, under long-term charter to Dominion Coal Company. These ships were requisitioned during the period of the war by the British Government. Immediately following the termination of the war, representations were made by the Canadian Government to His Majesty's Government, requesting that these vessels should, with the least possible delay, be returned to the chartering company. In a despatch from the Secretary of State for the Colonies to the Governor General dated 26th June, the contents of which despatch were communicated to the House of Commons by the Prime Minister on 1st July last, and may be found in unrevised Hansard at page 4477, it is stated that of the five vessels in which Dominion Coal Company are interested, three have bfeen released from requisition and returned to the owners, and the remaining two are to be released as soon as present cargoes are discharged. It is understood that these two were undergoing extensive repairs, and if they have not already been released to the owners, they will be -as soon as they are ready to be placed in commission. We have not heard that they have not been released.

speechtext:
On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. 0. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) : I should like to say just a word about the procedure in connection with the matter which is at present the main subject of debate in the House, the Peace Treaty. The other day a request was made that at some period before the discussion on the resolution was concluded the House should go into committee upon it, and the Prime Minister expressed his willingness to meet that desire. Apart from that desire and the willingness to meet it, it is, of course, not necessary that there should be any committee stage on this resolution. That being the case, unless the desire which has been expressed still persists, it appears to us that w-e should not interrupt or curtail the debate for the purpose of putting the resolu-
TMr. Rowell. 1
tion into committee. If, on the other hand, the desire to which I have referred still persists, we, of course, would he willing, at such a time as may be found convenient by the House, to meet that desire.

maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: The understanding between the Prime Minister and myself was that we should finish to-day the business in connection with this resolution. No particular time was -assigned one way or the other, in respect either of the discussion before the Speaker or of the discussion in committee. My own view is that we should get into committee as soon as possible, when all members have spoken who wish to speak at this stage, and devote as much time as we can to the resolution in committee. I aim not, of course, in a position ito say when the committee -stage will be reached.

maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: I would like to ask, Mr. Speaker, by what right -two men in this House-, the leader of the Government, and the leader of the Opposition, come to an arrangement as to- the -time when this discussion should close, without doing their followers the courtesy of referring the matter to them? This is the most'momentous question that has ever come before this House : it has to do with the greatest event that has taken -place in the world since the birth of Christ. Unless there is some strong reason why we should get through-and if there is, the members of the House should have been consulted with regard to it-I do not see why this debate should he curtailed. After all, we are sent here -to represent our constituents and to express such humble views as w-e -may have on these questions. I would like to know, therefore, whether there is s-ome authority with which I, -as a green member, am not familiar under which these debates can be concluded at a certain time upon the arbitrary decision of the leader of -the- Government and -the- leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: The question is of course entirely in -the hands of the House.

maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: I m-ay say that I took the best terms I could get from the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext:
I should like to have it -clearly understood that in the making of -the arrangement there was no purpose of curtailing the liberty of debate, more especially no purpose or intention of preventing horn, members -from having opportunity of discussing as fully as they might desire the terms and conditions of the Treaty.

But there was this very important consideration; the Treaty will not be ratified until the Government of this country is in a position to advise His Majesty upon that subject. Prior to giving that advice, the Government have submitted the Treaty for approval by the Parliament of Canada.

maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. I understand that every member must speak to the Chair. It would give us a great deal of comfort if the hon. gentleman would speak to the Chair so that we may be able to hear him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was under
the impression that I was speaking to the Chair, though for the moment my face was turned in another direction. I trust that Mr. Speaker will appreciate the fact that no discourtesy was intended to him. I have, of course, every desire to make myself heard. '
It was because of the necessity of enabling the ratification of the Treaty to take place at as early a moment as possible that this arrangement was arrived at as to the disposal of this resolution.
I might add that there will be full and ample time for the most complete discussion of the treaty, on the Bill which has beep introduced into this House for the purpose of conferring upon the Governor in Council the necessary power to give effect to that treaty. There was not and is not any desire to curtail the liberty of debate, and, moreover, as the Speaker has said, the matter is, of course, in the hands of the House. I think, in so far as that latter observation is concerned, it would be well that members of the House should bear in mind the importance of promptitude, consistent always with fair consideration in dealing with this particular matter. That the treaty should be promptly ratified is of great importance by reason of the fact that it will become effective as determining all the delays provided for in the treaty, from the time that it has received the ratification of Germany and three of the great powers. The British Empire, of which we are one of the constituent nations, is one great power to be counted amongst those three, and it is important, in order that we, along with the rest of the world, may begin at the earliest possible moment to benefit by the further proceedings that may be carried on, that we should not retard that ratification by the British Empire of which we are a part. I understand the United Kingdom is in a position to act, and I think, other nations as well.

maintopic: THE DEBATE ON THE PEACE TREATY- DISCUSSION ON THE PROCEDURE.
speechtext: I have no particular views on the point of procedure which has just been referred to, but I am afraid I shall have to take exception to the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) that this treaty can be discussed in committee when the Bill is before us. The Bill does not ratify the treaty; the Bill deals with matters of detail, and I believe any hon. member raising the question can succeed in establishing that you cannot discuss the treaty in committee on the Bill. The treaty will then have been dealt with and approved, and you can discuss only ' matters contained in the Bill itself. I have no particular complaint to make, nor point of procedure to take exception to, but I question whether my hon. friend's suggestion will be found feasible.
