subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the following proposed motion of Sir Robert Borden, adjourned from September 10:
That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany (and the Protocol annexed thereto), which was signed at Versailles on the twenty-eighth day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen, a copy of which has been laid before Parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiaries therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.

speakeroldname: Hon. WILLIAM STEVENS FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I believe, Mr Speaker, that the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers on the one side and Germany on the other, which Treaty we are invited .to consider, is in the main a good Treaty. It has been described by .some one, I am not sure by whom, as being next to the Holy 'Scriptures, the grandest document in human history, and there is something in its character tq justify the description so given. That there should be some dissent from some of the provisions of the Treaty is certainly not a matter of surprise. If we have regard to the vastness of the problems with which the Treaty deals, if we have regard to the many rival and conflicting interests with which it had to deal, to the efforts required to reconcile those differences, the wonder is noit that there is still some difference but that the statesmen who were assembled around the table at Paris were

able to find, in so large a measure, an agreement upon that which they had under consideration.	[DOT]
As to the Covenant of the League of Nations, which forms a part of the Treaty, while it would be too much to say that it is not open to some criticism, and possibly some reservations, I think we should all regard it also as a noble effort to put an end to the horrors of war and to give to a distressed world the blessings of peace. I have no hesitation in saying that the statesmen, whoever they were, who had any active part in bringing about the completion of the Treaty, including the Covenant of the League of Nations, have rendered a service for which they deserve the thanks of the civilized world.
But we are discussing in this debate not merely the merits of the Treaty itself. The debate has taken a wide range, and we have been spending a good deal of our time in discussing the policy of the Government regarding the Treaty, and particularly the claim that they have made that, by this Treaty, and by the proceedings in connection with it, there has been a great advance in the constitutional status of Canada. That aspect of the question obliges me to express some dissent. I want to speak for myself alone, for I shall not be surprised if some of the views I may have occasion to utter will not altogether be endorsed by hon. gentlemen on either side of the House; but one must call a spade- a spade, and it is my emphatic judgment that the whole policy of the Government in relation to the Peace Conference and in regard to the proceedings which they are now asking us to engage in is a colossal .humbug, designed to impose upon an innocent Parliament and to bamboozle a too-credulous people, who have been led to believe that our statesmen who went over to Paris did some Canadian business, a belief for which there is no foundation whatever. It is my judgment that it was not necessary for our representatives to go to Paris under the terms and conditions which took them there. It is my judgment that the present procedure for ratifying, or approving if the word is preferred, this Treaty, is entirely unnecessary, and, therefore, I am unable to treat the situation with the gravity which some hon. gentlemen have been attaching to it.
Let me guard against a mistake. If any man in this House or out of it says that I am content that the interests of Canada shall at any time be disposed of by men who are not representatives of Canada, he

will be saying that for which there is no foundation whatever. Whenever there are Canadian interests at stake, I shall be found standing for the vindication of those interests, for their representation, before any tribunal which may be called to deal with them, by Canada's proper and responsible representatives, the ministers of the Crown, or by men chosen by the ministers of the Crown. If the question under consideration is one of our Imperial relations, one within our own family circle, I shall be among the foremost to insist on the maintenance of the autonomy of Canada; I shall be among the foremost to claim that we shall uphold and adhere to every constitutional right that has been won for Canada by the efforts of our statesmen who have passed away. If a question is to arisd in relation to some foreign country, I shall be prepared to maintain, as in the past, that in the treatment of that question Canada shall be represented by responsible ministers of the -Crown, or somebody- chosen by them. In these two cases, the one of our own Imperial relations, the other as to our relations with a foreigv country, wherever there is a real interest of Canada at stake, I want Canada to be represented by the ministers of the Crown, the chosen representatives of the people. When there is something going on in which Canada has no interest, when there is something in which Canada, if she has an interest at all, has only that remote interest which comes to every citizen of the British Empire, an interest which we share in common with our respected fellow-citizens of the Fiji Islands, when there is that kind of a question or a group of questions to -be considered, I would not waste the time of four ministers of the Crown and a great deal of public money in having the representatives of Canada try to deal with such questions. In short, I would have Canada represented, and adequately represented, when there was any Canadian business to be done; I would not be over anxious to have her represented when there was no Canadian business to be done, and the latter ' seems to me to have been largely the situation with regard to the proceedings in connection with the Peace Treaty.
There is a sentiment in this matter, I suppose, as well as facts, and the two should be considered, I do not undervalue sentiment; far from it. Noble sentiments move men to noble deeds, and very often there are times when we may put aside all other considerations and be moved by high and noble sentiments. But sentiment is only of value when it can be harmonized with

facts. When .sentiment runs up against cold facts it does not weigh very much. Now there are some cold facts in connection with the Peace Conference which we should consider. There is one great basic underlying fact that I am anxious that this House and the country should absorb, because it is the foundation of my contention, and that underlying basic fact is that there was no business of Canada before the Peace Conference at Paris. Our representatives first went to England. That was quite right. The British Government had given the assurance that the Dominionsi would be consulted when the time for peace-making approached, and it was a very proper undertaking for the British Government to give. Undoubtedly it was the right thing for our ministers to go over to England and discuss the matter fully with the British Government, but when they found that there was no Canadian business coming before the Conference I do not think it was a wise policy to press for representation, especially for representation separate and apart from the British Empire. We had some little discussion of the matter last year when I presented a little evidence, as I think Hansard will show, of how our delegates were obliged to spend their time over there. Let no man say for a single moment that I am desiring in any way to undervalue the talents of our representatives over there, still less, that I desire to belittle them. It would be a silly thing to do, and the man who would attempt it would only succeed in belittling 'himself. The gentlemen who represented Canada are eminent public men of unquestioned ability and large experience in the public life of this country, and if there had been any Canadian business to do they would have done it. They did not do any Canadian business, through no fault of their own, but simply because there was no Canadian business to do. The evidence which I was able to submit to the House last session went clearly to show that these gentlemen had the greatest difficulty in filling in the time; they did not know quite what to do. There were a number of committees appointed on a variety of subjects, and the managers of the Conference distributed our friends over these committees and their names were published in the press. There was a system which I mentioned to the House last year of what one of the delegates expressed as " eyewash," which meant that with nothing to do they were making an effort to lead the public to suppose they had something to do. That was all set forth in the House
last session. It had a humorous side then, but time, experience, and this Treaty now show that those statements were substantially cgrreet. These gentlemen did not do anything concerning Canada, not because they had not the ability-they had it-not because they had not the desire-they had it-but because there was absolutely no Canadian business coming before that gathering.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman if the sacrifices we made in the field, and the 55,000 dead we left in the fields of France and Flanders, did not give us the right to say something about the conditions of the Peace that was to be concluded?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: IT there were any Canadian interests in the world affected there would be no question of our right. The sacrifices that were made by the 50,000 or 60,000 Canadians now lying on the fields of the Continent would give us a claim to any position that we want in considering the affairs, of the nation, but they do not give us a claim to make ourselves ridiculous by undertaking to deal with things of which we know nothing.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that the Canadian people have no interest in the peace of the world?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
We are a part of the
British Empire, and I desire that we shail always remain so, and I therefore regret the policy of hon. gentlemen in pleading for separate recognition apart from the British Empire. By their demand for separate recognition apart from the British Empire they are beginning-they may not have meant it so-to break up the British Empire. There is no question of our rights as within the Empire to participate in all its deliberations. We have in the representatives of the British Government in London statesmen who would take due account of the interests of the Empire at large. I again say that upon any point where Canadian interests were particularly affected it would be desirable that we should have special representation, but when there was no Canadian business before them, when no Canadian interests were affected, I say it was not wise for us to insist upon having representation of Canada when there was really nothing of importance from a Canadian point of view for our representatives to consider.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend object to our

representation if the Old Country had asked for it?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I should like to have the correspondence before answering that question.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I will produce it

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Will my
hon. friend permit me a question? Were we not as Canadians interested in the ports of Hamburg and Dantzig?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes. The only interest we have in them is one which would certainly have been adequately protected by the British statesmen, and that interest is that we should have free access to them. But there is no provision that Canada should have any particular access to them. Will mys hon. friend suggest that if Sir Robert Borden had not gone over, Lloyd George, Clemenceau, and Orlando would not have taken the greatest care to ensure that there was no discrimination against them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I merely suggest this,
that where Canada as Canada has interests, even though other nations have the same interests, our interests should be looked after by those who represent this country and are responsible to it, and not by those selected by any Parliament or people not answerable to us.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Is that a question?
iMr. FIELDING:	I do not object. We
have no interest that is not the common interest of the world at large in that port question, and it is preposterous to contend that it was necessary to send over delegates from the Dominion of Canada to arrange about the waterways of the Danube, the Elbe, the Oder and the Niemen. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if we have any interest in these things it is the common interest of the Empire at large, and there was no special interest to Canada which called for special representation.
Then my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster),
we are told, was Chairman of a commission on economic questions. Well, Sir, if you read over the forty or fifty clauses relating to economic questions you will find no reference to anything in which Canada is particularly interested.	_
The great purpose of the economic clauses was to see that Germany, in the new order of things, did not discriminate against the Allies. Will my hon. friend suggest that, if our delegates had not gone there, Germany would have been permitted to discriminate against the Allies? Was it not one of the most natural things in the world that the Allied representatives should insist that Germany should- not be permitted to discriminate against them? My hon. friend the Minister of Interior (Mr. Meighen) will hardly' ask us to believe that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce had not been present some exception would have been made by which Canada could have been discriminated against while all ^ the rest of the civilized world enjoyed free access. During the time that these hon.	gentlemen wdre absent,
serious conditions were prevailing in Canada. Never in the history of this Dominion was there more need of the concentrated attention of the ministers of the Crown than during the past year. When we consider the unrest that existed, the strikes that were growing almost to revolution in one of our great cities-,-when we regard all these things, surely we must admit that it was a time for ministers to be at home and not elsewhere, if their presence abroad was not imperative. If their presence was necessary over there, if they were dealing with Canadian questions, then . undoubtedly much could be said in defence of their absence. But inasmuch as they were not dealing with Canadian business, I am one of those who say that it would have been wiser had they come home. Was there unrest? Yes, unfortunately; everybody knows there was. But if the men who thought that our ministers ought to have been at home at that time still entertain that view, I beg them to take comfort in the reflection that while they were not here they were carefully considering the navigation of the Danube. If in the presence of the strikes which existed there were men who thought that our ministers should have been at home to join with their colleagues in the consideration of these grave matters, I ask these men to be patient and enduring, because the explanation is that our ministers were exceedingly busy in arranging the affairs of Czechoslovakia. And if our Budget was delayed, if the business of Can-

arrant humbug. The ratification by Great Britain is beyond all question effective. There cannot be a debate about that. I do not believe that any of my hon. friends in the Government-and they include some able lawyers-will stand up and say that in his opinion, if we did not pass this resolution, the Treaty would cease to be effective. One does not need to be a lawyer to see that. An ordinary layman, like myself, can easily see that when the British Empire, through His Majesty the King, ratifies the Treaty, it is ratified for every part of the British Empire. Therefore I think the procedure here is really a' bit of humbug; it is not necessary.
The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) put a question the other day to the President of the Privy Council which was very pertinent. He asked: What about Newfoundland, what is her status? Has she not the same status as we, and what is she doing? The President of the Privy Council replied that it was as much as he could do to answer for Canada, and he was not called upon to answer for Newfoundland-a very fair and proper answer. But the idea that was in the question of the hon. member for Dorchester remains: What is Newfoundland's position? In all that 'Constitutes status-that overworked word "status"- Newfoundland stands on even terms with Canada. She is a smaller country than Canada; she is an older colony than Canada; she is now known as the Dominion of Newfoundland. For all purposes of constitutional discussion Newfoundland is exactly in the same position as Canada. The Premier of Newfoundland went ovct to the Conference in England. I am not sure, but I think he went to Paris; if he did so, he speedily discovered that there was no business there concerning Newfoundland, and he had the good sense to come home and attend to Newfoundland's business.
_ Our ministers, when they made a similar discovery respecting Canada's business, were content to stay there and go through the tomfoolery of attending to business that was not Canada's.

speechtext: I do not object to the question of the hon. gentleman. From my point of view it was out of order, except on the point that no member can interrupt another member who is addressing the Chair. But I do not take the objection that the question is out of order, although I do not think in this instance it was a wise question to put. Shall I tell the hon. gentleman that I have only one son? He enlisted as a private soldier in the month of August, 1914, he saw service, and is now home with an honourable discharge, having won his commission after two years in the ranks.

speechtext:
I have said that in my judgment the ratification or approval of this Treaty is not necessary by this Parliament, and-I hope the word is not offensive *-it seems to me that it is a part of the general humbug surrounding this matter.
I suppose the ministers can fool some people over this question, but I know they cannot fool their own friends over it. They cannot fool that.eminently respectable Conservative newspaper the Montreal Gazette, for a few days ago the Gazette said:
The Bill to ratify the Peace Treaty, which is the excuse

Oh, I want you to notice that word "excuse".	'
-for the special meeting should go through as a matter of course. The Parliament of the United Kingdom has given its sanction to the instrument, and no matter what any legislative

todies of the colonies may do, in due time the Empire will he at peace with Germany.
So the Gazette sees through this foolish pretence that we have to ratify or approve of the Treaty. The Gazette is right; the ministers are wrong.
Then there is another thought: I do not think ratification is needed at all, I do not think approval is needed at all; but if approval were needed, it did not require a special session of Parliament for that purpose. I am not as well informed as I would like to he regarding events in the Sister Dominions, but so far as I know there has 'been no special session of any Parliament of the Sister Dominions. Perhaps my hon. friends the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) or the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) can inform me if that is so.

speechtext: My information is that Parliaments in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand have been convened for this month for the purpose of dealing with the Treaty. Whether the- sessions are special or regular, I do not know. The South African Parliament is now in session; I think New Zealand has already approved the Treaty, and it is now, I believe, before the Australian Parliament.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
The point I desire to make is this: If approval was necessary it could have been had without a special session of Parliament. We made a change in the fiscal year some years ago, for a distinct purpose. It was found that when Parliament assembled, as it usually did, at the end of January or in February, the sessions were protracted into the summer, and it was thought desirable to make a change whereby the sessions could begin much earlier and end much earlier. Formerly the fiscal year ended on the first of July. It took about seven months to get papers and records together, and that threw the session into the months of January or February. Therefore we changed	the fiscal	year so that
it ended on the 31st day' of March. Allow the same seven months and Parliament could meet in October or November. It is as easy now for Parliament to meet in October or November as it formerly was to meet in January or February. So with a diligence on the part of the ministers after they came home, a little diligence on the part of the officials, instead of meeting on the first day of September we could have met in October and had the advantage of a very early session of Parliament, so that we would not need a special session. Now we are called together in a special
session w'hich I do not hesitate to say is not necessary; I join the Montreal Gazette, which is a strong Conservative paper not accustomed to deal rashly with public questions, in stating that the Peace Treaty is only an excuse for this parliamentary session. We are unnecessarily, wastefully, called together in a special session of Parliament which will cost at least a million dollars of public money. We are asked to practise thrift and economy; we are called upon to exercise all the virtues that men ought to practise to-day-and the Government sets the example by calling a special session of Parliament which is not needed at all and flinging away at least a million dollars.
With regard to the status to which my hon. friends attach so much importance, 1 really think it is very much magnified; as I said a moment ago, the word has been very much overworked, We have a written constitution; by it the status of Canada is fixed, and there can be no material change in our constitutional position except through an amendment of the British North America Act. There has been no such amendment; there has been no change in the status of Canada; actually at this moment there is no change in Canada's constitutional status. We have gained in prestige-you may call it status if you like, if you do not use the word in a constitutional sense.
Canada plays a much higher and a much bigger part in the affairs of the world than she ever did, and of that we are all proud. Canada's increasing prestige has been brought about in our time by three events. The first was in 1897, when under the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier the commercial system under the British preference was introduced. Undoubtedly that added much to Canada's prestige in the eyes of the world; undoubtedly that added prestige to Canada's position throughout what I may call the colonial Empire. And may I not pause just to remark that whatever prestige we gained by the ,step which was then taken, whatever increased status came to Canada as a result of that step, was accomplished in the face of the strenu-our hostility of the present Prime Minister.
The second thing which added to the prestige or the status of Canada, if you wish to call it that, was the South African war. Then hundreds and thousands of the sons of Canada volunteered for service and went away down to South Africa to fight for the flag. Undoubtedly that made a deep impression upon the British mind everywhere.

do we want? That is practically giving us the right to make our own treaties. I cannot understand the meaning of this cry from time to time about the need of enlarged status. I have no sympathy with the cry that something must be done. I do not believe for a single moment that we have any reason to fear Canada's political future. The British Constitution has developed a remarkable capacity for adapting itself to the changing conditions of the times, and I believe it will continue to do so. I believe that, from day to day and from month to month, by various methods, by our conferences, by the communications that are taking place, by greater intercourse, by all these things, we shall gradually come to have a stronger and stronger power in our relations with the Mother Country. I do not know how you are going to define it; I do not attempt to define it myself; I am content to express my hope and belief that it will come. I had occasion in a previous discussion, a little while ago, to use some words which I can hut repeat, because they express the thought which is in my mind and that which I believe represents the thought of the people of Canada:
"I want Canada to have all the freedom that is possible in the management of Canadian affairs, all the unity with the Mother Country that is possible without the sacrifice of the freedom we now enjoy, and I want Canada to be all the time a part of the British Empire."
I have an abiding faith that if any circumstances shall arise in which a difference shall seem to exist between the Mother Country and ourselves, the statesmanship which has been developed in the past will continue, and we shall find a way which shall be consistent with our own freedom, our own autonomy, and with the unity of the British Empire.
There is one part of the Covenant of the League of Nations which has been the subject of very much consideration and discussion both here and elsewhere. I refer to Article 10 of the Covenant. It has been read before, but I must ask permission to. read it again because it is necessary for the comment I wish to make:
The Members of the League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all Members of the League. In case of any stich 'aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
Upon that Council Canada could technically have representation, but practically
TMr Fielding. 1
she cannot. The Council is composed of the representatives of the Five Great Powers who are always to be members, with four others to be chosen by the Assembly, Canada will have her vote in the Assembly. She could be chosen to be one of the members of the Council, but is it conceivable that the thirty odd nations are going to name Canada to fill one of these places when the British Government aueady has a seat on the Council? I do not think it. is possible. Technically, it is possible. If you say that. Canada could be chosen by all these small nations, I do not dispute that fact, but that it ever will be chosen is highly improbable. Therefore it seems that Canada by Article X is going to be, I will not say at the mercy, for that is not the right word, but at all events subject to the will in matters of vast concern of a Council on which she can have no representative. I am justified in making that statement. Instead of having an improvement in our status, I am going to submit to the House that we have an impairment of our status by this Treaty, unless we take pains to protect ourselves. What would be the position if we take absolutely no action? If this session had never been called, and if the Treaty had been ratified, as it will be ratified, by His Majesty; the King, what would be the effect upon Canada? It would bind the whole British Empire. It would bind every foot of soil which is under the British flag. But it would bind Canada subject to the terms of the Canadian constitution, and while Canada would be technically bound by that ratification no power under Heaven but the Parliament of Canada, so long as the British North America Act remains, could issue an order to send one Canadian soldier overseas. That was the position in 1914, Immediately the declaration of war was made in August, 1914, Canada was at war, because Great Britain was at war. If the German fleet had the next day bombarded Quebec; St. John or Halifax that would have been entirely within their rights. We were at war, but no power other than this Parliament could determine what part we would take in that1 war. That was our position then; that is our position today. The ratification of the Treaty by His Majesty the King would bind Canada, but it would bind her subject to the terms of the Canadian constitution. We are going to lose that power if this Treaty be ratified without any reservation whatever. I think it must be clear that under Article 16 this Council may determine that an act of war has been committed and can demand of any country within the League of Nations

that it shall contribute a certain proportion of the forces necessary to enforce the commands of the League. I do not^think there ought to be any doubt about that. However, I must speak with deference, because my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council said the other day that that was not the proper interpretation. I noticed my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) indicate just now by a movement of his head that he did not agree with me. He also claims, no doubt, that the interpretation I put upon it is not the correct one. I am only going to ask them to admit this, that it is a debatable question. It is a question upon which men may differ, and have differed. Able and brilliant lawyers in the United States have said that that is what it means. My hon. friend the President of the Privy Council says it does not mean that. The Prime Minister has said on different occasions that in anything that may be done with regard to our status the autonomy of Canada is going to be preserved at all costs.
I think he said so in his speech the other day. Again and again at different sessions the Prime Minister has declared " Do not be afraid of any of our negotiations. Whatever else may happen we are going to stand for Canada's autonomy.'' He brought a resolution to that effect from the Imperial Conference quite recently. All I ask my hon. friends opposite to admit is that it is a debatable question. They may be right; other men will think otherwise. Since my hon. friends opposite are of that opinion, I am going to ask them to join me in protecting the autonomy of Canada by an amendment which I am about to move; not an amendment to the Treaty, that could not be done, not even a reservation, but a declaration that in approving this Treaty we have no intention of abandoning Canadian autonomy. I beg to move, seconded by my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe), if I may use his name, that the following words be added to the resolution:
That in giving such approval this House in no way assents to any impairment of the existing autonomous authority of the Dominion, but declares that the question of what part, if any, the forces of Canada shall take in any war, actual or threatened, is one to be determined at all times as occasion may require by the people of Canada through their representatives in Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very sorry indeed to be any party to adding any contribution to anything that may have sounded discourteous in the present debate. I
congratulate this House that in the course of this debate there has hot been anything of that kind unless it be found in the somewhat emphatic expressions which the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Fielding) has seen proper to apply to men whose actions he would not belittle to save his veTy life. Inasmuch as he told us that the man who would belittle the ministers who went over to the other side to represent Canada would merely belittle himself,
I should like to ask him what we are to think of a man who spends from an hour to an hour and a half belittling, not any individual men, however great they may be. but belittling his own country. I ask the hon. gentleman to reflect on that. From start to finish of his speech he was intent on showing how insignificant Canada is, how utterly useless was any contribution to any question interesting the people of this world that might be made by the people of his own country through their representatives. We were implored to see how absolutely absurd it was to suggest that perhaps Canada, on any question that, interesting as it .might be to Canada was interesting at the same time to any body else, might like to say a word about the whole question. We were implored to confine ourselves to things that interested Canada and that by no possibility could be of the slightest consequence to any body else. We were lectured, because, forsooth, we were of opinion, and acted on that opinion, that in this world Canada holds a place, and holds that thing which the hon. gentleman so greatly contemns holds a status that entitles her to respect, and entitles her to expect that people will listen to her voice and to claim her right to express by her own statesmen her own views on those things which, because they do interest the civilized world, interest this Canada of ours that is taking and means to hold its place of influence among civilized nations. Mr. Speaker, if we are never to speak about any matter or any question that is not exclusively a Canadian question, might I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) why we felt called upon to send our 500,000 soldiers to pour out their blood upon the battlefields of Europe, and why we have imposed upon ourselves a financial burden which it will take us and our children after us years and years to discharge? There was no question in that war that interested Canada exclusively. Great Britain, the British Empire, France, Italy, Belgium, the civilization of the world, were interested in the questions at stake; and if the hon. gentleman were

logical, he would have asked: Why should Canada spend money and send men about a matter that did not interest her exclusively? I say, Mr. Speaker, that that language is language that belittles our country. The hon. gentleman stated that in what he was going to express he would probably find himself differing from other hon. gentlemen even on his own side of the House. I am glad to believe, even more glad to know, that in what he said in that regard he does differ from many men on the other side of the House, as well as, I venture to say, from all men on this side.
The hon. gentleman told us that this was a good Treaty, taking it as a whole. He told us that the Covenant of the League of Nations, taken as a whole, was acceptable to him; and upon a motion to approve that Treaty he proceeded to give us an argument directed to demonstrating the absolute inferiority of Canada's position as compared with any of the other nations of the world, and her position of absolute supordination within this Empire to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. And he did this because, he said, we had made on this side of the House extravagant claims with regard to the progress made by Canada in the paths that lead to nationhood. Then at very considerable length he fought with a bogey of apprehensions which he seemed to consider existed somewhere about the future relations between Canada and other parts of the Empire. He was at great pains to fight these apprehensions. He inquired again and again what reasons there were, and why it was that people were clamouring for a change. Mr. Speaker, I had not heard any clamouring for a change on this side of the House, but I had heard-and for the benefit of the hon. gentleman I shall endeavour briefly to repeat it-I had heard it pointed out that our country had grown from being a colony-that title which the hon. gentleman loves so much-to being a nation, just as the child grows from childhood to manhood.
^ It has not been claimed on this side of the House that this Treaty made Canada a nation; nor has it'been claimed that anything that happened at the Peace Conference made Canada a nation. Canada has grown to nationhood and Canada is a nation; and she does not go seeking anywhere to any of the Allied or Associated Powers, to any foreign power, to Great Britain herself, to the entire Peace Conference, to confer upon her the gift of nationhood. Peoples, starting under 
the tutelage of other countries that have sent forth their sons to establish colonies, in the course of time, as they grow, come to acquire qualities that belong to no colony. What is the proper position of a colony as towards its mother country? Why, it' is the position of the child in the nursery. It takes .the directions of its mother country; it follows the mother country without any question in whatever line of action that mother country chooses to adopt as governing its conduct towards the outside nations of the world. And when that line of conduct leads to conditions that call for the facing of those outside nations in arms, while the relationship is purely that of guiding and governing mother country and dependent colony. Then it is the business of the mother country to provide not only for her own defence, but to carry upon her own shoulders the burden that may result from the line of conduct which she and she alone has chosen to adoipt; and if her child colony over there, that had nothing to say about how those conditions were brought about, is exposed to danger, it is for the mother country to defend it. Was that the situation in regard to Canada? Nationhood is a matter of fact; it is not a question of what is written in a statute-book or what is declared by one nation in relation to another.
Nations may recognize the nationhood of another nation but nations do not make the nationhood of another. It was in the position of a nation that we in this country found ourselves at the outbreak of the recent great struggle and that, indeed, is the condition which had existed throughout all those preceding years in which the late distinguished leader of my hon. friend, without the mental reservation that he suggests, proudly proclaimed that Canada was a nation.
We went into that struggle as a nation and we played a nation's part. We played it nobly-our soldiers did-and we -who stayed behind did our best to make the glorious effort of our soldiers successful. We played a nation's part. We did not as a colony run to cover and say to the Mother Country: Oh, it is for you to do the fighting; it is for you to protect yourself and us too. No, we sprang to the front as a nation among the world's nations. We took our place side by side with the men of other nations and we did our share in the achievement of the victory1 that has made the world safe for civilization. We have never suggested that our growth or anything that happened in connection with

this Treaty, took us out of the British Empire. Our standing-I will say " standing " because I do not want to shock the sensitive ears of the hon. gentleman more than need be by the use of the word " status "-was voluntarily and willingly recognized on the part of all nations of the British Empire, led by the United Kingdom long before this war broke out. The hon. gentleman haa referred to the resolution of the Imperial Conference of 1917 which recognizes that any arrangement looking to the organization of the different component parts of this Empire should have as its starting point and its necessary condition the preservation of the rights of the Dominions as autonomous nations of the British Empire. Then, why should the hon. gentleman be so stirred up by that affirmation? Is it 5 p,m. that he does not want the country to be a nation?
.Mr. FIELDING:	If the hon. gentleman
means:	" Do I want this country to be
a nation separate and apart from the British Empire?"-no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I said a moment ago,
and I hardly needed to have said it, that we have made no claim for this country as a nation separate from the British Empire. There is nothing farther from our thought or our desire than that. But does the hon. gentleman know what the British Empire is? What is it that he does not want to be a nation separate from?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not regard me as being discourteous but I really cannot understand his question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
The British Empire is composed of different countries living together under one king and all these countries have unanimously and repeatedly recognized the fact that they-I am speaking now of the self-governing dominions and the United Kingdom-constitute a group of nations which group of nations is the British Empire. There is not some country somewhere rto which Canada is attached and which country is the British Empire. That would leave us outside of the British Empire, attached to it. if you will, a "dependency" of it-another word that the hon. gentleman loves. But that would not place us in the British Empire and that is where Canada is, in the British .Empire and one of the autonomous, self-governing nations that constitute the group which is known to the world as the British Empire.
I might perhaps advance -a little in the order in which I would follow the hon. gentleman if I followed him in the order in
which he spoke and refer in this connection to what be looked upon as a triumphant demonstration that the recommendation of this Government that His Majesty the King should sign the Treaty on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiaries recommended by the Government and that this should be stated in the preamble to the Treaty was not acted upon. He said: "You will not find the word 'Canada' mentioned in the preamble of the Treaty." Thqn he reads the preamble. He found the "British Empire" mentioned in that part of the preamble which defines the contracting parties but he did not find any special mention of Canada. But when the British Empire came to act what did he find? The British Empire, acted in the making of the Treaty by His Majesty ithe King, the sole treaty-making power within the Empire. WKen it came to the matter of getting the signature of the British Empire to that Treaty His Majesty the King acted for and on behalf of these different nations that compose the British Empire by plenipotentiaries representative of each one of these nations and appointed on the advice of the Governments of these different nations which enjoy constitutional government. When His Majesty the King came to act and the signature of the British Empire had to be attached to the Treaty, to provide the signature of the British Empire there were required the signatures of those statesmen specially representative of the United Kingdom and of the Crown colonies and dependencies plus the signature of Canada, plus the signature of Australia, plus the signature of New Zealand, not because they pretend to be nations separate from the British Empire but because they are the nations that make up and compose 'the British Empire.
Now, the hon. gentleman said that this proceeding of ours to-day is a waste of time, a colossal, humbug, and I am not sure that he did not also describe it as a piece of tomfoolery. I wonder if the hon. gentleman understands what it is that we are doing to-day. His Majesty the King has the treaty-making power of this British Empire, and he has the ratifying power with regard to treaties made by this British Empire. In the olden days the King exercised that power of his own authority, but as the Constitution grew and the people came to count for something, His Majesty exercised it with the advice, and only with the advice, of his responsible ministers. This Treaty will be ratified by His Majesty-I say " will be," not " has been."



The hon. gentleman read from a newspaper that the Parliament of the United Kingdom had ratified or approved of the Treaty, and that that settled it. It is not in the power even of the Parliament of the United Kingdom to ratify the Treaty. What that Parliament did was to approve the Treaty-not in the form precisely of this resolution, which has been introduced for expedition's sake-but by passing an Act on the lines of the Bill which will be submitted to this House, empowering His Majesty in Council to take all steps necessary to give it effect. By doing that they expressed their approval, and that having been done, the ministers of the United Kingdom are ready to-day to give their advice to His Majesty that he should ratify the Treaty.
But what is His Majesty waiting for? His Majesty knows, if the hon. gentleman does not know, that there are other nations composing his great British Empire than the "very great United Kingdom which is at the centre of it, and he is waiting for the advice of his constitutional advisers in Canada. And those advisers are here before this House asking for its approval, because they feel, and I am sure this House feels with them, that in this the first participation in our own right as a component nation of the British Empire in the actual work of treaty making we should start the good precedent; that treaties will not be ratified until the people, through their representatives, have expressed their approval of such treaties. That is what this "bamboozling tomfoolery" means. This "bamboozling tomfoolery" is participated in by His Majesty the King as the Head of the Empire, and the same "bamboozling tomfoolery" has been participated in by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, and, as my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) pointed out, has been or is to be participated in by the Parliaments of all the self-governing dominions. But we forsooth are told in the superior knowledge of the hon. gentleman-who would not for any consideration in the world have it suggested that his country is a nation-that this, is a piece of " bamboozling tomfoolery."
Now, having belittled his country, in the process of doing so the hon. gentleman thought it wise to belittle the usefulness of the men who went over to the Peace Conference-he would not for the world belittle the men individually; indeed, he had to give them a certificate of capacity as individual men. What paralyzed them? They were Canadians. " Why," he said, " the 
interests of labour were at stake; Mr. Gompers was there, Mr. Barnes was there; what need was there for Sir Robert Borden and for my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton)?" Why, he asks, was there need for any Canadians; surely the outside world produces the men of ability-our friends to the south of the line, our friends in the United Kingdom, they produce all the great men of this world; no Canadian is any use anywhere; He would not for the world belittle the individual men. But what is he doing when he uses such language? And let me tell him that though he may forget, the men who went over to represent Canada were not unmindful that there is a great labour population within this Dominion that has its own interests, its own points of views, and its own rights to be preserved and protected. And let me tell him further, that when he reads that part of the Treaty dealing with the great organization which has been created to give protection to the legitimate interests of labour

to give effect to those pious aspirations at which the hon. gentleman sneered as being contained in the declaration of principles which the right hon. the Prime Minister moved at the assembly of the conference-if he will look at the Covenant which establishes that organization, he will find that in the composition of that body the employers and the workingmen of Canada will have their representatives in equal number with every one of the nations of this earth other than the five great powers, and that they will have not only an equal number of representatives but an equal voice and influence in and an equal eligibility to the council of that great body. And may I tell the hon. gentleman-and I will be violating no confidence when I tell it-that it was not Mr. Gompers and it was not Mr. Barnes who secured that right for the industrial interests of Canada; it was the right hon. Sir Robert Borden and my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton). It was not by sneering at Canada that it was done. We did not go over and say: Oh, we are a little colony; please, now please do not listen to us on any question that might possibly interest anybody outside of Canada.
Please be good enough to understand that the contention of the hon. gentleman is that our vision is absolutely circumscribed, and that, in the world's peace we are not interested in the slightest degree. The peace of the world was broken through causes that did not interest Canada; sixty thousand

Canadians gave up their lives and the rest of us were called to the sacrifices that I have mentioned1-yet the question did not interest Canada. V^hen you are dealing with the matter of how things are to be disposed and ordered upon the continent of Europe- and it was conditions on the continent of Europe that gave rise to the war-when you are settling and determining those conditions in such a manner as may best tend to avoid the recurrence of such a war, be good enough-the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) would have us say-not to listen to any Canadian; will you kindly send us home again, because we are an economical country and the cost of living is high in Paris.
It was because we took an attitude very different from that that Canadian labour, the Canadian employer and the Canadian Government, vastly interested as it is, vastly interested as this whole country is in everything that affects the conditions of labour, will have a voice adequate and equal to that of all the other nations, with the exception that I have mentioned, in the determination of the decisions to be arrived at by the great international body that is to give effect to those high principles which evoke nothing but a sneer from the hon. gentleman.
The hon, gentleman (Mr. Fielding) asks: What was there over there that Canada was interested in? I have mentioned this labour organization. May I tell him that Canada was very materially interested in the proposed convention with regard to aviation, and in the legislation contemplated by the Parliament of the United Kingdom in that regard? In order that he may realize that Canada is sometimes very much interested in matters that he is satisfied to leave to be settled by Mr. Barnes and Mr. Gompers, may I mention the fact that legislation was projected to govern aviation, not only outside this country, but actually, in a general sense, within the limits of this Dominion? I am sure he will be surprised that the Canadian delegation protested emphatically -and what is more, protested effectively- against any such action. Yet, the British North America Act never took legal power away from the Parliament of the United Kingdom to enact that legislation. But over there, as among people in Canada who concern themselves with looking carefully into what is meant by the British Constitution, they know that the " fine-drawn distinctions," as the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) called it, of the President of the Council between legal power and the constitutional right to exercise that power,
13J
is as plain as daylight, just as plain as it is to every man who has ever opened or looked at a book on the law of the British Constitution. Recognizing that notwithstanding that legal power they had no constitutional right, as we affirmed, to pass legislation to govern the internal conditions of Canada, whether on the water, on the land or in the air. They yielded to our representations. We, therefore, will make our own legislation in connection with such matters, and that is an assertion-an awful assertion, I am sure, in the mind of the hon. gentlemen-of Canada's possession of one of the qualities of a nation; her absolute right constitutionally to govern herself in accordance with laws made by the Parliament of Canada. That right was recognized, although it is undoubtedly true that as matter of law the Parliament of the United Kingdom might have passed that legislation.
Just one word more upon the subject of the need of our representation on the other side. The hon. gentleman virtually asked what we were doing there. Does he realize what that gathering was? Does he realize that it was a gathering of the representatives of the triumphant powers of the world and that we had taken our part in achieving their triumph? Yet he says: Oh, Canada should not have had any representation there that derived its authority from the democracy of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am not lacking in respect for the great statesmen of the United Kingdom. But if in the dealings of this Empire with the outside world Canadian affairs are to be carried on on democratic principles, then Canada's participation in such dealings must be by representatives who hold their authority from the people of Canada and from no other source. And in the great world's democracy the great Canadian democracy i.s going to hold its place and have its say through the representatives who owe to it their authority.
The hon. gentleman sneered at the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden having anything to do with the fixing of the boundaries of Greece. There seems to be a horror of Greece on the other side of the House. The member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) told us the other evening that he might believe that the President of the Council was bringing to Canada the, by him highly appreciated, gift of nationhood, but he held back and he trembled because, he said, he feared the Greeks even when they bore gifts. The hon. gentleman is horrified because a great Canadian statesman repre-

sentative of this nation of the British Empire ventured to take part as representing that entire Empire in .a settlement of the boundaries of Greece. Does the hon. gentleman know that hound up in the question of the boundaries of all those different countries over there is the question of the future peace of the world? Yet we, who are certainly interested in that future peace, are to be condemned because the representatives of the British Empire as a whole thought that there was a Canadian man who would give valuable service in settling one of the most critical questions with which the Peace Conference was called upon to deal. Surely a prophet is not without honour save in his own country, at least in that very little country which Canada is in the eyes of the hon. gentleman.
I do not want to detain the House unduly as I know other hon. gentlemen are anxious to take part in this debate. I should like, however, to say a few words with regard to the subject of this Treaty itself. Before passing to that, however, might I just say a word of two in answer to the references made to Newfoundland's position and the argument drawn from the fact that Newfoundland was not represented. I do not know why it was that the representatives of Newfoundland were willing to forego representation; I do not know why it was that they did not assert their right. That is their affair; it is for their representatives who did not assert their right to settle that matter with the people of Newfoundland. I think we might safely say that Canada had a stronger claim for representation, because there is some difference between 250,000 people and 8,000,000 people. With all the good will that 250,000 people can possibly have, they cannot play the same part within the Empire as 8,000,000 people can. But it is not for me to tell the reason why Newfoundland was satisfied to go without representation. Canada was not; Australia was not; New Zealand was not, and I am satisfied that the people of those three countries will endorse the action of their representa-ives who insisted upon that representation.
As regards the constitutional question, the hon gentleman has told us, and a number of others have also stated, that we have a written constitution and that that is the last word. We have a written constitution enacted for what purpose? It was enacted to distribute throughout this Federal country the powers of legislation. The Privy Council is on record as having said that the whole field of legislation had been by

that Act conferred upon the Dominion of Canada, either upon its central Parliament or upon the Parliaments of its provinces. When that was done the last work that a written constitution could do was done. But because we had that written constitution, we did not cease to live under that British constitution that is not written in books, that rests upon the continued practice of the British people-of the people of the British Empire, which includes us Canadians as well as the people of the -United Kingdom. I was surprised the other evening to hear the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) say that the British constitution was limited to the United Kingdom, as though we had not all of us for years boasted-and no man did it more frequently nor more eloquently than the late great leader of the Liberal party-of our enjoying all the benefits and advantages of the British constitution-and it is not all written in the British North America Act. The British North America Act said the last word that could be said in the way of determining what our legislative powers were, but it left us there with those legislative powers, in the condition in which we then stood, still within the British Empire and enjoying the benefits and advantages of the British Constitution. And one of the principal of them is the, possibility of growth from smaller things to greater things, and we have gone on and we have grown from those smaller things to greater things and one precedent after the other has occurred, each going on broadening from one to the other and making more clear our right of self-government, our constitutional right to that self-government even though there be legal power in the .Parliament of the United Kingdom to enact laws binding on us. I am not going to weary the House with particular instances, but we have the instance of the discussion of the copyright with the result of the recognition that although the British Parliament had legal power, we exclusively had the constitutional right to legislate. There was the question of naturalization when a few years ago the British Parliament started.out by enacting a naturalization law that was to be effective in Canada. There is no question that they had legal power to enact that law, but we asserted our right and told them that they had no constitutional right to exercise that power, and they recognized that and they did not exercise their legal power. I have referred to the recent discussion with regard to the aviation law. Over in Great Britain they recognize our national status and that con-

stitutionally the whole field of Government of Canada is ours. It is only in this country that you find the little man who wants to hang on to the colonial status of his country and to insist that she is subordinate to and to- be governed by another portion of the Empire. However great that portion may be-and we all respect it, we all recognize what she was the source of for us all, and we shall all be happy to recognize her as the first among these equal nations-we contend that, as a matter of fact, we stand as an equal nation within the Empire.
The hon. gentleman pointed out things we could not do. We were told for instance that, when the Prime Minister wanted to communicate with the King the other day by an Order in Council of the Government of this country he had to hand it to the Prime Minister of Great Britain. He could not address it directly to the King, and we were told that all these things go to show that we are not a nation. I am not clamouring for a change; I would not like to disturb hon. gentlemen, but what these things go to show is simply that it may, perhaps, be necessary that in the performing of these functions which our nationhood brings to us we should find a different machinery. But because of our own free will, we should choose to communicate with His Majesty through His Majesty's Prime Minister in Great Britain, or because, if you will, that is the only practical method existing to-day of having that communication reach His Majesty, how can that be said to affect that other question of fact; whether or not we have all the attributes of a nation. That fact has been recognized not only within the Empire but by the assembled nations of the world. As I have said, I do not contend that any body on the other side, within or without the British Empire, has given us nationhood.
We have grown up to nationhood, and it is ours. What came over there was the recognition of our nationhood. May I read just two paragraphs from the rules of the conference. Surely there can be no better place to go to to find out what Canada is in the eyes of the other Powers who sat in that Conference than to that Conference itself. When that Conference was called upon to make rules as to who should sit in the Conference, and how those who sat in it should be divided, what did it do? It provided:
The Conference summoned with a view to laydown the conditions of Peace, in the first place
by peace preliminaries and later by a definitive Treaty of Peace, shall include the representatives of the Allied or Associated belligerent Powers.
The belligerent Powers with general interests (the United States of America, the British Empire, France, Italy, Japan) shall attend all sessions and commissions.
We have there five great States, one of them the British Empire, of which Canada is a part. To continue:
The belligerent Powers.with special interests (Belgium, Brazil, the British Dominions and India, China, Cuba, Greece, Guatemala, Hayti, the Hedjaz, Honduras, Liberia, Nicaragua, Pa-na'ma, Poland, Portugal, Roumania, Serbia, Siam, the Czecho-Slovak Republic), shall attend the sessions at which questions concerning them are discussed.
Now in the outside world we rank with Belgium, with the much despised Greece perhaps, with every one of the nations outside of the British Empire and of the four great States who constitute the principal Allied and Associated Powers. We rank with them in the eyes of all the outside world and are entitled to speak with the same authoritative voice that they do, and to be listened to as they are entitled to be listened to. And yet, forsooth, we are reproached because here within our own country we venture to call our country a nation. Let me add just one word on this point, and it is to present a wonderful contrast. The other day my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) fought for hours with the bogey of Imperialism that was hidden away somewhere in this Treaty or could be traced somewhere in the words or actions of somebody on thu side of the House. To-day, lo and behold, we have the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) his heart sad within him because we have started to break up the British Empire. The hon. gentlemen can perhaps reconcile these two views when they get together.
Now I proceed to the amendment which the hon. gentleman has moved. He has proposed that the following words be added to the resolution:
That in giving such approval this House in no way assents to any impairment of the existing autonomous authority of the Dominion but declares that the question of what part, if any, the forces of Canada shall take in any war, actual or threatened, is one to he determined a* all times as occasion may require by the people of Canada through their representatives in Parliament.
The amendment raises in the first place, I think, the question of what is the real meaning of Article X, not what is the nature of the obligation imposed upon Canada but what is the-effect of the second

phrase of that Article. A great deal has been said with regard to Article X in this House, and outside of it. and in this country and outside, and I am perfectly free to admit that there is a great deal to be said pro and con with regard to the nature of the obligation that is by it imposed upon and accepted by all the nations who are parties to the Covenant. I do not purpose here to take up or discuss the nature of that' obligation, nor whether it is one which the nations generally or Canada in particular should assume. I heard no criticism from the point of view of the nature or scope of the obligation. I do not purpose to express an opinion one way or the other upon that at the present time, for a reason which I will give very shortly. The amendment directs itself, if I understand it, to that part of Article X which deals with the manner in which the method of fulfilling the obligation is to be determined. The hon. gentleman, I think, shares the apprehensions of a number of other hon. gentlemen that by the second part of Article X " In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat* or danger of such aggression the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled," Canada's right to determine the question of what part, it any, the forces of Canada shall take in any war, actual or threatened is in some way put in danger. I think if he will read carefully the wording of the Article he will see that his fears are not well grounded. This is not an article which Canada alone is asked to sign; it is an article which all the nations who become members of the League are asked to sign. All of the members of the League undertake in unqualified terms the obligation to respect and preserve the territorial integrity and political independence of all the other nations who are members of the League. For the moment we are not concerned with the question wjhether or not they should have undertaken that obligation. What has given anxiety to the hon. gentleman and to other hon. members is the manner in which provision is to be made for the carrying out of that obligation. The second sentence of Article X reads as follows;
In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
There it is stated in words as clear as the English language affords that the Council
[Mr. Doherty. 1
is to exercise an advisory function, not that it is to order any 'of the nations to do anything. It seems to me inconceivable that it should be suggested that because the Council has that advisory power,-the power to advise how Canada ought to fulfil its obligation-that it can claim in any way power to step in between the Government of Canada and the citizens of Canada and order a single soldier away from Canadian shores, or . impose upon any Canadian citizen the obligation of contributing a dollar. I quite understand that when that advice is given there will arise a situation in which it will be for the people of Canada, who will be acting then through their Parliament, as they act now, to determine whether or not they should accept and act upon that advice; and it will only be if the Parliament of Canada decides to accept and act upon that advice that it will proceed to send soldiers and to raise money. Between the people of Canada and the operations of the Council, under Article X, there will always be standing the undisturbed power of the Parliament of Canada, and the same thing will be true with regard to the constituted authority, whatever it may be, in any of the countries which are members of the League. Now, it is to be admitted that the entering into this obligation will at that date put this country and every other country that subscribes to it in a position where it will have the duty of giving very serious thought to that advice. And I believe, with no hesitating belief, that if that advice presents itself in those days to the minds of the representatives of Canada as advice that is based upon a fair consideration that there has been unjust aggression such as is contemplated here, and that under the circumstances it is fair that Canada should be called upon; and if such advice as the council may give concerning the proportion of aid is fair advice, I have no doubt that the Parliament of Canada will accept it and act upon it. But if the views of the Parliament of Canada should be all the other way, there is absolutely no suggestion of any machinery in the Covenant of the League of Nations whereby a solitary soldier could be raised in Canada or a dollar of Canadian money spent. And as I have said, that is true of all the nations that take part in the Covenant. What the Article does is to recognize the soundness of the principle and the policy of a joint guarantee, so to speak, of the territorial positions and political independence of all the members of the

League. I am not dealing with the question of the nature of that obligation, and whether in its nature it is one that ought to be assumed. But when you come to the question of how far the power of the Council threatens the power of the Parliament of this country, I say without hesitation that it is impossible to suggest that there is any danger in that regard. More than that however, the advice that Canada should take part can never by any possibility come from a Council upon which Canada will he unrepresented; and coming from a Council upon which Canada will be represented it will not come unless it is unanimous; that is to say, unless the representative of Canada, who doubtless will be acting under the direction of the Parliament of Canada, has concurred in the advice, that Canada should act.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: That is just what I am going to do. My hon. friend the President of the Privy 'Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell), I thought, showed that clearly the other day.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: He showed us that we could have a representative but not that we would.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I purpose to read the
provision which says that we shall have a representative under certain circumstances. There are three categories of people who may sit upon the Council. There are the representatives of the five great Allied and Associated Powers who are to sit there for all time. There are four representatives of the Powers with special interests who are to be elected by the general body of the Powers with special interests, and among whom Canada may be one of those elected. As to the probabilities of Canada being elected it is not worth while speculating. And when it comes to a question affecting directly any power among the Powers with special interests which is not represented on the 'Council, then that Power will have the right to send a representative to sit as a member of the Council; and when it will be a question of what part or interest Canada should take in any future war, surely no one will suggest that that is not a question in which she has a special interest. Even my hon. friend, who is incredulous about any special interests of Canada, will, I think, concede that that is a question concerning which Canada will have a special interest.
Article 4 provides:
Any member of the League not represented on the Council shall be invited to send a representative to sit as a member at any meeting of the Council during the consideration of matters specially affecting the interests of that member of the League.
iMr. FIELDING: That would mean if that member were a party to the dispute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
There are two distinct
things which my hon. friend must bear in mind-

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Suppose that there is a dispute in which Canada is concerned. Let us admit that Canada would be entitled to send a representative. That is debatable and I do not admit it; but suppose for the sake of argument that Canada would be entitled to have a representative. Suppose that Canada is not a party to the cause except that twenty members are directed by the Council to contribute soldiers. Will each one of the twenty have a seat on the Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: If they discuss a question affecting each of the twenty at one and the same time, at the same meeting, then every one of those twenty will have a seat on the council.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Only when it is a party to the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
There are provisions for the Council dealing with disputes or cases, and there is a provision that stands by itself as to when there is no dispute, -when nobody is suggesting Ihe existence of a di-pute upon which the Council is to pass. The facts provided for in Article X are these: Someone, referring no dispute whatever to the Council, is guilty of unjust aggression upon the territorial integrity of a country. There is no question or case submitted to anybody. That country has violated its obligations; it has submitted no case, but has gone to war. Under Article X it is the duty of every other member of the League of Nations to take its part 'to defend and preserve that integrity, and the 'Council meets, with no dispute before it, to determine as between the nations which of them should take part and what should be the proportion of each. When the question arises someone suggests in that council: "Well, Canada ought to take a hand in this," and he gives this, that or the other reasori why it is proper to call upon Canada for a couple of hundred thousand men. The moment that is introduced to the Council, you have a meeting

to consider matters specially affecting the interests of Canada. That is the way that everybody I spoke to in Paris understood that section. I do not think I ever heard an explanation of Article X that did not conclude with the pointing out of that fact.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Under that interpretation the whole assembly would become members of the Council.
/

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: If the Council chose at one and the same meeting to consider the duties and obligations of all of the members of the League who were not members of the Council, and if it was thought necessary that they should be considered at one and the same time, then the consequence that the hon. gentleman points out would come to pass. But let me suggest that that condition is highly improbable. Supposing it happened, what would be the harm? If it was a question of all the member nations of the League joining in apportioning between themselves the share of each, the most right and proper thing in the world would be that all the members of the League should come to the meeting. But that would happen rarely and infrequently. If the Council, dealing with a situation of that kind, had to determine what they would do with the small countries that would not be represented: Belgium, Poland, or, perhaps, (Canada, that would involve the presence of a representative of any of these countries. The Council of Ten, in dealing with the Treaty, proceeded on the same basis. When the question came up where a nation not represented on the Council was specially affected, they called in a representative of that nation. That only meant that when they were dealing with something that affected, say, Poland, and another country, they called in a representative of each. If they were dealing with something that affected only one of the smaller nations, they called in a representative of only that one nation. The thing worked satisfactorily and I do not see why it should not work satisfactorily under this system.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Is it dependent on the Council's decision whether, say, Canada would be called in or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
If the Council contemplated advising that Canada ought to take part in a war, then the Council would have to call Canada in, because the provision is that any member of the League not represented on the Council shall be invited when-

ever there is a question specially affecting its interests.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: In what capacity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
