speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Of course.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Where is that stated?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.

speechtext: There is no special provision for the vote of a member who is invited to act as a representative. The evident purpose is to afford representation to the country that is invited to be present.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.

Certainly, excepting on these occasions. You make a provision that every member of the body shall have a vote and then in the next line you say that on certain occasions John Jones shall be invited to come in and sit as a member. Surely he has the vote that a member has.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice)-Resuming: Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at 6 o'clock I was answering the suggestion of the bon. .member .for Beauoe-(Mr. Boland), that although, when our interests were especially affected, we would be entitled to a representative to sit as a member of the Council, that did not, in his view, give us a right to vote. I have pointed out that the provision itself is for the sitting as j. member, and that where it is intended that a vote should not count special provision is made in Article 16. But there is something which is more direct and more absolute than that.. In the first place, -Article 4 provides in the last paragraph, that:
At meetings of the Council, each Member of the League represented on the Council shall have one vote, and may have not more than one representative.
So that at meetings of the Council, each member, without distinction, represented

there shall have one vote. But what perhaps is more conclusive is the provision in Article 5.

speechtext:
Will the hon. minister
allow me to interrupt him at that point? Each representative can have only one vote; that is .what the hon. minister has read. The British Empire already has one vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: How can Canada have one vote also?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Because Canada, as a member of the League of Nations, is distinct from the British Empire. If the hon. gentleman will turn to the provision determining who are the original members, he will find himself referred to the schedule of t'he signatories of the Peace Treaty-one respect in which it was worth while for Canada to be a signatory by itself. But in the schedule itself he will find specified as the members of the League the British Empire, then Canada, Australia, and so on. So that the British Empire is one member of the League and Canada is another member.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question?-But as a part of the British Empire. Because if you look at the appendix you will see that Great Britain, or the British Empire, is mentioned as a heading, and Canada, Australia, New Zealand and India are mentioned as sub-headings, indicating that they are members of the League of Nations, but as forming part of the British Empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: They are in a list under a sub-heading. But to give the interpretation the hon. member puts upon it is to suppose that the representatives of the United Kingdom conceded that the United Kingdom was not a member of the British Empire. That is not a complete list of the members of the British Empire; it is a list of those members who are distinctively members of the League of Nations, and the United Kingdom is not a distinctive member. To put the interpretation that the hon. member does on the mere fact of a difference in printed type means that he has to conclude that that is a list of the component parts of the British Empire, which forces him to the conclusion that the United Kingdom is no part of the British Empire. We have heard invoked as conclusive on the subject of interpretations the authority of the President of the United States. Might I point out to the hon. gentleman that upon this question which he is now raising my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) the _ other evening put upon Hansard the authoritative interpretation of Mr. Lloyd George, of Mr. Georges Clemenceau, and of Mr. Woodrow Wilson, in which they specifically state that each of the Dominions is eligible as among the Powers of particular interests entitled to have elected on the Council a member of the League each for itself.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: But-if you will allow me-when the British Empire is interested in a dispute concerning the British Empire as a whole the Dominions - will have a right to sit on the Council, but they will not have a right to vote because they will be members interested as part of the British Empire.	.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: That may possibly be true if you are dealing with matters which concern the British Empire as a whole.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: But when that happens, Canada will be entitled, as within the British Empire, to state her views as to who is to represent the British Empire. But once you come to the case-and that is the ease we are dealing with-where Canada has a particular interest as Canada, where the question is: How many soldiers shall Canada be called on to furnish, then Canada will have her special representative sitting as a member on the Council of the League of Nations, and that, notwithstanding the fact that Great Britain has a member sitting there.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
No. I do not think the hon. member was here this afternoon, when I pointed out that when the day shall arrive that the Council is considering what part it will call on Canada to play in any particular war, then Canada will be invited to send a representative to sit as a member of the Council.
I was going to point out that there is not only the provision in the last paragraph of Article 4 that at meeting of the Council each member of the League represented shall have one vote, but there is more than that. Article 5 provides:
Except where otherwise expressly provided in this Covenant or by the terms of the present Treaty, decisions at any meeting of the Assem-

bly or of the Council shall require the agreement of all the Members of the League represented at the meeting.
Now, Article 4 has said that at the meeting when they are discussing what con-tri-bution Canada shall be asked for, Canada shall have a representative to sit as a member; and Article 5 says, that every decision shall require the agreement of all the members of the League represented at the meeting. Therefore it is impossible to conclude otherwise than that when it will be a question of calling upon Canada, or rather of advising Canada-for it is not a question of enforcing an obligation-of advising that Canada shall make a certain contribution in men or money or otherwise, Canada will be sitting there as a member of the League, and for any decision at that meeting there will be required the agreement of every member represented thereat. Words could not be clearer. It is impossible combining those texts to persist in the suggestion of a doubt on that point. As io the sub-heading, I think I have sufficiently dealt with that. I may say that not only the three outstanding great powers understood that as I understand it, and said so, but if you understand it as the hon. gentleman does you must determine that the United Kingdom has ceased to be a member of the British Empire, because you treat this as a list of the component parts of the British Empire and the United Kingdom is not there. ' I need not say that that is an impossible conclusion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to come directly to the amendment and the proper method to deal with it. The hon. member has said thq.t we should add this amendment to our resolution because' the question which we have been discussing is at least debatable. Although the particular feature of it to which he attaches importance and which he looks upon as objectionable and seeks to correct by this amendment 'has been debated, with ai'l the profound respect that I entertain for those who in this House and outside of it have debated this question,
I oonfess that it does not seem to me to be debatable. But if we suppose for a moment that it is debatable, then one o.f- two things is true. Either that portion of the article does mean whiat the hon. member fears it may mean; either it imposes an obligation upon Canada which constitutes .am impairment of the existing autonomous authority of the Dominion and makes the question whether the part, if any, that the forces of Canada shall take in any war, actual or threatened, one which is not to be de-
	,
termined at all times as the occasion may require by the people of Canada through their representatives in Parliament, or it does not. If it has the effect that the hon. gentleman attaches to it, then certainly it imposes, not upon Canada in particular but upon all the nations that subscribe to it, a most important derogation to their respective sovereignties. If this clause means that, it is certainly a most important clause of the Covenant of the League of Nations, and the suggestion that our approval .should be accompanied with ia declaration such as is contained in this motion amounts to nothing more or less than a refusal to accept this condition of the Covenant. A vote for this amendment, therefore, is, in effect, a vote to reject this provision of the Covenant; and you cannot reject the Covenant for part and adopt it for part; nor can you reject any part of the Covenant and imagine that you are adopting the rest'vf the Treaty -it is one whole. So that if the hon. gentleman's fears are grounded, this proposal is that we decline to approve o.f the contract because we approve subject to the striking out of a substantial provision. On the other band, if the article does not mean what the hon. gentleman apprehends, then this resolution is absolutely useless. So that 'I cannot, for my part, contemplate for one moment the acceptance of the proposed 'amendment.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Does the 'hon. gentleman consider as an amendment to a treaty a reservation made by one of the contracting countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
A reservation made by one of the contracting parties either involves an amendment to the treaty or is absolutely worthless and of no effect. The hon. gentleman would not suggest to me that having been presented with a contract which I am asked to sign in my every-day business, I could sit down .and sign, the contract, and, simultaneously or a moment before, sit down and write a reservation. If I signed that contract, I might stack my library with reservations or load up the other party to the contract with them, but the .contract would mean just what it said and I would be bound by what I had signed. The only way that this amendment could be made to produce any effect would be if it were transmitted with our resolution of approval and if His Majesty, or whoever might represent him, when he came to impose his signature to the ratification, should insert that reservation

above his signature. But if he did that it would be saying, in effect: I do not sign the contract as it is; I sign it provided something else is put into it. And what about the other parties to the contract who have never agreed to that reservation? The hon. gentleman knows that a contract involves the consent of two parties in idem. The. hon. gentleman gave us a little Latin the other night; I should like to show that I know a little, too. If a reservation affect the substance of the contract; if His Majesty's ratification signature on behalf of Canada is subject" to a reservation that modifies the contract, then we stand as having refused the Treaty. If the hon. gentleman will turn to any of the books on international law he will find that instances are given. I recall in particular the instance of a treaty to which the United States was a party-I cannot recall the name of the treaty. The Senate agreed to it with reservations and all the rest of the parties t.o it said: Well, the United States has not agreed to it. And the treaty never became effective. If reservation is to have effect it can only have effect if in some way all the other parties to the contract assent to it.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Would not a reservation be considered as our mode of interpretation of a clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes, but that, I think, does not better the hon. gentleman's position. Let us come down to the simplest thing in the world and put this question: Does the hon. gentleman suggest that if a contract is presented to me in precise terms stipulating that I lease his house for $1,000 a year I can sign it and interpret it as meaning that I have to pay $500 a year? Is that a contract? These reservations or interpretations may be worth what they may be worth to salve the conscience of people who are hesitating to accept particular provisions. But if they modify the contract and have effect at all, it simply puts one of the parties in the same position as he would be in if he had not signed the contract.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I suppose that a treaty could be signed with a mental reservation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Well, I am afraid that a mental reservation would not be any help to the signatory. The hon. gentleman, entertaining that view, will, I fully expect, vote against the amendment, because the amendment is down in writing and he can have his mental reservation. All of us can
have many mental reservations about different provisions in the Treaty.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to refer to the amendment that is now before the House as affecting the Peace Treaty itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Is it not an amendment to the resolution which is under discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Yes, it is an amendment to the resolution, and the resolution is that we approve of the Treaty.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: But the resolution will not form part of the Peace Treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: No, but it is the basis upon which this Government will have to act in advising His Majesty whether he should ratify this Treaty -on behalf of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I thought that that would be decided by the Bill based upon the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
No. If the hon. gentleman will read the Bill, he will see that its purport is to empower the Government of Canada to give effect to the different provisions of the Treaty, but the advice that the Government of Canada is by His Majesty called upon to give as to whether His Majesty should ratify the Treaty, will be advice given pursuant to this resolution, and if this resolution be that this Government should advise His Majesty to ratify the Treaty with a declaration that His Majesty, acting as he will be on behalf of Canada:
In no way assents , to any impairment of the existing autonomous authority of the Dominion, but declares that the question of what part-
And so on. If that means anything, if it affects in any way the Treaty, then, as I have said, His Majesty will not have ratified the Treaty on behalf of Canada. If, on the other hand, it does not affect the Treaty, that is to say, if nothing in the Treaty at the present time impairs the rights referred to, then it is absolutely purposeless to make such a reservation. We are face to face with this proposition:	Do we purpose approving- the Treaty and advising, on the part of this Government, His Majesty to ratify the Treaty, or do we not?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Does
the minister consider that this reservation affects the meaning of the Treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: In my opinion, it does not in any way affect the meaning of the Treaty.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I have not the Treaty
under my hand, but as I remember it, the preamble of the Peace Treaty begins with the United States, and the second Power is the British Empire. Does not the British Empire, whether we ratify the Treaty or whether we do not, whether we accept this reservation or whether we do not, act through the King?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Yes, the British Empire acts through the King. -Canada is part of the British Empire. His Majesty entertained the view that when he purposed signing a Treaty on behalf of the British Empire, the way to do it was to sign it on behalf of each of the nations that compose the British Empire, and, therefore, he named plenipotentiaries to sign that Treaty on behalf of this nation that forms a part of the British Empire, and through them he signed that Treaty for Canada. His Majesty is proceeding now to ratify the Treaty, and he purposes following the same course, that is to say, he is going to sign it for the whole British Einpire, and in his judgment, whatever may be the judgment of hon. m'em-bers, he desires the advice of this nation of his Empire as to whether he, on behalf of the whole Empire, which will include us, is to ratify that Treaty. And before his Canadian advisers take the responsibility of giving that advice, they are asking this Parliament whether it approves their doing so. That is the absolutely simple operation which is taking place.
I have endeavoured to make clear the reasons why the proposed amendment seems to this Government absolutely unacceptable. One reason, and to me a conclusive one, why we should not adopt an amendment of this kind is that if it can be of any effect its effect will be to place us in the same position as though we had disapproved the Treaty.
But there is another reason why we should decline to entertain this amendment, and it is a reason to which I should like to call the attention of every hon. member who- and I think many hon. members are in that position

while he approves the general principle and the general plan of the Covenant of the League of Nations as well as of the Treaty as a whole, entertains doubts, and in some instances, very serious doubts, with regard to certain provisions and I am not going to say that the objections made have not been supported by arguments that deserve very careful consideration. But I

want to point out to all the members of this House and more especially to members who have raised the objections to which I have referred, or who may find that the Covenant is open, even to objections that have not been raised, that there is a method of having those objections met, which will be an effectual remedy, provided only that we approve the Treaty and having so approved it, and having, therefore, had it ratified on our behalf, we become a member of the League of Nations.	*
The Covenant of the League of Nations is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians, it is not a thing that is insusceptible of alteration and improvement. This great League of Nations is a new association that has been brought into existence. It is true that it has been furnished-a most unusual procedure-with a constitution to start off, which has been prepared and agreed to in advance by a certain number of those who contemplate becoming members; but there is provision in that Covenant itself for the amendment of the Covenant and there is furthermore provision for a right of withdrawal from the League for those who have gone in. Let me ask hon. gentlemen who entertain objections, that, in their judgment, are serious, to certain clauses of that Covenant: Is it better or wiser, because they do not like those particular clauses, because, in other words, this Covenant, the first attempt at making a proper constitution for this new association of an absolutely new kind, is not in every particular in accordance with their views, to reject it, with the consequences that would follow rejection. I do not imagine that our rejection would affect the continued existence of the League of Nations and its proceeding to do the good work that we all hope is before us, but it would leave us outside of the League of Nations.
Mr. DEViLIN:	It would. There is no
doubt about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
In my judgment, there is absolutely no question about it, and the converse proposition involves that Canada can be forced into the League of Nations against her will; and with all the respect that I entertain for hon. gentlemen who have suggested that it is -constitutionally within the power of the United Kingdom to force us to become members of the League of Nations, I for one do not believe that to be true.
And in the second place I am convinced, as I am sure we all are convinced, that if the United Kingdom had the power to do

20S
that she would not exercise it. The day has long gone by when there is any desire on the part of the United Kingdom to deal with Canada-or, with apologies Jo the hon, member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding)-with the other nations of the Empire with any assertion of the right to coerce.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
In what position would
the United States of America be as regards the Treaty if the American Senate adopted the report which has just been sent to them by the Foreign Relations Committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
I am assuming that the report referred to-I have not seen the last text-involves substantial modifications of the Treaty. If that be so, and the United States Senate adopts those reservations, the United States will in effect have declined to become a party to the Treaty. While on that point I should like to point out that there is a substantial and material distinction between the position of Canada and the [DOT] position of the United States with regard to this Treaty. The same distinction exists between the position of the United States and the position of Great Britain and possibly with some exceptions of the other nations that signed the Treaty. In these other nations there is one authority that has the treaty-making power. With us His Majesty the King has the treaty-making power. Now all treaties require to be ratified, unless under exceptional circumstances there is a stipulation to the contrary, before they are binding, and the authority which can ratify or authorize ratification is provided for in the constitutions of the different countries. The position of the United States is different. The President of the United States cannot make a treaty without the advice and consent of the Senate, so that up to the present time the United States has not actually made a treaty. We have made a treaty subject to ratification. The United States, having acted by the President of the United States alone has only acted by a part of its treatymaking power, and if the other part of the treaty making power should undertake to say:	" Well, so far as the President goes
he has made this Treaty, but we do not advise or assent to this Treaty being made unless this, that, or the other modification is made," it will in, effect be declining to become a party to the Treaty. I say this subject to correction. It is a perilous thing to undertake to expound the constitution of another country.	-
Coming back to the question of the Covenant of the League of Nations, there is in it provision for amendment. Speaking for myself I should have been glad to have seen provision making amendment more easy, but there is provision for amendment. What does that mean? It means that at the first meeting of the League, and it is expected there will be a meeting shortly-at one time the meeting was expected to be in the month of October, but the delays that have occurred in different countries with regard to ratification have made that date impossible-any member represented in the assembly, and nobody 'has disputed that we will be represented there, will have the opportunity of putting forward his objections to whatever provisions he finds objectionable, and there face to face with everybody concerned, face to face with the body that can effect a remedy without delaying or affecting the Peace Treaty itself, in any way, he will have the opportunity of lodging his objections and having the matter settled. With all the respect that I entertain for the great Conference that has delivered to the world this draft of the Covenant of the League of Nations, I permit myself to say that probably in that first assembly of the representatives of the members of the League you will find a body, I will not say more competent, but probably more favourably situated to consider calmly, quietly and deliberately such proposals as may be made and to give reconsideration to such clauses of the present Covenant as may be called in question. I say that without any reflection on the Conference, but one cannot lose sight of the fact that the Conference, in addition to dealing with this weighty problem of the creation of the League of Nations, had in addition intricate and complex problems of the very first importance that had to be solved to bring about the Treaty of Peace itself. I would therefore appeal to every member of this House who sees objection, and serious objection, to certain clauses of this Covenant to join with us in expressing that approval which will bring about ratification of the Treaty and ensure our membership in the League of Nations. Having done that, we shall have done our part to put in motion that great machine, if I might use the expression, with whose intended purpose I am sure we are all in absolute sympathy. Let us do our part to get that organization into active existence, helping thereby to set on foot and make -a practical thing what the world has sighed for and dreamers

have dreamed of for centuries. Nobody in the present day -can take to his soul the flattering unction that he conceived the idea of a League of Nations. There have been projects for a League of Nations for centuries past, different projects put forward by men of great weight in their day. They, all of them, failed of realization. We having got so far, let us have to-day no responsibility for the failure of the realization of this project to the extent of bringing it into existence so that it may start on its great work. And if part of that great work should be the amendment and improvement of this Covenant, its own constitution, the sooner it is put in a position to consider the desirability of taking that action if on mature consideration it is found necessary, the better for the whole world.
In conclusion, therefore, I have but to reiterate what I have said with regard to the position which the Government finds it necessary to take upon the proposed amendment, and to repeat my hope that this House will see its way to adopt the resolution unanimously. I think that, with what I have pointed out with regard to a better opportunity that will come for dealing with this Covenant, if it requires improvement, as soon as the League of Nations has been brought into existence-with that present to o'Ur minds, and with this further fact present to our minds, that if any of us consider modification essential or of great importance, or if this House upon further consideration should come to the conclusion that modification in connection with Article X or any other provision is necessary, it will be perfectly open and competent to this House, when it sends its representative to the League of Nations, to send him there with instruction as to the amendment, whether it be this or any other that, in the opinion of this House, is essential or necessary or desirable in the interests of Canada,
I trust that we shall unanimously adopt the resolution. You will send your representative, as I have said, to a place where, if he can persuade the other nations that the amendment is desirable he can have it effectively dealt with and should his effort so to persuade fail, then it is always open to us to withdraw should we so desire.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: May I ask the minister one question? Should Canada withdraw from the League, after giving proper notice, who would then decide if Canada had fulfilled her obligations to the League?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
The question, I may
say, does not seem to me from a practical * 
point of view to be of very great importance, because I cannot conceive that Canada during any period in which she would be a member of the League would put herself in, a position in which it would be questioned whether she had fulfilled her obligations or not. But if we do assume that Canada finds it necessary to withdraw, and if she be of opinion that she has fulfilled all her obligations and somebody in the League of Nations is of a different opinion, whoever it may be that may seek to hold Canada within the League of Nations, notwithstanding her withdrawal, because she had not fulfilled her obligations, will have incumbent upon him the duty of proving that she had not fulfilled them. So far as my reading of the Treaty goes, there is no tribunal established to determine whether or not a nation has fulfilled its obligations.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Could Canada withdraw and the British Empire remain in the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: In my opinion, I do not see that there is anything to prevent Canada withdrawing from the League of Nations even though the other nations of the British Empire determine to remain within it. Gentlemen all speak as though Canada were one thing and the British Empire another. Canada is part of the British Empire, and if Canada withdraws part of the British Empire will have withdrawn.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the minister because I realize he must be tired, but this is a very important point. We are a distinct member of the League of Nations, according to the hon. minister. Would we then withdraw as a distinct member and nevertheless remain a part of the British Empire?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: Everybody who agreed to the Covenant agreed that we, while remaining a part of the British Empire, should become a distinct member of the League of Nations. If we could become a distinct member-I say "distinct"; I do not say " separated from " or any other, word that implies that we are not still in the Empire- if it was possible for us to become a distinct member of the League of Nations, then I cannot see how it can be contended that such a distinct member cannot withdraw.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: What would be our position then as regards the British Empire?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
That would be a matter to determine between the different members of the British Empire. If that question

should arise, just as if any other question should arise as to what the members of the British Empire, or the British Empire as a whole, should do with regard to external matters, and if it should be impossible to arrive at an agreement as to what should be done, all I can say is that we would find ourselves face to face with a very serious situation. We would be a partnership whereof the members could not agree, and what the consequence would be I do not want to, foretell. I have confidence, and I am sure we all have sufficient confidence, in the sound sense, the common patriotism, the desire to meet each other that prevails among the different members of the British Empire, to go to bed and sleep .peacefully without worrying our heads with fears of what is going to happen when it is found impossible to agree. It is no more probable that we should find it impossible to agree as to membership in the League than it is that we should find it imppssible to agree upon any other question affecting the relations of the British Empire, or the relations of any of the nations of the British Empire with the outside world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I feel that with the co-operation of quite a few members of this House I have taken up more time than I should have had I been all alone. However, no one will dispute the importance of the question. I have had numerous appeals made to me for such information as it was in my power to give, and so far as I have been able to recall such questions as have been put to me, I have endeavoured to answer them to 'the extent of my knowledge. I venture to repeat my hope and my confidence that this House will reject the amendment and adopt the resolution purely and simply, and I trust that it may do so unanimously. After all, as I have pointed out, if you make the very most of the objections to which any one or more of the conditions of the Covenant may be open -our accepting it as it stands makes us members of the League, and thereby we create for ourselves the opportunity to urge our case for modification before a body that can grant effective modification. If our effort should fail there and we should still be convinced that there are insuperable, fundamental, important objections to any of the clauses of the Covenant, or if experience should show that they do involve us in a responsibility beyond what we understand to-night, or beyond what we may then consider it just or right that we should assume, there is always the open door for us.
What then do we risk by lending our aid to the attainment of what has been so long the world's most glorious ambition the leagueing together of the nations for the maintenance of Peace even if we think the plan has some defects? If any member feels that it has objectionable features what do we risk if we by our votes ratify this Treaty and place ourselves in the League of Nations thus providing ourselves with a proper forum in which to obtain improvement? If we should fail there to obtain any amendment we may deem essential, we shall be free to walk out of the door as untrammeled as if to-night we should vote to reject the Covenant in toto, or any of its conventions. Of the ultimate object to be attained the importance cannot be exaggerated. The risk to be taken is assuredly small. To those who doubt I would say have the courage to take it.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question with which the House is confronted is one of those problems in regard to which there might appear to be so much prejudice that^ it is with great diffidence indeed that any member of this House undertakes to participate in the debate. But the question is of such magnitude and 'it carries with it such a heavy burden of responsibility that I feel in duty bound to give my modest and humble contribution to the debate. My task indeed is rendered more arduous by reason of the fact that I 'am following the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who 'has had the privilege of attending the Paris Conference and who has introduced into the debate a lot of explanations. If I may be permitted to express an opinion upon the address which has been delivered by the minister, I would say that I was ' more favourably impressed by the last part of it than by the first. The last part was more the speech of a statesman than the first part, although I do not w.ant to show any disrespect towards the minister. He has charged my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) with trying to belittle the country and the plenipotentiaries who were sent to Paris. This may be good tactics hut surely it is not what might be expected from an hon. gentleman of the status or the standing of the Minister of Justice. We have been called upon to attend this session of Parliament, we are sitting here as members of Parliament, and when a gentleman of the standing and experience of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens rises in his place to offer criti-

eism and to take part in the discussion of so important a document as the Peace Treaty, he can do it on his own responsibility without being charged with trying to belittle his 'country or the representatives of the country who went to the Conference.
The Minister of Justice asked a question which was so to speak, the infancy of art. He asked: " Was Canada interested in the war?" Certainly our country was interested in the war. We had a war session and we gave a blank cheque to the ministers of the Crown. We suspended the laws of the country; we introduced conscription; we enlisted an army of some 500,000 men. There are 60,000 of our soldiers who lie entombed in the soil of France. Were we interested? Why did we participate? Because we decided to join hands with the Mother Country. We decided to take part in the war and to cast in our lot with the Allies in order that Prussian autocracy should be smashed and that future generations of Canadians should enjoy the liberties that our forefathers had won for us. We were interested in the war, and we have done our share. I would ask the ministers of the Crown:	"Are we not interested in
securing peace"? They say: "Yes," and I say " Yes " also. If we are interested in securing peace, and, if it be true that we cannot secure peace and obtain a cessation of hostilities until this Treaty is ratified by the proper authorities, why 'should the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) ask the King to wait, to stay his hand, and not ratify this Treaty until this Parliament has been consulted? It was first ratification, it was next approval, and it is sometimes approbation that is asked; -it may be concurrence or endorsation later on; we do not know what it is. But we claim, and we have a right
9 p.m. to claim, so long as we offer honest criticism, that the act which is asked from this Parliament has no value whatever. Have we not a right to our opinion if we have the courage to express it in a fair way why should some hon. members try to mis-state our position and to tell us we want to remain a colony and that we are Little Canadians? I believe that such criticism is out of the question and ought not to be introduced into a debate such as this. The question is too serious to try to make political capital out of it.
The Minister of Justice has said that Canada has grown from a colony to a nation. On this argument I wish to join issue with him. I would ask the House:

When did we emerge from a state of dependency to a state of nationhood? Was it before the war, was it during the war, or was it after the war? As a component part of the British Empire we were at war as soon as war was declared by Great Britain. We could have been attacked. We did not wait to be attacked, we decided to participate. But when our soldiers reached the soil of Europe they were incorporated into the Imperial army and formed part of it. Some hon. gentlemen claim that Canada being one of the sister nations forming the British Empire surely she was a nation. The day before yesterday the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) read before this House two documents, in one of which it was stated that we could not get copies of certain papers without securing the consent of the Imperial authorities.
'Ships that had been commandeered by the Admiralty could not be restored to this country and registered here without first securing the assent of the Imperial authorities. Is that the status of a nation? Did we acquire nationhood during the war? I say no. The only answer-and this is where we cannot agree-the only answer which need be used to refute the argument that we have changed from being a component part of the British Empire to become a nation is contained in the Order in Council appointing the plenipotentiaries who were supposed to go to Versailles and affix their signatures to the Treaty of Peace on behalf of .the Dominion.
I submit, Sir, that nationhood on our part cannot be attained except by the act of three powers: First, the Canadian people, who would manifest their intention of changing their present dependency for nationhood; second, a parliament regularly elected with a specific mandate; but I believe that in our position even on the initiative of these two powers, nationhood could not be secured without the participation of the Mother Country. And here is what I base my argument upon. Canada was ceded to Great Britain by the Treaty of Paris in 1763, together with a population of 65,000, to whom and their successors were preserved certain privileges and prerogatives, and Greaj: Britain pledged herself to safeguard them. In 1774 we had what we call the Quebec Act, and the same safeguard was embodied therein. Afterwards we had the Constitutional Act of 1791, followed by the Union Act of 1841, and finally the Act of Confederation of 1867. The privileges and prerogatives so preserved to the former population and

to their successors have been safeguarded by the Crown of England, and we claim, Sir,-I do not hold the same opinion as my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding); I hope that at some future time Canada will have her independence and become a nation-but I claim that when that time shall arrive independence could be given to us only by the will of the people, duly declared by Parliament, and concurred in by the Imperial authorities, so that the privileges and prerogatives granted under the signature of the King of England may be maintained for the benefit of the successors of those who were ceded by the Treaty of Paris.	.
Some hon. gentlemen want to believe that we are a nation. I claim, Sir, it is impossible for us to be a component part of the Empire and at the same time to be a nation. My hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) this question: Supposing that Canada, as a distinct nation, should retire from the League, and that the British Empire should remain in the League, what would happen to Canada? Well, Sir, Canada being a component part of the Empire, she would have to remain in the League. She would come out as a distinct entity, but she would remain there as a component part of the British Empire.
The Minister of Justice -gave us many explanations of the Treaty provisions, and I was very glad to hear them, because I had read in the New York Times of August 30' a report which made me feel somewhat uneasy. I was under the impression, from the explanations that we had had so far from the representatives of Canada at the Peace Conference, that this article referred to the Minister of Justice, as it is in this form was correct.
We quote from a statement made recently before the United States Committee on Foreign Relations (Part 17 Treaty of Peace with Germany) by Mr. Frank Walsh, who was one of the delegates sent to the Peace Conference on behalf of Ireland. Speaking before the Senate Committee, Mr. Walsh's statement is reported as follows:
" Senator Brandegee:	At the time this covenant was accepted by the plenary Conference was there any attempt to elucidate its provisions, to explain the various provisions in it, or any debate upon it, other than the formal set speeches of the heads of the nations which presented it to the Conference?
" Mr. Walsh:	Not a particle. It had been
presented before, there were some objections made to certain parts in it, and it went back, and this meeting was called, and I talked to one of the most powerful members of the Conference outside the Big Four. He is a lawyer of very fine ability. As we are going in to
have everything open, I will say that it was Judge Doherty, of Canada, representing the Dominion of Canada, and the night before he did not know what was in it."

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
If this report is correct I suppose that the hon. minister since his return to Canada has had all the time necessary to study the Treaty, because he gave quite an explanation of its provisions.
He said that we have a written constitution. Sir, it is because we have a written constitution that I consider-and I do not want the expression I am going to us to be regarded as showing a want of respect for the hon. minister or of other hon. members who share his opinion-I say it is because We have a written constitution that I claim it is absurd, without amending this written constitution, to state that we were a colony yesterday and that we are a nation to-day. Why, in a matter of this importance, should hon. members play with words? They may be pompous, sonorous and consoling, but no words however strong or grandiloquent can alter the written constitution that we have in the British North America Act; it is an impossibility.
The hon. minister (Mr. Doherty) in answer to a question put, I believe, by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), said that there was a difference between the American Senate and this House. I believe so, Sir; and the reason is very clear and very simple. The United States of America are a nation, we are not; they have sovereignty, we have not.
The President of the United States cannot be a pajrty to a treaty on behalf of the United States without the consent of the Senate; the representatives of the great powers cannot make treaties; they must go back to the proper authority-to the authority which is representative of the sovereignty of the land. The comparison, therefore, which my hon. friend seeks to make really does not exist.
I now come to the amendment proposed by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I listened with a good deal of attention to the speech of the Minister of Justice and I must say that I cannot agree with him. It is debatable whether we are a nation or not. I say that it is debatable, because some hon. members on the other side contend with a good deal of seriousness that we are a nation, while there are gentlemen on both sides of the House who affirm that we are not a nation. But whether we are a nation or not, we do not



want our privileges 'to be impaired. Why should the Government, through the Minister of Justice, refuse the amendment which has been proposed? If we are a nation, we are entitled to all the privileges of a nation; why should we not keep those privileges unimpaired? If we are not a nation, why should we take away from Parliament the privileges accorded to it by our constitution? The amendment of my hon. friend is a safeguard, whether we are a nation or not-but the minister does not want to accept it.
Let me put this question. Having always in mind the fact that the amendment is merely the addition of a safeguard and that it does not impair the resolution, can it be denied that when our representatives, holding a mandate from this Parliament, sit in the conferences which will subsequently be held, their position will be made stronger with this amendment than it would be without it? Why should 'the Government refuse this amendment? It is all very well to appeal to the generosity, to the philanthropy, to the sentiment of members who do not feel disposed to swallow this proposal without discussion-having first covered them with abuse of all kinds. Sir, I will try to explain why the Government does not want to accept the amendment, even though it would safeguard our privileges and strengthen the hands o' cur representatives at future conferences.
Basing the nomination of the plenipotentiaries who were supposed to represent Canada on an Order in Council passed under a law which was of a very exceptional nature, and doing so without consulting Parliament, the Government has, through the Canadian delegates to the Peace Conference, entered into the Covenant of the League of Nations which is embodied in the Peace Treaty. To my mind, the Peace Treaty proper is what marks the cessation of hostilities; the , League of Nations is simply a preventive of future wars. By this Order in Council, then, the Government took upon their shoulders a responsibility which they were not obliged to take. Why did they assume that responsibility? I am speaking only for myself, but I have my own suspicions. A few moments ago the Minister of Justice said that the nation of Canada would have to provide for the defence of this country. Well, Sir, that is no new obligation; that is an obligation which rests upon us under our constitution. >So that there must have been some other reason; what was it? The Minister of Justice says that the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) agitates

the bogey of imperialism. Who was interested in setting in motion the machinery which caused the Prime Minister of Canada to go to the Prime Minister of England, not at the request of the Prime Minister of England, but to ask a favour? Who was interested? Was it the British Empire? No; if they had been interested, they would have indicated their interest by requesting the Prime Minister of Canada to do that. Was it Canada that was interested? No; the people of Canada were not consulted about it. Who, then, were the parties interested? I contend, Sir, that the Prime Minister was obeying orders that did not emanate from the British authorities. In Great Britain there is a school of men who believe that the British Empire cannot attain its objects and ideals and realize the form of Government which Britain has given to the world without linking together all the Dominions which are the component parts of the British Empire. Our own imperialists are not satisfied with the sacrifices that Canada has made for the sake of freedom and liberty. They refuse to open their eyes to the significance of the events which brought ruin aijd devastation to the German Empire, that country whose imperialists and junkers of the Wilhelmstrasse declared war in order to create their proposed system of Mittel Europa and German domination over the world. They refuse to be enlightened by this example, and to-day the German war lord who at one time had the audacity to proclaim himself the partner of God is an exile in the'castle of Amerongen.
What is going to happen, Sir? Hon. members opposite have hurled across the floor of the House expressions which indicate if not their contempt, at least their disregard for the people whom I represent. But these things have no effect upon me; I stand by the rights accorded to my people under the constitution which was granted by my King, and within that constitution I want to remain.
It satisfies me, it is the safeguard of my privileges, my prerogative^ and my liberties, and I want to keep it; and whenever Britain will acknowledge that the time has arrived to grant us the full sovereignty of nationhood, I have confidence enough in Great Britain to say in advance that the nation which has affixed her signature to the documents that I have quoted will see that these privileges and these prerogatives will be safeguarded. We are not secessionists; we want to remain with Great Britain. And, may I be permitted to say, our only safeguards are His Majesty the

King, the Union Jack and the British authorities. I have confidence in no other. Do hon. gentlemen believe that we would be foolish enough to cast away our protection and our safeguard? Let them not be afraid. We will remain British subjects and we will remain faithful British subjects; but we claim that it is our privilege to look in advance and when we see dangers, when wreck threatens, we believe it is our right, oun duty, to say to the Government: Halt, stop and consider what you are doing, and beware that the act that you are committing to-day is not the beginning of a repetition of the sad story which the exile of Amerongen is at present weeping over.
Mr. FRED. LANGDON DAVIS (Nee-pawa): Mr. Speaker, it is almost certain that any speaker coming into this debate at this late hour will have to repeat some of the things that have already been said, and I trust that in that event I shall have the patience of the House. A little over five years ago, Germany entered on the destruction of the world, a world that had in a little over a hundred years built up a mercantile system, a system of economics and finance, which was unknown before that time. The greatest factor in that great development had probably been Great Britain. She had developed first her system of manufactures; she had developed the theory of free trade; she had seen that in the development of the world and in the development of nations lay her greatest safety and her greatest profit. Her moneys were spent in the United States of America, in Argentina, and throughout the dominions of the British Empire, building up other nations with which she might trade. During this time Europe, with a feeling of uncertainty, was trying, nation by nation, to build up a system by which each would be sufficient to itself. Even when alliances were formed for the protection of some balance of power, there were strategic territories which each sought ' to acquire for itself, and which its allies sought that it should acquire.
Such, p'erhaps, was the explanation of the aggressions of Germany when she sought Schleswig, when she sought Alsace-Lorraine. Such too was the attitude of mind of Austria when she acquired Bosnia and Herzegovina in direct conflict with the Treaty of Berlin. Such was the condition ol Europe. And when Germany upset the balance of the world and tried the strength of her system against all the remaining strength of the world, her hope of

success lay in one direction and in one event alone, namely, the speedy gain of her ends through her greater preparation. That end she was not able to attain for all her century of preparation. She first had adopted the system of conscription; she had gained the territory she needed for her support; she had the arms and equipment together to make an attack upon civilization. What beat her in the end was the system which Britain had supported. At the end of the struggle, we found Britain with every nation which had a surplus of food supplies her ally. All those were supporting France and freedom from the aggression of the military states. So Germany's attack upon the economic system of the modern world, upon its financial system, and throughout the war upon its social system in her denial of the tenets of Christianity, failed in the end and miserably failed, and now she faces the payment of the penalty for her offence. And great indeed was her offence. She has set back social and domestic reforms in all democratic States for probably two or maybe three or four generations. The moneys that were needed .for certain purposes we have had to put into the effort to defeat her, and should we now attempt to carry on the work upon the old separatist principle, that setback will undoubtedly be the result. It is only through a system which is made possible by a League of Nations that it will be possible for this world to recover itself and to put itself upon the road towards renewed freedom for social and domestic reforms.
It seems to me that when we speak of British Imperialism, we should draw a distinction between that and every other Imperialism the world has ever known. The fact of the matter, as I see it, is that the British Empire grows from its circumference, that its Imperialism arises on its confines and not at its centre. It has been truly said by one that "the expansion of England is carried forward by the Overseas Dominions; that British statesmanship did not broaden the Empire, but British statesmanship is coloured by the expansion of England. And such, indeed, is the fact. If we go back even sixty-five or seventy years, we shall find that Britain was prepared to see each of her colonies set out on a road of independence. That road was not taken because of the choice of those colonies. We in Canada hoped for a greater thing. Lionel Curtis, in his book, has said, and I think truly said, that "we will have a higher organization of the commonwealth

when that is the road to a higher freedom." Such to-day we do not see. Indeed, it may be said that in the development of the outlying parts of the Empire, we have taken the road of autonomy; we have gone so far along that road that now it is practically unthinkable that we should turn back and reverse ourselves and be an Imperial federation.
Indeed, if you will read the reports of addresses upon that ninth resolution of the Conference of 1917, you will see that all who spoke upon it spoke with one mind. They spoke then of equality of nationhood; they spoke of the colonies as nations. In listening to this debate I could not help thinking that it would be well if some of our friends on the Speaker's left were to recall the time when Sir Wilfrid Laurier came back from the Jubilee and spoke of Canada as a nation. The Conservative party then called his expression mere rhodomontade, and it seemed to me that that word was in the minds of many of those who have spoken in this debate, when similar expressions as to Canada's status as a nation were heard from your right, Sir. The fact is this: It is recognized not only in the confines but at the centre of the British Commonwealth that we are citizens of one Empire, subjects of one Kiiig, and that the citizens of one part of the King's domains are not sovereigns over their fellow-citizens in another part. That is our comprehension of our situation. It is -true that we have been granted a charter in the British North America Act for this nation of ours. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr Fielding) properly drew a distinction between the ways in which that word "nation" is used. The word "nation" may be used when you speak of a sovereignty, and also when you speak of a people. For instance, we see resuscitated to-day, after a hundred and fifty years of submergence, the "nation" of Poland. Who will say that Poland through the years of her disasters has not been a nation? She knew no tie of sovereignty, she governed not herself; but she was a nation. What makes us a nation? Is it not the thought and the aim in the hearts of you and me and the people like unto us? Indeed, it is that thought that makes us Britishers, and while that thought is the same for Britain we shall be Britishers, and when that thought and that sympathy cease we shall cease to be Britishers-God forbid that the time should come soon; I doubt if it will ever come, but that is the fact. Why, to-day, have 
we no feeling of inferiority, when we meet this British citizen whose vote -may settle our destiny? Do you or I, when we meet him, ever have that feeling in mind? No. Why? For this reason: The grant that has been made by the British Crown to us can never be taken back, and it lies in our hands to make that grant complete. If this Parliament or any other Parliament chooses to declare Canada a sovereign state Britain will raise no hand against it. Our fate lies in our own hands. That we have not gone on to independence in the past, that we do not seek to. go on to independence now, is because we have a higher and a greater hope. We know that in the British Empire we can be a greater force for righteousness, a greater controlling influence in this mundane sphere than ever we could be .as a separate state. Once an American asked me why we did not think of becoming Americans. I chanced to think of an illustration and took a coin from my pocket and said, " When that coin is worn to a wafer that you can .twist between thumb and finger the effigy of His Majesty can still be discerned upon it," and I said " Such is the spirit of the people of Canada." That I believe; that I know. We sent 55,000 men to their death not merely to- defeat militarism and to maintain the freedom of the world, but to demonstrate our oneness with the British Empire.
With regard to the League of Nations, I fully agree with what the Minister of Justice has said as to the meaning of Article 10, and I cannot see the effect or importance of the amendment which has been proposed. I think that if hon. gentlemen will read Articles 16, 4 and 5, after reading Article 10, they will see that there can be no other meaning than that we as a nation coneerned shall be consulted, and on that consultation we have a veto as to' any demand that may be made upon us. That, after all, is hut a sensible provision. If Canada should be asked in a case of that sort to contribute forces and we did not wish to do so, there are a dozen ways in which we could refuse without declining outright the request of the League of Nations. We could so delay in making our preparations that our forces would not land upon the field in time to be of any use. It would be no use trying to compel any state to take any such action unless there was good will and co-operation behind its efforts.
The Covenant of the League of Nations also recognizes, most sensibly, that there

will yet be wars among states, and recognizes that there should probably be defensive alliances. That I understand to be the meaning of section 21-that there may still be defensive alliances between states for their protection. That is what France has been demanding for herself. She is not, I believe, willing to rely entirely upon 'the conditions of this Covenant, but seeks rather the assistance of those tried and true friends, Great Britain and Italy. It is true that the League of Nations does not live up to all that some of us would like to see, but then very few of us ever make a bargain even between man and man that turned out just as we would like to have it; and that the nations of the world should come together and be able to form a covenant that would be entirely in conformity with any one's ideals is unthinkable. It is true that Italy at one stage left the Conference because *she could not get her way with regard to the Dalmatian coast, and that Japan seized that opportunity to raise the question of Shantung. It would have been fatal to the League had two great associated powers left it, and in the circumstances a concession was made to Japan that is certainlv contrary to the spirit of the League, and that future times, I hope, will correct. This Covenant is but the prospectus of the development we hope to see. We hope that some day the League will be a great success.
With regard to Canada's part, I think that in the past we have been satisfied to be in the position of members of a company. To-day we are asked, to go beyond that; we are asked to take the position of one of the directors who shall guarantee the company's liabilities. For my part, I do not think it would be advisable for us to decline. As for the contention that we are but a colony, it is. true that we are a dependent province of Great Britain, that we lack many of the rights of sovereignty. We cannot take away or add one foot to the territory which the British North America Act has given us to govern; we have not control over our merchant shipping; we have not treaty-making powers; we let our appeal cases go to the High Court of the Empire, the Privy Council. In many respects our sovereignty is still incomplete, and that is a matter that rests entirely in our hands. I observe also that there is not a complete uniformity about the way this Treaty is made. The Dominion of Newfoundland is not a party thereto. As I understand the situation, treaties are brought
before Parliament, in modern times at least, because Parliament holds the purse strings.' In the past the Executive signed treaties without reference to Parliament, although when fiscal measures have been necessary Parliament has usually been, and now always is, consulted. The Parliament of the United Kingdom, it is true, has the right to ratify this Treaty, and our approval perhaps is not strictly necessary. But there are fiscal provisions. If you will look at sections 6, 23 and 24 you will see that there are certain measures that call for the expenditure of money, and I have little doubt that the Dominion of Newfoundland has expressed her assent to the Imperial Government, for which reason she is not a party to the Treaty. We as a greater State and a more important section of the British Empire, upon whom these obligations may some day lay claim, are asked here to approve. Holding as I do the view that there is no reason at all for the amendment and that our autonomy is protected-and I think you will see New Zealand particularly taking that position, for Sir Joseph Ward says he will never be a party to the control of the defence forces of New Zealand going into any other hands than those of New Zealand-I think that the proposition would not have been put up to us in any other way than in the light in which the Minister of Justice has propounded it. I purpose, therefore, to vote in favour of approval without the amendment, which in my opinion is' entirely unnecessary.
Mr. EMMANUEL B. DEVLIN (Wright): Mr. Speaker, I did intend to say a word to the House, but I find that there is no member of the Cabinet present, and I should like to know if the Cabinet has resigned. There is some information which I desire to ask of some member of the Cabinet if it is at all possible to have one present, and I ask in all seriousness, Sir, who is at present leading the Government?

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks this'evening will be very brief. I want to thank the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) for coming into the House and giving to a member of the Opposition the attention that one would naturally expect he would give, as he has done this afternoon in the enlightening speech which he has delivered. I have listened with considerable attention to a debate in this House relating to constitutional law. Men eminent in constitutional law have given us their views, and

the only clear, concise and useful information that has been given to the House in order to guide it upon this momentous question which we are called upon to decide was given this afternoon by a man who is capable of giving and is authorized to give views upon the legal aspects of a case referred to us by the Crown, and that is the Minister of Justice. This question respecting the Peace Treaty is one which may mean absolutely nothing to the Canadian people and the Canadian Parliament, as some have argued to-day, or it may mean a total change in our relations with the Empire, it may mean a total change in the status of Canada. I have carefully weighed the question in order that I might take that action which I believe that, as a representative of the people, I should take, independent of political parties, or of what others may think or say, and wishing only to do towards my country what I consider to be in my country's interest.
At times it must have been amusing to the House to hear some eminent gentlemen argue that the Empire v as ours. This proposition has been quite seriously put forward by hon. gentlemen on previous occasions. It has been suggested by the right hon. the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Porden), who, I must say, I regret is not enjoying at present the best of health-and 1 want to say that although I am speaking upon this question to-night I will not vote upon i't, because I am paired with the right hon. gentleman. I felt, Sir, that I could not refuse, when asked, to pair with the Prime Minister, because he is not as well as he generally is, and I was informed that he was confined to his bed. Nevertheless, I shall be constrained at times, in the course of the very few remarks I intend to make, to refer to him. For instance, the right hon. gentleman, speaking in the year 1915, said:
The events of the past six months mark a new stage in our nationhood; a new chapter in the hook of our destiny has been opened. The strength of our Empire

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext: He is he King of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
He is the King of Canada, but you cannot divide the personality of the King. The King is one being. The King is the King of Canada, he is the King of the other dominions beyond the seas, he is the King of Great
10 p.m. Britain and he calls himself the Emperor of India. I respect my hon. friend but I cannot follow him in so far as to say that the personality of the King can be divided. But if my hon. friend would like me to apply that, and I am sure he would, I would refer him to the preamble of the British North America Act. It reads as follows:
An Act for the Union of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswiok, and the Government thereof, and for purposes connected therewith. *
Whereas the Provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to he federally united *into One Dominion under the Crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a Constitution similar in Principle to that of the United Kingdom:
And whereas such a Union would conduce to the Welfare of the Provinces and promote the Interests of the British Empire:
And whereas on the Establishment of the Union by Authority of Parliament it is expedient, not only that the Constitution of the Legislative Authority in the Dominion be provided for, hut also that the Nature of the Executive Government therein be declared:
And whereas it is expedient that Provision^ made for the eventual Admission into the Union of other Parts of British North America:
Be it therefore enacted and declared hy the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, hy and with
the Advice and Consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and hy the Authority of the same, as follows:
Mr. [Speaker, there came the Lords Spiritual and the Lords Temporal-some have called them the Booze Barons, others have called them the Industrial Barons, and names have been applied to them that made me shudder, Sir; hut, nevertheless, they are the Barons who, with the Lords Spiritual and the Commons, too, of England, gave us authority to exist as a Confederation of Provinces.
No doubt my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) remembers, through reading Lord Carnarvon's and other interesting speeches of some of the Lords Temporal, that the Canadian delegates who went to London did not like the name of "colony," and therefore they said:	"We
do not want to he called a colony any more." "Well, what name do you want to be called?" they were asked. They replied, " We want to be called a Dominion." " All right," the answer came, " We will call you a Dominion." And a Dominion Canada was called, nothing more nor less. That is how we got the name " Dominion," through the authority of the Queen, the Lords Spiritual, and the Lords Temporal, and the Commons of England. Other colonies of the Empire found that the word " Dominion " sounded rather big, so they wanted to be called Dominions too. They made representations to England, and England said, " Well, to satisfy you all, we will call you Dominions." And hence England refers to us as " of her Dominions overseas"-existing, mark you, toy the authority of the King, and the Lords Spiritual, and the Lords Temporal, and the Commons ol England.
Now, Sir, I am not citing this to make an argument; to me it would be ridiculous to argue so plain a matter. I do not mind hon. gentlemen calling themselves a " Dominion," 1 do not mind hon. gentlemen calling themselves a "nation;" but I do take some objection to my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) wishing us hack to the family of colonies. May I be personal for one moment and say that on one of my first trips to England I went to see London, the West End and the East End, and therefore I went to the West End in the afternoon. There I saw the wealth of London displayed. I saw the King in his box looking at a horse show, I also saw our departed and good friend, Lord Roberts, sitting in his box; in fact, I saw a number of the

Lords Temporal, but I did not see any of the Lords Spiritual, and few of the commoners of England.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: At a horse show!

subtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON THE MOTION OP THE PRIME MINISTER TO APPROVE OF THE TREATY OF PEACE.
speechtext:
At a horse show. And, if I am not mistaken, the delegates from Canada went to horse shows, too, when they were over there. If they did not go to horse shows they should have done so, and they would have seen some good horses. They went to dinners and banquets and theatres-I speak not of any hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) when I say this, because he has been referred to by other authorities as one of the most eminent legal gentlemen before the Commons-but-whilst he was enjoying a well rested night, others of his friends were going to banquets and theatres,-and they could have seen good horses if they had followed His Majesty's example or the example of the Lords Temporal.
Whilst the wealth of London was enjoying this horse show-and only the wealth of London could enjoy it-<many of the commoners of London at ten o'clock at night were engaged in the pigeon market buying pigeons, and not only pigeons, but pieces of fish so as to have something' to eat. I presume that the jarvey who was .showing me London must have been more familiar with the pigeon market than he was with the West End. He drove me along Victoria street-I think it was; this is many years ago-where Canada had an office, and he said to me, with his chest well out, "Sir, that is an office of one of our colonies." I said, "One of your colonies?" "Why, yes," he said, "one of our colonies." I said, "What colony?" He replied, "Canada, Sir, Canada."

There is one word that I want to say in all earnestness, and I hope the hon. President of the Privy Council .(Mr. Rowell) will convey it to the Right Honourable the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), if the Right Honourable the Prime Minister is in a condition to have it conveyed to him. him to go to the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), or to some other member who is not in disagreement just at present with the Right Honourable the Prime Minister, and get him to act .as messenger. Sir, I find that there was some fighting over on the other side. It has not been told us in .so many words upon the floor of the House, but it has been hinted that some of our delegates had to " fight like blazes"-excuse the expression, Mr. Speaker; I am simply repeating their words.

speechtext: An historic expression.
