House and to ask them to investigate the situation in Quebec and judge by themselves, as have done some members from the West whom we had the honour to receive in our city some weeks ago and who have taken advantage of a view at close range of the situation I speak of. I am sure that if more members iwere acquainted with the situation, active steps would he taken to prevent so .much public money being wasted in Quebec, and elsewhere.
I wish to draw the attention of the House, Mr. Speaker, to the way in which public money has been wasted since 1911, and particularly to direct attention to the situation in Quebec city. In 1910 the Government formed a commission, known as the National Transcontinental Commission, with the Hon. S. N. Parent as chairman, for the purpose of constructing the National Transcontinental railway. It became necessary to decide on the best site for the Terminal in Quebec city, and after very careful consideration the commission in consultation with eminent experts of the railway and steamship lines interested in the matter, came to the conclusion that the Champlain Market site, with an area of 230,000 square feet and fronting on the St. Lawrence river, was best adapted for the purpose. The Government then decided to proceed immediately with the work of construction, and a contract was signed for the building of a union station at a cost of $750,000. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that this very valuable site was the property of the city of Quebec. The city was very reluctant to part with the property, which it valued at $250,000, but in response to a request from the Government the city consented, after serious and careful consideration, to grant the property in order to facilitate the erection of the Union Station, and a contract was entered into in August, 1910, between the Government and the city under which the Government agreed to build the Union Station, to spend not less than $2,000,000 on the St. Lawrence river frontage in docks, tidewater wharves and elevators, and to build, on the main line of the National Transcontinental, railway workshops at a cost of $2,000,000. The Government then purchased three miles of frontage on the St. Lawrence river at a cost of $2,000,000, and built the railway from the Quebec bridge to the Champlain Market, a distance of six miles. After the change of Government in 1911 the Conservative Government cancelled the contract for the erection of the Union station, aH the plans which had been the study of

expert men were abandoned, and a small Union station was built in partnership with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Had the original plans been carried out the National Transcontinental would have had a railway yard of 12,000,000 square feet, area, free of street crossings, instead of the restricted accommodation which they are now using in conjunction with their competitor, the present yard having an area of only 1,000,000 square feet, and as it is only 1,000 feet in length, every freight train, while passing through the yard, blocks the most important streets and greatly inconveniences local vehicular and pedestrian traffic.
The Government, after they had laid out what they called a general plan for the city of Quebec, decided to go on with some other great improvements, including improvements in the St. Charles river at Quebec. Owing to the fact that the city had handed over to the Government our property, consisting of the Champlain market, the city of Quebec had to provide for another market and also for the accommodation of small craft and boats. After the Government had given serious consideration to the work on the St. Charles river for fifteen or twenty years, they decided to proceed with the construction of the lock, and the dredging of the river, and a contract was entered into in 1912 with the firm of Quinlan and Robertson, of Quebec. The Government at the time told the city of Quebec that they were disposed to proceed with the work on the St. Charles river, but that they had some conditions to impose on the city. They asked the city of Quebec if they were willing to renounce all claim fwrodfemage that might, by raising the level of the water, be caused to the sewers which empty into the St. Charles river. The city of Quebec agreed to this, and an agreement was entered into and signed between the Government and the city, and then the Government granted a contract to the firm of Quinlan and Robertson, which proceeded with the work. In answer to a question which I put to the exMinister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) on the 31st of March, 1919, I was told that the contract " was originally suspended on account of the war, but now the question of continuing and completing the work is left for future consideration." I also asked the minister what was the amount spent to date for the St. Charles river works, and the minister's reply was $1,683,094.16. Moreover, my information is that the Government, in cancelling the contract with the Quinlan and Robertson company, have ac-[iMr. Lavigueur.]
quired all the plants of that firm at a cost of pretty nearly $300,000, which means an expenditure by the Government of about $2,000,000 on the St. Charles river. The Government, if my information is correct, are selling the plants by auction on the 21st instant, and I suppose they will .realize 25 or 30 per cent of the amount expended in purchasing them. As I have stated, the Government, after expending on the St. Charles river $2,000,000, have decided, for no reason whatever, to suspend this work. We told the Government that we were urging that this work on the St. Charles river should be proceeded with, and that the city of Quebec relied on the good faith of the Government that the work would be done, and the promise of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), who came to our city in 1913 when the citizens of Quebec tendered a banquet at the Chateau Fron-tenac to him and his colleagues, the Hon. Mr. Rogers, the Hon. Mr. 'Cochrane, the Hon. Mr. Hazen and the Hon. L. P. Pelletier, the minister then representing the district of Quebec. The Prime Minister came to Quebec at that time to inaugurate the works on the St. Charles river, to inaugurate the works on the Transcontinental, and to lay the corner stone of the St. Malo workshops. He told us that was only the beginning of large expenditures which the Government felt justified in proceeding with immediately in the city of Quebec. All these works have been suspended, and I wish here, for the information of the House, to put on record the declarations and promise made to the citizens of Quebec by the Prime Minister and liis colleagues on the 22nd October, 1913. The Prime Minister spoke as follows:
Mr. Mayor and Gentlemen:
Will you permit me in the first place to express my grateful appreciation and warm acknowledgment of the kindness and hospitality of my fellow-citizens of this city in tendering .me this banquet and in extending to me so cordial a welcome and reception. Whether we worship at the same altar, whether we are affiliated with one political party or the other, we are all united by a proud confidence in the resources of our country, in the possibilities of their development, in the freedom of our institutions and in the greatness of Canada's destiny.
Welcome an Inspiration.
Your welcome is of itself an inspiration but apart from that one cannot fail to be inspired by the memories of the past when visiting this city. Here', more than three hundred years ago were laid the foundations of the Canada of to-day. If even in later years and since the birth of this Dominion it required faith and courage to persevere in this task transmitted to us by the founders of Confederation, how shall we estimate the faith, the courage, and

the strong purpose of those who consecrated their energies and their lives in reclaiming for the cause of Christianity and civilization what was then a vast wilderness in this western world. May the soul and purpose of our nation ever be strengthened by the memory of the ideals which inspired the pioneers of Canada when first they undertook the task which is now committed to our keeping.
Quebec is thus unique among Canadian cities, in the associations and traditions to which I have alluded. But apart from these, when one considers its majestic situation, at the portal of the greatest inland waterway of the world, its commanding position at the head of the Gulf of St. Lawrence which lies like a great land-locked ocean almost at your feet, the vast territory largely undeveloped which lies tributary to this city, and the unbounded opportunities for the development of industry and of commerce which are thus afforded, one realizes the immense importance that this harbour should be so developed and equipped as to enable it to compete on at least even terms with any port on this continent for a legitimate share of the world commerce flowing to and froan our shores.
Whatever differences may exist between the policies of political parties in Canada, I am sure they will be found united in the view that the great national ports of this country should be adequately equipped for the purpose which I have stated. It is in this view that I desire to set forth to you to-night the works [DOT]which the Government deem necessary and which they have already undertaken for the proper equipment and development of this harbour.
Must look wTell ahead.
In approaching a question, one realizes that we must build not for to-day or to-morrow or for ten years hence, and that no proposals can be regarded as adequate unless they are so comprehensive in their character as to permit of proper extension to meet the necessities of the large future. We can estimate to some extent the probable development within a few years; but one would need a prophetic vision to foresee the enormous increase in our commerce and the equipment necessary to cope with it during the life-time of even a single individual. Considering the resources of this country, still on the eve of development and the population flowing in marvelous streams to our shores, one may conjecture that the bright eyes of children to-day at play in your streets may still be undimmed when this Dominion shall have surpassed in population the British Islands, or that favoured land from which came the ancestors of more than two million Canadians.	[DOT]
Transcontinental Works.
The approaching completion of the National Transcontinental Railway naturally render it important and even urgent that every needful facility and equipment should be provided without necessary delay. Let me put before -you in a few -words the proposals of the Government in the provision of terminals.
Pending the completion of the Quebec bridge which will probably not be finished before 1917, it is proposed to provide a ferry boat of large dimensions capable of handling a whole pas* senger train at one crossing. Such a boat has already been contracted for in Great Britain and will be delivered early next season, ^he
ferry landings for this boat are already under construction both on the Levis side and the Quebec side, the necessary land having been acquired for the purpose. It has been thought in the public interest that instead of constructing the shops at .St-Foy as originally proposed they should be erected at St. Malo in this city. These shops will occupy an area of about 200 acres and a large number of men will be employed. The establishment of these shops will, I hope, be a marked advantage in the development of Quebec and it will mean the upbuilding of a prosperous community in that portion of your city, as the operation of the shops involves the steady employment of a high class of labour and all the advantages that necessarily result from increased business and commercial activity.
Freight and Passenger Stations.
The site originally selected at St. Foy will nevertheless be utilized in the first instance for a large through freight yard which is necessary at that point in order to provide for the distribution of cars on different roads. Moreover a large handsome station has been completed at St. Foy as well as an eighteen stall engine house and every building neeessary for the efficient operation of the railway. Between the Quebec Bridge and the Champlain Market a double track has practically been completed. There is also a connection with the Canadian Northern Railway at Cap Rouge which permits entrance to the St. Charles side of the city and which can be utilized for this purpose pending the completion of the tunnel that will connect the St. Lawrence waterfront with the new Union Station on the Palais site. While that tunnel is essention to the National Transcontinental Railway for effective access to the Union Station and to the St. Charles side, it will be equally neeessary to other great railway systems which will naturally require access to the great frontage terminal of the St. Lawrence. The new Union station will be a very handsome edifice worthy both of this city and of the great railways by which it is to be used. Not only will this building be handsome and spacious, but its arrangements and accommodations will be of the most modern and approved designs. Its location is in the most populous part of the city and it will therefore accommodate most conveniently the greatest number of people. The advantages of a union station for all railroads where such a course is reasonably practicable are so obvious hardly to need enumeration. It is sufficient to say that when this station shall have been completed, Quebec will be as well equipped with terminal facilities for passenger service as any city in Canada.
Must Obtain Western Traffic.
Having regard to the probable enormous development of western traffic to this city and its w'onderful possibility by reason of the situation which I have described and seeing also the necessity of providing adequately for future development, the Government thought it desirable to possess an extensive waterfront on the St. Lawrence. With this view we have acquired three miles of the best waterfront in Quebec extending from Sillery to Cap Diamond; and portions of the waterfront from the Cap Diamond to the Champlain market have also been secured. This magnificent waterfront will give to the Government and to the Harbour Commission the opportunity of almost unlimited development of port and terminal facilities; and I hope you will agree that in thus looking forward to the possibilities of the future the Gov-

ernment have taken no unwise course. In adopting this policy, we feel that we are acting not in the interest of Quebec alone -but in the interest of all Canada, for Canada as a whole is concerned in the provision of modern and effective facilities necessary for the outflow and inflow of commerce at all great ports.
Whenever necessary we can also arrange for connection of the tracks between the Champlain Market Station and Louise Basin for the transfer of freight which can largely be carried on at night without disturbance or inconvenience to the business activities of the city. While the great Union Station which the Government is to occupy jointly with the Canadian Pacific Railway will subserve the principal requirements of traffic it is also desirable that there should be a station at the Champlain Market for the convenience of that portion of the population in the immediate vicinity. The plans for this station are now in course of preparation and the work will be commenced at a very early date and will be carried to completion with no unnecessary delay.
Gigantic I>ry Dock.
It is not difficult to understand that the St. Lawrence route cannot hold its own in competition with other routes unless vessels of the largest tonnage can be docked and repaired in case of necessity. The conditions of the past, in which at least a score of the large liners sailing to the St. Lawrence could not be accommodated in any available dock in the gulf or river St. Lawrence, could not possibly continue if we seriously contemplate not only the maintenance but the increase of the existing transportation facilities across the Atlantic. Accordingly the Government have undertaken the construction at Lauzon of one of the largest and finest dry docks in the world. According to a statement compiled by the experts of the Department of Public Works no larger dock is either in existence or in contemplation in any British or American port than that which is being commenced within the city limits of Quebec Harbour. Last year in London we sought and obtained information as to the requirements of the Admiralty in respect of the character, dimensions and the possible use of such a dock. The information thus gathered was of great value and it has been acted upon in determining the size and character of this dock, which primarily will be utilised for commercial purposes to the marked advantage of the St. Lawrence route, but which will also be capable of use in time of need for the purposes of the Admiralty. Whatever differences of opinions may exist upon the question of preparation for defence, there can be no sound objection to a policy which subserves in the first place the necessities of commerce and the requirements of peace and which can also be made available for naval purposes in time of need. It is to be hoped, and, indeed, anticipated that, with the construction of this dry dock, there will come the speedy development of such an enlarged repair plant as is needful at this port. Without assuming the role of prophet, one may well anticipate that from these beginnings there may in the future spring up a great shipbuilding industry surpassing even that which in the old days of wooden ships flourished in and around the harbour of Quebec.
Harbour Commission Work.
Let me now advert to the work which has been carried on by the new Harbour Commission since its appointment less than a year ago. Two English Engineers of eminence famil-

iar with the problems of harbour development were instructed to draw up a general scheme for future as well as for immediate development. The plan which they proposed was most carefully considered by the Commission which consulted with the Railway Companies, the steamship lines, captains of steamers, pilots and other competent persons and eventually concluded that the recommendations of these engineers should be carried out. Plans have accordingly been prepared in accordance therewith and the work is now under construction. The bulk-head wall on the St. Charles' side is in course of construction, and dredging contracts involving no less than three million cubic yards have been awarded for dredging at the mouth of the St. Charles. A contract has also been given to capable contractors for the construction of an elevator having a capacity of one million bushels which will be ready early next spring. This elevator can be increased to a capacity of two and a half million, which will probably be accomplished next season. In addition to this, new freight sheds have been constructed for the Grand Trunk and Intercolonial and new tracks laid in connection with the car ferries. Shunting engines have been purchased and are now in use, with good results in increased efficiency. Indian Cove has been acquired by the commission, a small mill has been erected for the purpose of working up the timber for the cribs, and a number of large cribs have been constructed there for the purpose of the work which is being carried on in the St. Charles.
St. Charles River Locks.
The acquisition by the Government of so large a portion of the waterfront of the St. Lawrence naturally restricted very much the opportunities of the large fleet of smaller craft which hitherto have availed themselves of that frontage. In this view the Government thought it both important and desirable that provision should be made for the utilisation of the St. Charles above the railway bridge near the Louise Basin. The construction of a dam and other works at this point, will enable some six miles of the St. Charles river to be used for transportation and will afford necessary accommodation for the smaller craft which hitherto have carried on their operations on the St. Lawrence waterfront. The transportation facilities thus afforded will doubtless be untilized not only for these purposes, but to the advantage of many industries w'hich I trust will greatly increase both in number and capacity in that vicinity.
In this brief exposition of the proposals of the Government for the development of this port, I trust you will find evidence of our determination to spare no reasonable effort for the proper development in the public interest of this city and port.
Ministers Favour Quebec.
Holding strong opinions as to the necessity of adequate equipment for our ports, I have taken a warm personal interest in the proposals for the equipment and development of Quebec. I need not assure you that Mr. Pelletier has been indefatigable in his efforts to reach a satisfactory conclusion in these matters. Let me add that Mr. Cochrane, Mr. Rogers and Mr. Hazen have given sympathetic consideration and careful attention to every reasonable suggestion for the effective carrying out of our proposals. The works which I have described will involve the expenditure of very large sums, but the national purposes which are to be served amply justify that expenditure.

On behalf of the Government let me express our appreciation of the sympathetic co-operation of the mayor and council of the city, of the harbour commission, of your board of trade and of other important bodies. In common with them it is our desire and determination that adequate facilities shall be provided for Quebeo and that in the future no man may truthfully say that the " Ancient City " lags behind for lack of equal opportunity. And we are not unmindful that modern science coupled with Canadian enterprise and courage may increase very materially the period of navigation available to this port.
I conclude by thanking you once more for your generous and cordial welcome, and let my last word be the expression of my sincere wish that the works now projected and under construction, as well as those which in the future will be their necessary consequence, may be attended with all the advantages to your city which are now within the bounds of reasonable anticipation.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the plan for the construction of the Union station at Quebec has been cancelled by the Government and arrangements have been reached with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to have a joint railway station at the Palais site, to cost approximately $200,000. How does this $200,000 station compare, for the capital city of Quebec, with the $12,000,000 station which is being erected in Toronto, the capital city of Ontario5
It was stated by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) in an eloquent speech that he delivered to the citizens of Quebec that there would be another station in the Champlain market. The members of this House whom we had the honour to receive in the city of Quebec a few weeks ago, had an opportunity to judge for themselves as to the station that was built for the Transcontinental railway there in place of the $700,000 station that was to be built. The station that has been built on the Champlain market site is a disgrace to the city of Quebec, it is a disgrace to the Government of Canada and it is a disgrace to the Transcontinental railway. This station was erected. I believe, at a cost of $30,000 or $35,000. It is a brick building, more suitable for use as a cattle sh'ed than as a station.
The valuable property that the city of Quebec has handed over to the Government and which is worth at least $250,000, was damaged by flood last December. Every effort was made by the city, the board of trade and the citizens of Quebec to have the Government repair the damage to the property which the city has given them. Not a cent has been expended for the repair of this property. I have communicated with the hon. the Minister of Railways and
Canals (Mr. Reid), and several times with the Canadian National Railways commission, but they never gave us any satisfaction. We in the city of Quebec to-day are considering the question as to whether we shall close the street, as we do not feel that we should be compelled to repair property that we have handed over, almost for nothing, to the Government. I am pleased to see the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sifton) in his seat. I hope the minister will give his attention to the situation as soon as possible. I know that he has been newly named to the important of Minister of Public Works, but I make an appeal to the minister to-night and ask him to look into this situation which is very urgent, and to render justice to the citizens of Quebec.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that millions of dollars had been wasted in the city of Quebec. I think I have proven most conclusively to the hon. members of the House that the situation in Quebec is very grave. Millions of dollars have been wasted there. The Government should proceed with the work which it has undertaken in Quebec, and not allow the money which has already been expended there to lie idle as it has for years.
The Government have purchased the Ross Rifle factory in Quebec at a cost of millions of dollars. I do not pretend to blame the Government for the position that they took at the time. It was reported that the Ross rifle was not suitable for our soldiers, and the contract which was given to Sir Charles Ross, proprietor of the Ross Rifle factory, had to be cancelled. The Government deemed it necessary to expropriate the Ross Rifle factory at a cost of millions of dollars. This important factory employed thousands of people, who were sent away from their work with only a few hours' notice and the doors of the Ross Rifle factory were closed. These valuable properties, for which the Government paid millions of dollars, are lying idle to-day.
The Government last year erected in Quebec a number of huts for soldiers, at a cost of over a million dollars. These huts are not utilized, and the money which was expended thereupon is practically wasted. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I do not see the necessity of such an expenditure by the Government on these buildings when the money thus spent could have been devoted to the carrying out of important public works.

At a cost of some $2,000,000 five railway shops were constructed but they have remained closed since their construction. The city of Quebec, the Board of Trade, and other public bodies have urged the Government to utilize these shops for the repair Of rolling stock for the Canadian National railways, but those appeals have remained unheeded. In the month of February last year we had a visit iat Quebec from Mr. Hanna, Chairman of the Canadian National railways, and the members of the Railway Comtnission, who came down to investigate the situation in regard to these shops and they have decided to put the shops in operation. While the shops remained idle the rolling stock of the Transcontinental had to be hauled from the Quebec section to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,350 miles. Let me ask why not use the shops at Quebec for the purpose, especially in view of the fact that their construction has involved an expenditure of $2,000,000? Last spring it was stated that the shops at St. Malo would be in operation and by the month of June would be employing at'least one thousand men. . On the 27th of June last I was officially informed that the number of men employed at the St. Malo shops did not exceed fifty, and if I aon right in my information the men now employed there number only about 200.
What do the records show in connection with this matter? In 1898 the city of Quebec entered into a notarial contract with the Lake St. John Railway and the Great Northern Railway Companies, whose systems now form part of the Canadian National railways, whereby the city subscribed $650,000 towards these railways, and a special agreement was also made in accordance with which the city subscribed $200,000 of stock with the express condition that the railway repair shops should be erected at Limoilu, in Quebec and give employment to a great number of men in the repairing of rolling stock. It was decided, however, to transfer the staff of the Canadian Northern shops to the St. Malo shops amd only to utilize the Limoilou shops for the, repairing of freight oars. If my information is correct the personnel so transferred consisted only of about 200 men when we were anticipating *that from 3,000 to 5,000 men would be employed at this branch ishop.
I ask the Government, and I- make the appeal to every member of this House, to investigate the way in which the management of the public works and the railway facilities in Quebec has been carried on,

and to immediately remedy the situation, 'I am sure, Sir, that if more members of this House would imitate the example of their colleagues from the West and go down to Quebec and investigate the situation for themselves they would appreciate the injustice which has been done to that city. Once more, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Minister of Railways is not in his seat, because I would have preferred to have described the situation to him- personally. Recently an organization' comprising the most eminent citizens of Quebec has been formed to interview the Government in the hope of bringing about a remedy of the present [DOT] state of affairs. Before concluding my remarks I wish to refer to the matter of the treatment of defaulters. Every true citizen views unfavourably the campaign carried on against defaulters under, the Military Service Act-even the returned soldiers do not endorse it. They would much prefer to see the Government display the same activity against war profiteers, whose extortions are causing so much unrest at the present time. The defaulters in many cases had good grounds for acting as they did, but those who are maintaining the high cost of living have no excuse whatever. Furthermore, why should our Government deal more severely with military defaulters than the French Government, for instance? The authorities' in our former Motherland have pardoned those who did not fulfil their military duties. It is rumoured that even a former Prime Minister, M. Caillaux, charged with treasonable dealings with Germany during the war, will benefit by the general amnesty. It has been realized that the work of reconstruction will require the full energy of the whole nation and that nothing is to be gained by such useless proceedings. Why not adopt the same course here?

Let us not forget that, according to many of our statesmen, this Dominion was under no constitutional obligation to participate in the great war. But we did participate, and our soldiers, volunteers as well as conscripts, immortalized themselves, toy their gallantry in many a hard fought 'battle. Let us not forget also that in the province of Quebec our people were not treated as they should have been by those who were asking that she send the best of her young men to the front. Insults, slanders, lies- nothing was omitted that would irritate French Canadians. In view of this no one needs he surprised at the number of those who failed to fulfil their military duties; on the contrary, it is rather a matter for congratulation that so many answered the call of the federal authorities, and the devotion of these men should help to efface the remissness of the defaulters.
Therefore, let us drop these proceedings against them. A nobler and greater task requires all our energies and statesmanship, namely, the urgent necessity of ameliorating the condition of the people by taking drastic action against profiteers, and toy reorganizing our agriculture and our manufactures. Let us cease these rancourous personal quarrels, unworthy of a nation wishing to 'become great and prosperous, and instead let us devote ourselves to promoting the union of our citizens in an entente cordiale.
Mr. JAMES McliSAAC (King's, P.E.I.): Mr. Speaker, in supporting the resolution before the House, I desire to add my congratulations m those which have already been expressed w'ith regard to the admirable manner in which the mover and seconder of the Address discharged their duties.
I wish also to refer to the visit of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, who by his demeanour has apparently completely captivated the hearts of the Canadian, people. His simplicity of manner and undoubted sincerity of speech and action have endeared him to the people, and his evident desire to be among them prove him to be a democrat of the best and purest type.
It is unnecessary to dwell at any length upon the extraordinary causes which necessitated the calling togethef of the representatives of the Allied and Associated Powers in connection with this Treaty of Peace. The great war was of a nature more stupendous than anything of which we have any record in the history of the world, and after the enemy was vanquished it surely was imperative that those engaged in bringing about his defeat should meet together in
order to arrive at such conclusions as would tend to prevent a recurrence of a similar calamity. As is well known, this was the most important Conference that had ever taken place. It was felt that its deliberations would have the most far-reaching effects, that they would have a regenerative force, as it were, and would result in the establishment of such principles as would make it very difficult, if not impossible, for any nation to again disturb the peace of the world.
Now, Sir, starting from these premises, it is not unnatural for us to inquire: What was Canada's position at the Conference? What was her attitude in the tremendous struggle that necessitated the conference? What was her participation in the war? What were her energies? What were her sacrifices? Their remarkable and transcendent Character is known to the world. Canada's contribution was most extraordinary, whether in wealth or means or sons, who so valiantly acquitted themselves and wrote their names in letters of gold on the battlefields of Europe. Not only the participation and the glory of her arms, lout the tremendous sacrifices that Canada made in the cause of liberty and civilization, were extraordinary, wonderful and equal in every way, population and other things being taken 'into consideration, to those of any other nation that participated in the struggle. Canada having so participated, having been such an important factor in the war, is it not quite natural that she should have an equally important part to play in the arrangements that were made in consequence of the war; that she should participate equally with those other nations, with whom she had fought side by side, in drawing up the conditions by which the defeated enemy should be bound, in taking part in the regulations which were so far reaching, so important and intended to have such a tremendous, influence in regulating the conduct of all the nations that took part in the war? Is it a patriotic sentiment, is it worthy of our country or our country's representatives, that any one should deny the right, privilege.and duty of Canada to participate in the Peace Conference? I would suppose that all patriotic Canadians would feel a thrill of just pride in the knowledge that Canada's Prime Minister and his Cabinet colleagues participated in the memorable conference side by side with and of equal importance to the representatives of other nations taking part therein.. Would you, Sir, have us take a full share in the prosecution, the glory and

the sacrifices of the war and deny us the right to have an equal participation in the conference at which the peace terms were to be decided upon? That would be unworthy of us.
Let us inquire what Canada's position was at the Peace Conference, what place her representatives took in the discussions at that conference and what the representatives of Canada accomplished and placed in the completed Treaty. The representatives of Canada, the Prime Minister, Sir Koibert Borden and his Cabinet colleagues, his co-delegates to the conference, side by side with the delegates of the other Powers, were not in any inferior position to them, and let it be said here that there is no doubt at all that Canada's important position at the conference was perhaps not conceded to her immediately; but through the energy, wisdom and perseverance of ,the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues we were accorded that position which was in proper proportion to the importance of our participation in the war and our sacrifices in connection therewith. Would you have Canada refrain from taking the position she did at the Peace Conference? Would you have her different from all other Allied and Associated Powers participating in the war? Would you have her different from the other Dominions of the great British Empire? On the contrary, Canada not only took her place of importance at the conference, but led the way for the otter Dbminions of the Empire. It was the perseverance, wisdom and judgment of the Prime Minister, in conjunction with his colleagues, that showed the way and that won for him ithe assistance of the otter Dominions of the Empire in persevering in exerting tteir energies to get their rightful place at the conference.

speechtext: Was that before or after Union Government?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I will leave that to the judgment of the hon. gentleman himself. His memory is possibly equa} to the occasion. I was going on to siay that had Canada been denied that position, ia cry would have arisen from this country, and I think the 60,000 who made the supreme sacrifice, giving their lives for .the cause of liberty and- civilization, would have spoken from their graves and said: We gave our lives freely for the cause of civilization .and liberty, for the cause of Canada, and we would consider our sacrifice was in vain if you were not there to see that no right of Canada would be jeopardized; that every

right and privilege to which she is entitled would 'be properly guarded and placed before that conference.
What did the Canadian delegates accomplish at the Peace Conference? Sir, it is written in the Treaty. Many of its most important articles were framed, or partially framed and advocated, .by the Prime Minister of this country. The labour clauses in particular were his work. Through his perseverance and -unflinching fidelity to the duty which he believed devolved upon him as Prime Minister of this country he had the labour clauses inserted against a great deal of opposition. Have we not therefore reason to be proud of the part that Canada's delegates took at the Conference and of what they accomplished? Surely no one in this country is unwilling to accord to them tteir due meed of praise.
In virtue of the promise made by the Prime Minister to this Parliament, the Peace Treaty was laid before this House for ^ approval before ratification by His Majesty the King. This same action is taken by all the other Dominions of the British Empire. The Parliaments of South Africa, of New Zealand, and of Australia are all either in session or have been summoned in order to ratify this Treaty. His Majesty the King awaits the approbation of the Treaty by the Parliaments of the Dominions before he ratifies it. It is, therefore, extraordinary that we should have heard so much from hon. gentlemen opposite that was calculated to lower the prestige of Canada. Are we to have the privilege of participating in the war, contributing our means, our soldiers ' laying down tteir lives by the thousands in the cause, and then to be told that Canada should not participate in the Peace Conference? Is that just or is it reasonable? Hon. gentlemen opposite instead of desiring to see Canada rise from plane to plane would degrade her in the eyes of the world and put her back to her colonial status of forty, or fifty or sixty years ago. A.s the President of the Privy Council truly said, there are a number of Kip Van Winkles on the other side of the IHouse. Hon. gentlemen opposite made no attempt to put Canada' in her best light before the world and maintain for her the prestige she had won during the war. On the contrary everything was said that would tend to degrade her, and deprive her of the proud position she has taken and is destined still more to take among the nations *of the world. We can only call their attitude " little Canadianism." We have heard

of the " little Englander," who is not regarded as much of an intellectual asset in the Mother Country. It would seem that we have " little Canadians " in Canada who occupy not a more distinguished or honourable position in this country. What' was the reason for their attitude? They tell us that it was altogether unnecessary for us to discuss the Treaty, as the King could ratify it independently of this Parliament. That is possible, but His Majesty's advisers in Great Britain, fully conscious of Canada's status in the Empire, would never think of asking His Majesty to ratify the Treaty until it had been approved by the Dominions of the Empire. So far as Canada is concerned, the Treaty could *have been approved by Order in Council, but if that had been done what a different tune would have been heard from the other side of the House. We have often heard them object to conducting public business by Order in Council, and if that course had been taken in this case there would have been a clamorous demand that the Treaty should be brought before Parliament for consideration. I think we can venture that assumption, judging of the future by our knowledge of the past; for that is the nature of the reasoning which we have heard from the other side during the last two or three years. The conduct of. our representatives at the Peace Conference has been described by such high-sounding, rhetorical and admirably classical language as "arrant humbug" and "tomfoolery." These are the expressions which emanate from those whom we would expect to have a full knowledge of matters of this kind and who should deal with public questions in a temperate manner instead of endeavouring to throw ridicule on them.
I would animadvert for a moment on an expression which I have heard from quite a number of those on the other side who have participated in the debate on this subject.

speechtext:
I bow to your decision Mr. Speaker. I realize that I cannot quote
anything that has been said in a former debate, but I suppose I am at liberty to express my opinion of the conduct of those who participated in that debate. I think that the conduct of hon. members opposite during that debate had for effect, ostensibly if not in reality, to degrade Canada and deprive her of the proud position she occupies. Their remarks tended to give Canada the status she held half a century or more ago, and scarcely anything that came from those hon. gentlemen was calculated to elevate this country in the eyes of the world and to place her upon the high plane to which, in consideration of all that she has done in behalf of humainty, she is entitled. Why did hon. members opposite go so far afield as to place themselves before the world in a position of antagonism to our plenipotentiaries, and to criticise their conduct in the most unfair manner possible? This was an occasion when the people's representatives, in Parliament assembled, should have been big enough and willing enough to rise above party feeling and to accord to the right hon. the Prime Minister and his associates at the Peace Conference that due meed of praise which they richly deserve. It is unpleasant to think that one section of Canada's representatives in this Parliament have placed themselves on record in direct opposition to what has been accomplished in this world-wide and all important matter. The Peace Treaty is an instrument which, in its scope and magnitude, and in the multiplicity of subjects^ which it embraces-all for the benefit of humanity and the proper government of nations-reflects abundant credit on those who framed it. Possibly it is not perfect. Nothing human is perfect. It has its limitations, but it is marvellous that the representatives of thirty-two powers, after discussing these questions horn their naturally variant viewpoints, and considering the diverse interests which they represented, should unanimously sign their names to that memorable document. It is a marvellous historic achievement, and the people of Canade, in common with the rest of mankind, should, regardless of political feelings, be only too proud to approve of this Treaty. As regards the League of Nations, I shall say very little, because it has been pretty well, discussed, and the constitutional and legal aspects of it have been admirably presented to the House by the Minister of Justice and the President of the Privy Council. But this question was raised on the other side during the debate. A fear was expressed that Canada-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this special session summons us before you to achieve a .purpose lying outside the acknowledged bounds of our constitutional .powers-the ratification of tire Peace Treaty of Versailles. True, it is That we Canadians, loyal subjects of

the British Crown, enthusiastically showing our devotion to the Mother 'Country and our fondness for the Royal Family by acclaiming the son of our beloved Sovereign, the Prince of Woles, have many a reason te rejoice over the brilliant victory of Great Britain and .the Allies. Moreover, the heroes of the Canadian army who went and fought under the British flag, the noble offering of their lives by 60,000 sons of Canada who1 fell upon the battlefields have made us realize, value and hold1 sacred the advantages of the victory won by the Allies and sealed by 'the Peace Treaty of Versailles. It seems to me that on those grounds 'the Canadian .people ought to be proud to see their Parliament assenting to that document and sending it overseas after their representatives have reverently and joyfully heard, of the advantages accruing from victory.
But these advantages., compensations and indemnities' to. the Mother Cbiuntry and the Allies are satisfactory to us in so far as the Mother Country with whom our boys have cooperated in. defeating the common foe, and in so. far as the Allies who. were our brethren in arms, are satisfied with the treaty they victoriously dictated.
'The noble act of Canada during that great war was not the interested1 but the free act of an independent State asking that outrages be atoned for, 'that treaties disregarded as scraps of paper be respected; no, the act of this Dominion was more than that, for it was 'the .act of an .autonomous colony which of its own accord lent assistance to the Mother Country and fought for the prevalence of the Christian slogan: "Dieu et mon Droit" over the barbarous political motto1: "Might supersedes right."
So, for us, the day of final victory was the eleventh of November, 1918, the day of the armistice, rwhen the enemy, vanquished as he -was, craved for quarter from the commander-in-chief of the armies. We had nothing more to claim, nothing more to expect from the Peace Conference which might cause us furthermore to rejoice at the victory, for we had taken part in the great war as a British possession, or, if you will, as a self-governing Dominion under the protection of Great Britain, and we had sent forth our quota of men on the very day when the Mother Country had rushed into the conflict. War, .for us, was at an end.
So great was the sacrifice and so noble the stand as to make it unnecessary to pledge our future participation in the conflicts which may eventually take place be-

tween the nations of the world. Before going over to sit at the Peace Conference, the representatives of the Canadian Government should have 'been vested with certain powers by the Canadian Parliament. Parliament might properly have asked: "What interest had we in having Canada represented separately from Great Britain at this Conference?" To put the question is to solve it. We had apparently no interest in being so represented. No one of the belligerent powers had invited us; far from it, we were first denied the right to be represented, and it was only as .a consequence of the entreaties made after the meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet, that we could secure admittance, fictitiously, as 'being included among the representatives of [DOT] the British Empire.
Therefore, our participation in the Conference, the sequel of which is this invitation to approve of the Peace Treaty, was not prompted by the Canadian Parliament, but imposed by the Empire and with the view of serving the ends of the leaders of Imperialism. It is Imperialism which we fought against on the battlefields of Europe and which we will never 'suffer to be imposed upon Canada so long as we are in a position to claim as ours this country of our ancestors, and so long as we cherish it above all others.
This statement of mine is quite in keeping with the platform of my party, and I may assure you, Sir, that we on this side of the House, together with all the Liberals in the Dominion, have approved of a proposal which tends to crush any project or attempt calculated to impose Imperialism upon Canada. Here is the resolution adopted at that Liberal convention, concerning the autonomy of Canada: " Be it resolved that we are strongly opposed to the idea of centralizing imperial control and that no organic change in the constitution of Canada with respect to the relations of Canada with the Empire, should come into force, if adopted by Parliament, before and unless it has been ratified by a vote of the Canadian people in the form of a plebiscite."
Mr. Speaker, according to the speech delivered by the hon. leader of the Government in the Senate, we axe a nation, a separate nation, enjoying full autonomy, though forming an integral part of the British Empire. According to the hon. President of the Privy Council, we are, within the British Empire, a sister-nation to the other nations of the Empire. It
being admitted that the Canadian Dominion constitutes a nation, here is the argument I have to offer against taking any such steps as the Government proposes to take in a coming Imperial conference to evolve towards Imperialism. The first privilege of a nation is to be the arbiter of its own destinies, and the supreme end of a nation is to preserve and to strengthen its existence as such. Full autonomy is the essential condition of this privilege of 'being a nation, and the main object of its existence. Now, the imperialist doctrine which the Government is at present advocating in order to bind us constitutionally to that immense British Empire about to be established, appears to me as inconsistent with .a status of full autonomy for us, and consequently with our very existence as a
nation.	.
My first contention is this: The imperialistic view voiced by hon. gentlemen on the Treasury benches coincides with that which has prevailed in the United Kingdom of Great Britain, only on an enlarged scale so *.as to embrace all the Dominions. Now, this United Kingdom scheme has proved manifestly injurious to the kingdoms of Ireland, Scotland and Wales in their association with England. Under the folds of the Union Jack, England developed wonderfully through the disappearance of Wales, Scotland and Ireland as separate sovereignties, while England has evolved into a Great Britain, and correspondingly has maintained, extended and strengthened its autonomy, while its associates were deprived of their own.
Well, by copying those united kingdoms, it is intended .to .establish a vast British Empire in which England shall unceasingly develop her attributes of self-government, but in which the Dominions shall enter and remain, deprived of their autonomy as is the case with Ireland, Scotland and Wales in the United Kingdom.
Indeed, I shall prove that we are going to lose our autonomy. Who will govern the Empire? An imperial parliament, I fancy. For should the answer he that it is the Government in London, as now constituted, it is obvious that we would be deprived of our autonomy. Therefore, we are no more a nation. If the answer be that to govern the Empire an imperial parliament shall be established in which the Dominion of Canada .shall, of course, have representatives, then I say: In that imperial parliament, naturally, England will have a majority of the votes. Giving way to an awkward sense of generosity, she will not com-

mit her fate to an imperial parliament in which her representatives should be in the minority. Consequently, under the proud name of an imperialist .system, we are asked to accept a parliamentary form of government under which we should no longer be the masters of our destinies and we should be deprived of our autonomy; but a nation is no longer a nation from the moment it ceases to be self-governed and master of its fate. Therefore, the imperialist doctrine now advocated is the doctrine of national suicide for the Dominion of Canada. We should not be in that case a nation in the British Empire nor in the League of Nations; Canada would be the servant, the slave of sovereign nations.
I said that the highest aim of a nation is to maintain and to develop its existence. Now, the policy of an imperialistic system, the policy of the League of Nations, utterly defeats our purpose by ruining our autonomy and leading us into ventures entailing a great loss of lives and money. In order to reach our loftiest end which is to develop our existence, the policy of the Government should be confined to the reconstruction of the country, to the establishment of an economic condition which together with the actual welfare of our farming community, of our manufacturing and trading people, which constitute a *splendid nation truly autonomous and living in a happy state of civilization.
The policy of the Government should be directed towards the internal questions rather than towards the external problems.
I repeat once more that should we be forced by the present conditions to concern ourselves with these, let it -be in this Parliament and let us not allow new responsibilities to be imposed upon us by two or three members of the Canadian Government empowered by an Order in Council to bring us under the subjection of the sister nations of the Empire. As the representatives of the Canadian people, it is our lot to be the masters of our destinies, ,to maintain and develop our existence, to perfect the work of our forefathers .who have established Confederation.
The fathers of Confederation had the foresight of themselves framing on Canadian soil the new charter of our constitutional rights. In 1864 when in the old city of Champlain the representatives of the five large Canadian provinces signed the federal covenant subject to the approval of the provincial legislatures and of the Imperial Parliament, Canada gave herself a constitutional charter.
	-
If we are a nation to-day, if we can cry out, as during the debate just closed, that we have the status, of a nation, it is far less on account of the part we played in recent events than on account of the enlightened will of those fathers of Confederation who foresaw in this federation of provinces the ongin of the Canadian race.
May I be permitted to quote to the 'House the words uttered 'by Sir John Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier, in 1865, when they asked for the establishment of Confederation?
Macdonald said: " If we will become a great nation and form a great race capable of imposing respect to the world and of upholding our institutions!, if we will have uniformity of government, an economic system which will be homogeneous for the four provinces depending on a single nation, obeying one sovereign only, bound by the same allegiance and for the most part sprung from the same blood, we must be united under a single government.''
And Cartier added : " If we become united we shall form a political nationality regardless of the racial origin and creed of individuals." He also said: " It is not to be feared that there will ever be an attempt to deprive a minority of its rights."
Underneath the cold memorials dedicated to his memory in Ontario, he must be shedding bitter tears and deploring his blind trust in the fairness of those majorities.
However, in the minds of our forefathers, Confederation was a political aggregation governed by the new charter they had framed for themselves, and consequently the provinces made but one nation composed of various races, which, although distinct, had a common aim: to weld a free Canada within a free Empire.
For my part, I am content with the present status of my country, that of a self-governing Canada within the Empire, and that condition, I think , is even the best suited to the development and progress-of this vast country and to the political aspirations of its inhabitants. I most strenuously protest against the dangerous proclivities of this Government who thoughtlessly call upon the centre of the Empire to consider new political questions which might irretrievably affect our relations to the Mother Country and forever endanger our national existence. Nothing is more degrading for a member than to hear what was said from the Government benches in this House: That as soon as this short session is over, the Prime Minister and his colleagues, without consulting Parliament, will

again go overseas to receive from an 'Imperial conference of sister nations a new principle as the basis of our constitutional charter.
The Government is bound to attend to Canadian affairs, and not to matters of Imperial concern alone. This House has just approved by its vote the Peace Treaty of Versailles. There are important events which must come to pass to ensure' a better administration of the common weal. I shall not go into them all; I shall spare the House protracted remarks, pointing out however that this country is in need of a reversal to pre-war conditions. Why should we not start by repealing conscription? England does so; the Allies prescribe it in the Treaty of Peace; the trades unions call for it, and the whole country demands it. Would it not be an act of justice to repeal all those Orders in Council quickly begotten by war conditions and no more justifiable now than the War Measures Act? For God's sake, let us have peace!
Another matter which I dare say is still more pressing is the repeal of all those vexatious measures enacted by Orders in Council so as to punish defaulters or slackers. These criminal proceedings are obnoxious, and the Government is well aware of it. There are defaulters in every province of the Dominion, and that is no wonder. Conscription was enacted at the last moment and was quite open to criticism; it was rather an exemption measure as far as military service was concerned. We had been led to believe by the very utterances of the Prime Minister himself that compulsory service would never be enforced in this country. For the most part, those who are prosecuted are farmers exempted by orders of judges of the Superior Court, and who were in such circumstances as to be granted leave according to the regulations, as their help could not be dispensed with at home.
Their only fault is the neglect of a mere formality. They are only guilty of having failed to assert their right to an exemption; they sincerely believed they were exempted, having only an imperfect acquaints ance with this intricate Act, and. relying upon the postponements granted to farmers, such as appeared in the newspapers under official sanction, Moreover, war is at an end; we have a well-earned peace and why should these young men be punished now? Would it not have been wiser, more far-seeing and faireT to wink at their failure to respond to the first call and to call them to
the colours in the thick of the fight, if the Government intended to indiscriminately enlist the farmers? But they purposely left those farmers in the fields, thus tacitly yielding to- their claim for exemption. It is unfair to chase them now as wild beasts in some quarters, in order ito feed the demon of bigotry, and to carefully avoid doing so in other quarters. Everybody favours a general amnesty, and the Government would be well advised not to turn a deaf ear to the people's voice. Nobody desires the continuation of this vexatious system. Great War Veterans in my own city have shown their disapproval of such a course, and those from every part of the country, no doubt, harbour the same feeling.
To hold a different view would be to deny their sense of fair-play, their generosity and magnanimity. Moreover, do we not know they came back to us with a greater fondness for their beloved country and willing to devote themselves to the work of reconstruction, united with their fellow-citizens by the bonds of a new friendship.
I appeal to the Government and especially to the Minister of Justice, and I ask him to give his immediate attention to those just requests coming to him from all sides and praying that defaulters be pardoned. It is the Department of Justice which attends to the enforcement of these Orders in Council and is entitled and bound to show the Cabinet the uselessness and unfairness of these arrests. The minister is well aware of the anxiety which belabours the father's mind when his boy is wrongly suspected of having infringed the Military Act. I lay before him the sorrows and sufferings of mothers whose sons have been arrested and brought into another province to appear before an outside court where they have no relatives, no friends, no spokesmen to plead for them, and are sentenced to imprisonment for a term of two or three years.
I beseech the honourable minister who presides over the administration of justice, and is one of the most prominent members of the Cabinet, to take in hand that important question concerning our young farmers and to grant to our drafted men a general amnesty such as is- proclaimed in victorious countries. The honourable minister knows how to rise to the occasion, and the country expects- from him that noble deed.
On motion of Mr. Joseph Archambault (Chambly-Vercheres), the debate was adjourned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT AMENDMENT ACT.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT AMENDMENT ACT.
speechtext: The Bill is the one I referred to in the statement made to the House on Friday. Legislation was enacted last session for the creation of a Department of Soliders' Civil Re-Establishment, but the work of that department has been carried on under the provisions of certain Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act which lay down the scale of allowances to be paid to soldiers who are taking training under the department and also define the classes of returned soldiers who are entitled to the benefits of the provisions contained in the other Orders in Council, there being some four or five Orders in Council in all defining the work of this department. As, with the coming of peace, the Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act will come to an end, it is necessary that the department should have power to carry on the various branches of the work which it is now carrying on, and the object of the Bill is to authorize the department to make the necessary regulations for that purpose. As I intimated on Friday, when the Bill comes up for second reading, which I hope will be to-morrow, it is my intention to ask the House, after the measure has received its second reading, to refer it, together with the Orders in Council which I have mentioned, to a Special Committee for consideration and report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL RE-ESTABLISHMENT AMENDMENT ACT.
speechtext: Is it not a Bill involving the expenditure of money?

speechtext:
No, the Bill simply provides for the making of regulations. The money provision, so far as any money is necessary, was covered by the vote of last session. The Bill itself contains no money provision.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed with considerable diffidence that I bring this matter before the House, for I realize that when a question of such supreme importance as this comes to the attention of the public through a discussion in the House, the member who introduces the subject always lays himself open to the accusation that in his action, however laudable, he is self-seeking or desirous to obtain some degree of public advertising. Involved in this question also there is the possibility that I may be charged, being myself a returned soldier, with an attempt to institute class legis-tion. Permit me to say, Sir, that so far as

I am personally concerned I am by no means disposed to discuss either class or class legislation of any kind. I am too deeply imbued with the ancient idea of parliamentary government to desire that this House should spend its time in any discussion of class legislation. But in view of 'the fact that there has been a widespread agitation for further gratuities to the soldiers, and that there have been some public disturbance as the result, I feel that the House and the country will excuse me for seeking to bring this matter before Parliament at the earliest possible moment. My experience in parliamentary life, as well as the experience of those who have studied parliamentary law and history, shows that nothing will clear the atmosphere as readily as a discussion of questions of this kind on the floor of the House. For that reason, Sir, I was pleased beyond measure to see the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) to-day withdraw his motion, because, if the motion of a young member hfs stood in the way, he might have been accused of blocking the discussion by his motion on the Order Paper.
I remember very well that when I was in Opposition in this House, a certain young gentleman from the West used to come here every session and place upon the Order Paper a motion referring to the removal of taxation from farm implements. Then he would disappear every time that order was called and nobody could discuss that question during the session. It is only right and proper that the rules of the House should be rigid in every regard, but I notice, Sir, that you have modified your resolution dn this case, no doubt in accordance with the new rule of the British House of Commons, which leaves matters of this kind largely to the discretion of the Speaker.
The Bill that has been brought before the House by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) deals with Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. That Bill can be obtained in the distribution office. It deals with one department of the Government and with returned soldiers who are not yet discharged or demobilized. The discussion I wish to carry on to-day will not deal with that phase of the question at all. I will try to avoid that in every possible way and discuss this question purely with reference to the soldiers that have been, demobilized.

I think the House understands that. I know that all the old members understand that, but there has been a great deal of camouflage in the press over the committee that is going to be appointed by the House and it has been spoken of as being something very wonderful. This House has a right to appoint a committee. That does not appertain to any particular member; it is the duty of the House. I think that in. so far as this House is concerned, its scope and its duty-

speechtext:
Unfortunately the minister brought to my .attention this Bill, and, of course, I must answer the remarks that he made. It is the question of the returned soldiers that I propose to take Up to-day. I am endeavouring to bring a difficult subject before the House. It is the duty of every member to bring matters before this House for discussion so that members of the House may have an opportunity of discussing it in a public way. Putting the soft pedal on a difficult question such as this only creates dissatisfaction in the mind of the public and the belief that Parliament has lost its old-time vigour and is no longer the mouthpiece of the people.
In reference to the subject matter that I am going to deal with, I understand that an association has been formed in the city of Toronto by returned men and that it has been named the Returned Soldiers' Gratuity Association or something of that kind. The members of that association waited on the Government on Saturday last and made certain propositions with reference to further gratuities to returned soldiers. The question of gratuities to returned soldiers falls roughly under three heads. There is a demand for a cash gratuity for returned soldiers, especially those who cannot or who did not take up land. There has been a demand, emanating at first from Calgary, that the men who served in the trenches should get $2,000 in cash; those who went to England $1,500 and those who were enlisted and served for a term in Canada but who through disability were unable to go to the front, should get $1,000. That question came before the Great- War Veterans Association at Vancouver, was discussed there and a committee was appointed to deal [DOT]with it and to bring it to the attention of the Government. They brought it to the attention of the Government as the House will observe in the correspondence from Mr. McNeil, the secretary, which correspondence was laid on the table, of the House on Friday last.
I understand that the Great War Veterans Association, of which I am one of the oldest members, only represent a small fraction of the number of returned soldiers, possibly not 15 per cent. There is a tremendous number of soldiers who have returned and who have not identified them *selves with any of these associations. Consequently, it would be very difficult to speak entirely at large for the returned soldiers. No small organization-perhaps no organi-

zation .so far in Canada-is in a position to speak entirely for the returned soldiers; consequently, the only place that the returned soldier really can be spoken tor is in the House of Commons. The House of Commons contains a number of returned soldiers and these gentlemen from time to time during the last session held meetings for the purpose of dealing with the question of pensions and of keeping this matter before the House and the Government. But the committee of returned soldiers in the House does not contain all the members on both sides of the House and I do not think that we would be justified in assuming that its decision should be taken as final on any _ of these questions. We are not designated a committee of the House and we are not designated a committee for the returned soldier. After all, the only place where this question can properly and generally be discussed and where everybody can take part ' in the discussion is on the floor of the House. After all, Parliament represents the people and under our consWtution it is the proper place for the discussion of public questions. For this reason I feel justified in bringing this question forward here, having it discussed and then leaving it to the Government to take any action they deem , advisable.
I make this explanation because the newspapers have been drawing attention to the fact that I did not represent the Great War Veterans in bringing this question up in the House. I do not represent them-I confess. Members of the Army and Navy League, the Veterans and the Gratuity League desired to discuss this matter ' with me the other day but I told them that I preferred not to discuss it at all because .1 wanted to be a free member in a free House of Commons and that is my position in the matter.
Another matter that i.s desired to be drawn to the attention of the House is that of a gratuity to widows and the mothers of those who have given their lives in France. There is a widespread feeling amongst the returned men that the Government should give these women a gratuity equivalent to what their sons would have received had they returned home. This strikes a responsive chord in the hearts of a great many men as it does in the hearts of all the women of the oountry and it is a matter which should be discussed in this House.
Another matter that has been brought before the House and which should be attended to before we depart this session is the question of gratuities to students.

There is no class of the community in Canada who so cheerfully rushed to the colours, went to the front, and gave up their lives, as the boys who are attending the universities and colleges of this country. We all know that at one time the Princess Pats were decimated in France-decimation would be a mere figure of speech to characterize what happened to them, because there were only seventy or eighty men left in the whole regiment. When that battalion was completely wiped out it was recruited by young men from the universities of Canada-the university of Toronto, and the university of Laval, and the universities of McGill and Queen's. The students rushed in a body to take their places in the ranks of that regiment; and I am sorry to say the .records will show that fully fifty per cent of that student body that went to the front from this country perished in France. Now, those of them who have come back have given up a great deal. Many of them were young men of eighteen or nineteen when they enlisted.. They have returned men of twenty-three and twenty-four years of age, and it is exceedingly difficult for them to find their old places in the community; the cost of living, and of everything else, has grown so great that these young men have found themselves in a very, difficult position in re-assuming their studies.
Now these are the three questions that are being discussed. I want to take the three matters up, one after the other, place some arguments before the House and leave the decision in its hands. Of course a division on the motion I have brought before the \House is to a certain extent impossible. I know that the sympathies of members are with the returned soldier- the only question asked is: " Where are we going to get all this money?" But there are many people in the country who do not look at the question in that way and they slam the door in the returned soldier's face.. Now, the returned soldier who has come back from the war is just like a poor shipwrecked swimmer who has just reached the shore. He is exhausted from his struggle, he has been badly beaten and buffeted by the waves, the roar of the tempest and of the surf is still ringing in his ears, he does not understand his orientation, he does not know the north from the south, or the east from the west. He has changed greatly since he went away, and when he returns he finds that everything at home has changed. A dollar will
not bring him as much as it brought him before. He finds tha,t his former associates have changed. Some of the young fellows who worked alongside him have become rich men since he went away. When he comes to take back his position in the factory he finds that he has to take exactly the same position that he occupied when he left, .and that many o;f the fellows who "slacked" at home are his seniors. He finds also that the law has been changed. Perhaps somebody, on his way home, hands him a flask in Montreal, and when he gets to Toronto the first thing he knows he is picked up by a policeman), brought to the police court, and sent to Burwash. I am told that 4,000 soldiers have been sent to Burwash and I do not quite approve of the operation of the law in that regard.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: As I say, the returned soldier finds that in his absence the laws have been, changed. In speaking as I do I am merely expressing the views of my comrades. They come to me an the street and ask me the question: "Don't you think this is very unjust? Here is my chum Jack who fought with -me two years in the trenches. He -comes home -and gets a flask of liquor at Halifax. When he reaches Toronto, he is picked up, he is pinched and sent up to Burwash to serve six months." That is what the soldiers -are saying. Four thousand -soldiers have been sent up there, -men who have fought right in the trenches -and helped to keep our liberty, but when they come home they have riot got liberty, they find that something -else has taken the place of the old-time liberty. Now the *situation with the returned soldier is peculiar. His former friends do not seem to be very glad to m-e-et -him. Some of his old churns who stayed at home pass on the other side of the road-they do not pay very much attention to him. When he has been back in Canada 'a -couple of weeks he is a worse wreck than he was when he left France because the sudden change has. not been of benefit to him. The form of demobilization that w-e have adopted is not, and never was to my mind, a proper form, because when the soldier -comes back from the war he must have something to lean on, -and you should -not take the returned soldier-s, as we have taken them, march them on to the parade ground, and then give the order: "Pile arms. Take your uniform off, and if you wear it longer than a certain period you will he sent to jail." That is pretty drastic treatment with re-

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question? Does the Imperial Government pay to a Canadian who left this country and went into the Imperial service the student gratuity that he has just spoken of, if such student wishes to complete his education here?

speechtext:
Unfortunately the British Government limit the grant to those students who go through Cambridge, Oxford, or the British universities; I do not think that is fair. However, I think this country should do as well as England does. I want the House to understand distinctly that when I speak of the returned soldier I make no distinction, as far as I am personally concerned, as to whether he served

in the Imperial army or in the Canadian army. '
The question arises: Where are we going to get all this money? I suppose the House is anxiously looking around and listening' to the plea that we are going to become bankrupt. Now, I am not the Finance Minister, nor do I like to give lectures on finance, except when the question is before the House; but this subject involves a financial question, and unless some method can be shown whereby the money can be raised we could not very well ask the House to make the necessary grant. I know, Mr. Speaker, that it is only by your courtesy that I am permitted to make this digression. Of course, I should not talk finance unless there was a Bill before the House dealing with it, but, Sir, you will bear with me for a moment while I proceed, and I hope the House will show me similar indulgence.
We read in the press recently that Australia was going to get $300,000,000 or $400,000,000, as her share of the war indemnity. We have not yet heard what Canada is going to get.
