speechtext: Nothing at all.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am going to take occasion to point out to the House what Canada did in the war, and what I think we should be entitled to, and if I am able to do that the discussion will be worth something. Now, what have we done in the war? We went to war for freedom. We went of our own free will. There was no clause in the Constitution, there was no bond, there was no League of Nations Covenant or anything else; there was nothing to take us to the war but that great ideal of liberty which we wanted to defend. We did not go over to get a few acres of snow-we had lots. Somebody suggested that we should have Greenland, until it was discovered that Greenland belonged to Denmark, a neutral nation. But we could not expect to get any territorial advantage. We have taken our part modestly and our men have fought as well as those of any other army in the field.
General Currie, who recently returned, has 'told you that it was not the expectation Ithat the war would end as it did last year.
If you read Haig's despatches and those of the other generals you will find that nobody expected the war would end last year. It Was a surprise. Soldier^ will tell you that when they were sent in to the final drive Ithey were not expected to drive through, for the simple reason that if they had been expected to do so they would have been supplied with new boots to continue the 
inarch up through 'Mons into Germany. 'Many of them struggled along barefooted until they reached German territory-all glory to them who broke the line. Who do you think broke the line and ended the war as it was ended, a year earlier than it was ipxpected to end? The Canadian soldiers. :I do not wish to cast any reflection on any (of our Allies, but the fact stands out that When our men were given fifteen miles of line to break through-to make a demonstration is really what the generals expected-they went through, and they went through so fast that supplies and equipment could not keep up with them, and they fought the Germans to a finish and kept them on the run until they had driven them back into Germany.
The men who really broke the line were our own men. I do not wish hon. gentlemen to think that I am boasting about our men; the war despatches of General Haig and all the other despatches testify to this fact. I bring this point to the attention of the House for the purpose of showing that we were not laggards in this war; we were at the front and we did our duty every time we were asked to do it. The glory of winning the war really rests with us, because'it was our final charge that counted; we were the " Old Guard " that broke the German line, and we take that credit to ourselves, because it is given to us by all the other Allies. But for us the war would have lasted another year.
That being the case, we now come to the Peace Treaty. We were represented at the Peace Conference, and through the Peace Treaty, which this Parliament has approved, we received at the Peace Conference our place in the sun. I did not speak in the debate on the Peace Treaty for the simple reason that, to my mind, we imist treat it as we would treat a Hamburg steak-we must not inquire too closely into its antecedents. - But one thing it did do: it gave us a seat at the council table of the nations; it showed that we were recognized by the nations of the world as a free people, as a people equal to those of any other nation. That was sufficient; that is really what we got out of the war.
Now. what did the other countries get out of the war? France gets Alsace and Lorraine. We do not begrudge her that. She gets the Saar Valley. She gets millions of tons of iron and coal in that district, a small royalty on which would pay the whole cost of the war to all the Allies'. These iron and ore fields that she has won from Germany are greater than all the ore fields of Minnesota and the Western States-and you all

know how large those are. France, therefore, is to get back her old territory and she is to get a large acquisition of territory in Africa. Belgium gets an indemnity. Italy gets territory-and she is not satisfied with what she is getting'.
We turn now to the other British colonies, who fought just the same as we did-and I am going to make this point as an argument in favour of special consideration of our case. All the colonies, dominions, or dependencies that went into the fight alongside of us are receiving something out of this war which is far above and beyond any money consideration. South Africa is getting an empire greater than the whole of the United States. Great Britain is getting Palestine and Mesopotamia with its oil fields, its coal and gold, and its free route on British territory to India. Australia is getting. a mandatory power over the islands in the Pacific, German colonies worth hundreds of millions. Our good friends to the south of the line, the United States, stayed out of the war a good while, and what do they get? All the loose change that is lying around1 in the world-that is what they get. As for Canada, we get no territory. If Australia is getting $400,000,000, the least Canada should get to recompense her for her part in the waT should be $1,000,000,000, or only a hundredth part of the total indemnity-and surely we did more than a hundredth 'part of the fighting in this war. We are entitled to it, and out of that amount we could very well, pay our pensions and any gratuities that we require to pay, without its costing this country a single dollar. If we do not spend the money that way, we will spend it on railways, at the rate of from $20,000,000 to $50,000,000' a year. Or there may be demands for a further navy, though no one has yet decided what a future navy .shall be like. But if anybody is entitled to a gratuity, surely it is the man who fought overseas I do not think this country should hesitate one minute to see that they get it.
Mr. Speaker, for the last three 4 p.m. years this House has been doing its best to shift the weight of the burden of taxation from one shoulder to the other; it has adopted virtually what 1 would call a policy of free trade. We have taken the duties off a great many articles, and there is a constant cry that the duty should be taken off everything. Several years ago I pointed out, in an address delivered in this House, that if we wished the soldier to have a place for himself and to have employment after he came back from the war, the fiscal policy of the country should be such as would build up great industrial institutions within our borders. I do not think that any one in this House can point out to me one new industry that has been established in Canada as a result of the war. No hon. gentleman can rise in his place and say that the Government during the war so adjusted its programme as to facilitate the establishment of new industries in order that employment might be given to the returned soldier.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend meant that to be a challenge. But I should like to ask him whether he does not think there is enlightenment along the line of his question as to the ability of our country to build up industries without special feeding for years, in the fact that Canada, during the brief period of the war, turned to what for her was an absolutely new industry-the making of munitions; and that she made munitions profitably and in quantities beyond the possibilities of exaggeration?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I -am quite well aware of the hon. gentleman's ideas -along that line. But no thanks are due to this House or to the Government for the large proportions which the munitions industry assumed in this country. The directors of companies, the private individuals who put up the funds, were responsible for the development of that industry, not the Government. But in England, whence the member for Red Deer came, there was not a manufacturer who was not deluged with money which was advanced to him for the buying of machinery and the building of factories for making munitions. That money came from the Government; and we can readily understand how it "was that the Government, after seeing that the manufacturer had recompensed himself, asked him for a part of his [DOT] profits in taxes, which he willingly gave. If any manufacturer was'given a large factory full of machinery and a contract so that at the end of a year the cost of bis plant and equipment is amortized and everything is paid for, I do not think any one would object if the Government went to him then and said: Next year we want half your profits.- That is what happened in England, but it is not what happened here. No thanks are due to the Government, nor the country, I repeat, for having, through any part of its programme, caused the munitions business to become such a large business in Canada. The only man in the Government who had anything to do with it, so far as

I know, was the former Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). He did his best; certainly he blazed the way, and others followed. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. M. Clark) cannot base any argument along that line upon the fact that the private individual put his money into this business and made it successful.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman not see that he is admitting imy contention that private enterprise is sufficient, under special circumstances, especially when there is a market, to build up industries? Does he not see that he is really conceding my point?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may think so, but I do not, and I do not think anybody else does. The hon, gentleman is very sore because his position during the war was antagonistic to the establishment of any industries in this country to help out the returned soldier, and he is 'afraid now of what will happen when he gets back to his riding .and has to face his electors.
These young men, when they come home will want positions, and if you cannot give them farms, then you must provide factories for them, or things of that kind. We all know what position our country took in the manufacturing of the world during the war and no one is prouder of it than I am, but our exports have fallen off already since the war ceased. No effort has been made to continue our war export trade. Nothing to my mind has been done by the Government to help restore our industries to their normal condition. Anything of that kind that has been done has been entirely due to the private individual, and God knows he has difficulty enough. There are hundreds of factories idle in this country, and the reason soldiers are walking the streets discontented is because business is not being carried on as usual in this country, whereas imports from the United States have virtually doubled. The Americans who never went to the war are getting the money, making the boots and shoes and hats and everything else for our returned soldiers. That is not right, and I think my friends the farmers will agree with me. We simply have to go to their relief. I said in this House last year that we would have to fix a price for wheat, and a lot of free traders, my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), for one, said that was against free trade principles. But the Government had to come to that idea, .and so did the grain growers and the farmers, because things were not normal, and until they are the Government must
[Mr. J. A. Currie.J
assist. I say that an additional tax on everything brought into this country of from five to six per cent-the average is now only twenty-two per cent-would give the Government a sum ample to pay all the gratuities for the returned soldiers and to set aside a sinking fund and wipe out the debt in ten or fifteen years. Anybody who knows anything about finance knows that. He knows that from that twenty-two per cent duty we are drawing to-day about $165,000,000, and yet we have men saying that all the taxes should be put on the shoulders of those who have a few dollars. Why should our method of taxation bear hard upon one class of people of this country? Everybody knows that income taxation is the hardest and most disagreeable kind of taxation in the world. It is like the hut tax on the poor African negro who has to pay five dollars a year for nothing. There are lots of cranks going around who say there should only be one kind of tax and. that should be collected from the land. If that method of taxation should be adopted my friends the farmers would have to pay every dollar of the war debt. The best form of taxation is that which bears most lightly on the people. Suppose we had not won the war. Suppose our soldiers had not broken the Hindenburg line. Suppose we had not been victors in this fight. Apart altogether from the $500,000,000 or $1,000,000,000 that it would have cost this country to carry on the war for another year. Suppose we had lost the war, how much do you think every farmer and every other man in this country would have had to contribute to the German tax that would have been immediately put on? There is not an acre of ground in this-country that would not have been sold over again to the farmer. There is not a bushel of wheat that would not have been taken, just as they took the wheat from the Roumanians and paid nothing for it. Bear in mind that the .men who prevented that condition from existing today are these very men whom I am endeavouring to represent in my modest way in the House here to-day. These are the arguments which the men themselves have, and I think they are arguments that can be repeated to this House and to common sense people everywhere, in support of further gratuities to the men.
I have told you how the money could be got by the German surtax from what they have to -pay for the war, and they will pay it. They will have to pay that $100,000,000,000, and if they cannot England will lend them the money just as England and Ger-

many bought the bonds of France to help France pay off her indemnity to Germany. Now we are going to get a piece of that in* demnity and this Government will be derelict in its duty when the question comes up as to how much of that indemnity we are going to get if it does not present these arguments and point out that we are not receiving millions of dollars' worth of territory, we are not receiving empires comparable with South Africa or Mesopotamia, or that we went into the war without any hesitation and did not expect anything out of it, but as $100,000,000,000 of an indemnity is coming from Germany, and I hope something from Austria too, Canada is entitled to some of that coin, and we are desirous of putting that money in the hands of the men who fought for us.
Now comes the question how this matter can best be dealt with by the House. The Bill to which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has drawn my attention is not sufficiently wide to my mind.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Before discussing that phase can my hon. friend say whether the returned soldiers who have asked for $2,009, $1,500 and $1,000 for those respectively who went to France or England, or remained in Canada, make any distinction as to the length of time a soldier may have served in France? W'ould they give the $2,000 gratuity to the soldier who was in France a week, and the same amount to a soldier who had been in France three years?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
There has been no distinction made by the men. Ever since tne men started to come back efforts have been made to raise these distinctions by outsiders who wanted to break up the men's organization. The first effort was mane before the Pension Committee to see that the men got the same rate of pension as the officers. Coming back to my hon. friend's question, I have seen a man come from England and go right into the trenches and be killed inside of five minutes. 1 know another young man who was in the trenches only six minutes when he lost his left leg and left arm. (He draws the same pension as the man who served five years in the trenches. There is no distinction made. It does not matter whether he was in the trenches five minutes or ten minutes or ten years.. There is no argument in favour of quibbling of that kind. But they have made a distinction between the men who did not get to the trenches and those who did. The men are all agreed that the gratuity for the former should not be as
much, but so far as the men who were in the trenches and were under gun and shell fire are concerned it makes no difference whether they were there ten minutes or ten years. It is just luck whether he gets killed inside of five minutes or not. None of the soldiers would support these distinctions. The last men to make distinctions between themselves and the officers are those who fought under the officers. The junior subaltern who led his platoon with rifle and bayonet and fought just like one of the men, the little lad whom they followed over the top at the zero hour was not drawing as good pay as an armour sergeant, and his wife at home suffered [DOT] more than any private in the ranks for the simple reason that the Patriotic Fund would not allow her to receive a cent. Hia average pay would not 'be more than from $3.50 to $4 a day; the sergeant was drawing more money and his wife was receiving assistance from the Patriotic Fund. The men I have spoken to say: "We want the officer to get his proper place, if there is any proper place for him. There is an occasional officer who is a rotter, but there are rotters everywhere and you run across them occasionally. That cannot be helped."

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I did not quite gather the full effect of my hon. friend's reply to the question of the hon. member from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards). Did I understand him to advocate that all men who served in France should receive equal gratuity, that the military landing officer at Boulogne for instance should receive the same gratuity as the man who fought in the front line trenches?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The law has clearly distinguished between the man who is entitled to the war medal, the man who has fought dn the actual war-zone and the man who has not. The distinction that has been made is, to my mind, amply sufficient. One man might have been in the trenches for nearly five years and have been fortunate enough to have escaped without being wounded. I know of several who have never left the trenches except for a furlough of ten or twelve days and have emerged unscathed, whereas, on the other hand, others have not been in the trenches ten minutes-indeed, in some cases, three minutes-when they were killed. The widow of the man who unfortunately was killed 'at the end of the war and the widow of the soldier killed after only ten minutes of struggle should be placed in the same category so far as

compensation i-s concerned, for their sacrifice to the nation's cause is precisely the same. There is no difference between their position, and it is not in the interests of the returned soldiers that any distinction (should be made between oases off this nature. Great efforts are being made to create such distinctions, which are not only invidious but, from a national standpoint, should be severely discountenanced. A good deal has been said derogatory of the conscript, but for my part I raise my hat to the man who went overseas after the enactment of conscription. It was the conscript forces that broke the Hindenburg line; the Canadian army contained over fifty per cent of conscripts, and the irresistible advance of these men shattered the enemy. So it ill becomes us to say that they were not just as good fighters as the volunteers and not entitled to every consideration. You cannot divide the returned soldiers by any such line of demarcation, because the moment you argue in that way you give him to understand that you are antagonistic to him, and he takes it for granted that you are stirring up trouble between him and his comrades. A considerable amount of far-fetched criticism is indulged in at the expense of the returned soldiers, and an attempt is being made to intimidate the farmers and others with absurd stories about the alleged recklessness of the men who have come from overseas. All kinds of yarns are told about them, one example being the story of the returned soldier who, hired by a farmer, was sent to milk a cow and finding the animal refractory killed it with a pitchfork. The soldier, however, cannot be found.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Did any one find the
cow?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No-I am afraid this tale is on a par with fabulous pair of socles which the woman knitted for use overseas and which were found at Hudson bay. That is an innocent story compared with some others, but the evident intention is to prejudice the farmers against the employment of these men. As to what we should do, I think the Government could appoint a special committee of the House to deal with the whole question, so that there might be no possibility of narrowing the scope of the committee. I think myself, it would be a very good thing to have a motion passed in this House to investigate some of the new departments with a view to ascertaining just what they are doing. The returned

soldiers are not pleased with the Department of Soldier's Civil Re-Establishment. I have received a number of letters in reference to that organization, and I think that the entire subject should be inquired into by a parliamentary, committee. I know a pamphlet has been sent to the members stating that it is not the intention of the committee 'to go into anything that has been done by this department. If it is necessary I will introduce a resolution, and I should like to see this committee, if it is appointed, take up that matter and carefully consider it. The returned soldiers are sending all kinds of complaints to me, and other mem-, hers are receiving complaints also to the effect that this department is of no earthly use. The complaint is made that a man is being taught about automobiles, for example, by one who does not know the difference between a carburettor and a muffler, and men are trying to teach telegraphy by a system in vogue twenty years ago. This subject should be investigated, and the President of the Privy Council will, I hope, introduce a resolution giving us the assurance that this committee when, it is appointed will have the power to inquire into all these questions, and will not simply deal with this particular question alone.
I have spoken at greater length than I intended, Mr. Speaker, but I have endeavoured to answer all the arguments against the proposition that the returned soldier is entitled to further consideration. I have shown the House that he is -not asking too much, and I think I have made it quite clear that he is a good and eminently loyal citizen, who is ready to stand up for law and order when revolution threatens. His whole object in life is to see his country worthy of its position as one of the greatest, and I have every faith in his honesty and integrity. No one has <a greater -stake in the country than has the returned soldier, and we must bear in mind that if in our efforts to help him the country is put into debt, he is helping to liquidate that debt.
I am -a returned soldier and I pay my income -tax. I pay my income tax on the enormous amount I receive as a member of Parliament. We are all willing to pay our share, 'and1 the -returned soldier is willing -to take off his coat -and work strenuously to make hi.s country worth while. I trust therefore that we will stand behind these men and give them every advantage which it is in our power -to bestow. I will be willing, Mr. Speaker, to -answer any questions that may be asked of me, and I hope that we shall reach the conclusion that these returned men deserve everything

which a grateful Govern orient and country can do in their behalf.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. member has told us what the returned soldiers want .and what the resolution passed at Calgary meant, but he has not told us what he himself wants. He has not 'told us whether he is in favour of the proposition or not.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will read my speech he will find that I endorsed the gratuity to returned soldiers in accordance with the Calgary resolution. I also said that I consider the widows and orphans and mothers of men who were killed in France are entitled to a gratuity the same as men who oame home. Further, I am infavour of a substantial amount to every student going to the university. That is my position on the question.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
In rising to speak on the subject before the House I desire at once to express my gratitude to the hon. member for Simcoe North (iMr. Currie) for bringing this matter up in the way he has done. I quite agree that this is the place in which to air grievances, the place where allegations can be proved or refuted as the case may be. With much that my hon. friend has said I am in hearty accord, but with some of it I do not at all agree. However, with regard to his statement that the soldiers (fame back rolling through foam and spray and did not'know what they were doing, I may say that that cannot apply to me personally.
I think, Sir, that this is a proper matter to come before the House. When' everything has been said to the contrary, the fact remains that there is unrest amongst the returned fighting men. This unrest, in my opinion, is caused solely by the inevitable injustice of war. With your permission, Sir, I will cite a couple of illustrations of the injustice consequent upon war. There are two brothers, one of whom went overseas and into the trenches, the other going into a munitions factory. The poor boy who went overseas remained there for a year, suffering all the horrors and hardships incident to modern warfare. He never slept in a bed, he was greatly inconvenienced by vermin, and eventually, a big shell dropping near him, he was disem-bowled-his comrade takes him back to the dressing station where he dies. The 'brother in the munitions factory has slept every night in a good bed, and has made more money than he ever made before. He is alive and. has married since. Both these
men were doing absolutely essential war work. The lad in the trenches could not have lasted one week unless the fellow at home supplied him with the necessary munitions, but I think it will be conceded that there is no comparison between the sacrifices of the two men. Take a second example, a couple of doctors. One of them goes overseas and the other stays at home. They could not both go. The man who went overseas returns and sees some of his old patients going into the other medico's office. These patients had to go_ somewhere. He also notices that the medical stay-at-home is living in a much bigger house than when he went overseas, and that he drives a much more expensive car. So we have it right down the line from the lawyer, the doctor, the civil engineer to the -man digging; we find that the felloF who went [DOT]overseas got the bad end of the stick. There is no use in denying that. We find, since the beginning of the war, lavish display and luxury cropping up. The streets are filled with new motor cars. In my own province in 1914 there were 10,000 odd licenses for cars; the last return shows that there are now 27,000.
I am not going to try to speak for all the returned soldiers in Canada. I speak for myself. I do not begrudge any man a car; I would like to see every man own a car, but if there are spare cars going around, I would like to have one, too. That is my personal feeling, and in expressing these thoughts to my comrades I find that they are met with at least a smile; they understand what I mean.
The average man did not go to the war for the money that was in it. He does not come back expecting to be paid for it. You could net pay him if you tried. But the fact -does seem to me apparent, Mr. Speaker, that if any man during the last five years really earned a new motor car it was the man who risked his life for his country. There is one other phase that has appealed to me personally, and that is the psychological end of it. I yenture upon this question with a certain amount of diffidence, for I do not know much about psychology, but the soldier comes back to Halifax and he is still very largely influenced by the spirit which took him over and bore him up through all the trials and troubles that he encountered over there. He is in a heroic mood. He is cheered and acclaimed by the people at home. He wears his medals with pride, he is smiled on by the ladies and everything is just as he hoped it would be when he was on the

other side. But in a few weeks he is de-mobolized, and you cannot demobilize the soldier too quickly to please him. It is something he has been looking forward to for a long time. He, has been looking forward to the time when he would, be back safe and sound in old Canada and at work again. But once you get back to civilian clothes and get back to work you seem to miss something. It begins to gall you under the collar. I do not know what it is that [DOT] the men miss; perhaps it is the comradeship, but personally I think the smiles of the ladies have a good deal to do with it. It is a fact that all women love a fighting man. , If he is in uniform he is received with a proud smile, but for some reason or other when he gets back to civilian clothes they size him up in a little different manner. Sometimes I think they size him up for his ability to keep a house -going, to support a family and to maintain a car. But there is a distinct difference between the soldier in uniform and one in civilian clothes. That cannot be helped.
I have tried to bring before the members of this- House some of the points of view that have a bearing upon the question of the returned soldiers and some of the causes for the prevailing unrest. Now that we have the unrest I shall try to suggest, if I may, the remedy. First of all, I think we must realize the tremendous job ahead of us. The successful re-establishment of the returned soldier is so intimately hound up with the general prosperity of this country. The job of reconstructing the ravages of the war is such -a big one, that it is going to take all the men, all the returned soldiers, all the women, all the babies for the next twenty years to accomplish -it. We want to -realize that it is a big job just as the w-ar was a big one, and we can only deal with it successfully iby having goodwill and an absolute desire to accomplish the end. Goodwill is something which only comes by sacrifice to the common end.
It is hard -perhaps to express to you -exactly what I.mean -by comradeship. There is nothing quite like it in the world. With it you can do anything; without it you can do nothing. I remember that once it was my duty to help 'bury in one orchard all classes and all ranks of the sons of Canada and there lie, if my memory serves, the son of a senator, the son of a millionaire and the son of a labour union leader in one shell hole. I have yet to learn that any one class in this country has all the virtues or all the good points which go to make up

this common, citizenship and goodwill without which we can -do- nothing. *
Right here I should like to say -a word on another phase of the subject. I want to register here and now my protest against the loose way in which we are using the word " profiteer." Who is the profiteer? Is it the man who makes profits? That sounds very like a good business man. - Can any hon. gentleman suggest to me that we could run this country successfully if we eliminated or hounded out of business our successful business men? Is it likely that we will ever get that goodwill and unity that I have spoken of by c-alling some of our men profiteers? I can never -believe that ninety per cent of the business- -men, of this country are profiteers. God only kn-ows, I hold no brief for the man who has made money out of the distress and turmoil of this war, but there is not in -my acquaintance a man of the calibre who might -properly be called a profiteer -and I w-an-t to register my protest right now against the loose way in. which profiteers are being spoken of in almost every newspaper in- the country. It was brought to my attention more particularly during the labour parade in- Ottawa. They had a -dummy on a string labelled "profiteer they were hauling him up and down on a derrick and every time he went up to the top the crowd -cheered. The question just struck me: What is a profiteer? The more I thought of it the more satisfied I w-as that it was time for me to stand up and say something on the subject.
Last session- it was my duty to place on record my protest against the use of the word " Bolshevik " with reference to a few men who were striking to better their conditions of life and I equally and just as emphatically wish to go on, record as protesting against the loose way in which the word "profiteer" is being used.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it-has been my -privilege to be very closely connected with the work of re-establishing the returned soldier. I am proud to be able to say that in my opinion of all the countries engaged in the task of re-establishing the soldier, Canada stands second to none.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
But I would say this:
there is much yet to be done. I believe we can do it, I believe we have the will to do it.
In 1917 the election programme was: The last man, the- last dollar if necessary to win this war, and you will remember that I was returned by the biggest

majority ever known in Canada. That, I believe, was the true spirit of Canada. It is the spirit which prevails now, and we shall win in our efforts to surmount the difficulties that confront us.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as one of those who served at the front for some time and saw the courage, sacrifice, tenacity, and cheerfulness of our men under most appalling conditions, I feel that it is perhaps my duty to take pome slight part in this discussion. I agree with the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that a discussion of this kind is perhaps wise for tne good of the country at the present time. I have become more or less convinced that free and open discussion on practically all occasions lets off steam, so to speak, and perhaps does good in the country. I also agree with the hon. gentleman that in' certain cases injustices have been done by the Government in the handling of the returned men, although at the same time I submit that this Government has done exceptionally fine work in its handling of the men. Still I agree with him that there have been injustices done. For example, in my own city, I have seen the appointment made of a man who was not a returned soldier to a $3,000 position, which I protested against. That position might well have been filled by the selection of a returned soldier from some other part of the country.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Sir, I think that cases of that kind should not have occurred. They are the small items in the handling of the returned soldier which have caused a great deal of the dissatisfaction and unrest in this country. But I submit also that the Government of Canada, just the same as the other governments of the wrnrld, was inexperienced in the handling of such vast problems as we have had to handle since this war began. Therefore, I think that the Government, whichever party happened to be in power, could easily be excused for having made a number of mistakes in the handling of the men who came back from the front.	,
Now, Sir, I wish to disagree with the hon. member (Mr. Currie) on one point which he made. He stated that only fifteen per cent of the returned soldiers are members of the Great War Veterans' Association. I have it on the best authority, from one of the high officers'-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I said active members.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member now states that he said " active members." I did not so understand him; I thought he said " members." I was about to say that I have it on the authority of one of the high officers of the Great War Veterans' Association that over 200,000 of the soldiers who "came back from the front, which is something like fifty per cent of the total, are members of that association. However, the hon. gentleman may be correct in his statement of the number of active members; I am not a very active member of the association myself, so I cannot check up his figures.
I also wish to make one allusion to the remarks from my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews), who has just taken his seat, who said that the existing unrest is very largely the result of the inequalities which existed between the men who served overseas and those who did not serve overseas. I agree with him mat a great deal of the unrest is caused and brought about by, perhaps, an accentuation of the differences which really existed before, and for centuries before. But I believe that the recent war will, perhaps, bring about a type of civilization in this world whereby the people of the world will not stand for those vast inequalities which have existed in the past.
Mr. Speaker, as a returned man, and as one who made a fair amount of financial sacrifice in going to the front, I do not know [DOT] anything that I could accept more easily than $2,000, unless, perhaps, it were $3,000. And, by the way, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask you if you could tell me who it was that' originally set this cheap price of $2,000 upon the glorious individual actions of our men at the front-

In making that observation, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I used to think that was only a figure of speech, but since serving overseas and seeing the work of the noble boys who fought over there, I firmly believe1 that the Canadian corps was at least the equal of, if not the superior to, any other corps that fought on the western front. their courage? I should like to ask further. -I should like to ask the hon. member for Simcoe, or anybody who advocates that $2,000 be paid to our soldiers-if the men are willing to sell that heritage of glory for a mess of pottage, in the shape of $2,000, which is mentioned?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I should like to ask if our boys ever expected to get $2,000 when they went to the front as an extra gratuity? As one who went and served over there I submit they did not expect any $2,000; I never heard a gratuity of any kind discussed over there. I did not expect a gratuity and so far as I am concerned the gratuity which I received was a total surprise to me. Mr. Speaker, there is nobody in this House or out of it who thinks more nobly of our boys who -served, so courageously at the front than I. There is no person in this House or out Of it who thinks they should receive better treatment from this country than I think; but at the same time I wish to say that I have yet to discover any man, in this House or out oi it, who does not hold the same view as I do regarding the very finest treatment o! our boys who have returned1 from overseas. And, Sir, I resent, as a returned soldier, the imputations which have been cast upon serious, high-minded public men, who do not wish to blindly promise $750,000,000 to the returned soldier unless they see some possibility of raising that sum, unless they see no fear of bankrupting our country in doing it, and unless and until they feel sure that they will not bring about the collapse of the whole financial structure of this country by attempting to pay that sum. Mr. Speaker, anybody I think will agree with me in thqse remarks when he looks.at the immense increase in the debt of this country since the war began. Let me briefly review our financial position: Canada owed $330,000,000 before the outbreak of hostilities or a matter of $40 per head for every man, woman and child ip the country. Canada to-day owes 
$250 per head, amounting practically to $2,000,000,000. The interest on our national debt was about $15,000,000 per annum before the war. -The interest on our national debt to-day is $115,000,000 per annum. Our pension bill, which was nil before the war, or practically nil, is to-day something like thirty to forty million dollars per annum. Another $125,000,000 is being spent on the Soldiers' Settlement Board. Another thirty cr forty million dollars-I have forgotten the exact figures as I am giving them from memory-on the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. Then there is the upkeep of the country, the deficits in the operation of our railways, and vast other sums which have to be raised. Therefore, I think it is a reasonable view to take that we should seriously consider how we are going to obtain the $750,000,000 for the purpose in question. I admit the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) has informed us that we are going to get it from Germany, but before we undertake to spend money we must obtain it, and. we certainly have not yet obtained any indemnity from Germany. But I agree that if eventually Germany does pay the indemnity which has been imposed on her it will be the duty of the British Government to see that Canada gets her just share.
I think this- Government will look after that part of it, and if they do not they will be derelict in their duty.
Personally I think that one of the greatest menaces in this country to-day are the demagogues who are ready at a moment's notice to accede to the irresponsible demands of any class of people. In my opinion they are panderers to popular prejudice, who are ready to promise anything which the people demand, so long as they do not have to give it themselves; and all they demand in return, Mr. Speaker, is the vote of the people to whom they are pandering. Unfortunately it is a sad comment Upon our public life that too frequently these demagogues get the votes, and the high-minded, serious citizens, citizens who love not only the returned soldiers but this country of ours, are shoved aside.
Mr. Speaker, $750,000,000 is an immense amount of money. Outside of this imaginary indemnity which we are to receive, I have not heard it discussed where this money is to come from, nor how it is to be raised. I have not heard or read of its being discussed in any public meetings whether th^ vast majority of the men who have served overseas desire this proposed gratuity of $2,000, nor have I heard it discussed whether it is the best thing for

them. 1 have heard the fathers of soldiers, and soldiers themselves, in fact most of them I have met knocking about this city-one who served with me and lost a leg-say they were not in favour of this $2,000 indemnity. We need production in this country. Will a payment of $2,000 to each of these returned men help production; or, as some people claim, will it send fifty per cent of them out on an extended holiday and lessen production? These are vital questions, and they are not generally discussed at public meetings.
The men who have returned from the front should receive the best treatment this country can give them. But I wish to repeat what the President of the Council gave to the House the other day, that so far as this country is concerned we have treated our men better than any other country in regard to monetary arrangements.
I agree with the remarks made, I think, by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) that no money can repay the men who have been out there-$2,000, $3,000, $10,000, $20,000, could not repay them for the sacrifices they made. But, as a matter of fact, Sir, these men did not go out there for money. What one of these men would have gone to work at a job like that for $1.10 a day? One compensation' to those of us who served out there-and it is rarely mentioned-is the satisfaction of knowing that in this war we played the parts of men. Is not that a priceless possession for us to hand down to our .children? Mr. Speaker, I would not sell that possession for any figure you could name. And what about those who do not need or do not want this $2,000 gratuity-men who perhaps, as the hon. member for Simeoe mentioned, do not require the money, men who are well fixed financially? Some of these returned men do not wish .to get anything else but a good position, and are they to be forced to take $2,000? Then there are the men who have better positions to-day than they would ever have had had there not been this war; are those men to be given $2,000? I admit that such men are vastly in minority, I admit that the majority of the men who went to the front made financial sacrifices-and if I may be excused for a personal reference, I am one of those who did -make a financial sacrifice. But as far as I am concerned, I am ready to accept that financial sacrifice as part of the price I paid for the privilege of going out theie .and helping in my humble way 21
to .preserve civilization by curbing the abnormal .ambitions of the German Emperor.
Mr. Speaker, let us think of our dead- our noble dead, those men who but a short time ago lived and loved as we do now. Would they demand $2,000 to be permitted to come back and join us here? I think of two of them at this moment, two who assisted me when I was medical officer of the Twenty-first Battalion-Private Boswell and Corporal Holden. They were among those whom I grew to admire, to respect and to love out there. They were charming, gallant boys, one of them with a little wife and family waiting here and longing for him to come back. I can see them now, Mr. Speaker, as they strode smilingly into danger zones that the bravest hesitated to enter. I can see them for days and nights after the battle of Vimy Ridge standing under heavy shell fire in an open trench dressing wounded .men, snatching an odd hour of sleep in the snow and mud at the bottom of the trench, and never uttering a complaint. Those men were recommended by me for decoration for that act, and it was only one of a thousand noble deeds which they performed. Do you mean to tell me, Mr. Speaker, that those men would demand $2,000 to come back to life, and love, and health and youth here in 'Canada? If the dead know what we do here on earth-and perhaps they do-must they not smile sometimes at the demands of the living? How they must say to themselves: Are you not satisfied that you came back in health, while we must lie out here in the cold soil of France and Flanders? Let our country keep its $2,000, but give us back our lives, our loves, our youth. When we think of them and the price they paid, does it not seem petty that we should be demanding money for the price we paid?	.	,
I do not wish to be misunderstood in speaking of this $2,000 gratuity, or in speaking of this question at all. Let me repeat .that this country must do everything it can possibly do to help these men who have come back from the front, and cases of injustice must be righted. Some system, it appears to me, must be devised whereby cases of real hardship can be helped; cases which require assistance to start them anew in life should be given that assistance.
I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Simeoe regarding the university students; a lot of whom enlisted when they were about to enter the university and they gave up their future to serve their country. It seems to me that some system of loans might be devised whereby those



boys would foe assisted to complete their education and be put in a position to qualify for a professional career. In addition to those, some system should and must be established in this country whereby all classes suffering hardship should be helped, because I do not believe it is the opinion of our people that any man who played a noble part over there should suffer hardship, or any of his dependents accept charity.
As the hon. member for Simcoe explained, Great Britain has organized an institution of this kind and is helping students to complete their university course and qualify for the professions. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that some such system as that applied not only to the students but to all other classes would meet with the support of the people even if it cost $100,000,000 or $150,000,000. I believe the country is very desirous of repaying our gallant boys for the noble part which they took out there at the front; the only thing they ask is that the price be not prohibitive, that it be within the resources of this country.
What would it profit our soldier boys if they gained these demands at the cost of the destruction of our country?. I think that blatant demagogues should not be encouraged; ranting, irresponsible agitators should not be tolerated, because they are neither friends of the returned soldiers, nor good, loyal citizens of our country.
As a returned soldier who has at heart not only the interest of the returned soldier, but also the interests of my beloved country, I appeal to our heroic men to show the same steadfast qualities here in Canada that helped to hold the line in France, and not to allow petty politicians looking for votes or irresponsible agitators looking for notoriety and power to seduce them into betraying the country which they so recently offered to die for.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
* Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few practical words upon what is, after all, a very practical and urgent question-we should not be discussing it if the House had not voted that it was an urgent question. I would wish from the bottom of my heart that we should approach it with the utmost sincerity and with absolute freedom from any party bias. The speeches which have preceded what I have to say in this debate have been admirable from that point of view. I think we are indebted to the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie); he need have made no apology for bringing this question before the House; I think he has'

done a public service. The advantage of approaching it without party bias, if we have regard to the urgency of the subject, is that there will be a possibility of our arriving unanimously at a wise method of handling what is, after all, a somewhat difficult question.
I do not intend to be debarred from saying what I have to say upon the subject by the appeals, and even the attempted dictation, of those reckless and "blatant demagogues "-I think that was the expression of the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion)-who outside this Chamber have shown considerable inclination to draw party support for themselves from a federal question in a field of political endeavour which is not federal.
I shall very likely be misunderstood by many friends whom I have amongst the returned soldiers. I have been for years a much misunderstood man, so that the experience of being misunderstood will not be a new one to me. I purpose, Sir, in the short time that I shall have the good fortune to retain the attention of the Chamber, to say what I have to say on this subject with courage and with an attempt to put ideas before the House for its practical solution which will meet the demands of fair play to all classes of the community.
There need be no surprise that this question has been brought to the doors of the Government and to the doors of Parliament. There need be no surprise, Sir, because the returned soldiers have been invited to bring it, both by the Government and by the official Opposition in this House. I am afraid that at this point I shall not receive the support of many members of the House of Commons. But I repeat that both the Government and the Opposition have invited this approach.
What did we have at the last session of Parliament? We had a housing scheme introduced, mainly for the relief of the returned soldier. We had ah incursion on the part of the Government of this country into road building-which, in my judgment, is a purely provincial enterprise-an incursion which was made with all the encouragement possible from considerable portions of the Opposition, especially those of them who came from Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia is a splendid province, but its in-
5 p.m. habitants have Scotch blood in them, and they can never resist the attraction of something that is going to do them good in worldly affairs.
Then, we had a shipbuilding scheme brought before the House, largely it was

said, for the benefit of the returned soldier, as the roads were. I trust we shall hear how many houses have been put up for returned soldiers, hofv many returned soldiers are working on the roads, and how many at shipbuilding. There again the Opposition, in the person of the most capable gentleman who still temporarily occupies the position of leader (Mr. McKenzie), gave every encouragement to the Government-no doubt not losing sight of the fact that the plates for the ships were to be bought in Nova Scotia.
Then we had a large scheme of land settlement-a huge scheme of land settlement-for the benefit of returned. soldiers. But a far more serious invitation than any of these held out has been held out to returned soldiers to present such a claim as this by the neglect of the Finance Department-not so particularly of this Government as now constituted as of the previous Government-to curb profiteering in the only way it could have been curbed-that is, by drastic taxation imposed from the first war session of Parliament. I want to say here, Mr. Speaker, that it is within my knowledge, as the result of intercourse with all ranks and conditions of returned soldiers, that they have been incensed and their whole nature has been revolted by the thought, on the one hand, of what they have gone through and what they have suffered, of their comrades who have died to the number of sixty thousand; and, on the other hand, of what they have seen since they came back-men who had not two dollars to rub against one another at the beginning of the war but who are now riding in their motor cars and owning their hundreds of thousands and in many cases their -millions of dollars. So I say, Sir, that there need be no surprise that the returned soldier is corning to this Parliament and asking that his immediate needs at least receive consideration for a little longer.
Now, I have referred to the invitations that have been held out to the soldier by the Government. But so far as I can see, the official Opposition in this House are still more culpable. I studied, Sir, with much interest and with very great care, a document which will lend itself to- extended consideration, probably, in a future session of this House-the platform of a convention which met in Ottawa in August last.
I do not know precisely what was done on that platform in the way of promising gratuities to the returned soldier-we shall no doubt hear from the Opposition on this
question; I hope they will tell us exactly where they stand in regard to it- but I know there is a large body of belief in the country that this question of a further gratuity to the returned men was one of the planks of their platform. It is an open secret anyhow that it was supported by many of the members who attended that convention, and that it was discussed in the Resolutions Committee. Everybody knows that, but as I say, although I have studied the somewhat extended and interesting document very carefully, I could not find precisely what it was that they were prepared to do for the returned soldier, and we shall listen with interest to the official expositors of that document in this debate and hear exactly what it- was that they held out to the returned soldiers.
There was more in that platform that invited the returned soldiers to knock at the door of this Parliament than- any direct reference to the gratuity. Why, there was a plank in that platform which engaged to take care of human Canadians from the cradle to the grave, by means of the State. The maternity fee was to be -paid when the Canadian came into -this world. I suppose for a brief period he was to be handed over to my hon-. friend the President of the Privy Council (\Mr. Rowell) to have a house provided for him when he was at the prime of life. If by any chance he became sick he was -to be insured by the official Opposition returned to power on this platform, against sickness; if he lost employment he was to be insured against unemployment-all by the State; and when he got old, in a country with less than two people to the square mile and an infinity of resources, he was to be provided with an old age pension, and, I suppose, finally he would be returned to my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council who would no doubt give him the necessary consolation in his last moments.
Now, what inference was a returned soldier, with all the weariness of war on him, and all the hardships of a pretty severe climate in front of him -to draw from the policy of the Government and the platform of the Opposition? Why he could draw only one inference, and that was -that we had money to burn in this country, that we had so much money we did not know what to do with it. The poor fellow, after all, had been at war, and he would- like a little consolation. I listened with interest to the poetic assurance of my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) that all the wealth of the Indies

could not reward the soldier for what he had done. That is perfectly true, Mr. Speaker, but all the verbal appreciation of a more eloquent man than my hon. friend would not fill his stomach three times in one day. There are two sides to that poetry business.

speechtext:
Besides verbal praises for the men who served at the front, did I not advocate assistance in every possible way for the returned men who required assistance?
Mr. :M. CLARK: Since my hon. friend has asked me a question, I must say that his speech was the most admirable specimen of facing both ways on a question that I have, ever seen in my life. He said in general terms that he was willing to do anything in the world for the returned soldier-so everybody in Canada has said who could speak-but the next moment he said that all the wealth of the Indies could not reward him. What was the meaning of that sentence? He uttered many other sentences along the same line. I did not make my remark ill-naturedly, although it has provoked a somewhat ill-natured retort. We will leave it at that. The public and the House will form their own appreciation of exactly where he stood on this question.

I hope so.
Mr. M. 'CLARK: I was trying to elaborate the point that official politicians are largely responsible for the fact that the soldiers are , at the door of Parliament with this demand, and I think I have given considerable evidence that there is some foundation for that statement. If these things have not happened, if these are not to be the policies of the parties in Canada, there will be every opportunity for reply. I said, before I was led off the line of my thought, that it was perfectly natural, indeed almost inevitable, that the returned soldier should, from a great many considerations, have arrived at the conclusion that there was money to burn in this country. Mr. Speaker, I think the time has come when somebody has got to say, not only to the returned soldier, but to every citizen in Canada, that there is not mon.ey to burn in this country.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I think the time has come when that must be stated in ia loud and emphatic voice not only to the Federal Government but to the Provincial and Municipal Governments of this country. The real truth, Sir, is-and we had better

all realize it, we shall be the better patriots the sooner W'e do-that fo.r a small population of eight millions such as we have in Canada, we are carrying a debt and obligations as a result of the war which are well-nigh unbearable. The country is in a condition of enormous debt and facing insolvency almost. Don't let me be thought for a moment to have any doubt of Canada's ability to bear her burdens? Canada will bear the burden 'and clear the debt, but the facts about our financial situation at -the moment ought to be stated, and stated in the plainest and most unmistakable terms. To take any other course, for political ot *any other reasons, is to be dishonest with ourselves and dishonest with the country.
Now I come to what, after all, as I said to commence with, is a very practical question, and I do not think it is very abstruse or very difficult. We can look at it from two angles in the main, and I think we can look at it from two angles only. We can look at it from the angle of the nation, and we can look at it from the angle of the returned soldier.
Another statement that has to he made emphatically which was made by my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River, and which I am very happy to endorse, and which the Government are taking steps to make by these very publications which we have ordered printed this very day, is that Canada has done far and away better in the matter of financial help for her soldiers than any other belligerent country within the Empire or outside of it. We stand at the top in that respect. Sir,
I am proud of what Canada did in the war and I. am proud of what she has done since the war. It is worthy of Canada. We are a big people and we know it. We have a big country and we know it, and we are out to do big things in the world; and as our men veritably did what my hon. friend from Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) claimed for them,-as they made the first break in the Hindenburg line, so we in the civilian trenches behind the ranks are at the top, as they were, in what we have already done in sheer gross material assistance to our soldiers. I am not now referring to the other things that have been * done, which may or may not be of assistance to the soldier or the country, according as they were wisely conceived and will be wisely carried out. We have not only given this aid, hut we have done an enormous amount in the way of the re-instatement of our men in civil life at the sacrifice of others of our citizens, and that is a con-

sideration that ought to affect the mind of this House, as well as the minds of the veterans in their attitude on this question.
I wonder if those who are most insistent npon this question ever reflect that there were many civilians who held positions in the Civil Service both of the Federal Government and of the Provincial Governments, who have had to step down, and have in many cases, I am sure, gladly stepped down in order that the returned soldiers should take their places. In many cases these civil servants stepping down are tender girls who did their bit in the war according to their ability and upon whose earnings parents are dependent for their support. Numbers of them have already been dismissed and others will be dismissed in the course of coming weeks. They will be dismissed not merely in the interest of economy but to provide places for returned soldiers. If it be true-and it is substantially true, I think, as it has been stated to-day-that each man or woman who stayed at home and did the .best they could in their own work here was morally as virtuous and as heroic, if you like, as the soldier himself, then the civil servants who are suddenly deprived of their occupation and income would be entitled to come to us and ask for relief. But we know that they will not do it. That consideration, however, should modify our attitude on this question.
I have referred to the financial position of the country, which is as serious as my language can describe it. What the country has done for the soldiers; what those who are giving up positions are sacrificing for the soldiers now; and the very serious financial position of the country at the present moment-these are the main thoughts that ought to be in the mind of the committee which will deal with this question, and that ought to be in the minds of hon. members when they approach the consideration of it.
I have said that the subject can also be looked at from the point of view of the soldier, and at this point let me say that I should like to know from some member of the Government who may speak on the subject later-as I have no doubt some member of the Government will-whether there are any statistics as to how many soldiers have been replaced in civil life. I understand that when my hon. friend the Minister of Militia demobilized a man, that man passed from the Militia Department's care and was handed over to some other department of Government. I should like some
minister to state whether there' are any accurate statistics as to the men who have already been replaced in civil life and those who have not been so replaced. I think that that is a consideration of the greatest importance. I had occasion to address a meeting on Celebration Day, July 19, in the little town where I live, and I told the audience there with very great pride that from that little town and district 150 men went to the war. A very considerable proportion) of them, I am sorry to say, will not come back, but those who have come back are replaced to a man. Statistics have been kept by the people in that neighbourhood, and those who have come back have been all replaced either on the farm or in the village, or in the service of the local Government of my province. I have similar information about other districts in my constituency, and I have not the least doubt that this is the case with regard to the rural districts all over Canada. However, the practical point I am trying to bring to the attention of the minister is that we ought to have as near an approximation as possible in statistics to the actual numbers of men who have been replaced and those who have not. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) that there is something very alluring about the policy of giving $2,000 to a man-at least for the man who is to receive the $2,000. It is a policy which, amongst the recipients, would not need any active propaganda to make it reasonably popular; I quite agree with my hon. friend in that respect. But this Parliament has responsibilities, and one of them is to ask, in regard to the soldier himself: Suppose he got the $2,000, would it do him good or not? Now, Sir, I am certain it would do some men good. I know of some returned soldiers whom I could trust with $2,000 to put it by and let it breed and take care of the interest as well as the original capital. But I know some others who are now on the farm-I know them intimately-who, if they got a *hack of $2,000 would immediately go off the farm. They might not stay off. but they would have a look at old 'London again. It is the duty of this House to consider seriously whether, if this demand were acceded to, we should not be doing more harm than good to the soldiers themselves. From the soldiers point of view

and here I have no doubt I am going to make enemies in the ranks of the soldiers-I think it is .necessary to say that there is no heroism 'in mendicancy. If there is any man among 'the returned veterans who has the spirit of

la mendicant, then he should lay that truth .to heart, that there is no heroism in mendicancy. However, we shall have light on the subject when we know exactly what has been done for the soldiers since they were .demobilized.
Now, in regard to the Government's attitude so far on this question, I think the ,statement of the Prime Minister, which has been very much criticized and in which he expresses the view that he did not see the need of a commission, was a most courteous and reasonable statement, as indeed his statements always are. It not only said .'that the Government did not see the need of a commission but that they had all the 'facts in their possession which were necessary to settle the question. Well, that being iso, one arrives at the point at which the (Government's position is not quite so strong, (because if they had all the facts at their 'disposal necessary to settle the question, Iwhy in Heaven's name do they not settle lit? Why appoint a committee? This com-knittee cannot ascertain any more facts than the Government has, if it has all the facts. I do not therefore understand why .this matter is being handed over to a committee, after the Government have told ;the people from the Atlantic to the Pacific 'that they themselves know all about it. .After all, they are the parties who are primarily responsible.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
wants to go into a little business. Well, I trust the Government won't, without very great and very grave consideration, try to find embryo Rockefellers in the ranks of those who are most urgent amongst the veterans for this 32,000. I trust the Government will not look there for the best business men that they can find. I do not want to say anything to hurt the feelings of any man. who- went to the front, but I do say this: That for building up .a business, and every man almost in this House knows what I am saying is true, you want in the first place business inspiration-that -must be your calling-and you want very great mental astuteness and you want determination. Every business man listening to me knows that what I am saying,is true and it is a great doubt in. my mind-especially if the description of the returned soldier given by my hon. friend from 'Simooe (Mr. Currie) has even a glimmer of truth in it-* if large numbers of successful business men could be found in those who are most urgent for money under this particular head. What are we to do then?
I have said that we should not leave the men without something for this winter; and personally, having regard to all that I have said about the gravity of Canada's resources, I believe we should start this winter as beginning from the first of November to the last of March. That is what I do in regard to the feeding of my cattle-I always try to have feed enough for all the cattle I have from the beginning of November to the end of March. Now having said that as' to the winter, during which these returned men may suffer want and suffer want to the point of becoming a menace to the public safety-and here the national question joins the personal question, here the nation's interests join the soldiers' interests- looking at this as a practical question and seeking a wise method of dealing with it, I would give a gratuity to the soldiers from the first of November to the end of March. Limit it as you like, make it the lowest thing that you can call a living wage. I may be asked "Why do you urge that, after you have .said that Canada has already done more for her soldiers than any other country?" My answer is this: Canada has, but Canada also has a climate which is vastly more rigorous than any other country in the Empire, and that I take it is a complete answer to that question. There is no inconsistency in claiming a high position for Canada and yet bearing in mind that we have so much of our work closed down in winter and that our climate is so

rigorous. That is what I would say for the returned soldier. "For whom mainly would you do it?" I may be asked. I would do it for every man among them; I would make no distinction between the humblest private and the commander-in-chief. This is a democratic country. I would do it as an urgent public necessity and an urgent necessity for the soldiers themselves; 1 would do it along the line of seeing that every returned soldier, at least, had enough to keep body and soul together in this severe climate for the first five months, for the first winter that- they have been at home altogether with us once more; and I would do it as a democrat-I would treat them all alike. In that way you would relieve yourselves of all the heart-burnings, and they would be numerous, which would arise if 'you dealt with special cases and you would put yourselves in the position of saying: When the month of April-comes we shall all be living in the finest country in the world to get along in, if you have a man in you. We shall be able to say: This is the final decision, this closes the question, and next April we are all going to settle down to be good Canadians.
I intended to say something about how I would get the money. I would not get it the way my hon. friend from Simcce talks of getting it, because he would not get it that way at all and it would be a very poor way of getting it. Talk of getting money from Germany to relieve the soldiers this winter is not to be considered for one minute, just as I think giving $2,000 to each soldier is not to be considered for one moment-I do not believe the majority of the men are considering it, and certainly the majority of our fellow citizens are not considering it. I would get the money along the lines of the policy that was laid down by Mr. Asquith in a very lucid and powerful speech which he delivered the other night-delivered in a way I could not deliver a speech, but I could say all the things he said, and have been saying them continuously during the last five years, and the House will recognize them when I repeat what he said. He said: " I have no panacea, no special panacea for the condition of England at the present moment; you have got to remove all the restrictions from imports which you put on during the war"-and strangely enough the Government did it from the first of September. That is Number -One. He said further: "And the next thing you have got to do is to institute drastic economy.'1' Why, we could save what would pay for the soldiers,

what I have said should be done for them, if the departments of this Government were handled by business men upon business lines as the business men of this country handle their own business. Drastic economy; and I would get it by bringing Parliament down early in the new year and giving every member of it a primer on political economy and let him get to know something about the proper methods of taxation. I would do it by taxing the rich.
I would do it by direct taxation.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Class taxation.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Well, there must be class taxation to the extent that you cannot get money from a man who does not have it. If my hon. friend says that; if his zeal for not going along the lines of class taxation carries him to the length of saying that paupers should pay taxes, then I take his point for what it is worth. The point is not mine-it was Mr. Asquith's recommendation to the people of Britain. I desire to impress these three points of a great speech upon the Government and upon the House: Take down your import restrictions; trade to make money. Money was never made in any other way. Make the nioney first.
Economize; do not spend. That is the way tc get rich whether you are an individu il or a nation. Make money on the one hand and do not spend it on the other. Mr. Asquith's third point, which he sa'I would be more disagreeable, was more drastic taxation-and	that in England, Mr. Speaker, where some incomes are paying sixty per cent income tax. Let me at this point repeat, that what is rankling in the minds of the returned men is that, against advice, the Finance Department, under the ex-minister, did not put on an income tax at the beginning of the war. Our debt would have been less, and what would have been vastly more valuable than that, our people, rich and poor alike, from the first days of the war would have learned 'the lessons of service and of sacrifice.
I have given the House my poor thoughts upon this question honestly and fearlessly, and without any party feeling, as behooves one -sitting on these cross benches. When we arrive -at spring, if we shall have tided over the winter in this way, we shall be all Canadians together, let me repeat, in a country which I have learned to love, and which is capable of the greatest things for ourselves both individually and as a nation; but I want to say that we shall only be a people equal to the record we
have made in the war, we shall only be a people worthy of the great natural resources which Divine Providence has given us as a magnificent heritage, if, whether we be veterans or civilians, we bring into civil life the same qualities of courage, of endurance, of holding on to the end that has sent Canada's name to the very topmost pinacle of the Temple of Fame. Those are the qualities we must cultivate if we would build up Canada.
This country is amply able to provide for -all of us. Do not let any of our soldiers hunger this winter. Deal with them all alike on democratic principles; give them at least a living wage for the first five months of the winter; leave no heartburnings by giving it to one and refusing it to another, and when April comes, this decision having been recognized by Parliament and Government and people and soldiers as final, let us stand as men before the world, and may every one of us be able to say about his civil life as our soldiers are well able to say about their military life:
In the fell clutch of circumstance,
I have not winced nor cried aloud;
-Beneath the bludgeonings of chance
My head is bloody but unbowed.
It matters not how straight the gate,
How charged with punishment the scroll.
I am the master of my fate,
I am the captain of my soul.

After Recess.
