subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I declared in Calgary last summer that I was opposed to the $2,000 bonus to each of our returned men, which meant a total payment of $800,000,000 because I believed that the country could not pay it. On the other hand, there is a large field of reasonable inquiry -to which we should devote our attention. The subject which is before us to-night, Sir, is this, what has been accomplished by the present schemes of re-establishment? What further is required; how much money will it take to meet these further requirements, and what part, if not all, of that money can our country afford to pay?
There are several proposals before us. There is the -proposal of a new organization known as the Gratuity League, or something of that kind, in Toronto, -that a flat gratuity of $2,000 be -paid. There is the proposal of the Great War Veterans' Association, passed by their Vancouver convention last July, that the Government

pay a bonus to the soldiers, that bonus to be limited by the ability of the country to pay. I need hardly point out that the Great War Veterans' Association is the most powerful body of returned men in Canada; that it has within its ranks-I should think that this is a fairly correct estimate-some
200,000	returned men, and that it has as its sympathizers the dependents of these soldiers, and I think, many soldiers who belong to no organization. This being the case we should consider to what organization we should give the greatest consideration.
I do not agree with some hon. gentlemen who have said to-day that this very intricate and involved subject can be settled by one debate in this House. I believe that the subject should be gone into by a committee or commission which will ascertain with the greatest care all the facts which are relevant to such an inquiry and which will survey all the possible remedies to meet the needs of the case. With this end in view I put a resolution on the Order Paper some days ago which, as I have previously explained, I withdrew because the Government saw fit to appoint a parliamentary committee. I understand, from the assurance given by ministers in this House, that the appointment of that committee will be based upon a Bill already submitted, or that the Bill will be so amended as to enable such a committee to go into the entire question of soldiers' civil re-establishment and in doing so to have the broadest possible scope.
I believe that such a committee will be more satisfactory even than the commission which was first suggested by the Great War Veterans' Association, because its personnel will consist of members of the House, who are now available for action; a staff is also available. In the second place, such a committee will be made up of men who are responsible to their constituencies. The inquiring body will not consist of men who may have no special qualifications for the work, or who may even b.e biased one way or the other. Another reason why a parliamentary committee will be more satisfactory to soldiers than a commission is that the committee must report during the present session of Parliament, and when the report is in an opportunity will then be presented to the Government to bring forward any money Bill which may be necessary in order to give effect to the recommendations of such a committee. Moreover, in the original resolution of the Vancouver con-fM. Redman.!
vention, a joint parliamentary committee, not a commission, was asked for. No such body as a joint parliamentary committee is possible under our constitution, so that a parliamentary committee is the nearest approximation which can be had to comply with that request. Having served during the last two years on the Pensions Committee of this House, I am certain that a parliamentary committee will accord to the war veterans and to all interested parties the fullest possible consideration of all the facts which bear upon this complicated subject. I am certain that such a committee can adequately deal with this question.
Now, taking my definition of the subject which is before us and having in view the desirability of surveying the existing schemes for demobilization and for reinstatement into civil life of our soldiers, let us first see what the present schemes are.
On Friday the President of the 'Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) gave us a great deal of very useful information and a number of very interesting figures showing that the provisions which Canada had made for her soldiers were infinitely superior to those which had been made by other countries. Let us examine .for a few moments the charts and figures which he gave us.
In the first place, it may be pointed out that pensions1 affect only those who have been wounded or dependents of those who were killed in the war. While our pensions are admirable, even their limit is not adequate to meet the cost of living which at present prevails in our country.
, Then, the question of re-education. While (Canada has proceeded further and more successfully in this matter than any other country, only a limited number of our returned soldiers are assisted in that way. In fact, it is questionable whether the courses which have been given to many returned soldiers adequately fit them for the new vocations which they have taken up, or whether it has really put them in a much better position than they were before.
The question of medical treatment has been adequately dealt with, but that applies only to those who have been wounded; it *does not go far towards re-establishing the returned soldier in civil life.
. It was shown that France, England and Germany have not dealt as generously with their soldiers as Canada has dealt with hers. While that is true, we must not forget that France, England and Germany are impoverished by this war to an extent .which we in Canada have not begun to approach. Moreover, in the countries men-

jtioned other schemes are carried out, in '.addition to the gratuities ankl pensions, comparison of which was made with ours. In .England there is unemployment insurance; [DOT]and they have been more generous in the affording of facilities for the education of soldiers in universities than we have. It is .quite true that United 'States compare very unfavourably with Canada in this matter. In that regard I can only say that in my *opinion United States has not dealt fairly, let alone generously, with its soldiers. Moreover, the United States soldiers were only in the war a very short period compared with our men, and the sacrifices which they were called upon to make were as nothing compared with the sacrifices made by the Canadian soldiers.
, In respect to the gratuities which have been paid by the Government, and which were generous and voluntarily given, the soldiers have made several complaints, gome of these complaints, in my judgment, are well founded. In the first place, these gratuities were given according to rank. That was a fundamental mistake in a matter of principle, because gratuities were .given for the purpose of re-establishing soldiers in civilian life as civilians, not as officers or privates in the army. There has been resentment and there is still resentment among private soldiers on account of ..the adoption of that principle, which seems to me to be an unfair one.
, In addition to that, I think the Government would have been wise had they made .arrangements whereby some board could have sat in various centres and instead of paying monthly to the men this wage or allowance which was given monthly, that board should have afforded a man an opportunity of getting the amount in a lump sum if he could show that by so getting it .he would be able to re-establish himself forthwith in some business.
A great deal of agitation and irritation has' also been caused among soldiers by .reason of the fact that a certain number of the dependents of soldiers who returned to Canada, since the day of the armistice have had their way paid home, whereas ,those who, at the invitation of the Government, were patriotic enough to send their [DOT]dependents home from England previous ,to the date of the armistice, had to pay [DOT]*their way, and no effort has been made ,to re-adjust that unfairness.
A great deal of complaint has been made by those Canadians who, instead of enlisting in the Canadian army, for various .causes enlisted in the army of Great Britain or in the armies of our Allies, with the result that their fellow .Canadians who enlisted in the Canadian army are receiving .infinitely better treatment than they are.
, Last session the Government brought forward a housing scheme-an excellent .scheme, well-timed; a scheme which, had .full advantage been taken of it, would in .many communities have solved the problem of the shortage of housing accommodation. .That scheme was brought in, as we understand, mainly to provide houses for returned soldiers.
I am sorry to say that in the province of Alberta, and I believe in many other provinces, the scheme up to date has been ineffective. I do not think that is the fault of this Government, but of the various Provincial Governments who have refused to take advantage of the scheme. In any event the soldiers who have been looking forward to getting homes under that scheme have seen their hopes disappointed, and ' have in consequence a feeling of justifiable irritation.
The land settlement scheme of the Government has been an excellent one and has provided foT many soldiers. I do not agree with those who say that the land settlement scheme is not of advantage to soldiers. I think a man who can borrow several thousand dollars and get on a half section of land in our western country with its splendid possibilities, and with the almost certain increase in land Values about to come, with full equipment, has an excellent chance of getting ahead in the world and is pretty well on the road to re-establishment. While that scheme is of advantage to a great many of our soldiers, you can understand the feelings of the others who wish to go into business' of some other kind. , It is bound to cause dissatisfaction amongst them. I think that the land settlement scheme, while not the underlying cause, was perhaps the proximate cause of the birth of the 82,000 bonus scheme.
Let us consider the position of those of our soldiers to whom none of these schemes have been of any advantage. Many of our soldiers, it is true, have been able to reestablish themselves, but a large proportion of our soldiers have not. I have said in this House so often that it must be getting monotonous, though I have never said it as well as or as fully as the cause deserves, that our soldiers returning to Canada are entitled to be absorbed into our economic life; they are entitled to the best positions they are capable of filling. They have come back to this country after two, three or four years' absence overseas, having sacrificed

the positions they held when they left, and are returning to us perhaps slightly more unfit for economic strife in proportion to the time they were overseas, some of them suffering from physical handicaps, and some perhaps from mental handicaps, on account of the experiences they have gone through. They come home to Canada where we in the meantime have had every opportunity, owing to the exceptionally good financial conditions prevailing during the war, of improving our own financial condition. Many of these men have not yet been absorbed into our economic life. I claim it is th^ir absolute right to be absorbed by the Canadian people into the economic life of this country.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How are you going to put them back into civil life without some money?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to that question. My objection is to offering to give them a sum of money which I think every reasonable human being knows we cannot give them.
As I said last year, I think the Canadian Government might have gone further in absorbing more soldiers into the various departments of the Government, not only for the good of the soldiers so employed, but for the example it would set to other employers of labour throughout the country.
I need, hardly remind the House that Great Britain has recognized so clearly her obligation to re-absorb her soldiers into civil life, that she has made arrangement whereby if a soldier cannot obtain a position during the first twelve months after his de-moblization he is entitled . to a certain stated sum each month he is idle. I believe, Sir, that no comprehensive scheme has yet been offered by this Government at all commensurate with its obligation to re-absorb our soldiers into the economic fabric of our country. It is true that last session a great amount of money was voted for public buildings in various centres. If this work had been gone on with it wrould have been of very great assistance, particularly in our larger centres. A vote was passed for the erection in Calgary, for instance, of a post office, which we greatly need, but no work has been done on that yet. Had the contract been let I believe that to-day we would be able to employ two hundred stone-cutters in Calgary cutting the stone for that building. We have stone-cutters who came out from the Old Country to Calgary on account of the quantity of stone we have in that vicinity. If the contract had been let many of these 
men would to-day be employed, and many more still next summer. So I think it is the duty of the Government, if no other solution offers, to afford work of this nature in, the various centres in order to relieve the unemployment which I believe is coming. I am not saying that there is a great deal of unemployment in Calgary or other cities in Canada to-day, but I would point out that a large percentage of our men in Western	Canada are	now at
work in the harvest fields and in a very few weeks they will be coming into the cities. While I do not wish to assume the role of prophet, I do believe that thirty or at all events sixty days will not elapse before we will have in Calgary and in every other city in Canada a large number of soldiers who have been, back from overseas but a short period, and who, through no fault of their own, and in spite of their best efforts to get employment, will not be able to get a job this winter. I need hardly say that we are responsible. These men are still the wards of the state until they [DOT]are re-absorbed into our economic life. The proper note was struck here to-day when it was suggested that the comparison which these men must draw between their own position and that of those who have been financially Successful during the war must aggravate the situation. All of us in employment in this country to-day and receiving some emolument know 'that it is hard to keep up with the cost of living, but what would be our position if we had been away from this country for several years and come back with a feeling that we had not the opportunity of getting into the industrial or commercial world of this country but were on the outside looking on, with a conviction that our country did not realize its obligation to us. Possibly the Government might assist by grappling more energetically than they have with the problem of the high cost of living. I believe that problem is being grappled with in the United States much more effectively than in Canada to-day, and this session should not come to a close until we have passed all enabling legislation that is required to enable our Government to deal with this problem as effectively as it is being dealt with in the United States. That might have its influence.
I think I have gone over the various schemes which have been suggested, and whether I have convinced you, Mr. Speaker, or not, I have at least convinced myself that the present schemes for the re-establishment of our soldiers are not adequate,

but that something further is required. What is required? This problem is much too complicated and intricate to be solved in one debate. It must be referred to a committee that will take evidence and make full inquiry into the matter, and on the facts adduced finally form their opinion. Some of the suggested remedies which will come before that committee will be the following: The cash bonus scheme which has 'been suggested; the Great War Veterans' scheme for such bonus as the country can afford to pay. I think they will also consider some such scheme as has been suggested by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) here to-day, of a bonus during the winter months. Perhaps they will consider the question of unemployment insurance.
That is now a practical possibility in this country because the Labour Bureaus, which under recent legislation have been instituted from one end of Canada to the other, provide the machinery whereby we can ascertain clearly whether a man has had an opportunity to obtain work, and whether he is unemployed through no fault of his own. Perhaps they will consider the question of industrial loans which Australia is now grappling with and which have been discussed by the soldiers throughout the country. In dealing with the problem of the re-establishment of soldiers in civil life, one matter of importance which should be earnestly considered is the assumption by the State of that proportion of insurance premiums which will represent the amount of disability which a soldier may have sustained and for which he will be taxed by the insurance companies when he seeks insurance. Some men have returned with various disabilities, such for instance, as an impairment of the lungs or heart, and it is their right to insure their lives for the projection of their wives and families. They are willing to pay the ordinary premium which we are all ready to pay, but they may find that the disability which they have suffered in the service of the country is such that probably they will be called upon to pay two or three times the premium ordinarily paid. Surely that added proportion of the premium it is the duty of the State to shoulder. We have a responsibility to see that the man who has been overseas shall be enabled to protect his family by means of insurance at the same rate as before he went to the war. All these are questions which this committee should carefully examine into.
We should not come to a definite conclusion here to-day. Certainly we should not get the idea that there is nothing in this discussion but the alternatives of granting or refusing a gratuity of $2,000. In any event, we cannot arrive at a definite conclusion until the evidence has been submitted to the committee and we have had an opportunity of perusing it and very carefully weighing it. After we have done that we shall be in a better position to come to a proper determination in regard to these various questions that are involved in the problem which is now engaging the serious attention of all thinking and responsible citizens of the country. In all this discussion to-day if we do nothing but survey the question in a general way and come to the conclusion that some further substantial scheme of re- * establishment is required we shall have done a great deal. We must realize that something further is required in order to constitute an adequate re-establishment of our soldiers in civil life. Something further is required before the State shall have fulfilled its obligations to the men who went overseas risking their very life for the national ideals and the national wealth, a portion of which may be required to adequately re-establish them now that they have returned. We should approach this subject, I think, from an entirely unbiased standpoint, unbiased by the voting strength of any organization which may make representations, utterly uninfluenced by the clamour which extremists may create, and solely with a view to ascertaining just what is required. When we have definitely decided what the requirements will demand in the way of financial aid, we should then undertake the raising of the money for that purpose with the same zeal and enthusiasm which characterized our efforts in securing the necessary money to carry us 'through the war, because the care of the returned soldiers, the proper and satisfactory treatment of the wounded, and the duty which devolves upon the State to see that full and complete justice is aocorded the wives, and children of those who have suffered for us, are all equally as sacred a trust now that Peace has been consummated as was our duty during the heat of the struggle to put forth our greatest efforts to prosecute the war to a .successful con-elusion.
i Mr, JOHN H . BURNHAM (Petebboro West):	I think, iSir, that every member
on such an occasion as this should express

*as far as possible the feeling which prevails in the district he represents. I am ,not one of those who think that every question should be relegated to a committee, because I am convinced that this House has some brains and that its members are capable of imparting to one another the information which they severally possess and *that, having a certain degree of judicial .faculty, they are well aJble to exercise it. At the same time, of course, we must .bear .in mind that matters of detail are always .referred to a committee and in that respect there can be no objection to that procedure. The soldier wants one thing and one thing only, and that is employment. ,To give him money is simply to postpone .the evil day, if he has not employment. ,To give him money when he is unemployed ds merely to attempt to cure a disease by .administering a palliative. The soldier, I repeat, does not want money as much as he wants employment and the opportunity .to settle down seriously to earn something .for his family as he formerly did. Under the circumstances, therefore, when I heard ,on former occasions the exdVfinister of Public Works, the hon. member for Carleton .lay down the dictum that in order to .effect economy in this country we must realize that there was no necessity for engaging in public works, I felt that the death knell of the soldier had been sounded, and ,the soldiers thought so too. They said that .they evidently were to fight the battles of .the country and were to be compelled to pay for the war on their return. Naturally the soldier was very much irritated. It is .apparent, Sir, that it is a short-sighted policy to leave any considerable proportion of the population without employment, .for this is only to create another disturbing element in 'the community even if the soldiers are provided for. The country stands .in a position exactly similar to that of the man who wishes to borrow money. If he goes to a money-lender and asks for money .inevitably the question is put to him: What purpose is it needed for? If it is intended for improvements, then ten chances to one the money will be lent; if, on the other hand, improvements are not contemplated it will not be advanced. You can borrow the money in a country that has more money than it knows what to do with, namely the United States. This 'Government could and should borrow money for .public works and give employment now and during the coming winter to the soldiers and every other idle man in the country. The Government can raise $350,000,000 more; for what purpose? To waste it? Not 
by any means. It is only using it as a medium of exchange, and we could have the soldier translating his work into buildings for the betterment of tbe country at the same time benefiting himself. I think that the Government did the worst thing in the world when it conceived the idea and gave expression to it that economy consisted in cutting down expenditures in necessary public works. I say we should go on with public works. Borrow money and proceed with public works which will be an enduring monument to the technical ability of the country and which will serve the very urgent purpose of giving employment to those who are in need of work, thus amply justifying the expenditure. Build good roads and .bridges and erect buildings; do anything you can conceive of that will be of permanent benefit .to the country for the future and that will give [DOT]much needed work to those who are suffering, and you will render a magnificent service to the soldier who wants employment above everything else. That is the service he wants. He does not want a donation as a means of pacifying him; he wants work. iHe went to the war as a man and at home he desires to be treated as such, and it is altogether unfair to the soldier to portray him as a beggar. He is not a beggar. Give him work; give every honest man work and there will be no fear of rebellion or revolution.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find that most of
what I had intended to say has already been stated during the course of this debate. I quite agree, as I hope to show later on, with the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Burnham) and I also agree with the hon. and very gallant member from Calgary (Mr. Redman) who spoke before him. I say " gallant " member advisedly, because he must be gallant -and I am sure he showed his gallantry to-night as much as probably he ever exemplified it on the field-when, as a member from the constituency from which this demand for $2,000 arose, he was able to say to the voters who sent him here that he was not in favour of such an extravagant demand on the public purse of Canada. For this I congratulate him. I also agree with him that the gratuities as they have been distributed so far have not met with general satisfaction. For instance, we have at the present moment staff officers drawing staff pay with their war service gratuity. I think it is absurd, unreasonable, and unjust. There may have been a reason, but

hitherto I have not been able to ascertain it, for staff officers drawing increased pay. (Since they have returned to civilian life at all events they should not receive a larger gratuity than is given the average soldier.
, It has been said during this debate that ,we should all approach this subject from a non-partisan standpoint. Up to very recently, I too had been endeavouring to approach all subjects in reference to the soldier from a non-partisan standpoint. I was one who voted at the convention of the .Great War Veterans, and in my own branch *in Quebec, to keep the soldier out of politics. I am sorry to be forced to come to the conclusion that all questions relating to the soldier ought to be considered as *partisan questions. Under our system of Government it is only through party politics that the common people have ever been able to achieve anything. We sit down *supinely in this House, the members on *the one side and the members on the other *saying:	We will not make this a party
question; everything is lovely; we have done so much for the soldier; we are all favour-, *able to doing everything we can for him- ,and the result is that the soldier gets nothing. I believe that such things should not ,be. Therefore, when anything is brought up in regard to the soldier, I am a partisan. I shall begin being a partisan by renouncing *my own party in regard to the soldier. In the Liberal party platform there was a clause, which advocated a cash bonus. I am absolutely opposed to any further payment of a cash bonus to any soldier. I am under the impression that the gratuity has been wasted, that we have already treated our soldiers generously in reference to gratuities and that we have done enough.
. There is another reason why I am a partisan in this matter. The present Government-I call it the Tory Government

have been playing politics with the soldier. They have been endeavouring to take the soldier to their bosom for political purposes only. *They have been endeavouring to control the soldier's vote throughout the country. *Even before the soldiers were a force in this country, and whilst they were still a *force in politics overseas, they sought to control the soldier's vote. Now the day of reckoning has arrived and it is for 'the Government to make good their promises to the soldiers. Let those who promised the soldiers everything during the election in ,1917 make good. I have in my hand an extract from the minutes of a meeting of honourably discharged soldiers held under the auspices of the Grand Army of Canada, .Vimy Post No. 4, at the Irish Rangers
Armoury, 91 Stanley street in the city of Montreal, on August 1, 1919. This document is written on the paper of the Grand Army of Canada. The motto appears there **-and I commend it to the Government-
We will not break faith."
It was moved by Comrade H. B. Jones, seconded by Comrade J. E. Lapointe, accepted by the majority and unanimously resolved' as follows :
"Whereas the Grand Army of Canada, Vimy Post No. 4, in resolutions passed on April 30th, May 6th, and 13th, 1919, reminded the Government of various promises given, and
"Whereas among them was one previously given on behalf of the Government in December, 1917, before the election, of a peace gift to each soldier of $2,500, and
"That we honourably discharged soldiers gathered at this meeting (open to all returned men) remind the Government that as Peace is already officially proclaimed, and that it is now time to fulfil its ' You have a vote ' pledges, and pay to all discharged men who served in France, $2,500 and to other pro rata,
"We ask the delegatee of the G.A.C. to present this resolution in person to the Right Honourable Prime Minister in Ottawa,"
I hereby certify the foregoing to be a true extract from the minutes of said meeting.
With reference to this resolution, I suggested to the soldiers that it would be well to collect the $2,500 from the people who had promised it

from the Unionist party- and that there was no reason why this money should be collected from the people of Canada who did not make this promise. This promise apparently was made in France by the Unionist party canvassers, and therefore I should think that the Unionist party, which had so much money at the last election, ought to collect this $2,500 and pay it over to these soldiers.
This Grand Army of Canada is a wonderful organization. It has a paper entitled The Grand Army of Canada Weekly Journal, and in it I find some most interesting things. I"n the " Open Forum," page 14, of the issue of May714, 1919, we have a letter to Sir Thomas White from W. E. Collins, Secretary of Vimy Post Grand Army of Canada, Montreal. It is rather long and I will not tire the House by reading it all, but among other things he refers to the fact that when Russia had signed the Peace Treaty some difficulty was found in paying separation allowance to the wives of certain Russian soldiers in the Canadian army. The writer says that:
The Canadian Government opened an office at India House in London for Canadian Russian soldiers and placed same in charge of Major Yurkevitch, of Montreal, who was assisted by his own daughter and Lieut. Novitzky. It is claimed, however, that this office was incompetent and incapable of handling the matters under dispute.

In case he does not attempt conscientiously to learn a trade in which he can earn more money, he is not a good citizen and we should le't him look after himself as he probably did before the war I would solve the difficulties of the students in a similar way. The Vocational Training Branch of the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Department could be extended to the students also in such a way that they could finish their university course, and their tuition fees, with perhaps some personal compensation, should be paid by the depaitment. So that, in fine, my solution of the problem-take it for what it is worth; it may demand a great deal more study-is simply to Jiave public works carried on by the Government in order to give employment to the men at fair wages and under decent working conditions, and to train in the vocational training corps those other men who cannot obtain such work.
Befor# closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read an extract from a letter written some time ago by one of the men in the platoon which I had the honour to command at one time. He comes from Toronto -and he is a very good man in spite of that. He was looking for a job, and he says:
Our Royal Canadian Army gave me my grand finale with a huge gratuity of seventy-five dollars.
I am glad to say that that is abolished now.
I am back in the bank again and hate the damn place like poison. Also X can't live on the money they pay. Mr. Power, if you know of any position you think S.C. as you knew him could fill, you might let me know. Can't see how I can make enough to live on in the blooming bank, and I prefer outdoor work.
Then he proceeds:
Do you ever feel a hankering for the billets in some old Belgic barn with all the boys lying around, scraping the mud off their clothes, etc., while waiting for the rum, to come up? Sometimes, when I feel I should like to be with them again, I think" how naked it would be with all the old boys gone. Army life surely has that miserable way of making a chap restless and giving him a great big longing for something, not definitely put forth in any way, shape or form.	.
That, I imagine, is one of the things wrong with the returned soldier to-day. He has been led away by agitators, until he has that hankering for something which he 	Vl
cannot put definitely into any shape or form. It is true that lately he has put his hankering into the definite shape of $2,000, but as a general rule he has not been able to give it any definite shape or form. . He has been spoiled to a certain extent. Now we blow on him hot, now cold. We told him he was a fine fellow; the next thing we did when he asked for a job was to throw him down. He has been sent from pillar to post and has obtained no satisfaction. I am sorry to say that among a large number of our returned men this dissatisfaction has led to agitation, which ' must be stopped if the Government of this country is to be respected.-As an ex-soldier I, for one, must enter my protest most emphatically against those agitators who are endeavouring to stir up strife, to make out of the returned soldiers a militaristic class, and to force them to ask for something which we cannot concede; in fine, to make the returned soldier something else than the good citizen which he should be. According to the press despatches, certain returned soldiers prevented one of their own members from explaining his views in contradiction to* theirs; and other soldiers, having invited the editor of a very reputable paper to address- them, afterwards refused to listen to him and so ill-treated him that he was obliged to flee. I protest that soldiers such as these are not worthy of our consideration. If our men went over to fight for anything it was for liberty, and another thing which they also should have included was free speech. I deny to any man, be . he a soldier or be he a member of the Government, the right to refuse the right of free speech to any citizen of this country. Our soldiers should learn-I think a large number of them have learned-that to settle down in civil life requires a certain amount of time. They had pure physical courage; in fact, in point of physical courage the soldiers of Canada yielded place to none in the world; hut they will find when they return that to be good citizens they will require a higher kind of courage still- that moral courage, higher than the courage which made them carry Vimy Ridge, higher than that which made them assault Passchendaele-that courage to bear disap- , pointments, ill-luck and the vicissitudes of the ordinary life of a citizen without grumbling, and taking upon themselves once more a spirit of sacrifice almost.as great as the sacrifices which they made when they were fighting for us overseas.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to detain the House but a very very moments to express my opinions upon this matter and to explain my position. I desire first to disassociate myself from that cheap despicable demagoguery which is playing to a certain class of returned soldiers. I have a different conception of the returned soldier than seems to be entertained by some people who describe him as an imbe-
9 p.m. cile and in a shaken condition very much like that of a man after he has 'had a very' good night, and that he is going to be a great charge on our hands. I had perhaps as good opportunities of seeing our soldiers at the front as any one. As I saw them leave the trenches on those gray battlefields on many a morning and charge against the best troops of Europe, I thought they were supermen, and that is what they were. While I maintain that a man cannot have gone through the war without a certain impairment of his mental and physical powers, at the same time I think when our men come back here they are not going to need these tears of pity that are showered upon them. All the returned soldier wants, Sir, in my opinion, is not to be mollycoddled and pampered, because, as has been already stated in this House, no money can recompense him for what he endured. Many a man must have endured at times sufferings which a million dollars a minute would not have induced him to undergo; but he knew his duty was to stand in that terrible hell-theatre of war and meet every danger. So when he comes back what I think the returned soldier wants is nothing but a square deal and a reasonable opportunity to make a living.
I had the temerity to interrupt my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to-day, and I want to explain my attitude. I do not intend to camouflage my position in any iway. It seems to me that my hon. friend may not perhaps have understood the early stages of this movement, The executive of the Great War Veterans' Association came to Ottawa and approached the Government upon this question of gratuities and other questions, and they asked, as I understood it, that the Government should appoint a commission to examine the question of gratuities and all other questions that appertain to the returned soldier. The Government assured them that if they wished to do so, they might examine the records of the different departments, but such an examination was not necessary.
Then some members of the- House who are returned soldiers had a meeting. I do not think this is any secret; in any case, it should not be, because there is nothing to hide in these matters. So far as I am concerned, I do not want any camouflage. Then it was decided that these members should interview the Cabinet, and this was done. Many of these hon. gentlemen, like myself, took the position that a commission should be appointed. I do not desire commissions should be multiplied, because governments often answer a demand by appointing a commission. But a commission is one of the instruments of Government whereby we often obtain a scientific idea of public opinion. These members, therefore, asked for a commission, and I supported them in that request. But the Government did not agree to that suggestion; they wished to appoint a committee, and a Bill has been brought down dealing with the subject. I thought that a commission- was the best means of obtaining this information, because it could go from place to place in the country and if its personnel was made up of good, honest men it would obtain more valuable information than could be obtained by a parliamentary committee.
My friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) who has such a mastery of debate in this House, rather reproached me as not being an old parliamentarian. I do not know that that is any very great disgrace; at any rate, his remark does not make me angry. But, Sir, I know enough of politics in this country; I have studied the politics of this country long enough to- know that a parliamentary committee often involves a great deal of camouflage. I am not going to say anything against this committee; God forbid that I should, -because I want to do everything I can to help in the attempt to deal satisfactorily with this question of the re-establishment of the returned soldier. But I say that a great deal of camouflage is often employed in these parliamentary committees; they are sometimes loaded, and it has been noticeable from time immemorial that parliamehtary committees have brought in reports that were suspiciously favourable to the Government. So I thought that the appointment of a commission was the better way. I have to stand by my position and the Government may stand by theirs. However, I do not mean to throw up my hands. Sir. When the Government appoints that committee we should enter into the thing in the proper spirit. I hope that returned soldiers and all the

various bodies who are interested in the returned soldier will present before this committee their views concerning the objects which they have in view.
With regard to the question of a gratuity, I hope to explain my position in a way that will not be ambiguous. I do not believe that it is possible, having regard to the finances of our country, to grant all the extreme demands that have been made in regard to gratuity. I simply say that I think something might be done. Any man who has examined this question will certainly say that the gratuity should be readjusted, because it is a notorious fact that men who have suffered most and have served the longest have not received commensurate reward.
There is also the question of pensions- what we shall give to sustain the widow and the orphan. On three occasions in this House last year I took the stand that the pension to widows and orphans was not adequate. I take that stand now, and I intend to maintain it. What I say now applies also to pensions to disabled men, the wounded and the afflicted. As I explained once before, Sir, the question is one which does not so much concern those who have come back to Canada in the full possession of their physical strength; it affects those who have been left to us as a sacred charge by those men whose last thoughts on the battlefield were of their dear ones at home. So I say that these pensions to the widow and the orphan, to the wounded and afflicted, should be increased. I stand for that now and will always stand for it.
I associate myself with a great many of the remarks that have been made by hon. and gallant gentlemen who have preceded me, especially those of the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) in regard to education. I think that a great deal might be accomplished in that direction. We might extend the work which has already been done so that it would include all young returned soldiers in the vigor of life who wish to obtain a professional or technical education or a training in the trades. If we did that, we should be doing just as much to increase production as we are doing under the land settlement scheme.
I agree with the hon. gallant gentleman from Quebec South (M.r. Power) that we should not introduce any party, consideration into our discussion of or dealing with this matter. We should render our tribute -honest men will do it; the soldier will always do it-to those to whom credit is due; to the Government for the things that they have done for the returned' soldier.
[Mi Peck.]
Some people have sneered at the Soldier Settlement Board. I think that is most unfair. This country and the returned soldier owe ,a great debt of gratitude to the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) for the courage, the ability and the confidence with which he introduced the measure for land1 settlement, 'and for the manner in which' the plan has been prosecuted. In my part of the country the land settlement scheme has been a splendid success; the returned men are entering into it and great results are being achieved. I look forward to its success with a great deal of hope and confidence. I am anxious, therefore, to render my tribute to the hon. gentleman who is responsible for that plan of land settlement. In all ways I want to render to the Government any credit that is due to them for what they have done- and they have done a great deal. Hon. members have said that the Government of this country have done more than the Government of any other country has done for returned soldiers-.all the more credit to them. Canada had the greatest soldiers in the world; therefore she wanted to give them advantages and benefits very much greater than those which were offered to soldiers in other countries.
Although I differ from the Government in respect of the method of inquiring into this matter, I .think that we should all go at it with a view of trying to achieve some definite results and of giving to our returned .soldiers everything that can possibly be given, everything that the country is capable of giving them, not only to reward them for their great services, but also to re-establish them in civil life.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my only excuse for rising to take part in this debate is that my silence might be misconstrued'. I may say at the outset that I agree with very much that has been said on the floor of this House to-diay and to-night. We all agree that the soldier did not go to fight for money and that this country cannot pay him for the services that he gave. Furthermore, we should be thankful to the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) for bringing to the attention of the House the subject which 'is now under discussion.
It is a subject on which I think every man ought to take_ a stand for the good of the country and for the good of the returned soldier. If we look for a moment at the causes of the dissatisfaction which exists in this country to-day, and it does exist T

think we shall probably get an inkling as to the remedy, if the Government only had the courage to apply it. The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) was right when he said this afternoon that the cause of the unrest among the returned soldiers is the fact that on returning they find the men who stayed at home while they were fighting, have become rich. They feel in consequence that they have been more or less victims of circumstances which were beyond their control. They see that men have been promoted and had their salaries increased and some have become rich, while the soldiers come back comparatively poor. They find out, which is absolutely true, that the Government has failed to get from the profiteers an adequate portion of their war profits, and I think if the Government had the courage, and some government will yet have the courage in this country, to take from the profiteers the undue profits which they made while the soldier was fighting to keep them and their families and their business in existence, they would hit upon the first thing to relieve .the unrest in this country.
There are other causes, and they are not far away from the one I have just mentioned. I raise the question of insurance for the disabled. There are men in this country to-day crippled from wounds and disease, who see dissolution approaching in the not very distant future. They know they are going to leave their families unprovided for, and I say it is the paramount duty of this Government to look after these people, and to look after them at once.
Now I come to the different soldier establishments in this country. I said on the floor of this House last year that it was nothing less than an insfult to suggest that there was not among 300,000 returned soldiers a man competent to become deputy minister of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. I have nothing to say against the man who occupies that position, but I say this-I have said it before, and I will continue to say it until these things are redressed-that in all departments pertaining to soldiers alone, such as the Pensions Board, and the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, the officials must of necessity be men who have served at the front. Under no other conditions .will the returned men have confidence that they are getting a square deal. I had read on the floor of this House a year ago a list of the higher-paid officials of the Pensions Board, not one of whom had seen service
at the Front. These are some of the things that are agitating the men who fought for this country during the war. This Government will yet have to take hold of this mess and clean it up, and until they do, we shall have dissatisfaction; we shall have people coming to this House and demanding $1,000 or $2,000, not as their just reward, but in order that they may be into it as .well, for they have a sense of justice and equality. 1 agree with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that the soldiers are fair and have the interests of this country at heart, but they must have a fair and square deal. We have seen too much of the military autocracy that stayed at home lording it over the people of this country. The day for that kind of thing ought to be past. I agree with my hon. friend that that has been a source of dissatisfaction to the returned men. This.military autocracy that stayed at home received promotion and salary increases. They have been riding around in Government automobiles at Government expense. But what happens to the returned soldier when he comes home? If he is twenty-dour hours'' late he gets ten days' pay deducted. These-things are bound to cause irritation and trouble.
. This Government deserves considerable credit, but I do not think we deserve any credit at all for looking after the widows and orphans and the disabled, because that is simply our duty, and our stern duty. The war gratuity was an act of graciousness on the part of this Government which I think the soldiers have appreciated. If they have not done so, they should have.
I agree with the; hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that the land settlement scheme has also been [DOT] a good thing for the soldier. It raises a man's earning power from $1 or $2 a day to $10 or $15 a day, and if he has the necessary energy and' ability it affords the soldier a ready means of re-estalblishing himself into the civil life of this country
, One other thing that is irritating	the	people of this	country' is the fact that this Government have put	out	all their loans	free of
taxation. It is indisputable that that has been the avenue through which millions have been sunk away that were made by men during this war. The loans offered them excellent security at a good rate of interest, and enabled them to escape the taxation which they knew was bound to come. These are some of the things which the returned men are thinking about, and they are going to think about them until they are adjusted in a more equitable way.

As to the solution of this trouble, I say frankly I do not know what it is. I do not agree with the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that this country can raise $600,000,000 or $700,000,000. I do not believe we can; I think it is impossible. If we are able to get $1,000,000,000 from Germany I might revise my ideas about giving the $2,000 gratuity, but at present I do not think we can possibly do it.
There are some things which must be done. .1 have mentioned insurance as one of them, and it is a very important thing. It might also be possible to give the men some other assistance in re-establishing themselves in civil life. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to-day, in a very brilliant speech, suggested a possible remedy for this winter. These things must be considered. What the remedy is I do not know. But I do know that there is a great deal of discontent among the returned men of this, country which has a just and righteous foundation. They did not enlist for money, and I repeat their great demand to-day is not for money. That is only the outward expression of a dissatisfaction which they feel at the conditions they have found on returning. I am very glad this matter is going to a committee of the House. I think that nothing pays like the truth. Let the light of day in on this question and let us see where we stand. If we cannot do anything, let us tell the people so, -and give our reasons, but if we can do anything it is up to this country to do it.
I hope that some men either in this House or out of it will be able to furnish the necessary ability, intelligence and good judgment to guide this country safely through the troublous times which are undoubtedly ahead of it during the coming winter. As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said to-day, we have a hard and rigorous climate. We know that work is going to toe scarce, and it is imperative that these men shall be looked after. I heartily agree with the hon. member when he expresses the opinion that the country will not allow these men to go in want during their first winter' -after the war, and I trust, Mr. Speaker, that some solution will he found that will satisfactorily settle this question in a peaceful and amicable way.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I have listened with close attention and great interest to every speech which has so -far been made in this debate, -and I will pay this tribute to every gentleman who has

spoken, that whether or not his views -agree with mine, I can freely give him credit for sincerity in the expression of them. I may frankly say at the outset that I do n-ot agree with some of the opinions which have been advanced this afternoon and evening by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me. It is true we owe -a great debt to the Canadian soldiers who went t-o France, not only those who are sleeping their last -sleep there, but those who have been fortunate enough to return to Canada. They acquitted themselves in a manner which has brought undying honour and fame to the name of Canada. They did their whole duty as soldiers on the battlefield, and it is -for us as men. occupying responsible positions in the gift of the people to realize our -responsibilities and do our duty -as fearlessly as did the men who fought -for us across the seas. The easier thing for a man to do on an occasion of this kind is to fall in lin-e with the clamour, and agree with those who are demanding this, that or the other thing. That, however, is not fulfilling one's duty -as a public man, at any -rate, not as I conceive that duty. We require in this country to-day, more than- -at any other time in our history, -men whq will exhibit in public life tire -fearlessness which characterized our boys overseas-. We require men who will have -courage enough to face any issue, however unpleasant it may be, to face perhaps even unpopularity in the expression of their honest convictions, and when necessary to say "no-" in the interests of their country.
I wish to commend very highly indeed the excellent speech which was made by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). It was thoughtful; it was carefully rendered; it was a sincere expression of the opinion of a man whose interests in the returned soldier no one will question or doubt for a single moment. And when that hon. gentleman concluded,, I for one had no misgivings as to where he stood on this question. I was therefore sorry to hear the expression which fell from the lips of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), charging the hon. member for Fort William with duplicity in this matter, and accusing him with facing both ways. I d-o not agree with the member for Red Deer in that opinion. I say that at the conclusion of the speech of the hon. member for Fort William I was left in no doubt as to his position on this question, and in regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from Red Deer, until the last- ten minutes of his speech I certainly felt that he was

going to agree in principle with the member for Port William. It came therefore very -much as a surprise to me when the hon. member for Red Deer took a right about face on the matter and seemed to favour the granting, if not of $2,000, 'at least of a portion of it. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member or Simeoe (Mr. Currie), in bringing this matter before the House, has ex pressed opinions which I dare say will find approval on the part- of very many soldiers in Canada, but I have sufficient confidence in the intelligence and fair-mindedness of the returned soldiers to believe that a great many of them will not approve of the attitude and the words of the hon.. member. The hon. member for Simeoe, for the purposes of his speech, divided the soldiers into three classes. The demand was made for $2,000 for every man who had gone to France; $1,500 for the man who got as far as England; and $1,000 for the man who had enlisted but did not leave Canada. He gave his approval to those demands on the part of certain soldiers in this country.
