subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Not at all. My hon. friend from Simeoe is congratulating himself to a greater extent than I had any intention of doing. I did not credit him with having fathered the resolution. I said that my hon. friend from Simeoe endorsed the resolution. He has acquainted us with the fact that he was not responsible for the resolution, and if I had allowed this matter to pass at that, I suppose the impression might have been created in some minds that he did not endorse it. I thought, therefore, that it was as [DOT]well to clear the matter
up, and the hon. member now says he does endorse the position taken in that resolution. Now, my hon. friend has a perfect right, if he sees fit, to endorse that resolution, but I will say from my place in the House that I do not endorse it, nor do I approve of the position taken in it.
The proposition contained in that resolution is one which is impracticable and which could not possibly be carried out in this country without serious loss and damage. It is a proposition which I believe the majority of returned soldiers, when they fully understand the situation in Canada, will themselves agree was unreasonable. I asked my hon. friend from Simeoe (Mr. Currie) when he was discussing this matter if he would give the same amount to a man who had been in France only a week as he would give to a man who had stayed there for three years, but he made no distinction; he said one should get the same as the other. Well, I have in mind a certain gentleman in this country who went over to England. He took a Cook's tour as far as France, was there four or five days and came back to Canada. While I am speaking I have in my mind's eye a gentleman who for twenty years or more attended annual drill twelve or fourteen days in the year, paraded around with all the gold braid arid feathers he could put on himself, and was a big man for the time being, and was elevated to the rank of Colonel.
When the war broke out he did not offer his services until public sentiment became so strong against him that he did join up with the army and went overseas as second in command. He went as far as England with his battalion. It was broken up and he had his choice of reverting to a lower rank and going to France to fight or taking a Cook's tour, going over to France for the purpose of observation for four or five days, then back to England and then home. He took the second course. He went over to France for four or five days, came back to England and then came back home. Under the proposal contained in the resolution which the hon. member for Simeoe endorses, that gentleman would receive $2,000. I feel fairly safe in the county of Fron-tenac. I do not intend to boast of my majority or of my personal popularity there. It was not my popularity that got me that majority; it was the popularity of the Government I supported. Although I had pretty nearly 2,000 of a majority at the last election, if any such'course were pursued as that which the hon. member for Simeoe would endorse, or if a man of that kind was given $2,000 of the money of this coun-

try, I do not believe I could get elected again in Frontenac. I pay that tribute to the intelligence of the people of Frontenac. I do not believe they would endorse any such proposal as that. Nor do I think it would be reasonable or fair to give the same consideration, in the matter of paying $2,000, to every man who has set foot on the soil of France whether he had been there for twenty-four hours or four years. Yet that is what the resolution which my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) endorses calls for.
The other class to which my hon. friend refers is the class of soldiers' dependents, the widows and children of those who gave their lives in the Great War. Mr. Speaker, I want mv position in regard to this portion of out population to be defined as distinctly and clearly as my position in regard to the grant of $2,000. I, for one, am willing to mortgage this country, if necessary, to the hilt, in order that the dependents, the wives and children of the men who gave their lives in France, shall live as comfortably and as well as they did before their sons or husbands went overseas. I am willing, and I believe the people of this country are willing to go the limit in looking after the dependents of those who are sleeping their last sleep in Flanders' fields. There should be a full endorsation in the Dominion of Canada by its people of anything the Government may do along that line. Our treatment of these people cannot be too generous.
Let me come to the other class-the student class. I gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Eed Deer (Mr. Clark) that he rather favoured this Government giving assistance to students to complete their course with the exception of theological students who would not get much consideration from him.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
permit me to correct him in what he gathered? I made no distinction in regard to students at all. I made a statement about the kind of student I admired and that was the student in all faculties at the Scottish university, at which I got my own degree, who went, supported by the slender means of his parents, carrying a bag of oatmeal, and in many cases became a professor. I did not refer to any faculty whatsoever.
I want to correct my hon. friend's false impression.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am very glad to be set right in the matter and I will do myself the honour of entirely agreeing with my hon. friend in regard to the class of people to whom he has referred. I was

under the impression that he rather favoured the idea of Government assistance in the way of a grant to students to enable them to complete their course in Canada. But in that he has corrected me. There are quite a number in my own county who have approached me in regard to this matter and who think that the Government should put up money to enable them to complete their courses at college. Whom are you going to define or designate as students? Is it just those who are fortunate enough to be able to attend the universities? Are these the only ones who should be classed as students? Every person who is acquiring knowledge from thos.; who have had the advantage ahead of him deserves to be classed as a student whether or not he goes to a university. Therefore, the apprentice to the plumber, or the carpenter, while he is learning his trade and getting little or nothing in the way of wages is entitled to be called a student. The returned soldiers in that class would be excluded from any of the benefits that you would give to the boy who had been attending a university. The boys who gave up their university course, made great sacrifices to go overseas. There are thousands and tens of thousands of others who also made great sacrifices but who could not qualify as students for any grant of public money. The objection I have to any such method as that is that you could not discriminate, that if you made a grant to certain of the returned soldiers who had partly completed their courses you would be discriminating against others who had perhaps never entered a college but who could not qualify under the definition of student and who would have just as good claims as the man who had attended college for one or two terms.
But some say: There is discrimination any way under the Land Settlement Act.
I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer who said that he believed that that Act was not passed with the primary idea of assisting the soldiers but rather with the idea of assisting to get men back on the land. I do not take that view of it myself but let us consider that for a moment. We have passed an Act which gives, certain assistance to men who proposed to take up farming. Is the returned soldier who asks for assistance to enable him to open up a corner grocery in the same position? I do not think so. The Government in the ease of assistance given to the man who goes on the land, takes a first mortgage on the land as the Government's

security. They would not be dealing fairly with the people of this country if they did not endeavour to secure them for every dollar which they loaned on land or loaned on any other thing. In regard to an amount of money put into a grocery store, what security could that man give? He gets the money from the Government, buys goods and puts them on the shelf. They are perishable; they are easily convertible into cash.	.
If his books show him that he is going behind there is great temptation for that man to avail himsell of the privilege of disposing of what goods he has and getting out. The Government has got to have security. But there is another reason which is worth mentioning; every man whom the Government might assist in opening up another line of business, such as storekeeping, is adding one more to the army of consumers in this country, whereas every man whom the Government might assist in placing on the land is adding one more to the army of producers, and to that extent in the latter case is attempting to solve in a practical way the high cost of living by greater production, just as our difficulty in that regard would be increased in the former case by opening up positions for people in cities and towns. I, therefore, do not agree in that respect with an editorial published a few days ago in the Toronto Globe from which, however, I wash to quote just a few words. I do not agree with that part of the article which says that:
" The Government should try to do for men in the cities and towns who are unfitted, or have no Inclination for agriculture, what it is doing for men going on the land."
I do not think the Government would be warranted in following that line and for the reason I have attempted to give. But because of certain remarks which were made by one or two hon. gentlemen this afternoon in regard to the Land Settlement Act, I shall place on Hansard a few figures published by the Toronto Globe quite recently. I think it was the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) who rather made light of the Act and of the Government's loans to men going on the land, arguing that such men were being loaded up with a debt. I think there is a very great advantage to the man who avails himself of the terms of that Land Settlement Act, and I think the Government is deserving of very great credit indeed in having put that Act through. _ The Globe says:
The exact number of applications received by the Soldiers' Settlement Board up to August 23
was 30,903. The applicants wished to be located
by provinces as follows:
British Columbia	 5,313
Alberta	 7,6'72
Saskatchewan	 6,932
Manitoba	 4,720
Ontario	 3,027
Quebec	 1,282
New Brunswick	 864
Nova Scotia	 709
Prince Edward Island. . . .	384
Of these, 23,087 had been approved.
That is to say of the 30,000 applications for loans to go on the 'land, 23,087 have been approved.
The number who actually received loans up to 23rd August was 9,691, and the total amount of money advanced was $29,038,901, an average loan of $2,996.
It may be of interest to follow those figures just a little bit further.
The $29,038,901 has been divided among three classes of loans:	(1) on purchased land;
(2) on Dominion (free) lands; (3) on lands already owned by soldier-settlers. Most of it has been advanced on purchased lands-$15,-627,579 for the land itself, $2,027,139 for buildings and other permanent improvements, and $5,387,339 for stock and equipment.
You will see from these figures that of the $30,000,000 in round numbers which had , been advanced up 'to the 23rd of August in loans to those who want to settle on the land, the majority of those taking advantage of the Act are prepared to buy farms rather than go and get free grants of land. Over a million acres have already been handed over in free grants to soldiers, but the majority of them prefer to buy improved farms, and I take it one reason for 'that preference is because they have a certain amount of money to put into the proposition themselves. As a matter of fact, the $15,-
627,000	which has, been advanced as loans on lands purchased indicates that the soldiers obtaining that money put in one-tenth of that amount themselves, or over $1,500,000, because under the Act, as I understand it, they have to put up one-tenth of the amount of their loan on lands purchased.
Now, Sir, I noticed from my reading of 'the statistics just quoted the pretty general distribution of the soldiers so far as the provinces, are concerned, and that it seems to me is a good thing for this country. It indicates that not alone in the western provinces, but in the older provinces in the East as well, the returned soldier has availed himself of the provisions of this Act, and many thousands of them are going to the land. I believe, Sir, that if no more of them went on the land than have gone up to the present time, there has been ample justification for the Act which has been passed. No hon. gentleman in this House, I am sure,

will question that it has been something which has added materially to the permanent assets of this country, that these thousands of men already have shown an inclination to go on the land, have applied for this loan, and are in a fair way, not only of making a good living for themselves, but assisting in greater production by themselves becoming producers in this country. Therefore, it seems to me that those who make light of this Act are not taking the broad view of it that I think the measure warrants.
I would like to ask one or two questions before I take my seat. Several hon. gentlemen have made comments on the suggestion made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I fully agree with the motives behind the suggestion of that hon. gentleman. I am sure every member of the House will agree with him in his statement that we must not see any of our returned men in want during the ooming winter; (but I question very much, indeed, the wisdom of the suggestion the hon. gentleman has made. He would hand out to the returned soldier, beginning with the first of November, a certain amount which he did not mention, but which I presume would be along the line of the gratuity which was granted to them, for a period of five months.
, Now, let us take one or two cases. John Brown arrives at Halifax this morning from overseas. Some days are required before he is finally discharged. He is under pay, of course, until he is discharged. We will say he gets his discharge the last day of September. Immediately that happens he starts to draw seventy dollars a month for six months. 1 am, of course, assuming that he has been overseas for three years or more. So far as John Brown is concerned, he will draw seventy dollars for October, November, December, January, February and March! ,But the suggestion of the hon. member for .Red Deer would mean that, in addition to drawing that money, he would also draw a further seventy dollars a month, .beginning with the first of November of .this year, for five months. I do not think you can argue that in his case he needs the other seventy dollars a month in order to keep him from starving this winter. .Then we will take the case of a man who got back here on the first of January. He ,was discharged on that date. Up to that time he was drawing pay. He then started to draw his gratuity and drew it for six months. At the end of six months 'his gratuity stopped, but during that period he has had an opportunity of supplementing 	"
his pay in other ways in order to put him [DOT]through the coming winter.
( How are we going to justify ourselves in making a grant for five months to carry men through the winter of 1919-20, and not make .a similar grant next year to carry men through the-winter of 1920-21? What better reason can we offer for saying that the public generally must take it for granted that that ends the gratuity business than .we can offer in regard to the gratuity which has already been granted? Is it not conceivable that a year from now there will be soldiers who have just got out of hospital, who have been kept going for all those months, gradually getting stronger and stronger, looked after by the 'Government of course until the time came for their discharge from the hospital, and who when they get that discharge are told: You are now recovered and you must get out and make a living for yourselves? If those men are unable to find work, what are we going to do with them? I do not see, Sir, how it .will be possible to do otherwise than treat them in the same way as. the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) suggests we should treat the returned soldiers now.
Those are cases which I have put in the form of questions, and I would like some hon. gentleman who may discuss this matter further to give me their opinions thereon.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
May I intervene? I had given some thought to the considerations which my hon. friend raises.
I would like to point out to him in the first place that the number of men drawing the double gratuity under the cases which he has portrayed would be extremely limited, and that there would be a certain rough justice in the men who are last in getting their release having a Kittle extra money to afford them a little extra chance to get on in the world. I do not think there is a man in this House or in the country who would grudge them that extra chance, especially as those cases are limited in number. If ifoffered a chance of a final settlement, the number being so .small, I do not think any one but my hon. friend, who is a very close and clever reason,er, but whose reasoning is very fine sometimes, would really grudge the little extra in what would be exceptional and limited cases.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a very unfortunate habit, I may say, Mr. Speaker, of always concluding that when he expresses an opinion upon any matter the last word has been said upon it, and that any person who has the temerity to

differ from him is in a class by himself. Now, the hon. gentleman is so sure of his position that he includes with himself every other hon. member of the House ex* cept myself. I am extremely unfortunate, of course, in that regard, and. I appreciate the unfortunate position in which I find myself; hut notwithstanding that, I have on many occasions'-and I say it with extreme regret-followed the arguments of my hon. *friend very carefully and found what appeared to me, with my limited intelligence, very serious defects in his line of reasoning; and there are defects in his present argument which appear to me, and which 1 venture to think may suggest themselves to other hon. gentlemen, despite the evident assurance of my hon. friend that he has everybody else thinking his way.
Now, Sir, I take exception 'to one word which my hon. friend has used, and I take exception .to it in the very strongest terms. He has the right to differ from me in opinion, as I have the right to differ from him; but he has no right to assume, nor has he any right to imply to this House that I stand [DOT] as one who would grudge to the returned soldier any sum which he in his generosity would give him. I wish to tell my hon." friend that I will go just as far -as he will in generous treatment to the returned soldier, tout in pointing out wihat I think are defects in the suggestion which he makes-, I believe I am taking -a course which though it may not appeal to returned soldier voters-it will not be popular in that regard-is more in line with the welfare of this country than is the course taken by my hon. friend. He ih-ad no hesitation this afternoon in speaking very strongly in opposition to the idea of acceding to the demands of the soldiers for the $2,000 grant, and. if 1 recall his words correctly, it was in his estimation something which would bankrupt this country. He said that we did not have the resources to make such a payment. I wonder where the length of our resources comes in to provide the hon. gentleman from 'Red Deer with the money to carry out his proposal. To meet the $2,000 grant -would mean an expenditure of $750,000,000 or $800,000,000. If the suggestion of my hon. friend were adopted it .would cost this country about $250,000,000. If we are justified in asking in all seriousness : Where are you going to get $800,000,000 to meet this demand of $2,000 each, I think, without being accused of grudging the soldiers what is due them, I have a Tight. to ask: Where does my hon. friend propose to get his $250,000,000 which would
be required if his suggestion were carried into effect?
The hon. member for Red Deer has not told us in definite terms where it is to come from, nor has the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), t The memlber for North Simcoe suggested that it would come from Germany, but that suggestion was repudiated, and very properly so, by the member for Red Deer. Just as properly we might repudiate the suggestion made by the member for Red Deer, because his was just as indirect as that of the member for North Simcoe. I submit that the member for Red Deer should follow up his suggestion by stating definitely how this money is to be obtained. Of course, it would be entirely 'wrong, from his point of view, to get it from the tariff. The hon. gentleman in one breath denounced such expenditures as those involved in the housing scheme and the good roads proposal, and he very kindly enunciated a great economic principle when he told us that the way to get rich was toy making all the money you could get and not spending any. He told the Government that the way to get rich was to raise revenues by direct taxation and so on, and not spend the money. But in the next breath he deviated from that economic principle by advocating the expenditure of $250,000,000, without even telling us where the money was to come from.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I should like to follow the Scotch practice of answering my hon. friend's question by putting one to him. If war had lasted another year-I do not doubt for a moment that my hon. friend agrees with me this time, that we should still have kept in it-where would the money have come from?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is a question which I cannot answer; I doubt very much whether my hon. friend could answer it. We did not have to cross that bridge. I think we would have found the money, though.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
But it is to be remembered that money was coming into this country while the war was on that is not coming into it now. Hundreds of millions of dollars were flowing into Canada for the purchase of munitions and supplies which are not coming into the country now. That suggests to me, as it does, no doubt, to my hon. friend, that had the war continued another year, sources of obtaining money would be open to the people of Canada at

the present time which are not now open demnation goes to me as well as to the Gov-to them because of the conclusion of the eminent; it goes to every member of this war. But merely to ask where the money House, including the member for Muskoka, would come from if the war had continued for we all allowed the measure to go through another year does not tell us where the in the form that it did, and we were silent
money is to come from to meet his suggested expenditure of $250,000,000.
As one who represents a farming constituency, I point out to those who advocate this expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars that they are advocating a course which, if adopted, would compel the Government to place a federal tax on every farm in Canada. If that should happen, farm values would immediately tumble. I was talking to a man the other day, a farmer who had returned from overseas, and he asked me what I thought of this proposed gratuity of $2,000. I said: "The Government will not do it; they cannot do it." He said: "Don't you think they should do it?" I said, "I certainly don't think they should do it." I added, "How would you like it if in addition to your municipal taxes you had to pay a federal tax of $50, $75 or $100 on your farm?" "Well," he said, "I would simply sell the farm." I said, "To whom would you sell it? I suppose you would sit up at night watching for some fool to come along who was eager for an opportunity to pay taxes that you were running away from."
Mr. Speaker, I am willing to go as far as any person in this House in doing what we can for the returned.soldier. Our first duty in that regard is to the wives and children of the men who lie buried in France, and I will go the limit, and then some, so far as they are concerned.. Our second duty is tp the men who are partially or totally disabled; I will go the limit so far as they are concerned. I am willing to mortgage this country in order to assist these two classes. But il should not be- doing my duty as a member of this House if I were to support a proposal to meet the clatter coming from certain men- in this country, without giving due consideration to what bur- -den we were thereby placing upon the people. That, I say, I will not do; -whether or not that course causes me to obtain support is a secondary matter and one which I do not think I or any other member of this House in a similar position should consider.
Permit me to refer, Mr. Speaker, to a remark made by the member for Muskoka (Mr. P. McGibbon) with which I do not agree. He criticised the Government very strongly in respect of the non-taxable feature of the Victory Loan. Well, that con-
at the time it went through. I do not feel like kicking myself in that regard, nor do-I feel like taking any kicks from any hon. gentleman who is in the same position as I am so far as that is concerned.
I wish to express -my entire agreement with certain sentiments which have been voiced by hon. members of this House in regard to pensions and gratuities to returned men. Gratuities were given to these men not in recognition of their services, but in order that they would not have to take the first job that came along; in order that they might have the choice of a position in getting back into civil life. Moreover, the private soldier is entitled to just as large a gratuity as is the major, colonel or general;
-i would have made no distinction whatever. And when it comes to fixing pensions for the widows and children of dependents of those who were killed overseas, I see no reason why the wife and children of the officer should receive any more consideration than the wife and children of the private soldier. Speaking as a medical man.
I know that the wee babe of the poor man will -suck just as much milk out of the bottle as the babe of the millionaire.
It will cost just as m-uc-h to feed it, and I do not see any reason why more dollars should be allowed for feeding the Child of the rich man than the poor man i,s allowed for feeding his child of the same age.
I believe that this debate has resulted in good. There has been a candid expression of opinion, and we will arrive at correct conclusions by criticising one another's views, doing it kindly, and I hope, courteously. I believe that it was the wisest course to 'appoint -a Parliamentary committee rather than a commission to inquire into this matter. No matter who may be chosen to sit on that committee, whether from this side of the House or the other I believe they will sincerely try to do -their duty regardless of politics or -anything else.
A Parliamentary committee in touch with the people and the soldiers will enable the returned men -to place their views before this House through the committee, and I believe will result in great good.
Mr. W. K. BAtLDWIN (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, many members have expressed the opinion that we should -all take a baud' in -this debate. I shall endeavour to confine myself strictly -to the question. There is

one question that requires to be dealt with perhaps more urgently than the question of unemployment among returned soldiers, and that is the land settlement scheme. This work was commenced early in the spring. I saw the man in Sherbrooke who had charge of it, and he had then found forty-three farms, but he bad not found a *single soldier to go on the land about the beginning of haying, because he could not get title to the farms. The men who sold these farms had not planted any crops, had not cultivated a garden, and had no potatoes in the ground. Things were generally running loose. He did place one .soldier on one of these farms; this soldier was a bachelor. There were no crops on the farm. In another instance a man who sold his farm to 'the Government had planted no potatoes or crops of 'any kind. I will guarantee that this Government in three or five years will own a considerable number of farms 'because the soldiers who go on them will be starved out. I know a farm that, cost $900 four or five years ago that was sold with four cows and a double *wagon to a returned soldier for $4,500. Before Christmas he will have to work by the [DOT]d'ay to feed his family or else abandon the farm. That is an abominable state of affairs. The Government could have found practical farmers who would have not asked a sou marquee to find farms of producing value for the'soldiers that could have been purchased at a reasonable figure, and on which the soldiers could have made a living. A senator has said, not in the Senate but outside of the Chamber, that it was simply criminal the way things were going in connection with locating soldiers on the land.
1 think the returned soldiers who have spoken in this debate have been the most moderate of all the speakers. They have not endeavoured to exact anything from the Government, because they know the country's financial condition. But there is something in this country that we could give to the soldiers who are deserving. We have *enormous areas of land in the great West which, in my opinion, should have been bought in large blocks for the use of the soldiers, who could have been put under an instructor, just as in the United States many counties have farm instructors They would then have had a chance to make a success of farming.
I think it is absurd to suggest that the soldiers should be paid a flat bonus whether they have been in the service only a week, a month or a year, and regardless of
whether they went to England or Scotland or France. Men have crossed the seas who have never heard the sound of a gun, and they have come back deep-chested, rugged fellows.	Their	families	have takencare of their money and have perhaps	$700	or $800	saved up.
Probably seventy-five per cent of the Great War Veterans believe in doing right and have got positions. I had the pleasure of speaking at a Great War Veterans' meeting in my county, at the county seat some time ago. 1 went there without hesitation not knowing what to say. I heard two young men speak, one from this city and one from Montreal, and it would be unparliamentary for me to use the language they used in flaying the twenty-five per cent of the Great War Veterans who are slackers, who would sell the last stitch they own to get money to get drunk on paregoric or Jamaica ginger to keep them in a state of inefficiency. Give them a flat rate. Why, as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said this afternoon, some of them would soon see London again, and go ahead destroying themselves as long as the money lasted.
I agree with the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) that we cannot do too much for the returned man who is suffering from disabilities, or for the widow and orphans of one who is lying in France. We received in our boxes to-day a paper showing that the Canadian married soldier gets $600 and the single soldier something less than $500, whereas the United States gives only $60. It is true that the United States has insured her soldiers, but when the men get back they have to keep up the insurance themselves. From time immemorial soldiers have been looked after by a pension system, and that is what I advocate. Let a pension be paid in accordance with the years of service and the degree of disability sustained. That is the system in England and in the United States. After the great Civil War in the TJnited States the rate was $4 a month to commence with, and a few years afterwards it went up to $20 and $30 a month. They gradually paid more until now practically all the veterans of that war have passed to the great majority. The annual total pensions paid in the United States on account of thatr war amounted to only $42,000,000, whereas in Canada we have practically reached that amount to-day.
I do not see how in all reas,on we can give to the soldiers much more than we are giving, and the advocacy of this enormous grant is altogether incomprehensible to me. We have a tremendous debt, and I am con-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What does the Government say?

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
If I recollect rightly, the Prime Minister gave a very definite statement on the matter. I secured from the Great War Veterans' Association a copy of a letter written by the Prime
Minister that seemed to me to leave no ground for the question which the hon. member has asked, as to where the Government stands. If I can comprehend the English language the Prime Minister pointed out very clearly where the Government stood. Every man in this House or out of it will agree that it is our duty to do everything in out power for the returned ' soldier. We must do everything possible for him for his good and for the good of the country. But to say that you should establish a system of cash bonuses to keep him in idleness, is to contradict yourself when you express the conviction that you should do something for his good.
. I agree, as I believe most men will who have studied this question, that there was a necessity, and that there is a necessity, to provide for the returned soldier during the transition period from military to civil life, to give him an' opportunity of getting his feet, so to speak, and to provide him with an opportunity for getting back into civil life. The next thing necessary for the physically fit returned soldier is to provide him with an opportunity for getting back into civil life and if the Government and the country can do that they will be doing the best thing they can for the returned soldier. To continue the system of cash bonuses beyond the time actually required to enable him to provide for himself is to begin to pauperize the returned soldier and you cannot have a virile man and a pauper in the same suit of clothes.
There is, however, a class of returned soldier, outside of the physically fit, that we can never lose sight of, and that is the class represented by those who have come back maimed in any degree whatever. There are also the dependents of those who will never come back. I cannot put my position any more readily than by saying that if any disabled returned soldier, or if the dependent of any soldier who will not return, is ever permitted to suffer in this country after the service that they have given in this war, the country will not .be doing its duty to the men who upheld the honour of 'Canada, as they did, in France and Flanders. My judgment is that the country will never permit them to suffer. Canada, as has been said so well and so many times on the floor of this House and throughout this country, has done, and is doing, more for her returned soldiers and her soldier dependents than any other country that went into the war; she is doing almost double as much as Great Britain, the United States, Australia and New Zealand.

, There are, however, some other problems in connection with these men that will have to be faced. There has been pointed out the problem of the men who during this coming winter, or during the next winter, may find it impossible to secure adequate employment and it will be necessary to find some means of taking care of that class of men. With the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. iClark) that we should grant a flat rate to .all returned soldiers for five months during this winter, I cannot agree.
, There are two bases upon which payment of any description might be made to returned soldiers. The first is: Do they deserve it as a class? Can we by any system of cash payment compensate a man for the sacrifices that he has made in going over to fight for us in France? I say we cannot. ,To even suggest that you can compensate a man by a cash payment for his services in this war is to offer insult to the men who .were over there. The next basis is that we must as a matter of necessity do something to provide against the contingency which has been suggested this afternoon

the possibility of returned soldiers, or the families of returned soldiers, suffering during this, the first winter they are back in Canada, due to lack of employment. That is another question altogether. That is dealing with a situation that becomes a matter of actual necessity on the part of an individual and does not apply to a class. It does not include the majority of returned soldiers. I believe that I am within the mark when I say that the great majority of returned soldiers who have come back home, and who are physically fit, are to-day in positions equally as good as those which they occupied before they went overseas, if not better. I meet a considerable number of returned soldiers I know a number of employers of labour and I know hundreds of returned soldiers who will tell you that they are in better positions than ever they had before and that they have better incomes than they ever had before as a result of those positions.
There is a point in connection with that to which I would like to refer briefly. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) this afternoon, in dealing with this subject,
. consciously or unconsciously, left the impression on my mind that there was an attitude of mind on the part of a large number of people in this country antagonistic to the returned woldier and that there were a considerable number of employers who were not treating their ex-employees

who had gone over and given service in this war fairly when they returned. I have made it a part of my business during the past year and a half, since the men began 'to return, to see if I could find one such case on the part of any employer. I have written to the Great War Veterans' Association in different parts of the country and up to date I have still to find one case of an employer failing to give his ex-employee on his return a position not only as good as he had before but as good as he would have had if he bad remained. I do not say that there are no cases to the contrary, but what I do say is that when any general statement is made that would imply that there are such, the case should be cited in order that returned soldiers and the country as a whole will not be under the impression that all employers of labour are in that class because to my personal knowledge they are not.
There are one or two classes of returned soldier to which I would take the opportunity of briefly drawing the attention of the Government in connection with this whole matter. One belongs to that class of Canadian citizen who went out of this country voluntarily, paid his own transportation to Europe, joined up with one of the Allied armies in France or Flanders, served during the whole period of the war, as in many cases he did, paid his own transportation- back to Canada and then finds himself stranded practically without one cent of consideration and without any recognition notwithstanding the fact that he, a Canadian citizen, fought side by side with other Canadian citizens practically in the same army and for the same cause.
There is another class, the reservist, whether he be British, French or Belgian, who was called home at the outbreak of the war. He comes back to Canada now and finds himself in a similar position. I commend to the judgment of the Government the advisability of dealing with these men exactly in the same way as they would have been dealt with had they been in the Canadian army. For my part I fail to be able to discriminate between the man who fought with the Canadian army and the man who fought side by side with the Canadian army whether in the British, French or Belgian army. They will not be a very large class; yet there are many individual cases of actual hardship as a result of the fact that .these men are not getting the treatment that the Canadian soldiers are getting. Not only is it a case of actual

hardship, but there is a sense of inequality that must always rankle in the heart of the man who feels that he has done exactly the same as other men did but who, because he was doing it in a little different way, or under different auspices, finds himself discriminated against. I do not believe that the Government has been doing that from anything else than a sense of its duty to the country but it is worth while in my judgment considering whether these men should not be treated as Canadian soldiers have been.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me just conclude by saying that in so far as I am concerned I am in identically the same position as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). It may not be a popular position to take, but it is the position I conceive to be right in the interest of this country and in the interests of the soldiers-and that is that a system of cash bonuses under which we would undertake to compensate men in dollars for their sacrifices and services at tthe Front, is an insult to -the men themselves. Apart from that my judgment is, that this oountry cannot conceivably meet the demand that has been placed upon it. When we talk of finding $800,000,000, and when we hear people suggest that we might ha^e found it if the exigencies of the war had made it necessary, 'had the war gone on for a year or two or three years more, it seems to me that there is -an utter lack of -appreciation of wihat the -whole subject means. I have not any doubt whatever in my mind but that should conditions develop during this winter which-will bring [DOT]about hardship or suffering, or anything nearly akin to either one of them, a means will be found to alleviate that distress and to make it possible for the returned soldier to get back on his feet-those of them who are willing to- get back on their feet as the majority of them are.
I had the privilege of meeting a command of the Great War Veterans' Association on Sunday night last, and they told me to a man: "We do not want anything in the nature of a gratuity to the returned soldier whatever; we feel that the people of Canada, through the Government, has dealt most 'generously with him; they are doing everything in our judgment that the country can afford on behalf of the returned soldier, and that is all that we can legitimately ask."
Mr. FREDERICK F. PAR.DEE (Lambton West):	I intend to occupy only a few
minutes in expressing my views upon this subject. It appears to me the first thing we have got to realize is that amongst a certain percentage of the returned men [DOT]there is a very considerable amount of unrest. That -has been voiced in various public meetings that have been 'held, in the deputations that have waited upon the Government, and in other ways. We know that amongst -that percentage there is very considerable dissatisfaction. It -always appears to me, Sir, that when a crisis arrives -perhaps the present situation cannot be dignified with the name of a crisis in so far as the returned soldier is concerned-but when any great question arises before the people the surest and best way to get over it and the surest and best way to give satisfaction to all concerned is that each party should speak its own mind1 and should come out fully in public discussion. Therefore, I think at the present time it is very fit and proper that the members of this House, being the people's representatives, and representatives as well of the soldiers that have come back from overseas, should discuss this matter very frankly. Speaking for myself, I am in favour of the appointment of a committee. I am in favour of the committee taking up the various questions that have caused this unrest and this disquietness and looking at them in all their phases, and if possible bringing down some recommendations to the House that would be best in the interests of the country and in the interests of all the people. I am, however, just in this position, perhaps through no fault of the Government, that I am not quite certain what this committee proposes to do. Some of us served last year and the year before that on a Pensions Committee. That committee gave much time and much thought to the matter of pensions, and so far as I can see, having been a member of it, having regard to our means the provisions brought down in the Pension Bill enacted as the result of our recommendations were just and generous. Is the committee which is now suggested to look into the question of the $2,000 payment? Is it to look into any further gratuity to the soldiers? Is it to look into a further increase in the pension? Or is it generally to look into the complaints that the soldiers have made and that have been spoken about here to-day? I may say very frankly at the moment, and I have no hesitation in doing so, that in my opinion a gratuity of $2,000, or $1,500 or $1,000,



that has been spoken of by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), is purely without the question. I cannot think for one moment that the great majority of the men who went overseas, as was so eloquently put by the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) to-day, feeling that they were doing a man's work and that they were doing their full duty to their country-they went and served in that respect and under those auspices-or at least a very small percentage of them only, are coming back here to-day and asking the country to put up dollars and cents for the services they have performed. Those men I know, and I have the pleasure of knowing a great many returned soldiers do not look upon the matter in that way. I think we are very safe in saying that the great percentage of the returned men do not so regard it; I feel certain that the great percentage of the people at large are not in accordance with any such demand as stated. But, Sir, I do think that it is the bounden duty of the people of Canada that they should take this into consideration: The returned man who to-day has come back lessened by a great percentage of his earning power, lessened by a great percentage in the joy that he gets out of living, lessened in a great percentage in the pleasure he can get out of his home life and his family, is to-day entitled from this country to more than a pittance in the way of a pension-he is entitled to something that will put him at least on an equal, if not a better, footing than on the day he enlisted for service overseas. I think with regard to the returned men who have come back disabled, I think further with regard to the dependents of those men-the wives, the mothers, and the children-that it would be a standing disgrace to the people of Canada-no matter to what extent we would have to go in the way of financial aid and in the way of incurring financial obligations-that we should permit those people to become charges upon this country or in any way to^ suffer for the loss that they have sustained in the latter case by reason of the fact that their own men and their own support gave up their all in order that we might enjoy the benefits of peace and prosperity. To those classes of people I say the very utmost consideration ought to be shown. As to the men who have come back in health and strength, I admit that to me they are all they ought to be. They are men who were prepared to make the great sacrifice, who were prepared to give their
fMr Pardee.]
all if necessary, in the defence and in the saving of the country. To them every honour should be due, and every honour is due. But I say, and I do so knowing that the vast percentage of them agree with every word I utter, that those men who thought this country was good enough to go and fight for, and if necessary die for, fully realize the responsibility that is upon them and know that this country is good enough to again fight for in the arts of peace and make it a country worth living in. Those, I am satisfied, are the ideas that the vast majority of the returned men hold. Those ideas are the ideas they ought to hold. Those ideas are the ideas that influence the greatest manhood that a country could possibly have, and which must necessarily make this country go on and prosper and grow great, as she ought to. I say again that a $2,000 gratuity to all the men who have served overseas is financially an impossibility. I say that so far as appointing a commission to inquire into the financial position of this country would be a surplusage. The financial condition of this country was disclosed last session in the Budget speech. We know our assets and we know our liabilities; we know our income and we know our outgo; we know as well as any private corporation possibly could exactly where we stand. Canada to-day to my mind-although 'far from being bankrupt with our great resources and our splendid people-has reached the position in which we have got- to say that a halt must be called, and to-day is the day that a halt should be called.
There should be retrenchment in every way. There is no question that there have been extravagances, and those extravagances must cease. We must cut our coat according to our cloth, and, as a nation, we must live accordingly.
In closing, Sir, let me say simply this: That to the disabled men and to the dependents of the men who, as I said before, fought and died that Canada and the Empire might live-to them the greatest consideration must be given. Failing to give that consideration, the people of Canada wall fail to do their full duty.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHEETY (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has taken an exceedingly wide range-a wider range than, perhaps, the motion justifies. However, I am not saying that in any regretful or critical mood, for I think that we have had a debate of very great value. We have had expressions of opinion-not all of them in accord-upon a very wide range of subjects, very many of those opinions, in-

deed, being entitled to our most careful consideration. But I think it is well that I Should come back to the motion which is before the House and confine myself to it.
The question of urgent public importance to debate, which is the purpose of the motion before the House, is " the claim of the Gratuity Association of Returned Soldiers and the interview of its representatives with the Government." I am not clear that beyond the mention of the existence of that association we have heard anything in particular about it in the debate, and I do not recollect-I may be mistaken-that we have heard anything about the interview, save, indeed, some observations which were made about the slamming of doors in these peoples' faces. Let me say at once in connection with this whole matter that there has been absolutely nothing in the nature of the slamming of doors in anybody's face. Whoever has approached the Government upon this subject has been received with perfect courtesy by the members of the Government, and I am quite satisfied that none of the gentlemen who called upon us will state that any doors were slammed in their 'faces.
It is quite true that when the delegation from the Gratuity Association of Returned Soldiers waited upon this Government they got a perfectly frank answer. The question of the granting of a gratuity indiscriminately, without regard to the needs of individuals, with no connection whatsoever with affording a means for reestablishment, this Government very carefully considered and reached the conclusion that neither the financial condition of the country, nor the best interests of the men themselves properly understood, would justify the granting of such a gratuity. And the Prime Minister wrote in frank terms and announced that conclusion. That was the question, that had come before the Government in the first instance. The statement of the Prime Minister is contained in the correspondence which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) read to the House a day or two ago, and certainly that statement left nothing to be desired in the way of clearness.
The representatives of the Gratuity Association of Returned Soldiers asked for an interview on Saturday last, which interview was granted, and wre heard most fully what they desired to say. The only answer that could be made, and that it would be fair to give to that deputation, the Government having looked into the question as carefully as it w'as capable of doing, was
23J
to tell them perfectly frankly that so far as the Government was concerned it had reached its conclusion that theie was no way out-if I may use the expression-in the direction of granting the additional gratuities such as were proposed in the resolution of the Calgary gathering which has been read to us and which the deputation was pressing for.
As regards the question of a Royal Commission, the position of the Government was equally clear. The facts which led to the conclusion that the Government reached seemed to us so palpable that no Royal Commission could add to or detract from them. But it was made a ground of complaint, and it was stated, if I followed more than one of the speakers rightly, that there was a grievance in this; that the refusing of a Royal Commission implied the refusal to put before the soldiers the-facts on which the conclusion was based;: and it was stated that if that had been granted and the facts referred to properly established, why, the soldiers would have: had no cause for complaint. It is perfectly true that the Government declined to appoint a Royal Commission, but in the letter of September 5 conveying that refusal it was clearly pointed out that the means of information were absolutely at the disposal of the representatives of the soldiers or of any committee that they might choose to appoint. These are the words of the Prime Minister in that letter:
You will realize, I hope, that it would be undesirable to establish a commission or appoint a committee to inquire into facts which are within the knowledge of members of the Government. We are quite ready, however, to place all avail! able information on the subject at the disposal of a committee to be named by your association. If such a committee is designated to me, I will see that it is put in touch with accredited representatives of the Department of Finance, the Department of Militia and Defence, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment and the Department of the Interior, which are those chiefly concerned with the matters in question.
I trust that this suggestion may commend itself to the judgment of the Executive Committee.
I think I have made it clear that there has been nothing in the nature of closing doors in the face of any representation of soldiers or anybody claiming to represent any section of them; that they have been received, their representations have been heard and we have put absolutely at their disposal every source of information that would enable them to appreciate the facts bearing upon this question. I take no credit to the Government for that; that is

a courtesy that we owe to the public ot Canada generally and a courtesy that we certainly do not owe in any less degree to the soldier who has deserved so well of Canada. But I point that out because I understood it to be suggested-or at all events I gathered that it was felt in some quarters-that there has not been a perfect readiness to receive and listen to and consider representations coming from any source, more especially representations coming from the soldier, and to put at the disposal of those interested every information under our control.
There are two perfectly distinct things. One is this proposal for a system of gratuity based merely upon the fact that a man has served in a military capacity, having no connection with what that man needs, the gratuity to go equally to the man who is in the enjoyment of large wealth, to the occupant of a position-a position under this Government, even; a position in any walk of life-that gives him ample revenue, that makes of him even a wealthy man; and to the soldier who may be in absolute need. I am not going to elaborate an argument in support of the view of the Government that that is an impossible way out. The gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Pardee) has put it very forcibly. The member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), numbers of hon. gentlemen, have made perfectly clear to this House that the one request with which this (correspondence was concerned is one that can not be entertained. That, at all events, is the settled view of this Government.
But side by side with that view there is the totally different question of soldiers' civil re-establishment. A good deal has been said about the committee that i3 to be appointed. It is well that there should be no possible misunderstanding; certainly the statement of the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Howell) the other day left no room for nlisunderstanding. Side by side with this question of additional gratuities-or, rather, occupying the field alone, because there is, in our judgment, no room for this question of additional gratuities of the kind that I have referred to-occupying that field alone, then, is the question of possible improvement in our methods of dealing with the matter of soldiers' civil . re-establishment. Now, the great bulk of the suggestions, if not all that we have listened to this afternoon, have had to do with a possible improvement in our method of dealing with the question of soldiers' civil

re-establishment. With regard to that matter the President of the Council announced that a Bill was to be brought down, and that Bill has been introduced. When that Bill reaches the proper stage it will be referred to a special committee and there these suggestions will have opportunity of being made and being supported by such arguments or such proof, if necessary, as gentlemen interested may think it wise to adduce. It has been said that there is nothing extraordinary about this; that that is what is done with every Bill. It is not coptended that there is anything extraordinary about this; on the other hand, I hardly think it is correct to say that that is what is done with every Bill. It is proposed to submit this Bill to a special committee, which will afford the opportunities that I have mentioned.

The hon. gentleman will
pardon me, because I am very anxious on this point

That committee will
not be concerned with the question of the adoption of a system of gratuities such as I have described. That I have tried to make perfectly clear. Whether its judgment be right or be wrong upon that subject, the Government has reached a definite conclusion for which it must assume responsibility before this House and before the people-a definite conclusion that there is no way out, as I said before, in the direction of the system of additional gratuities that has been proposed.

As I understand it, then, this committee cannot-and the Government will not give it power to do so-discuss the question of gratuities such as those which have been referred to? If that question is to be discussed, then, and if the matter is to be dealt with by this House, there will have to be a motion for a special committee for that purpose?
, Mr. DOHERTY:	It is, of course, open
to my hon. friend or to any other hon. member who wishes to have a further dis-

cussion of that question, to take steps to do so in accordance with the rules of the House.

speechtext:
The 'Government do not
intend to initiate any method of having the members 'discuss that question further?
, Mr. DOHERTY:	The Government does
not contemplate initiating any proceeding calling for the discussion of that question. My own impression is, judging from the discussion we have had this afternoon, that the sense of this House endorses the view which I have expressed on behalf of the Government. However, if any hon. member thinks it desirable to have further discussion of that specific question, it is for him to take such steps as the rules of the House [DOT]permit him to take with a view to having that discussion.
, But I was going on to say that there is open in connection with this Bill the whole question of anything that properly pertains to soldiers' civil re-establishment. I am [DOT]not going to go over all the suggestions that have been made in that regard, It is not impossible that in connection with suggestions which may be found acceptable and which in the judgment of this House ought to be acted upon, it may be necessary to provide for some additional expenditure. But that is quite a different thing from this precise system of gratuities to which I have referred.
. Mr. REDMAN: When the minister mentions this " precise system of gratuities," does he mean the straight $2,000 bonus? Or would it be possible for the committee to consider some monthly payments or the payment of some sum which would naturally come under civil re-establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Anything that comes under the heading of soldiers' civil reestablishment will naturally be open for discussion in connection with the Bill dealing with soldiers' civil re-establishment, and as I said a moment ago, it may involve the expenditure of money. What I hope I have made clear is that there is no intention. to provide a committee to look into this question of the system of gratuity as a gratuity. The gratuity that has been already granted, it might be well to point out, was not granted as a gift or reward for services rendered. It was granted because it was thought that it was a fair thing to grant a reasonable time for returned men to look around .for employment, and that was the sole idea with which the gratuity was granted. It was not in. any sense a payment for services rendered. Certainly
nobody imagined it was an adequate reward for the services rendered.
Having then, perhaps, made the position clear I might leave the subject here, but so much has been said in the way of criticism of what this Government has done, or rather, of what they have not done, that I think it is perhaps worth while to correct some of those observations at all events, and to point out some of the existing conditions which do not seem to have been brought to the knowledge of hon. members generally. Before I proceed to that might I say that I gathered from the address of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that he coupled with this demand for a cash gratuity the question of gratuities to widows and mothers, and gratuities to students, So far as the suggestion of gratuities to widows and mothers is concerned, the question it raises is whether or not the pensions provided are adequate. Now the subject of pensions was dealt with most fully and most carefully by a committee of this House last year, and we have as a result the pensions provided in the present statute. Of course, nothing in this world is perfect. It is perhaps open to question whether in some respects these pensions might not be modified or increased, but that is a distinct and separate question by itself unconnected with this question of gratuity. As regards a gratuity for students, that I think is a question that bears directly and pertinently on the question of soldiers' civil re-establishment. I am not going to express an opinion at the present time whether it ought to be granted or not, but it may be looked upon as a question pertaining to soldiers' civil re-establishment, and is therefore a question that may come up for consideration in connection with the Bill.
My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie >
pointed out the source from which he said this money could be got. I think I can satisfy 'the House in a moment that there is no source 'there from which we are going to get additional money to pay these additional gratuities if we ever did determine that they should be paid. Under the Peace Treaty Germany will pay every dollar that Germany can pay, and s'he will pay every dollar that she can pay whether we pay these gratuities or not. The fact of our paying additional gratuities will not increase Germany's paying power.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman will forgive me for putting it in -a blunt way, if I say he is entirely mistaken. If he will look at the provisions of the Treaty he will find that there is no fixed sum payable by Germany, and that the system is this: Germany, having acknowledged her responsibility for the entire cost of the war, the Allied -and Associated Powers on their side recognized that Germany was unable to pay the entire cost of the war, and that it would be worse than useless to try to collect it from a country absolutely denuded of means to pay 'that large sum.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Nothing has been decided as to what Germany is to pay. There was a very long discussion upon the question of what was the nature of the claims that could be advanced with the hope of their being paid, not the particular amounts that were claimed by each nation, but what was the nature of a claim that could be entertained. Having compelled Germany to acknowledge her responsibility for the entire cost of the war, the Allied and Associated Powers acknowledged that it was impossible to collect that amount. But they did not proceed on the basis of fixing a particular amount. They went on then to enumerate the kind of claim which Germany should be compelled to pay, and speaking roughly-I do not suggest this as covering everything-that claim is the claim for damages of different kinds and classes done to the civilian population of the different countries. I can safely say that the cost of the war does not figure 
among the things that may be claimed, with this exception: that you may include in the claims that may be made the pensions and the allowances which are made to soldiers and their dependents, which are to be capitalized. But let me point out that they are to be estimated at. the rates allowed by Prance.
These claims are to be put before a commission which is to hear the parties with regard to them, determine which are to be allowed and which are to be rejected, and, according to those determinations, to establish a sum total amount,-not an amount for France and an amount for Great Britain or for Canada-but a sum total amount by adding them all together; *and then to provide means as to how Germany shall pay and in what instalments. That sum total so paid is to be divided among the Allied and Associated Powers in accordance with an agreement to be arrived at by them. The hon. gentleman will see therefore that we are not dealing with any fixed sum, and when we get reports from Australia that they will receive $400,000,000 I can only say that I have great respect for the statesmen of that country, and I presume they have figured out what they anticipate, but they are not making a statement based upon any settled amount which anything that can be found in the Peace Treaty, has ever determined as being due to Australia.
Mr. CURRIE? The hon. minister is directing his remarks chiefly to me, and I think a question and an answer will help matters. Is it a fact that no effort was made by the representatives of this country at the Peace Conference to make representations to the various Governments and authorities that we were entitled to a certain indemnity? It is not a matter of the cost of the war; it is indemnity according to Treaty. The Germans did not take ten minutes to decide how much they wanted from France in 1870 and they got it.

speechtext: They decided how much they wanted from France and they got it. That is true.

speechtext: And you would have got it from Germany if you had said how much you wanted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
