speechtext:
I suppose the hon. gentleman was there and knows of the procedure and is aware of everything that happened. However, let me say that no country demanded any specific amount or

received it. Once the unanimous conclusion was arrived at that you had to limit your demands to certain classes of claim; once the most competent people that could be found to deal with the subject had determined that Germany could not pay more than would meet, without fixing a specific sum, the full amount of claims of the classes referred to, it became useless at that time to discuss any definite amounts because a commission was appointed to determine what those amounts were.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I understood that the first levy on Germany was to be twenty-five billion dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There have been discussions in regard to various suggested amounts and twenty-five billion dollars was spoken of as being the maximum that by any stretch of imagination Germany could possibly pay; but it never took the form of a claim. No man could say to-day what is the amount of damage done to Northern France and Belgium by the German invasion. That is a matter that must be most carefully gone into. As I understand it, all these things are to be determined by the commission appointed, and it will be open to us to put before that commission all the claims that we may have that are of the nature covered by the Treaty. As I mentioned a moment ago, the unanimous view was that you could not include the entire cost of the war in that sort of claim, because it would be utterly futile to do such a thing.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister will pardon me, but I do not want any misapprehension to exist in regard to his words. He states that the sums that are to be payable to those who took part in the war are to be in proportion to the damage done to the civil population. I presume therefore that the only amount which Canada could get would be compensation for the trawlers destroyed off the coast of Nova Scotia, and that we shall be debarred from receiving other remuneration, by reason of the fact that our civil population have not suffered in the sense in which the people in the war zone suffered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I said I was speaking generally. I did point out that there was to be included an amount to represent pensions, and allowances to dependents of soldiers, because that is treated as damage to the individual. But I also pointed out that that was not necessarily to be based
on our scale of pensions or allowances. To secure uniformity the French scale was agreed to.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take up so much time, but I was led into this discussion by questions. I will point out that whatever may be the amount that we get, we shall not receive any more by reason of these gratuities, so that there is no way of getting the money in that direction. We shall get our share of all that Germany can pay and we will have to make that go as far as we can. If we assume an additional burden of eight hundred million, whatever we do get we may devote to the liquidation of that sum, but we shall not have it to meet pensions with, nor to meet any of the other things that are necessary, and we shall have to go to the people of Canada in the last resort to raise that money, including of course among the people of Canada all of the returned soldiers, all of their friends and their connections and relations, who I suppose would amount to twenty-five or thirty per cent of the population. They will have to pay this money if it is to be paid. That, therefore, is the answer I make to the suggestion that we have only to go to Germany to get this money.
We have had criticism from one side and the other. We have been criticised because we did not carry on sufficient public works in order to give employment to the returned soldiers. We have been severely condemned by the hon. member from Red Deer, amongst others, because, on the other hand, we did a great deal too much in the way of public works. Witnout trying to settle which parties to that discussion are right, may I point out that there are some things that have been done? It is said that these men are entirely out of employment, and the suggestion has been made that the Civil Service 'Commission, which makes the appointments, have not fairly treated the returned soldiers. I hold in my hand a return from the Civil Service Commission showing that some sixteen thousand returned men have been placed in public employment. The return is up to the 29th of August, and in the last five weeks of the period we were placing them at the rate of over fifty a day in the public service, and in the period preceding that, at about forty a day. I have not been able to secure such figures as the hon. member for Red Deer requested, showing what has become of every demobilized soldier and how many have been re-established in civil life, because it has not been found possible for us

to trace the soldier after his demobilization and, above all, to trace the one who finds permanent employment and is absorbed in the civil life of the country. But I have some figures that are significant. Of 30,000 applications for employment made to the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment, eighty-nine per cent have obtained employment. Out of 6,000 re-trained men, that is, men who have been injured and have been given training, ninety per cent have been placed. These are the people we have under our eyes, and when you find such percentage in employment among those of whom we have knowledge, it is not unfair to assume that similar conditions prevail throughout the country. The member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) himself told us that in his neighbourhood all of the returned soldiers had been absorbed into civil life.
I am sure we all, in our respective neighbourhoods, know of many and many returned soldiers who have been absorbed into civil life and who are in the enjoyment of good positions. It was suggested that it was only the inferior Government positions that Went to the returned soldiers. The credit is due to the Civil Service Commission and not to the Government and the responsibility is with the Civil Service Commission and not with the Government; but we find amongst the 16,000, men occupying such positions as those of Pension Commissioners and other positions whose designations show on their faces their importance.
It is not well to run away with an exaggerated idea of the position in which returned soldiers as a whole find themselves. Certainly it is not well to assume that the Government is indifferent to the position in which the returned soldier finds himself. We have suggestions as to particular things and as to particular classes of soldiers. For instance, there has been the suggestion in regard to insurance for disabled men, that we pay the difference, as I understand it, in the premiums resulting from the condition in which they find themselves. That is a matter that might very well be considered in connection with some phases of soldiers' civil re-establishment.
For the benefit of those who have complained that we did not have sufficient public works to provide employment, let me say that we had sufficient to bring down criticism upon us last year. Provision was made for public buildings at London, Hamilton, Toronto, Montreal and Calgary, work on the Welland canal, shipbuilding in

which very large numbers of returned soldiers have been employed; road building, which afforded work not only directly to the returned soldier but to others; millions have been spent in railway construction and we have endeavoured to make provision for housing which has been referred to. It would take too long for me to go through the enumeration in addition to the statement which has already been placed upon Hansard showing what has been done. As I have said, if there be room for improvement in connection with Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, in that field we are absolutely open to suggestions. Of course, that statement implies that any such suggestions will have serious and real consideration and there should be an opportunity for such consideration in connection with the Bill that I have referred to.
In conclusion, let me congratulate the House on the manner in which this debate has been carried on. I was a little bit surprised-I do not know whether I understood him correctly or not-to hear the hon. member who brought up this subject make some reference to introducing this disagreeable question. Let me say from the Government's point of view there is absolutely nothing disagreeable in a discussion of how best we can do our duty.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is mistaken. I said that it was made disagreeable for me; not that the question was disagreeable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. gentleman will never regard as disagreeable the discussion of a question in which he is so thoroughly interested. Neither to this Government is the discussion disagreeable of anything that may open to us a way that is practical and feasible of being of real service to the soldier. May I add just one word? I think the tone in which this discussion has been carried on is an example to others who may be interested in discussing questions of this kind. I think we all want to be on our guard in the discussion of questions of this kind, and questions that affect the soldier, in whom we are all interested, to avoid urging claims that may present themselves in such a way as to create a false and exaggerated idea in his mind as to what it is possible and feasible to do for him and what it is fair and reasonable for him to expect.
Above all, I am sure every hon. gentleman in this House will join in deprecating anything in the nature of an appeal to the soldiers urging them on to the making of

claims because it is believed that they are strong enough to force their granting. I saw that a gentleman who was here with a delegation the other day-I sincerely trust that he is mis-reported-is reported to have urged persistency in pressing this claim for a gratuity because, as he said, they are afraid of us down there in Ottawa. Let me say to the gentleman who makes that statement, or to anybody else who may be labouring under that delusion, that while we are anxious to do that which the resources of the country will permit us to do and that which may be of advantage and assistance to the soldier in restoring him to civil life, we are not open to be led into any course of action by dread or fear, or by anybody's threats whether those threats take the form of suggested possible violence, or whether they are confined to the threat of dealing judgment out to this Government through the vote at the polls.
We are, of course, in the judgment of this House, in the first place, and we are, through this House, and ultimately directly responsible to the whole people of the country and, of course, we fully recognize the right of these returned soldiers, or others, who may think we are wrong on this particular question, to exercise their judgment in the regular way and through their franchise. But though we quite realize that, we realize also that our duty is to follow that policy, which, after giving the most careful thought to this very important question, we think is the policy that our duty to the people of Canada as a whole requires that we should adopt and follow.
Mr. DANIEL D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria): Mr. Speaker, I (have very little to add to what has been so well said in connection with the question that is indirectly before the House. The discussion which we have had this afternoon and this evening must necessarily be more or less of an academic character because the real motion before you, Sir, is whether or not this House shall adjourn. Whichever way the motion is decided, it will not settle any question, it will not establish any policy, it will not sustain or refute any position which the Government may have taken, upon any public question. Therefore, I do not wish to go at any very great length into what may be the policy of the Liberal party on this question of soldiers' civil re-establishment, or what is the policy of the Liberal party in dealing with the returned soldier. It is not necessary because the question is not before the House.
I observed with great satisfaction, indeed, that the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) is showing signs of coming into the proper faith. Although holding on per-tinaceously to tihe Tory party, he finds that there is no light or leading there, he finds there is no unction for his soul there, and he wants to turn to the Opposition to see if there is any light or leading here. Well, Mr. Speaker, we shall be glad, indeed, to offer any consolation that is possible to the hon. gentleman in order to lead him along proper lines and to give him proper ideas on public questions.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am afraid it will 'be very meagre.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I did not catch the observation of my hon. friend and therefore I am afraid that his statement, whatever it may 'be, must go without answer as far as I am concerned.
This question, before discussing it very much further, seeims to take a very strange position. We were told by the President of the Council that there was no necessity to press for a royal commission, when he spoke at great length, in placing figures upon Hansard the other day, showing the reason why the Great War Veterans' Association should not be looking for this commission of inquiry. He wound1 up with a statement that a special committee was to be appointed to deal with the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Act, but incidentally, and as an incident of the work of that committee, it would deal with the question of the gratuity, or the granting of money, to the returned soldier as asked for by the War Veterans' Association or by the committee that has recently been appointed in the city of Toronto. I presume, Mr. Speaker, that we will not be permitted to refer to any discussion that took place recently in this House, but Hansard will show what the President of the Council said, and Hansard will show what the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) asked. The latter distinctly and clearly put the question to the President of the Council: Is it a fact that this committee, which the minister says he is going to appoint, will deal fully with this matter? The matter that we were discussing was whether or not a commission should be appointed.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will allow me to say one word, I know he is not intentionally misquoting me, but what 1 asked, according to my recollection was, if it would be permissible for the war veterans to appear before this committee, and

it was distinctly understood they would be able to appear before it.
, Mr. McKEiNZIE:	That is exactly what
I am saying. That is what the hon. member said, and I would ask you, Sir, what was his purpose in putting that question? What did he put the question for? Was it not for the purpose of ascertaining whether the object of the Great War Veterans' Association's committee would foe accomplished just as well by going before that Parliamentary committee as if they had been granted a commission? I contend that was his purpose. If I am1 mistaken in that contention I want the hon. member to put me right. What further evidence does he require? The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) had a notice of motion on the Order Paper. Clearly that motion was for the purpose of giving the war veterans a royal commission. Clearly that is what he asked for by his motion; but, Sir, the Rules of the House were suspended this afternoon to enable the hon. gentleman to withdraw his motion because it is no longer necessary for the reason that the President of the Council had declared this matter was to foe dealt with before a committee. Nothing can be clearer than that. Now, what do we find? The Minister of Justice, tells us flat-footedly that the matter is not to be dealt with before that committee- nothing of the kind. We have been in a fool's paradise all this day listening to this discussion and on the point of going home satisfied with the declaration of the President of the Council that his committee was to deal with this matter absolutely. In dealing with the matter, following observations of the President of the Council, ,we went even so far as to ask how the witnesses would be provided for-that is how the veterans coming from different parts of the country were to be provided for in coming before the committee.
Mr. RiOWEDL: I am quite sure my hon. friend does not wish intentionally to misrepresent what I said, but if he will turn to page 255 of Hansard he will find that I distinctly stated what the Bill provided for and that it would be referred to a committee-that was the (Bill dealing with the re-establishment of the soldier in civil life, and relating to disabled soldiers and the matter of employment. When the question was asked by the hon. member for Fort William my answer'was:
What I stated was that the Bill would be referred to a Committee of the House just as the Pensions Bill was referred last session, and I would anticipate that the committee thus appointed would give the same full facilities for

any representation that might he made in reference to matters referred to it as the Pensions Committee gave last year. They will be empowered, of course, to hear all parties as the committee was then.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Certainly. Absolutely
does the President of the Council mean to say that he is using language with a double meaning? Does he mean to tell this House that while he- was satisfying the hon. member for Fort William that the war veterans would go before that committee, have their case presented and be heard and dealt with in every particular, that he did not mean that?-that he was guarding himself with language which would silence the hon. member and at the same time safeguarding himself so that no evidence would be given? If he says that that was his position, we can understand it. Does he mean to say tlhat he used language that caused the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) to withdraw his motion this afternoon because ;he was led to believe by the language of the President of the Privy Council that 'there was another court provided and another avenue opened which would give the Great War Veterans greater facilities and enable them to go fully into this matter? Does he mean to say that he did not mean that, and he allowed that hon. gentleman to lose his opportunity of going into this matter and moving bis motion under a misconception of the real situation, intending when the real time came to put another construction entirely upon his words? I am sure that when the President of the Council made his speech there was not a man in the House that had any other understanding than that this committee was to deal fully and solely with every phase of the question which the Great War veterans could present before it. Now, we have a different position entirely; the President of the Council says he meant nothing of the kind, that no evidence is to be taken, and the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) finds he withdrew his motion without anything to show for it, and the war veterans are entirely shut out. That is the situation and I submit, Sir, that while I realize the gravity of dealing with a subject of this kind, and while I recognize that every member, whether in opposition or supporting the Government, should with the greatest possible care approach a question of this kind and say nothing that would tend to create difficulty or dissatisfaction in this country, it appears to me it was not absolutely square to tell the representatives of the War Veterans' Association the other day that 'they'were to

be heard before the commitee, and now for the President of the Council and the Minister of Justice to declare that there is to be nothing of the kind.
If they go there they have to confine themselves entirely to the- terms of this Bill, nothing else, because the Government has delivered its judgment, and there it is. If I were a war veteran and had been given to understand that I was to receive a hearing, and were told afterwards that I was not to receive a hearing, I do not think I would be pleased. That is exactly the position in which the Government puts itself and its friends in connection with this matter, and I would be disposed to describe it as not dealing in good faith with a question of a most serious character.
If the letters which passed between the Prime Minister and the representatives of the War Veterans are read-they were put on Hansard by the President of the Privy Council-it will be found that one of them is dated the 29th of August, 1919, and is signed by the president, W. P. Purney, the vice-president, R. B. Maxwell, the second vice-president, S. Stalford, and also by a committee consisting of seven or eight members, who style themselves Members of the Dominion Executive Committee; that letter demanded a Royal Commission. The Prime Minister replied that he did not think a Royal Commission was necessary. The secretary, Mr. C. G. MacNeil, writes on the 3rd of September renewing the demand, and on the 5th of September they are again told that they cannot get that Royal Commission. Then the heather is afire and news comes from every quarter that something must be done. Thereupon the resourceful and ingenious President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) comes forward with about three thousand yards of tables containing no end of figures, and in presenting them he explains that a Bill is to be introduced and in connection with it there will be the fullest possible inquiry. That allayed the trouble, and the War Veterans, I suppose, were willing to take what they could get, and if it was not the best it might be good enough, for they would be able to give their story to the Government and to the public, and it mattered not so much in what form it was put. Let me repeat, Sir, that that is all off now, and there is no avenue left open for them to put their story before the Government or before this House.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the discussion, and I thought that the
President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Doherty) were going to adhere to their former position, that this question of what should be done in the way of further gratuities to the soldiers was to be heard by the committee referred to, and I did not think it was necessary that either myself or any other member, on this side of the House at all events, should express any opinion, because 1 am sure the training and experience of the Acting Prime Minister and that of the President of the Privy Council would lead them to conclude that when a case is to be submitted to a properly constituted court it is not only unnecessary but highly improper to comment on what the findings of that court should be. I was sitting here happy and contented that the facts, so far as the soldiers were concerned, were to be submitted to a properly constituted committee, that they would deliberate on the matter, and that we would then adopt, amend, or reject as the case might be, the findings of that committee. But now really there is nothing at all to be expected from the Government except a blank refusal, as appears from an alleged interview with the Acting Prime Minister which appeared in the Globe on September 14, and is as follows :
Asked to give a further statement of the position of the Government on the question of $2,000 gratuity to veterans, Hon. Judge Doherty, Minister of Justice and Acting Premier, said:
*' Sir Robert iBorden had already given the war veterans his decision on the point, and it is the decision of the Cabinet Council as well. Clearly it must toe adhered to. We want to be sympathetic with all the demands and aspirations of the returned men, and do all for them that is humanly possible. But there must be some place where we have to make a stand.
"As I pointed out to them yesterday, it is the people of Canada who would have to pay the extra money if it were given, and there is some limit to what they can pay. The figures given by Hon. Mr. Rowell in the House show that we have done very much better toy the returned men than any other country engaged in the conflict has done.
" I am sure that the demand made upon us does not represent the view of the great body of the returned men. Most of them are well able to gauge the situation and understand the impossibility of adding to our debt the immense amount that would be involved."
That is the decision reached by the Government, and that is merely a repetition of what is contained in the Prime Minister's letter hearing date the 5th of September. If the President of the Privy Council had stood by that decision and had not suggested that the question would be considered by this committee, I presume that the hon. member for Calgary

East ,(Mr. Redman) would have gone along with his notice of motion and the question would have come squarely before the House. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is evidently nothing on which an opinion can be expressed. Nothing is to be done by this committee, the hon. member for Calgary East has withdrawn his notice of motion, and there is nothing before the House of a practical character as to what shall be .done in respect to the demands of the War Veterans' Association.
I think, Sir, that as far as we on his side of the House are concerned, we should wait until something practical is brought forward by the Government, which alone can move in matters of this kind. The hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) and others may find fault with the Opposition for not doing anything, but we have no control over the finances of this country at present, and anything we might bring in here (by way of legislation dealing with public moneys would be ruled out of order by you, Sir, because it is impossible under our rules for the Opposition to bring in any money Bill. It is therefore without the slightest foundation that fault is found with hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the member for North Simcoe, (Mr. Currie) was right in bringing this question before the House in order that hon. gentlemen might express their views in regard to it. I do not, however, agree with all that the hon. gentleman has said; nor do I concur in the demands which he has made in this connection.

Although the discussion has taken the whole of the day and has lasted well into the night, I think it has been well worth while.
A few days ago a deputation waited upon the Prime Minister to ask for a commission or a committee to consider the matter of a gratuity to be paid to the Great War

Veterans. The Prime Minister did not accede to that request. I had a telephone message from one of the Great War Veterans informing me that they had been unsuccessful in securing the appointment of a committee to meet representatives of the Great War Veterans' Association. My reply was that I thought a committee should have been appointed to hear their grievances.
It is apparent that while many of the Great War Veterans were asking for a gratuity of a'certain amount, they were not, I think, disposed to confine themselves specifically to that demand. They feel that they have certain grievances with regard to pensions and re-establishment and they would like a committee of the House to straighten them out. I think it is right that a committee should be appointed and that they should be heard. I am very glad that the Government changed their mind on this question, because while a few days ago they were not disposed to appoint a committee, they subsequently decided, upon second consideration, or, perhaps, in view of further pressure, that a committee of inquiry should be appointed.

speechtext: I have but one observation. 1 am afraid I cannot congratulate my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition on the illuminating character of his address tonight, at least 'as indicating his own views on the matter under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The difficulty . with my 'hon. friend to-night was the difficulty he experienced last week, 'and that was in distinguishing between things thait differ. Last week he failed to distinguish between legal authority and constitutional right. To-night he failed to distinguish between a general war service gratuity and the question of the re-establishment of the individual soldier in civil life. If my hon. friend would turn to the statement I made the other day he would see the distinction I made between, the two. In the opening statement I said:
Mr. 'Speaker, at the request of the Prime Minister X desire to make the following statement with reference to the position of the Government in the matter of a further bonus or war service gratuity to returned soldiers.
The position of the Government is set forth in a statement prepared by the Prime Minister on Saturday last for submission to the House in answer to a question placed on the Order Paper by the hon. member for West Edmonton.
Then I went on to give the Prime Minister's statement, as set forth in the letters I read to the House. I made the position of the Government perfectly clear in reference to the two points, namely, the war service gratuity of $2,000 (the Calgary resolution), and secondly, in reference to a royal commission to investigate the financial ability of the country to pay it. That position was that the Government could not accede to either of these requests, and that is exactly the position which the leader of the House here to-night (Mr. Doherty) has taken. I pointed out on that occasion that the Government had already introduced a Bill in the Senate dealing with the Department of Soldiers' 'Civil Re-Es-tablish-inent, that the work of the department was covered by certain Orders in Council under the War Measures Act, that it was the intention of the Government when the Bill

received its second reading to refer it together with all Orders in Council relating to the matter to this Committee, which would have full power to hear witnesses and to summon witnesses if it saw fit. That Committee will have before it everything that relates to the re-establishment of the soldier in civil life, and I am quite sure that it will hear whatever representations may be made on that important and vital question. That includes the questions mentioned by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Foster). The question of making provision for returned men out of employment is one of the very points enumerated. Representations may be made on all these points- by the Great War Veterans' Association or any other association that chooses to come before that Parliamentary Committee, and I am sure that the committee will give the same generous and sympathetic consideration 'to representations that may be made to it as- did the committee appointed last year to consider pensions. My hon. friend's difficulty is that he fails to distinguish between things that differ.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
If we were asked to vote upon this question of a $2,000 gratuity, I certainly would not be able to record my vote in favour of it. It is well for us to remember that the Great War Veterans' Association, while they began by asking for that gratuity, modified their claim later and only asked for an investigation. Of course, I presume they had in mind ultimately the same thing, but we must take their request as they made it. Even their request to the Prime -Minister, I understand, was not for a specified sum, but for an investigation. Now, it is always -a difficult thing to refuse an investigation to any large body of men, and when we consider those who compose the Great War Veterans' Association and the services which they have rendered I think we should go a long way towards meeting them to the extent of giving them a hearing whenever they demand it on any question.
I regret -that the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) imported a party question for a moment into this matter. I do not think it is necessary. The general tenor of the debate has been excellent, and I think it has served a good purpose. It has been illuminating in the way of eliciting opinions from all sides, and to that extent I think my hon. friend who introduced the motion has served a good purpose. Yet, perhaps, it was not necessary, because there has been a change of attitude on the part of the Government, which has to be recog-

nized. I find no fault with the letter of the Prime Minister, but it is a fact that the attitude of the Government at that moment is not their attitude to-day. I am not complaining of that. I think they were wise in modifying their attitude so far as to say they would give an inquiry to the war veterans.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been in the House and has heard the statement. They would not allow that.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I have heard most of the debate, and I suppose we may all interpret it in a different way. I understand that while the Prime Minister at first refused a commission, he has, through the Minister of Justice and the President of the Privy Council, offered to give an investigation before a committee. That is the whole situation.
How far that committee may go is a question to be considered, but we cannot alter the fact that the refusal which the Prime Minister gave-and I am not finding fault with that-has been modified; but instead of granting the commission he has intimated that he is willing to have an investigation before this committee. I understand through the public press-the ministers can correct me if I am not right- that the representatives of the 'Great' War Veterans waited upon some of the ministers in view of that change of attitude and said that they were content with what was then proposed. I do not know whether that is correct or not. I .am merely stating what appeared in the press, that the leaders of the Great War Veterans' Association were -satisfied with the situation, and if they are satisfied I -am not disposed to complain. 1 take it for granted that while the commission is not to be granted, this committee to be appointed will afford the War Veterans an opportunity to- make out the best case they -can, -and to -that extent I commend the attitude of the Government to-day.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
To what committee does the hon. member refeT?
-Mr. FIELDING: I refer to the committee mentioned by -the President of the Privy Council.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: He has not stated that any special committee will he appointed.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I think it has been stated repeatedly that the Bill to be referred to the committee appointed for its consideration will afford the opportunity incidentally-that is the word-of discussing the whole question, of gratuities. It is with that understanding, I believe, that the War Veterans have expressed their satisfaction. I do not think that any of the statements made to-night have been so emphatic as to prevent an inquiry by that committee in-to the whole matter. At all events, the impression I have ds -that the War Veterans are satisfied with the position of affairs, and if they are -satisfied with it I have no disposition to find fault. I -am not advocating a gratuity of $2,000. The matter appeals to me as a grave and serious one, and I -am glad that the Government have so far modified their attitude as to be willing to give the War Veterans a hearing; and whether this ds done through a commission or a committee the principle is not altered.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not wish to detain the House very long in closing this question. First of all I desire to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). His utterance was brilliant, but he assumed an attitude altogether beside the question. In the first place, he endeavoured to impute certain motives to myself and other people with reference to this matter. Now, it is a very bad thing for any man, especially a member of Parliament, to impute motives to anybody, and I leave the hon. member to the Great War Veterans of Fort William, who will doubtless -attend to him. As regards his position in the (House and the way in which he got in here, I shall say nothing.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. CURRIE TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THEIR INTERVIEW WITH THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I have the floor. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it was Burke, the famous Irish orator, who repeated the -story that Addison used to tell about a man who lived at the time of Addison and who amassed a great fortune by the sale of bread pills to people in order to prevent earthquakes. So far as the speech of the hon. member had any effect as an appeal on behalf of the Great War Veterans or of any of the returned soldiers, I can only say that- in my opinion it is a case of -bread pill. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) also wandered far -afield, making uncalled for remarks about a gentleman who went to France on a Cook's tour. A number of gentlemen from this- House enlisted and raised regiments. They went to England and, owing to the fact that they were over age were not permitted to go to the front but were allowed to go to France for a time to see a little of the show. I think, Mr. COMMONS
Speaker, that we should have heard the last of this matter of Cook's tourists. As a matter of fact, only five members of the House got into the trenches, but these other men, many of whom were far over age, served their country well, and they did their duty when they took their units to England. The hon. member for Frontenac, whom I am sorry is not present now, did not make an attempt to go to the front, but many of those who endeavoured to go were older than he. Now, Sir, the position is this:	It has been assumed in the
press and even by the hon. member who has just resumed hia seat (Mr. Fielding) that the Government is going to appoint a committee for the special purpose of considering these gratuities, but the minister, who spoke frankly has told him that this Bill would be referred to a committee like any other Bill, and that the Government were not going to initiate any kind of movement to enlarge the scope of the committee, which would discuss it. But all along it has been assumed that the Government is going to appoint a special committee to deal with this question. The Government has absolutely refused a commission, and it has also refused to appoint a special committee, as it might well do in regard to this question which is one of supreme importance and is attracting a great deal of attention. There is a certain word in use among the Tommies at the front in regard to matters in which there is any shuffling, and that is the word " wangling." There has been a great deal of wangling about this question, when nobody ' seems to understand the position of the ministers and no one can give a clear statement concerning the exact position of affairs in the House, except to make speeches assuming that the Government is going to do this, that, and the other thing and that everything is highly satisfactory. Nothing has been given by the Government to satisfy the demand of the Great War Veterans. They asked for a commission or a committee of the House to discuss this question and the Govetnment has absolutely refused to grant this request. The minister can correct me if I am wrong. I assume from his silence that I am right in this statement. What, then, is the use of evasiveness? We must face the facts. I advocate a gratuity for the returned soldier, a gratuity for the widows and children and mothers of those men who have fallen, and a gratuity for the student. To listen to some of the speeches of hon. members, especially the hon. member for Bed Deer, who I regret is not in his place, one would 
think that the returned soldiers could be satisfied with mere temporizing and fine iwords. It is a helping hand that the soldier needs. So far as the hon. member for Bed Deer is concerned, free trade and work seem to be all that occupies his mind, and it seems that we are going to send the returned soldiers to work houses if they have no money. I do not assume that position. The men who went to the front served for a very small sum daily. They did their duty for a meagre remuneration, looking at the matter from a purely commercial standpoint. It is eminently unjust to suggest that a man who has done his utmost at the front and has made great sacrifices for his country should be asked to continue sacrificing. Are we to say to the men who cannot get food and clothing:	You sacrificed
your all in the trenches and though it is true that within twenty-four hours a coffin may have to be provided for you we will ask you to continue sacrificing in the interests of your country. Is that the position which this country is to assume? These men went overseas and served for a dollar and a dollar twenty-five a day, and now they come home to find that during the whole period of the war their comrades who did not go to the front but were given exemption by the Government have been working in munition factories making four times as much money as they did before. These are the stern facts which the returned men are putting forward, and we must honestly face them. The returned soldiers are not making threats against this House or the country and it is absurd to make that suggestion as an argument. There are no people in the country who will support Parliament and the Constitution more than the soldiers and their dependents. I do not think there is any other question raised that is worth while referring to. We have reached the end of the debate. The speech of the hon. member for Calgary has been wiped aside by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Doherty), and the hon. member for Fort William has the consolation of knowing that he made a brilliant argument in support of a position which the Government has not assumed and does not intend to assume. All the other speeches, as the leader of the Opposition has said, leave us faced with the bare fact that nothing tangible is offered the returned soldier. The Government has nothing to offer to these men who have asked for a fair consideration of the matter of gratuities. If they belong to the category of the sick or are in want of a hand out they can go to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Be-Establishment

which finds them jobs but as far as granting them a gratuity, or discussing it, is concerned, they cannot discuss it before that committee. The President of the Privy Council after spending a number of days trying to ward off the Great War Veterans and trying to make everybody believe that it was all right, that there was going to be an investigation, thus endeavouring 'to create a fool's paradise, reverts to the cold facts as I have stated them. Fortunately I read the statement of the President of the Privy Council, and I was not deceived by it. I read it in cold print and I asked myself the very question that seems to have fooled the leader of the Opposition:	Is
there any committee granted, or is there any promise of a committee in that statement? I found that there was none and that is one of the reasons why I would not back down or withdraw my motion. I wished the whole question to be brought up plainly here so that the House would understand the situation and that none of the members would go home and place themselves in a false position without knowing what had been said or done here. I did not believe in that moonshine and I hope the leader of the Opposition will not be influenced by any more of this moonshine because politics are politics, and things are going on.
I have endeavoured to present the arguments of the returned men on this question whether they are my own views or not. I confess to the House that at first I was of the view that this country had done as much as possibly could be done for them and that it was impossible to raise this vast sum of money. But my attitude on that has changed and it has changed because I feel that there are ways and means by which this amount or a similar amount can he obtained. It is not a new thing for a Government to remunerate its returned soldiers, after coming back from a victorious war such as this. If they had not won the war we might have had some excuse. (Anybody (who reads history will know that after every successful war from the days of the Romans down the country has given grants in money and land to the soldiers who have come back. Why should we single ourselves out and take the attitude that such a thing is a new idea and that the soldiers are not entitled to this money? It has been the custom for ages. I think it was a Biblical custom, was it not? The leader of the Opposition will tell us that it was an ancient Biblical custom dating from the days of 24
Moses. Why should we assume an attitude of alarm, and because the soldiers make a demand for land and money, slam the door in their faces, as the leader of the Government has said? I do not say that the Government have slammed the door in their faces, but apparently they have no money for them. Such being the case, having heard all theqe arguments, having discussed the question here, I am sure that the discussion being academic has not suffered by reason of that fact or by reason of the fact that under these circumstances the arguments can be presented pro and con on a question of this kind because there cannot be any party division. That is why I brought the question forward in this way. Anybody can take part in the discussion, the question can be discussed by ministers quite freely, and members behind them and on the Opposition side can state their views upon the matter. We have heard a great many opinions expressed. But one thing has come out of this discussion and that is that this House wants a committee to discuss this matter with the returned soldiers, and we will have this committee if it is possible before the end of the session.
There has been no argument advanced against my view that we can get the money.
I say we can. That argument was advanced against the first home loan that was proposed in this country. The bankers, who surrounded the late Minister of Finance, when he said that we must have a domestic loan, of the large amount decided upon, pulled enough whiskers out of their grey beards to stuff a sofa. They said that it would put the country into bankruptcy. But the Minister of Finance assured them that after the money subscribed to the loan was got in, the bankers would have more money than ever before, and that turned out to be true. I would not take the responsibility, after this experience, of saying definitely that I thought the money could not he raised. Any man who suggests that is entirely wrong.
A question has been raised as to whether we can get it from the Germans. I am sorry that a more practical attitude was not assumed towards the Germans by those who took part in the negotiations of the Peace Treaty, especially if we are going to get damages to the extent of the damage done to our people and our land. The only people who can claim any damages to their property, if the Minister of Justice is right, will be the owners of the trawlers sunk



off Shelburne and Halifax. We have had no bombs dropped in Canada. I believe there was an attempt to blow up a bridge or two, and possibly damages will be allowed for that. But over and above that there should have been a very sharp decision made and our representatives should have placed the question of damages in such a light that they could come home like Mr. Hughes of Australia, and say that Canada is going to get $100,000,000, $200,000,000 or $300,000,000 in round figures. In so far as I could see, the argument of the leader of the Government tonight was to the effect that we were not to get anything. But I assume that is not quite correct. We are entitled to a share of the indemnity just as much as any other country that fought over there. A share of the indemnity could be given to our soldiers first and to the country second. The navy is getting prize money. When a vessel is captured it is taken into the prize court and the prize money is awarded to the soldiers and sailors. Our position is the same and we should be entitled to share in the indemnity. We should not have haggled too much with the Germans as to what they are able to pay. They are able to pay far more to-day than the people of Canada are able to pay proportionately.
The hour is late and I would be presuming very much upon the good nature of the House if I were to ask for a division on the question to adjourn. I do not regret that I have brought this matter before the House because, although it may be unpopular, I am not unmindful of the maxim of the aged statesman Pericles, that he judges rightly who chooses the unpopular side of a great cause. I am quite willing to take the unpopular side and I am quite satisfied that after the arguments that have been advanced in this House, and the arguments that will be advanced outside of it during the next few weeks, the House will take a more mellow view of this question and will see its way to unanimously appoint a committee to discuss the whole question of gratuities as proposed' in the remarks which I have addressed to the House. I ask leave to withdraw the motion.

speechtext: Consideration- of the motion of Mr. Howard Primrose Whidden for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Monday, September 15.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I concur with what is said in the remarks made by the previous speakers on the Address in offering sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder, who have made excellent speeches. Indeed, Sir, it would be a misfortune if I should not speak in a eulogistic strain of my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. McIntosh), whose speech was one continuous congratulation to every one he thought of.
I do not desire, Sir, to discuss at great length the matters included in the speech from the Throne, but I will rather discuss the omissions from that speech. The welcome to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales was fittingly placed in the opening passages of the speech from the Throne. I humbly and heartily join in the welcome which has been given in this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to the most valiant, the most popular Prince who has visited our shores and who has endeared himself to the hearts of the Canadian people.
I might remark that His Royal Highness must have scandalized many of my hon.

friends on the other side of the House by his knowledge of the French language and the pride he had in using it. Of course, I am referring to those hon. members on the other side of the House who have such a horror of the French language that if'God Almighty was French they would be atheists.
As to the Peace Treaty and the League of Nations, we have had resolutions on the matter and a long discussion; therefore I will defer my remarks on this question until Bill No. 3 is before the House. The next item of the Address relates to measures and legislation necessary on the advent of peace. Until these measures are brought down I will refrain from making any statement except to express my sincere wish that they will be real peace measures; that we will return to constitutional government by majority through the representatives of the people duly elected; that we will re-establish the sanctity of our courts as the protectors of individual rights, and that we will re-introduce liberty now that peace has come.
I may say that we in Canada, as well as the people of Great Britain, have been at peace with Germany for a long time; even during the last session we were said to be at peace with Germany. If I refer to an Order in Council dated June 23, 1919, I see that persons resident in Canada are allowed to resume trade with Germany. Mr. Speaker, in my humble opinion, we are either at peace or at war. There is no middle ground and if we are not at peace and if this Government has allowed persons resident in this country to resume trade with Germany, they are guilty of trading with the enemy and are subject to a severe penalty.
Now, Sir, although it is not included in the Address, may I be allowed to discuss the high cost of living? I might have waited until the House had been moved into Committee of Supply but I have read in the newspapers that our ministers intend to return to England very soon for the Imperial Conference and I am most anxious to bring this matter up while the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and his travelling colleagues are on a visit to Canada.
This session has been called especially for ratifying the Peace Treaty. On arriving here we were practically told by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) that it is already ratified, that it is already signed by the King and signed by our representatives, but that unless we give 
it our approval it will not be dealt with in Paris and we will have to start all over again. Why not say in this House what everybody outside of this House says, what everybody knows to be the truth, that this session was called by the Government to placate the ire of some of its supporters who were disappointed because the Prime Minister did not agree to increase the sessional indemnity? The calling of this session is outrageous in face of the financial status of our country, but we are here, and now that we have been called to attend it-and it is our duty to attend-why not get down to some real work? Why not earn our indemnity by taking up questions of interest and trying to solve problems that are vital to the welfare of Canada? It is with this desire that I will offer a few considerations on the high cost of living and its most obvious cause, the profiteers.
First of all I wish to state that outside of profiteering there are many other reasons, for the high cost of living, such as lack of production, diversion of production of the necessaries of life to the production of luxuries, strikes, the increased cost of production, high tariff, etc.
But as I am convinced that profiteering in its most aggravated form exists in Canada,
I will confine my remarks to this special cause. At the last session I gave the House some figures regarding the profits made by the millers-I am now able to add a few more. I told the House then that the Ogil-vie Flour Mills Company for the year previous to the outbreak of war, had made $470,000 profits. But their profits for the year ending August 31, 1917, were $2,100,000. This increase is enormous. Yet, Sir, the profits of 1918 were $3,551,821 consisting of net profits for dividends, after payment of bond interest and war tax of $1,955,414, and a special contingent account of $1,596,407. This special contingent account, according to the president of the company, was set aside to take care of a sudden change in the value to meet a post war slump. This was camouflage, Mr. Speaker, because according to the company its total stock on hand on August 31, 1918, was valued at $1,462,916, or $1,174,900 less than in August 1917. Therefore, the company provided $1,596,407 to meet a possible decline in value of stock, valued at $1,462,916. Besides the company had its old contingent account of $2,501,000 now termed a rest account, making a very respectable reserve of $4,096,407. The total invested capital of the Ogilvie Flour Mills Company at the beginning of last year being $7,-
200,000,	the net profits of $3,500,000 are

equivalent to fifty per cent. Therefore the company which up to 1916 earned a dividend of eight per cent, now earns a dividend of fifty per cent. The Lake of the Woods Milling Company is in the same position. Again the amount of common stock issued by the St. Lawrence Flour Mills Company was $1,200,000. Of this $150,000 was paid in assets-the rest is water. Up to 1917 there was no dividend on the common stock. In that year the profit on actual invested capital was 16.2, and in 1918 it was 29.6. Instead of a debit of $61,000 in 1913 a surplus profit account is now shown of $251,154; and the manager of the company, who is a stalwart supporter of this Government, makes the statement that the millers are making far less than those engaged in any other industry.
An Order in Council passed by the Government, dated March 9, 1918, limited the profits of all meat-packing companies to 11 per cent on the invested capital, all profits above that percentage going to the State.	I wish to draw the attention
of the House to this point: had the Order in Council in question been made applicable to the milling companies, the Ogilvie Flour Milling Company would have had to pay an extra tax of $2,750,000 to the treasury, a very interesting amount you will admit. You have seen how great the profits of the principal milling companies who turn out the basic product of bread, have been.
Now what about the textile companies? The Dominion Textile Company last year made $1,559,888 or 31.2 on its common stock against 21.9 in 1917 and 15 per cent in 1916. If the Order in Council applied to the packers had been made applicable to them, and if the Government had seen fit to collect the extra dividends, this company would have added $1,006,380 to the treasury. We had an inquiry into the high cost of living last year and amongst other things it was shown that a certain clothing company bad made 72 per cent, and the Dominion Textile 300 per cent on the capital invested.
It is impossible for me to give you the exact figures respecting the packing industry, I could not obtain accurate data, but let me remind you of certain facts. The Prime Minister last session when discussing the high cost of living stated that most drastic taxation had been imposed by Order in Council on those engaged in the packing industry-so drastic that the companies affected came before the Government and implored them not to go so far,
that their business would be absolutely ruined; but that the Government was firm and passed the Order in Council under which the State collects all profits above 11 per cent, which legislation was still in force. Now let us see what the President of 'the Privy Council said on the same matter. As reported 'at page 3521 of Hansard of last session, the hon. gentleman, whom I am very glad to see in his seat, said:
Take the question of the profits of packers and cold storage men which has been so much discussed in this House. What was done under the administration of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture? Regulations were imposed which, in the first place, limited the profits on the turnover of the leading cold storage men and packers. They were required under regulations, which were administered by the Government, and under license issued by the Department of Agriculture, or the Food Board, -I forget which-to so carry on their business that their profits should -not exceed two percent on their turnover. Notwithstanding that^ if they earned a profit on the capital invested in the business of over 7 per cent, and up to 15 per cent, one-half over 7 per cent went to the Government as revenue, and the other half went to the packer. All over 15 per cent went to th>-Government. The result was that no packer could earn more than 11 per cent on his total actual capital invested in the business. The packers very strongly resisted these regulations
and protested against them	The Canadian
packers protested against our regulations....
In no country at war have such stringent regulations been imposed upon the packers and cold storage people as have been imposed by the Government on the packers of this country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I remember the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) telling us one day last session that this Government was owned by Sir Joseph Flavelle. He probably knows more about that than I do. But what I do know and what every other member knows is that the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and. the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) never let an opportunity escape to make a brotherly defence of this most deserving titled profiteer. Early last session the President ot the Council was in the House the "chevalier servant" of this notable food king, and related the martyrlike sufferings of the packers under the drastic Order in Council of the 9th March, 1918.
In the face of all these declarations every hon. member has been under the impression that these poor cold storage companies, -which according to the O'Connor report *constituted a monopoly and made enormous profits,-have contributed a tremendous amount of money to the Treasury by giving away all their profits above 11 per cent, especially as the price of bacon instead of declining has been making a skyward

jump, and has now reached an altitude of 65 to 70 cents a pound. But, Mr. Speaker, please do not forget the fact that when the Order in Council touched their very close friends they lavishly indulged in the policy of laissez faire. What huge sums have been collected from the cold storage companies since that Order in Council was issued? What fortunes, large enough, 1 might say, to jeopardize their existence, *have these companies been forced to contribute to the public Treasury? The answer of the Government to a question which I put to them on the 28th of May last will enlighten us. It will be found at page 3008 of Hansard of last session, and I beg permission to read it'
1.	What sum has the Government collected from cold storage warehouse companies since the Order in Council limiting the profits of the said companies to 11 per cent has been passed?
2.	What amounts have been collected from each one of said companies, and what are the dates when said amounts were collected?
Sir Thomas White:	1 and 2. Persons,
firms and incorporated companies engaged in the slaughtering of live stack or the manufacture of products therefrom liable to taxation under the Order in Council of 9th March, 1918, are assessable for all profits in excess of 15 per cent upon capital and one-half profits in excess of 7 per cent up to 15 per cent upon such capital. Regulations under the said Order in Council were in effect from 1st January, 1918.
And listen to this:
The Commissioner of Taxation has been engaged in investigating the business and accounts of all persons, firms and incorporated companies who might be liable to assessment under the Order in Council. These investigations are not completed, but so far as they have proceeded they do not disclose profits in excess of the ' mount exempted by the Order in Council Many firms and companies engaged in the busi

oneerned, sustained heavy losses 'iur-;* ** -1918 calehdar year, which year was most unfavourable to the packing industry.
The President of the Council, who is more prone to defend proflteeis than to defend himself personally, has shown more grit in defending a profiteering company than he did last year when the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Munphy) made precise accusations against him. I read from Hansard at page 3525 what the President of the Privy Council said:
Ret me mention the case which the hon. member for Marquette mentioned yesterday about the Dominion Textile Company and the large i rofts they had earned. Yesterday, by a strange coincidence, Sir Charles Gordon, president of-that company, happened to be in my office, before my hon. friend had spoken. Some question came up about this announcement in the paper showing their large profits, and Sir
harles told me that more than 50 per cent of the profit was made owing to the increase in

value of raw cotton and other raw material they had on hand during the year. In other words, 'hey had bought at a fortunate time; they had exercised good judgment in buying.
Yes, Sir, they had bought at a fortunate time; they had exercised good judgment. Very well. I admire the foresight of traders-especially when they do not use that foresight against the people in order to extract their life blood. But what the Textile Company did is the principal cause of the unrest in this country. Why, Sir, the buying of the necessaries of life in huge quantities at a low price and the holding of those necessaries until an artificial scarcity is created and the price goes up, is the essence of profiteering. This company made 300 per cent on money invested in the handling of an essential necessity of '[DOT]ife, and my hon. friend, the President of the Privy Council, approves, protects and encourages such methods, and he cites this instance as a clever and keen piece of commercial intelligence. Was there ever a more glaring defence of the profiteer?
Sir, when the Kaiser left Germany after his defeat he carried with him a huge sum of money. I fail to see any other reason for the behaviour of the President of the Privy Council than that, realizing the rapidly approaching debacle of the Union Government, and that the people armed with whips are only waiting occasion to flagellate the Pharisees, he wishes to carry with him into private life the gilded friendship of the Flavelles and the Gordons.
Another reason for the high cost of living is that there is no restriction on exportation. Charity begins at home, but before permitting the unlimited exportation of foodstuffs the Government should see, first, that there is enough left in the country for the Canadian consumer; secondly, that the foodstuffs which are now filling the cold storage plants to their capacity should be put on the local market, and, thirdly, that the consumer should not, on account of unrestricted exportation, be made to compete with the markets of the old world, now at abnormal heights. It is absurd and criminal that in a country like ours, with its abundant production, a sham, and artificial scarcity should be created under the benevolent and paternal eye of the Government.
I have said that charity begins at home. But if the people of Canada had been deprived of their foodstuffs to prevent friendly Allies from starving, such a course might have been improvident, but at least it would have been generous. But, Sir, instead of feeding the Allies, or instead of

feeding any one, Canadian foodstuffs are rotting in the warehouses of Europe. Let me read an extract from the Montreal Star of September 4. It is a despatch from Paris:
A tremendous drop in food prices in the United States may be expected in the next few months, Herbert Hoover said in continuing his testimony yesterday before the committee investigating war expenditures.
The speculators have reached the end of their powers, Hoover declared, and are no longer able to maintain corners in stocks, owing to Europe's inability to purchase America's over-production.
" Warehouses in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Copenhagen and Stockholm are now full of foodstuffs from America," he said, "but no outlet exists, as the countries needing food are unaJble to pay for it at present prices."
On that same day certain statistics were published with regard to Canadian exports of foodstuffs. I quote:
Ottawa, Sept. 3.-Statistics of Canadian exports of foodstuffs in the twelve months ending July 31 may tend to substantiate the theory o ' H. C. Hoover that a factor in the cost of living is European imports for speculation in such commodities, many of which, according to him, have not reached the market.
Canadian exports in the period mentioned include 16,2'Q2,320 pounds of butter. 145,208,450 pounds of cheese, 55,486,266 bushels of wheat, 181,819,455 pounds of bacon, 131,246,513 pounds of beef, 12,414,976 pounds of canned meats and 33,572,004 pounds of pork.
Now, the Government was not only permitting, but encouraging these accumulations. During the month of May last Mr. Henry B. Thompson, Canadian Trade Commissioner, was sent to Europe by the Administration, at the expense of this country. The Government, therefore, are certainly responsible, if, as a consequence of Mr. Thompson's going to the other side, prices soared to heights inaccessible to the Canadian consumer. In a despatch published in the Ottawa Citizen of May 25, Mr. Thompson makes the following interesting statements, among other things:
The prospects for Canadian bacon, he thinks are especially rosy. In a characteristically racy phrase, he says: " Canadian bacon has the chance of its life. Producers can sell all they can make for the English trade as fast as they can get it over."
Mr. Speaker, the prospects for 'Canadian bacon are rosy, I admit that. Canadian bacon has, indeed, the chance of its life, but what about the prospects of the Canadian people? The prospects of the father of a large family are not so rosy when starvation is facing him every day. Notice, Mr. Speaker, the paternal solicitude of the Government for the hog. " Canadian bacon has the chance of its life "-but the Canadian people have no chance at all, except those
people who, like the bacon, are closely related to the hog, the profiteers.
Of course, there are certain of our products which are not rotting in the warehouses, but these are sold to bankrupt countries like Roumania and Greece. The producers of these foodstuffs are not paid by these countries-oh, no; that would involve too much risk for the friends of the Government. The moneys are advanced by the Government of Canada with no sound guarantee of repayment; the profiteers are paid and the Government will have to do the best they can to recover these amounts from countries like Roumania, which is already disobeying the order of the Allies by marching on Budapest.
These accumulations of foodstuffs exist not only in European warehouses, but also here in Canada. The cold storage warehouses of this country are overflowing with goods. Not later than Friday last, Mr. O'Connor, of the Board of Commerce, made the following statement to the press: " All the cold storage houses are bursting with goods." The Montreal Gazette of Thursday last stated also that it was understood that a large quantity of cheese and other products were accumulating in Montreal, awaiting a favourable opportunity for export.
On the first of May last there were in cold storage in Canada 2,381,151 dozen of eggs, 35 per cent more than the previous year; 35,995,954 pounds of beef, 80 per cent more than the previous year; 2,619,097 pounds of mutton, 86 per cent more than the previous year. Now, what afoout the food which is rotting in the warehouses of Canada? 1 need not recall the disclosures made last year with regard -to the antediluvian chickens which rotted in Winnipeg, the property of the William Davies Company, or the carloads of potatoes which were dumped in the fields. Let me cite more recent figures.
Between January 1 and August 22, 1919, enormous quantities of food were confiscated in Montreal as unfit for human consumption: 215,667 pounds of meat, 884 pounds of fowl, 60,076 pounds of fish, 1,147 pounds of fruit, 3,383 pounds of vegetables. In the city of Quebec 95,813 pounds of meat were confiscated during the same period and for the same reason, namely, being unfit for use.
