speechtext:
The English Government, of course, not this Government. Great Britain has always looked after the welfare of its people in a generous way and has always enacted laws against profiteering. May I be permitted to read a very ancient piece of legislation which, in its simplicity and fairness, is a credit to the Mother Country? I quote from a very old statute enacted in 1349 in the reign of Edward III, namely the Statute of Labourers:
Likewise let butchers, fishmongers, hostlers, brewers, bakers poulterers and all other vendors of any victuals, he bound to sell such victuals for ' a reasonable price, having regard for the price at which such victuals are sold in the adjoining places ; so that such vendors may have moderate gains, not excessive, according as the distance of the places from which such victuals are carried may seem reasonably to require; and if any one sell such victuals in another manner, and be convicted of it in the aforesaid way, he shall pay the double of that which he received to the party injured, or in default of him, to another who shall be willing to prosecute in this behalf; and the mayor and bailiffs of the cities and boroughs, merchant towns and others, and of the maritime ports and places shall have power to enquire concerning each and every one who shall in any way err against this, and to levy the aforesaid penalty for the benefit of those at whose suit such delinquents shall have been convicted; and in any case that the same mayor and bailiffs shall neglect to carry out the aforesaid, and shall be convicted of this before justices to be assigned by us, then the same mayor and bailiffs shall be compelled through the same justices, to pay to such wronged person or to another prosecuting in his place, the treble of the thing thus sold, and nevertheless, on our part too, they shall be grievously punished.
In Belgium, prices are also fixed, and, furthermore, foodstuffs come into that country free of duty. Recently, I had occasion to meet the Hon. Philippe Roy, Canadian Agent at Paris, who assured me that foodstuffs in Brussels were selling 30 per cent lower than in Paris, on account of their free entry. Besides, as I said before, prices are fixed and every infraction is punishable iby jail and fine, not an alternative punishment, but both, and the goods are seized, confiscated and sold by the State.
Let us see what has been done in the country to the south of us. The real campaign started on the 28th of July last. On August 9, the President of the United States

delivered his message ito Congress, and in that country-with which it was a crime in 1911 to have any truck or trade, but from which this administration, after being safely seated in the Government benches, has borrowed many ideas and suggestions -the campaign, effective, in earnest, without any sympathy or any back-door escape for friends, started at full speed, and is rapidly bringing to their knees the gamblers in human distress. First on the 9th of August, stringent legislation was passed, and an appropriation of $1,500,000 was voted to enforce the anti-profiteering law.
Orders were flashed from the Capitol at Washington to hundreds of special detectives of the Department of Justice all over the United States, instructing them to cooperate with Federal district attorneys in the profiteer hunt. Instructions were given to open warehouses and to put stored food on the markets in order to force down prices. Then the ball started. The five big packing companies were indicted by the Grand Jury, namely, Armour, Swift, Morris, Wilson, Cudahy. On August 14, $55,000 worth of butter was seized in Chicago. At Toledo eight houses were seized and a retailer was fined $500 for having sold a pound of sugar for thirteen cents when the price had been fixed at eleven cents. Instructions were given to prosecute nineteen large companies. On the 15th, 2,400,000 pounds of meat were seized in cold storages and prosecutions were commenced against thirty companies;
13,000,000 dozens of eggs were seized in St. Louis. The Sugar Equalization Board was formed by which all the sugar either produced in the country or imported, was bought by the Government and sold to the refiner. On the 16th, Commissioner Drennan, of New York, assigned 375 men to inspect warehouses and several other arrests were made. In Detroit on the same day, 442,762 dozens of eggs were seized. On August 20, proceedings were instituted against all the big cement companies. These companies were; Atlas Portland Cement Co., Allentown Portland Cement Co., Alpha Portland Cement Co., Bath Portland Cement Co., Coplay Cement Manufacturing Co., Dexter Portland Cement Co.. The Edison Portland Cement Co., Giant Portland Cement Co., Glens Falls Portland Cement Co., Hercules Cement Corp., Knickerbocker Portland Cement Co.. Lawrence Cement Co., Lehigh Portland Cement Co., Nazareth Portland Cement Co., Penn-Allen Cement Co., Pennsylvania Cement Co., Phoenix Portland Cement Co., Security
Cement and Lime Co., and Vulcanite Portland Cement Co. I could go on and cite many more drastic and effective measures that were taken, and if I were asked what the results were I would read from the Montreal Star of August 12, the following;
American wholesale food dealers making heavy cuts in prices.
Wholesale food dealers have begun to make big reductions in prices' of vegetables, dressed meats and fruits, Government reports showed to-day.
With the campaign to reduce the high cost of living in full swing, comparison of quotations of July 28 with those of August 11 showed a marked decline, which set in after the attack on unjustified prices began.
Potatoes have been cut from 50 cents to $3.40 a barrel since July 28, according to quotations collected by the Bureau of Markets.
Slashes in the price of dressed meats range up to five cents a pound for pork loins.
The cutting also has been extended to beef, the figures show.
Big drops are noticeable in quotations for Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Chicago. A few price increases are shown for some grades of meat. The figures indicate the downward trend is general and that increases are exceptional.
Let us see, now, what the Canadian Government has done. Although receiving reports from the High Cost of Living Commissioner, and aware of the enormous profits that were being made, the members of the Cabinet who perchance were in Canada last year went strenuously to work and did nothing until the last days of the session when, realizing, after the strike at Winnipeg, that the high cost of living iwas the primary cause of the unrest in this country, they named a Parliamentary Committee which after many sittings, in which profits as high as three hundred per cent were disclosed, presented a minority report, accepted by the supporters of the Government, stating that there were no profiteers in Canada, but advising the people to eat less and be more economical. Pressed by public opinion, however, and a threatening cloud of unrest, two. days before the end of the session the 'Government introduced a Bill creating a Board of Commerce. I may be excused if I use an expression which I have used before, and describe this Bill as mere camouflage, because sections 41 and 47 take all the sting from the other sections which 'look formidable enough in the rest of the Bill, and for which reason we protested against the Bill in committee. These two sections, 41 and 47, practically nullify the effect of .the Bill. Section 41 reads:
The Governor In Council may in his discretion, either upon petition of any person interested, lodged within one month after the

his products dearer. I read lately in a Montreal newspaper that the profiteer is ten times, nay a hundred times, more guilty than the common bandit who waits in a dark corner to kill and rob his victim; the bandit kills one man but the profiteer takes, or endeavours to take, the life of the whole population by starving them. He takes the life of the hard worked labourer who, as things are, cannot recuperate his strength, after his day's work. He takes the life of the labouring man's wife and family for whom the husband cannot procure nourishing food. The profiteer is also the worst of parasites. He has cultivated nothing, he has sown nothing-he has not taken care of the herds-but he lives and thrives on the work of the toiler. He comes between the consumer and the producer. He buys everything before it is ripe; indeed he is the worst of criminals because he allows food to rot in order to obtain a higher price and he is diverting these products from the purpose for which God created them. The profiteer is the primary cause of unrest in this country. What the Government should aim at is the common good and the comfort and the happiness of all the people in this country. Society is a contract entered into by all the people under which they consent to abandon part of their privileges and part of their rights for the benefit of all and those who fail to realize the truthfulness and put into action the principles of this definition are blind to the approach of a conflict which will completely put in the shade all the horrors 'of the last war.

speechtext:
This special session which has brought us together will go down to history under the name of a Peace Session.
We are assembled here mainly to consider and approve the terms of the Peace Treaty signed at Versailles.
Mr. Speaker, nowadays everybody is crying out and shouting for peace, but, truth telling, we are far from enjoying the blessings of peace.
Ages ago peace was promised to men of good-will. As peace does not reign in the Government we are bound to come to the conclusion that men of good-will are the few in the Cabinet. The Unionist Government is rent by intestine wars, as to which I may say a word later on.
The Unionist party, that incoherent and ephemeral amalgam, is vainly struggling against the morbid/ elements which must ultimately bring about its downfall.
Whenever, in the midst of their clashing interests, their jarring elements, their discords, these gentlemen come and talk to us about peace we have a presentiment-I was going to say that we already have a vision of the approaching end of the party, and that pretty soon we shall say: " Let it rest in peace."
[Mr. Steele!
The war is over-so they proclaim. It is true that war is at end between the Allies and Germany, but it is still raging in the ranks of the Unionists, whose ministers hasten to leave the ship, while the several groups into which they are divided are looking askance at each other.
Instead of launching out into long speeches about world peace, let the hon. gentlemen first make peace in their own household and thereby have it reign in the country.
Those politicians, those would-be statesmen, arrogate to themselves the ridiculous role of contributing to international peace adjustments, unable as they are to give peace to their own country.
A general state of unrest and agitation is now prevalent in Canada. One has but to open his eyes1 to see what is going on in all social classes and agitating the minds of a dissatisfied and restless proletariat. Unless one is unwilling to listen and pay attention to what is transpiring in the country it is easy to hear the clamour of the strikes rising on every side, the complaints of the masses protesting against the persecution of the conscripts and the actual reign of terror in our rural districts.
Does it not ill become the Government to come and talk of foreign policy at a time when in the very midst of our country such a great unrest is prevailing, brought on by the high cost of living, as to .which the Government has remained indifferent?
For many years we have insisted upon the Government controlling cold storage, prosecuting profiteers, fixing prices, limiting exports. They have turned a deaf ear to our demands and prices have kept soaring.
A few months ago the hon Minister of Labour, in a letter sent to the city council of Montreal, made this strange statement: " That the high cost of living in Canada was owing to the shortage of farm products."
How could he make such a statement, considering we have it from official statistics that during the twelve previous months Canada had exported agricultural products valued at $180,000,000? It is quite evident that the Government was unwilling to open its eyes and its ears. The United States, so to speak, had to take them by the hand and show them the way, and it is only from that moment that we hear of the organization of a board of trade that is to give us the reforms which we have been asking for years.
Up to that date the Government had accomplished nothing, notwithstanding the issuing of commission after commission, the

holding of numerous investigations and the publication of countless reports. The Government have not done a single efficient move and when they appointed a commission to inquire into the high cost of living, they were simply burying the question with all due honours.
The Government are extolling the ministers who have worked in the interest of universal peace, but they have not been able to prevent labour troubles and bp-risings amongst the returned soldiefs, to whom they .promised the moon; they have not been able to prevent the uprisings of the farmers; they could not even pacify the families* disquited by raids of the Federal police. So Mr. John Bruce had every reason to say yesterday, at the National Industrial Conference, that "it is no use for the Government to try to settle the troubles in Europe, if they cannot solve the problems that confront us in Canada."
The wrongs we are complaining of in this country are not irretrievable. A wiser and more alert Administration than the one we have at present, could greatly improve the situation. A much more difficult task will be to find a remedy to the political acts of the Government that pledged the future, that modify the constitutional status of the country, and bind future generations. Allow me. Sir. to dwell a few moments on this phase of the question. In the first place, our ministers, are ingenious enough to believe that war is a thing of the past, because they have signed a Treaty of Peace.
Let us take a broader view of the situation ; let us put aside, for one moment, the petty doings of the narrow-minded statesmen of the Union Government. The Peace Treaty of Versailles deals with peace, but does not secure it. It is a self-delusion-a delusion that will soon fade away-to believe in a permanent peace.
So long as the people of most countries will continue to be guided by the same ideals-and these ideals are not likely to change, before a very long time, if they ever do change-the countries of Europe will have to be satisfied with more or less ephemeral periods of peace.
And, beware, the wars of the future will be much more ruinous and bloody than the wars of the past.
It has been said of the Peace Treaty, that, owing to its hardness, it will soon become obsolete and will not attain the purpose it had in view. I do not agree with that statement. The Treaty is stern, but not over harsh.
1.	Because the Central Powers-Germany and Austria-Hungary-are responsible for the war that has shed such disasters and ruins.
2.	Because that treaty is far more lenient than the terms that would have been exacted by a victorious Germany.
If there could be any doubts about it, they would be dispelled by the following statement from Count Bernstoff, German Ambassador in- the United States:
He was proceeding from the principle that France must be crushed, and reduced to the rank of Portugal, even if five million Frenchmen had to be killed. Going into the details, he undertook the dismemberment of that country in tearing away fifteen million inhabitants outside of a line from 'Saint-Valery to Lyons; that territory was to be given to Belgium which would become, of course, an appendage of Germany. An indemnity of ten billions was to be exacted from France; her fortifications were to be dismantled and her armament ceded to Germany. France would have to terminate her alliance with England and Russia and make a new alliance of twenty-five years with Germany. Finally, William II was to buy Russia and crush England.
tn a confidential memorandum to the Imperial Chancellor of Germany, on the peace terms, signed by all the large industrial and agricultural associations, the dis-iderato of the German people are clearly set forth:
Belgium must be economically subjected to Germany. The coasts portion of France, next to Belgium, as far as the Somme River, must be included in the German Empire. Germany will take possession of all the fortifications on the east boundary, particularly Verdun and Belfort. The coal districts of the Nord and Pas-de-Calais shall belong to Germany. The proprietors in the said districts shall be ejected and the iand shall be occupied by German subjects. As regards Russia, we shall take whole of Poland and of the Baltic provinces.
One may easily gather from the above how Germany intended treating her enemies, had she won the war.
In the third place, the Treaty of Versailles is not too severe, because, had it been less rigorous, it would not have proved a sure guarantee against future wars; and it would not have annihilated the factors which will ever make Germany redoubtable.
The character of a nation cannot be destroyed by a peace treaty.
Borrowing from a well known psychologist, Dr. Gustave LeBon, the following considerations which I make mine, I may say that:
A superficial Inquiry into the causes of the European War, which sees in the armies and the instruments called into play scientific and clever combinations, might have led one to be-

lieve that it was governed toy an infallible rational logic.
But a more careful introspection, a more searching analysis would have revealed that superior forces directed the thoughts, the feelings and actions of the combatants.
The real leaders of those armies were psychological forces.
Immaterial forces are the actual leading and guiding influences in battles.
So that a peace treaty, even though it rested on good grounds, cannot help it.
Rational logic reigns exclusively in the laboratory of the scientist, but it exerts but a slight influence over the conduct of individuals and nations. It is mostly by effective, mystical and collective elements that their existence is conditioned.
Were it not that we are cognizant of the real springs and motive powers, the life of nations would prove a baffling enigma. Their thoughts and actions but seldom take their bearings from reason.
It is exactly by affective and intellectual forces that the character of a nation is shaped and moulded.
Character is the great force by whose impulses we are guided through life. The intellect shapes all our thoughts and conceptions; character guides to right action. The intellect is the power of operative thought; character prompts us to action.
Therefore, character is of the utmost import in the existence of individuals and nations.
Affective influences figure conspicuously among the factors in history. While imparting their strength to ideal concepts, they bring us on to view things in variable ways, according to our sensibility.
So that a treaty of peace, even though it were grounded:, as I said, on reason, is powerless .against the effective and collective forces which sway nations.
The mentality of men collectively manifests itself as quite dissimilar to their mental aotivity, in an isolated state. A multitude of men differs as much from the individuals who compose it as a living being differs from the cells which help to form it.
The collective soul is but slightly actuated by reason. As the feelings of human masses are at once intense and mobile, they rapidly pass from adoration to hatred.
Collective opinion represents a considerable force, but it is seldom spontaneous.
A multitude, in fact, is an amorphous being, unable to exert itself without a leader.
A multitude is swayed and influenced to action by a leader through .persuasive methods pertaining to affective logic, such as affirmation, repetition, prestige or moral influence and contagion stirring up emotions in the masses.
Leaders are always needed in order to create or orient opinion, even in the case of national conflicts.
But the actual starting point of opinions is a leader or an epochal event, as a substitute for the former.
So, in spite of any treaty we may sign, Mr. Speaker, we are at the mercy of an agitator or an event-.

One of the forces of the German Government in the last conflict was to have shown itself able to orient, long beforehand, in its own way, the opinion, of the nation. Journalists, professors, writers compliantly did the bidding of the government and yielded implicit obedience to it. It was thus enabled to transform a European conflict into a national war. It was neither a sovereign nor a military caste which were battling, but the whole German nation.
What can a treaty do, even though it were grounded on -reason, against the mystical forces which sway public opinion in a nation?
Mysticism and reason belong to two spheres which do not interpenetrate each other.
Mystical convictions are born of suggestion or mental contagion, but never through reasoning. No more can reason generate them than it can destroy them.
Mystical impulsions take no account of material needs nor of rational arguments.
Through mental contagion, mysticism easily becomes collective and then exerts a potent impulsion on believers. It ever proved beneficial to nations, such as the Jews of old, the Arabs in the Middle-Ages, the Germans of to-day, to believe themselves predestined by God to regenerate mankind.
Among the various prime movers and springs of conduct in human actions those of mystical origin have eVer proved the most potent. Of them are born those illusions, which are history makers. Under their influence empires were destroyed and others built up. It. is on the very same motives that civilizations are still resting.
The modern world believes that it is no longer under the sway of mystical forces. Yet never wa-s mankind more enthralled by them and brought under their overmastering influence than it is to-day. Whether political, religious or social, those forces belong to the same family, exert an identical action and obey the same laws. They are not governed nor controlled by reason.
If I were ask-ed why a bloody war was let loose on the world, why so many youths fell and yielded up their lives in those battles which have turned the world into a slaughter-house, why so many families have sunk into despair, the reason is that a nation which believed it was called upon to regenerate the world, strove to impose on nations its mystical -chimera of world domination.
Therefore I am right in stating that a peace treaty, be it even that of Versailles, along with the Covenant of the League of Nations, cannot ensure a permanent peace. The causes of military conflicts will always exist, throughout the world.
Whether we 'base the new conditions on the old dogma of the 'balance of -power or on the principle of nationalities, we may he able to delay future outbreaks, but they shall never be suppressed.

Thai peace, even after the Treaty of Versailles, is really a "generous illusion" is evidenced by the fact that in order to prevent retaliatory attempts on the part of 70 millions of people a formidable standing army has to be indefinitely maintained, which, however, will not prevent such attempts or other conflicts which may spring up everywhere.
Such is the explanation of Clause X of the Treaty which embroils even Canada in future wars.
We are required to sign a momentous document in which it is explicitly stated that:
The members of the League undertake to-respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all members of the League. In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or dianger of such aggression the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
They want to belittle the importance of that obligation by quoting other clauses of the Covenant in which it is provided that the differences between the members of the League shall, be submitted to arbitration or to the Council of the League. But should a nation outside the League declare war, the arbitration machinery stops; should even a single member of the League ignore *the Covenant and wage war without arbitration, such as it is provided in Clause 16, what will happen? The clause says that in such case, it shall be' the duty of the Council "to recommend to the several Governments concerned what effective military, naval or air force the members of the League shall severally contribute to the armed forces to be used to protect the Covenants of the League." We are well caught in the gear. Everybody is aware that the issue is a most serious one and everybody admits 'that it is useless for us to approve or disapprove the Treaty. However it is our duty to ask of those who bound Canada in the Treaty of Versailles on what authority they did so.
The Prime Minister and his colleagues, who in 1911 were such obstinate advocates of a referendum and who were opposing with all their strength the least little change in our national status without consulting the people, were the same men who, without consulting not only the people but even Parliament, sent delegates to a congress where they bound this country to all future wars.
Of course we want peace. In order to secure it we have increased our national debt by more than a billion, we have overburdened our budget for half a century to come with such heavy liabilities as will necessitate heavy taxation, and then 60,000 of our fellow citizens gave their life for that same purpose. But we will not have peace at the cost of our liberty and autonomy.
Therefore it may be properly stated again, , as it was stated before in this House, that "we do not accept any restriction of the present autonomous authority of our Dominion and that the question of determining what -part Canada may take in any war, must be always settled by the people of Canada through their representatives in Parliament."
I think that such a correction is necessary, for I see in Clause X a clever and < cunning move on the part of military imperialism, which is the most dreadful form of all.
The imperialists unanimously exclaim: "Canada is a nation. Laurier said so, and we treat you as a nation." But, beware! When Laurier said that. Canada was a nation he was looking for our wider autonomy as well as for the greatest prosperity and highest reputation for our country, which were assured by his policy, whereas the imperialists, now as ever before, disguised under several names, will impose on us solely the obligations and responsibilities of a nation. When we demand onr autonomy and liberty, they hurl at us the word "colonials."
The title of nation which is conferred upon Canada at. a time when our country is driven into the whirlpool of future wars is but a fallacious one. Canada is verily that "unfortunate guest," mourned by the poet, and it will act wisely in exercising fear and caution while sitting at the banquet of nations.
Let us make clear the meaning of the expression: Canada is a nation. During the fifteen years- of the Laurier Administration, Canada progressed in .accordance with the natural law governing the evolution of nations, while the general tenor of its constitution remained unchanged.
In other words, the country has kept abreast of the times. During that memorable period; the conditions in trade, commerce,_ agriculture, means of transportation have liept evolving; the needs and aspirations of each class in particular and of all classes in general, have been modified, but the armature of the Canadian constitution has not varied.
Our legislation hi every sphere, social, fiscal and administrative has followed a rapid drift towards progress and has trans-

Such are 'the principles which should prevail in this country and such are the underlying principles' of the Liberal programme.	[DOT]

The President of the Council, who is more prone to defend profiteers than to defend himself personally, has shown more grit in defending a profiteering company than he did last year when the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) made precise accusations against him.
The hon. member (Mr. Archambault) must think that there is only one passage of Scripture with which I am familiar, and that I am determined to practice it under all circumstances and conditions, that is: " Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." I would remind my hon. friend that there is another passage which I think he should not overlook: "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again."

wide increase in prices, growing inevitably out of the war, is attributable to the Government of the day. Statements of that kind only tend to inflame popular feeling, to create unrest and distrust of all forms of Government, and to feed the Bolshevik sentiment in the country. Hon. members should appreciate the importance of a sense of responsibility in dealing with matters of this kind. As I pointed out last session, we had the Canada Food Board und'er the administration of the ex-Minister of Agriculture. I desire to repeat that I have the highest respect for the ability, the earnestness and the sincerity of the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) in the performance of his public duties; and I believe that in that important and responsible post he did everything which he considered could properly be done in the interests of the country to meet the situation in regard to food distribution and food prices in Canada. In addition -to that, there wajs the work of the Cost of Living Commissioner in the Department of Labour. Last session we had a committee appointed on the cost of living with my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) as chairman, 'and we can still almost hear the echoes of the debate in this House on their report. Yet, with a knowledge of that report, and /with the sound of that debate still ringing in our ears, the member for Ohambly and Vercheres censures this Government for not having taken more vigorous action. When -the report was brought in recommending the creation of -a board with full jurisdiction to deal with the situation, what was Hie attitude on the other side? They moved that it be referred hack for further consideration. The Minister of the Interior pointed out that it would mean delay and the killing of the report for the session, and it was because of the strong stand of the Government and its supporters on this side, that the report went through, that the necessary legislation was introduced -and passed and the board duly constituted which is now in active operation. Judge not by professions but by deeds. Who were the friends of the profiteers last session when the question was under discussion in the House, those who urged action or those who urged delay?
Now, any hon. friend referred to Mr. W.
F. O'Connor, a member of the board, and said that he had been appointed after having been dismissed from his former position because he had made a report on the packing business, and after having
Cllr. Rowell.]
been-I am not sure whether he used the expression, but he conveyed the idea- thoroughly spanked for his public service; and that he would therefore be careful in his present position. I want to say to my hon. friend that Mr. O'Connor did not resign by reason of any report he had made. My -hon. friends on -the other side must know that his resignatiofi occurred a year or more -after he had made the report to which the 'hon. member referred. One cannot but express surprise, and- profound surprise, that Mr. O'Oonnor, so long -as he was making reports which my hon. friends thought they could use to advantage in an endeavour to discredit the Government, was an angel of light and a veritable Daniel come to judgment, but when he takes a public position and is administering the law -and seeking to keep the profileers within bounds, hon, gentlemen opposite have not words of condemnation strong enough for him. I appeal to the members on both sides; I appeal to their sense of justice and of fair play. Is it fair to Mr. O'Connor; is it fair to the Board of Commerce; is it fair to the public interests of the country, for hon. members to take such a position on the floor of Parliament? The Government has been criticised and blamed for its delay in the appointment of the commissioners. As a member of the Government I cheerfully take my full share of responsibility for that delay. The Government sincerely desired to secure the appointment on that board of the very best men in Canada, not only because of their ability, but because of the confidence which the public would have in them. The very first time the matter came up for consideration the Government concluded that Judge Kobson of Winnipeg, if he could be secured as Chairman, would be the best man in Canada for the position, and accordingly we took means to secure him. It took over a month to do so, but the Board is not a thing of a day or a week, even of a month or a year; and I think that the Government could not have done better than to secure a man of such great ability, such high integrity, such splendid capacity for public service as Judge Robson. Hon. gentlemen opposite will not make friends with the public-spirited people of the country, particularly with the people of Western Canada where Judge Robson is so well known, by suggesting that the Board is mere camouflage and is- not sincerely prosecuting its work. It -is not a breach of confidence to say that Judge Robson, for the opportunity of rendering to the people

of Canada the great public service which he believed he could render on this Board surrendered a lucrative position in which his salary was many thousands of dollars more than the remuneration he now receives from the people. In these two men, Judge Robson and Mr. O'Oonnor, devoted to the public interest and sincerely anxious to meet the situation, the Government has the nucleus of a Board which I am confident will go down in history as one of the best bodies any Government has constituted, one which in the end will render a great public service. 1 am sure that when the permanent appointment of the third member of the Board is made it will meet with the same public approval as those already made. Why, Canada is ahead of both Great Britain and the United States in the practical steps it has taken in providing machinery to reach the best possible solution of the problem of high prices so far as the prevention of profiteering is concerned. I need not dwell on that matter any longer, because it shows the position of the Government in regard to this very important question.
Now I desire to come to the second question. I think I have sufficiently answered the first. I have never defended a profiteer, and if it were possible I should like to see a situation in which all profits made'by men during the war-the amounts by which they increased their wealth over the wealth they possessed before the war

were turned into the public treasury, as a contribution on their part, not commensurate with but bearing a relation to, the contribution made by the men who offered their lives for their country.
I never defended a profiteer and I am not going to discuss the question of the bacon business. I have discussed in this House the position of Sir Joseph Flavelle as Chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board. I have not one word to withdraw in the statement I made in reference to Sir Joseph Flavelle. I believe that the people of Canada will some day recognize the wonderful service he rendered to the country during the war as Chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board. It may be unpopular for a public man to recognize the distinguished services of a fellow-citizen. But the public man who is afraid because of some cheap criticism of doing justice to a man who has rendered such great service to the country would be unworthy to occupy a seat in this House. 1 stand here prepared to say that I will not withdraw one word from what I have said with regard to the magnificent service he rendered to Canada at that time.
The statement was that I was more concerned with defending profiteers than with defending myself from the specific charges of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy). That hon. member is not in his place in the House. If it had not been that my hon. friend from Chambly and Yercheres 'brought this matter up this afternoon I would not have discussed it without sending notice to the hon. member for Russell in order that he might be in his place when I came to deal with the matter.
It has been said in the press that I was in the House or at least in this building on the night in March, 1917, when the member for Russell made his attack. I think Le Devoir and some of the other papers reported that T was around the House that night but kept out of the Chamber. I regret to say I was at home in bed that night under the doctor's orders. There is a custom which has become an honourable tradition of this House, that when one member desires to rise in his place and make an attack upon the position or character of another, he gives that hon. member due notice.
I received no notice. I was in the House in the afternoon, and notwithstanding my indisposition, if I had received any notice. I would have come back that night. I would have been in my place in the House and I should have promptly answered the false statements of the hon. member for Russell.
I got no notice. The debate closed that night. Next day I spoke to the Speaker and asked him,: "Is there any way by which I can make a reply to the statements of the hon. member for Russell?" The Speaker replied: "The rules of the House are clear; the debate having been closed, it would not be possible for you, during this session to deal with the subject matter of the debate in any other debate or discussion." The hon. Speaker told me that I could not deal with the matter during that session of the House. Of course, I could have risen to a question of privilege and made certain specific denials, but I could not have discussed the statements made by the hon. member for Russell on that occasion. If my colleagues in the House had not permitted the debate to close that night I could have replied. The reason they gave for not adjourning the debate, a 'reason which seemed to them good, and probably was good, was that in view of the inflammatory character of the speech of the hon. member for Russell, if the debate had been adjourned and the House had entered

upon the discussion of such inflammable matters as had been presented to the House by the hon. member for Russell, we should have had perhaps a week or more of heated debate and discussion involving .religious and racial matters at, a time when the Government was putting forth every effort to compose the feeling in the province of Quebec in order that the military service law might be enforced and that men should be secured to reinforce the battalions at the front. In view of the necessity of securing men to support our battalions at the front, I accepted that view of the situation and for over a year and a half these false accusations were carried from one end of this country to the other without my dealing with them. My only reason was a concern for the public interest and the desire to do the right thing and not stir up the racial and religious controversies which might have resulted from my answering the statements of the hon. member for Russell.
So soon as hostilities ceased I did take the opportunity in^my own riding, where these same stories were being circulated, of making an answer to the statements made by the hon. member for Russell, and other members of the House. I delivered an address in my riding at Bowmanville in which I dealt with these matters. I had hoped that the matter might end there, that in the public life of this country men would have a sufficient sense of decency and fair play, when they had received the generous treatment that had been accorded to them by not characterizing these false accusations as they deserved to be characterized, to let the matter drop. But that is not the case. These matters have been brought up again to-day and therefore I feel called upon to deal with them.
I shall not attempt this afternoon to go through in detail the lengthy address of the hon. member for Russell but I shall take up the salient features of it and deal with them. Let me quote, Hansard 1918, nave 40:	6
Now, Sir, what happened when the hon. gentleman entered the provincial field of politics'? With his usual .presence of mind he arranged with his friends to form a committee for the purpose of raising a fund to guarantee him against any loss while engaged in his work as provincial leader. Mr. A. E. Ames, of Toronto, was Chairman of the committee, and in addition to Sir Joseph Flavelie, the contributors included several other Toronto gentlemen. The fund itself was called the " Secretarial Fund " and I am informed that it varied in amount from $9,000 to $11,000 a year.
I ask any hon. .member of this House: What inference, what impression, did the hon. member for Russell desire to convey [Mr. Rowell. 1
by that statement? There could only be one impression, the impression that hon. members of this House did draw-for many of them spoke to me afterwards about it- namely that if I was to be leader of the Liberal party I stipulated that a fund should be raised out of which I should be compensated for my loss of time in serving the country as leader. The impression conveyed was that I was receiving possibly as much as $9,000 or $10,000 per year. Let me give you the facts. There was no salary paid out of the public treasury to the leader of the Opposition in Ontario at that time as there is a salary paid to the leader of the Opposition, I am glad to say, in this House and as:	there is a salary
paid to the leader of the Opposition now in the province of Ontario. There was no salary at that time. I believe that my immediate predecessors in the-Liberal leadership in Ontario had received as salary a modest sum subscribed by party friends. I make absolutely no criticism of that. I think a salary should be paid, but I think it is much wiser that it should be' paid by the country. I think the position of leader of the Opposition is so important that there should be a salary attached to it.
I am glad that the leader of the Opposition in this House draws a salary, and that it is now provided in Ontario that the leader of the Opposition shall draw salary. A delegation of Liberal members waited upon me and asked me to accept the position of leader of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario. I am sorry that I have to go into these matters of domestic political history in Ontario. I should riot have done so if they had not been spread upon Hansard by the hon. member for Russell and brought up again to-day by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres. Mr. Bowman, the then Liberal whip, was at the head of the delegation, and he said to me: " Mr. Rowell, we present to you the unanimous request of the Liberals in the legislature and of the Liberal convention "-which had been held-" that you consent to 'become leader of the provincial Liberal party. I am authorized to guarantee you a salary of $5,000 per year, because we know the acceptance of the leadership will mean a substantial loss in income from the practice of your profession." What was my reply to Mr. Bowman? I mention this, not to reflect credit upon myself, but simply to give the facts and to show how grossly unfair and untrue were the statements made by the member for Russell. I said: " Mr. Bowman, no; if I accept the leadership it must

be without any salary attached "-because I was determined that I would be independent even of the contributors of the Liberal party to such a fund.
I refused the offer of $5,000 per year. I held the position of leader of the Liberal party in Ontario from the 31st of October, 1911, till the 11th October, 1917. During that whole period not one cent of compensation was paid me, by the Liberal party or by any person whomsoever, in respect of my services as leader of that party. A man engaged in the practice of his profession, with good practice as I had-and members will pardon me for referring again to these personal matters-could not give the time required for the discharge of the duties of leader without serious financial loss. When I resigned the position of leader of the Liberal party in Ontario, in October, 1917, I had served the party and the country at a loss of many thousands of dollars per annum during the whole period.

It is no harm to say that the federal Liberal members from Ontario, or some of them at least, were not anxious to be identified with that policy. Did he then rise in his place as an hon. gentleman and withdraw the statements? You sat through the session and you know that there was no withdrawal; and despite his knowledge that they were untrue, either he, or those associated with him, or the Liberal information bureau-I do not know which-had his speech printed and distributed throughout Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, containing those statements that he knew to be false. Is that what a public man has a right to expect from even his bitterest opponents on the other side of

the House? Surely public life in this country has come to a sorry pass when men for the sake of impairing or destroying the influence of their political opponents will print and distribute broadcast through the country statements which they know to be untrue reflecting upon the character of an opponent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me deal with another point. The hon. gentleman said this was a fund raised for the purpose of supplanting Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I have stated the object for which it was raised. One might say with some sense of truth, that it was raised to prevent embarrassment to Sir Wilfrid. The provincial Liberal party had no desire to embarrass the federal Liberal party if the latter did not wish to identify themselves with the policy to which I have alluded; they would work through their own organization, we through ours, acting in co-operation as much as possible. The hon. gentleman then goes on to add, and let me quote his own words:
The hon. gentleman engaged for several years in a conspiracy to supplant Sir Wilfrid Laurier as leader of the Liberal party.
Well, if it is possible to have one statement falser than another, this is such a one. It is even more false than the statement that I stipulated a fund should be raised to pay me as leader of the Liberal party when I accepted the position. Here again, if the hon. member for West Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee) were in his seat, he would say to this House-there are hon. members opposite who know what I state to be true -that throughout the whole course of the negotiations for Union Government, from the time they started until they closed, I kept in close touch with him as Chief Whip of the Liberal party, and he had knowledge of the proceedings from beginning to end. I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his place at present to tell the House so. Some day the story will be told, some day the record will be produced, some day the correspondence will be brought down, and I think I can perhaps leave any further consideration of the matter until that time comes. Having shown you the falsity of some of the statements, you will appreciate how false the others are.
I have only this one thing to add: no one can regret more than I that the old and honoured leader of the Liberal party, the late Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, is not in his place in this House, so that he too could give his denial to the statement in question. Some day, I repeat, the correspondence will be brought down, but I

might quote one sentence from a letter which Sir Wilfrid wrote me shortly after I joined the Union Government:
I may frankly add that I have too much respect for your convictions to allow an action which I cannot approve to interfere with our old personal relations.
We honestly differed on a great matter of public policy, but Sir Wilfrid recognized my right, just as he recognized the right of the hon. member for West Lambton and other Liberals in the country, to take a different view. I never questioned his sincerity in the course he took, and I am perfectly sure he never questioned mine. What was the situation, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal party faced at that time? They faced just the situation that was faced in the year 1864 at the time the coalition government was formed to carry out Confederation.
At that time, it will be recalled, Hon. George Brown was an ardent advocate of Confederation. His illustrious colleague in the province of Quebec, Mr. Dorion, did not believe in Confederation under the conditions which -George Brown supported. An offer came from Sir John Macdonald to form a coalition government in order to carry out Confederation. The Liberal party in Ontario in those days [DOT] faced exactly the situation which ithe Liberal party faced in 1917. George Brown was asked to join with Sir John Macdonald to make Confederation possible, but to do so he had to separate himself from his old associates in the province of Quebec who wtere opposed to the policy of Confederation. If the course suggested by my hon. friend be the right one, that we should stand by our party through thick and thin, George Brown, for the sake of preserving party unity and continued harmony with his colleagues in the province of Quebec, would have said to Sir John Macdonald: "No, I will not join you in order to promote Confederation. We are going to put party unity before national interest." Was that the position of George Brown, of Oliver Mowat, and of the other Liberals of that day? No. They said: " National interests first. Canadian Confederation is vastly more important than maintaining the unity of the Liberal party." And there is no brighter page in the history of Liberalism than the magnificent stand of George Brown and his colleagues in associating themselves with their old bitter personal opponent, Sir John Macdonald-a bitterness so intense that Brown and he did not speak to each other-in order that the provinces might be brought together in a

confederation which would make possible the development of a great new nation on this half of the North American continent. But for the courage and patriotism of George Brown and his colleagues Confederation would have been impossible at that time.
What was the situation in 1917? Our gallant troops were facing the foe at the front and urgently in need of reinforcements. Every man conversant with the situation knew that the voluntary system could not continue to supply the men needed. The position I took was not a new one, for I had for months urged the Government to adopt compulsory military service. In fact, I urged that in an address which my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) listened to at North Bay, before the Prime Minister brought down any proposal to that effect And I still want to thank my hon. friend for the eulogy he pronounced on me at the banquet that evening even after he heard that statement of mine. In that address I urged th? national necessity of a Union or War Government and of compulsory military service to back up our troops at the front.
I am sorry to have to refer so much to myself, but to prevent misapprehension let me quote the statement I then made in an address delivered at the Canadian, Club in North Bay during the holding of the Northern Ontario Liberal Convention, .at which my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) was present and delivered a very eloquent and able address. I spoke on the war situation and Canada's duty, and in the course of my address I made a statement from which I quote the following sentences:
Let us frankly admit that we cannot reinforce our men at the front by the existing voluntary measures. We must either use the Militia Act or adopt other measures no less effective to meet the situation. Surely after nearly three years of war the time has come . for us to realize that this issue is vastly bigger than any party or all parties combined. What matters it if parties fall so long as Canada and liberty live, and the great democracies triumph in their struggle against autocracy? Do you see any prospect of our being able to do in Canada what none of the Dominions or our Allies have so far been able to do, namely, to adequately meet the situation with a purely party government, and to administer the grave affairs of the war on a party basis? Do you see any hope of our moving forward as a united nation, exerting our utmost efforts to win the war and grappling courageously with our own domestic problems, unless we also create a war Government? Is not this Canada's present and most urgent need?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
I am not going to say how far back I had been advocating this policy; but whether earlier or later, we were both agreed, anyway.
The issue the country faced was that of reinforcing our men at 'the front. The Prime Minister stated that we could not secure the necessary men by the voluntary method. My knowledge of the need of men at the front and of the recruiting situation convinced me that that statement was absolutely right. I know my hon. friends may criticise the manner in which recruiting was carried on; I did so myself .in the different provinces; but criticism of recruiting methods in the past would not get the necessary men for the future, anti however much I might differ from the policy the Government had pursued in the matter of recruiting, I recognized, as every other Canadian citizen must have recognized, that vastly more important than party differences was the question of adequate reinforcements.
There was an acute difference of opinion in the Liberal party on this issue. The great majority of the English-speaking Liberals in the House-in fact, all the English-speaking Liberals west of the Ottawa river with a few exceptions-were in favour of the policy of compulsory military service. The Liberals from the province of Quebec took the other view-and they were absolutely entitled to take it; I am not here at this time offering criticism of their action in that respect. That was the issue, cutting as deep into our national life and as important for Canada's future-in fact, more important-than the issue of Confederation. It went to the very basis of Canada's continued war effort, and Canada's continued war effort was of great importance to the success of the Allies in the fateful struggle which then hung in the balance. The Liberal party had to face this issue.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
That was the issue
facing the people, and the Liberal party had to decide what the first consideration should be, the supreme national issue of the reinforcement of our troops at the front and Canada's continued and whole-hearted participation in the war, or the question of continued party unity.
I	had an opportunity of visiting the front in 1916; the member for Russell makes reference to that occasion. I am son*y that he did not have the opportunity of visiting the front; I am sure that had he been there he would have been more active in recruiting throughout Canada than he was. But I had the opportunity of visiting the front and of talking with many soldiers there; and I shall never forget the inspiration that came to me from talking to these gallant men. They did not think of themselves, their own lives, or their own future. I asked man after man, " What can I do for you when I return to Canada?" Did they

say, " Get me home?" Not a man. They said, "Send us reinforcements." Almost all our regiments were then under strength, reinforcements were urgently needed. They wanted men to back them up so that when they fell carrying the flag in the face of the enemy, other gallant Canadians would be there to pick up that flag and carry it on to Victory. The last man who said that to me was the man who drove me down to Boulogne to take the train to Paris-a French Canadian from the county of Essex.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: No cheers from the Government side now.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
Why didn't you cheer
on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
There were no finer
troops in the Canadian forces than the French Canadians who went from the province of Quebec; there were no finer troops in the Canadian forces than the French Canadians who went from Ontario. I had the opportunity of seeing them in 1916 and in 1918. I had the opportunity Of going into the line of the Twenty-second battalion on the 30th of June, 1918, when they were holding the section of the front before Arras, and the one thing heard from all quarters was a magnificent tribute to the courage and patriotism of these men, their brilliant fighting qualities as soldiers and their great achievements. Those with whom I came in contact in 1916 said, " Send us reinforcements " and " Take good care of our wounded comrades who have gone home." I can imagine nothing finer than that spirit and attitude on the part of our soldiers. One promise I made was that to the limit of my ability I would help to secure reinforcements to back them up. And when the issue was raised in Canada, the Liberal party had to face it. The question was whether a man should stand by the men overseas and the cause for which they were fighting, or for the unity of his party. Others could do as they saw fit, for me there was only one course open; I determined to -stand by the men at the front. So long as I advocated national government and -compulsory military -service and the then Administration, the Borden Government, did not advocate them, there was very little criticism of my course; it was embarrassing [DOT] the Government for me to advocate a national Government and compulsory military service. There was absolutely no public criticism, although one or two expressed the view privately that I

was going a little too far. Generally speaking, however, there was no criticism. But when the test came whether I should stand by my convictions and by the policies which I had advocated and the Government now proposed, and whether I should help the. Government put those policies into effect, I had to choose between being true to what I believed to be right and in the country's interest, and forsaking principle and the country's interest by standing for party unity. I made my choice, and by that choice I stand; I have no regrets for what I did. Attacks may be strong and vene-mous, but any sacrifice a public man might be called upon to make is simply as dust in the balance compared with the services rendered and sacrifices made by the men who went overseas. Therefore I count as nothing the service I was able to render when it is compared with the service our soldiers rendered in this struggle.
The members of the Liberal party faced the issue; should they accept the views of their confreres in Quebec and oppose compulsory [DOT]military service, or should they do what they believed to be right and in the national interest to help win the war, join with Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues, just as George Brown joined Sir John A. Macdonald, and form a coalition or national Government to carry out a law of compulsory military service? Certain members of the party chose as George Brown did. To-day Quebec rejoices in the decision that George Brown made; to-day Quebec recognizes that George Brown was right and that Dorion and their own leaders were wrong; to-day Quebfec realizes that the right and patriotic thing was done by George Brown in bringing about Confederation. And inside of fifty years Quebec will recognize that the Liberals who helped to form Union Government and to put compulsory military service into force did the right thing; they took the course that served the highest national interest. George Brown and his colleagues, by their courage and patriotism, made Confederation possible; the Liberals from one end of Canada to the other who, for the sake of the national interest in time of war, forgot party feeling and party prejudice and joined in helping to form and support a Union Government, saved Confederation and made possible the glorious and triumphant achievements of our troops in 1918.
Now, let me come to the last of the important matters mentioned by the member for Russell. It has been proclaimed from one end of Canada to the other, by the press
and from the platform, that in an address which I delivered at North Bay I publicly slandered the Roman Catholic Church. Now, I recognize that one cannot discuss such a question without subjecting himself to the danger of being misunderstood, of having his motives misinterpreted, and partisan feeling and prejudice raised against him. I shall, however, attempt to discuss the question this afternoon as free from any feeling as possible; I discuss it only because of the attacks which have been made and continued throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that every man's religion is entitled to respect. A man is doing no service to himself, to his country or to' his party who seeks to belittle the religious_ convictions of any other class in the community, no matter how much he may differ from them in that respect. So that in whatever I said-and I shall come to that-nothing would be further from my thought than to. belittle the religious views or convictions of any class of the community.
Far be it from me to do that, for I had no better friends in the world than my Roman Catholic friends in my province, men who. had been not only my friends but my strong supporters.
Let me briefly review the situation in reference to this now famous North Bay address which has received much more prominence than the first one, although I think the first one was more important in its statement of policies than the. second. Unfortunately, I have no stenographic report of the address delivered at North Bay and I, therefore, read from the Globe report on that occasion. I cannot profess to say whether it is an exactly accurate report or not, but I take it as setting forth substantially the general views I presented at that meeting. It was delivered at North Bay on December 6, 1917:
" When I last visited North Bay, in the early part of the month of May, I spoke to you on the issues of the war, and urged, in view of the critical situation which faced us, that the time had come for compulsory military service, and the formation of a Union or National Government, and that without these Canada could not throw her whole energies into the war. At that time Sir Robert Borden had not proposed either. My presence here as a member of the Government is an evidence that I believed ,u the policies I was advocating. But there are further and other reasons why I am a member of the Union Government.
The vote on the Military Service Bill disclosed what Mr. Bourassa had continuously asserted, that Quebec's attitude towards the war was different from that of the other provinces, for while the members from the other

provinces by an overwhelming majority were in favour of the Military Service Act, members from the province of Quebec were almost a unit against it.
May I say here that it has been charged that I not only slandered the Roman Catholic church but the French Canadian race. No man can point, I challenge any man to point, to any address of mine or any statement that I have made that belittles the position of the French Canadian people of this country. I have too gret t a respect for them, for their history and traditions, and their place in Canadian Confederation to utter any such words. But that does not prevent me from differing from them, if I find myself compelled to differ on conscientious grounds, nor of stating my views on an important national issue.
The attitude of the province of Quebec is not due to any lack of courage or any other fine soldierly qualities on the part of her citizens, for no Canadian troops have fought more brilliantly or successfully than the gallant 22nd Battalion from the province of Quebec.
That is what I said in this North Bay speech which has been so denounced as an attack on the province of Quebec.

speechtext: Is that all?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
No, there is more.
What those soldiers have accomplished overseas shows what might have been done had Quebec joined with the other provinces in whole-hearted support of Canada's effort in th-. war. The fine manner in which the French-Canadians of this district-
That is the North Bay district. I was speaking to an audience composed of both English and French Canadians.
-responded to the call to the colours is the best evidence of their willingness to share the burdefis and responsibilities of this war, if the facts are fairly put before them. '
I then believed, as I believe to-day, that if the facts had been fairly and squarely put	before our	fellow	citizens ofthe	province of	Quebec, and had
they realized the magnitude of the issues in this war, they would have just as promptly and cheerfully responded by the thousand as did the English-speaking Canadians. That is my firm conviction.
The present attitude of the province of Quebec may be due to several causes. Undoubtedly the persistent agitation carried on by Mr. Bou-rassa and his Nationalist associates against Great Britain and France and Canada's participation in the war has most powerfully influenced the feeling and attitude of the province of Quebec.
Does any hon. member opposite challenge that statement? I have never seen it chal-

lenged; I believe it to be absolutely true, and I believe it will not be challenged by any responsible person, either English or French Canadian.
And apparently the majority of the cures throughout the province shared his Nationalist, clerical and reactionary attitude.
I have never seen that statement publicly challenged, and I do not think it can be successfully challenged. Do any of my hon. friends opposite challenge it? My hon. friends know that Mr. Bourassa's paper circulates widely .amongst the cures and clergy of the province of Quebec and that the cures and clergy throughout that province are largely supporters of Mr. Bourassa. As regards this statement, the only criticism I have heard is that I did not make it broad enough; that I would have been nearer the exact truth if I had stated "almost all the cures and lesser clergy". Now I come to the point particularly emphasized by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) :
In this attitude they were undoubtedly encouraged and abetted by the members of the religious orders from France, who found an asylum in Canada and used that asylum to undermine Canada's strength in the struggle. It is a misfortune that they did not follow the example of the priests of the Catholic church in France-
I am accused of belittling the work of the priests; I am magnifying the work of the priests.
-who threw themselves into the' struggle of their people to preserve their national existence, and by their courage and sacrifice, won for themselves a new place in the hearts and affections of the French people.
That tribute I paid to the priests of the Roman Catholic church in France, I desire to repeat. Every man who knows the conditions in France, knows that the part the priests of France took in this struggle in France has greatly increased the power and influence of the church in France, because the French people have realized that the church stood with them in the hour of their country's need. The cures and priests went into the trenches with them, fought with them side by side, shared their perils and their triumphs on the field of battle. No one can speak disparagingly of the work of those men at- that time.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend simply anticipates the point I am coining to. At

the time I spoke at North Bay I was not aware that the French law of compulsory military service covered members of the French-speaking clergy of military age who had come to Canada, and who remained citizens of France; that they were obligated by this law to return to France for military service; and that those who were physically fit, and were not exempted temporarily or otherwise, did return to France when called by their Government to do so. As I did not know this, I could not specially refer to their service, but my attitude to all who went forth to fight was clearly shown by my reference to the clergy of France. if I had known of the position of these members of the French clergy, I should have paid a tribute to them, but I also should have pointed out how privileged were the clergy under our law of compulsory military service, as compared with that of France, and that this imposed an additional obligation npon them to respond to the call of Canada, and to oppose, and not to support Mr. Bourassa in his attitude toward Canada's participation in the war, an obligation to do all in their power to aid in the prosecution of the war for human freedom, and to support, and not to oppose, our military service law, as the great majority of them were doing. Again I repeat, my references at North Bay were not to the men who had gone forth to fight, but to the men who stayed >at home, men who were in the province of Quebec during the [DOT]war supporting Mr. Bourassa. Had I known that the law of military service had applied to those men and that they had gone forth to fight, I should have paid a tribute to them with greater cheerfulness than I paid the tribute to the French clergy in France.
I regret that the magnificent service of those gallant men who left Canada and went overseas to fight for the cause of liberty in which we were all interested was not emulated by others. I do not question * the figures set out by the hon. gentleman in his speech, as illustrating the part which those men took in the struggle, and I say I regret that their splendid example was not used by him and more of his associates to appeal to others of their own religion, to inspire them to similar service. I have no hesitation in saying that if the general expression I used hurt the feelings of any in that I did not recognize the fine service of the men of whom I did not know, I would be the first to withdraw any such suggestion. I recognize the service they rendered. But when my friends say that I
have attacked the Roman Catholic Church, I say there is no foundation whatever for that statement. Taking the preaching and teaching clergy together, every one knows that the great majority of them were opposed to the law of compulsory military service in the province of Quebec. I do not question their right to be opposed to it, any more than I question the right of the Protestant clergy in Ontario or the Roman Catholic clergy in that province to support it. Indeed, there was no finer supporter of compulsory military service in Ontario than the Roman Catholic Bishop of London, and I did not hesitate upon the platform through the campaign to pay tribute to the splendid service he was rendering Canada. As I say, I do not question the right of the Catholic clergy. I differed from their view on the issue and I set out the issue on that Oocasion fairly, as I believed it to be. May I read to the House my statement as reported in the Globe. Some of my friends on the Government side may not like this statement, but I will repeat it as I said it on that occasion:
As Liberals we have claimed that the surrender in the year 1911 of the Conservative Party in the province of Quebec to this Nationalist-Clerical influence was a grave national blunder, from which we have suffered through the whole period of the war. But the surrender of the Liberal party to-day in the province of Quebec to this same influence, when Canada is at war struggling for her existence is a national calamity, from the baneful consequences of which Canada may suffer for generations and the only hope of averting the .full measure of the calamity is to decisively defeat the effort now being put forth by these influences to dominate the political life of Canada and take Canada out of the war.	*
If Sir Wilfrid Laurier had been twenty years younger I believe he would have fought this sinister influence in the province of Quebec, just as lie did in 1896, and would have triumphed over it.
I was opposed to the Nationalist propaganda in 1911 when Canada was at peace. I am doubly opposed to it to-day, when Canada is at war. The Liberals of Ontario were united in opposition to this Nationalist propaganda in 1911; they should be doubly united in opposing it to-day.
When Sir Wilfrid Laurier announced his policy of a referendum Bourassa endorsed it, and gave as a reason for endorsation that it was his policy which he had already advocated. A Nationalist policy is no more palatable to us, even if covered with a Liberal veneer, but it is vastly more dangerous, because, thus disguised, it may secure the support of thousands of honest, sincere, public-spirited Liberals throughout Canada who would repudiate it and fight it to the end if it were naked and undisguised nationalism.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the House to read the rest of my North Bay address, but I shall read the closing paragraph:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY.
speechtext: They feel that they rendered Canada a service in the most critical period in. the country's history, and I venture one more prediction, Mr. Speaker. When the history of this period comes to be written, the noblest chapter in the annals of the Liberal party throughout this time will be the fact that in the face of a grave national crisis they put the country's interests before those of their party; they stood for Canada, they stood for the cause for which Canada was fighting, for the gallant men overseas who were pouring out their life's blood to preserve our homes and liberties and the liberties of all mankind. They helped to save Confederation and they made their contribution to the limit of their ability to help *win ,this war for Canada and democracy.

In the few moments that remain before six o'clock I desire to make a short review of the speech of the hon. minister, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). Whatever may be thought of the acrobatic feats of our hon. friend, no person will contend that he is a man who rushes quickly to conclusions. The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), at the first session of this Parliament, made certain charges and statements against the President of the Privy Council.
Since that - time both hon. gentlemen have faced each other in this House day after day. No reference was made by the. President of the Privy Council to the charges of the hon. member for Russell, while that hon. gentleman was in his seat, and no attempt was made to reply to them. Eighteen months afterwards, when the hon. member for Russell is out of the country, sick, the President of the Privy Council takes advantage of the opportunity, in the closing hours of this debate, to make an attempt to reply to the charges of the hon. member for Russell. I shall leave it to the President of the Privy Council and the member for Russell to settle their own personal quarrel.

What I rose more particularly for was to congratulate the President of the Privy Council upon his change of heart as regards the people of the province of Quebec. Like the hon. gentleman I desire unity throughout this country, and I only wish that he had had at heart, at the time of the election in 1917, the same thoughts that he has expressed to-day. No person took a larger share in organizing the forces of the Union Government party in Ontario during the election of 1917 than did the President of the Privy Council. Indeed, we are told that he had charge of the campaign in Ontario, that he had charge of the advertising. .

In order that my hon.
friend may not be under a misapprehension, I may say that his information is quite inaccurate. I was speaking throughout the country. I had charge neither of the organization nor of the advertising.

My hon. friend will not
deny participation in the organization of those who took charge of the advertising for the Union Government party in Ontario, in the election of 1917? I am sure my hon. friend will not go that far.

that he is preparing for another campaign-he will get down to the' facts presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault), leave out sectionalism, devote his energies to the great problems of the day and try to reduce the high cost of living. You will never reduce the high cost of living by sending out a paid profiteer who, before the war, had a very small salary and who, to-day, we are told, is doing very well under this Union Government-sending out a gentleman like Mr. O'Connor who makes the statement to the farmers of this country that if they put up the price of their milk to what it is worth in the United States he will fine them $1,000 and put them in jail for a year. That is not the way to increase production in this country. That is not the way to reduce the high cost of living. If the President of the Privy Council and his associates will look about them they will find that milch cows are going out of this country by the car load. Why? Because there is an agitation to keep down the price of dairy products in this country. These products are worth more in the United States, and if the farmers cannot sell their products at a reasonable price in their own country the milch cow is going. The people in the cities who are carrying on this campaign through the newspapers are going to pay more for their product than they have been paying. They are the people who are responsible, because of the campaign they are carrying on, for discouraging production throughout the agricultural districts of the country.
