speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hearts of all the members of this House have gone out in sincere sympathy to our 
friend and colleague Sir George Foster, on learning of the very sad and irreparable bereavement that has come to him. I know that this House will feel that it is fitting that it should give some expression of its sympathy. We all realize how utterly inadequate any expression of sympathy must be if looked at as consolation for such a loss as that which our colleague has sustained. But at the same time I feel that the House will agree with me when I say that, in so far as any expression on our part may serve, if not to console, at least to bring to our colleague, in his sorrow the assurance that it is our profound desire, if it were in our power, to offer him consolation, it is fitting that we should tender him that expression.
T't would perhaps not be proper that I should allow myself to say any word in regard to the lady who during so many years has been the helpmeet of our distinguished colleague. Those of us who have
known her

and no doubt all of us havehave learned to admire the estimable lady who went about quietly doing good, interesting herself in so many things that contribute to the uplift of our people and who did not spare herself in the direction of giving aid in the course of the recent war, doing everything within her power to assist those who were engaged in various activities and those who suffered as a result of the war.
Of our colleague himself I do not purpose to say anything. He is the father of this House in years of service here. We have-all come to look upon him with respect, to appreciate his personal qualities and to regard him as in very truth a father to us, the members of this House.
I beg to move, as a tribute of respect to our colleague and of sympathy with him in his great loss, that when this House adjourns this evening it do stand adjourned' until four o'clock to-morrow afternoon, inorder that we, the members of this House, may be permitted to pay the last tribute of respect to the spouse of our colleague and thereby express our sympathy with him, in his irreparable bereavement.

Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Council): Mr. Speaker, the Bill now before the House, the second reading of

Then as hon. members are aware, Mr. Speaker, there are in Canada a very substantial number of men who were residents here when the war broke out, but were either reservists in the Imperial Army, or enlisted in some branch of the Imperial service and went overseas to serve in the army of Great Britain. speechtext:
reciprocal arrangements are feeing worked out whereby the Government of Canada, through the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, will act for the Imperial Government in giving the necessary training or medical treatment to soldiers who formed a part of the British army; and, on the other hand, the British Government through its proper administrative branch, will give corresponding care to soldiers who served in our army and took their discharge in Great Britain.
The same situation exists as between Canada and the United States. A very substantial number of Canadians, residents of the United States, responded to the call and enlisted in the Canadian forces and fought side by side with our men. There are also in Canada a number of Americans by birth who were called up or enlisted in the American army and fought with that army in France and have now returned to settle in the Dominion. Here, again, a reciprocal arrangement has been worked out between the Government of the United States and the Canadian Government whereby Canadians wha fought in our Expeditionary Force, but who are residing in the United States, will be looked after by me proper department of the American Government, we in turn looking after, through the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, American soldiers who are residing in Canada.

That includes residents -before enrolment?
Mr. ROWEiLL: Residents at the time of enrolment, I believe, although under the reciprocal arrangement it would not make much difference, because the expense is to be borne by the country which is responsible for its own soldiers'. In other words, we will be recouped all expenses we are put to in looking after American soldiers in Canada, and the American Government will be recouped all expenses they are put to in looking after Canadian soldiers in the United States; and the same arrangement will apply as between Canada and Great Britain. Negotiations are now under way for a similar reciprocal arrangement between Canada and France, Australia and New Zealand, and it is anticipated that an understanding will be arrived at with those countries. I mention these matters because in this particular it is absolutely necessary that there should be legislative authority to enable the department to enter into and carry out these reciprocal arrangements and to make the necessary expenditures; our existing legislation is not adequate for the purpose.

Before proceeding to review more in detail the general provisions of the Bill and to give the reasons why the legislation is necessary, may I be permitted for a few minutes to draw the attention of the House to the important character of the work that is being carried on by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment? I am sure hon. members will realize that no more important or responsible task can face the Government than that of endeavouring to bring back into civil life at the earliest practical date and with the minimum of industrial or economic disturbance the men who have fought so gallantly in our forces
men drawn from civilian life and who now desire to return to civilian life-and to bring them back under conditions as advantageous to them as possible. I am sure we all agree that it is not only in the interests of the soldiers themselves, but in the interests of Canada as a whole that they should get back into civilian life without delay. It is the desire of an overwhelming mass of the men themselves that they should get back into civilian life at the earliest practical date and form part of the producing forces of the country, because during the period through which we are passing one of the most vital factors in our ability to bear the burdens which the war has imposed upon us is the productive power of the nation.
The work of the department may be divided into four branches. So far as the care of the widows and dependents of the fallen are concerned, they are looked after by the pension law which was passed last session, and which is administered by the Board of Pension Commissioners. While that board is attached to the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, it exercises its own authority and jurisdiction under the legislation passed by this House last session, and the Government has no control over its decisions. But not only must the widows and dependents of our fallen soldiers be cared for, but also those who are wholly or partially disabled by reason of war service, and those who are suffering from wounds or disease likely to involve protracted illillness, or from disease which is incurable. All such are discharged from the army as soon as possible and pass under the care of the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment. The department, therefore, has to provide the necessary hospitals and appropriate treatment to care for men of this class. One of the most important

branches of the work of the department is the vocational training.
In the case of those who come back from the front either wholly or partially disabled through wounds or disease due to or aggravated by service and are prevented from pursuing their pre-war occupations, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment undertakes- to give vocational training to lit them for some other useful occupation.
Another branch of the work relates to securing employment for the soldier who is physically lit. A man who has been discharged from the army desires to secure employment in some useful occupation, but having been away at the front, and there being no opportunity immediately available, he requires the cooperation and assistance of some branch or department of the Government. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment co-operates with the Dominion Labour Bureaux and with such organizations as tne various provincial governments have established in an effort to secure suitable employment for discharged soldiers. In every one of the Dominion Employment Bureaux throughout Canada the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment has an officer whose special duty it is to meet, give information to, and assist all returned soldiers who may go to that office to secure employment for which they are qualified and which they desire to undertake.
In general terms I have now outlined the character of the work carried on by this department. May I indicate a little more in detail what has been accomplished in connection with the different branches of the work?
Take, first, medical treatment. I have referred to the incurable cases or the cases of protracted illness. In all such cases the pay and allowances which the men had been enjoying in the army are continued during the whole period of his illness until his recovery. If he is totally incapacitated from any disease-in the case of insanity there is some special provision as to pay-[DOT] from which he cannot recover and if he is quite incapable of looking after himself, as an insane person would be, he becomes the ward of the nation; the State takes charge of him until his dying day. Provision is made for him and for his dependents. If is is a tubercular case requiring more or less protracted treatment, the State accepts the responsibility of caring for him until he recovers, if possible, or
until he dies, if he is beyond recovery. The pay and allowances continue not only for the man but for his dependents also during the whole period that he is under treatment by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment.
I am sure that the House will be'interested in learning something of the extent, of this medical work. The number of patients receiving treatment in September 1918 was approximately 1,150. The number of patients treated during the week ending September 6, 1919, was 12,230. This shows the great expansion of this branch of the work. The hospitals operated by the Department for general treatment is 19, and the number of general treatment hospitals with which the department has made arrangements for treating patients is 16. The number of tuberculosis sanitoria operated by the department is 11 and the number of tuberculosis sanitoria with which the department has made arrangements for treatment is 12. This makes a total of 58 hospitals or institutions either directly operated by the department or with which the department has made arrangements- for the medical care and treatment of patients under their charge.
In the case of insane patients who need special treatment-that is, special nurses to look after them on account of the violent nature of their trouble-does the Government bear all the expense?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To answer that question I should have to refer to the Order in Council covering the matter. I shall come to that later.
In addition to the provision for the totally incapacitated and for those whose illness is likely to be protracted, the department accepts responsibility for the medical treatment of all those whose illness is due to or aggravated by service; and that obligation continues during the whole life of the ex-soldier. He may undergo treatment and may be cured, so far as cure is possible, and be discharged from the hospital. But if illness occurs one year, five years or ten years thereafter, due to or aggravated by his service in the field, he becomes entitled to be re-admitted to an institution under the charge of the department, and so long as he continues to undergo treatment he is entitled to the pay and allowances which he enjoyed in the army, as well as to free medical care and treatment. Let me make the position clear. The Government has undertaken to provide that every man who has served in the

Canadian forces and who suffers at any period of his life from disease or disability contracted or aggravated by service in the field shall have free medical treatment, and that during the period of his illness, no matter when it occurs, he shall receive the same pay and allowances to provide for himself and family as he would have received had he continued in the army.

Suppose a man is drawing a pension, and that in connection with the injury for which he draws pension some complication arises and he comes back under the care of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment and draws the pay and allowances which pertained to his rank when he left the service, do I understand that he drops his pension during that period ?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In effect, yes, depending on the conditions. Probably the pay and allowances would be in excess of the pension, in which case the pension would be credited on the pay and allowances, and the man would be paid simply the surplus over and above the amount of the pension.
He receives the larger amount in any case?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes,'if the pension is in excess of the pay and allowances, then he receives the pension.
The department has also accepted responsibility for the medical care and treatment of every soldier Who served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, for one year after his discharge, no matter from what cause the illness may ensue. In other words, it is recognized that the men who served overseas and who came back not suffering from any disease or from any physical injury, have in many cases been compelled to undergo such a strain and subject themselves to such hardship that their resisting power to disease is more or less weakened for some period after their return.
So the department accepts full responsibility for medical care and treatment for one year after the discharge of the soldier, but in that case the soldier does not receive pay and allowance; he receives simply free medical treatment.
Will that be made retroactive in cases of those who have not received it in the past?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not remember the date when the Order in Council came into operation or the terms of it, but that is the general law governing the matter at the [-Mr. Rowell.]
present time. I think it came into operation the first of the present year. Whether. it would be retroactive or not would depend upon the terms of the Order in Council. I find the Order in Council was passed on the 24th February, 1919, and it would apply from that date.
W7ould the minister mind reciting the terms of the Order in Council covering that point which he has just explained?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
(Reading):
The question of providing re-treatment for former members of the forces in cases where the disability is not clearly due to service, has. been considered by the department, and the following ruling has been made:-
When any ex-soldier applies for re-treatment, and it is questionable whether his disability is due to, or aggravated by service, the Unit Medical Director should give the ex-soldier the . benefit of the doubt, if in his opinion, the general resistive power of the ex-soldier against disease has been lowered by war service to such a degree that it has induced the disability from which he suffers when he presents himself for re-treatment.
That was the ruling made under the prior Order in Council. Then this Order in Council recites:
That on the return of the member of the forces from overseas, it has been found in many cases that there is a lowered physical resistance, which sometimes results in a disability not directly attributable to war service, but which undoubtedly is indirectly caused thereby. It is considered that this lowered resistance will prevail for some time after the retirement or discharge of the former member of the forces and that the department should be empowered to grant treatment and medicines only, to all former members of the forces who fall i'll during the twelve months following the date of their retirement or discharge, when such treatment or medicine is not caused by a war disability.
The actual clause in the Order in Council concerning the matter is revised, clause (b) of paragraph 1:
Any former member of the forces resident in Canada who, within twelve months after retirement or discharge from the forces or if he has been transferred to the department by the Department of Militia and Defence, or the Department of the Naval Service, for further continuance of treatment, within twelve months of the completion of such treatment requires medical or surgical treatment for a disability which is not due to or aggravated by service, shall be entitled to such medical or surgical treatment, provided that such disability is not due to vice or misconduct on the part of such former member of the forces, and that it shall be competent for a medical officer of the department to decide whether such disability is or is not due to such vice or misconduct; and provided also that the granting of such treatment shall not entitle such former member of the forces to receive pay and allowances from the department, nor shall it be deemed in any way

to entitle him to pension in respect of any disability not due to or aggravated by service.
That answers the question of my hon. friend. In addition to the foregoing, provision has been made for medical treatment by means of outdoor clinics in those centres where there are a sufficient number of discharged soldiers who may require treatment to justify the establishment of those outdoor clinics, and any soldier coming within the provisions of the Order in Council, who is entitled to treatment, may receive treatment readily at those places. If a soldier is too far away so that he cannot attend to receive medical treatment without loss of time, provision is made to pay his expenses and an allowance is given for the time he must spend in attending to receive treatment. The desire of the Government in the matter is that every facility should be provided in order to ensure that every returned soldier shall have the medical attention which he requires, even if his illness be not due to war service, for one year after discharge, if due to or 'aggravated by war service, through the whole period of his life.
The House will appreciate the magnitude of the work which has been carried on. When I point out that the amount paid for the month ending the 31st July in pay and allowances ito ex-soldiers receiving treatment under the conditions I have mentioned, was no less a sum than $413,261. In other words, the Government is paying out, in pay and allowances to ex-soldiers and their dependents who are undergoing treatment in the hospitals under the charge of this department, a sum of approximately $5,000,000 a year. Of course, in the earlier months of the present year the amount was not so large; but owing to rapid demobilization and the bringing over from England of those who -are in the hospitals there, the amounts may be increased during the latter months of the year.

With respect to points that are some three hundred miles away from an established centre-I have in mind Peace River in Alberta, 300 miles away from Edmonton-is there any proposal in the mind of the minister for provision for medical men to render assistance to soldiers so as to prevent a man from having to come in that distance for medical treatment?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must admit that I am not aide at 'the present time to answer my hon. friend's question, but I shall be glad to get the information for him. I do not know just what the provision is in such a oase.

From what the minister states, it seems to me that it is going to be a merging between civil re-establishment and pensions. Last year we passed an Act pioviding for the support of disabled men and dependents. I understand now the same men are going to get under this civil re-establishment or the Orders in Council or the regulations which are being made, some more money and their dependents also are to be taken care of by the State. Where does the parting come in between the two Acts?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The point of severance is this. If a man is undergoing treatment for an illness which is likely to be protracted but which is of such a character that he could receive treatment at home as well as in a hospital under the charge of the department, and if it is probable that his illness will not be cured within a reasonable time, he may be discharged from the hospital and in that case awarded his pension, and he would then be dependent upon his pension for the support of himself and his family. If, however, his condition became such that he required to return to the hospital for treatment, he would then become entitled to be restored to the position of receiving pay and allowances. If his pension were less than- the pay and allowances, it would be credited on account of the pay and allowance, and he would receive simply the additional amount over the pension to make up the amount which he would have received if still in the army.
If his pension is more than the pay and allowances, he would continue to draw his pension and receive treatment in the hospital. That is a case where the work of the Pensions Board and of the department compliment each other.
Mr. BUREAU.: They touch pretty close. The line of severance is not very clear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is pretty close. It has to be worked out in a practical way as best it can be done, in dealing with a more or less difficult situation.
The Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment provides vocational training for any member of the forces, who is so disabled through war service that he cannot carry on his pre-war occupation, so as to fit him for some other useful occupation. During the time he is taking re-training he becomes entitled to the pay and allowances set forth in the Order in Council, which does not differ very materially from the pay and allowances he received while a soldier in the army. Hon. members will

recall that during last session, the question was raised in the House whether special provision should not be made for the young men under eighteen years of age who enlisted and served in our army overseas. They were not liable to be called up under our Militia Act or under our Military Service Act. They were under military age, but they were accepted and served overseas. The Government decided that these boys were entitled to exceptional treatment, and therefore all who enlisted under the age of eighteen years become entitled to the benefits of re-training, or other training in some useful occupation on the same basis as a disabled soldier, with this one qualification, that while the schedule of allowances is the same, if the department on investigation finds that the young man does not need this allowance, if his parents are in a good position and well able to give him the necessary training, the department is empowered not to grant pay and allowances That is the only respect in which the pay and allowances granted to the boys under eighteen differs from the pay and allowances granted to the disabled soldier.
Did the Government consider extending the advantages of the vocational training to a still wider field?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The matter has been considered by the Government, but up to date the Government has not seen its way clear to extend it further, but that is a proper question for the committee which I intend asking the House to appoint to consider. There are the two classes: vocational training for the men wholly or partially disabled from pursuing their pre-war occupation, and for the boys who enlisted under eighteen years of age.
In many cases this vocational training is started before the man leaves the hospital. When a man comes back from England and is in the hospital for treatment, if he is physically fit to commence his retraining, it is commenced in the hospital to the extent of his capacity to undertake it. It has been part of the policy of the Department,-and in that respect- the policy is in entire agreement with the views of the Great War Veterans' Association,-to g'-v? these young men the privilege of taking their retraining as an apprentice in an actual factory or shop, so far as practicable, so that they will learn how to do the work by actually doing it. A substantial number are receiving their training in this way.
The number of men receiving re-lraming on August 31 of the present year was 11,134. 
The total number who had completed their course of training at that time was 5,955. The House will be interested in knowing how far the men who have received their re-training have taken advantage o: it- by engaging in seme useful occupation for which they have been trained. Of the total number who had been trained up to 'list August last 67.94 per cent were employed in the occupations for which they had been trained; 22.26 per cent had sought employment in some other occupation. The total number who have taken their places as civilian wage-earners after re-4 p.m. eeiving restraining was 90.20 per cent. Of the remainder 3.23 per cent were sick, .83 per cent had died, and 5.74 per cent were unemployed, making up the total of 100 per cent of those who had graduated from the institutions under the department up to 31st August. Each graduate is followed up monthly until hh permanent re-establishment in civil life is beyond question. The follow-up is of a double character. The Social Service Branch of the department, to which trained nurses are attached, follows up the man in his home with a view to rendering assistance, so far as it may be required in re-establishing his home. The inspectors oE Industrial Survey also follow -up the man in the factory to see that he ds properly placed and is able to do the work committed to his care.

Can the minister tell us the number of college students whose courses were interrupted by enlisting? I think we should have that information, as an application has been made by the principals of various colleges for assistance to these young men so that they could complete their courses.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know some statistics have been compiled, but I am sorry I have not the figures here. The number would run into some thousands. The question of the students is a most important one and is receiving the consideration of the Government. The hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) presented a strong argument in favour of that proposal, and the hon, member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) presented strong considerations against it. It is a debatable question. We each may have our own views on it, and I think it is a perfectly proper question for the committee to consider and report upon.
Has the minister the figures by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think they would be available, but I am sorry I have not got them here. Personally, I feel, a very deep interest in the position of the student whose education was interrupted, and very strong reasons may be urged in the national interest why he should have the opportunity to complete his course.
The House will be interested in knowing the pay and allowances for the soldiers who are undergoing retraining. While undergoing training the allowances payable to a former member of the forces who is without dependents is $G0 a month. If he has partial dependents such additional allowance may be made as in the opinion of the department may be deemed necessary, provided that the additional allowance paid to or on account.of such partial dependent person or persons shall not exceed $25 per month. If he is a married man he gets $85 per month For one child he gets $10 a month additional, for two children $18, for three children $25; if more than three children, $25 per month, plus $6 a month for each child in excess of three. If he is living at a point where he cannot take this retraining and remain at home, he receives an additional allowance of $8 per month and his wife receives an additional allowance of the same amount. I believe the members of the House will say that the provisions for re-training are an evidence of Canada's determination to do justice to her partially disabled soldiers.
In order that the soldier may not be placed at any disadvantage as compared with the position he occupied in the army, a flat rate allowance is given to take the place of the grant from the Patriotic Fund. The soldier therefore receives practically the same pay and allowances under this department wdiile he is undergoing training as he received when he was serving in the army.
Mr. SfLEARD: I did not quite understand how long the Government pays during that training. For what period is the payment made?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is supposed to be for the period necessary to enable a man to fit himself for some other occupation. It is estimated that that should be done in a period of six months. In some cases it goes beyond that time and in other cases it is less.
Is there a limit of time beyond which it cannot be paid?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, it is in the discretion of the department. If a case appears to
be one in which there should be an extension, the department has power to extend the time. To indicate the magnitude of the operations being carried on by this branch, I would point out that the pay and allowances on account of vocational training for the month ended July 31, amounted to $940,725.
For how many men?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not the exact number. This is not the whole amount the Government is spending in order to fit men, wholly or partially disabled, for resuming their places in the civil life of the country. This amount only covers the payand allowances to the men and their dependents while undergoing training. There is the expense of carrying on the operations in addition.

It would be only fair to point out that there would be a decrease in the payment of pensions to the same extent and that that must be credited against the amount mentioned by the bon. the President of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, if a man is receiving a pension, it is applied on account or suspended as the case may be during retraining. He gets whichever is the larger.
Does that include the expense of carrying on all these operations, paying the officials and so on? And if so, can the minister give us some idea approximately of how much that is per month?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not that information here.

I understand that it is
exceptionally large.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount is large- there is no doubt about that. For all branches we have voted this year approximately $30,000,000. For pay and allowances to men undertaking this retraining, for pay and allowances to men receiving treatment in the hospitals, and for all other expenditures in connection with the work.
On the basis of the minister's statement that would only amount to $5,000,000 a year if the expenditure is $400,000 a month.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: $940,000 a month would be about $10,000,000 a year.

And the other $5,000,000 would make $15,000,000. Surely it does not cost $15,000,000 a year for official and other ex-

penditures to provide for this branch of the service?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; my hon. friend is not correct in his statement, but all this information will be put before the committee when it meets. My recollection is that I gave a good deal of this information at the. last session of the House when the Estimates for this department were under consideration. Had I known that the information would have been asked for to-day I would have been very glad to have secured it.
Another important branch of the work which is being carried on by the department is the assisting to secure employment for soldiers physically fit who have been discharged from the army.. As I explained in opening, the department works in cooperation with the Federal Department of Labour. There are ninety-five free Government employment offices throughout Canada extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and carried on under the Department of Labour in co-operation with the provinces. In every one of these the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment has its representative. The total number discharged from the army since the armistice up to August 31, 1919-that is between the 11th November, 1918, and the 31st August, 1919 -was 316,589. -Of these, 22 peT cent, or 68,673, sought the assistance of the department to put them in touch with employment opportunities, or applied for assistance to secure positions. Of the number who applied for assistance, namely 68,673, 61,278 were placed in positions of a more or less permanent character. In that 61,278 the department has not included those who only remained a few days or changed several times. In addition, before the armistice, some 50,000 men had been placed in positions through the department in co-operation with the labour bureaux and provincial agencies, making a total of 111,278 men assisted by the department in securing employment in useful occupations. The 50,000 forms no part of the 316,000. The remainder of the 316,000 have not sought the assistance of the department to re-establish them in civil life, and it would be fair to assume that they have, largely or almost entirely through their own efforts, secured useful employment and have been absorbed back into the civil life of the country. Hon. members 'will therefore see that, either due to the efforts of the soldiers themselves or due to the co-operation of the labour bureaux and the Department of Soldiers'
fMr. Ross.]
Civil Re-Establishment, the overwhelming majority of the soldiers who have been discharged from the army have secured some useful employment and have been absorbed into civil life.
The House will be interested in hearing how many returned soldiers have secured employment in the Civil Service. According to the figures furnished me by the commission, for the six months ending August 31, 1919, 7,823 submitted themselves for examination for temporary employment; 1,970 submitted themselves for examination for permanent employment, or a total of 9,793. Of those who submitted themselves for examination, 6,277 passed for temporary employment and 758 for permanent employment. Seventy-two per cent were successful.
Successful in passing or in securing appointments?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In passing. During that period the Civil Service Commission appointed to positions in the Civil Service
5.320	returned soldiers. During the same period the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment gave temporary employment, in carrying on the work of the department, to 3,000 soldiers, making a total of 8,320 who secured employment, temporary or permanent, 5,320 in the other branches of the Civil Service, and 3,000 in the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Department.
What percentage would that be of the total number?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The total number of civilian males employed during that period was 867, most of whom were labourers. The House will see, that of 9,187 men appointed to various branches of the public service for the six months ending August 31, 1919,
8.320	were returned soldiers and only 861 civilians, most of whom were appointed as labourers. In addition to the foregoing, large numbers of men who had been in the Civil Service enlisted for service overseas. I understand that approximately 5,000 civil servants enlisted; 477 or thereabouts fell in action or died of disease. Of the remainder every man who was permanently employed and who was capable of resuming his position in the public service has been restored to his position if he cared to have it. So far as my information goes, practically the entire number have been restored to their posts in the service. If you add this number to the new appointments of soldiers to the public service for the period I have mentioned you will see how large a factor the

Government itself has been in restoring to civil life and to positions in the public service the men who served overseas.
Just a word or two with reference to another branch of the service, the Government provides ex-members of the forces who require them on account of disabilities due or aggravated by active service, with new limbs, splints, trusses, artificial eyes, elastic bandages and other orthopaedic or surgical appliances free of charge, and keeps these appliances renewed during the life of the ex-soldier. These are supplied at the expense of the Government, and during the period of fitting or adjustment-that is in the case of a soldier who requires to have an artificial limb or any other artificial appliance fitted-he is taken on the strength and receives the same pay and allowances as if he were undergoing medical treatment, so that every precaution is taken to see that the soldier is properly cared for.
I have already referred to the reciprooal arrangements which have been worked out, or are being worked out, between Canada and the Mother Country and between Canada and the United States. In the case of Canada and the Mother Country, the matter is now before the Government and full details will be announced in the very near future. But I think it will be found, as was announced by the Minister of Pensions in 'the Imperial House of Commons, that the Imperial Government will, as a result of the efforts of the Canadian Department of Soldiers'Civil Re-Establishment, supplement the allowance to the. British soldiers living in Canada by an amount sufficient to bring the pay and allowance granted to them up to the pay and allowances given to our Canadian soldiers who are taking vocational training or are undergoing treatment in our hospitals. I said a moment ago that we bad a reciprocal arrangement with the United States. That is, we look after American soldiers in Canada, provide them with medical treatment and give them vocational training, the American Government paying the expense. On the other band, they agree to do the same for us. But when it comes to the re-education or the vocational training, what is Ithe situation? The Department of the United States Government which looks 'after that branch of their own service and of ours is the Federal Board for Vocational Training. This board examines the ease, and if it 'approves sends it forward for the approval of the department, and if the department is satisfied that it is a proper case for retraining, the man is asked to come to Canada for training. Why? Because thfe provision made in Canada is so much in advance of the provision so far made in the United States that the re-training can be given much more effectively and satisfactorily in Canada.
How is the cost determined as between the two countries?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

This Bill, Mr. Speaker, is necessary in order that the department of the Government concerned may have power when peace comes and the War Measures Act is no longer in operation, to make the necessary regulations to carry on the work which is now being carried on. All we ask to-day is approval of the principle of the Bill, and I am quite sure that all hon. gentlemen are in hearty sympathy with it. When the Bill goes to the committee they will [DOT]consider its provisions and what changes they think should be made, and report back 'to the House their considered judgment on the matter.
The Bill deals with the whole work of the re-establishment of the soldier in civil life, and the committee will be authorized to consider everything relating to this great subject, which is of such vital moment to the ex-soldiers and people of Canada,

The hon minister has stated that reciprocal arrangements are being entered into with Great Britain with regard to the treatment of soldiers. He will remember that last session the Pensions Committee recommended that the pensions of Canadians, who fought in the Imperial army should be augmented by Canada, but we did not deal with the question of gratuities. The fact is that Britishers in this country who went back to Britain and entered the Imperial forces as privates received very small gratuities from the British Government, and I would like to ask the hon. minister if the negotiations he has referred to deal with the question of supplementing those gratuities?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a question upon which I am not able to give my hon. friend [DOT]any information to-day, but I shall be glad to look into it and furnish him with the required information. The House will be interested to know that while last session in our Pension Act we provided for supplementing the Imperial pensions out of the Canadian Exchequer, I believe, when the negotiations are completed and the documents are brought down, we will find that, thanks to the efforts of the Government and tlft Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment, the British Government will itself assume that responsibility.

Will it be a proper subject
to come before this committee?
rMr. Rowell.]

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If it relates to the reestablishment of the soldier in civil life it will. It is for the committee to decide. I would expect, Mr. Speaker, that the committee would act as the Pension Committee did last year-hear whatever representations might be made to it in reference to any matter relating to the re-establishment of the soldier in civil life.
iMr. PETER McGIBBON (Muskoka): The hon. minister will remember that he asked me to remind him of a question I put to him.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The pay and allowances to the insane are provided for by an Order in Council dated September 28, 1918. I will read the provisions so that hon. members will have the information on Hansard, starting with the fourth paragraph:
4. Former members of the forces who are insane may he divided into three classes as follows :
A.	Retired or discharged owing to insanity entirely caused hy service;
B.	Retired or discharged, owing to insanity only partially caused by service; ajid
C.	Retired or discharged owing to insanity not in any way caused by service.
Each of the these classes may be sub-divided as follows:
(1)	With dependents.
(2)	Without dependents.
Class A. Former members of the forces retired or discharged owing to insanity entirely caused 'by service.

Class B. Former members of the forces retired or discharged owing to insanity only partially caused by service, (in this class the word " dependents " shall mean only those proving actually need and dependency).
