speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have received a great deal of information from the hon. minister upon the subject matter of soldiers' civil re-establishment, but it is rather 'to be regretted that we are not dealing with the minister in charge of that
department. We have on several occasions taken up the question that departments of such a character as that with which the hon. minister has just been- dealing should be under the control of a member of the popular branch of this Parliament. It is all very well to get matters second-hand, as we have been getting them this afternoon but I think it is only right and proper that this Chamber should insist that the heads of these departments should be in the popular branch and directly responsible to the people.
It is an extraordinary condition of things if it be true that so much is being done for the returned soldier as has been told us by the President of the Council this afternoon, that every returned soldiers' association from the Atlantic to the Pacific is continually petitioning hon. members, and expressing in every newspaper its dissatisfaction with what is being done by the Government, and protesting 'against the way in which the Government is dealing with the returned soldier.
There is a conflict of opinion somewhere. The speech of the President of the Council this afternoon would appear to leave nothing to be desired so far as the treatment of the returned soldier is concerned. The Great War Veterans' Association and other organizations of a like character all over the country are petitioning this House and petitioning their friends, and expressing in the press and publicly in other ways on frequent occasions, their entire dissatisfaction. If we are to accept the facts and conditions as set forth by the President of the Council there is nothing to be desired, but if we are to accept the testimony of the returned soldier himself as expressed through the agencies which he is enabled to employ, we must come to the conclusion that he is entirely dissatisfied. As a private member of this House I am not in a position to decide between the Government on the one hand and the returned soliders on the other.
On the night of the 7th of July, 1918, just at the close of the last session, some interesting information was communicated to the House by a former officer of high standing in the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment. I have reference to the speech that was made in this House and the correspondence which was put on record by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy), who was at one time Parliamentary Secretary of this department. According to him, he was too conscientious to remain in the department and to draw



a salary where he could get nothing to do and where nothing was being done. That is the testimony of a member of this House who is responsible to a constituency and who was responsible to this House as an official of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. That information, to say the least, did not reflect any credit upon that department; it rather showed that no energy was exercised in dealing with the returned soldier; it demonstrated that the department bad really not shown any anxiety with regard to the question of what was to become of the returned soldier. So far I have heard no answer to the statements made and the explanation given by the member for Colchester, who felt it incumbent upon himself to retire from the office which he held because he was simply receiving money under false pretences and doing nothing along the lines for which he was appointed.
I give this as a supplement to the very eloquent speech of our good friend the President of the Council. I am getting so used to those eloquent speeches and to his practice of painting rosy conditions that I must measure them and ask our members to measure them according to the evidence of such officials as the member for Colchester. That hon. gentleman had first-hand information; he had the experience of being in the department, but our good friend the President of the Council simply has what is handed out to him by the department. If I were hearing evidence as a court-and we are more or less of a court here-I would be obliged to take the first-hand testimony of the member for Colchester in preference to the second-hand case made out by the department on its own behalf and passed over to the able advocate who presents it to this House.
That, then, is the situation-entire dissatisfaction so far as the soldiers are concerned; entire dissatisfaction on the part of an official of the department, a member of this House, who presented his explanations to Parliament. On the other had, we have the glowing account which has been given to us by the President of the Council.
The Bill which we have before us is an amendment to chapter 42 of the Acts of 1918. On the 24th day of May, 1918, the Act creating the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment received the assent of the Governor General and became the law of the land. Since that time the officials of the department have had experience with this

law. They know the powers that were given to them; they know their requirements; they know what they have to deal with. I submit, therefore, that such legislation should be introduced to this House as will embody these requirements. Surely the department should know by this time what powers ought to be vested in them by statute to enable them to conduct properly the affairs of the department. But instead of coming to us to-day with a Bill embodying those requirements and those powers which are necessary to the department in order to enable it properly to carry on its business, which powers and requirements we would be in a position to scrutinize and to approve if we thought them proper, the President of the Council comes to us asking that power be vested in the department to legislate for itself. The people of Canada and this Parliament are tired of that second-hand way of enacting laws. What are we here for if not to draft such legislation as may be necessary to carry on the affairs of the country? There was a reason for very wide latitude in the matter of making law by Order in Council while the war was on. Matters of emergency would suddenly arise for which a statute could not make provision, and it was desirable and proper in the interests of the country that the Governor General should at once provide for such contingencies by Order in Council. But these things are past. The war is over, we are back to ordinary conditions. I repeat that the department should know by this time what powers they require, and that those powers should be incorporated in a statute.
The Act provides simply that the Governor in Council may make recommendations for the control and management of hospitals, workshops, and so on; for the marking and stamping of artificial limbs; to forbid any false statement, suggestion or representation with respect to artificial limbs; for the disposal of any money payable by the Crown to the estates of deceased officers; for prescribing the pay and allowances to persons undergoing medical treatment or vocational training. It provides also that the Governor in Council may make regulations:
" (f) with respect to reciprocal or other arrangements with the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or the Government of any British Dominion or the Government of any of His Majesty's Allies in the late war, or the Government of the United States of America, for the treatment and training and the issue of pay and allowances to ex-members of the forces of any such

Government when undergoing treatment or training, or to their dependents; and,
"(g) with respect to any matter placed under the control and management of the minister:
Those are all very simple matters which could be dealt with by this House and the legislation passed. I understand the department has those powers now in the form of Orders in Council, and if it has, all that the minister would have to do would be to transform his Orders in Council into the shape of a Bill, submit it to the House and have it passed, and we would know once and for all what the powers of the department were. Is it not extraordinary for the minister, in time of peace, to ask us to vest in the Governor in Council, particularly, I may say, in the head of this department, powers to make laws in respect to anything that the Government, in its wisdom or otherwise, may submit to that department, because we are asked to give that department power to make laws with respect to any matter placed under the control and management of the minister? That seems to me an extraordinary latitude that is asked for, and taking it all in all, I am appealing to this House to see to it that our rights are restored, and I trust that hon. gentlemen will realize their responsibility to their constituencies, our duties as a Parliament, and will insist that this House shall deal with any laws that are to be passed in Canada in connection with the protection of our seamen and soldiers on the one hand and the moneys that come out of the pockets of the people on the other, the money too much of which has been extracted out of the pockets of the people of this country and which has been expended to such an extent that the Government tell us that they are at the end of their tether and that if our soldiers require further aid they must look elsewhere for it. That is the position at which we have arrived. Nevertheless, we find this Bill asking us to give further power to this department lavishly to expend money wherever they may get it without submitting the expenditure and the reason for it to this House for approval. It is well known to hon. gentlemen before me on the Government side of the House that it is not in our power on this side to enforce these things; all we can do is to appeal to hon. members to exercise the proper functions of Parliament and to deal with those matters. If they choose to give up those functions and to say: We will simply delegate all our powers to one or two ministers and let them legislate as they see proper; that responsibility rests upon the shoulders of hon. gentlemen supporting the Government, and it is only for us to bring the matter to their notice. Sometimes I see newspapers supporting the Government finding fault with the Opposition for being too easy, and saying that we do not raise enough trouble in the House; that we do not storm the Government sufficiently. Why, Sir, if they are dissatisfied on that point, perhaps it is not too late to level our batteries on the Government now. Of course, it is true that a broadside on the Government would not kill very many, because there are so many vacant seats.
We would lose our shot.

And we would be sorry to annihilate them altogether. But the time has arrived, now that the war is over and the troops which we used to maintain have been demobilized, when it is possibly quite in order for myself and other hon. gentlemen on this side to satisfy the Unionist and the Tory press that we shall not spare in any way whatsoever the backs of the Government, but shall give them every inch that is coming to them.
Lay on, MacDuff.
That will keep us busy.
It's a big order.

I have to-day pointed out some of the things which possibly some people may find fault with us for not having found fault with. Now that we are back to the days of peace, there being no particular rush or hurry about putting legislation through this House, except so as to give it due thought and attention, the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) should be called upon to lay upon the Table for the discussion of hon. gentlemen and in a proper way to bring before the House such legislation along these lines as he may require and to do away with Orders in Council. Those are things regarding which we on this side of the House discharge our responsibility by bringing them to the notice of the Government. The burden is then shifted to the shoulders of hon. gentlemen who are, as a Government and as supporters of a Government, responsible for legislation that may pass in this House.
I should like to say [DOT]something to the minister in charge of this Bill regarding the enormous expense that he has been disclosing to us. Of course we must be and we are sympathetic with the soldiers and we want to do everything we can for them.

As was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in whose remarks in that regard I f'.dly concur, the man who is crippled, or the woman whose bread-winner is taken away, or any person who is in any way dependent upon the public by reason of the war, should receive our full sympathy and support. But there is a vast quantity of loose machinery kept agoing by the Government in connection with the war, and involving an enormous expenditure of money of which the soldiers get very little. We have in the Dominion of Canada splendid hospitals; we have in my little province of Nova Scotia the Victoria General at Halifax; we have a splendid hospital at New Glasgow in the county of Pictou; we have four very excellent hospitals in my county of Cape Breton, all of which are willing and anxious to take hold of this class of work. Private or local arrangements could be made with these hospitals so that any returned soldier would receive the treatment he requires by the local doctors just as effectively as these returned men are being treated under the machinery created by this Government, and the expense would be very much less. I am mentioning Nova Scotia because I am familiar with the excellent doctors in those hospitals, but the same is true of the other provinces. Probably a little over a year ago we had in the city of Halifax the experience of the Victoria General Hospital, which is a provincial institution, offering to provide for all the returned soldiers in that city or thereabouts that might require treatment. Instead, however, of the Government making a simple arrangement with the authorities of that hospital, either one or two-I forget how many altogether -new hospitals were started and completed at an enormous expense and they will be kept going indefinitely at the expense of this country when a simple arrangement could have been made with the local hospital by which the same work could have been done equally well and very much more cheaply. I am reminding the minister of these things so that he may. not only take cognizance of them himself, but bring them to the notice of the Government. I fear that vast machinery of a military character is being kept going throughout Canada which could very well be dispensed with and the same work done by other means in a very much cheaper way. I do not know whether it applies in this case, but representations were made to me last winter that certain 
officials were keeping men in the city of Halifax in connection with the Niobe doing nothing, simply for the purpose of giving the officers an excuse for staying there and drawing large salaries. I brought that matter to the notice of the Government, and the Minister of Militia took cognizance of it and in a very short time the men were disbanded. An expense was saved to the Dominion by dispensing entirely with an institution which had no right to exist and which brought no return to the country for the money expended. I am bringing this matter up simply in order that the Government may carefully inquire whether or not we have an army of officers on the pay list of this country who could be dispensed with, so that every dollar that we can save may be saved. I remember very well in the early days of the war, when extravagance and unnecessary expenditures were brought to the notice of the Government, hearing the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) say that he would begrudge the expenditure of any ten cents that could be avoided. That was in the early days of the war, when we had something to save, but now I am afraid we have reached the stage where recklessness has gone mad and we have nothing to save. Our reputation for saving has gone to the four winds of Heaven, and the Government have evidently come to the conclusion that there is no use trying to regain it. They tell us plainly that they have no money and are at their wits' end to know where to get any. However, they must take courage, be thrifty, and save. They must cut down every possible expenditure, for that is certainly expected of them by the good people of Canada.
The real point I wanted to make in connection with this Bill was that we should insist upon putting in the Act itself whatever powers this department requires. We should not be called upon to grant any more of those loose powers to be vested in the Governor in Council or any particular department. I have read the headlines, the real substance of everything in this Bill, and I find nothing there that requires a committee. I do not know what a committee has to do with the question whether we shall grant those powers to the ministers or the head of this department. It is true that if the minister in charge of this Bill is going to submit the Orders in Council to the committee, there will be some discussion and the committee may be of some assistance To us, but if those Orders in Council are not to be submitted to the committee, if they are

not drafted and we do not know what they are, I do not think the committee will be in any way armed with the facts that will enable them to decide whether those powers should be granted or not. I submit, therefore, that I can see very little to expect from the deliberations of a committee, as far as the facts contained in this Bill are concerned.
It is possible that the committee may travel from this Bill to other subjects, although we were told the other night they would not. We had a hope at one time that the request of the Great War Veterans would be dealt with by this committee, but we were entirely disillusioned on that point by the acting leader of the Government (Mr. Doherty), who told us there was nothing to decide on that point, as the Government had already decided, and he is too good a lawyer and too old a judge to think of hearing evidence in connection with any point which has already been decided by the court and the decision filed. I am sure I sympathize with the distinguished judge the other night when he was listening for hours to evidence being poured upon his head on a question which he had already decided, and which if he had been sitting on the Bench he would have regarded as contempt of court. I hope that when this Bill comes before the Committee such points as the House may regard as important may be brought out and dealt with.

I do not rise to discuss the Bill at very great length. In fact, I had intended only to ask a question. Before doing so, however, I should like to refer to some of the remarks made by the leader of the Opposition. He states, and very properly, that there are good grounds for objection to government by Order in Council. I heartily agree with him in the enunciation of that principle.
In theory, but not in practice.

In theory and in practice. But we must be fair and recognize that there are some steps which it is absolutely necessary to take by Order in Council, for if we were to deluge this House with Bills covering every move of a Government and of its departments, not only would we not have sufficient, time within the compass of a year to legislate, but it would be utterly impossible for this House to deal with the details of administration.
The Bill before the House provides for
certain things, and I think my hon. friend should have applied his criticism directly to the actual facts before us. What are those facts? We are simply empowering the Governor in Council to deal by regulation with certain things; (a) the control and management of any hospital, workshop, institution, and so forth connected with the Department of Sol-
5 p.m. diers' Civil Re-establishment. I submit that it would not be reasonable to bring down to this House a Bill covering all the details of the management of a hospital or an institution of that kind, and I would invite hon. gentlemen to consider that point. For instance, suppose we provide for the bringing into existence of a large hospital in a city or province. We appoint a Board of Governors and the legislation provides for certain main powers. That Board of Governors in turn, draws up the regulations for controlling the hospital in all its details. That is exactly what we are doing here. By the original Bill we brought into existence an institution, and we are now empowering the authorities administering that institution to deal with the administrative details.
That is not in this Bill. That was covered in the Bill last year relating to pensions.

By the original Bill we brought into existence the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Under this Bill we are providing for details in the management of the hospital, the workshop and other institutions established 'and arranged by Order in Council and I do not think we are violating the principles of parliamentary government in that regard. Paragraph (b) provides for the marking or stamping of artificial limbs. Such things as artificial limbs, which, unfortunately, must be provided for in very large numbers, have been, in connection with this department, brought into a veiy efficient state. We are simply providing for regulating the marking of artificial limbs. Surely it does not need an Act of Parliament to provide for a matter of that kind?
(c)	To forbid any false statement, suggestion or representation with respeat to any artificial limbs.
Again, I submit, this is a fit subject for regulation by Order in Council or by the minister at the head of the department.
(d)	For the disposal of any moneys payable by the Crown to the estates of deceased or insane officers, soldiers or other persons.

There is already in existence legislation dealing with that matter. This simply provides for detailed regulations.
This is legislation to amend Chapter 42 of the statutes of 1918 whereas the law that deals with pensions and payments is chapter 43 of 'the statutes of 1919'

I submit that the point raised by my bon. friend makes no difference because we are dealing with details. I't does not matter how many statutes you put through you will have certain details that must be dealt with by Order in Council and I submit that this is the proper method.
Without going any farther into this, I wish to call attention to the point raised by the leader of the Opposition with reference to the expense in connection with ithe hospital arrangements. To the extent jjhat there has been a duplication of hospital arrangements in connection with our -military affairs-those under -the Militia Department and those under the Re-establishment Department-steps have -already been taken by the Government to solidify or consolidate these -and bring them into one institution. As rapidly as possible 'that is being done and in many oases that has -already been accomplished. The criticism which my hon. friend has directed against the Government in that regard has been anticipated by the Government and the condition of which he complains is being rectified as fast as it is practicable to do so.
I do not agree with my hon. friend when he states that no committee is required. Unquestionably, we require a committee on this Bill not only to study the provisions of the Bill but also to hear any representations which may be made by those interested in the re-establishment in civil life of our returned men. They have already been assured by the leader of the Government and by the minister in charge of this Bill that an opportunity will he given to their various associations, or to individuals, to be heard by the committee. I think that is not only wise but absolutely essential; otherwise, without any question, this House would be in duty bound to provide for some tribunal to hear what the soldiers or their representatives have to say on this subject. I think the Government should be commended and I differ entirely from my hon. friend in that regard.
Before taking my seat I would ask the minister if under clause 7 it will be competent for the committee which is to survey and deal with this Bill, to hear and consider the claim of Canadians who enlisted in the

Imperial forces that their gratuity should be brought up to the level of the Canadian veterans' gratuity. I would ask if the committee can consider that request under that clause. If not I would like to ask the minister to consider an amendment which would make it possible. My own opinion is that the committee should do so and that assurance from the minister would be quite satisfactory to me.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I hardly think that the gratuity which my hon. friend mentions is a matter contemplated by the terms of the Bill. It is for the committee to settle its own procedure and to decide who shall be heard. I know that in the case of the Pensions -Committee last year, they heard representations from anybody, and particularly from the bodies of returned soldiers, who came to present any matter connected with the subject to them. It will be for the committee to determine whether they care to consider a representation on the matter mentioned by my hon. friend or not. I am sure that they will deal with the utmost liberality with the question as to who shall or shall not be heard in connection with the matter.
Hon. HUGH M. CLARK (Parliamentary Undersecretary tor the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment): Mr. Speaker, I do not propose -to discuss the Bill at any great length for the reason- that it is to go before a committee. I just wish to make a reference to the remark made by the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) with respect to the deluge of criticism that has been coming towards this department largely from the Great War Veterans. I may say that in so far as I can recall, nearly all the criticism coming from the Great War Veterans has been based upon the view of the Great War Veterans -that the department has not gone far enough. Representations were made to the effect that vocational training should be given to nearly everybody who had returned from overseas. Representations were made that assistance should be given to returned men should they desire to go into any other occupation than farming. Then, their education- being interrupted by reason of the war, a good many men made representations that they should be given -assistance for the completion of their university studies. All of these things of course would have meant a great increase in the expenditure of this department. The leader of the Opposition himself appreciates that the expenditure is very high as it is. I agree

with him in the statement that the expenditure is high. It is high largely because Canada is doing more in this way than any other country in the world. We have increased our pay and allowances for vocational training beyond the point that any other country has reached and we have been giving medical treatment in a way that no other country does. All this costs money but I think it is safe to say that we shall have reached the peak of the load probably in February next and that from that time onward there should be a very sharp decline in the expenditure for these purposes, particularly in reference to vocational training.
In connection with the criticism to which I have referred, I think it is a very good thing that the whole matter is to go to a committee so*that all these subjects may be threshed out before that committee. It will be well to have a committee if for nothing else than to make known just exactly what is being done in each branch of this department because a good deal of the criticism has been uninformed criticism and ilt would be a great advantage for the members of the committee to know the limitations of the department, just how the work is being carried on and also to know that -a great deal of the criticism has been caused by reason of the fact that the department is not authorized to go as far as a great many think it should go. Then the committee, too, can pass upon the question as to whether or not the criticism was right that the department should go beyond that point; as to whether or not we should extend our educational courses beyond the point to which they have been limited and as to whether or not the returned soldiers should have the facilities if they want to go into business, such as are now accorded under the Land Settlement Act and many other matters that might very easily be suggested to the committee.
It is not necessary that I should go into details now, because they will all be laid before the Committee and afterwards presented to the House. I merely wish to make that observation-that our expenditures were large because we were doing more for the returned soldier than any other country and, furthermore, we were attempting to educate men in a great many occupations in our vocational training schools. I think in Great Britain they give training in forty-six trades, whereas we train in over three hundred trades. We train in that large number of trades because we do not wish
to glut the market in any particular trade; but it will be obvious to hon. gentlemen that to train in so large a variety of trades is a good deal more costly than confining the training to a smaller number. I say again that I think the minister of the department who, as hon. gentlemen will admit, is exceedingly capable and effcient, will be very glad indeed that some committee of the House should be placed in a position to go fully into the work of this department and to recommend such other steps in the direction of the rehabilitation of the soldier as they make think wise and proper.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough and Antigonish):
speechtext: I think it is unfortunate that the Government has not introduced a Bill which would admit of soldiers placing their case before a committee. There are a great number of matters that are omitted in this Bill, and the questions that are dealt with in it are of comparative unimportance. For example, the first clause in the Bill relates to the management of hospitals and workshops, and the next clause to artificial limbs.
The marking of artificial limbs.

Yes, the marking of artificial limbs. The third clause forbids any false statement regarding artificial limbs. For the life of me I cannot understand why it is important to make regulations to prevent people from saying things about artificial limbs. But my criticism is that there are important questions relating to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment that this Bill does not admit of being considered. For example, take the advances that are made to returned soldiers engaged in farming. I do not object to that policy. It is right and proper, but I have never been able to understand why advances should be confined to men who desire to embark in that industry. Why not consider the great fishing industry of the country? I represent a constituency in which hundreds of men identified with that industry, who enlisted in the forces and have returned, would like very well to have an advance of a few hundred dollars to enable them to buy a motor boat, or fleet of nets. The amount of money required to equip a fisherman to carry on his business would be comparatively small compared with the sum the Government is advancing to farmers. I submit that the security in the case of the fishermen would be

just as good. There is no worse security you can find than an old farm that has been abandoned because the man who worked it cannot make it pay. Taxes have to be paid on it, whether it produces anything or not, and in its worn-out state it is of no value to any body, and will be a very poor security indeed for the Government. To my mind the security of a fishing boat and a fleet of nets which would be properly insured and cared for by the owner, would be much better and the loan would be just as likely to be returned to the Government. I might also refer to the lumber industry. I have in mind the case of a young man in my constituency who returned from the war. His father had died during his absence at the front and the only occupation that the young man knew anything about was the lumber business. His father had left a few hundred acres of timber land and the young man wanted to purchase a portable mill in order to help maintain his mother and sisters, and keep the family together. He did not need very much, ten or eleven hundred dollars would have sufficed, and he could have given the security of the mill and the lumber; but when he applied to the proper officials in the province of Nova Scotia, he could get no help because he was not a farmer. I say that is an unreasonable position to take and that the Government would have avoided a great deal of the discontent that has arisen among the returned soldiers if it had opened up a little and been a little more liberal in connection with the administration of this department.
The question of students whose course in college was interrupted by enlisting in the forces has also been pressed upon the Government, but I understand the Government has refused to do anything in the way of advancing money in the form of loans to students who are anxious to complete their college course. This matter has been brought to the notice of the Government and urged upon its attention by the leading educationists of Canada, and I submit it is one of very great importance. The Imperial Government, according to my information, has adopted measures to help the students who wish to complete their college course. It is also pointed out in a statement submitted to the Government by the educational authorities referred to that the Australian Government has taken a very liberal step in the same direction and in order to remind ministers of what has been done in Australia, I will read an extract from the statement in question which is

signed by W. A. E. Kerr, of the University of Alberta; Dr. J. J. Tompkins, of the University of St. Francois Xavier; Joseph Sirois, of Laval University; and K. F. Euttan, of McGill University, and was submitted to the department on behalf of these colleges by Sir Eobert A. Falconer, Principal of the University of Toronto:
So generous is Britain that she is educating at public cost young Canadians who have been in the British service. We know of several who, returning home, and finding no financial help here, have gone back to Britain to be educated at the expense of the British taxpayer. That this should have happened is not creditable to Canada.
In Australia also, the Government has taken the following action: (1) Where an applicant for assistance produces evidence to the satisfaction of the State Board that he had, prior to enlistment, entered or intended to enter upon a university course or other course of professional training, the State Board grant to the applicant assistance.
Provided that an applicant who had not before enlistment entered upon such a course shall only be granted assistance if (a) He is not more than thirty years of age at the date of his application, and (b) He applies for the assistance within six months after discharge.
(2)	Where the State Board is satisfied that assistance should be granted, the State Board may, if it approves of the course selected:
(a)	Pay by way of gift from time to time the fees payable in connection with the course.
(b)	Grant to the applicant, by way of loan, such sum as is necessary to purchase the books, instruments, and other articles required by him in connection with his course.
(c)	Pay to the applicant by way of gift such allowance as will insure him a weekly income inclusive of his own pension of 42s. for one academic year, including the period ordinarily required to enable him to attend the qualifying examination for that year.
(d)	Pay to the applicant by way of loan such allowance as will insure to him a weekly income (inclusive of pension) of 42s. for each subsequent academic year of his course, including the period ordinarily required to enable him to attend the qualifying examination for that year.
Provided that no allowance shall be paid under this regulation during the period between the termination of one academic year and the commencement of the next, except for such periods as the attendance of'the applicant at the university or other institution is compulsory.
(3)	The applicant shall give personal security for the re-payment of the amounts granted under paragraphs (-b) and (d) of the last preceding sub-regulation.
(d) The continuance of the granting of the assistance provided by sub-regulation (2) shall be subject to the receipt from time to time by the state board from the university or other institution of a report that the applicant is making satisfactory progress with his studies.
That is what the Government of Australia is doing for its students whose college courses were interrupted through enlistment, and I submit that the Government

of Canada should not do less than Australia has done.
A well-known educationist in the province of Nova Scotia has written to me on this question, and I would like to be permitted to quote 'an extract from his letter:
I do not see why the Government could not loan money to bona fide students as they do to farmers. What we want in Canada to-day is trained brains. If we have not that how shall we bear our burdens? We must have brains to make two blades grow where one grew before. We can only do this by training our young men scientifically and otherwise. Think of the enormous educational progress of the United States of America. Even England is up and doing beyond all expectation considering her financial burden.
Now, Sir, I submit that it would be only proper to include in this Bill clauses providing that consideration should be given to the case of fishermen, lumbermen, students, and also to the case of every returned soldier in any station in life, who requires assistance to complete their college course, or to become settled in civil life.
A question that seems to me of urgent importance at the present moment is the care of those returned soldiers who, with winter approaching, are still without employment. That condition of affairs is admitted but, so far as I know, no provision has been made by the Government to meet it. The very least we must do as a temporary measure, and with as little delay as possible, in view of these facts, is to provide unemployment insurance for our returned men. If we are unable to find them immediate employment so that they cam settle down in civil life, then I say it is the duty of the Government to provide at once for that state of affairs, otherwise those men will be in want during the coming winter, and it will be generally admitted that the best way to meet that situation is by providing for unemployment insurance. The Government cannot and should not refuse our soldiers any reasonable request they may make, and certainly the matters that I h'ave brought forward are very modest. I am disappointed that the Bill has not a wider scope, and that it is not such a Bill as would enable the returned soldier to come before the committee and ask a cash bounty or anything that he thinks that he has a right to. The committee could then report on the requests, and this House could afterwards decide whether they should be granted or not.

Mr. DUNCAN C. ROSS' (Middlesex West):
I wish to say a word or two before the debate is closed, Mr. Speaker. I have no objection to this Government spending all the money that may be necessary for the re-establishment of what the President of the Council always calls "our gallant men." He rather over-works that phrase sometimes; but overlooking that fault, I can join with him and every other hon. member in saying that I am always favourable to doing anything that is in the interests of the returned soldier. But at the present time, Sir, there is a great deal of unrest among the returned men, and recently I have had occasion to see a good many of them in regard to it-not of my own motion, but theirs-and I find that one cause of this excessive unrest is the fact that the soldiers argue this wise: That the Government refuses to grant the returned soldier an additional gratuity-and I am not stating whether that refusal in my opinion is right or is wrong-giving as their reason that the ' country cannot afford it.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question? What is his opinion on that matter?

That matter has apparently been closed by this Government. I may say frankly that so far as granting a gratuity of $2,000 to each soldier, irrespective of his service and of his necessities, is concerned,
I am not in favour of it. If my hon. friend wants any plainer answer I can give it to him.
- Mr. BUREAU: No, no; that is enough.
* Mr. ROSS: However, that is not the point. We have had ministers of the Crown in this House and out of it saying that this Government cannot spend any more money to assist the returned soldier in the way of additional gratuity because the country cannot afford it. Last session the hon. Minister of Public Works-who has since taken a place of safe refuge on the Railway Commission -told us of the dire necessities of the country and that we were in a dangerous condition financially. The ex-Minister of Finance, in his Budget speech, told us the same thing. I think there is a great deal of truth in what they said and that their warnings are worthy of serious consideration. But

what the returned soldiers say is this: That the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment and the Department of Militia and Defence are at the present time wastefully spending sufficient of the peoples' money to provide more liberal treatment for the soldiers, and that if the Government would only make the necessary changes in the public services they would have suffi-'cient funds in hand to meet the just demands of the soldiers. They further say that in connection with the manning of these two departments, not merely hundreds of thousands of dollars could be saved per year, but actually millions of dollars- that there are thousands of absolutely unnecessary officials employed in these departments who are drawing excessive salaries although they have nothing to do, and, in short, that their retention is simply a waste of public money. I noticed the other day in the press that two hundred women had been dismissed from the Separation Allowances and Assigned Pay Branch, and in the same item the statement was made that these women had been absorbed by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. If that is so it confirms what these returned soldiers say to me. I noticed, also, in the remarks made by the President of the Council this afternoon several things mat lead me to believe that these statements of the returned soldiers are true to a great extent. He pointed out in regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment that the Government had actually manned thirty hospitals, nineteen in one branch and eleven in another, and were using another twenty-eight throughout the country. That seems to me a great many hospitals to be used in that way, but, (of course, it may not be more than is necessary. He pointed out, moreover, in connection with the allowances paid to the soldiers who were sick in these hospitals and to their dependents, that a sum of $420,000 per month was disbursed, or in round figures $5,000,000 a year. He also pointed out that in connection with vocational training $940,000 a month was being disbursed, or about $10,000,000 a year. In other words, the whole amount being spent on returned soldiers' pay and allowances seemed to be about *ro,000,000; yet we know that in the estimates last year $30,000,000 was appropriated for this department.
When this Bill goes into Committee, I would like some information from the minister with regard to how the other $15,000,000 that was appropriated last year for this department has been spent. I should like

the full details; it seems to me that there is a very large hiatus there which needs explanation. If we are to go at this thing properly; if we are to see to it that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment is administered honestly and efficiently, we should have these details. I ask the minister to furnish also a statement of the number of employees in, say, District No. 1 -or in all the districts, for that matter. I would like him to give their names, if possible, though I will not insist upon that. I would like to have them classified in some way in order that their salaries-or wages, if you cannot dignify their remuneration by the name of salary-may be shown. I refer to all employees and officials of the department; I would like to know the details of expenditure in this connection all down the line.
I am told that in small towns where only two or three men are taking vocational training, four or five officials go there weekly in order to see that this vocational training is being properly administered. I am informed that in London, Ontario, at least half a dozen medical boards are operating and that their work is overlapping; that there are three doctors on each board, receiving large salaries; that half of them are not necessary, and that, as a matter of fact, although there are so many doctors on these boards they -are not attending to their duties as they should and are not giving the soldier the prompt examination and treatment that he should get.
As I said at the outset, I have no fault to find with the expenditure of any money that is honestly and properly spent to help re-establish the soldier in civil life. But I think it is very unwise for this Government to allow a situation to prevail with which, it is quite apparent, the soldiers are dissatisfied, and which leads them to believe that the Government is squandering money in a most wasteful manner that might better be given to them and to their dependents.

One of the objects of having the committee consider the matter is in order that they may give attention to the question whether the present provisions are adequate or not, or whether provision should be made for other classes of cases. One of the important matters which will be dealt with by that committee is undoubtedly the question of assisting our students. I intimated that at an earlier stage of the debate. The other question is a proper matter for consideration, but it is subject to the observations made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) with reference to such a class of expenditure. speechtext:
I move:
That Bill No. 10, An Act to amend the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Act, and the Orders in Council relating to the work of the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment, laid on the table of the House
on Tuesday, 16th day of September, be referred to a special committee composed of Messrs. Calder, Arthurs, Beland, Bolton, Brien, Chisholm, Clark (iBruce), Cooper, Copp, Edwards, Kennedy, Lang, McLean (Royal), Nesbitt, Pardee, Power, Tremain, Tweedie, White (Victoria), for consideration thereof, and of all matters pertaining thereto, with power to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time, and that Rule 11 be suspended.
Rule 11 is suspended because it limits the number of members on a special committee to fifteen.

Before that motion is adopted I should like to know why we are not following the ordinary procedure in this case. In 1918 we passed the Bill which my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council is now seeking to amend, because he claims that under that Bill he has not the power to impose penalties for violations of the Orders in Council which it may be necessary to pass to give effect to the Act. We are now asked that this Bill should be referred to a special committee with power to send for persons, administer oaths, and make an investigation. Why? I say that the whole subject ought to be discussed in Committee of the Whole. On, the second reading questions have already been raised by different members of the House. There seems to be a conflict. between two Acts. We are seeking to amend the Act passed in 1918, giving the Governor in Council power to dispose of moneys which might be due to estates of deceased soldiers, or of deceased dependents. Then we had the Pensions Act last session. I do not think this Bill ought to be sent to a special committee. We all know what is done to a Bill when it goes to a committee. The members of that committee hear evidence and make a report to the House, and when the report is presented to the House we take it for granted that the members who were picked for that committee were the best ones for that work and that they will make a proper report, and nobody outside the committee takes much interest in the subject. Of course, it may be said: " Why don't you go to the committee?" Now, these committees generally sit during the sittings of the House, and we cannot be present at both. We have had experience of these committees in the past. We had a special committee on the Railway Act, and afterwards we had to thrash the whole matter out in. the House. If the Government are not satisfied with the administration of the Act, or if they think people outside are not satisfied with it, let a committee be named to consolidate the different Acts, or

let these Orders in Council be enlarged or emasculated or re-arranged in some such way that they shall be acknowledged as being the regulations necessary for giving effect to these Acts. I do not think it is fair that five or ten members of this House should consider this matter in a special committee and make a report-, while the rest of us are attending the sittings of this House. My hon. friend might answer that the evidence will all be printed and that I shall be able to read it, but he knows very well that half the members of this House do not read the evidence taken before these committees to whom matters like this are referred. They have not time to read the evidence. If there is any particular reason why this course should have been adopted I would be disposed to acquiesce in it, but I say that the President of the Privy Council has given absolutely no reason why the various clauses for amending Chapter 42 of the Statutes of 1918 should not come before the Committee of the Whole House, where we would have the privilege of putting questions, reading the Orders in Council, and having them explained by those responsible for them, and of going into all these matters. As it is, I cannot see my way clear to vote for the second reading.

Mr. Speaker, just before six o'clock I had intended to say a few words about this motion sending this Bill to a committee. The minister assures us that the different phases of the management of the military system in Canada will be dealt with by that committee. When the Soldiers' Land Settlement (Bill came before the House, I pointed out to the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) that the policy of the Government in connection

with the assistance to be given to the soldiers should be put on all at once; that every phase, whether it was by grants of money, grants of land, or whatever it was going to be, should be placed before the public and before the soldiers so that they would have an opportunity of selecting for themselves whichever branch of. that assistance they would care to avail themselves of. The land settlement policy was placed before the country and a great many have taken advantage of it. There is talk about other assistance that has not yet been disclosed. I would suggest to the Government that when this Bill is dealt with, whatever policy the Government is going to put forward in regard to other branches should be announced so that we will have it all, and so that -soldiers, sailors, or whoever are entitled to assistance by the Government by reason of their services to the country, should have an opportunity of selecting for themselves whichever branch or phase of that assistance they are going to adopt.
I was pointing out when the Bill was up for the second reading that I thought the hospital treatment that soldiers are now receiving is rather too expensive and could be carried on much more cheaply. I wish to remind the Government again that from Halifax eastward in the province of Nova Scotia we have quite a number of hospitals. I am not so very well acquainted with the hospital facilities west of that point, but I know that in Windsor, Kentville, Yarmouth and at other points they have hospitals. I think it is at Kentville that they have a hospital in which they treat tubercular cases and I think such cases would be treated in that hospital. The cheaper way would be to arrange with the province of Nova Scotia and to equip that hospital so that any tubercular cases could be received there. In Halifax we have the Victoria General Hospital, which is a large well conducted institution. In New Glasgow, Antigonish, Sydney, North Sydney, and Glace iBay there are well equipped hospitals while in Sydney there are one or two hospitals at least, one of which is a firsts class hospital. I venture to suggest that in all these hospitals- patients who require treatment either at the present or some future time, as pointed out by the minister, can be dealt with and treated very much more cheaply than by maintaining hospitals and- staffs particularly for these cases. These hospitals that I have mentioned have private staffs and- they must maintain them. If we -are going to have separate hospitals for soldiers -we must maintain staffs when perhaps there will be

very little to do. The minister tells us that for at least a year they are going to receive any cases of this kind and to give them sufficient treatment, and that if, at any time in the future, a soldier becomes ill, or has any trouble which may be traced in any way to his service in the field, he shall be entitled to free hospital treatment *and such allowances as he received when he was in the service. I am sure that it would be a bad policy, and a very ex-ipensive one, for the Government to maintain hospitals in different parts of Canada so as to be ready to receive men of that kind. However desirable it is that they should be received, I think it is better that a private arrangement should be made with the hospitals in different parts of the country in which they would receive patients and be paid specially for any services that they would render.
I trust that the general policy of the Government in the different lines in which they expect to assist the soldiers will be announced and also that 'the question of hospitals, and the treatment of cases, not only in the province of Nova Scotia but elsewhere, may be arranged for on the basis that I have mentioned. I only mention the province of Nova Scotia because I am familiar with the hospitals there, but I am quite sure that all the other provinces are equally well equipped to look after cases of this kind. I trust that the committee under the direction of the minister who has charge of this Bill, and of the Government generally, will see to it that the fullest possible information is obtained in connection with the matter and that officials, no matter how capable they may be, will be dispensed with if it is found that the country can get along and that the service which they render can be obtained as well and with less trouble and expense to the country. These are the only observations I wish to make in connection with this Bill before it goes to the committee.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. ISAAC E. PEDLOW (South Renfrew), moved the second reading of Bill No. 2 respecting Thanksgiving Day. He said:
As the House is well aware this is a Bill which has been before Parliament for a great length of time. The subject was introduced by me by way of resolution on the 11th of March last. On the ensuing 4th of April I brought in a Bill and it received its first reading, but owing to the pressure of business last session the measure made no further progress and was held over until now. Since I gave notice of my resolution last March, and doubtless owing to the publicity which it was accorded in the press of the country, I have received many communications from citizens and associations and organizations of various kinds, endorsing the principle of the Bill. So that hon. gentlemen will thoroughly understand its provisions I will read the measure which is very brief. It is entitled "An Act respecting Thanksgiving Day," and reads as follows:
His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
The annual thanksgiving day, heretofore held on a day fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council, shall hereafter be held on the second Monday of November in each year, as a perpetual memorial of the victorious conclusion of the recent war, in addition to such other reasons as may be prescribed by proclamation of the Governor in Council for that purpose published.
Then the Bill proceeds to enumerate the various alterations to the law that would be rendered necessary by the enactment of its provisions.
Now, Sir, it may be wise on my part to make a reference to the Thanksgiving Days that have been observed in this country for some time past. As a matter of fact I intend to go back to the early history of Canada, draw attention to some of the dates observed as Thanksgiving Days, and give the reasons therefor.
The earliest date i,n Canadian history recognized as a day of special thanksgiving was observed in Lower Canada. This was proclaimed on December 22nd, 1798, and observed on Thursday, 10th January, 1799. It may be of special interest, perhaps, to those present here at this time, to know that the reason for this day of thanksgiving was because of "The signal victory over our enemy";-our enemy at that time

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
being France. The Thanksgiving proclamation also stated that the day was observed for "the manifold and inestimable blessings -which our kingdoms and provinces have received, 'and daily continue to receive." The next date which was observed as a day of thanksgiving in Lower Canada was on Thursday, August 12, 1802, and the reason then announced by proclamation was "for Hi® mercies." No doubt that had reference to a bountiful 'harvest, and peace and prosperity in the land. The next thanksgiving day was observed in Lower Canada on Thursday, April 21, 1814, "for glorious victory over our enemies- "France." Another day of thanksgiving was observed on Tuesday, 13th September, in the same year, 1814, for "the end of the sanguinary contest in Europe and to give the Dominions the blessings of peace." Then on Thursday, April 6, 1815, wiais observed as a thanksgiving day by Lower Canada, "as the end of the war with United States of America arid the restoration of the blessings of peace." Tuesday, May 21, 1816, was observed by Lower Canada a® a day of thanksgiving, "for the end of the war between Great Britain and France," -the Napoleonic Wars. Wednesday, February 6, 1833, was the next date observed as thanksgiving day by Lower Canada and the reason was "for the cessation of cholera." Wednesday, November 1, 1834, was observed as thanksgiving day because of the inauguration of quarantine of ships at Grosse Isle, and Monday, February 26, 1838, was observed as thanksgiving day by Lower Canada for the termination of the Rebellion. This was the last thanksgiving day observed by Lower Canada separate from the province of Canada.
In Upper Canada, the first thanksgiving day of which there was any record was observed on Tuesday, June 18, 1816, "because of the end of the war between Great Britain and France." This was about a month later than the date on Which the same event was celebrated in Lower Canada. Thursday, 14th February, 1833, was the next thanksgiving day date in Upper Canada, observed "to continue His mercies." Thursday, 30th October, 1834, was the next thanksgiving day date, and it was observed for the same reason as in 1833. On Tuesday, 6th February, 1838, the last Thanksgiving Day was observed in Upper Oanada. The formation of the province of Oanada followed. This thanksgiving was for the same reason as in 1833, namely, "to continue His mercies." No notice, apparently, was taken in the pro-tMr. Pedlow.]
ciamation in Upper Canada, 'as was done in Lower Canada, of the termination of the Rebellion, so as to whether Upper Canada was thankful or not for the termination of that stirring event, the Rebellion of 1837-38, the citizens of the Dominion at the present time 'are left in doubt. After the formation of the province of Canada, which comprised Upper and Lower Canada, the 3rd of January 1850 was the first thanksgiving day date observed in the province, the reason assigned being "for His mercies and cessation of grievous disease, Asiatic Cholera." Wednesday, 4th June, 1856, was (the next Thanksgiving Day date which the province of Canada observed, "for the restoration of peace with Russia," this being at the termination of the Crimean War. The three subsequent dates on which Thanksgiving Day was observed in the province of Oanada were Thursday, 3rd November, 1859, Thursday, 6th December, 1860, Wednesday, llt'h November, 1863, all observed for the same reason, namely, abundant harvest and continuation of peace." Wednesday, 18th October, 1865, was the last Thanksgiving Day date in the province of Oanada before Confederation, and it was observed "for His mercies." This came after the termination of the American Civil War. No attention was paid to the many important events in Canadian history that took place between 1865 and 1867.	-
After Confederation in 1867 Monday the 15th of April, 1872, was the first thanksgiving day observed, and that was " for the restoration to health of H.R.H. the Prince of Wales,'' afterwards King Edward the Seventh just eleven years after his visit to Canada. Since Confederation thanksgiving day has been observed yearly without interruption, beginning with Thursday, the 6th of November, 1879, and continuing right up to the present time, and in every case it has been observed " for the blessings of an abundant harvest." Twenty-two of these thanksgiving days were observed in the month of November on dates running from the 3rd to the 28th; eighteen were observed in the month of October as early as the 8th and as late as the 31st, one on Wednesday- in 1880-and afterwards always on Thursday up to the year 1908, when Monday was decided on because of special representations made by business representatives and the commercial travellers associations of Canada. Since Confederation special days of thanksgiving have been observed, in addition to the one I have already referred to in 1872, on the following dates: Tuesday,

the 17th of November, 1887, to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Queen Victoria's accession to the throne of Great Britain and Ireland; Tuesday, the 22nd of June, 1897, was observed as a special day of thanksgiving on account of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee; on Thursday, the 26th of June, 1902, the coronation of King Edward VII was to have been observed, but owing to the serious illness of His Majesty the date was changed to the 9th of August, 1902.
Now, Sir, the proposal embodied in the Bill before the House has been endorsed, as I have already stated, by many institutions and associations, the principal of these being:	The Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada (Toronto); the Dominion Commercial Travellers' Association (Montreal) ; the Ontario Commercial Travellers' Association (London); the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada; the Ontario Associated Boards of Trade-in annual convention assembled, representing delegates from fifty-seven Boards of Trade of Ontario; the Hamilton Methodist Conference-assembled at Kitchener on June 2; the president of the Great War Veterans' Association, Captain W. P. Grant, of this city, and many other citizens in every walk of life as well as hon. members on both sides of the House.
I might perhaps call the attention of the House to a few of the resolutions to which I have referred. The first is from the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, which association represents over 200,000 commercial institutions in the Dominion. I read this communication because in their discussion of the proposition they decided very sensibly on the day of the week instead of the date of the month as the most suitable to. meet their requirements. Their communication is as follows:
Moved by- seconded by-
" That it is the opinion of this meeting that in order to preserve the memorable date of November 11th as a day of Peace, we ask the Do-miniBn Government to have Thanksgiving Day of each year fall upon this date."
After considerable discussion, it was resolved that, owing to the fact that November 11th might fall on Saturday or Sunday and greatly inconvenience the general public, as well as the retail merchants, it would be inadvisable to support the resolution, but the members felt that, in tReir opinion, it would be appropriate for Canadians to celebrate a Peace day, which could very well be considered a day of Thanksgiving, and they would recommend that if it was the intention of the Government of Canada to combine a Peace day with Thanksgiving day it should be permanently fixed so as to fall on a (Monday.
I read that with much pleasure, because it endorses absolutely the position which I have taken. I might also read the resolution adopted by the Methodist Conference held at Kitchener. I take this from a copy of the Toronto Globe of June 3 last. It is in the form of a despatch from Kitchener, dated the previous day:
The delegates at this afternoon's session of the Hamilton Methodist Conference almost unanimously passed the amendment to the report of the Committee on Conference Memorials recommending that the Monday nearest November 11 be fixed by the Government as Thanksgiving Day in Canada hereafter, and supported the proposal to fix November 11 of each year as Armistice and Thanksgiving Day. This latter proposal was submitted to the Conference by the Simcoe district.
The Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada addressed me in the following terms:
Our American Allies have for years past fixed the fourth Thursday in November as Thanksgiving Day and as the Armistice was signed on Monday, November 11th, 1918, we would be fully in accord if your motion read fixing said day on the second Monday in November.
You will notice that while endorsing the principle of observing the day on which the Armistice was signed ending the great World War, they prefer the second Monday in November to the date on which the Armistice was actually signed, so that the Thanksgiving Day would always fall on the same day of the week in each year. They further state:
We have always understood that Thanksgiving Day was set aside for returning thanks to Providence for his many blessings during the year. It was understood, that people as a general thing would attend divine service, in the different churches. Until Thanksgiving Day was set on Monday, this part of it was a total failure and churches were meagrely attended and a great many of them did not open their doors, while outside the theatres, picture shows, horse racing, sham battles and everything of a secular nature was engaged in.
That was an argument in favour of Monday, so that the Thanksgiving service should be held in the churches on Sunday and horse-racing, sham battles and other amusements could be indulged in on the following day. The same idea runs through the communications of the Dominion Commercial Travellers' Association, having its head office in Montreal, so that Montreal and Toronto are a unit in that respect. I am glad to find that they agree on some things, and in particular on Thanksgiving Day. The Commercial Travellers' Association of London, Ontario, passed the following resolution :
That Parliament be requested to fix the second Monday of November of each year as a public Thanksgiving Day.

I have also a communication from outside our own borders. It is from the editor of one of the most important trade journals published on the American Continent, if not in the world, and he says, in replying to my inquiry:
It seems to me that your suggestion that the Dominion and the United States should celebrate Thanksgiving Day on the same day each year is a very sound one.
The arguments which I adduced in its favour were that it would be a great convenience to commercial, banking and stockbroking institutions of the two countries, and would obviate the necessity of disturbing business on two different dates.
As I have already intimated, I have received many favourable notices through the press since the Bill was introduced. As a matter of fact, some newspapers were advocating it before the matter was -drawn to my attention by a commercial traveller whose name I should like to associate with the proposal, because I do not wish to claim credit for originating the idea. The idea originated with Mr. David Adair, a commercial traveller, of Ottawa, who has given a good deal of study not only to this matter but to other important questions of considerable interest to Canada. The following letter from Mr. Adair appeared in the Montreal Star of March 13th last:
As Thanksgiving Day is usually held late in October or early in November, and as there is no special date named until a few weeks previous, we would suggest that Nov. llth, the day we celebrated the triumph of right over might in the war waged by Germany and her allies against Great Britain and her allies, 19141918, and in memory of our illustrious dead soldiers and in honour of our gallant living heroes and noble nurses who have represented us so splendidly in the great conflict just ended, be permanently settled by the Government as our future day of thanksgiving, to be known as " Armistice Day." By doing so we would he able to call up some of the enthusiastic comradeship and thanksgiving which touched the heart of all Canada on this ever to he memorable day, the most glorious in all our history.
It would also give future generations a splendid opportunity of doing honour to the memory of their forefathers who suffered, bled and died for the freedom of the world. We believe the setting apart of Nov. llth as Armistice Day for all time to come is a national duty and ought to he taken up by the House now in session.
I wish to read also a short editorial from the Montreal Star with reference to this subject, and then I will not weary the House with any further extracts of that kind. This is one of many that I have clipped from various newspapers:

A National Thanksgiving Day.
The Star is glad to note that a Bill is to be introduced during this session of Parliament to make November eleventh, the anniversary of the day on which the armistice was signed, the national Thanksgiving Day of Canada. A suggestion to this effect was made-
You will note this, please.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
in this column of The Star on the day following the signing of the armistice. Hitherto Thanksgiving Day has been unfortunately a vague festival. The date of its observance has varied from year to year, and has been fixed by Order in Council annually. It has never been associated with any particular event in history and has meant too little to most of us.
I think that' the editor is somewhat in error in that, because judging from the list of events that I have read to the House tonight, a different conclusion could be reached. However, that has not much bearing upon the matter which I have under consideration. The editorial continues :
The opportunity is now presented of making this day the most significant and in many ways the most important of all our holidays, a day in which Canada can give solemn thanks for deliverance from the most terrible crisis in its history, a day of real thanksgiving, not only for our safety but for the splendid record of our sons, in a word a day which can be consecrated to patriotism in the best sense of the word. We should not let this opportunity go by of fixing once and forever upon a day for national remembrance of a great moment in the world's history.
That opinion has been endorsed by many leading newspapers in all the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, every nation has its memorial days. " What mean ye by these stones " was the question provoked in their children by the setting up by the Israelites of their crude memorial at Jordan. During the past year we have heard much oi the various kinds of memorials, but is it not exceedingly fitting that we should have memorial days and memorial services wherein sorrow sits with gratitude, enthroned in the. memory of noble deeds?
We have in mind the memory of such stirring events in the Great War -as Ypres, Passehendaele, Valenciennes, the Hinden-burg line, Mans, the Marne, Courcellette, Vimy Ridge, Amiens, Cambrai, Festubert, the Somme, Givenchy, Loos, and many other events of equal interest and importance where our Canadian boys from the farm, the shop, the college and .the office covered themselves with imperishable glory and engraved these names upon the flag of -Canada, not in flaming letters of such base metals as silver or gold, but in a pigment more precious s-till-even in the

heart's blood of the nation's noblest, best and most beloved sons. It is to the memory of these brave men that, if the Bill now before the House is approved of, this day-Armistice Day-the second Monday in November each year, is to be consecrated throughout all the ages of our history. They brought not only to their relatives and friends, but to the whole of Canada, undying glory to the fullest measure, and although the bodies of many of these noble lads lie buried in foreign soil far from the Canada they loved, their memories shall live forever in the land they died to save.
I trust, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the Bill will receive the favourable consideration of the House and will become the law of the land during this year, so that there may be no break in the observance of this memorial.

subtopic: BILL, TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the eloquent address with which the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) supported his motion for the second reading of this Bill. There are doubtless very many reasons why we should desire to bear in mind the great cause for thankfulness that we had on the eleventh of November, 1918, when Ithe great struggle einded in which our men, in common with the men of the Empire as a whole and with the men of the allied powers, took so glorious a part. The hon. member has enumerated a number of days in the course of the war when the sons of Canada covered themselves with glory and earned for themselves and for their country a name which I am satisfied will never die. Each one of these days would be worthy of commemoration. Perhaps each one of them is as worthy of commemoration as the day which marked the termination of the struggle; some of them, indeed, may be more worthy of commemoration. Because, after all, we are, I think, not disposed to forget the fact that the war ultimately terminated. But that, perhaps, is not the thing that we have most reason to be proud of. It is the achievements that brought the end, rather than the mere fact that the war ended, that we have special reason to be proud of and special reason to desire to Temember. I point out this consideration which I think it is worth our while to have in mind in dealing with this question.
There is another point of view from which they may be viewed. Thanksgiving Day has come to be with us an annual
28i
festival; it has come to be associated with the special thanks which, as the years go by, we owe to the Almighty for the blessings and mercies that have come to us during that year. It would seem to me that, if it be thought that Armistice Day required a special day to be set aside for its celebration lest we should forget it, we should consider whether we should not give it a day for itself. It does not seem to me to be desirable that we should abandon the custom, which has become time-honoured, of setting aside one day in each year for thanksgiving to the Almighty for His blessings during that year. The day after all, in its nature as we have observed it up to the present, is not a day intended to be a day of commemoration; it is one day out of the whole year that the country sets apart to thank the Almighty for the blessings that he has bestowed upon us during that particular year, and for my part I would be sorry to see that custom of setting aside a day for that particular purpose departed from.
We should also give thought to certain practical considerations. After all we desire this day, which in its nature is a day of thanksgiving, to be a day of rejoicing, of happiness, of enjoyment, for our people. When you take this country from one end to the other, I think I may safely say that past experience has shown us that selecting a day in the month of November exposes us to falling upon a day which will very probably be entirely unsuitable for anything in the nature of enjoyment of outdoor amusement of any description. That, perhaps, is the most wholesome form of amusement, and it is well to give consideration to that fact in determining the day upon which we should celebrate our day of thanksgiving. It is true that for quite a number of years our Thanksgiving Day was fixed in the month of November. I would not speak positively, but I think that, to some extent at all events, that fixing was influenced by the desire to make our Thanksgiving Day fall upon the same day as was fixed in the republic to the south of us, and no doubt there were advantages to be derived from Thanksgiving Day being celebrated on the same day in both countries. But, notwithstanding that consideration and ki response to what was the expression of a very general and widespread opinion in the country, Governments for quite a number of years past, now have found it wise, with a view to meeting the desire of the public and in view of the considerations that I have already mentioned, to fix Thanksgiving Day at an

In view of all these considerations and the desirability of marking for all time our thanksgiving for this great victory I have very cordial feelings towards the proposal of my hon. friend, and if he would consent to making the date the 11th of November instead of the second Monday of November I would have very great pleasure in doing all I could to help him carry his resolution.
