speechtext:
I think I should not let this occasion pass without saying a word on the matter. I wish to say a few words on behalf of the retailers. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has said that he would have no objection to seeing Thanksgiving Day fixed for the 11th of November. Now the 11th of November might fall on a Saturday, and there are a great many retailers who do not observe Thanksgiving Day when it falls on a Saturday. Why not make it the second Monday of November as proposed by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow)? Then every retailer and merchant would know exactly on what date it would be. You can thank God as well on a movable day as on a fixed day, and if we decided on Monday for Thanksgiving Day we could thank God on the Sunday before, and then enjoy Monday. I am also speaking on behalf of the Montreal Live Stock Association, of which I am a member.
I have no objection to the day being fixed as Monday, but Saturday, which is the day on which the retailers do a large amount of their business, is the worst day that you could choose. If you choose Monday I think I am safe in saying that every one will be satisfied to have it on a fixed day as the hon. member for South Renfrew has suggested.

subtopic: BILL, TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my views on this subject are very much the same as those which have been expressed by my hon. friend from Westmount-St. Henry (Mr. Leduc). I would be in favour of a fixed day for Thanksgiving. My first reason is that the calendar would mention Thanksgiving Day as any other non-judicial day is mentioned as a federal holiday. The business people would be prepared to observe that day and would know exactly how they stood. It makes a difference whether the day on which we 
are to thank our Lord is fixed by statute or by Order in Council. I think I would rather have it fixed by statute. The Government might fix a day by Order in Council that would perhaps not suit the business community. The peeople would be taken by surprise. It is not everybody who knows what an Order in Council is. A day that the calendar would mention would be a day that would be known to everybody. I second this motion with pleasure, and I think in doing so I represent the views of the people of Montreal who would like to know exactly how they stand in reference to Thanksgiving Day. The Government has decided that Thanksgiving Day shall be in October. It varies by two or three weeks sometimes. Some people are expecting it to be fixed for November, but it has been set for October this year. That is not a good thing for the country and we would be very pleased if the Government would see fit to accept this Bill. I understand that the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) does not make it a party question. When it is stated that Montreal and Toronto agree it seems to me that this Parliament should not interfere but should allow it to go by common consent.

subtopic: BILL, TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
If I correctly understand the suggestion which is before the House it is that Thanksgiving Day shall be fixed for the second Monday in November. I agree that the day should be set for Monday. We are accustomed to celebrating some of our holidays on Monday. Labour Day is the first Monday in September. As far as the workingmen are concerned if a day in the middle of the week is fixed it interferes with the week's work. If a holiday happens to fall on Tuesday or any other day of the week, except Monday, it puts the men in such a position that they suffer a great loss of time and it is a loss to the community commercially as well as economically speaking. There is a Saturday half holiday in a great many of the cities in Canada. Any body who wants to visit friends can start on Saturday and he has the benefit Of Sunday and also of Monday, if Monday is the day fixed for Thanksgiving. Every one knows that the workingmen have very few opportunities to visit their friends, and they can thank God as well in a country town as they can in the city. I would strongly support the proposal to have a fixed day and, in order that it might be beneficial to the labouring classes, I would urge that Monday be decided upon so as to ensure

that the people would have two days of rest instead of one and a half. I feel that the change would be of great advantage to all classes of people.
Mr. HERBERT M. MOWAT (Parkdale): As representing a constituency which contains, probably, the homes of the greatest number of commercial travellers, I desire to throw any weight I may possess in this discussion on behalf of a fixed day, and that day Monday. Commercial travellers would not then need to start out on Sunday night, .as is usual, to be at their work on Monday. They would have a much longer time to spend with their families, and if it is to be a day of thanksgiving, how better can a man give thanks than when he is at home with his family? For that reason I hope that the Bill as drafted by my bon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) will pass.
There is another reason that should be given for the acceptance of this Bill, namely, that it is a new Bill for Canada and it gives recognition to Canada's effort in the war. Our ancestors, and those of us whose ancestors came from the British Isles, had no special thanksgiving day. They gave thanks for a bountiful harvest every day after the harvest was gathered in. We are no more pious than they were and yet we -think we ought to observe a particular day on which to give thanks. We adopted a thanksgiving day from another country and not our own. Therefore it is a matter of rejoicing to me to see that we are starting out, as we will by this Bill, with a thanksgiving day to give thanks not only for a bountiful harvest but for the greatest event in the history of our country that probably any of us will ever experience.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time.

speechtext: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) .moved -the second reading of Bill No. 9 to amend the House of Commons Act, .and to provide that polling days at elections shall be public holidays.
I would like the hon. gentleman to explain the Bill.

This measure, Mr. Speaker, is designed to correct certain abuses which have arisen under the House of Commons Act with respect -to electoral matters. It provides for automatic bye-elections. As is well known, under the present system there
is no provision for elections to be held at a certain stated period when- a seat has been declared vacant and -the result is -that v-acant seats have been made political footballs by the party in power ever since the House of Commons Act was placed upon the statute-books. I submit that the law as it now stands is undemocratic, -that it is not according to British precedent, and that it is high time that some change be made whereby constituencies which have become vacant shall not be kept disfranchised for periods ranging from six months to three years.
I might say that under the Liberal rule vacancies were filled much more expeditiously than they are at present, but I am free to admit that very much was left to be desired, even under that Administration, with respect to this matter. I have only to mention the case of the disfranchised county of Glengarry; no representative from that county has sat in this Parliament, although we are now well on into our second year. We also have the ridings of North Ontario, Quebec East, Assiniboia, and other divisions, which have been disfranchised for many months. I submit this should be put an end to- and this measure seeks to accomplish that result.
The second section of the Bill makes provision against two seats being held by the same member. It is inconceivable, Mr. Speaker, that the present system should continue. One would imagine that the importunities of the electors of a single constituency would be quite sufficient to satisfy any one member; but to be obliged to submit to the demands of the electors of two divisions seems to my mind to be a cruelty from which the member ought to be protected. Now, this system of electing one member to occupy two seats is mannestly something which should no longer continue in Canada. The voting strength of tne parliamentary party to which the member belongs is lessened and weakened by the present system, often a first-class man is kept out of the House, and it is certainly time that we should make some change whereby a member can sit for only one seat.
The third section of the measure is one which I almost hesitate to refer to at this moment, and it is this: That election day shall be declared to be a general holiday throughout Canada. In view of the fact that we are abo-ut to add an additional holidav. it seems to be-
No, not an additional holiday.

At any rate we are fixing Tnanksgiving Day for a particular time. Prom the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) in the Thanksgiving Day debate, one would be led to believe that we ought to have a Thanksgiving Day and also an Armistice Day, that both of them are so important that they afford particular occasion for thankfulness by the people of tins country. However, tfie rule which is incorporated in the Bill, whereby a holiday is to be declared on voting day, is one which, I think, will make for actual benefit-actual tangible benefit-to>
the people of this country. The reason for incorporating it in the Bill is that every voter "should be given an opportunity of going to the poll free from restriction and untrammelled so far as action by his employer,, or some person who has some supervision over him, is concerned. We know it to be quite often the case that in elections, particularly by-elections, where it is almost vital that the Government should carry the seat, pressure is sometimes brought to bear by employers to see that the voter goes to the poll and votes according to the wish not of the voter but of the employer, or the superintendent, or the manager of the department where he works. This should be done away with. The voter should go to the poll untrammelled and unafraid, and I think a measure of this kind will make for general benefit. The whole measure, I submit, is one in line with legislation throughout the world. In England, as is well known, elections take place automatically -within, I believe, three weeks after the seat is declared vacant. We pride ourselves on being fashioned on the English system. Why not adopt this rule? I submit, the Bill ought to receive the support of members on tooth sides of the House.
I may say before closing that this was the view of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) when on January 16, 1908, he introduced a measure and spoke as follows:
The Bill has the same purpose as a BUI introduced last session or the session before. It is to provide that, in case the seat of any member of this House is vacated for any cause and the writ for the election of a new member is not issued within a prescribed time, it shall be the duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to issue the writ for a new election.
It is rather curious that measures of this kind, fixing elections automatically, are usually introduced by the Opposition. When the Opposition succeeds to office, interest seems to toe lost in the measure, probably on the principle that "When the devil was sick the devil a monk would
['Mr. Jacobs.]
be. When the devil was well, the devil a monk he'd be." However, I intend to hold the Prime Minister and his cohorts down to the view he expressed on January 16, 1908, and I trust the Bill will receive the approbation of the members to your right, Mr. Speaker, who are following the Prime Minister.

I have one objection to the hon. gentleman's Bill and that is that it proposes to make election day a public holiday. I must confess I may hold extreme views with respect to this question of holidays, but I am absolutely opposed to a multiplication of public holidays. It is a serious interference with business and, speaking of my own profession, a handicap in the publication of a daily newspaper. I very much dislike the prospect of election day being proclaimed a holiday. In the city from which I come the polls are usually located in the schools and an election results in a school holiday. Children have a holiday on polling day, but there would seem to be no good reason why the general business of the country should be suspended because an election is being held.
Perhaps I might be pardoned for introducing the matter, but I felt more like supporting the views of the sponsor of the previous Bill because the 11th of November would occasionally fall on the Sabbath, and I do not see why we should not give thanks on the Sabbath as well as on any other day. It also occurred to me that this Government ought to approach the German Government with the view of getting them to adopt the 11th of November, ' Armistice Day, as a holiday, 'as I think they have more reason to rejoice at the signing of the armistice than we have.
As to the by-elections being held automatically, I quite agree with my hon. friend that it would appear to be a desirable practice. It is the practice in England, and I suppose that is a very good country to look to for an example. I have always observed that the party in opposition is strongly in favour of having bye-elections brought on expeditiously, but when in power it is not so anxious to have that practice carried on.
It may be that that sentiment exists to some extent even at the present day; I remember it did in the old days. I have not considered the merits of the Bill and therefore have not any further remarks to offer in regard to it, but I am entirely opposed to making election day a public holiday.

If I understand the wording of this Bill

aright, it means that a bye-election at any time would be made a public holiday. If that is the case, I am opposed to the Bill. Let us take a large city where there are ten or twelve subdivisions:	Are we going to
proclaim a legal holiday for one corner of the city and order all the stores and factories to close, and leave those in the'other parts of the city open? Is that fair? The proposal might work very well in the country, but it would not be practicable in a city. It would be absolutely unfair to deprive a great many working men of their wages because they happened to be in a certain section of the city in which a bye-election was being held, and it would be equally unfair to the manufacturers and other employers. At first I thought the proposal was restricted to a public holiday during a general election, which I have always been in favour of, because a date can be fixed to suit everybody; and I believe when the people are choosing a Government for three or four or five years they should be given a chance to go to the poll, for it is *an occasion of great importance, and probably we are celebrating other holidays which are not nearly as important. Especially is a general holiday needed for a general election with women now in a position to exercise the franchise, and it is quite likely that in the very near future they may ask that the day be set apart as a public holiday. I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) would not want to have the shops and factories closed in his own little riding wedged in among four other ridings-and the shops and factories in the adjoining ridings open for business. It would be absolutely unfair for every one concerned. I would therefore ask my hon. friend not to press that part of his Bill.

I am not wedded to that
section.
Mr. RICHARD -C. HENDERS (Macdonald) :	Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to say
anything about the matter of holding bye-elections at a stated time after vacancies occur, I desire rather to deal with the other feature of the Bill. As a farmer representing an agricultural constituency I would like to call the attention of the House to the inconvenience that would be experienced in the event of an election coming, say, at this time of the year and a public holiday being declared for it. Take the western part of our country where the threshing machines are running and we have hundreds of thousands of dollars of interest at stake. If it was a suitable day
for those machines to run, would you tie up the threshing of perhaps one or two million bushels of grain for the sake of giving everybody a holiday to vote, particularly if we had weather like that which we have been passing through during the last ten days, with the machines tied up every other day on account of rain? I am quite sure that if we declared a holiday under those conditions we would have the people up in arms about it. It is quite possible for every voter to have an opportunity to register his vote without stopping threshing for a minute. Suitable arrangements to this end are made from time to time during elections, and I do not think any serious difficulty" is experienced in doing so; but to tie up every machine for an election and particularly a by-election I think is going entirely too far.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this Bill introduces what may be regarded as a very useful reform in connection with elections. I have very little to add to what has already been said in regard to it. I agree altogether with the mover of the second reading and the author of the Bill (Mr. Jacobs), that it is desirable to have elections held as soon as possible whenever vacancies occur. We have noticed from time to time that even in the midst of the war whenever a vacancy occurred in any constituency in the United Kingdom the Mother of Parliaments immediately brought on an election and the constituency was again represented in Parliament at the earliest possible moment, as it ought to be. As that system has worked very well in the Old Country-where I am sure they would not adopt such an obsolete system as we have-I think it will be a wholesome law for us to establish. I trust therefore that as far as the general policy of the Bill is concerned the Government will decide to adopt it.
I am in favour of a general election day being a public holiday. My good friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders) spoke against stopping people from working, but as far as I know there is nothing to prevent any person working on a holiday if he wants to.

He won't work,
though.

If he has a threshing
machine working, or is taking in his hay, or is engaged in any other farm work, and he finds it would be a great loss to him to observe the holiday, there is no punishment to deter him from continuing opera-

tions; but as a general rule the holiday would be observed. I am in favour of the general election date being a public holiday because I think it will tend largely to greater purity in elections. I run about as cheap elections as any man, otherwise I would not be able to run them at all, but I have been told that in some other parts of the Dominion some voters will say : " I will not lose my day's work unless some provision is made for it." That is " put up *' to candidates very often, and they have got to do a lot of " arranging " or they will probably lose the support of such voters.
If the day is a public holiday and factories and works of that kind are closed, that condition is not put up to the candidate. The adoption of this measure, therefore, making election day at general elections a holiday, would be a great step in advance; it would tend to make elections less expensive and, indirectly, to bring about purity in elections, as we call it. I can see the force of the argument put forth against declaring the days on which byelections are held to be public holidays, particularly in large cities, because that would interfere with the people outside of the riding in question. But general elections do not come round more than once in four years; under our Constitution they are required to be held at least once in five years; and a public holiday once in five years will not he very much felt in the long run. If the Government will accept the Bill, I believe that they will be bringing about very wholesome reforms in connection with the different points which the Bill covers.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. L. DAVIDSON (Digby and Annapolis) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is much to be said in favour of the proposal that has been brought forward by the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). The question, however, is a somewhat complicated one. When I first saw a reference to it on the Order Paper, it occurred to me that it was a matter upon which I would wish to speak at some length. I am sorry that the discussion was brought on so speedily and so unexpectedly this evening for 1 should have liked to be in a better position to discuss it.
But there is another reason why, in my opinion, this matter should not be disposed of at this sitting. The House is somewhat slim and the only member who might give us a valuable opinion on this thing based on actual experience is absent from his place; I refer 'to the hon. member who

represents the constituency of Maiisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). We certainly ought to hear from him on a matter of this kind before we advance the Bill any further. I therefore move the adjournment of the debate in order that we may have an opportunity of discussing it later.

maintopic: BOARD OF COMMERCE-SALARIES OF THE COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: My recollection of the Act creating the Board of Commerce is that the salaries of the commissioners are to be determined by the Governor in Council. Has it been found necessary to depart from the provisions of that Act and to resort to the present procedure?
