That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to assist repatriation and civil reestablishment by advancing moneys to provide houses; that these houses should he erected in model townsitets or garden cities, one in each province; that land sufficient for market gardening should go with each house; that oocupants should be encouraged to buy their holdings by payments extended over twenty years ; and that the properties be so constructed that the owners can work at home w'th electrical power.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I propose this
motion again not for the purpose of discussing it at length, because I did so last session, but in view of a statement made by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Hon. J. A. Calder) at the conclusion of the debate last session. He said:
The subject introduced to the House by the hon. member (Mr. Mowat) is an exceedingly interesting one. I am sure he realizes that it is a matter that should not be pressed at the present time. The Government should have the fullest opportunity to consider the matter in its various details and I am sure hon. members will desire very full light on this question before committing themselves to it.
Nothing so far as I have heard has been done by the Government in this very important matter. I desire shortly, without discussing the particular arguments advanced last session, to state to the House what seems to me to be the present opinion of the country on this question.
There is no doubt that discontent or unrest prevails among some of the returned soldiers. The particular cause for unrest is the fact that they are unable in the large centres of population to obtain suitable houses for themselves and their families. The returned soldier has become a domestic man. Many returned soldiers married in the Old Country, and upon coming here they find it impossible to get houses which are suitable for themselves and their families. In Toronto, where I come from, the soldier very often has to house his family, consisting perhaps of a wife and two or three children, in two rooms in an apartment house at a very high rental; he cannot obtain a house which is suitable for his purposes. The consequence is that the matter has been taken up by the different branches of the Veterans' Association and by the press, with a view to pointing out that this is one of the particular causes of discontent. If a man is uncomfortable in his life, if he cannot look forward to having a comfortable home in the future, that worries him more than anything else, even more than the fact that he may for the time being be out of work, and throughout the country there has been this demand for increased housing facilities. This particular proposition does not come under the housing resolution which was passed last year for giving aid to Provincial Governments in- housing schemes, because that resolution referred particularly and, indeed, only to housing schemes, housing settlements and townsites in congested districts already in existence. That is the very thing to which the people who favour the scheme I am now proposing, object. As an eminent architect said, we do not want to be tied down to some old settlement which has already got anything but a good reputation; we want to start anew. The result is that we have as yet no scheme for homes in an entirely new settlement, such as the schemes they have in England and other parts of Great Britain and in the United States. It is to prevent Canada from being backward and behindhand in this most important matter that I bring this resolution to the attention of the House.
The idea is that land should be acquired initially near cities, large centres of population, so that the man who has never lived outside of a city shall not be taken away to an environment and conditions to which he is not accustomed. We have done a

unless the Government eventually follow the best thought of Great Britain and the United States and erect these villages at not a great sum, taking security for the repayment of the houses which are to be put up, we shall have a crying discontent in Canada which will exist for many years. If there is anything we desire in Canada it is that we shall not be backward. If we are not able to initiate good schemes for the reconstruction of the returned men-and we have initiated many good and novel things for that purpose-the next best thing we can do is to adopt the schemes which have been tried out and found by experience to be successful in other countries. I do hope that the Government will see its way clear, not to put the matter off by saying it must consider it, as it did last session, but to elaborate some scheme in the early future by which this matter can be taken up with energy and brought to a successful conclusion.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: HOUSES FOR SOLDIERS IN GARDEN CITIES.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) who presented the resolution to the House is to be highly commended. I do not know whether my view will prevail with many of the members, but I think this is one of the most important questions with which the Government of Canada has to deal. While I think both the civic and provincial governments have a greater responsibility, there is aq opportunity now, as pointed out by the hon. fnember for Parkdale, to take the initiative in this movement in connection with the repatriation of our soldiers.
I submit that comfortable housing is the first essential for the moral and physical well-being of a community. It is quite impossible for children who have been brought up in the narrow streets of a great city, where two, three or four families are living in one house, to turn out as well morally as they might have done if their parents had houses of their own and were living in the clean countryside with a garden about the house, such as my hon. friend has described.
There is another side. Nothing will add so much to the efficiency of the worker as good home surroundings. The man who goes to work in a factory at 7 or 8 o'clock in the morning, and works eight or nine hours a day, will do more work in that period if he owns his own house in a healthy quarter than the man who comes from a congested section and shares his house perhaps with two or three other families. He finds a greater satisfaction in

his work and gives better results to his employer.
He is a better workman and a better citizen and under present conditions does not live, as so many have perforce to live, not as matter of choice but of necessity. If the plan which the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has outlined were put into effect it would make for the steadying of public sentiment to a degree that very few of us really appreciate. I have given this matter some thought in the past, and I am quite satisfied that if we could make it possible for every man who works in a factory or in an office to own a piece of land and have on it a house which he could feel some pride in being the sole owner of, it would be a tremendous stride in the direction of national contentment; for such a man could bring up his family under conditions that would tend to sound morality, and in the final result we should have a far better citizen in every respect, a man who would' be of great value to the country and would exercise a potent influence on the life of his particular community. In regard to some of our big centres-and I refer particularly to my own city-the reason why there has not been more unrest than exists to-day is the fact that at least 'fifty per cent of the people of our city, for instance, own their own homes. Now, I should like to see the time when ninety-five per cent, indeed, a hundred per cent, of the people could own their own dwellings. In such a condition you would have better communities from every standpoint, physically, mentally, and morally; and what the hon. member has proposed tends in that direction, and therefore h as my unqualified approval. The greatest menace to the good order of the country is the large city with its crowded quarters and oftimes its unwholsesome slums. It could not be other than a menace. When a group of men living in places contiguous to one another for two or three blocks go home after a hard day's work and have nothing to do but sit around the doorstep or stroll idly around the pavements, inevitably they become discontented with their lot, and their discontent breeds the same feelings and sentiments in others. So that very soon the spirit of discontent permeates quite a large field and is found to prevail wherever tractable material affords it lodgment. I say that it is the business of the Government to cortect that state of affairs and make it possible for every man who works in a factory to have his own home so that he may rear his family under heal-

thy and hopeful conditions in order that they may he useful and admirable citizens.
Nothing better could be done for the country, if it were possible, than to take 200,000 people out of the city of Toronto, or out of Montreal, and distribute them around in the smaller centres of the provinces. If
10.000	people could 'be taken from Toronto and transported to Woodstock, and 10,000 to Guelph, a similar number to St. Thomas, and so on, the result would be wonderful. If some of these smaller places could be increased in population to 25,000 or 30,000 and Toronto be reduced to 300,000, the advantage in the social conditions would be mutually great. Every one of the places increased would be better, and it is unquestionable that Toronto would be greatly benefited; certainly it would be a better place to live in. In a town of 25,000 or
30.000	it is possible for a man who works in any factory to cultivate his acre or half acre at least. His family is then brought up under the very best conditions available anywhere, and the hope of this country is in the health of its children and their home influence. If ,we put the citizen in the position to instruct his children in the principles of hygiene and sound morality, and above all to enable them to get out into the fresh air where they will have every opportunity to develop themselves physically, we shall do something that will show an immediate benefit in every corner of the country and in every class of our people. In a campaign in which I was interested in Toronto, I discovered the fact that, in one section of the city, men had come out from the big centres of the United Kingdom, Manchester, Birmingham, London, and so forth, and a minister who was working in that neighbourhood informed me that they were, nearly all undersized and anaemic people. He said, however, that their children would compare favourably with those in any town in the province because they had gone out a distance from the limits of the city, had acquired their own little homes-some of them, comparatively speaking, hardly any bigger than packing boxes -and had given their children plenty of opportunity to play around in the fresh air, with the result that they had benefited immensely in physique, as was evident in their faces and figures every day of their lives. That is the kind of thing in which this and every other Government ought to be interested. I do not think that this Government could take 200,000 people out of any city and spread them around, but I am undoubtedly of opinion that the men who are operating the big industries of the
country would find it in their own interests, as well as in the interests of the whole country, if they would scatter, one here and another there, so as to distribute the population a little more evenly over the province than is the case at present. I believe they would have more contentment among their men and would experience fewer labour troubles, and I am quite sure that the men who work in their factories, together with their wives and children, would benefit to an enormous extent. I do not see how we can do it in any other way.
As I see this project I think that the civic and Provincial Governments have responsibilities. If I understand the motion of the hon. member for Parkdale. he takes the ground that as we are now engaged in the great work of repatriation and reestablishment of the men who fought overseas, that particular work can be made use of to initiate a movement which ought to be taken up by the Provincial and civic governments and extended practically without limit. If this Government could find it a wise and profitable enterprise to use the moneys, or at least part of them, that are to be expended for repatriation ini the way suggested by the hon. member, I have no doubt whatever that such a step would inspire the Provincial Governments, and the provinces might very well undertake a large campaign in that direction, because it is a form' of legislation that comes peculiarly within their purview. After the provinces had done their part, there would still be something to. be done by the civic governments in the great cities within reach of which such model communities might be established. I am not familiar with the geography of the surroundings of Montreal, but I know that in our own city a community such as the hon. member for Park-dale has suggested might be established a little west of Brampton, or going up Yonge street at Thornhill. For an expenditure of a few hundred dollars per acre, and with an electric line running up the main street and easily accessible, sufficient land could be obtained averaging four or five acres upon which these soldiers would make a handsome living if they were able and willing to work. It would be in close proximity to the market, and for all they could produce they would obtain the very best prices that can be commanded in Canada. In my office I have had returned men who formerly were among the steadiest in my employ, but when they sat down to their machines they could do nothing. They would say to me : "Mr. Hocken, I cannot



possibly- do this job." Before the war they were on the job every day, and were in every way steady, industrious and reliable. But three or four years of war had made it impossible for them to settle down before their machines and resume their former occupations. They could not do the work and consequently left the job that had been waiting for them. Now a man of this type if he were assisted to go on five acres of land and were given such advice and guidance as could be provided by the Agricultural Department, would I fancy in a couple of years' time make enough from the produce of his, little farm to keep him in comfort, and he would be living under conditions of outdoor life which his service at the front had made indispensable.
The proposition made by the hon. member for Parkdale ought to be received with very great sympathy by the members of this House and the 'Government. I hope, as he does, that this matter will be taken up seriously. I do not think it is something we should throw aside and say that it is a dream-that it is something that is impracticable. It is one of the most practical questions that has ever been introduced into the House, and it goes right to the fundamentals of our community life throughout the Dominion of Canada. T s'itneerely 'trust that -the question will receive immediate attention.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: HOUSES FOR SOLDIERS IN GARDEN CITIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is just a word or two that I desire to say on this resolution brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat). The matter was before us last year. It was not discussed at very great length; as a matter of fact, I think the hon. member for Parkdale was the only member of the House who spoke on. the resolution, which he introduced at that time.
The proposition which he has placed before us is merely one phase of a very large question .and I am sure that every member of this House will realize that. It is but an. aspect of the general question as to what shall be done in the direction of re-establishing the returned soldier in civil life. I am in. thorough accord with all that has been said-and I think properly said- in- regard to doing everything that is possible in the way of providing for the proper housing of our people in Canada. I do not think there is a member in this House who will disagree with the proposition, that it is the duty of the Government to see to

it that all of our people are housed to the greatest possible advantage and that it means a great deal not only to the people themselves but for the nation as a whole. I think I can say as well that conditions in this country are not just similar to the conditions in the old country. While we may have our housing problem, it is nothing in comparison, to the
4	p.m. housing problem which they have in Great Britain. I am not saying that for the purpose of intimating that nothing should be done in. this direction in Canada; far from it. We will remember some istatement's that were made here when, the question of housing loans, to our provinces was up for discussion; we will remember the pictures that were drawn, by one of the hon.. members for Montreal .and by members from other parts of 'Canada as well.
But, there is a phase of this question that this House would be bound to consider, and that is the question as to the extent to which this is a Federal duty, and the extent of jurisdiction over a matter of this kind. Personally I am inclined to think that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hoclten) has put his finger on at least one of the causes that has led to the conditions prevailing. If the managers or owners of the large corporations which have established industries in this country had just given a little thought to the care of their employees I think we would not have had the crowding of these industries into our larger, centres. The tendency would have been to place these industries in villages of the class that has been referred to by the hon. member for Parkdale, and they might very well have been started there.
The most important work that is now being carried on in Great Britain in the way of establishing garden centres and model cities is being very largely undertaken by those who are interested in the establishment of industries. That is true to a very large extent; although it may not be entirely true. It seems to me that if something can be done in the future to prevail upon those who are establishing industries, not to establish them in or near our large cities, where we have crowded conditions, very much can be done in this direction. I thoroughly agree with what the hon. member for West Toronto said. This is not a dream; it is a practical thing. It would be the easiest thing in the world to put through a law to establish model

cities such as have been referred to by the hon. member for Parkdale. We could buy land, put up houses and, I dare say, get people to go there and live, but do not make any mistake about it-that sort of thing costs money. It is a question of finance. The whole question to iny mind, is: What shall we do in connection with all these various schemes and proposals that have come before the Government? Which is the most practical; which is the one that will do the most towards securing the results that we have in mind ? That is something that must be considered.
We know that the committee that has been appointed by the House to consider the question of re-establishment will have before it, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty different schemes for carrying out that work. We have had a number of clear intimations from the House that endorse the carrying out of some of these schemes, but the Government is limited only by the financial condition in which we find the country at the present time. Although we may desire to carry out certain classes of work, the general financial conditions of the country are such as to make it impossible. This problem will come before our committee. It should be dealt with there just as various other propositions will be dealt with, and I would suggest that the hon. member for Parkdale himself attend in order that we will have an opportunity of going into the question, of taking it up from every aspect and of seeing whether or not it will be possible to come to some conclusion that will be practicable and that will be in the interest of those whom he desires to serve. I am quite sure that he does not desire to press this motion to a. vote at the present time, particularly as that committee has been appointed by the House and will be sitting during the course of the next two or three weeks for the purpose of considering problems such as this in order that it may make a report to the House upon which the House may take action.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Oape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: HOUSES FOR SOLDIERS IN GARDEN CITIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I wish to assure the hon. member (Mr. Mowat), who introduced this motion, that I am in full sympathy with any proposition to provide proper housing for our people particularly in the large centre of population and in other places where the question has become an acute one. I believe that the hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) touches the point of the matter when he brings to the attention of the House the question of jurisdiction involved in this motion. Jurisdiction in regard to property and civil rights clearly belongs to the provincial legislatures. The question of the size of a man's house, the accommodation that he provides is largely a municipal affair to be dealt with by city and municipal regulations. We have no authority in this House to say to n man what the size of his house shall be, whether he shall connect with a sewer, how he shall connect with a sewer, what the sewerage system shall be-questions ail of which pertain to the life of the citizen and which are all important. Hnder our constitution and the division of power in this country, we have nothing to do with such matters. True, we passed a Bill last session, under which by some compromise between our own jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of the provinces we have assumed certain control over health, whether the health of the individual, the health of the family or the health of the people generally. By the use of that Act and the powers which we have taken to ourselves, we could possibly, to some extent, enter into the question of proper housings a proper system of cleanliness, etc., in cities and in centres of population.
Some good may result from this discussion, and if any of the ideas expressed shall lead large corporations and provincial and municipal governments to take steps to better present conditions we shall have done something for the benefit of humanity generally. But I think, Sir, it is very clear that under our Constitution we have no power to buy land and build houses thereon and then say to men who are working in factories: " Here, we have become landlords and we are looking for desirable tenants for our houses. Become our tenants." I do not think it was ever the intention of the Fathers of Confederation that we should go into that kind of business. -I think we should confine ourselves to the encouragement as much as possible of local and municipal governments and employers of labour to take action with a view to bringing about the very desirable conditions so well advocated by the mover of this resolution (Mr. Mowat) and the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). Undoubtedly much can be done to make employers of labour provide better housing accommodation for their workmen. I come from a part of Nova Scotia where we have thousands of men employed in the ceal and steel industries, and I am glad to say that in at least 80 per cent of the housing systems there

provision has been made for small gardens of the type described by the hon. members who are behind this resolution. I trust the day will come when our provincial parliaments will take cognizance of the fact that every employer must see to it that proper provision is made for the housing of his employees.
I have no objection to this motion going to that place which the hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. -Calder) has found as a cure for all the ills that flesh is heir to. He has appointed a committee with blanket jurisdiction to deal with all manner of cases, and I have no doubt that if given an opportunity the hon. member from -Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) will be able to inform that committee what he is seeking to accomplish, and then that committee will, of course, advise him that the matter must, under our Constitution, be dealt with by municipal and provisional authorities.
Mr. SPEAKER- Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

I venture to differ from my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition on the constitutional point, for it seems to me that we have ample authority to take up a matter of this sort. We took these men from Canada and sent them to war, and when they come back it is our bounden duty to look after them if they are without the amenities which decent citizens should have. When the men come back we provide hospitals and soldiers' homes for them, and although it may be said that those are only temporary measures, the principle is the same, and there is no reason why we should not erect suitable dwelling houses, which those men can pay for in due course. I recognize, however, the cogency of the reasons given by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) for referring the resolution to the committee he mentioned, whose powers seem ample enough to discuss this scheme; and while I did hope to press this motion to a vote -and I am quite sure hon. members would *support it-yet I know that under our system if a minister of the Crown asks that a certain course should- be taken, it is only in very exceptional cases that his request is not concurred in. I therefore withdraw the motion.

speechtext:
Moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, whereas the struggle for existence expresses itself largely in the cost of production and the co-st of consumption and whereas confusion and therefore injustice and unrest are developed by the constant struggle to maintain a due relative proportion between these two costs, it is desirable that this House should discuss the situation to the end that the scientific method may be applied in Canada -to the struggle for existence, and whereas it is desirable that the directing head -or Government of the nation should conduct itself and all business, according to the s-aid method to the end that such order and success as attend, for example, the affairs of a department store should he applied to the national business, therefore, be it resolved, that a definite plan of Government in this respect -he laid before the people at the next General Election, and that a committee be appointed for that purpose.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will, with your permission, make a statement with regard to this resolution in order that- that statement may express shortly what I refer to, and after that I will with your permission, make a more extended comment.
1.	Eliminating the weak and the vicious, 90 per cent of the population may be considered as- trying to do its duty and to perform a faithful part in the struggle for existence, ninety per cent therefore may be considered a constant quantity.
2.	Should this constant quantity be considered as a number of free units, or as a united totality? The economic record from the earliest times of the different countries of the world which is most extensive and instructive, furnishes the .answer. The evolution of society shows that what began in free and rival units has developed in theory at least, into a society composed of both free and allied units. In the early era each family is supposed to be free to do as it pleases in its own home, but, later on, when it goes forth from home to earn its living, it inclines to unite with other families. At home it is still comparatvely free. The tendency is towards union everywhere.
3.	The invasion of the freedom of the family in its own circle is being proceeded with, however, chiefly in a moral way. The argument is being put forward that society must be considered only as a vhole. This involves the final stage of development. What has been known as freedom is being put aside for the interest of the majority. The rule of the majority is becoming absolute industrially and morally, but not relig-

iously. Morally and religiously are really one. Hence it will not be long before the rule of the majority will be extended to the religious on the ground of aggregate right as against individual right. This of course, upsets the whole theory of man's responsibility to God, which is supposed to concern the individual. The modern doctrine substitutes the ways of man for that of God. This fact is worthy of note because it shows how surely the national, if not as yet the world aggregate, has come to be considered as one. The constant quantity is becoming so well defined that it is affected only by itself, moving by means of a majority in a certain given or ascertained direction. It may be considered therefore as one man, that is, man and woman.
4.	The struggle for existence has to do with necessaries only. Therefore we simplify the problem we are now considering by eliminating the weak, the vicious and the element of luxuries. It is the man struggling for necessaries of life.
5.	In the last analysis the man whom we
have taken as our unit, to simplify matters, gains his living and that of his family, from nature. When, however, he said to his neighbours:	"Some of you do some
things, some of us will do others, and we will trade," the problem which we are now considering began.
6.	The basis of this trade became nominally the unit of labour cost. Labour produced wealth, and part of the wealth was used as capital. So long as the unit of labour-cost was paramount there was little difficulty. But when men begin to trade so as to obtain where possible, something for nothing, otherwise known as profit, the struggle, not with nature, but against each other, began, and it has continued and become intensified to the present day. It has been partially counteracted by organization, but it expresses itself very largely and terribly in what is known as sweating.
7.	Until the unfair element of securing something for nothing is banished, it is impossible to obtain order in the trade world.
8.	When it is banished and a unit of labour-cost is ascertained and established, it will be easy to calculate the true rate or price of exchange, or trade.
9.	The world really is divided into two parts, economically, the producing and the consuming parts. They trade with each other. When the fair exchange price is based upon the fair exchange value as ascertained for a constant quantity, by a constant unit of labour cost, the problem of the struggle of existence so far as it applies to the trading world, will be solved. The rest depends as they say, upon the individuals themselves. It will be no longer, as at present, a struggle to obtain order out of chaos. It will be no longer an unequal struggle. It becomes a fair fight, definitely ascertained quantities seeking definitely ascertained results. The problem ought to be as simple as one in simple equations. Why is it not solved then, if it is so easy, you ask? I answer:	What
can you do with people who believe in profit, who instead of reducing their common efforts and needs to a common basis, fight them out as if they were all different? We are fast beginning to see the first light of dawn, and then how we will laugh at ourselves, when daylight shows us up.
The modern system of method of science, of course, tests theories by experience, principles by practice. We have not yet. learned to do this in the business or trade-world, and it is to this absolute necessity-that I am presuming to direct your attention to-day.
That the unrest in connection with trade-and business still continues and has no particular likelihood of early settlement is very plain from the fact that we have had sitting in Ottawa during last week an Industrial Conference, the chief bodies represented at which failed to agree. This sort of thing has gone on ever since the modern industrial world developed. It went on under the guilds; it went on under the old village common system when they settled.everything in the vestries, and it is likely will go on till the end of time, attended with unrest, strikes and possibly bloodshed. It is no sign of common sense on our part that we still go on in this blind way. We have asked for the development of State control, but State control cannot fetop it. If the 'State seeks to control any branch of industry and the men in charge of that branch of industry says: Well, take it; we are done with it; then the State has to take it up. In the last analysis, therefore, State control means State ownership.
There was a time when people like free traders called upon the law of supply and demand to solve everything. Well, I have here the report of the Committee on Trusts which was submitted to the Minister of Re-Construction in the British House, Sir Auckland Geddes. I myself sent for this, report, and a more absolute condemnation of that idea could not be found anywhere. This report says:
Sir, we have held fifteen meeting's, and have-heard verbal evidence from witnesses representing the principal trade associations and com-

binations in the United Kingdom. We have also considered written statements submitted to us, in response to invitations issued by representative Trade Associations, combines, large amalgamated concerns, Chambers of Commerce and fedarations of manufacturers, and from individuals and firms in a position to judge the effects of combinations on outside interests. We have received communications from traders in competition with combinations, from merchants, from Government departments, from labour leaders, and from representatives of the Trade and Technical press. We have also made use of such reliable documentary evidence as was readily available, and have considered certain memoranda prepared for the use of the Committee by Sir John Macdonnell and others.
We find that there is at the present time in every important branch of industry in the United Kingdom an increasing tendency to the formation of Trade Associations and Combinations, having for their purpose the restriction of competition and the control of prices.
And believe me, the same thing exists in Canada to-day. The report goes on:
Many of the organizations which have been brought to our notice ha.ve been created within the last few years and toy far the greater part of them appear to have come into existence since the end of the nineteenth century. For reasons which we shall presently discuss, there has been a great increase in the creation of trade associations during the period of the wo r.
The following list of associations connected with the Iron and Steel industry, nearly all of which are definitely known or believed to be 'engaged in regulating prices and output, affords some indication of the extent to which the creation of Trade Combinations has now proceeded. The list does not purport to be at ail exhaustive, even of this one industry.
Then follows a list of some associations in the iron and steel industry, including the following:

The report goes on to say:
A large proportion of them are either permanently or Intermittently price associations, concerning themselves, as a rule, only indirectly with output. In the majority of cases they do not comprise more than a small number of firms, but generally a large proportion of the trade.
Amongst the associations encountered by the Ministry of Munitions there are here about fifty very large British associations, such as the Northeast Coast Steel Makers' Association, the Bailway Makers' Association, the Ingot Makers' Association, the Billet Makers' Association, the Brass Wire Association, Copper Vessel Makers', Silversmith Makers' and so on; an immense list, all engaged in the control of price, at least, if not both of price and output.
There has been also, as you are Aware, a tremendous development in the chemical industry; everything is fast becoming chemical in its nature. Even iron and steel, clothes, etc., are now being tested in a chemical way, and there must be added to this report, as found-by this committee, the whole chemical industry. These are the conclusions and recommendations of the committee :
In the United Kingdom, combinations operating in restraint of trade ,are, though not criminal, unlawful if shown to be against public policy, as public policy is understood by the English courts, where these words are construed in a somewhat narrow and technical sense.
We are unanimously of opinion that it would be desirable to institute in the Unite! Kingdom machinery for the investigation of the operation of monopolies, trusts, and combines, similar to the commissions and other tribunals created for that purpose in the United States of America and the British colonies above referred to. The problems to be considered, before any just conclusion can be arrived at with regard to the actual existence of abuses tending to the detriment of the public, or with regard to a form of safeguard or control which it would be practical to prevent such abuses, if proved, are not matters On which it is possible for a committee such as this to form any final or considered judgment. But we are satisfied that trade associations and combines are rapidly increasing in this country, and may within no distant period exercise a paramount control over all important branches of the (British trade.

We are satisfied that considerable mistrust with regard to their activities exists in the public mind, and that the effect of such mistrust may be equally hurtful to the political and social stability of the State, whether or not the public mistrust and resentment be in fact well-founded. We consider that it is desirable that means should be provided whereby the fullest information as to the activities of trade associations may be made available to the public, and complaints may be promptly and thoroughly investigated, so that doubts and suspicions may be dispelled, or, on the other hand, the true facts ascertained as to evils for which a remedy is required. We believe that it will be found necessary ultimately to establish further machinery for promptly and effectively dealing with such abuses as the Tribunal of Investigation may discover.
In addition to that, there is an addendum signed by Sidney Webb and several other well known men on the committee. The very best men in England are on the committee. This is the addendum:
The fact is that free competition no longer governs the business world. The common assumption that the rivalry of traders affords a guarantee that the price of commodities will oscillate closely about the necessary cost of production-whatever may have been its degree of truth in the past-is now, in this country, nowhere to be implicitly relied on. It is nowadays open to doubt whether we ever buy anything at the cost of production. We find that capitalistic combination, in one or other form, and at one or other stage of production, transportation and distribution, now loads in varying degrees the price of practically everything that we purchase.
To this has been added by the British Government in this pamphlet to which I refer, a report, a study of trade organizations and combinations, in order that it may have a complete bearing on this question. John Hilton, of the Gaston Foundation prepared this for the committee, and he says with regard to the law of supply and demand:
According to those doctrines, evolved In the course of the industrial revolution, supplies, prices, profits and wages could safely he left to adjust themselves. Leave the business world to its own devices, and, competition would ensure that all was for the best. Competition would harmonize supplies and requirements ; would lead to the survival of the most efficient business concerns; and would ensure that the level of wages, prices and profits in any trade or industry would always be "just about right."
The reasons given were as follows:-(a) If demand exceeds supply, competition between buyers sends up the price; (b) a relatively high price spells a relatively large profit; (c) a relatively large profit attracts capital find enterprise to the business; (d) supplies increase; (e) competition between sellers brings down the price to normal, and (f) in the struggle between sellers each endeavours to improve his processes and methods, the more capable succeed, incompetents are driven out, and the general level of economy and efficiency is raised throughout the industry.
This is what he says with regard to that:
The passing of competition.-The assumptions are, however, no longer valid. In the modern industrial and commercial world competition, which indeed never was wholly "free," -is becoming less free with each passing year.
In very many branches of trade and industry, business concerns whose inter-competition is conventionally supposed to maintain prices at a competitive level have, in fact, working arrangements of one kind or another which prevent competition.
Appended to this report is also a very-learned summary by the celebrated Sir John Macdonald, prepared for the Committee on Resolutions, at the instigation of the British Parliament, and he says with regard to modern economic conditions:	x
In proposing remedial or amending measures,
I assume that the law should be based on the existing economic order, and that it should take note of certain prominent facts, a'mong . them these:-
That competition is often wasteful; that it leads to needless multiplication of plants and
staffs, and standing charges; that it increases cost of dti&tribution in many ways ; thait it is often short-lived and precarious; that it is generally followed by combinations; that competition is not an end in itself, and that the motives for encouraging it often cease.
That monopoly does not necessarily mean " artificial dearness "; that monopoly in production and distribution may be attended by substantial advantages; e.g., economy and stability of prices, reduction of standing charges, facilities for standardizing; that there is a tendency towards larger units of production and distribution; that almost everywhere the tendency is towards production on a large scale and the suppression of small businesses;
That combinaton may facilitate interchange of experience and useful technical research work; that it permits of specialising in production and of reduction in the cost of advertising and marketing; that it is favourable to collective agreements and negotiation with labour representatives.
He goes on:
It is suggested that the law as to combinations should take note of all the above-mentioned facts. In the long run courts have followed, though slowly, the teaching of economists. It is suggested that they should come abreast of that teaching.
The remedies here proposed fall under four heads:
(A)	Preventive;
(B)	Disabling or disqualifying;
(C)	Punitive or penal;
(D)	Changes as to procedure and as to courts administering the law.
The remedies belonging to the first category, to which I attach more importance than to the others, are numerous. I do not profess to give a complete list. But they should, I think, include the following:
(a) Accurate and, as regards the chief articles of commerce, fairly complete statistics of prices, which would enable consumers to judge whether a particular combination is abusing its power and raising prices unduly.
We have there a pronouncement by the leading authorities in Great Britain at the

present time upon a subject which is causing the very greatest excitement in this country. It is something, therefore, to which we should give our immediate and most intelligent attention. It is no use our going on from year to year in the way we have been going on in the struggle of one portion of the body politic and of one portion of the industrial world against the other, in a wild effort to find an equilibrium, which cannot be found until certain fundamental principles are applied. When those fundamental principles are recognized and applied we shall be .able to give an intelligent and effective attention to the great problems before us, but in the meantime you see what effects are being produced. It has come very near to revolution in this country, and actually has produced revolution in places like Russia. It has produced revolution before this in France, and is on the very brink of producing' it to-day in Great Britain. Are we then going to confess that we must let evolution and Fate work out their own ends, rough-hew them how they will, and that as for ourselves we are unable to solve the problem and do not propose to try. Is that the attitude of this House? I trust it is not, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have asked the House to give their practical attention to this matter by appointing a committee which will bring in a report to which it is hoped Parliament will give some attention, and if it does, we will get better results than conferences can produce-conferences such as we have seen, where men come together and do not agree. They cannot agree, because they represent opposing rival interests and are not trying to find the fundamentals upon which they can come together.
, Let me say once more that the object of this proposed committee is to ascertain the fundamentals, to present them to the people, and to ask the people to recognize them and govern themselves accordingly.

The motion, as I read it, has two objects in view. It proposes, first of all, that there shall be a discussion by this House. To that, of course, there can be no objection, and the opportunity is now afforded by the motion of discussing the very important question of what remedies it may be possible to devise to meet the conditions on which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burnham) has dwelt.
I have had some difficulty I must confess, in seizing precisely what is the scientific method that the hon. member suggests fMr. Burnham.]
*should be supplied. There have already been suggestions how we might endeavour to meet the conditions to which he refers. We have had a conference, which has just closed, and which the hon. member describes as a conference which had failed to reach agreement. W'hile there may not have been absolute agreement on every-point between all the parties in the industrial life of this country represented at that conference, I think we have reason to congratulate ourselves that with regard to some very important matters it was possible to reach agreement, and with regard to many, progress was made.
As to the practical proposal contained in the motion, if I grasp its meaning rightly, the hon. gentleman proposes that this House should resolve that a definite plan of Government with respect to the application of the scientific method- of dealing with questions concerning the struggle for existence should be laid before the people at the next general election, and that a committee be appointed for that purpose. This last portion of the motion, I must say, seems to me to be hardly acceptable. We are very glad indeed to have an exposition of the views of the hon. gentleman, and if this discussion should be further extended we shall be very glad indeed to have the views of the other members of this House. The expression of all such views furnishes in the first place information, and possibly valuable guidance, to the Government in the formation of any plan of Government to be submitted at the next general election, but to suggest that this House should select a committee for the specific purpose of formulating a plan of Government seems to me to be practically proposing that this House should supplant the existing Government, which, after all, in a sense, is a committee of this House, and hand over to the newly appointed committee what is the proper function of Government, namelv, the preparing of proper plans of Government for submission to the people when it will be proper and we will be called upon t-o go to the people and submit our actions and our then present policies for their consideration. I think perhaps the hon. gentleman, having attained the first purpose of his motion, so far as this House desires to discuss it, will realize that the Government can hardly be expected to accept his second suggestion, which would produce the results I have just pointed out.

speechtext:
The resolution says that it is desirable that the House should discuss the struggle for existence, etc., " to

the end that such order and success as attend, for example, the affairs of a department store should be applied to the national business, therefore be it resolved, that a definite plan of government in this respect be laid before the people at the next general election, and that a committee be appointed for that purpose." National business may mean one thing or another. Whether it means, as is evidently considered by the leader of the Opposition, a commercial policy, from a trade point of view, or whether it means the internal conduct of the affairs departmentally of the Government is what I have not quite clearly before me. The resolution might reasonably be urged upon the Government to devise a plan whereby the internal economy of the Government's own affairs would be reached through the medium of a committee and thereby the expenses of Government be greatly reduced. If the hon. gentleman means that I am very much in favour of the proposition, because in ordinary conversation and parliamentary dissertation we hear continually about the overlapping in the Government service. We hear that instead of having, as in a departmental store, just a sufficient number of employees to do the business a we have one man treading on another's coat-tail and kicking his heels because there are too many clerks in every department. That is said to be true. It may be true, and no doubt under the old system, before patronage was abolished, it had necessarily to be true because every member of Parliament had to bring some one from his constituency to Ottawa for a job. My mind, however, is directed to this point: So far as the resolution relates simply to Canada it relates to a minor portion of the world, and to be effective the hon. gentleman's motion should be world-wide in its scope For instance, how can Canada to-day by a committee provide for its national business in a world sense, in view of the unrest and the unsettled conditions that exist, when Canada does not know the policies of the different nations with regard to trade and commerce and industrial life? Viewed from that standpoint, I think the resolution is rather premature. We have to wait for more normal conditions before we shall know in Canada exactly what kind of policy this country should adopt. Reference has been made to the present period of unrest and revolution in Russia. As I view the situation in Russia, there never was a revolution there. A revolution was manufactured for Russia by intriguers in

Central Europe, principally Germany. I remember a statement made by Rudyard Kipling once, when he said, at the time the Czar was threatened by Nihilists and Anarchists, that owing to the peculiar construction of the Russian nation-a high class of few and a low class of many, the lower class being practically serfs-they were not constitutionally fitted for revolution, and therefore there would be no revolution until the serf learned enough to put his shirt inside his trousers, to quote the exact words; They were mere clods. The revolution in Russia was made for these people. It did not spring from them. It had no hope of being successful. That manufactured revolution has spread until there are fifteen or twenty areas of civil war in Russia today, and she is no nearer the end than she was.
To my mind, the conditions in Canada are not so bad if we will let them alone. We have had the influenza. It was worldwide as the unfortunate conditions arising out of the war have been world-wide. The influenza ran its course, it petered out, and so I feel that the unrest we have noticed in the industrial life of the country lately will also disappear, if we talk a little less about it, think a little less about it and do not strive to raise up nightmares and bugaboos. God knows there are enough outside of this House, on every railway train and on every street comer, who are doing that. The condition of the world because of the terible strain of the war is very much like a disturbed physical condition on the part of a human being. Things come up which decentre a man's nervous system and he becomes a shattered wreck. So the world, because of the great strain under which it has been labouring, is in a condition of nervous prostration, it is suffering from shattered nerves and, as with a man whose nervous system becomes decentred, the only way is to try and get back to normal. It seems to me that it is our duty in Canada to try and get back to that condition. Let us sing more, let us have a little more band playing, a little more music, a little more healthy sport, accompanied by reasonable business activity on a fair basis, and then we will be approaching that era when we will come back to normal conditions.
It is a most remarkable thing that while unrest prevails, our industrial establishments are doing well. Hon. gentlemen seem to be sorry that they are doing so. The wage earner of Canada is getting

higher wages than he ever did in history and even in comparison with the cost of living, because the wage earner, while he lives well, can teach some others how to live reasonably, frugally and well at the same time. The working man to-day is enjoying the advantage of a higher scale of wages than he ever dreamed of. Yet, strange to say, the unrest is there. I have not yet heard it very well explained why there should be this unrest amongst the labouring population when one workman has four or five requests to work for others. It does seem to me that we are getting into a chronic state of mind. I think sometimes that, in this House we have the spirit of pessimism rather than the spirit of optimism, and it is high time that we should allow Canada to have a little breathing spell, a little recreation, coupled with reasonable business activity. Let 5 p.m. the influenza run its course and some day the sun will begin to shine, we will bring the country back to a condition of normal health, and we will get ahead as Canada, in common with every other nation in the world, has a right to get ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon.
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), I would like to say that the proceeding which I have indicated was supposed to be, and is in fact, entirely in line with the usual method of procedure in introducing some variation, or considerable novelty, to the attention of the Government. For example, when they wished to overhaul the Civil Service they asked Sir George Murray to come here and make a report. It was brought into the House, discussed and adopted. There was no reflection whatever upon the Government then. I am making no reflection upon the Government now, nor upon the Opposition, but I am endeavouring to arraign the condition of affairs which exists at large, and if in any manner I have succeeded in pointing out any major propositions worthy of attention, and if the Minister of Justice wishes to suggest that there should be any other body than a committee, and so that we shall not go on here and discuss it and not come to any conclusion, I will agree to anything the Minister of Justice may suggest as to the manner of dealing with the resolution, provided he considers the main principle. I think he rightly understands that it is not the intention to compel him and his confreres to abdicate the functions of Government. I hope they will long continue to ornament the positions which they occupy, but at the same time these things must be gone into, even though the heavens, let alone Governments, should fall.
I have been very well pleased with the position which has been taken by the hon. tlie leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), who, in his usual well-known practical manner, has struck the nail straight on . the head. It has been found by the best men in the world that there is no legitimate competition. How can there be rest when the people of this country, who are trusting to the members of this House to look after their affairs, cry out to them in vain: "If there is no legitimate competition, if when you find that we are being pilloried, that we are being sweated, why do you not do something?" How can we reply and say: "We do not know what to do; we will call a conference; we will think it over, but we will not promise anything; we will go on from day to day and from week to week committing the same blunders?" That is not satisfying the people. That is not right, that is not true, and no man who has a modicum of economic information can say for one minute that a restful condition of equilibrium has been attained.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) has arraigned the Government fearfully. He says that they ought not to have called this conference; he says not to give out to the people that there is any unrest or any cause whatever for perturbation. He says it is true that there is unrest in the country, but on the other hand he assures us that he is an optimist. As you know, the optimist is the man who does not care what happens so long as it does not happen to him. That is a well-known and thoroughly well tried definition, but I believe the hon. gentleman is too kind-hearted a man to think anything like that. He has been led astray by the glibness of his own tongue. He is arraigning the Government more seriously than anybody I know of ever did when he says that they have no business to call this conference and have no business to hold another conference with the farmers, that they should take everything as read and as settled. Grip once pictured Sir John Macdonald as extending his hands over the people and saying: "Be ye warmed and fed," and expecting them to be warmed and fed accordingly. Of course, that was satirical, but it is typical of what is happening to-day. We want no more of that. If we do not understand, or if we are wrong,

let us find out the cause of the conditions of unrest and let us not stand idly by and take no measures to deal with these unfortunate conditions. I therefore press the resolution.
Motion negatived.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first intention when placing this proposition on the Order Paper was to name the date instead of the day as the proper time on which to observe Thanksgiving Day as a memorial of the termination of the great world war. As soon as that resolution had been reported in the press I was deluged with telegrams, and even had a deputation come all the way from Toronto, on behalf of the 'Commercial Travellers' Association and other bodies, agreeing with the principle of observing Armistice Day, but expressing their desire that it be observed on a day instead of a date. Armistice Day, as the House will remember, was observed on Monday, the eleventh of November last. The day lends itself very conveniently to the business of such an intelligent and representative body as the Commercial Travellers' Association, comprising a membership of over 30,000 travelling men, and I had the Bill drafted with a view to meetr ing their desires. It was also called to my attention that prior to 1908 Thanksgiving had been observed on Thursday, and in response to representations made by the same body of men it had been changed from Thursday to Monday.
The reasons for their request are obvious to any one who will consider the situation. The month of November is one of the most important months in the commercial life of this country, for during that month the commercial fraternity place a large proportion of their business for the ensuing year, and if Thanksgiving Day 
should come on any other day of the week than Monday it breaks into a whole week of their business, entailing, of course, a great commercial loss. The day therefore can be as well, if not better, observed on a Monday as on any other day of the week, and it is a well known fact that up to 1908 the observance of Thanksgiving Day, which was on a Thursday, was not as enthusiastic or as general as had obtained in the earlier years. It was easily conceded, therefore, that by changing the day from Thursday to Monday it was an advantage, because the religious part of the Thanksgiving could be observed on the Sunday prior to the date set aside for the holiday, and so Thanksgiving Day developed into a holiday instead of a holy day. I think from both the religious point of view and the point of view of thankfulness there was no loss in that connection.
There is also another feature in connection with this matter which has been emphasized during the past year, and it has been called to my attention in an announcement in the Acadian Recorder, published in the city of Halifax. This is from the issue of May 3, 1919, and is headed " Holiday Mix-ups ":
Halifax always seems to be in a mix-up as to holidays, particularly in the summer season as these days draw near. Victoria Day falls on a Saturday this year, and the Board of Control decided on Monday for the holiday. This will certainly suit those who can leave their employment at 1 p.m. Saturday and do not have to return again until Tuesday morning. But it will not suit those who have business with the banks and public offices. They will be legally closed on May 24, the shops will be open, while on May 26 the banks would be opened, while the stores would be closed. Besides, people in the country who will observe May 24 will find that their order cannot be attended to in Halifax on account of the stores being closed on Monday May 26. If the Ottawa government will declare Victoria Day postponed throughout the country until May 26 there would be no objections, as then there would be uniformity, but if one place celebrates May 24 and the other May 26 it will be a great mix-up. It is understood petitions are being circulated to ask the Board of Control to rescind their resolution. The 21st of June also falls on Saturday this year, though that is a local holiday.
This shows clearly that a movable day is certainly not as desirable as a fixed day in the week for a holiday. In the discussion that took place on the second reading of this Bill, the view cf the speakers was practically unanimous, if we except, possibly, the remarks of the Minister of Justice. The member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), while partly favourable to the date, was, I think, quite satisfied with the proposal that a day, not a date, be fixed.

The member for Brantford shakes his head; so I am not correct in that. But the other four members who spoke were agreed on this point. I refer to the member for West-mount-St.Henri (Mr. Leduc), who was very positive in the matter; the member for St. James (Mr. L. A. Lapointe); the member for St. Denis (Mr. Verville) and the member for PaTkdale (Mr. Mowat). There is no question that it would suit all parties concerned much better to observe the day rather than the date; the event can be equally well observed on Monday as a date that might fall on any day of the week. Anyway, only about four days in a great cycle of years would be out of line so far as the holiday occurring on Saturday, or Sunday is concerned. If it fell on Saturday or Sunday, it would as a natural consequence be observed on the Monday following. I ask the committee, therefore, to grant the expressed wish of the intelligent body of men to which I have referred, the Commercial Travellers' Association. The holding of the holiday on a certain day has also been endorsed by the Methodist Conference which was held at Kitchener on June 2 last, in the form of a resolution which I have on file. It has been endorsed also by the Retail Merchants' A -sociation of Canada, a body representative of over 200,000 establishments doing business throughout the country. It has been endorsed also by the Associated Boards of Trade of Ontario, who held their meeting in March last, before the decision had been reached to change the wording of the legislation from that of the resolution to that of the Bill as drafted by the Parliamentary counsel. I had a visit from the vice-president of that association, who assured me that had the meeting of the Associated Boards of Trade known that it was desired to set a day instead of a date, they would have incorporated that in their resolution.
Subsequent to the second reading of the Bill, I directed the attention of the Chairman of the National Industrial Conference to this matter, who very kindly had the subject discussed on the floor of the House while that convention was in session. He has sent me a statement setting forth the discussion that took place. I quote from the report:

Are there any other delegates desiring to express an opinion on the subject?-Then the secretary will kindly communicate with Mr. I. E. Pedlow, M.P., the message that the subject matter of his Bill was discussed by this convention, and that all the opinions expressed were favourable to its adoption.
Mr. R. A. Rigg, who, I understand, was a representative of the labour element at that convention, made the following remarks with regard to the matter:
Mr. Chairman, in the interval, while we are awaiting something else, I have had my attention called to a Bill which has been introduced into the House of Commons this morning, I think, for the purpose of making the second Monday in November a Dominion holiday, jointly to observe Thanksgiving day and Armistice day, and the member who introduced the Bill, Mr. Pedlow, I believe, is desirous of ascertaining the opinion of this Conference as to whether such a statute is desirable. I think that from the point of view of the representatives of the employees there will not be the slightest objection to that, and I do not believe there will be any from the other side of the House. X beg leave, Sir, to move that this Conference express its opinion in favour of such statutory action being taken.
Mr. S. R. Parsons, a representative of capital at the convention, said:
Mr. Chairman, I believe that we are all ready to approve of the suggestion that in some way we should commemorate Armistice day, and I believe further that the second Monday in November is a far better day for Thanksgiving day than the earlier date on which we have celebrated it in past years.
That remark has reference to the practice which has prevailed in past years of setting aside a day in October as Thanksgiving Day.
I think also that the fact has been made clear that Monday is in our estimation a preferable day for it seems to suit all of us workers better than any day in the middle of the week. We used to have Thanksgiving day on Thursday, and I suppose the United States still have it on that day, but we have come to believe, those of us who work so hard, that it is better to have two days of rest coming together. I certainly am in favour of the sugestion which has been made here and which, I understand, has been embodied in a Bill before the House of Commons.
I noticed an item in the Toronto Globe of Saturday last, as follows:
There is a very general opinion that the day on which the great war really ended-Armistice day, November 11-should hereafter be chosen as Thanksgiving day in Canada. Thanksgiving day in early October, comes too soon after Labour day.
That is another feature of it; if you select as Thanksgiving Day a day in the second week in November, you select a day which will be about midway between Labour Day and Christmas Day.

I am quite in favour of the idea that Armistice Day should be celebrated. But if you set aside as Thanksgiving Day the second Monday in November, you depart altogether from that idea,

because the holiday will not fall on the 11th. The whole idea is to keep fixed in the minds of the people the thought that the nation is called upon to give thanks each year on that day because of the great event that occurred on November 11.
"Mr. PEDLOW: If November 11th should fall on Saturday or Sunday, what then?

speechtext:
Why, just hold
Thanksgiving Day on Saturday or Sunday, that is all. Can the nation not give thanks just as well on Sunday as on any other day? If you celebrate Armistice Day on the 12th, 13th or 14th, the people of the nation, especially the children, will lose sight of the idea of commemorating the 11th of November, for the special event jvhich it signifies. Unless you stick to the 11th, what object is there in dealing with the matter at all? We might just as well pursue the old practice and allow the Government to fix the day. As to its falling on the Sabbath and thus, in some respects, taking away from the holiday, that is an additional reason why I support the proposal that the holiday shall he observed on the Sabbath if it falls on the Sabbath. In my judgment, this country is cursed with too many holidays; they are a vicious interference with business. Perhaps a good many professional men who are members of this House do not realize what it means to have holidays projected into the business of the country every few weeks. If we are going to celebrate the idea of the armistice and to give thanks on Armistice Day for the armistice, in Heaven's name, let us stick to the eleventh, whether it fall on Saturday, Sunday or Monday, or otherwise, let the Government fix the date.

speechtext:
Personally, I have not very strong views one way or the other in regard to this matter, but it seems very largely a matter of sentiment whether we have Thanksgiving Day on Armistice Day or not. But if we are going to have Thanksgiving Day on Armistice Day, or as near to it as we can, I favour the suggestion made by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow) to have the day instead of the date. He told us, very fairly to my mind, that the idea of changing Thanksgiving Day from Thursday to Monday was largely because many men who are known as commercial travellers try to get home for the week end, and in that case they can remain over Monday and have the two days' holiday without its interfering with their work so much as would be the case if Thanksgiving Day occurred in
[Mr. Richardson.!
the middle of the week. It is not necessary to repeat that argument because it was a very strong one, and the Government, in proclaiming Thanksgiving Day on a Monday in recent years, were influenced very much by that.
Another very strong argument is this, that a very large number of students attending college in the different college towns-I happen to live in a college town and I know this from experience-who are half a days railway ride from home can, if Thanksgiving Day falls on Monday, leave on Friday afternoon and remain at home over the week end and spend Thanksgiving Day with their parents. The same thing is true with regard to school teachers, particularly in the rural districts. Teachers who are living away from home can close the school on Friday afternoon, get home for the week end and spend Saturday, Sunday and Monday at their homes. If we made Thanksgiving day always fall on the 11th of November, when the 11th of November would fall on a Saturday, a great inconvenience would result to the business world, because it is very important to have business houses open on Saturday, not only to the business men themselves, but, as we all know, to the people in making their preparations for Sunday.

speechtext:
I spoke on this matter on the second reading and I have very little to add. If there be any sentiment in this matter at all-and I judge that sentiment is at the bottom of the Bill- the eleventh of November and no other day is Armistice Day. If we are looking for a holiday, I quite agree that Monday is the most suitable day. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) says that we have too many holidays, but I do not want to discuss that feature. But if there be any sentiment that leads us to select the eleventh of November for the purpose of thanking Almighty God for the blessings received by the termination of the great war, no day other than the eleventh of November can fill the bill. The hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) was of that opinion when he put his resolution on the Order Paper in the first place. As I said when I spoke on the second reading, at the solicitation of the Brantford Chamber of Commerce I placed a similar resolution on the Order Paper of the Associated Boards of Trade of Ontario, and when I referred it back to them, they said: Stick to the date, so that having referred the matter back to them, and in view of all the conditions that have been brought forward-and I admit they

are important and that we could argue a good deal as tq the propriety of having the holiday on a Monday, and I am sure that would carry if we are looking for a holiday -I am obliged to support the amendment. If we are looking for a Thanksgiving Day, meaning something and having in view blessings received from a certain great thing that happened on a certain day when the enemy was delivered into our hands and the armistice was signed and the world became, to a large degree, at peace, if that is what actuates us-and I think it is what actuated the hon. gentleman when he introduced his Bill-then there is no other day than the eleventh of November on which to celebrate this. If you want a holiday, that is another question altogether, and a great deal of my support for this Bill is taken away if the day is fixed for the second Monday, because I think that destroys the sentiment of the thing altogether. I have, therefore, pleasure in seconding the amendment, and if members will look at the matter in the light in which I have endeavoured to put it in these few words, they will find that the eleventh is the proper day on which to hold this day of Thanksgiving.

speechtext: I wish to express my unqualified approval of the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) for introducing this Bill, but I had no idea that any other date than the 11th of November would have been mentioned. If the second Monday is the day chosen, our children who are growing up will not know without inquiring just on what day the armistice was signed and the world delivered of this war cloud that was hanging over it prior to that date, and as this is a day of great importance in the making of history, the eleventh is the only date. There are three " elevens " connected with the signing of the armistice. On the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the year was the armistice declared and signed, and it is very important that we should stick to the date, the eleventh.

I would like to call the attention of the House to another fact. A good deal of emphasis has been placed on Thanksgiving Day's coming on Monday. Thanksgiving Day was a date arranged by Government, and it was not celebrating any particular event; it was celebrating an annual thanksgiving for a bountiful harvest for the returns for the year, and consequently it could well be fixed on any day that the Government thought would best suit the convenience of the people.
But when we come to commemorate specific days, we say: The first of July was Confederation Day, Dominion Day; we do not say: We will celebrate that on the second or third Monday in July, but we think of it on the first day of July, and if the first day of July happens to be a Sunday, we may defer the celebration until the Monday, but the date in the mind of the people all the time is the first of July. The same is true in regard to Christmas Day and all those days that celebrate or commemorate specific events. I am very much in favour of the resolution except on the point of changing from the date to a day. Let us stay with the date.

speechtext:
If it falls on a Sunday it is celebrated on the Monday. Good Friday and Easter Monday are different, always falling on the same days of the week, although the dates differ every year. I believe that Easter Sunday is the first Sunday after the first full moon after the 21st of March. These two holidays are always celebrated on the same days of the week, so we have a good precedent to guide us.
As to holiday and holy day, I think I covered that fairly well in my previous remarks. Thanksgiving Day up to 1907 had always been regarded as a holiday rather than a holy day, on which there was horse racing, sham battles, and all kinds of sports. Very little church work was done on Thanksgiving Day up to the year when that day was last celebrated on a Thursday, in 1907. The day was then changed at the request of this important body, the Commercial Travellers Association of Canada, and other organizations, and I think the point was well taken by them that the Thanksgiving services could be conducted on the Sunday previous, and the Monday be celebrated as a holiday. That is my idea regarding the celebration of Armistice

Day. There was a certain 'amount of thanksgiving in the minds of the people on the first Armistice Day in 1018, but far more a spirit of jollification. I had mo're fun on Armistice Day than I ever had before in all my life. The telephone girl had me up at 3.30 a.m. She knew I was anxious about the event. We had in Renfrew through a mistake celebrated the signing of the armistice on the Friday previous. On the Monday we went at it again and kept it up from half past three in the morning until after midnight. It was a real jollification. The lid was off all over the town, and we had a real good time, and I think it was the same all over Canada. If we set aside Armistice Day as a day of thanksgiving, thanks could be given in the churches on the Sunday, and Monday be celebrated as a holiday.
As I said on the second reading of the Bill, the children of Israel very wisely set a pile of stones at the river Jordan as a memorial, because it provoked their children to ask questions about it. It will be the same with this memorial day. When it does not fall on the 11th of November, children for all time to come will ask why the day is being celebrated. Judging by the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Doherty), the other evening, he does not think we should celebrate Armistice Day on a certain date every year, but that it would be all right if it came any day within the week.
I submit that we should consider the convenience of the Commercial Travellers' Association and of the retail merchants and the business community generally, as well as the convenience of the schools and colleges. The students at college will naturally want to be home with their parents and friends who may have taken part in the war. We could tell them the story of Passehendaele. Festubert and Givenchy on Sunday and then on Monday we could have horse racing, and those who did not care for that could indulge in other sports to suit their taste.
