speechtext:
There are some objections, I think, to the proposal made in the Bill to observe Thanksgiving Day in November. November in this northern climate .is not an attractive month in which to celebrate a holiday. As a rule, we are not in a very thankful spirit in November. That month may be all right in the United States, where winter does not set in so early, but our bleak November days, when, as Longfellow says,
When the vine still clings to the mouldering wall, And at every gust the dead leaves fall,
[Mr. Pedlow.f
are not conducive to thankfulness. However, 1 can see one reason for the change. By making the change we would be able to commemorate a day on which we were delivered from a great national peril. If we make Thanksgiving Day come on an anniversary like that it will mean something, but if you do not keep the 11th of November, the actual day on which the Armistice was signed, but some other Monday in November, you might just as well celebrate some Monday in September or October, when the skies are bluer and the devotee is in a more thankful spirit. As a matter of fact, if you celebrate as late as the second Monday in November, some considerable time will have elapsed since harvest and we may have forgotten our blessings. The grapes are all eaten by that time and many other fruits. The sentimental argument has some weight, but it does not apply in the case of the Bill, which does not propose to commemorate the 11th of November. I think there is no justification for the Bill as it stands.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) say that in his constituency they celebrate Thanksgiving Day with horse racing. I come from a province where Thanksgiving Day is regarded as a religious anniversary, and I could hardly conceive so devout a man as my hon. friend sitting on a grand stand giving thanks by watching a horse race. He has said that we have a good parallel in the case of the children of Israel, but I am sure they never celebrated Thanksgiving Day in that fashion.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Bill No. 6, to amend the' Criminal Code- Electrocution!-Mr. Mowat-read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Davidson in the Chair.
On section 1-death sentence to he carried out by electrocution:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext:
times carried out sentences of capital punishment; from bodies of citizens; from citizens on grand juries and in county and city councils-in Ontario, anyway,-setting forth the desirability of a change. While I have no doubt that the committee is of opinion that some change should be made, I shall quote some of these expressions of opinion which I have received, with a view to confirming and strengthening that opinion. The Attorney General of Alberta says:
I beg to say that in my opinion electrocution is to be preferred to hanging in the case of a criminal condemned to a death sentence. As the facilities for guarding prisoners are better at the penitentiary than at any of the provincial jails, I am also of the opinion that immediately a prisoner is condemned to execution, he should be confined to the penitentiary. There have been several escapes of condemned murderers during the last few years which is very regrettable from every point of view.
The sheriff of Montreal says:
I endorse unreservedly the proposition to have the Criminal Code amended so as to put execution of capital punishment under the direotion of the warden of the penitentiary in each province. The actual practice of hanging in the jail of the district where the crime was committed is costly and has been the cause of much trouble in many instances.
The difficulty of finding a reliable hangman adds to the hardships of the situation and too often the mishaps of amateurs have been more derogatory than beneficial to the administration of justice. Electrocution is more in accordance with progress and1 a central place of execution in each province, is in my opinion the best method of dealing with the law of capital punishment.
The sheriff at Winnipeg says:
I am in hearty accord with the provisions of the Bill. The present system in force is antiquated, uncertain, and unsatisfactory and I hope you will succeed in having the change in the Criminal Code made in so far as the mode of enforcing the death penalty is concerned.
Under the law we have capital punishment for murder, treason, piracy where force is used, rape, and for the offence committed by persons who are subjects of a friendly State and who try to carry on war in Canada. But the question of capital punishment, concerning which there is great difference of opinion, does not come up in this debate.
I quote the opinion of the (sheriff of Calgary:
It is very satisfactory to me to know that at last this matter is being brought to the attention of Parliament and I trust that the Bill will be passed in due course.
I have had a number of cases of capital punishment where the sentence of the Court has had to be executed, and in some of these cases

the conditions surrounding the execution of the death sentence have not been satisfactory.
The carrying out of the sentence of death by hanging is in my judgment a most inhuman manner, to say the least, and the results obtained by electrocution, according to all the information I have had on the subject, are much more uniform and humane.
This is from the Sheriff of Sudbury:
In counties and districts there is usually no death cell apart from other prisoners; it is difficult to get a death watch and expensive to secure the services of an executioner, and sometimes inconvenient to secure carpenters to build the scaffold, while a lack of experience of most of the county sheriffs is easily understood.
There is a further objection to local executions in the fact that it has a very serious effect on local citizens of high-strung or nervous disposition and temperament, and serious illness has been known to result to numerous people residing in the neighbourhood where the execution has been slated to take place.
The sheriff of Halifax says:
I am strongly in favour of changing the mode of capital punishment to electrocution; also that the death sentence should be carried out in the penitentiaries. I do not think there can he any argument against the change, as it can be carried out with more privacy and safety to all concerned.
The sheriff of Toronto says:
The sheriffs have great difficulty in securing a competent man to carry out the sentence of the Court, and even with a man who has had large experience there is great anxiety for fear that something may happen that cannot be provided against. There has been no bungling at Toronto jail that I have known or heard of except on one occasion many years ago when the executioner arrived at the jail in a state of intoxication. On that occasion the death of the prisoner was delayed very much longer than it should have been by a mistake of the executioner that was not perceived, though very intelligent men were assisting him. There is also a danger that the man engaged to carry out the sentence becomes ill at the last moment or is delayed by accident to the train on which he is travelling. I only know of one man with skill in this matter, though I understand there are several who at times undertake the duty, hut I am told there have been several painful accidents.
The experience of that sheriff is no doubt the experience of other sheriffs, namely, that ithe executioner is nearly always in a highly nervous state. When he gets off the train and it is generally known what his mission is, he is the most execrated man in the community. He is boo-hoo-ed by the boys on the street 'and insulted by everybody in the lower walks of 'life. It is hardly to be wondered at, therefore, that he resorts to means to "buck him up" for his gruesome task. I venture to say that every sheriff has had trouble with the man who is paid to undeAake this duty.

The sheriff of Brant says:
In the first place an execution, especially in a small city or county town, is a shocking thing, where for weeks before the occurrence it is the principal topic of conversation. It is discussed amongst the school children, and I know from experience that every kind of^scheme is devised by certain people to gain access to or interview the condemned man. An execution in a local town has to greater or lesser extent a degrading influence on a certain class of the population. The average jail is not equipped with a death cell or the appliances for the carrying out of the death sentence. In some cases owing to lack of space other prisoners have to be kept in the same corridor. It also frequently happens that the officials, sheriff, governor, etc., are new officials who have never had any experience in capital cases.	[DOT]
The sheriff of Lambton says:
May I be permitted to express my approval of the Bill introduced in Parliament to amend the Act so that capital punishment shall be electrocution, instead of hanging, for the following reasons.
In the first place, the old method is so gruesome as to be repellent, not only to the officials in charge, but to the whole district in general.
A great difficulty will also be the securing of a death watch in such a case; also the uncertainty and difficulty in securing some one to carry out the extreme penalty. In brief, your amendment is a step in advance along the line of humanitarianism. I hope that you will be successful in getting this Bill through.
So, with the sheriff of Lanark. Most of the sheriffs who have written me are of the province of Ontario. It may be said that the sheriff naturally wants to evade a disagreeable duty; but even provided that that is so, it must be remembered that by so doing he relinquishes a considerable part of the remuneration of his office. Therefore, the statements may be received, not entirely qualified by the idea that they wish to evade their duty. Some sheriffs have executed men and they have not done their work well. When Grover Cleveland was running for President of the United States, it was charged against him as a campaign piece of propaganda that he had executed a man. He had; the reason being that he was at one time sheriff of Buffalo, and being a man with a very high sense of public duty, he thought it was his duty to carry out the execution personally. Whether it was done properly or not, I do not know, but that shows the strong feeling that can be aroused in the unthinking public-I will put it in no more offensive terms than that^as to the unpopularity of carrying out the law. The sheriff of Huron says:
It is simply a disgrace that in this day and generation such crude, barbarous and slipshod methods have to be resorted to and allowed, to carry out the sentence of death pronounced on any condemned person, or in other words,
to kill the condemned with the material provided the best way one can under the circumstances. The arrangements may be good or they may be bad, and local conditions for aarrying out an execution are generally pretty bad.
So with the sheriff of Prince Edward county and the sheriff of Essex. The sheriff of Middlesex says:
I beg to say that I am heartily in accord with the proposed amendment for several reasons. The first reason being that we are not supplied with a death cell, that is a cell apart from other prisoners; secondly, the difficulty in securing a competent death watch ; next, the want of experience of sheriffs, the securing of an excutioner, and also the expense of dispoeing of the body, etc.
I have also a communication from the sheriff of Parry Sound. The sheriff of Haldimand says:
I notice that you have a Bill before the House asking to amend the Criminal Code re prisoners who are sentenced to death, that the punishment should be carried into effect on an elecric chair instead of the old barbarous method of hanging. I am astonished that in this Christian country, this system of capital punishment should exist to the present day.
I have also communications from the sheriff of Halton, and the County Council of the county of Halton. The sheriff of St. John, N. B., says:
My attention has been called to the introduction in Parliament of "An Act to amend the Criminal Code (Electrocution)" and to-day I learn that you are the promoter of the Bill.
I am very much in favour of the Bill and hope you will succeed in having the Bill enacted into law.
I have also communications from the sheriff of Algoma and the sheriff of the county of Dufferin. The sheriff of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry says:
I had an execution on March 28 and had trouble getting the scaffold built. Several carpenters and one building firm refused to build it. I finally hired a man at $10 a day and he put it up with the assistance of two prisoners.
I have also communications from the sheriff of Bruce, the sheriff of Welland, the sheriff of Hastings, the sheriff of Peel, the sheriff of Grey, and the sheriff of Prescott and Russell. The sheriff of Kenora says:
People are very largely what their heredity and environment have made them, and it may be necessary to put some people to death for the protection of the community, but in doing so there should be no spirit of revenge connected with the act, hence it should be done in the most humane way, and certainly electrocution is a much more civilized and humane way of putting them to death than hanging, especially where the executioner makes a bungle of the business as he sometimes does.

The sheriff of Thunder Bay says:
The common jails of the province have with one or two exceptions no provision made for the carrying out of the sentence inside the jail so that a scaffold must be built in the yard. The walls surrounding the same are not high enough for the scaffold and therefore a hole has to be dug lin the ground to allow of the drop. It is impossible to get any carpenter to build same here. I could not get one four years ago and I have been unable to get one to promise to do so for the execution that is fixed for next month.
I have also communications from the County Council of Haldimand, the County Council of Norfolk, the sheriff of Norfolk, the Board of Control of Hamilton, the Wentworth County Council, the Grand Jury of Peel county, the County Council of Lambton, the Grand Jury of Brant, the County Council of Prince Edward, the Municipal Council of the County of Fron-tenac, the Middlesex County Council, the Town Council of North Bay, the Grand Jury of Wentworth, the County Council of Perth county. The County Council of Huron say:
This council approves and strongly recommends the passage of the Bill, being of the opinion, that hanging is a barbaric method and one which cannot be effectively carried out in county jails.
I have also a communication from the Grand Jury of Middlesex. A fine point arises here; one of the ever-recurring conflicts in constitutional law between the Dominion and provinces. The point has been raised-I must say I anticipated it- that the Dominion cannot carry out this provision. It will be noticed by looking at the whole Bill, that in the clauses subsequent to clause 1062, the words " warden of penitentiaries " are substituted for the word " sheriff." That transfers the carrying out of the sentence to the warden of the penitentiary in each province. It seems to me essential that this should he done in one place in each province just as is the case in the state of New York, in a perfectly equipped place, and the proper place will be the penitentiary, because there is no county jail, I should imagine, in any province where proper rooms could be had or where it would be fair to make certain counties assume the whole expense of carrying out all the executions in that province. Under section 92 of the British North America Act there is committed to the province, "the administration of justice," part of which would be this: that is to say, the carrying out of capital punishment comes within the realm of the administration of justice. Under section 91, subsection 27, the Dominion has power to deal with

" criminal law, except the constitution of courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters." Of course, this is not procedure in criminal matters, because when a man has been condemned, the eniminal "procedure" .stops. The Dominion dlso has charge of:
The establishment, maintenance, and management of penitentiaries.
What I had in mind when drafting the Bill so as to make the warden the executioner instead of the sheriff was that this constitutional difficulty could be bridged over by making the warden a provincial officer ad hoc for carrying out the sentence. There may be difficulties in that which I do not wish to take on, and I am willing, if the House will allow me, to ask that all the clauses in the Bill shall be withdrawn except clause 1062 which provides:
Section one thousand and sixty-two of the Criminal Code is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:-
1062. In all cases where an offender is sentenced to death, the sentence or judgment to be pronounced against him shall be that he be electrocuted.
All the other matters which are supposed to be matters of provincial jurisdiction, such as the inquest, the persons to be present, the certificate of death, the declaration by the warden, the identity and death to be proved, the place of burial and so on, shall be cut out and left for discussion between the Minister of Justice and the attorney generals of the several provinces, and I am sure there will be no real difficulty in their coming to a conclusion as to what should be done. As the matter stands now, the public hangman is a joint nominee. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is disposed to correct me in that, but he can state the fact as it is.
What I understood was that in view of a lot of bungling and the dreadful things that have taken place in the gaols, the provinces and the Department of Justice, before my hon. friend became minister of that department, agreed that there should be one person nominated hangman for the Dominion, and that the expense in connection therewith should be contributed in proportion by the province or the sheriff, and the Dominion. If that is not so, I shall be glad to correct the statement.
That there have been dreadful bungling and scenes revolting in character owing to the inefficient carrying out of our present method, nobody can deny. In the last few months there have been two cases at any rate which stand out in the public mind

as examples of a condition that should not be tolerated any longer, and which I am quite sure have prepared the public mind to accept this Bill. I need not go further than allude to the execution at Edmonton in April last. I wrote to the reporter of the Edmonton paper who witnessed that execution, and he was good enough to send me this report of what took place:
The execution took place at the provincial jail at Fort Saskatchewan about 5.45 on the morning of April 23. Every detail had been arranged beforehand. The convict with hands tied behind his back was placed upon the scaffold and when properly hooded and the noose adjusted, the executioner pulled the lever. The trap door swung apart. The body hung still and apparently lifeless. The hangman hoisted the black flag and left the scene, everything for the moment evidently satisfactory.
In a few seconds, however, the man began to kick and wriggle his body and succeeded in getting his hands unfastened. The hangman being recalled, re-adjusted the rope and the man died in about 10 minutes. It was stated by some one that the neck had not been broken but that the man had been strangled to death. The verdict of the jury was ''justifiable homicide."
Only this month in such a city as Montreal another mistake was made by the public executioner, and this is the account as telegraphed from Montreal to an Ottawa paper-I shall quote only one or two sentences :
Untold Agony is Suffered by Murderer.
An (hour after the bolt was released which launched his body into space he was still alive, the drop failing to break his neck. Ten minutes after the man was cut down the jury went to see the body, but found him alive although half strangled. Dr. Benoit declared that the heart ceased beating eight minutes after the hanging, but there was great muscular twitching until 9.02, when it ceased. He could not say the man was dead as long as this continued.
This is a horrible state of affairs, and when it can occur in a great metropolitan city like Montreal what can we expect of little jails where the sheriff has an execution perhaps only once in ten years? The Globe, of Toronto, in commenting on these events in Montreal, said on September 13:
Hanging as a method of capital punishment should be abolished after the disgraceful bungling in Montreal, where an Italian lived for more than an hour after the drop.
Surely the House of Commons of the present day cannot but see its way to accept this legislation amended as I have suggested, substituting electrocution for the worn-out and barbarous method of hanging by which a man, instead of having his neck broken, may be strangled and suffer untold agony struggling to be free from his pains.
Let us show that we are alive to what is demanded by the public and demanded by humanity itself.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext:
Before this amendment is adopted I have a suggestion to make to the House, which I trust will meet with its approval. I congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) in the efforts he has made to make the death penalty less barbarous and less repulsive to our modern thought and feeling. I was very much struck with the statement of a certain sheriff which he quoted-I think it was the sheriff for the united counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry. That officer stated that he had found it hard to get carpenters who would work for even ten dollars a day in the putting up of a scaffold.
I know that for years past it has been with the greatest difficulty that the authorities could find men who would perform the service of hangman, and I think that to substitute electrocution for hanging is a step in the right direction. But when we are at the business, could we not go a step further, could we not abolish the death penalty? If we did that we should put ourselves in line with fully three-quarters of the most advanced people on the face of the globe. We should not encourage crime, but discourage it, because, strange as it may appear, history teaches that the more brutal and the more awful the punishments the less repressive their effect seems to be. I have merely to refer hon. members to the history of British criminal law. A hundred years ago there were scores of offences upon the criminal statute-book punishable by death. If a young man stole a few shillings' worth of food he was liable to be transported, or even hanged. Hanging was quite an ordinary occurrence. I remember attending a meeting at Montreal a few years ago where a very prominent man from the United States came to speak on this question of capital punishment. I went to that meeting with an open mind, but the arguments which he brought forward on capital punishment convinced me. He pointed to what other civilized nations which had abolished the death penalty were accustomed to do in regard to serious crime, and then he made this assertion: The death penalty, he said, encourages crime in this respect, that the riien who go to the electric chair are regarded as the heroes of the underworld; just as the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church in other spheres of life, so the death of these men raises them in the estimation of all the underworld, and they are looked up to with what is akin to veneration. This may appear inexplicable to us,

but this was a man who had been, if I mistake not, governor of Sing Sing penitentiary, and he was one of the recognized authorities in the United States upon this subject.
It has been proven by the history of many European countries that when they abolished death penalties they did not, by so doing, increase the number of murders.
The statistics of murders in one state, the name of which I cannot recall at the moment, were most 'illuminating. They revealed the fact that in the period during which the death penalty was suspended the number of murders decreased. The death penalty was re-imposed, and concurrently with its re-imposition the percentage of murders increased. If that fact can be taken as an exemplification of a general rule, then it was perfectly clear that the death penalty was not a deterrent of murder. Now, there are those who will quote Scripture to me and say: " He that taketh a man's life shall be-" I cannot quote exactly, I am sorry to say.

What about the leader of the Opposition? (Mr. McKenzie).
Mr. MdMASTER:	The point I wish to
make is this, that the old Mosiac law, " An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,'' has, in my opinion, been superseded by a different system. We are living under a more magnanimous and humane dispensation. Is it not rather humiliating to our civilization that when a man commits a heinous crime the only thing we can do with him is to put him to death? Does it not to a certain extent smack of the old idea of vengeance? I move, therefore, seconded-by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow), that instead of section 1062 of the Bill there should be substituted these words:
The death penalty Is abolished and all crimes heretofore punishable by death shall be punishable by an incarceration not to exceed the remainder of the life of the accused.

That is kind.
Mr. MoMASTER:	Perhaps an amendment like this would come with better grace from the gentleman (Mr. Doherty) who is in such a distinguished manner leading the House to-night. There is, I grant you, a smack of Hibernianism about the amendment which I propose, but I do not wish

to suggest that the life penalty must be imposed in all cases, and that is the reason why I hawe framed the amendment as it is worded. I commend it to the good-will of the House, and although the Bill proposed by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) is a long step in the right direction,-for which reason I intend to support it,-I believe that if my amendment is received it will constitute a still longer step in the right direction and make the other provisions of the hon. member's Bill unnecessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) that the House is at present in Committee and that no amendment can be made in Committee which changes entirely the principle of a Bill which was adopted by the House upon its second reading. The principle of this Bill is to replace hanging by electrocution, whereas the principle involved in the sub-amendment which is submitted by the member for Brome is to abolish the death penalty altogether. That in my judgment should form the basis of a new Bill and I therefore rule the subamendment out of order.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext:
I am opposed to the
measure introduced by the hon. member for Parkdale, on the ground that it is an invasion of provincial rights. Hanging is within the purview and scope of the provincial authorities and to seek to foist it upon the Dominion authorities is to my mind unconstitutional. With regard to the change from hanging to electrocution, I fear that the glowing picture which the member for Parkdale has drawn of the simple manner in which the life of the *convict can be taken by means of electrocution might act as a stimulant to crime rather than a deterrent. The gruesome scenes which the hon. member depicted of the hanging of various murderers 'throughout the country, with sometimes more or less abortive results, would in itself, it seems to me, be the deterrent which society requires to put an end to murder as far as possible. The member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), kind-hearted man that he is, wished to make it more simple even than would be possible under the system proposed by the member for Parkdale. The member for Brome suggests that instead of execution the convict should, as he picturesquely put it, be incarcerated for a period not to exceed the term of
9 p.m. has life. The hon. member evidently does not agree with the

Irish writer who 'thought that life imprisonment wiajs much more serious than death itself; for that writer says that by life imprisonment you take away the man's life but you do not give him death- I do not know that there has been such a Strong desire throughout the country for a change of the system as to justify this Parliament in instituting a change. The system is a good old English one, consecrated by a thousand years of practise, and so long as there are murders, just so long, I suppose, we shall have to resort to capital punishment. We all know the famous expression of the French writeT, Alphonse Karr, who said he was in favour of the abolition of the death penalty, but that he was also in favour of the murderer first 'adopting that principle. I think that under the present system we have worried along fairly well. The member for Parkdale has spoken about the views of sheriffs; they would like to shift the responsibility on to the wardens; but we have not had any expression of opinion from the wardens as to whether they would care to assume -that responsibility. There ought to he throughout the country a strong agitation demanding a change before this Parliament should seek to disturb the present system. I am rather surprised that a stalwart Britisher like our good friend from Parkdale should desire to abolish the British system and substitute the American. "No truck ot trade with the Yankees" was, a few years ago, almost a classical quotation.

speechtext:
Not from the member fox Parkdale, then.
Mr. JACOBS. The member for Parkdale must have been inoculated with the idea at that time, because I do not think he could have undergone a change so suddenly. Now, if this system is good enough for the British people I am inclined to think that t'he member for Parkdale should he content to let it continue for some time yet in Canada. For these reasons therefore I declare myself opposed to the amendment.

speechtext:
First, I think the bon. member for Parkdale has made a very excellent case in support of the proposition which he submits to the House. I quite agree with him when he says that the method to which my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) has just referred as being a classical one and having been in use for more than a thousand years, is decidedly unscientific, very barbarous and something which we have outlived. The hon. member
for Brome (Mr. McMaster) advanced the interesting argument that hanging encourages crime, if I gathered what was suggested correctly. He told the committee that when a criminal was hanged he became a martyr to his fellow-criminals of the underworld. I can advise the hon. member for Brome and the committee that in the territory I have the honour to represent hanging never encouraged crime.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext: What is that?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext: The hon. member for Brome says that 'hanging encourages crime.

speechtext: In his county, perhaps.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-ELECTROCUTION.
speechtext:
In his county, perhaps, but it does not in the Yukon Territory. We have hanged every man that ever committed a murder, we hanged him quick and it has had a very deterrent effect Ujpon other would-be murderers. Just across the line the Americans have the territory of Alaska. I do not know how many capital punishments have taken place since the Americans purchased that territory from Russia in 1867, but there have been very few, and murders in Alaska are comparatively common, simply because the would-be murderer knows that he has a remarkably good chance to escape the gallows. In Alaska life is held cheap by the criminal class as compared with the way it is regarded by the same class in the Yukon Territory. Ia the Yukon, if a man goes out to kill another, he knows that the law is going to be after him from the time he thrusts the knife or pulls the trigger, or in any other way takes life. They never let up till they get him, they bring him to Dawson, and he is hanged on a scaffold in full sight of anybody who wishes to see the gruesome deed done. It is a gruesome deed, but it has to be done. I am absolutely opposed to the abolition of capital punishment, and if the hon. member for Brome had lived on the frontier as long as I have, I do not think he would be in favour of its abolition. . I am glad the amendment offered by the hon. member for Brome was ruled out of order. I am in favour of the method proposed by the hon. member for Parkdale of carrying out the sentence of the court. It is much more humane and scientific; it is no experiment; it has been tried, and tried successfully, for thirty years, by one of the most intelligent commonwealths on this continent, namely, the state of New York. The evidence submitted by the hon. member for Parkdale, given by the physician in

charge of Sing Sing penitentiary, goes to show that the sentence is carried out with remarkable simplicity and -with equal effectiveness. I have great pleasure in supporting the Bill submitted by the hon. member for Parkdale.

speechtext: I understand that what is now before the Chair is a proposed amendment by the hon. (gentleman (Mr. Mowat), striking out all the clauses except the clause to substitute electrocution for hanging. I would suggest that the committee might perhaps adopt that amendment before the committee rises, because it is my desire to move that the committee rise and report progress in order that it may be possible to adjourn, the House so as to permit of the members having an opportunity of paying to our late confrere and colleague, the Hon. Mr. Cochrane, that tribute of respect which would consist in following his remains to the station. The funeral, I understand, is to take place in Toronto on Wednesday. Though it may not be possible for us to attend the funeral there, I think it would be a satisfaction to our feelings and to our desire to express our regret if we should have the opportunity of accompanying his remains at least to the station this evening. I would suggest that before doing that the amendment should be submitted, and then I propose to make the motion that the committee rise.

speechtext: Before the committee rises I desire to record myself as being in favour of the Bill of the hon. member for Park-dale. I cannot -conceive why, in a modern, humane world, this should need any argument. It seems to me that all men who have the cause of justice and humanity at heart, if they still wish to retain capital punishment, should desire at least to make it .as humane as possible to those who may be the victims of it.

What is proposed now is to allow the hon. member to with-

draw part of it.	The effect of the
present amendment is simply that the hon. member who proposed the Bill withdraws the measure with the exception of one section which would remain and which, as the Chairman has pointed out, would come before the committee again for consideration. The hon. gentleman in withdrawing these sections has acted upon a suggestion of my own in which I have pointed out that it seemed to me quite clear that we should not mix up the administration of justice in the way proposed. The administration of justice belongs to the provinces; the execution of these sentences is the execution of the judgments of provincial courts, and they are executed by officers of these provincial courts. The hon. gentlemen, in deference to my suggestion, desires to withdraw these sections of his Bill. We are not accepting anything by passing the amendment. These sections will be struck out, and there will remain before the committee the point in regard to the substitution of electrocution for hanging which will be dealt with later on. However, I have no desire to insist upon disposing of the amendment at the present time if it is thought better that all these provisions should still remain before the committee. I thought that would be a definite step of progress before the committee reported. I suppose we can report progress without having done that but I would like that in any event we should be enabled to rise now so that we may be able to perform the duty which I have mentioned.

That is why I said we could not accept any part of these arrangements.

I shall do that as briefly as possible. I was informed, then, that the hon. member had delivered himself of a series of evasions, half-truths, and absolute falsehoods which he had characterized as a reply to some observations I made in this House on the evening of March 19, 1918. Now, .Sir, since my return to the city I have had an opportunity of reading Hansard containing the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman on Wednesday last, and to-day, with your permission and the indulgence of the House, I desire to occupy a few minutes in dealing with such of these statements as are of a personal character and that reflect upon .my alleged conduct as a member of Parliament and upon what I am alleged to have said, but which, as a matter of fact, I did not say.
The rules of the House, Sir (as the hon. member for Durham and all other hon. members in this House know), prevent me from dealing with falsehoods of a general character contained in the speech made by that hon. gentleman on Wednesday last; therefore I cannot do more than state that I will deal with these statements at the first opportunity at the beginning of the next session.
Now, Sir, in reading Hansard of the seventeenth instant, I. observe that the hon. member for Durham characterized my speech of March 19, 1918, -as. an "attack." In point of fact, Sir, my speech was a review of the general election of 1917, and in part was a reply to an attack made by the hon. member for Durham, in a speech delivered at North Bay, upon the members of certain French religious orders and upon others whom he assailed for alleged lack of sacrifice. My references to the hon. member for Durham were merely to compare his sacrifices with those of the people whom he attacked during the general election. In Unrevised Hansard-

I was just about to do
that, but I did not think that either you, Sir,-with all respect-or the House would be fully seized of the denial unless I made that preliminary explanation.
Now, in Unrevised Hansard of September 17, at page 406, the hon. member for Durham is reported to have spoken as follows:
It has been said in the press that I was in the House or at least in this building on the night in March, 1918, when the member for Russell made his attack.
" His attack," you will observe, Mr. Speaker-I have explained that my remarks were a reply to an attack. I have had to correct even a Toronto university professor for the misuse of that word.
I think Le Devoir -and some of the other papers reported that I was around the House that night but kept out of the Chamber. I regret to say I was at home in my bed that night under the doctor's orders. There is a custom which has become an honourable tradition of this House, that when one member desires to rise in his place and make an -attack upon the position or character of another, he gives that hon. gentleman due notice. I received no notice. I was in the House in the afternoon, and notwithstanding my indisposition, if I had received any notice, I would have come back that night.
You will observe that the hon. gentleman admits that he was in the House in the afternoon of March 19, 1918. He was here when I rose to speak just before six o'clock, and when, through your courtesy, Sir, and the courtesy of the light hon.

Prime Minister, an adjournment was granted so that I should not be obliged to begin my speech until the House resumed for the evening session after eight o'clock. The [DOT] hon. gentleman, therefore, knew that I had the floor, but he says that he was indisposed and did not come back that evening.

speechtext:
I think on Tuesday last the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) made inquiry of the Government as to the constitution of the membership of the Industrial Conference which was in session last week, and whether the evidenae taken by the Royal Commission on Industrial Relations in Canada, which was appointed earlier in the year, was to be printed. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) and his deputy were very busy with the conference last week and it was impossible for me to obtain the answer before Friday last, when, owing to an oversight, the answer to my hon. friend's question was not given to the House. There was not an opportunity for me to do so yesterday, so with the leave of the House I should like the question and answer to he incorporated in Hansard.
Questions by Mr. Archambault:
1.	Why were the National Labour Unions of the Province of Quebec and the Circles Catho-liques who represent a very large number of employees and who, according to the report of the Commission on Industrial Relations in
Canada, are an important labour factor in the province, entirely ignored by the Minister of Labour in issuing invitations to the National Industrial Conference?
2.	Why has the evidence taken before the Commission of Industrial Relations in Canada not (been printed, and why is it not available for the instruction of the members of the National Industrial Conference, who have asked for it?
3.	Is it the intention of the Government to have this evidence distributed before the end of the conference?
4.	Is it the intention of the Government to have this evidence printed before any legislative action recommended by this conference is considered?
Answer:
1. In securing nomination of delegates to the Industrial Conference it was impossible to have regard to each isolated unit of labour organization, and nominations were therefore requested only from (a) the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, to which the great mass of local trades union branches are affiliated, and (b) Canadian Railway Board of Adjustment No. 1, as representing the Railroad Brotherhoods, these important organizations not being affiliated with the Trades and Labour Congress. National and Catholic unions are not, so far as has been learned, affiliated to any central body and it was not deemed practicable to request nominations. Returns collected by the Department of Labour show a trades union membership in Canada at the end of the calendar year 1918 of 248,887, including 2,787 members reported by the National and Catholic unions of the Province of Quebec.
2 and 3. The evidence taken before the Commission was undoubtedly of much value and deserved and received a careful scrutiny at the hands of the Commissioners before the latter made their reports. The evidence was of a voluminous character and would, if printed, occupy some thousands of pages. It has not been deemed in the public interest to incur the large expenditures which would be entailed in printing and distributing the same.
4. The matter will receive careful consideration.

I shall try and set a good example, Mr. Speaker, in observing the rules of the House. In view of the fact that the Belgium Government some time ago presented a very suitable site at Ypres, and the French Government a suitable site at Vimy Ridge, for the erection of memorials to our Canadian 'boys who fought and have fallen in those places, I should like to ascertain from the Government-I do not want the answer to-day-[DOT] what steps they are taking for the erection of these memorials, of whatever description they may be.
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia): I saw the article to which my hon. friend has reference, I think, in the paper some time ago. It was proposed that the Canadian Government should erect in Flanders memorials commemorating the various actions of the Canadian corps at the front. The matter was taken up by the Overseas Ministry and the High Commissioner, and an officer of the Canadian Engineers, Colonel Hughes, was delegated to look over some sites and try and locate suitable property. I do not think that Colonel Hughes is a relative of my hon. friend.

He is a good man all the same.
Major-General MEWBURN: He made a very exhaustive survey of the various grounds, the details of which I have not with me. Eight sites were to be selected on which it was proposed to erect memorials in commemoration of the various battles in which Canada took part and of the sacrifices she made. Memorials were contemplated to commemorate Vimy Ridge, the Somme, and other celebrated battles. A minor survey was made of these properties, and it was understood that the French and Belgian governments would convey them to the Canadian Government. Colonel Hughes is now in France endeavouring to arrive at a satisfactory arrangement with these respective governments in order that the particular sites that are finally selected

speakerposition: stagedirection

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3 for carrying into effect the Treaty of Peace between His Majesty and certain other Powers.
'Some hon. MEMBERS: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
The Bill which is now before the House is very brief knd clearly sets forth the purpose which it seeks to attain. This, together with the fact that the Bill has already received an explanation on its introduction and its first reading, and the further fact that we have had a somewhat prolonged and, I think, a very exhaustive debate upon the Treaty which is to toe given effect to under the provisions of this Act, should make it unnecessary for me to speak at any length in moving the second reading of the Bill. In its terms, the Bill is similar to one which has been adopted in the British Parliament in order .to attain so far as Britain is concerned, the same end. There it served the purpose which is not necessary here; it served as a means of expressing the approval of Parliament of the Treaty itself, that approval being inferred from the fact of its conferring upon the executive government the powers necessary to carry out the Treaty in all its provisions. This House has already expressed its approval, so that this Bill is to . enable the. Treaty to be carried out and give effect to its provisions. The Bill, in order to attain that end, proposes to confer upon the Governor in Council the power to make such appointments, establish such offices, make such Orders in Council, and do such things as appear to he necessary for carrying out the Treaty. That is the provision of subsection one of section one. Subsection two is merely a provision to enable such orders as may be made to he properly enforced, providing for the imposition of penalties in respect of breaches of its provisions.
The third paragraph provides merely for the expense to be incurred in carrying out
[Sir George Foster.!
the Treaty and which is to be defrayed by moneys provided by Parliament.
I think it may safely be said that the steps which it is proposed that the Governor in Council should have power to take in virtue of this Act are of an executive character or nature. The Treaty itself determines the rights and obligations of Canada, in common with those of the other parties to it. There remains, we having approved 1'reaty, to provide for the means of giving it effect, for the method in which the rights conferred are to be exercised, and likewise the method by which any obligations which may result from the Treaty and which call for action on the part of the executive government, may be given effect to and carried out. I think it is safe to say that the orders which will, require to be made will not be, properly speaking, in the way of legislation. They certainly will not involve legislation of any permanent character, but it will be necessary to make provision from time to time for carrying out the different provisions connected with the Treaty. As giving an instance, one might refer to the economic provisions of the Treaty. I refer particularly to those provisions which confer upon Canada the right of liquidating property of German nationals situated in this country and of making provision for how the proceeds re-sultmg from that liquidation are to be applied. It will be necessary no doubt to lay down regulations prescribing the mode of procedure in connection with that liquidation and the means to be taken for the disposal of such moneys as may result from it. We also have provisions in the Treaty in regard to the relations of debtor and creditor which may exist between nationals of the respective countries-the nationals of Canada on the one hand and the nationals of Germany upon the other. For the purpose of giving effect to the . provisions it will also, in all probability, be necessary to make regulations prescribing just the particular manner in which they are to be carried out. That manner will differ accordingly as this .country .should decide to adopt the system which in the Treaty is described as. the clearing house system, or should exercise its right of refraining from availing itself of this privilege. These I give only as instances, and I think that probably they are instances of the most important matters in regard to which it may be necessary to make orders in the nature of regulations.
I think that what I have said should serve to make clear what may be described

as the principle of the measure. What the House is asked to assent to, in so far as the principle involved is concerned, is the conferring upon the Governor in Council of the power to do those things which will be necessary to the execution of the Treaty. Having approved, as this House has unanimously approved of the Treaty itself, I should anticipate that there could be no very serious ground of objection to the power being conferred that is necessary in order to give effect to the Treaty. I would like to point out that there is no general power of legislation conferred. The powers to be exercised are strictly confined to the limits of the Treaty itself and to such regulations as may be necessary and will have to do with the enforcement of the rights of the kind that I have mentioned and with the performance of such duties resulting from the enforcement or execution of those rights as may result from the terms of the Treaty.
I beg therefore to move that this Bill be now read the second time.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I wish to refer very briefly to the Bill but before doing so I would remind the Minister of Justice that according to a promise made by himself, .and I think also toy the Prime Minister, every member of the House has the opportunity to discuss any phase of the Treaty when considering this measure. The hon. gentleman .may have forgotten that promise, but I wish to remind him of it so that any hon. gentleman who wishes to discuss the Treaty may, according to the promise made by the Government, avail himself of the privilege now.
When -we were discussing the Treaty itself I pointed out to the Government that I did not think we had power on our own account to make .a Treaty. This Treaty which has been consummated, and which we have discussed, is a Treaty between Great Britain and some other powers. It is perhaps not a treaty in which any body specifically undertakes to do anything for Great Britain, but it is an undertaking, or an arrangement by which Great Britain binds herself to do certain things, in which treaty foreign powers concur. It is therefore a mutual obligation and contract between two or more countries and is in the nature of a contract, or otherwise a treaty. Under the arrangement at the Peace Conference Great Britain has entered into the Treaty, and having done that I do not think that we, as a part of the Empire, have any power to enter into another or concurrent treaty, under the sections of the British North America Act which I quoted at the time we were debating the Treaty itself. Section 132 of the British North America Act reads:
The Parliament and Government of Canada shall have all .powers necessary or proper for performing: the obligations of Canada, or any province thereof, as part of the British Empire towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the Empire and such foreign countries.
Now in respect to obligations in connection with the Treaty, arising by reason of any undertakings that Great Britain entered into and which require money to carry out, we have power to provide those moneys under the section I have quoted; but if we start out to make treaties ourselves then, as far as I can read the Act, we have no power to at all events so far as the letter of the Constitution is concerned-supplement those obligations by money votes, or

by providing for the expense of carrying out the provisions of a treaty which Canada itself has entered into. It is perfectly clear that we have power to furnish the money to carry out any obligations that fall upon this country as a whole, or any province of it, by reason of a treaty entered into by Great Britain; hut I find no authority for providing money to carry out the terms of a treaty which we make ourselves separate and apart from the Mother Country. I simply point this out to the Minister of Justice as he may have some understanding, or explanation, from the constitutional standpoint to give as to why, or upon what principle, we depart from that section of the British North America Act.
Now we come back to the old difficulty of Orders in 'Council. I want again, Mr. Speaker, to register my protest against this country dealing with foreign countries by Orders in Council.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
It is a 'loose and lax enough system that we should be dealing among ourselves, or dealing with our own people, by Orders in Council; but when we come to make regulations enabling the Government to enter into foreign relations with the United States, or with France, or Belgium, or any of the other kingdoms of the world, by Order in Council I think it is carrying that privilege much further than we should allow it to go. The Minister of Justice tells us that most of the matters for which we are to provide are set forth in the Treaty itself. If these matters are set forth in the Treaty in plain language there would appear to me to be no great difficulty in putting them into the form of a statute and giving power to the Government to carry them out if this House should so desire. But we are left in ignorance of what those things may be, and we are asked to vest in the Governor in Council such powers as may be necessary to make rules and regulations to carry out conditions as to which we are not informed. I am not quite sure that the Government itself fully appreciates the length to which it asks us to go. This Treaty requires us to join in war if it is necessary. Should the Council of the League of Nations decide that war should ensue then it would be the duty of Canada, as a nation so constituted under this Treaty, to participate in that war. That is one of the things to be done under the Treaty-take ,a part in world-wide wars. I am not saying that is wrong, perhaps it is not, but it is one of the undertakings to which we have obligated

ourselves. Now, does the Government say that the Governor in Council should get together and pass an Order in Council by which the military forces in Canada shall be called out and sent out of this country to fight wherever they may be called upon to go? It is certainly no strained construction upon this Act to say that that is possible. I submit, Sir, that very few members of this House, if any-in fact, I do not think any member will be found-who would agree to vest power in the Government, no matter how strong their faith in that Government might be, to pass an Order in Council by which such action would be carried out -without reference to the people or reference to the will of Parliament at all.
Subsection 1 of the Bill says:
The Governor in Council may make such ajrp-ointments, establish such offices, make such Orders in Council, and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the said Treaty, and for giving effect to any of the provisions of the said Treaty.
The Minister of Justice, w(ho has had long experience on the bench, will surely agree that at least a liberal interpretation of the power conferred by this subsection is that it will enable the Governor in Council to miake an Order sending the military forces of 'this country to wiar. If such an Order in Council were called into question as having no Statutory basis', those supporting it would have good) reason for saying that provision for such ian OrdeT in Council was made under ithiis subsection.
When the Treaty was- before Parliament, it was .pointed out by 'the Minister of Justice, 'the President of the Council and others that under the Treaty, or by reason of our acceptance of it, none of the powers of the Parliament of Canada would be in any wav interfered with or impaired. The member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) submitted an amendment the purpose of which was sdmlply to make it plain -and clear that Canada's position with regard to the settling of questions concerning war was to be the .same after the acceptance of the Treaty as it was .before the Treaty was signed. That amendment, supported by bon. members' on this isdde, was turned down by the Government land its supporters, 'the assurance being given 'that our powers would be just as they were before this Treaty received 'the approval of the House. If that be the case, is not my contention strengthened that whatever we do in the way of implementing this Treaty should be clearly set forth in an Act of Parliament; that we should not he left to
conjecture as to what an Order in Council may be? Particularly is this necessary when we are dealing with such a vital question 'as that of whether Canada as a nation should enter into, a conflict with any other nation of the world. We .should not be <asked to give these extensive and practically limitless powers to the Governor in Council. I may be told that we cannot put these details into a statute. But many Acts of Parliament go into details. Take, for instance, the Grain Act, with which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is very familiar. That Act sets forth minutely every detail of the operations of that department; it leaves little or nothing to be dealt with by Order in Council. If that procedure was necessary in that case; if similar procedure was necessary in the many other cases which I could mention,, it is even more necessary in connection, with the establishment of means of communication between ourselves and the outside world. Nothing should be left to conjecture; the powers conferred upon the Government or upon any agency which may he-established under this Act should be put in the form of a statute, i I see that this Act provides for the imposition of 'penalties. I do not quite understand the purpose of that provision. Certainly we cannot impose penalties upon any person outside of our own country who may fall short of the terms of this Treaty. Possibly it has in contemplation the doing of something in violation of the Treaty by one of our own citizens. However, I assume that when we get into committee these things will be more fully explained. But I repeat that the House should consider seriously whether it is not better that we should legislate with regard to these questions rather than leave them to the judgment of the Governor in Council.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the principle of this Bill is consecrated, I should like to express my approval of the position taken by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). It is unfortunate that under the rules the House must resolve itself into committee after the second reading, not after the first reading, of a Bill, because when a vote, if any, is taken upon the second reading of a Bill, then the principle is consecrated.
To certain subsections of the only two sections in this Bill I wish to take very strong objection. So far as I can see, the only purpose of the introduction of the Bill is to continue a system which has become very unpopular in this country, the

system of Government by Orders in Council. We on this side of the House, believing that we were acting in the best interests of the people, assented in the early days of the war to the War Measures Act, an Act which gave the Government power to legislate between parliamentary sessions upon all matters which required to be dealt with before the following session. The Government passed Orders in Council relating to everything which, in their judgment, the War Measures Act gave them power to deal with in that way, and for some years, we had in this country what was known as Government by Order in Council.
The preamble of this Bill, which is entitled " An Act for carrying into effect the Treaty of Peace between His Majesty and certain other Powers," has two divisions. The first sets forth that the Peace Treaty was signed and given effect to by the plenipotentiaries therein named-and these plenipotentiaries were named by an Order in Council.
The second portion relates to the expediency to do certain things proper and expedient for giving effect to this Treaty, those things being:
The Governor in Council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such Order in Council, and do such things as appear to Him to be necessary for carrying out the said Treaty, and for giving effect to any of the provisions of the said Treaty.
The objection I take to this is that, without knowing what the Government may do, we are asked to give them a blank cheque to establish offices' wherever they may desire, to make appointments in Europe or in this country without the people knowing beforehand anything about them, and to make such Orders in Council andi, besides that, do such things as appear to the Cabinet, because the Governor in Council is the Cabinet, to be necessary for carrying out the said Treaty and giving effect to its provisions. The second subsection reads:
Any Order in Council made under this Act may provide for the imposition by summary process or otherwise of penalties in respect of breaches of the provisions thereof, and shall be laid before Parliament as soon as may be after it is made, and shall have effect as if enacted in this Act, but may be varied or revoked by a subsequent Order In Council.
That savours too much of the history that we have gone through during the last few years. We have had instance after instance in the operation of the Military Service Act of young men by Order in Council being brought from one province before a military tribunal sitting in another province, of the courts of this land not having been re-

[DOT]spected, of habeas corpus having been suspended, all by Order in Council. We have had cases where ministers of the Cabinet, and notably the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), have stated to their electors that all hoys who. were required at home need not enlist, afterwards stating that if the tribunals conscripted them, they, the Government, would see that the judgment of those tribunals would be set aside, and that if the tribunals did not conscript sufficient, they, the Government, would see that the judgment of the tribunals would be set aside. This country has for some years been practically in a state of anarchy, and by consecrating again this similar provision in this Bill, we give to the Government a blank cheque by which they may repeat the actions which have transpired in this country during the last three or four years. Therefore, as this is my only possible means of protesting against government by Order in Council, I want to do so most emphatically now. The time has come in this country when a democratic form of Government should be renewed. There is amongst the civilian population of Canada enough trouble now that we should revert to the old system of Government for the people and by the people, and cease government by Order in Council.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

speechtext: What share?

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says that Sir Herbert Ames is to be appointed by the League of Nations. Of course, the League is not yet organized.
I suppose this means that Sir Eric Drummond had the power to appoint him and that he appointed him.
,Mr. DOHERTY:	I understand Sir Eric
Drummond is forming an organization. Of course, it is strictly speaking premature, because the League of Nations not having been constituted and got together, no one can make an appointment to the Secretariat of the League; but it was thought wise that an organization should be formed in advance; that a deal should be come to by those immediately interested as to the project of the organization of the Secretariat. When the League of Nations gets together all that will fall to the ground unless the League adopts it and is satisfied with it. This is all in the nature of project at the present time. Nobody can at the present moment undertake to pay Sir Herbert Ames a salary on behalf of the League of Nations. But a plan is being formulated and, with a view to carrying out that plan, I understand different officers have been suggested. The only one who is designated in the League is Sir Eric Drummond, and I understand his appointment will not become effectual until the treaties have been ratified and the League of Nations actually constituted. What has been done is in advance and with a view, when the League of Nations, which we hope will come into existence, comes together; that it may have at its disposal to adopt or to reject, as it thinks proper, an instrument by which its business affairs, if I may use that expression, may be administered.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I think Sir Eric Drummond has the power to appoint assistants in the Secretariat. He is designated in the Treaty, and I take it for granted that Sir Herbert Ames was appointed by Sir Eric Drummond, who is the only authority that could appoint him. I do not think there is any doubt he has that power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
He will have that authority when the Treaty is ratified. In the
meantime he is acting in advance on the authority that the Covenant proposes to give him, tout, of course, the Covenant, like all the rest of the Treaty is subject to ratification. I think, however, he is safe in taking for granted that that wilj be done.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Would the holding of this new position to which Sir Herbert Ames has been appointed, and in respect of which this country is going to contribute a portion of his salary not be incompatible, under the Independence of Parliament Act, with his remaining a member of this Parliament? Does Sir Herbert Ames intend to occupy both positions-Secretary of the League and a member of the Parliament of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
As to what his intentions may ultimately be I am not in a position to speak, but if my hon. friend will refer to the Independence of Parliament Act I think he will find it refers to offices to which some emolument derived from the Crown is attached. I think it would be very difficult to say that a salary derived from a body such as the League of Nations, merely because of the fact that Canada may be a member of the League and as a member be assessable for the provision of a portion of the general expenses, would bring Sir Herbert Ames within the terms of the Independence of Parliament Act. However, that is a question which it will be for him to consider in the first instance, and for this House to consider if it should be properly raised. At the present time I am not quite certain that the office has been officially accepted by Sir Herbert Ames, or that he is therefore actually in office. As I pointed out a few moments ago I do not think he can possibly be in office as>
an officer of the League of Nations until the League of Nations has been formed, which will only be when the Treaty has been ratified by a sufficient number of the parties interested.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I understand that he has already sailed to assume his new duties. The press has given that information to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
Sir Herbert Ames has sailed, I understand, for the purpose of looking into the whole matter; and it is not at all impossible that he will assume the performance of the duties; but surely the hon. gentleman understands that there cannot arise a contractual relationship between him and the League of Nations until

the League of Nations has come into existence. What is being dome at the present time is purely provisional or preliminary. Sir Eric Drummond, very much interested I have no doubt in having a proper organization of his secretariat ready as soon as the League comes into existence and is in a position to act, is taking time by the forelock and providing that organization notv. If the Treaty should not be ratified and the whole thing falls through, neither he nor Sir Herbert Ames nor any other person will have come into any contractual relationship with the League of Nations.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Has Sir Herbert Ames' salary been discussed, and if so, is the minister in a position to tell us what his salary will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: That is a matter for determination by the League itself when it will be constituted. What salary Sir Eric Drummond may recommend, I am not in a position to state.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: It would be reasonable to suppose that the matter has been the subject of 'communication with Sir Eric, and that Sir Herbert Ames has ibeen nominated by the Canadian Government.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

If Sir Eric Drummond thought it desirable and that it would perhaps be showing some consideration to Canada to select a Canadian, I should think it would be a very natural thing for him to consult such Canadians as he came in contact with. I am not saying that he has not done so, but certainly he did not consult with me.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is not aware that the Government has been consulted, he is not a careful reader of the public press, because it has been announced that Sir Herbert Ames has been named for that position by the Prime Minister of Canada. I am not finding fault with that, but when my hon. friend says 'that the Canadian Government had nothing to do with the appointment, I have a little difficulty in understanding that.
[<Mr. Doherty.]

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I have no knowledge- let us limit it to that.-of any action on the part of the Canadian Government in connection with the matter. I am not in a position to say whether or not any consultation with regard to Sir Herbert Ames' qualifications or otherwise was had with the Prime Minister. I am not in a position to say yes or no. I am not saying I do not 'know not because I think there would be anything improper in such consultation, but simply because I do not know.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Perhaps it would be fair to assume that Sir Herbert Ames' fame preceded him and that it was not necessary to have any recommendation from any member of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: That is not impossible.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Does this preliminary organization of which the minister has spoken include representatives of each of the nations affected?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I do not think the .matter is dealt with at all in that aspect. To put it very simply, without any desire to depreciate in any way, it is a matter of employing oflicials or clerks. Their functions are higher than those of clerics, but these officers are simply the officials who are going to look after the work of the organization. They are not going to deal with international questions, or anything of that sort. It is very much the same organization as the Clerk and the other officials of this House, for instance. The people who form part of the secretariat will not take part in the deliberations of the Conference or of the 'Council. They are-I do not think it is a term that ought to be considered offensive at all-purely and simply the servants of the organization to look after the details of carrying on the office work that will require to be done in connection with the League of Nations.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend from iShelburne .and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that a recommendation has been made to Sir Eric Drummond by the Prime Minister of a Canadian official such as Sir Herbert Ames. That was openly stated when Sir Robert came back from the Conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: He certainly is not a Canadian officer. I know that from conversation with Sir Herbert Ames himself. It was pointed out to him that the official must realize that he is becoming the official of all the nations of the world, and that he is no national representative.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I am not disputing that. I just wanted to emphasize that it would be nearer the truth to say that the Prime Minister did make a recommendation of Sir Herbert Ames. Sir Herbert Ames has been selected to be Assistant Secretary to Sir Eric Drummond because the two languages to be used in connection with the League of Nations, as was the case in the deliberations on the Treaty of Peace, will be French and English; and it is to the credit of this country that there was found in the Parliament of Canada a gentleman who was sufficiently proficient in both French and English to be appointed to this office. It is a great compliment, and at the same time a great lesson.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) that we are signing .a blank cheque, and a very large one, in giving the Government these *vague and, possibly, very large powers. The minister might help us a little by giving us some idea of what is likely to happen under these powers. " The Governor in. Council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such Orders in Council, and do such things as are necessary." What appointments are likely to arise? I quite agree that the minister cannot be very definite. We have to deal with things in. the future as they arise, but probably the Government have some inkling of what appointments and offices are contemplated under that clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I shall be glad to give the hon. member information in regard to that point. First, in reference to some things said by the leader of the Opposition. He need not have any anxiety that we shall read this provision as conferring on us authority to go to war. I think we made pretty clear what was our conception of the obligations under the League in that respect, and that when it comes to actually going to war there is nothing in the Treaty that enables any one to impose that obligation upon us, and therefore there would be no question, in carrying out the Treaty, of our undertaking to go to war.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.

In realizing on the

speechtext: Might I remind my hon. friend of the question that I put regarding the probable appointment of officials which he has overlooked? He did mention as amongst the classes of officials to be appointed that there would be legal advisers and officials of that kind,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Yes, legal advisers, sequestrators, liquidators, and people who could carry out the liquidation of these properties and who would manage a clearing house if we should determine to adopt the clearing house system.

speechtext: Are there any officials other than' that class contemplated by this Bill?
