subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I have no other in my own mind.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Is Canada to be represented in the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I would not consider that the appointment of the representative of Canada in the League of Nations would be the making of an appointment for the purpose of giving effect to the Treaty. That is one of the rights which will enure to Canada after full effect has been given to the Treaty. One of the effects of the Treaty will be the right of Canada to appoint a representative, and it will be time enough then, I think, for us to determine what the class of representative shall be. I confess that it had not occurred to me in connection with the Bill that what was in mind was the appointment of persons to represent Canada at the gathering of the League of Nations. As regards our rights in connection with the League of Nations, the Treaty produces its full effect when it has assured to us those rights. The appointment of a representative would rather seem to be
something done in the exercise of the right than something done in order to give effect to the Treaty. I confess, and I think I can safely speak for the Government, that we had not in contemplation the appointment of a Canadian representative to take part in the Assembly of the League of Nations when using the word " appointment." These appointments are for such work as is necessary to make this Treaty effective. As regards the League of Nations, I understand it is made perfectly effective. I do not see that anything further requires to be none to assure us of our rights in connection with the League of Nations. These rights once assured to us, it is our privilege to exercise them in our own behalf.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: The Prime Minister of Canada, being the head of the Department of External Affairs, would he not likely be the one who would represent Canada at the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: The question whether the representatives should not be settled in the Covenant itself on some basis of that kind did receive consideration. At one time that idea prevailed and in the original draft provision was made that the Ministers of Foreign Affairs-which in our case I have no doubt would be the Secretary of State for External Affairs-should, by the Covenant itself, be determined upon as being the proper persons to represent their respective countries either in the Council or in the Assembly of the League of Nations. But after discussion the provision was left as it is now in the Treaty for determining the right to representation, leaving to the respective members the privilege of determining in the manner they thought best who should represent them in the Council and in the Assembly.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I must not dare to express any legal opinion contrary to that of the Minister of Justice, and anything I say is submitted for his consideration. I do not think that the Treaty or the Covenant of the League of Nations-either or both-will give the Government of Canada the power to appoint anybody to anything. Therefore, I think any appointment that may be made of a representative at the Assembly of the League of Nations would have to be made under this Bill, because, except under this Bill, His Excellency the Governor General would have no power to appoint anybody. I am offering this suggestion in order that the hon. gentleman may think it over. Either the ap-

pointment would have to be made under this Bill or not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I will certainly give consideration to that. In the event of there being an Assembly of the League of Nations called before we have an opportunity to have another session of Parliament, it undoubtedly would be desirable that there should be power somewhere to appoint a representative. I am not prepared to say that it is not desirable to make it possible under this Bill to make such an appointment. But speaking quite frankly, I had not in my mind at the time the idea of the appointment of officials to exercise on Canada's behalf the rights secured to her by the Treaty itself. What was in contemplation was the appointment of officials to do those things which might be necessary to make this Trpaty effective; that is to say, to secure to us all the rights we have under it and to carry out anything we are called upon to carry out. I will look into this question.^ As my attention is called to it,
I might say that I do.not see that there ought to be any very serious objection to the suggestion, even giving to the word "appointment" an interpretation which would cover a representative of the kind mentioned. Undoubtedly this country ought to be represented, and if the call came at any time hereafter, or at any time when it was not possible to proceed otherwise, the only body that properly ought to exercise that power would be the Government of the day.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Instead of a representative of Canada being appointed on the League of Nations from time to time, is it not possible, that a permanent appointment >may be made? The remarks of the hon. gentleman are rather suggestive of that. When the assembly is called, if it be called, then of course Canada would have the right to make an appointment. Looking into the whole situation it strikes me that what will probably happen is that some gentleman chosen by the Government of Canada will be designated to be its representative, and so long as he holds office, I presume during pleasure, he will be the permanent representative of Canada on the League of Nations. It looks to me as if that is contemplated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I do not think that the Covenant, or the officers of the League, contemplated constituting a body composed of persons permanently appointed. I do not want to speak too positively about that but I think I am fairly sure that the Cov- , 
enant itself makes no provision for the same individual continuing for any period of time to be the representative of any particular country-I tlhink I am safe in saying that there is no provision of that kind in the Covenant. I think much would depend upon the frequency of the meetings that might be called as to the desirability, or otherwise, of the same gentleman being the representative of a country during a period of time, or a period of time that might cover a great many meetings. I must confess that I had not given thought to the question of whether it would be more desirable to appoint a man to be the representative of Canada for, say, ten years or to appoint a representative according to circumstances. I think it would be well to consider that meetings will be called under different circumstances when different classes of questions are going to arise; and the man that might be most suitable to represent a country and discuss certain classes of questions might not perhaps be the very best man to represent that country in the case of other classes of questions. The impression I had in my own mind was that each country would, at all events, be free to select a different representative on the occasion of each meeting as it is called and-though the question never came to my own mind; I cannot say I recollect having looked at the Treaty from the point of view of ascertaining that-I think I can speak with fair assurance when I say that there is no provision in the1 Covenant that would limit each of the countries concerned as to the manner of its choice of a representative or as to the period of time during which the particular individual should continue to be the representative. It would seem to me to be only reasonable, however, that each country should be free to change its agent according as it thought proper.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: In the case of Sir Herbert Ames, if his appointment should be permanent and confirmed by the League I would understand that his salary would be paid from a fund assessed upon all the countries forming part of the League; but in the case of the special representative, say of Canada, or of Australia, or of New Zealand, has it been decided whether the salary paid to such -representative shall be paid out of a common fund assessed by the League upon all countries interested, or paid by the particular country for whom the representative acts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
There is a clause providing that each country shall pay the cost of its own representation. The expenses

that are to be paid, as I mentioned a few moments ago-distributed or apportioned on lines similar to those of the International Postal Union-are the expenses of carrying on or of running the machine, if I might use the expression-

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Office expenses practically.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
-but I cannot lay my hand on the precise article at the moment. There is a provision, I think, which expressly states that the respective countries are to meet the expenses of their representatives, but at all events provision as to the expenses of the League is to be found in Article VI:
The expenses of the Secretariat shall he borne by the members of the League in accordance with the apportionment of the expenses of the International Bureau of the Universal Postal Union.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I quite agree with the minister that it is not necessary-perhaps it is not possible-at present to reach conclusions as to the manner in which Canada would be represented, but it seems to me what is likely to happen is this: If the League of Nations goes into effect, as '.ve all hope and believe it will, should any trouble arise in which a meeting of the League is required the notice will be a short one. When war is at the door you cannot wait for formal proceedings. I have no doubt at all in the case of the Great War the British Government would have preferred if they had had an opportunity of getting the advice and concurrence of the Parliament of Canada before they gave the declaration of war; but with the Hun at the gate they could not do it and they had to go on. So it may be in the case of the League of Nations. Things will press; and if for example the hon. gentleman himself were chosen as Canada's representative in the League of Nations andi a sudden call were to come requiring his presence at Geneva when there were urgent duties to be performed here he might find the situation very embarrassing. It seems to me that in order to have prompt action what is most likely to happen-it is only guesswork on my part as to the future-will be that when the League of Nations gets in full working order somebody representing Canada will -have to be available at any moment and that might mean a permanent appointment-permanent only in the sense that he can only hold his office so long as he has the support of the Government of Canada behind him, I think that is the way it will work out, but I quite agree with
the minister the matter is one we will have to leave to the future.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Aeroplanes will be in general use by that time.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: No doubt.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: I ventured in a most humble way to express an opinion upon the proper construction of section 132 and the Minister of lustice says that my views do not concur with those of Lord ^Jdilner. Now I thought that the people of Canada sent us here to exercise some judgment and discretion of our own and that we are here, upon the supposition at all events, that we shall use whatever judgment the Lord has endowed us with; but we are told to-day that unless that judgment corresponds with the view of Lord Milner it is to be wiped off the slate at once and it is unfortunate to express such views. The Minister of Justice without answering my argument at all said that my views, were most unfortunate. Well, the minister did not tell us in what way they were most unfortunate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: In respect of the statute that you read in support of your view; that is the unfortunate circumstance.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
Unfortunately for us
in- this country we have to read a statute and give it the best interpretation we can; we have, not got a vest pocket edition of Lord Milner-

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: And we do not want it either.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
-to give us the interpretation of these statutes. The courts of this country have managed to struggle along for the last hundred years without Lord Milner at their elbow, and I am not aware that when the British North America Act was drafted by the Fathers of Confederation, with such legal advice as they could get, Lord Milner was around.
But now we have found a new constitutional confession of faith, which has its beginning and end, its interpretation, application and execution, in Lord Milner. If we do not comply with him, of course everything is out of joint.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
Having discovered this new confession of faith, its beginning and ending, and so on, does my hon. friend intend to apply for a patent for it? It is his own original discovery.
Mr. McKENZIE': I am pleased to find that there is something yet to be discovered

which is not owned and controlled by this Government. I had thought that there was nothing in sight'that was not controlled by the Government, chiefly by Order in Council; I feel very much elated that there is anything left for me to discover.
Many of our good friends in this country seem to be very much interested in the fate of the beloved green island beyond the seas in connection with the troubles that are abroad there just now. The plenipotentiary from Canada should have some slight reminiscences in that regard, but his entire neglect to do anything in that 'behalf is now to be attributed to the leadership and control of Lord Milner over the proceedings of our plenipotentiaries, including the Minister of Justice. There is the explanation: Lord Milner would not permit him to say anything except what suited him. Let me assure the minister that I speak as a Canadian and for myself absolutely-and let Lord Milner mind his own business. For my part I propose to consult my people and my country, not Lord Milner and those who are trying to bring us under their wing and influence, and to break down the constitutional rights of this country. There is where I stand on Lord Milner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: Please do not "sit" on him.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
Section 132 of the British North America Act has been receiving interpretations in this country for nearly fifty years, and we must read the section in the light of that interpretation. This new status which we are supposed to have acquired is something that has developed within the last few years. How it developed we do not know. There was no amendment of the British North America Act; there was no different interpretation by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council of our rights under it. There was nothing to bring it about, unless it was this happy meeting between the Minister of Justice and Lord Milner. Possibly that was the beginning of those new conditions under which we are not to be governed by what is done by the King. If any member of this (House says that a treaty made by the King is binding on us in Canada, he is held up to ridicule; his construction is held to be a most unfortunate one. But it is absolutely within tl e power of the King in Council or of the King by himself to make a treaty which 13 binding upon the whole Empire, and we, as a part of that Empire, are bound by its [Mr. McKenzie.!
terms, unless it is provided in the treaty that there is no constitutional obligation on us, or that so far as we are concerned the treaty involves simply a matter of policy on the part of the King and his Council.
The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) took me very severely to task the other day because I was so exceedingly dull that I could not see the difference between constitutional right and legal constitutional right. Well, if I am still called upon to make such a nice distinction as that, I am still dull and stupid. As I understand it, every constitutional right which is binding and upon which we can base any structure, must be a legal constitutional right. For nearly fifty years it was thought in England that it was the legal right of the House of Commons only to deal with money Bills; that the House of Lords had nothing to do with them. But it was not a legal right which the House of Commons had been exercising and enjoying; it was merely a usage. Constitutional usage is one thing; constitutional right is another. Constitutional usage evidently does not mean very much. It did not mean very much to the House of Lords when they thought it proper to take a course which was at variance with nearly fifty years' constitutional usage by throwing out Lloyd George's budget because it did not agree with their ideas. It is not safe, therefore, to rely upon constitutional usage; the only basis upon which a sound structure can be erected is a constitutional legal right as established and affirmed. If we are called upon to sign treaties as an integral part of the British Empire, that is merely constitutional usage; it is not constitutional right. It is a usage from which the King in Council can break away at any time.
I am willing to leave to the interpretation of the best legal minds in the country the meaning of section 132 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows :
The Parliament and Government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing: the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries, arising under treaties between the Empire and such foreign countries.
That certainly contemplates the Empire which was in existence in 1867, and it was not intended at that time that Canada was a distinct and separate nation. It was not contended that Australia or New Zealand were separate nations. It meant nothing else than that the British Empire as it existed at that time, vested with

the power of making treaties. When the British Empire as it existed at that time entered into a treaty, we as a part of the Empire had the power to implement that treaty in such a way as was necessary to carry out our part of it. If it has since developed that we are called into council in the making 6f these treaties, that does not in any way change section 132. I say that when we are called upon to implement, by furnishing money and appointing officers, a treaty which we are priding ourselves upon making apart from the British Empire, there is no constitutional basis for our act. The Minister of Justice says that I said that we were at once bound by any treaty which Great Britain would make, and that we had nothing to say about it.
I said nothing of the kind; I put my interpretation upon that section. I have, and I ought to have, great regard for the experience of the Minister of Justice and his knowledge of the construction of a statute, and I expected that he would give us some construction of that section different from and more illuminating than mine, and that he would find in it some basis of jurisdiction for the Bill that is now before Parliament. All he did give was the statement that my interpretation was most unfortunate. Perhaps it was, but he should have given us one that was not most unfortunate. So far he has not done so. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has pointed out,-1 think very properly, that we should know what officers we are to appoint and what monetary obligations this country is assuming in passing this Bill. I can readily understand that the Minister of Justice has not given it very much thought, because it was not drafted in this country. I pointed out before that it was just word for word the English Act, and the British Government, or whatever minister had charge of that Act, gave some explanation and had some knowledge of what it meant. With us, this is simply a copy without any real explanation of what it means. An Act which might very well apply in Great Britain might not apply with us. In Great Britain there is no provincial jurisdiction, there is the one Parliament, with full, unlimited and ample jurisdiction over the territory which they profess to govern. We have a limited jurisdiction within a written constitution, and an Act of Parliament which might be quite in order in the Parliament of Great Britain might be restricted here and require some explanation. That is why I wanted the minister to tell us what our powers are under section 132, but he
thought proper not to give that information except to state that my understanding of it was most unfortunate. Until, however, I hear from the minister to the contrary, or until he gives his full explanation as he may be assisted by Lord Milner, I will stand by what I said.

subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext: As regards subsection (3) of section 1, the minister has said-and I quite agree in that view-that this subsection does not in itself appropriate any money. That is quite correct, but it distinctly takes account of the fact that we shall have to spend some money, and it practically obligates us to vote the money later on. We always have the freedom to say " No " when we like. My suggestion is that, perhaps, the minister has formed some impression of the extent of the financial obligation that this country will assume under this clause. I would not expect him to give us any details; but this is a very serious subject; we are going into a very large enterprise, and it is not unreasonable to ask, before we give that power to the minister, that we should have some general idea of what it involves in the way of expenditure. I do not contend that this votes any money, but the country would, I am sure, be pleased if the minister would give us now some idea of the probable obligation that we shall be asked later on to implement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL TO CARRY INTO EFFECT THE TREATY BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND CERTAIN OTHER POWERS.
speechtext:
I do not foresee that out of the execution of this Treaty there should grow anything in the nature of a permanent financial obligation, but to carry on the operations such as I have described will, no doubt, cost something. For instance, such officer and officials as we may employ in the liquidation of these businesses and so forth will all require to be remunerated, and incidental to the liquidation and distribution there no doubt will be expenses to be met. It would be difficult to speak as to the exact amount, but I should not anticipate that it was going to involve any very large expenditure, nor anything in the nature of a permanent obligation, because under the operations to which I have referred, we shall be liquidating this property which, with the information that I have as to the amount of property there is in this country of German Nationals, represents something between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000, if I am correctly informed, and I do not anticipate that this would result in creating a pecuniary obligation. But no doubt we shall, from time to time, require votes to enable us to carry on this opera-

tion. Beyond that I do not quite see that I can indicate any anticipated financial obligation that is to result to us from our giving effect to the provisions of the Treaty. 1 do not recall that there is in the Treaty any provision, the execution of which could create a financial obligation on our part towards any outside country, nor create anything in the nature of a substantial financial obligation on our part. I cannot, at the moment, think of any. What was had in mind was the necessary expenses for administering the different offices that will have to be created.

speechtext: I should like to know from the President of the Council (Mr. RowelH whether his attention has been drawn to the fact that General Smuts, Prime Minister of South Africa, a few days ago, when he introduced into the House resolutions with respect to the Treaty, is reported to have stated that he was asking the House to ratify the Treaty, not to approve it. speechtext: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Interpretation Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
This Bill, I think, has a deeper significance than might appear at first sight, because there are clauses in the Interpretation Act which carry into effect the provisions of a statute, even though it has been repealed. One might not think that such provisions would be found in the Interpretation Act, hut it is a fact. Of course, the word "interpretation" signifies that the Act is to perform some such service as is performed by a dictionary, either the ordinary or the legal dictionary, giving the proper use and significance of words or terms, but the Interpretation

Act goes further than that. Section 19, for instance, provides:
Where any Act or enactment is repealed, or where any regulation Is revoked, then, unless the contrary intention appears, such repeal or revocation shall not, save as in this section otherwise provided, affect the previous operation of any Act.
There are further provisions. I have only had an opportunity of glancing over the Bill, and I trust that when the minister comes to apply its provisions to the very many Orders in Council that have been passed during the war, he will consider well what the effect will be. I think we should know to which Orders in Council the force and effect of the Interpretation Act will be applied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bill proposes to apply the same rules in interpreting Orders in Council which Parliament has adopted as being suitable and proper rules for the interpretation of statutes, except, as the Bill provides, in cases where " any such provision is inconsistent with the intent or object of such Order or regulation, or would give to any word, expression or clause thereof an interpretation repugnant to the subject matter or the context, or is in any such Order or regulation declared not applicable thereto."
We have found by experience, not only with regard to Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act, but with regard to Orders in Council generally, that one is very apt to draft them assuming that the words in them will have the full meaning which the Interpretation Act attaches to those same words in the statutes, and it seemed to us desirable that we should not be bound in every Order in Council to start out (by saying " In this Order in Council, so-and-so means so-and-so ", but rather that in interpreting the Orders in Council we should apply the same rules which Parliament enacted, and which have stood the test of time, as 'being the proper rules for the interpretation of statutes. We had different instances where we were not able to apply the rule of the Interpretation Act in interpreting an Order in Council. We certainly had always contemplated applying that Act to the Orders in Council.	.
I have difficulty in seizing whether the hon. leader of the Opposition really intends to suggest that there is some reason why it would be undesirable that the particular section of the Interpretation Act which he read should be made to apply to Orders in

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Council. If I followed it correctly, it is the section which has to do with the effect of repealing provisions. If I recollect correctly the provision is in substance that the mere repeal of a previous law shall not be interpreted as meaning the revival of some law that may have been repealed by the previous law, unless the context shows that that was the intention. If that was the section the hon. gentleman read, I do not clearly grasp why it would be objectionable to apply that rule to Orders in Council, if that was what he intended to suggest. It seems to me a good general rule as applied to the statutes, and ,a good general rule as applied to Orders in 'Council. If some -other effect-it would be an exceptional effect- is sought to be attached to a Tepeal, it is simple enough to provide for it, but I can vouch of my own experience that on a number of occasions it was found highly inconvenient that we were not in a position to interpret Orders in Council generally by the rules' applicable for the interpretation of statutes.
There is no particular Order in Council in view in connection with the matter. We did pass an Order in Council under, the War Measures Act, which is about to lapse, making the provisions-of the Interpretation Act applicable to Orders in Council; and we found 'that of very great advantage. It simplified not only the interpretation of Orders in Council, but the drafting of them, because where you had a rule of interpretation you were relieved in many instances of putting in interpretation clauses.

I will try to make my objection more clear. If the Interpretation Act is to be used merely as a dictionary, and I say that advisedly, to ascertain the force and effect of any words in an Order in Council, I have no objection to that, but most of these Orders in Council which were passed during the war have legislative effect only for a certain period. The effect of applying the Interpretation Act, as I understand it, will be to extend the effect of these Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act, and that is what I want to provide against.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If that is a possible result of this legislation, I am quite willing when we are in Committee to insert a clause to the effect that nothing in this Act shall have the effect of maintaining in foree any Order in Council, passed under the War Measures Act, if you wish specifically to mention that Act, which but for this Act would have lapsed.
EDITION	,	,

I do not say that the hon. gentleman may not be right and I wrong, but I do not yet see how it can be said that if the provisions of the Interpretation Act are made to apply to Orders in Council, you are running the risk that the Orders in (Council, when /their legal effect |is exhausted, will be thereby revived. However, if there is any such danger I shall be glad to guard against it. I am not quite sure whether I correctly followed the section which the hon. gentleman read, but if I did I must confess that I have a difficulty in seeing anything in that section that would create the danger he apprehends. If there is such a danger, I shall be more than glad, as I say, to negative it by a provision in this Bill itself when we go into Committee.
I shall be satisfied if *the minister puts that short clause in.

Hon. Arthur L. Sifton (Minister of Public Works) moved the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection. Act.
He said: The other day when, this Bill was up, I gave .a short explanation and it is unnecessary to deal with it at length now. It is simply an amendment to the

Act that was passed a few years ago by which people were required to get permission or authority to build wharves upon or bridges over navigable streams. There was no provision, whereby any action could be taken in case such structures were made without permission. The present Bill is simply to provide that we may tear down obstructions to navigable streams in case they are, or have been, built without -legal authority.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee on. the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section. 1-section of Act respecting removal of unauthorized works to apply to *works built before 24th May, 1918:
That would affect existing rights. It has a retroactive effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: There would not be any existing right because, if people have built they have had no right to do so. I do not know of any cases to which it would apply hut if there are any cases they would not be existing rights; they would be existing wrongs.
They are assumed rights. At that time there was no law which provided they should get permission from the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: There has been a law for a great many years.

That required permission?
Mr. iSIFTON: Yes.

I desire to bring to the notice of the minister a very hard case in my own county-I think it occurred before there was any prohibition-of a man building a wharf in- front of his own property. A gentleman, in. my county built a very respectable wharf close to a lobster factory which he owned, and that wharf was used without any trouble for a great many years. But a few years ago the Government sent a dredge to try to deepen the channel of the navigable harbour in front of his property. Not intentionally, I believe, the dredging operations tore away the supports of the wharf and completely destroyed it. By reason of the deepening of the water by dredging operations, it was impossible to rebuild 'or support the wharf any further. The owner brought an action in the Exchequer Court for damages, hut the judge decided that under a construction of the Act governing the Exchequer Court, as long as the

damage was not done on the work-that is the damage was not done by the dredge on the job that it was performing-the Exchequer Court had no jurisdiction to deal with the case. The judge reached the conclusion that he could afford no remedy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That is a pretty fine distinction.

Since then, Parliament amended the Act. I think that if my friend had brought his action after Parliament amended the Act giving a right to damages caused by a dredge of that kind, whether upon the work or not, he would have been entitled to be compensated by the court. But in view of the conditions existing at that time, his property was destroyed and he received no consideration. I always had it in mind, if ever the opportunity presented itself, to bring the matter to the notice of the Department of Public Works. I think, under the circumstances, it would be a fair subject for consideration to ascertain whether or not, in the goodness of his heart, the minister could do something for the man whose property, built when there was no prohibition against such building, was destroyed entirely through no fault of his,

I see that section 2 provides, in addition .to the existing section 9 of the statute that:
Any work which is or heretofore has been built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water whereof the site has been approved by the Governor in Council, and which is so placed and maintained in accordance with plans or regulations approved or made by the Governor in Council pursuant to the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, shall be deemed to be and to have been duly authorized, and shall not be deemed to obstruct or to interfere or to have interfered with navigation or to be subject to abatement or removal or to give rise to any cause of action upon the ground that it unlawfully obstructs or interferes with navigation or any public right of navigation.
i I do not object, to the first clause because I understand that before erecting any of the works mentioned in the Act On navigable waters, you must get t)he permission of the Governor in Council and he must approve of the location and plans. In certain cases the approval was asked, but there were difficulties that arose in consequence of which the approval could not be got until the work had, been done. Then the Department of Public Works rightly said: We will not approve of a work that is done or of a location which has been built upon. This was extended last year or the year before
33i
to electric power wires crossing rivers. It was important to extend the wires, and they had to be constructed without approval in order to avoid great loss. The first clause would seem to apply to things of this kind, but the second says that if anything exists to-day that is an obstruction we declare it not to be such. May I ask the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Justice if there is any particular case in regard to whicth they want to avoid litigation, or has the department any litigation in mind in asking Parliament to enact this clause?
Mr. SlIF'TON:	There is nothing that I
have heard of.

Then, what is the object of the clause? The statute says that if anything becomes a nuisance, it may become the subject of discussion whether it should be removed or not. Here you say it shall not 'be considered as such.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That clause is for the purpose of avoiding lawsuits. If any work has been approved it shall not ibe interfered with.

That is the law as it
stands now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No; it has been questioned in the court.
I would like to ask the minister for a little light on clause X. Would he kindly explain the significance of the date fixed by this clause, the 24th May, 1919?	,

That refers to the last
amendment that was passed.

There is, another point
upon which I wish to ask for an explanation. I understand, of course, that the original Act provided that any person desiring to construct a wharf, building, or any obstruction, on any navigable stream or harbour should first secure permission to do so. Many persons apply for and secure Crown land grants, or leases, of water front property in various harbours in the Dominion, and when applying for these leases or Crown grants are required to submit a plan of the wharf or building they desire to place on it and to show what use they intend to make of the property. Upon their securing a Crown grant or lease many of these applicants consider that they have secured approval of the structure, or whatever obstruction they are about to put upon the property.
In most cases it was wharves and harbours. Now wha't I wish to ask the minis-

ter is this: Is it the intention of the Government to so apply this power given in this clause as, for instance., to remove, arbitrarily remove, a structure placed on water front property under such conditions? I submit to ham that the power is given in the clause and I think we ought to have a declaration from the Government as to its intention in that regard, because I do not think the Government wisheisi to use a power like that without precedent. Let me add, before I sit down, one other argument for the particuluar case of persons who acted in good faith. It is this:	In every
harbour in Canada there has been for many years either a harbour commission or else a harbour master who has charge of such matters as these and who must have known that these wharves or buildings were being constructed. Has it not been the duty of such a commission, or such an official, to look into the right of the placing of such a structure and see to it that the necessary powers existed under the Navigable Waters Act? In other words, while the person might have been innocently violating the law, or ignorantly-using that word perhaps more advisedly-has not the official of the Government perhaps been guilty of [DOT] neglect at the same time? I submit, in view of that 'consideration, that we should certainly be very careful in enforcing a clause which gives such a very drastic power as this. I would like to hear from the minister, or from the Government, as to its views on the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Certainly if I happen to
be at the head of the department there will be no such arbitrary exercise of power as the hon. member infers. It would be quite possible for many obstructions to navigable streams to be built-possibly not in large cities but over navigable streams and in navigable waters-without any Government official knowing anything of it for years after. It certainly would not be the policy of any Government I would think, and certainly not the policy of the department so long as I was at its head, to exercise power arbitrarily in regard to the removal of obstructions of that kind unless there was absolute interference with navigation or with improvements on the stream.

This section says the
work shall not be removable if proper authority for it exists under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
.
Mr. SIFTON.: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) was speaking of the other clause in the Bill.

There is another thing
with respect to these structures on navigable waters. If you purpose putting up a structure within a harbour you must apply, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, to the Minister of Public Works for authority to do so, and you must also apply to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for permission to use that particular part of the harbour, or get the location which you desire approved' of by the Government. I forget the particular section of the statute which provides that the Minister of Marine shall give his approval. Now suppose that any of the regulations referred to have .not been complied with and that some corporation or some person is hurt-, or has suffered prejudice and wants to remove that prejudice, then what? Technically, under the section, the Navigable Waters Protection Act has been complied with, the notice required has been given, the plans and the location have been submitted to the Minister of Public Works, and everything has gone through Council. But the parties have not secured any authority from the Minister of Marine. In that event this clause would prevent any recourse which might be exercised by the party injured. In the case of a structure in a harbour you have to go to both the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The same application goes to both in practice.

I would not think so.
Section .agreed to.
On section 2-approved works not to be deemed obstructions to navigation or to be liable to removal, etc.

I would like to get a fair idea as to whether the minister has any policy in dealing with structures of this kind, because I aim sure he will find that there are many cases in Canada of people having built small wharves upon what 'they , considered their own property. In the harbours along the Atlantic coiast there is such a thing as people getting waiter grants, with which .practice the minister is no doubt familiar. These people get those waiter grants in many cases from the local government, and the courts have held that as a perfectly good title while the holding of it does not interfere with 'harbour rights or the requirements of navigation. In many oases, people holding such waiter lots, believing that it was their own property and their own land'-except of course where the lots were covered by water-have built wharves and constructed buildings on the wharves and are carrying on a fishing or lobster business or a general trade on these wharves'. Now it would be a great hardship if some officer who- did not really understand the. full effect of the situation were to destroy those properties. I would like to urge upon the minister that the greatest possible precaution should be taken before any interference occurs and care taken - to see that at least as little harm as possible is done by reason of the change in the law.
Mr. MeMASTER: It is with difficulty that those who are not seated' upon the front benches of the Chamber are able to follow the discussion of a Bill of this sort, conducted as it is in the kindly and conversational tone which obtains to-night. If I might juist interject this remark, Mr. Chairman-for the last two sessions I have been making a sort of inverted bailiff of unyiself by shouting "louder" from day to day, from w'eek to week, and from month to month, but if I happen to be absent from the Chamber for a sitting, or even a few hours, I find the front benchers have slipped back into the habit of carrying on the discussion in a conversational tone which-and I speak now seriously-precludes any member outside 'a possible radius of about twenty feet, from understanding, taking part in, or enjoying the debate.	-
Section 2 of this Bill would seem to prevent the department from ordering a change
in any public work of this nature once it has been officially approved. That seems to me to be a dangerous provision. Suppose the Department of Public Works approves a bridge across a navigable stream, and' in the course of a few years a change in the' nature of the vessels using that stream-makes that public work an impediment t* navigation, this section would seem to provide that once the department has approved such a public work, that is the end of it, the department cannot do anything. Surely that would not be a sound position for a department of the Government to-place itself in.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) says. There, is across a portion of the harbour of Vancouver, known as False creek, a very old bridge which was erected twenty-four or [DOT]twenty-five years ago and which is owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is a frame or pile trestle bridge, with a very narrow draw. The pier in the draw goes diagonally across the channel and the bridge has been a menace to navigation for many years. Appeal after appeal has been made to the Public Works Department asking that the removal of this bridge be ordered. But it was discovered that while no official or formal approval of the structure was given, many years ago some deputy minister gave the assurance that the plans were O.K., and on that point the company rests its claim that the bridge should remain. Now, the member for Brome points out that under this clause- and if he is correct, the point is a very important one-such a work would be declared to be quite properly there. In recent years; a shipbuilding yard has been built above this bridge and every time a ship is-launched and sent to sea-about ten have been sent from that yard during the last two years-they have to take a span out of the bridge, the draw being too narrow to let the ships go through. This clause may put the Department of Public Works, which has been struggling unsuccessfully with the problem for seven or eight years, absolutely out of court. I suggest that the minister allow this matter to stand until he lias had an opportunity of consulting his deputy, looking into this particular case, and ascertaining whether or not the enactment of this legislation would prevent the department from dealing with the matter to which I have been referred-a matter which has been urgently pressed upon it for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: This section has reference only to any work which has been formally approved by the department. Certainly, after the department has formally approved of a work, it should not proceed subsequently to tear it down. If any work is believed to be a source of danger to the community it would have to be dealt with as such, under other legislation than- this. This Bill is simply to provide that once the formal approval has been given this department or nobody else can interfere and say that the structure is not a legal one.

The point made by the member for Brome is one which ought to be decided. I will give the minister a concrete case. Suppose he has built a bridge, with the approval of the department, over the St. Lawrence, the St. Maurice, or any navigable river, and through changes in navigation it is found that the bridge is too low.-The navigation company whose vessels are on the river says to you: We are going to submit new plans to you for your bridge, the location of which you have approved; we want to raise the floor of the bridge twenty or thirty feet in order that our ships may be enabled to pass-or, if it is a transmission line-we want to raise the wire towers. Under this Bill nothing coulu oe done in a case of that kind; nobody could secure the acceptance of such a proposal, even though the parties to be benefited undertook to meet the whole of the expense involved in making the change. Therefore the public interest is not served. Tne public interest- should always have precedence over private interest. If it is in the public interest that the style of a bridge should be changed in order to meet nefv navigation conuiuons, in order to provide for the free movement of vessels whose stacks or masts have been made higher, or which have been equipped with the wireless system, why should it be provided under section 9A of the Navigable Waters Protection Act that nobody shall have the right to touch that bridge?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: It does not say that.

It says that it cannoi be interfered with by any one. By this BiL1 such a case as I have mentioned is placed outside the jurisdiction of the courts or any one else, even outside the realm of private contracts between individuals.

speechtext: When this Bill was in committee, it was allowed to remain in committee at the suggestion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), because he said it would be desirable to elicit public opinion with regard to the matter. That gave some lion, members, including myself, the idea that this Bill would not come up so soon as it has done. May I inquire if public opinion has been elicited and, if so, in what direction has it been expressed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BIL.L TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
The Bill, of course, is
not under my control nor under the control of the Government. The Bill was introduced by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow), and he is entitled to proceed with it. I made the suggestion to him, and I would like to repeat it now-of course, I cannot force it-that it would be a desirable thing that the Bill should remain where it is, in committee, for such a reasonable period of time as might allow of the expression of public opinion on the subject. But, of course, that is only my view on something that would be desirable, and I have no power to insist upon the hon. gentleman's accepting my suggestion. I may say that I had not anticipated that we would reach the Bill again as soon as we have reached it, but the House with very considerable expedition to-day went through the business we were ready to put before it, with the result that the Bill has come back again. While I still would renew my suggestion to the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill, I do not feel I have any right to insist that he shall accept it.

subtopic: BIL.L TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
I have no desire to press the matter unduly in view of the expressed opinion of the leader of the House, an opinion which he has expressed before today. But in view of the fact that this Bill has practically been before the country for six months, and in view of the further fact that a few days ago, notwithstanding that

this Bill, to deal with the subject, was on the Order Paper, a date for Thanksgiving Day was unofficially announced through the press, there seems to be a considerable amount of misunderstanding and one can easily realize that-through the country.
I have a press despatch-I have not it with me at the moment-from St. Catherines stating that the people there were preparing for observing Thanksgiving day with the idea in mind that it would be decided by this House that Thanksgiving day would take place on Armistice day, in November.. Naturally, when this date was announced, although unofficially, through the press, they were in a quandary, or, to speak in common phraseology, they felt themselves up against it, that is to say, they had to hurry up the preparations for that event. Yesterday, it was reported in the press that it was practically decided by this House to observe Armistice day, November 11, as Thanksgiving day. Although this Bill has come around sooner than was anticipated when we were discussing it last night, yet, in view of the unsettled opinion that obtains in the country regarding the proposition, I think it would be better 'that we should deal with the matter to a'finish to-night and state whether we are going to observe this great event, Armistice day, as a national holiday, and couple with it Thanksgiving day, or whether we are going to abandon the proposition altogether.

subtopic: BIL.L TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
I have not heard from the Minister of Justice as to the method by which he purposes ascertaining public opinion. Coming as I do from Ontario, I might point out for his information, that some years ago an agitation arose there which resulted' in changing Thanksgiving day, which usually fell on Thursday, to Monday, for the reason that the change benefited a large class, not only commercial travellers, as the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow) pointed out, but school teachers and students throughout the country who desired to spend that holiday at their homes, .and who would thereby have Saturday, Sunday and Monday as a week-end. I was rather impressed by the arguments of the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) in giving weight to the representations made by the Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada, a very representative body of intelligent public opinion, and a body which is organized and which knows what its members desire. I should like to know in what other way than through
kindred organizations is public opinion going to be gathered.

speechtext:
I do not apprehend that there will be a public clamour on the part of any individuals throughout the country, and the only expressions of opinion we are apt to get will come from organized bodies.
If the Minister of Justice is depending upon the newspapers, I am not quite so sure whether the press has taken sufficient interest in this discussion in the House to worry itself about it. If the press takes any interest, I have no doubt but that there would be divergent views, and as regards the press, I always think, anyway, that editorial comment is just the opinion of one man who sits at the editorial desk and who, after all, does not carry much more weight than any man on the street.
I am very strongly inclined to the .view that the representations made by the Commercial Travellers' Association as to the great benefit that comes to the great number through holding the Thanksgiving Day on a Monday, ought to have the serious consideration of the Government. The question is one that ought to be decided soon, and I do not see any reason why we should not deal with the public opinion that has already been expressed. I have heard no great public opinion against the proposition. The only argument I have heard is that, the war having come to an end by an armistice upon the 11th day of November, that day is set apart and fixed in the public mind as a day of great deliverance from the horrors of war.
While from the historic point of view it might be considered a mistake to commemorate the signing of the Armistice upon any other day than the 11th of November, the* second Monday in November must always come very close to that date, and for many, many years to come the 11th of November will never be forgotten in the minds of the people as a day of great deliverance for which thanks should be offered up. Consequently, I would say that the second Monday in November, falling as it always, will near the 11th, will focus that day sufficiently in the people's mind to enable us to consolidate our thanksgiving for the signing of the Armistice with our thanksgiving for all other things for which we should be thankful, and the public mind will seize on that day as the anniversary of the close of the greatest war the world has ever known.

Having made that explanation, I want to say again that I am not at all in the attitude of insisting upon that suggestion. The committee, of course, is at perfect liberty to_deal with the matter, and to value that suggestion at what it is worth. Mr. DAVIlS: I was not present when the Bill was discussed before, but if we decide on the 11th of November then every fifth, or sixth, or seventh year there would be no holiday, as the 11th will fall on the Sabbath day. I do not know whether that view has been presented to the House, but it is an additional reason to my mind why we should choose a movable day, let us say, the nearest Monday to the 11th of November.

It was not my privilege .to be present when the discussion took place on this Bill the other day, and I 
should like to giive expression to my views. First of all, I think it was a happy thought on the part of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) to couple Thanksgiving Day with what we might call Armistice Day. We have been accustomed to the setting apart by proclamation of the Government one day in each year on which the people of Canada generally gave thanks for the many blessings, they had enjoyed throughout the year. I think every one will agree that there has never been an. occasion in the history of this country when we had such reason, for genuine thanksgiving as on the day the armistice was signed putting an end to the great war. I think it would be a very grave mistake to commemorate any other day than .the 11th of November. If we are going to suit our own convenience in regard to these holidays, if we who stayed at home during this terrible war cannot put ourselves out a little bit to celebrate the end of the war, what does it mean? It simply means that so far as giving^ real thanks is concerned, your thanksgiving is a farce. If you are going to suit individual' convenience in these holidays, let us pass a law here, and fix all these holidays on a Monday. What about the first of July? Do you want us to celebrate that on the first Monday in July?

speechtext:
Coming back to the
point-, the armistice was signed, I believe, at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of year. In all seriousness, I think it would be a very grave mistake to depart from that day. If we intend

to honour that day-and the idea of the hon. member for South Renfrew undoubtedly was that the people of Canada should honour it, for that, I presume, is his reason for wanting to couple it with Thanksgiving -I think the principle is eminently wise and I cordially agree with it. But to observe the day on the second Monday of November because that Monday should happen to be the one nearest the 11 th of the month would, in my opinion, be a serious and .an unfortunate impropriety* If it is desirable to have Thanksgiving Day on a Monday, then let us follow the established custom of the past and allow the Government to appoint the day in October or any other convenient month so long as it is a Monday. If, however, you want to honour Armistice Day and the great ideas for which it stands, honour it on the proper day, the 11th of November; but do not observe it five or six days before or after the actual day that sees the anniversary of the great event which means so much to us.

subtopic: BIL.L TO MAKE THE SECOND MONDAY IN NOVEMBER THE PERMANENT THANKSGIVING DAY.
speechtext:
In the consideration of this question one fact that strikes me as being of great importance has so far been apparently overlooked. In the great war, the peaceful conclusion of which we purpose to celebrate on Armistice Day, our brethren to the south of us joined us in a noble . effort to vindicate the right. Possibly the Government of the United States will within a reasonable time be considering this very subject that is now before this Parliament, and in view of the fact that our Government has already fixed the day for Thanksgiving to Almighty God for the year 1919, I do not see that there is at present any great urgency in settling this question just yet. I agree with the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), and personally I feel that no day would be as appropriate, sentimentally at least, as the 11th of November for the celebration, of the armistice. But if we desire to learn public opinion as conveyed through the medium of the Commercial Travellers' Association,
I may say that the choice has been strongly in favour of the second Monday. As has already been pointed out by an hon. member, for very many years in Canada Thursday was invariably selected as Thanksgiving Day; but representations have been forcibly, urged by the Commercial Travellers' Association and their organizations, supplemented I believe by expressions of opinion from Boards of Trade, Chambers of Commerce, wholesale houses and other bodies, to the effect that it is a distinct convenience
to the commercial travelling community and to the interests which they represent to have the day of thanksgiving on Monday. Probably the United States, which no doubt will fix a day for celebration of the armistice, may select the second Monday. On the other hand, they may select the 11th of November. Be that as it may, I submit, without any suggestion that we should follow in the footsteps of our southern friends or be guided by any action of theirs, that there is a great moral and a useful sentiment in the brotherhood of these two nations, and the holiday would appear to me to be a suitable occasion for the interchange of courtesies and visits if we could arrange our celebration for the same day.
I respectfully suggest, therefore, as Thanksgiving Day has already been fixed for this year, and in deference to the suggestion of the Minister of Justice, that this matter be allowed to stand for the time being, and possibly before the session is concluded it may be found desirable to defer further consideration of it to another session. If we could arrange a common day for observance of the anniversary of the Armistice by Canada and the United States it would conduce to an increased amity between two great peoples, and it would be a matter of mighty sentiment to have an entire continent returning thanks to God simultaneously for .deliverance from great tribulation, and for the conclusion of a peace which we all trust will be lasting. The Armistice was declared on the eleventh of November, and sentiment if nothing else would demand the observance of the event on that day. But notwithstanding that fact there is a great body of public opinion which- cannot be fully expressed in this House, and I really think we should not be too premature in dealing with this matter. T repeat my suggestion that we leave the question in abeyance for the time being, and before the end of the session something may occur to urge the desirability of leaving it over to another session.

As one who has taken some interest in this matter I think the proceeding to-night is extraordinary. I was not present when the discussion began, but I think the debate is quite unusual. The Bill has been approved in all its clauses, and I think even the title or preamble was passed and the Bill was ready to be reported. I asked the Minister of Justice at the time if this matter would be taken up again as regards the difference between the 11th of November and the second Monday, and he

assured me that it would not. At least, that is how I understood him. I therefore cannot see why we are now asked to retrace our steps, having come to a definite decision that the 11th of November should ,be the date. There is no doubt that the House decided that point, and the majority in favour of it would have been large had a standing vote been taken. While not wishing to take advantage of that fact, I certainly strongly object to the motion of the member for Brome to open up the question and refer it back again to the House, when the decision was as absolute as it was.

speechtext: I think it is well to have a holiday in connection with thanksgiving. If the League of Nations means anything it will have considerable work to do hereafter, and one of the first matters that will demand its attention- and it is one which is already under consideration in Europe-is the modification of our. calendar so that the months will begin always on the same day and each quarter have the same number of days. The result will be a great improvement in ithe conduct of business and in the observance of public holidays. As regards the suggestion that we should have the same day as the United States for observing the great event which will hereafter be the occasion of a national holiday, I believe That before five years have passed the League of Nations will have completed a modification of the calendar, and that public holidays will always come on the same day. Under those circumstances, if Monday should be regarded as the most favourable day for observing a holiday, there would be no difficulty in fixing it as a .permanent institution. \v hat-ever we may do now, however, I think that we shall find within the next five years that one of the great questions before the League of Nations will be the revision of the calendar, providing facilities along the Tines suggested to-night, so that public holidays will always fall on the same day of the week.
