speakeroldname: Mr. A. L. DAVIDSON (Digby and Annapolis):
speechtext:
When this Bill was before the
House at a previous sitting I had the honour to move the adjournment of the debate. It seems to me almost a pity that the Bill should contain three separate and distinct principles as I feel that some of these principles are good and some of them are bad; some of them might receive the support of members, whereas the remainder might evoke their opposition. The Bill, as I understand it, provides for three radical, or at least very distinct and separate changes in the election law. The second of these-I am not taking up the provisions consecutively-contemplates that any member who is returned for two or more

electoral districts shall make a selection, within thirty days, of which of such electoral districts he will serve. When last I addressed the House on this subject I mentioned that there was but one member in the House who had the honour to represent two separate constituencies at the present time, and that he, of course, had a very personal interest in this Bill, and I thought it well that the Bill should not be advanced until that hon. member was in his seat. I am very glad that the hon. gentleman in question is present to-night, because I believe his opinion on this question will be worthy of consideration. I must say, however, that I am inclined to agree [DOT]with this provision of the Bill. I do not believe that any member of Parliament- no'matter how clever he may be, no matter how distinguished, no matter what powers of speech or endurance in debate he may possess-is entitled to represent more than one constituency. If the principle of allowing a member to represent more than one seat were carried out you might just as logically permit him to represent 235 constituencies and let him run the whole show. I am sure I would object to that even in the case of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) who represents the constituencies of Maisonneuve and Gaspe.
What constituency did the hon. member first mention; I could not catch it?

If the hon. gentleman will refer td the list of members he will be able to find the constituency in question and give it the correct French accent. I repeat, there is some merit in the principle that no member should be allowed to represent more than one constituency at the same time, but it occurs to me that perhaps legislation is not altogether necessary in order to accomplish such a reform. If my hon. friend who is the sponsor of this Bill and for whose statesmanship I have a very high opinion
Ah, that's the word.

If he had conferred with the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve, and had pointed out to him the anomaly of representing two constituencies at the same time, I am quite sure the latter hon. gentleman would have yielded to his suggestion and no legislation upon this question would have been necessary. That is one amendment that is proposed by the Bill.

It is provided by section 1 that within sixty days after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons, such writ shall be issued. Now, I can see certain objections to that provision. If the Governor in Council were absolutely bound by any such legislative provision as that, an election might have to be brought on in some constituency at an undesirable or unreasonable time. I will give you a case in point. A vacancy in the representation of Glengarry and Stormont unfortunately occurred some months ago. The Government did not feel like bringing on an election in that constituency while the soldiers were overseas and unable to cast their votes, and they very wisely exercised the discretion which they are enabled to exercise under the law as it stands at the present time, by arranging that the election in this case be held after the return of the soldiers from France and at a time when the most worthy electors in that constituency would have an opportunity of expressing their opinion as to the representation.
How was it that the election in Lanark was brought on within a few weeks after the seat was declared vacant?
The Government was not so wise as all that.
I am not in the confidence of the Government to the extent of being able to say why that was done, but I have no doubt that there were good and sufficient reasons.

The point is not
well made.

Under the law as it
stands at present the Government are responsible to the people for any decision they make; if they leave a constituency without representation for ian unreasonable length of time, they must ultimately suffer at the hands of the people. While the Ross Government was in power in Nova Scotia, I think it was the constituency of Renfrew that was left vacant for an unreasonable length of time, without any possible excuse, ae I understand it.
Some hon. MEMERS:	Nova Scotia?

Ontario. Did I say
" Nova Scotia "?
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order.
If the hon. gentleman has any point of order to make, I shall be glad if he will state it.
My point of order is that Renfrew is not in Nova Scotia. Further, I have been looking for "Messinnee" in the official list of constituencies, but I cannot find it.

If that is the hon.
gentleman's idea of a point of order, I am afraid that his mentality is in a somewhat disordered condition.
I was going on to say that when an election was finally brought on in the constituency of Renfrew, the people of that riding indicated their disapproval by returning a candidate hostile to the Government which was responsible for the delay. That, after all, ?eem= to me to be the real remedy. If you leave the law as it is, the Government can consider all the circumstances and fix the day of polling at a convenient and proper time. If it fails to do that, it will receive the condemnation of the constituency concerned, when at length the people have had an opportunity of expressing their views.
The other provision of the Bill is that election day shall be a public holiday. I am entirely opposed to that provision. It has been argued that it election day were a public holiday, the facilities for electors to vote would be greater; more voters would be able to go to the polls, and a larger poll would be held. I do not believe that that would be the result. As a matter of fact, under the present system elections ara usually held on a Monday, for the accommodation of commercial travellers and ethers who may be away from home. If under the proposed new system a Monday was chosen as election day and it was a public holiday, a great many electors would be tempted to go off on a week-end holiday and not return until the evening of the election day, so that there would be even greater difficulty in getting voters to the polls on a holiday of that kind than there would be if there was no holiday. So far as my observation has gone, employers invariably give their employees an opportunity to vote. That privilege is never denied to employees by employers in my province; nor, I believe, is it denied generally throughout Canada. I believe that the labouring men of this country would resent the idea that they should not make .the slight sacrifice involved in the loss of time required of them in connection with their casting their vote. I believe also that employers would resent

the suggestion that-they should be obliged to give their employees a holiday simply in order that they might exercise what they regard as a sacred trust. There are enough public-spirited labouring men in this country who will vote without having a holiday;
I believe there is no general demand for this proposed change in the present system. For these reasons it seems to me that the provision is an unwise one. There is some degree of merit in the Bill, and my only regret is that it contains such diverse and distinctly different provisions.
Mr. DOHERTY; Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House deals with two quite distinct matters. Two of its sections have for their purpose to fix specific .periods within which vacancies occurring in the representation in this House shall be filled. There is also a provision for a public holiday on election day. It is perhaps difficult, therefore, to speak of any one principle as being the principle of the Bill.
I assume that it might be considered that the principle of its first two provisions is, broadly stated, that there should be a defined or an ascertainable period within which vacancies must be filled. I quite recognize that there is a great deal to be said for that proposal. I am not prepared to say that the precise limit fixed by the Bill is necessarily the proper limit, or that the cause of the vacancy is a matter not to be considered when the date upon which the election should be held is being determined. .
But if that result can be arrived at, subject to proper conditions, there is a great deal to be said in support of the proposal that it would be an improvement if we had some fixed period of time, perhaps not necessarily the period fixed by this Bill, or some determined method by which the period during which the seat may remain vacant might be terminated. As I said on rising, one can hardly speak of any one thing as being the principle of this Bill. It is a Bill that might very properly and that should rightly receive consideration at the hands of the Privileges and Elections Committee. We had this whole matter of the Elections Bill, and if I mistake not, in particular, a suggested provision for a public holiday on election day, 'before the House for consideration upon the report of a special committee-I think it was in 1915-dealing with the question of an amendment to the Elections Act. I do not want to speak positively, but my recollection is that the sense of the House at that time was rather against our having an entire holiday on election day. Perhaps everybody would

agree on the principle that underlies that proposal, that is to say, that people should have sufficient free time to do their voting; it is a question of detail whether a whole day is necessary or not. Taking that view of the Bill, and recognizing that there is merit in the proposal, without wanting to commit myself absolutely to that proposal or to the principle, at all events as it is sought to be applied-leaving that an open question-I would be disposed to assent to the Bill having its second reading with a view to its being referred to the Privileges and Elections Committee as, I understand that would be acceptable to the promoter of the Bill. I certainly think it is a matter that ought to have the consideration of a committee, and the Privileges and Elections Committee seems to be the most suitable body.

I do not intend to discuss this matter at length, but I want to express my disappointment at the course taken by the hon. gentleman who has seen fit to introduce this measure. The hon. gentleman has not, in one particular at least, gone as far as his courage should have, taken him. He apparently has no objection to a member of this House representing more than one constituency at the same time. In that respect, the hon. gentleman gives his consent to the disfranchising of one constituency.
May I ask the hon. gentleman in what way does the hon. member not object?

There is in this House one hon. member who, at the present time, represents two constituencies, who was elected for two constituencies in the province of Quebec. So far as I know lie has not elected for which one of those he will sit. He has, therefore deprived the people of one of those constituencies, I do not know which one, of having a representative in this House.
Quite right.
Quite right? Very well.

May I tell the hon. gentleman that he objects as much as my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman claims that my hon. friend who introduced this Bill dees not object to an hon. member sitting for two constituencies. He never said that, no more than the hon. gentleman did.
My hon. friend does not seem to appreciate the point which I am endeavouring to make.
Perhaps not.

That is my fault for
not putting it in clearer language. The point I make is that when the hon. member who has introduced this Bill makes provision whereby a man who is elected for more than one constituency has, within a certain time, to specify which it is he is elected for, he does not go as far as he should. By the provisions of this Bill he gives his consent to a man's being elected for more than one constituency for a time at least; he gives his consent to the disfranchising of that constituency for a time at least.

I see my hon. friend's
point.

The hon. gentleman
should go to this length, to make provision in his Bill that no member in this House shall run for more than one constituency in one election. For instance, how can the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux)-I am not going to name his other constituency
Yes, do.

-because I realize the fact that there are hon. gentlemen on the other side whose education has been neglected as much as mine has, like for instance the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow) who does not know when the name is	properly
pronounced. He might take me to task if I called it " Maisoneff," or " Maisonoove," or some other name. Hon. gentlemen, however, know to what constituency I refer. How can, the hon. member for Gaspe, who is also the member for that other constituency which I will not name, and who is a gentleman of great eloquence, great force in argument, get up and in his usual forceful manner support a Bill of this kind? If he does he condemns himself, because, if he says the hon. member for Georges Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs)-
Pretty good.

-I do not know whether I have the accent on that right, too-is correct in saying that a member who is elected for two constituencies should, within thirty days, specify which seat he wants to sit for, then the hon. gentleman is condemned because of the fact that he has represented -or misrepresented, as some of us may think at times-two constituencies in this .tiouse ever since 1917. We cannot have the benefit of the eloquence of the hon. member for Gaspe and that other constituency which
begins , with " M," because of the peculiar position in which he is placed. If the hon. member will just change the second suggested amendment by making it read:
No member shall be a candidate for more than one constituency in any election

I will support that part of his Bill, at all events, most heartily, and I believe it will receive the approval generally of the people of this country. But the hon. gentleman, for some reason or other, is not prepared to go that far.
As regards the holiday, what reasons can be advanced why there should be a public holiday on election day? It does not take a man a whole day to cast his vote. Provision is made, I think, for the labourer to have a couple of hours in the day in order to poll his vote, and I suppose his pay goes on for those two hours. Would you force the employer of labour to pay his employee for the whole day when he could poll his vote in ten minutes or half an 'hour? Would that be fair? If you would not force the employer to do that, would you force the labourer to do without bis pay for the whole day when he need lose only half an 'hour or one hour of his time at the outside? It will work an injustice to the employer or to the employee whichever way you arrange it. 1 see no reason for proclaiming election day a holiday. I also object to the other feature to which I have drawn attention, and if these two objection's are well founded there is not much left of the Bill. I think the Bill as arranged is inopportune at the present time. I hope, however, that the hon. member will follow it up, and if he does not I can assure him that at another session I intend to introduce a Bill along the lines I have mentioned providing that no man shall be allowed to be a candidate for more than one constituency in the same election.

The hon. member for Fromtenac (Mr. Edwards) has expressed the thoughts that -were engaging my own mind just as he arose to speak. I would not go so far as to criticise the hon. member who represents the constituencies, of Maisonneuve and Gaspe, but I do criticise the pernicious principle which allows a man under any circumstances to be a candidate for two seats at the one time. Even in a municipal government no man is allowed to run for school trustee and also for alderman at the same time. He must select in what capacity he chooses to represent the people. I think that the prin-

ciple of representing two constituencies imposes an injustice on the constituency. One of those constituencies must be unrepresented during the term of Parliament, or else the expense is imposed on the county of holding another election. I trust that this matter will receive the serious consideration of the House, and if iit be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, I trust they will submit a recommendation to this House for removing this evil that has existed ior a long time in this country'. If a candidate is going to stand for election to the House of Commons, I think there should be a means by which he would have to declare what is his intent, and his deposit should be paid .previous to nomination day, 60 that it will be impossible for one candidate to receive a nomination for two constituencies on the same day. There is absolutely nothing in justice, right or equity to justify the pernicious principle by which *a man is allowed even to contest two constituencies for the same House.
We have often discussed in this House the question of making election day a holiday; and there has been a difference of opinion. Some years ago the Municipal Act provided that the first Monday should be the date for the municipal elections; but certain cities had powers conferred on them by the Provincial Government to select New Year's Day instead. The arguments urged strongly at that time for making polling day a holiday was that commercial travellers and others would thereby be enabled to take part in the election, but the very reverse of what was anticipated has resulted. There was a very large shrinkage in the vote polled, and to-day in the city of Toronto, London, and other cities in the province of Ontario where municipal elections are held on a holiday there is a decided shrinkage in the vote polled, which is not in the interest of good government. Owing to the lack of interest in municipal elections, which should be a matter of concern to the citizens, men of mediocrity get elected to important positions in the municipal service.
I agree with the hon. member who said that this measure had points in it that were of value. However he did not say much on what he thought was of value. I agree that some definite limit should be fixed within which an election should be held after a seat has become vacant. Whether it should be sixty days or longer I am not prepared to state, but that is a matter which the Committee on Privileges and Elections,

if it was referred to them, could decide. I repeat, that the mere fact 'that the principle has been followed by the Dominion and Provincial Governments for many years past of allowing a member to represent two constituencies does not make that principle right. No constituency should be unrepresented for years, or even for too many months, and legislation against this pernicious principle should be enacted.
As the Minister of Justice has said, there are points of interest presented in this Bill, and I trust that they will receive proper consideration. I trust that if the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) introduces a similar Bill later on he will provide an amendment absolutely to prevent the possibility of any candidate contesting two seats for this Parliament in one election.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
There is a point I have not *
heard mentioned in the debate which I think would be worthy of the attention of the Committee, if the suggestion of the Minister of Justice is to be carried out. There are eight, unhappily, now nine, vacancies in this Parliament. Under this Bill now before the House we would be obliged to have these elections within sixty days of the date of the vacancy, but they would not all take place together. The Government might still pick and choose for itself. Now in our general elections we have accepted the principle of simultaneous polling. I would suggest for the consideration of the Committee that they should endeavour to find words the effect of which would be that where two or more vacancies exist at the same time, unless there is good reason to the contrary, the elections shall be held together. As far as possible we should have simultaneous polling, and no Government of either party should have the right to pick and choose, bringing on an election that might be helpful at one time, and another one later on. The House will generally agree that if we are asking for changes along these lines, that question deserves careful consideration.

It appears to me that there is a point that has not been discussed with regard to the question of dual representation. We know that very often protests are entered and it might be very convenient for a gentleman to retire from a constituency in which his election was being protested.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext: Provision is being made for that.

Protests frequently drag out one or two years and that is why on many occasions members who have been willing to retire from one of their constituencies have not been permitted to do so. While the matter is pending in court and the validity of the election is in peril a member is not allowed to retire even if he is willing to do so, and on some occasions seats have been held in that way for one or two years after an election. I would further point out that sixty days is a very short notice. In the ease of by-elections in Ontario, and I presume it is the same in most of the other provinces, the lists are not by any means ready. In a country district it is a very serious matter to prepare an electoral list. It may not have been got ready for one or two years prior to the vacancy and it is absurd to think that an election could be held within sixty days and. a proper list prepared for the particular constituency in such great haste. I submit these suggestions to my hon. friend, asking him if he has taken them into consideration, and if he does not think that the Bill should be modified in the direction I have indicated in both these respects. For-myself I agree with the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that no candidate should be per>
mitted to run for more than one constituency. I cannot remember it having been done in Ontario.
Is my hon. friend aware that it is the custom in England?

I believe it is. I
am not saying that it is not a time-honoured custom, but we are reformers sometimes even if we are called Tories or strong Conservatives, and I am a reformer to that extent. I believe that if an abuse exists, and I think it does exist, whereby a constituency can be disfranchised for a year or a term of years, it should not be	permitted	in any province, and
I say that with all deference to my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux), who is .an excellent member of the House; for if any man can represent two constituencies I presume the hon. gentleman can do so as -well as any one else. He carries great weight and is a man of breadth and ability. I am not disparaging his ability to represent two constituencies, but I think it is an entirely wrong principle, and if the Bill were amended in accordance with the suggestion of the member for Frontenac, at the same time having in view the points I have mentioned, I would have no serious objection to it, .although I have not considered it in all its details as closely as I should like to.

There seems to be some confusion in connection with the constituency represented by the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe. I do not see how the hon. member can legally hold two seats. Rule 79 says:
All members who are returned for two or more electoral districts shall make their election for which of the districts they will serve, within twenty days after it shall appear that there is no question upon the return for either district.
The hon. gentleman can therefore hold only one seat unless there was a protest against his holding either. It is interesting to know whether or not a protest was entered against the hon. member in respect of either Maisonneuve or Gaspe. The hon. gentleman would seem to be more interested in this question than any one else.

I am not more interested than any one else in this matter. I wish to obey the law and I have always obeyed it. I was the happy victim of circumstances at the last general election in the fact that I was elected for two constituencies. I must say that personally I do not think that any member of the House should monopolize two seats. I adhere to the principle of my hon. friend's Bill, for which I shall vote. But sometimes in an election party exigencies here a* in England make it necessary that a man should be a candidate for two constituencies. The law, however, is very wise. My hon. friend has just read one of the rules of the House providing that twenty days after the election a member who has been returned for , two constituencies must decide which of .them he elects to represent in the House, unless he is protested. Mr. Speaker, I would not have sat for both seats last session had I not been protested at the last election. There is a protest against 'my election in the constituency of Maisonneuve, and I am awaiting the result of that protest before electing for which constituency I shall sit in the House. I may say, however, that during the last Parliament our late lamented friend the ex-member for Charlevoix-Montmorency sat for both the county of Charlevoix and Montmorency, and there iwas no protest. I remember asking him at the time how he could sit for both seats without being subject to the consequences of the law. He told me at the time that he had taken the



advice of the Minister of Justice-I do not know whether he referred to my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) or to some one in the Department of Justice-and he said that, protest or no protest, there was no sanction to that rule. For my part, I have more regard for the sanctity of the rules of the House, and when a rule says that within a certain period the member who happens to represent two constituencies must elect which he shall sit for, I consider there is an obligation, at least a moral obligation, on him to obey that rule, and I stand ready to obey it as soon as the protest against my election in the county of Maisonneuve has been disposed of. In all sincerity, however, I say that although it is a great honour to represent two constituencies, I do not believe the principle is democratic. We should give each constituency in the' country the opportunity of having its own representative, and though a member may be able to serve the interests of two constituencies, the principle is undemocratic and should not prevail. The Bill introduced by my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) will therefore have my support.
Hon. Mr. (BROTHERS: Has the protest referred to by my hon. friend been disposed of yet?
ino.
It is nearly two years since the election.
It is not two years; it is only eighteen months.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg leave to make a statement in regard to what the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) has said. There must have been some misunderstanding between the late distinguished member to whom my hon. friend referred and himself as to the statement that was made. I certainly was not consulted on the question by the exmember for Charlevoix-Montmorency.

I think he said the
Department of Justice; I do not think he said the Minister of Justice. Perhaps that was not the intention of the then sitting member for Charlevoix.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no recollection
of having heard of it.

I am disposed to accept
the suggestion of the Minister of Justice that this Bill should go before the Privileges and Elections Committee. That committee, selected by the Government from both sides of the House, is particularly fitted to deal with this important Bill, I feel sure that

the committee will be favourable to the passing of this measure by the House.
I am sure we must all appreciate the delicacy of our good friend the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) in halting this debate on Thursday last in order to have the view of the hon. member .for Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux). I did not think it was in him, and I am sure that the opportunity given us of learning of his goodness of heart is something that we all appreciate particularly as it caused him to be somewhat severely castigated by the Montreal Gazette a day or two ago. I quote from the Gazette-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman is not in order in quoting any newspaper report reflecting upon the motives or statements of any member of this House.

There is no reference to any member of this House. It has reference to the policy of the Government. Inferentially, it may reflect upon the hon. member for Digby and Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). I quote''from the Montreal Gazette of yesterday:
The subject of the division of Thursday was the Bill of Mr. Jacobs to require the prompt filling by by-elections of vacancies occurring in the House of Commons, and the stopping of the abuse of members elected for two constituencies holding both seats through a Parliamentary term and depriving a section of the electorate of their proper voice in the decision of national issues. It should not have been the occasion of a party division, and the generalship that permitted one was' at fault.
I do not wish to make any comment.
Does the hon. gentleman blame me for the attitude taken by the other side when they made it a party question and voted against my motion?

I am merely referring to
the fact that the hon. gentleman who happens to be a whip on the other side of the House, .should have taken the action that he did in raising a question at the time, bringing about this comment from the Montreal Gazette which probably knows more *about the affairs of hon. gentlemen on the other side than I do.
Mr. DAVIDSON. It is a rebuke to those on the other side of the House.

The hon. member for
Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) stated he would support the Bill if it contained a clause to the effect that no. candidate should present himself for more than one seat. He seems to think that if he cannot get a whole loaf he is not going to be satisfied

with half. The rule which I have incorporated in my Bill in regard to candidates presenting themselves for more than one seat is the rule in England and my object in incorporating it in this measure was to bring it in line with the English law. The English Parliament has been functioning for six or seven hundred years and I do not think you could have a better pattern than the English system. When we fall away from the rule laid down by the Mother of Parliaments we always get ourselves into trouble. That is the case with the matter now under review. In Ontario there is a provision whereby practically automatic elections for the legislature must take place. I have not seen the Act myself but I am told that there is a provision that when two members give notice to the Speaker, signed by their own hand that a seat is vacant, it is the duty of the Speaker to take cognizance of it and cause the writ to issue forthwith. I am inclined to think that for the present we ought to be satisfied to permit candidates to present themselves for .more than one seat because there is always a danger that a candidate, no matter how good he may be, may be without honour in his own county, and for that reason we ought to permit him to try his chances in more than one division. So soon as he has a seat, so soon as he is elected in one constituency his duty is to see that some body else is provided with the seat which he himself cannot use.
If the principle which the hon. gentleman enunciated be right as regards running for two constituencies, why would it not be as right for a candidate to run for fifty constituencies?

The principle is the same and when' he obtains one seat he gives the other forty-nine to other people who can use them. I am rather inclined to think that the attack made upon my hon. friend from Maisonneuve and Gaspe by some of the members of the House is due to the fact that they cannot pronounce the word " Maisonneuve" as it should be pronounced, and they think that if he elects to sit for Gaspe it will make it more convenient all round.
With regard to the last clause of my Bill which has been subjected to a good deal of criticism, when the Bill goes before the Privileges and Elections Committee I will be prepared to amend it in a way which will suit the committee or I may ask that it be struck out altogether. As I said in introducing the Bill, I am not wedded to that particular section. I do not think it
34i
is as important as the other provisions of the Bill. I think it would be preferable that the voter should go to the poll untrammelled and unencumbered by the aid of his boss or employer. It sometimes makes for independence in the matter of voting, but perhaps we have not yet arrived at the stage in our development when a consideration of that kind weighs with members of the House. At any rate, the matter can be discussed and dealt with when it goes before the Privileges and Elections Committee. I feel that when it comes back to the House from that committee we will have something substantive upon which we can act.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty, the Bill was referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-FUNERAL OF THE LATE HON. MR. COCHRANE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before making the motion to adjourn the House, I would ask leave to premise it by another motion. There was among the members of this House, I think, a very general feeling that the House had taken no action to express the sentiment which it entertained in regard to the loss we have sustained by the death of our colleague and confrere, the late Hon. Frank Cochrane.
It is a matter of regret, I am sure, to all of us that, the funeral not taking place in this city, it is not possible for us to attend that ceremony and pay that last tribute of respect to our departed friend. But it has been suggested to me that as that is impossible, it would be a fitting thing that this House .suspend its sitting at 'the hour at which the funeral is to take place to-morrow in Toronto. Recognizing the sentiment that underlie.' the desire for that action, a sentiment which I am sure is shared by us all, I beg now to move that when this House adjourns this evening it stand adjourned until four o'clock to-morrow afternoon. In this way we shall refrain from carrying on the business of the House for the period of time during which the funeral ceremony will take place.

speakerposition: stagedirection

On motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 10.20 p.m.

speechtext:
Therefore, for the purposes of my argument and for the full presentation of this matter, I shall take it for granted that the telegram is authentic, that it -was sent, and that there is no denial of it.
Now the whole question is as-to the proper interpretation to be placed upon it, and the meaning that is to be assigned to its contents. If it is true that the message was sent, then inevitably we desire to know why it was sent and what was the purpose of it. If it was a proper legitimate transaction why were we treated to a secret code? If it was lawful for the Minister of the Interior, under the Act, to say to the Prime Minister: "You will gather up a thousand soldier votes in England or France and assign them to different constituencies in my province of Manitoba;"-if that was perfectly legitimate and there was nothing to conceal about it, one naturally would suppose that the telegram could be sent in plain English; since there was no mystery connected with it. But it is suggested to one's mind that when the message is clothed in these unusual and mysterious terms there is really something about it which the Minister of Interior is anxious that ordinary men shall know nothing about, and that he wants it to be understood only by the Prime Minister and those who would be concerned in carrying out the instructions contained in it. Now, it is true Sir that when the Military Voters' Act was going through the House in 1917 it was very strenuously pointed out by members on this side and members who are to-day sitting on the Government side of the House, that the measure was intended for this very purpose, that it was a piece of machinery that was created for no other purpose than this, and that for that reason therefore it should not be countenanced by Parliament. We were informed then that the intention was perfectly legitimate and that everything was to be entirely open and above board. Now, however, we find that the prophecies which were made when the Act was before the House have been fulfilled and that the fears of the Opposition have unfortunately been realized. If it is lawful under the Act for the Government to have absolute control of non-resident soldiers' votes, then, under such an interpretation of the statute, I should say that the Government is responsible for a piece of election machinery which is in utter defiance of the Constitution and the rights of the Canadian people. If ti e ministers of the Crown take the ground that the contents of this telegram, and the conduct to be followed in consequence of the instructions conveyed by the message, are 
both justifiable, I say that the Government is responsible for insidious legislation. Secondly, I make the statement that if on the contrary the law is not open to that construction-and I certainly believe it is not -then the conduct of the' Government in tampering with the soldier's votes is not only censurable, but constitutes a political crime against the freedom and the constitutional rights of the people of Canada. It is in that light, Sir, and in the belief that the telegram is not open to the construction which the minister will no doubt put upon it that I wish to devote some attention to this motion. This is perhaps an unfortunate occasion on which to introduce this subject; but gentlemen on this side of the House have no selection of their days. They have to be content with the days as they come to them and according as the rules of the House afford them opportunity. It is different with the Government. They can put their motions and Bills just where it suits their convenience. It is suggested to me that I should not take very much time this afternoon in discussing this subject in view of the fact that the House, under the rule, adjourns at six o'clock. Well, Mr. Speaker,
I have no desire to encroach upon the time of the House beyond doing what is absolutely necessary for the proper presentation in my case.
But I do say, Sir, that it is open to the Government to bring this up again at any time-to bring it up to-morrow if they like -if my taking more than half the time between my commencement and six o'clock should be regarded by them as unfair. If ever I won any success in politics, or at the bar, or anywhere else, it was never by taking an undue advantage of an opponent.
I have no skill in that line and I have no intention of attempting to take an advantage of any person by reason of any time that I may take in trying to discuss this matter this afternoon. If I should be regarded as trespassing upon the time which my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) may think should belong to him, I shall be very sorry. All I can say is that I will get along just, as quickly as possible.
What is the law 'that we are dealing with? What is the law under which the" minister justifies this telegram? I am not saying that he is going to justify the telegram. I am not saying that he is going to admit that he sent it at all. I do not know what his answer may be. This is not like a case in court where the pleadings are filed and you know to a great extent what the answer of the other side is. It is the privilege and right of hon. members themselves, as re-

ceivers and senders of this message, to bold their tongues entirely, to speak or not to speak at all, but up to the time that they will speak we have no means of knowing what the answer may be. But taking it fox, granted that they are going to justify this telegram, I wish to point out what the section of the Act is under which they were acting.
I think it will not be disputed or controverted when I say that the right to the franchise, and the use of the franchise by any individual, is one of tire most sacred and dearly prized possessions of a British subject and that any interference with that right is an offence of the gravest character.
I must say further, Sir, that as I understand the exercise of the franchise by any individual, it is a judicial act. Lawyers will have no difficulty in knowing what is meant by an executive act as distinguished, from a judicial act. The magistrate signs a summons ; that is an executive act. The man who is sued appears before him and he gives judgment against him; that is a judicial act. So, there is a difference between an executive act and a judicial act. I submit, Sir, that the man who goes to the polling booth and marks his ballot is not performing a mechanical, executive act, but lie is performing a judicial act. He is exercising his judgment as to the way in Which he shall vole and he is exercising his judgment upon the Government for or against which he is voting He is passing judgment on the concerns of the country in which he is entitled to exercise the ! rights1 of citizenship. Therefore I submit that when that man is going to exercise the right of voting he must do so by the proper exercise of his own judgment, that it should not be in the power of any other party to say to that man, or woman: " This way you shall vote," or: " This way you shall not vote, and you have nothing to say about it beyond the mere mechanical act of marking your ballot." The section to which I wish * to refer is section 3 of chapter 34 of the Act of 1917, which is called " The Military Voters' Act" Section 3 reads as follows:
(1) Every military elector shall he qualified and entitled to vote at a general election.
1 If he can state the electoral district wherein he last continuously resided during at least four months of the twelve months immediately preceding his appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service, or so particularly specify a place or places within an electoral district whereat during such period of time he so resided that such electoral district can therefrom be ascertained, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or to be ascertained, and his vote shall be applied thereto.
(3)	If he cannot state or so specify an electoral district or place wherein he has so resided for the time and within the period mentioned in subsection two but can state an electoral district or so specify a place within Canada wherein he has at any other time resided, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or made ascertainable and his vote shall be applied thereto.	,
(4)	If he cannot, because of non-residence or otherwise, so state or specify, he shall be deemed an elector of, and his vote shall be applied to, such electoral district as he may indicate.
This last subsection. 4 is the one that is right in point in connection with the matter that we are discussing. A person who had never lived in Canada, but who was made an elector under this section, although he could not name any spol in Canada which he knew, was permitted to designate some part of Canada where he wanted to deposit his ballot, which place he might indicate.
I will read that subsection again:
If he cannot, because of non-residence or otherwise, so state or specify, he shall be deemed an elector of, and his vote shall be applied to, such electoral district as he may indicate.
It is rather a hard proposition that men who know nothing about this country, who have never seen this country, who have never lived in it, who, in so far as we know, are absolutely ignorant of our institutions, who know nothing about the right to the exercise of the franchise, or what it is exercised for, should step in and interfere with our affairs. But if those men have such knowledge of this country as will enable them to exercise that rignt intelligently, it is not so very bad after all. But if a group of people of that kind, running up into the thousands, who have never lived in this country, who know nothing about our institutions, are put in the hands of the Government, or in the hands of anybody else-I do not care whether it is in the hands of the Government or in the hands of one party or another-and they have power to place them, just like so many sheep in any yard in which they wish to drive them, I submit, Sir, that it is a most extraordinary thing and a condition that no civilized people should tolerate for one minute.
Yet that was the condition that existed and it was under a condition of that kind and in regard to men of that class than uiis telegram was sent.
Will you suppose, or will any intelligent man in this House suppose, that this was the first intimation the Prime Minister had that this telegram was coming? Will anybody suppose that a man of the intelligence of the Prime Minister of this country could

be approached, even by one of his colleagues, and told to do a thing of this kind unless it was pre-arranged and understood that this thing was on and that it could be done? I submit, .therefore, that I am justified in stating in this motion that there was a pre-arranged and preconceived scheme by which this thing was to be done. Otherwise the telegram would not be put in the bare, bold, blunt manner in which it was put, except of course that it was in code.
Before I forget it, I wish to say that it was hinted in the interview of the Minister of' the Interior that this telegram was stolen. Let me assure you, Sir, that as far as I am concerned, or as far as anybody getting this information from me is concerned, the telegram was not stolen but was passed out of the inner court of my hon. friend's party in the city of Winnipeg and placed in the hands of those who brought it here; and if it is necessary, the finger-marks of those who were handling it, and every evidence of originality in connection with the whole business, can be produced and privately shown to my hon. friend at any time that he wants to see it. So that as far as I am concerned

It will be produced, Sir; the man who sent the telegram, and the man who delivered the code and the interpretation into our possession, will be produced, and then we will be able to tell where this thing came from. It would be a pity indeed that I would be going around peddling this thing from house to house. Nothing of the kind -it is in proper custody and will be produced at the proper place.

Now, Sir, I have already argued that in my judgment such a condition of things should not- exist and I now wish to point out that the grouping of men or voters into any counties to which they do not belong is a violation of the rights of the people of this country. Why is this country divided into ridings, counties, and subdivisions? Why would not the people of the whole of Canada vote for a certain group of men at large and send members at large to the House oi Commons if there was no purpose in creating subdivisions and counties? The idea was that a certain group of men in certain places would have, the privilege of being represented in this House, and for that purpose the Constitution provides, as set forth in section 51 of the British North America Act, as follows:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time as the Parliament of Canada, from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules:
1.	Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five members;
2.	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number of sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained) :
3.	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded; but a fractional part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number.
There is another subsection dealing with this matter, but I have quoted this section in order to show that the Constitution provides for the subdividing of the country or for giving a representative-or a vote in this House to a set number of people. The unit of representation at the last re-adjustment (was 30,819. That is every group of 30,819 individuals in Canada are entitled to a representative in this House; in other words that for every five thousand, or thereabouts of voters, there will be a representative. I think it is a fair statement to make that before women were given the right to vote and when this Act was made there would be only one in every -six of the population who had a vote. Therefore, when the British North America Act. was enacted, every five thousand electors were supposed to have a voice in this House through a member of Parliament. Are you going to destroy that unit by giving the electoral qualification to men all over the world who have

no interest in Canada at all? If so, when a group of men in any constituency in the Dominion wash to express their views by sending a man of their own choice to Parliament, you can always defeat that idea by gathering some of your cohorts from different parts of the country and throwing them into that constituency, and so defeating the will and wish of the people. That, Sir, is evidently the purpose of the Military Voters' Act, and that is the purpose of this telegram-at least- that is the effect of the telegram if I am to believe its contents and the instructions that were given under it. In this way the will and wish of the people and their constitutional rights can be defeated.
I am how going to quote some observations made in this House some years ago by a very distinguished Conservative, a gentleman who was for many years a member of Parliament, I refer to Sir Edmund Osier. That gentleman, who is well known and much respected in the Dominion and in this House, speaking here in 1900-and his words will be found at page 5508 and 5511 of the Hansard of that session, said:
I claim that if there has been fraud to the extent of only one ballot, that affected the whole election no matter even if the gentleman elected had 400 ballots of a majority in his favour. I say that the man who sits here representing that constituency is sitting here fraudulently	There is a greater dishonesty than stealing money from the treasury of the country-the dishonesty of stealing the franchise from the people. This country can stand the stealing of millions of money, humiliating and degrading -as that may be; but this country cannot stand the slighest attempt on the part of the Government or of any man to shield electoral corruption.
That is the view that was held by a leading Conservative, a view which no doubt he holds to-day; and when he expressed that view in the House, sitting then in Opposition as he was, I am sure it received the acclamation of the hon. gentlemen who sat around him on the Opposition side, which was then the Conservative Opposition.
Sir Edmund Osier is no longer a member of the House, but this principle which he enunciated is just as true now as it was then, and if there is any attempt to interfere with the law so as to thwart the will of the people the atmosphere should be made so hot that no Oovernment and no man attempting such a thing could live for one day in our democratic country.

If that be true, if that be the way in which this thing was done, if those men were not given any permit to exercise their 'God-given right of using their own brains and head and judgment as to how they should vote, surely this is not a matter that is going to be tolerated by the people of Canada and by hon. members in this House. We are asking only that this question should be fully and properly investigated and the truth made clear to the people of Canada. I do not know that it is necessary that I should make any comments now upon the views that were expressed in Parliament when this Military Voters' Act was passed. But I think I should point out some observations made by some hon. gentlemen who still have seats here and who would seem even then to have had some knowledge of what was going to be done. I find that the hon. member for Westmorland, N.B., said:
Mr. Copp: I would give every British subject the freedom that any citizen of this country is entitled to.
Mr. Morphy: Except the right to vote.
Mr. Copp:	My hon. friend is wrong there.
Take the case suggested by the hon. member for St. John, of a British subject who has enlisted in our forces after residing in the United States for a number of years. Now, although that man knows nothing about Canadian politics, he * is to be given the right to vote. Then subsection 3 of section 3 says: If he cannot, because of non-residence or otherwise, so state or specify, he shall he deemed an elector of, and his vote shall be applied to, such electoral district as he may indicate. He may not know a single candidate or a single electoral district in all Canada; so how can he intelligently indicate what district his vote shall be applied to?
Mr. Morphy: It will be done for him.
He will not be called upon to exercise any judgment; he will not be called upon to. know anything; he will be only a mere pawn 'on the chess board, and he will be told what to do.
Mr. Copp: By whom?
Mr. Morphy:	Don't ask me.
Don't ask me, says the good member for Perth, North. He would not disclose any secrets; he would not give away any of the machinery; but this slipped out of him, as much as to say to the hon. member for Westmorland: Do not worry; this thing is all arranged. As this officer said: "It was all cooked and dried," and the Government could not very well afford to keep my good friend from Perth altogether on the outside of this thing. He was too important a man. He knew what it was, but he would not tell. He said: Do not ask me,
I know all about it, but I will not tell. That goes to show that this was not a new scheme; that it had been well known for a long time. The hon. member for St. John at that time, the Hon. Mr. Pugsley, is a gentleman whose word must be received with a great deal of acceptance and weight by this Government, because they thought he wag good enough and deserving enough to be made a representative of the King in the province of New Brunswick. This Government, with all the wisdom and experience they had in a general way and the express and definite knowledge they had of this hon. gentleman who is now Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, thought he was the only man who should be given that appointment. Therefore, what the Hon. Mr. Pugsley said on that occasion must not and cannot be sneered at by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. He said:
Mr. Pugsiey:	If the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) is not going to resume his remarks, I would say that, in my judgment, the Minister of Justice ought to withdraw this provision to which exception has been taken. My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) made the statement before recess that he would not suggest that the minister had any ulterior motives, but I am prepared to say that if the minister, after his attention has been called to the injustice which may be done by continuing this provision in the Bill, insists upon its being continued there, he must not object if we suspect him of having ulterior motives and of having designed this Bill in order that unfair practice may be exercised and unfair advantage obtained in an election.
Further on he says:
What can be done under this provision? A Canadian soldier who has gone to the front is limited in his choice of a constituency to that particular constituency in which he has resided. He has one vote and one choice. The American

soldier, the man who is not a resident of Canada, who may happen to be a British subject, no matter in what country he may have resided, who has joined the Canadian Expeditionary Force, not necessarily enlisting in Canada, possibly enlisting in the United States, or in England, possibly enlisting on this side, because if he enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, his expenses across the ocean would be paid and he would receive a higher rate of pay than if he went to England and enlisted in the Imperial Forces, is to have the choice of 230 odd constituencies in Canada in the casting of his vote. That is grossly unfair. It gives opportunity for fraud of the worst kind. It gives opportunity for men who may not have been residents of Canada to join together, to make up their minds perhaps under proper guidance, as to the constituencies in which their votes shall be cast, in which the contest will be close, in which the majority will be a narrow one, and thus, they may possibly control many constituencies in Canada in favour of the Government of the day. The Government, under this Bill, appoints its own presiding officers; with the choice of those presiding officers the leader of the Opposition has nothing to do. That, in my judgment, is wrong. It is contrary to fair and proper administration, and it would not be too much to say that, if the minister persists in continuing this provision in this measure, it is designedly intended to offer an opportunity to steal the election from the people of Canada.
That was the expressed opinion of Dr. Pugsley at that time. We are not obliged, however, to rest entirely on the opinion of such a man as Dr. Pugsley, high as that authority may be. When this Bill was going through, fortunately we had sitting on this side of the House the present senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) now a member of this Government. Hon. gentlemen sitting to your right, Mr. (Speaker, cannot sneer to-day at any statements made by that hon. member, because they regard him as one of their big men, and as a man who would always express, his opinion as the truth came to him. What did he say about this Bill, about the machinery that it was creating, and about its possible effects? He said:
The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) stated that this Bill does not involve the question of what Government should be in control of public affairs; nor is it important to consider which party is in power in this country. In that statement I am sure we can all agree with him. For the life of me I cannot see how it is possible for the membership of the House of Commons to divide on party lines upon a question of this kind. I regretted hearing one or two hon. gentlemen opposite rather insinuating that, because one does not agree with the principle of this Bill, therefore, he is discriminating against the Canadian soldier. That is an unfair suggestion to make, and, as far as I am concerned, I resent it altogether. Personally, I would not care if every soldier enlisted in the Canadian force was given the vote. It would matter little to me personally; personally it would matter little to any member of the House, but we are dealing with a piece of sub-
TMr McKenzie.]
stantive legislation "which has to do with the franchise. The franchise has alwoys been in all countries a question of citizenship. We ^should settle this Bill upon some principle. "There - is no desire on the part of any hon. merriber on this side of the House to do an injustice to anybody who is fighting in the Canadian forces to-day. It is rather unpleasant to make any suggestion in the way of an amendment to the Bill which gives anybody an opportunity of making any insinuation. I do so simply because I believe the principle involved in the particular section which we are discussing is unsound. The member for Annapolis justifies his position by reference to the Franchise Act of Nova Scotia wherein it is provided that ownership of real estate carries the right to the franchise on the part of any British subject. That will only carry the hon. gentleman a certain distance because in most of the provinces of Canada residence in addition to ownership of real estate is necessary to qualification to vote. So, my hon. friend does not get very far with the argument, because the majority of the provinces require residence as well as real estate property qualifications. I doubt very much if England would follow our example, if they were enacting legislation of this character. Take the aviation service ; I am told that in the Royal Naval Air Service sixty-five per cent of the men are Canadian born. It is quite proper that "we should provide a method by which they could exercise the franchise at the first election, but I doubt if the British Parliament would give them the franchise simply because they constitute a large portion of that force.
Now I coma to the part of his speech that I wish to emphasize:
I think the suggestion in the Bill is fundamentally wrong, and it is for that Teason I oppose it. It is true, as the Minister of Justice says, that there are only a few men in the whole Canadian force who will be affected by the Bill, and by that reasoning possibly we might forego our objection, as little harm would come if they were allowed to vote. But there is a principle involved.
A little further on he says:
I want to protest against this legislation. 1 say it is in principle abominable, as were the motives which prompted its introduction. The whole thing is outrageous and unnecessary, and, besides, it is a cruel exercise of the powers of
the majority of this Parliament	
We shall a-ppeal to the people-
Here is where the good Liberalism of my quondam friend came to the fore.
We. shall appeal to the people of my province against this iniquitous legislation. I feel sure that they will not approve the miserable partisan course pursued by some members of the House in seeking at this stage to introduce an amendment into what is already a very cumbersome piece of legislation, the War-Time Election Act-an action taken purely for base political and partisan purposes. We will take our appeal, Mr. Speaker, from this House to Philippi, and we will meet hon. gentlemen there on this issue.	_
The only trouble is that my good friend worked Philippi off the map before the election. Those are the views of two of the

most reliable hon. gentlemen that we had on this side of the House at that date. One of them was taken into the bosom of the Government and given the highest position they could offer him. He was made Lieutenant Governor, and I presume that if the Government had had the power they would have made him Governor General. Not having that power they did the next best thing. They held him up to the good citizens of New Brunswick saying " Here is a man that the good populace of New Brunswick will delight to honour; we have made him Governor."
Although he received his gift at their hands, that was his opinion of their actions; and having accepted him as a man of such high standing they cannot very well now ignore the truth of his statement. On the other hand, we have the views of our good friend the member for Halifax, who is now a member of the Government. These are his statements and his views then, and they are his views to-day if he would care to express them and to find out where Phillippi is.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are other observations which I feel should be made but time does not permit me * to express thgm. My case, however, is. that such a power as appears to have been exercised by the Government in this connection was improper. I contend that it is a violation of every principle of civil government in this country and should not have been exercised. It is absurd to pretend that we enjoy responsible government when the Government of the day assume the right to dictate to free men just how they shall vote and where, and how many votes shall be taken here or there, altogether regardless of qualifications or legal procedure. This, I say, is a mockery and is absolutely subversive of all the traditions of responsible government. I think, Sir, that both you and the country as well as every hon. member in this House will fully realize that I am justified in bringing this matter to the attention of Parliament, and if this Act- allows a condition of this kind to exist, then it should be absolutely abolished. Are we to be told that an independent parliament such as this will have on the statute books an Act that places in the hands of the Prime Minister and two or three of his followers, or even one of them, the power to instruct their own officials as to how they shall act under circumstances of this kind, when there are certain constitutional and regular methods to be followed? Is a minister to direct the officials of the Government in this manner-their own commanders and officers and every one under their thumb and control, officers who were preaching to these men only the Sunday before the election in such terms as these: ''Gentlemen, we do not want 99 per cent of your votes; we want 100 per cent"? That was the exhortation of generals, colonels and others from the top to the bottom, and for the poor man who might attempt to exercise his own right, there was a place to which he would be consigned, and of which fact he was well aware. Such a condition should not exist in any country, far less should it prevail in the free air of Canada. I am not taking the case for granted. I am putting the matter as it stands. This telegram has but one meaning, which is that there was an arrangement by which any minister could sehd word to the Prime Minister who would set the machinery in motion to enable men to be elected by the switching of ballots from one place to another.
Now, Sir, I have put my case before the House. I do not know whether the facts are exactly as I present them; I take no responsibility. I give such facts as I have, and I say to the Government and to the members of this House that I am informed on the most reliable authority that abundance of the very best proof can be advanced to show a committee of this House and to show to the country that the soldiers had no voice or word in the casting of votes, and no opportunity of pronouncing their own judgment, but did exactly as the Government directed and as suited the convenience and the designs of the Government in their support of their own friends. My motion is seconded by the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and it is to the effect that a committee of the House be appointed and such inquiry be made in connection with the . subject matter of this telegram and everything involved in it as the committee may deem advisable, to the end that this matter may be thoroughly investigated and such remedy applied as will prevent the recurrence in the future of such conduct as has been disclosed, which interferes with the rights of the people and puts an unfortunate blotch upon the good name of the country.

speechtext:
One of the last remarks of the leader of the Opposition was an expression of regret that unfortunately time did not permit him to give to the House a great deal more information than he had imparted. Well, if there was anything in the world in relation to this motion which he ought to have said, it is a great pity he did not say it, because he occupied an 'hour and a quarter in saying a lot of things that had no relevancy whatever to the motion, chiefly in rehashing a debate of two years >ago on the merits of the Military Voters' Bill. He read a letter from a man whose name he refused to divulge; he read and re-read whatever he could find around him, but he never uttered a sentence to indicate, much less to prove, that there was the slightest semblance of dishonour or impropriety in anything alleged about myself in this motion. The hon. gentleman knows that there was not, and I will tell 'him why. I say he knows. He knows that if he could establish a charge there is a right and proper method by which he could bring that charge before the House. He knows that there is a proper method of levelling an accusation against a minister of the Crown or a member of the House, a method by which he would place his own seat and 'honour in jeopardy, but that method he very cannily refuses to follow.
Prior to the opening of the House to-day I addressed to the hon. member the following letter, which I had delivered to him:
September 24, 1919.
D. D. Mackenzie, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Mackenzie,-You stated on Monday that you purposed going on this afternoon (Wednesday) with your motion regarding myself, I have no objection at all to your going on to-
[S:r George Foster.]
day, or any other day, but as you are aware, the House rises at six, and does not sit in the evening on Wednesday, and should the debate not be concluded at six o'clock, the subject might not be again reached this session. I therefore recost that you arrange your speech so as to divide the time equally between us, as any other course, you will quite realize, would be quite unfair to me.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) Arthur Meighen.
In reply, I received an intimation through the Whip that he would not accede to this request. Pie stated that he would require an hour and a half to present his case and that he would not defer the motion unless I would personally request him across the floor of the House to do so. In relation to a motion of this character I would never make a personal request. I am ready to answer such a motion at any time. He has chosen to go on; has taken an hour and a quarter and left me 30 minutes.
I have said to the hon. member that if he believes that there was any conduct on my part that was inconsistent with the highest principles of honour and propriety, he knows the course which is open to him. That course is known to him as w'ell as it is to me, and if he follows it in this debate or ixf-morrow o*r any other time this session; if he makes his charges and alleges dishonour, stating specifically what was improper, he need not ask for an investigation; T will attend to that myself.
Pie comes before us and quotes a telegram which he alleges was sent. He remarked at the close of his speech that he did not know whether the facts that he was presenting were right or not, hut that he was presenting all the facts he had. No doubt he was: But he did not present any facts. He did not even present the telegram. He had not it with him and he has not it with him now. He says that I admitted writing the telegram. I admitted no such thing. I said immediately I heard of the message what I say now-I have no recollection of the telegram whatever. The message might have been sent; it might have been sent by me; it is a message which might have been sent by any honest man. U is not a message of the character *that I will refer to as I proceed with my address for I shal' quote, as I proceed, messages that could only have issued out of malevolence and mendacity.
Whether it was sent or not, I do not know. I do not think it was sent by me for the reason that I would not likely address that message to the Prime Minister. The matters regarding which the wire appears to have been sent, while quite proper, were

matters that necessarily could not have been attended to by the Prime Minister.
But if a man, however vaguely or obliquely alleges wrong-doing, surely the onus is on him to produce the facts; surely it is on him to establish the truth of his allegations ; surely it is on him to produce the proof. The time for a prima facie case is now-now. Where is the prima facie case? Upon what does it rest? Will any hon. gen-tlemarf answer me? There is no telegram; there is no signature. Upon what does it rest? I have no reply from hon. gentlemen opposite. If that telegram were produced and if there is anything wrong with it, it would be a prima facie case if my signature is there. Still more this telegram, were it actually produced to the world, would be no prima facie case at all for the reason there is nothing wrong with it whatever. The hon. gentleman himself has proceeded for most of his speech on the assumption that there was nothing wrong because he said this telegram intimates what was intended by the Act, and what is within the meaning and intent of the Act. If it is within the meaning and intent of the Act how is it wrong? He says that the Act is wrong- I say it is not, but that it is not the question now.
Furthermore, I say this on behalf of the Prime Minister who is not able to be here -although that is a matter of no immediate consequence because, I assure the hon. gentleman that the Prime Minister is not bothering his head about the subject at all -the Prime Minister never received the message. He has had made a most careful and thorough search and he says that it never was received. If it ever existed, it may have been sent by some one under the authority of the general committee-I do not know. If it was sent by the organization, then I have no desire to repudiate the message-none whatsoever.
I said in the statement I made shortly after the notice of it was issued in the press, at the time of the Liberal Convention, that I had no recollection of it but that its terms were quite in accordance with propriety and that the only thing in the way of turpitude about it was its theft. The hon. gentleman says to-day that he is not the thief. I never suspected that he was. He says that the message was purloined out of the committee rooms-I understood him to say so-at the time of the contest; in other words that the thief, instead of being a bandit, was a sneak. That is all the difference. There is a thief somewhere close back in the chain of possession
and the hon. gentleman is now his descendant in title.
The hon. gentleman read the law on this subject. He read it twice; why, I do not know. The law states-to paraphrase it, to hurry and not to delay the House-that there was a certain class of soldiers who, in the last contest, had the right to choose the constituencies in which they should vote. They were those who being British subjects had not resided for any four months of the year preceding enrolment in a particular county and who besides had never at any time lived in Canada. If a man had resided for four months or more in any electoral district, there his vote could count and nowhere else. If he could not specify an electoral district wherein he had resided for the time mentioned but could specify a place in a certain constituency in which he had at any time resided, his vote could count in that constituency and nowhere else.
If he was a British subject and had at no time resided in this country, there was no place to which Parliament could with propriety allot his vote and the only way to give him the franchise was to permit him to select his constituency. Will hon. gentlemen suggest any other way of giving that soldier the franchise? Did hon. gentlemen suggest any other way in the session of 1917?
