speechtext:
Before recess I had been discussing the inquiry held in St. Johns, Quebec, in reference to the military vote and the ballots cast there, a subject which was introduced into this debate by certain remarks to which the Minister of Interior gave utterance, and I had already placed before the House the documentary evidence to establish the fact that perjury had been committed. I then proceeded to quote evidence which was given at the inquiry. I had quoted from the evidence of Colonel Melville and when six o'clock arrived I was reading from the evidence of Major Keefer. I now beg permission to continue the reading of that evidence:
Q. (By Mr. Geoffrion, Crown Prosecutor) : You voted! at the poll at which Mr. Corbett was deputy presiding officer?-A. Yes.
Q. Will you look at the envelope I now show you and tell us if you are the T. C. Keefer whose ballot was enclosed in this envelope?-A. I do not want to quibble over the language but I cannot say whether that is so or not. That is my name and I have no reason to doubt that it is my envelope.
Q. You did give your vote to him?-A. I did.
Q. The answers on this envelope are:	"I
cannot say" and "Chambly-Verchdres." Do you remember giving these answers?-A. In the first place I would like to point out that I am not familiar with civil law. My conception of "residence" is a layman's conception of it, and in the question where you asked:	"Did you
continuously reside four months of the twelve months?" I concluded in my own mind that I could reside for six months or for two months not in any one particular place, in other words, my idea of residence, whether I am right or whether I am wrong, is that residence could

be shifted from place to place during a year; especially when it is asked "continuously."
Q. Did the deputy presiding officer swear you before he took those answers?-A. I was sworn, yes.
The crown prosecutor continuing:
Q. You will notice that you answered "I cannot say" to three questions, two of which referred to residence during the last four or the twelve months immediately preceding your appointment, enlistment, enrolling, or calling on active service. Question No. 8 asked you: "In what electoral district or place in Canada you have resided at any other time." Those questions combined asked you to mention residence whatever in Canada at any time since you were born?-A. My understanding of the question is this:-the first question I answered conscientiously, as I could not say where I had resided for four months. The 8th question is to my mind the corollary of question No. 7. It would read to me that I am required to go back to my twenty-first birthday, and state the places or electoral districts I have lived in. I cannot mention electoral districts in Canada.
Q. But you are asked to mention any electoral district or place?-A. What place could I select?
Q. Any one you liked, if there is more than one?-A. I simply could not select a place out of the mass of the places I have lived in.
Q. You have not lived outside of Canada?- A. Oh yes, I have lived in a great many places beyond Canada.
Q. And you could not give any of the places you have lived in in Canada?-A. I could not recollect any particular one.
By the Commissioner:
Q. Were you born in Canada?-A. I was born in Canada but I joined the British Army when I was quite young and I had about nine years service travelling in various parts of the world.
Q. When did you come back to Canada?-A. 1910.
By Mr. Geoffrion:
Q. From 1910 to 1914 you were continuously in Canada?-A. No, I was in the States for some time. I have lived a good part of the time in Canada.
Q. When did you join?-A. 1915. In that five years I had no home, I was unmarried.
I had railway contracts for a certain time and had an office in this place and an office in that place. I used to go away in the winter and spend my time in some part of the States or Bermuda.
Q. Your original place was Ottawa?-A. Ottawa.
Q. Your family live there?-A. Yes.
Q. You were unmarried in 1915?-A. I was married in 1915.
Q. And your explanation for your answers, for the court to appreciate is that you had lived in more than one place in Canada since you were born and were exempt from answering those questions in any other way than you answered them?-A. I honestly concluded that I should go through practically every place in Canada in which I lived. I did not know which place it was required of me to answer I had stayed in.
Q. Just before you enlisted were you four months in Canada?-A. Yes, I was four months in Canada.
Q. In what place?-a. No one place.
Q. Did you spend four months in one place during 1915?-A. No, no one place.

Q. Where did you live, where did your wife live?-A. My wife was in Ottawa some part of the time and in Toronto some part of the time.
Q. Were you with your father, or did you
have a house of your own?-A. I had a house of my own.
And this man had no residence:
I also had a house in the province of Quebec, in the country district.
Q. Where?-A. Blue Sea. I also have a house at Iberville.
Q. Since you are on service here?-A. Yes.
Q. Then we have it that the year previous to your enlistment you were married and had a house in Ottawa?-A. No, I will correct that; I did not have a house in Ottawa.
He was indignant. He said: "I had a house at Rockcliffe."
Q. Near Ottawa?-A. Yes, I was not very familiar at the time with the electoral districts as I am not much of a politician. and I could not say whether my house is now in the electoral district of Ottawa.
Q. Then you had a city house at Rockcliffe? -A. I suppose you would call It a country house.
Q. It was the nearest approach to a city house for you?.-A. Yes.
Q. Then you had another house at Blue Sea?

A. Yes.
Q. That is in the Gatineau valley?-A. Yes, north of Ottawa.
Q. And your wife and children lived in this house and occasionally visited her mother in Toronto?-A. Yes.
Now at page 170 the following evidence appears :
Am I right in saying that for one year previous to your enlistment you were married and had children and had a house near Rockcliffe and another house at Blue Sea?-A. Yes.
Q. And your family always resided at Ottawa?-A. Yes.
Well, this major, as I have proved and as the exhibits filed in the inquiry show, could not say or could not name any place in Canada where he had resided. The third witness, whose evidence I wish to quote, is Lieutenant J>. B. Armstrong and his testimony is to be found at page 185.
Q. You voted?-A. I voted.
Q. Will you look at the envelope I now show you and tell us whether this is your vote?-A.
I cannot say. I never saw the envelope.
Q. You voted at the poll at which Mr. Corbett was Deputy Presiding Officer?-A. I did.
Q. You answered questions 6, 7, and 8, " 1 cannot say " ?-A. Yes.
Q. And chose to apply your vote to Chambly-Verch&res?-A. Yes.
By the Commissioner:
Q. Were those answers given under oath?- A. Yes.
By Mr. Geoffrion:
<2. When did you enlist or join?-A. June, 1915.
Q. Then within the year previous to .1 ..ue, 1915, did you live in Canada?-A. I did.
Q. Had you a home there?-A. No, I had nc home of my own.

Q. You lived with your father?-A. I lived in several places, at the home of my father for one.
Q. Where else?-A. In Canada I have lived In Ontario and in New Brunswick.
Q. And you were travelling for business?- A. No.
Q. What was the reason for your changing your residence?-A. I was attending college previous to the enlistment.
Q. Give it as approximately as you can. You were unmarried and your home, so far as you had a home, was at your father's?-A. My father's home was in Westmount, Que.
Q. When you were not at college you lived there?-A. Well, while I was attending college I lived there excepting for the time I visited other places or resided at other places.
Q. What college were you attending?-A. McGill University.
Q. When did you finish your course at McGill?-A. I finished the third year at the end of April.
Q. The course began in October?-A. Yes.
Q. The beginning of October?-A. Yes.
Q. Therefore, except for brief absences, you were continuously attending MoGill and living in Westmount?-A. I was not continuously residing there.
Q. Did you drop your course for some time? -A. During those eight months I visited various places for some time, four or five days, and resided at other places.
Q. With friends or relatives or what?-A. I resided in the Laurentian Mountains for a few days at a time at various week ends.
Q. But your residence there, as you call it, for a few days, did not, I am sure, prevent you following your course at MoGill University?-[DOT] A. No.
Q. Therefore I take it that with the exception of a few week ends and the Christmas holidays, you must have continuously been in Westmount and Montreal, living in Westmount and attending lectures at McGill College, Montreal, for the eight months?-A. I believe I was most of the time, yes. I could not remember.
By the Commissioner:
Q. You always lived in Westmount?-A. Yes, but I have not always had a continuous residence there.
Q. The way the question is put on the envelope is as to continuous residence?-A. Now, in connection with question No. 8 I may say that I resided in Chambly-VerchSres County as well as other places in Canada, so that by answering " I cannot say '' there, I simply did so because I could not specify any other places. I might have specified Chambly-Vercberes just as well.
By Mr. Geoffrion:
Q. What was the nature of your residence there?-A. I resided at the residence of Mr. Joseph Ward.
Q. As a guest?-A. Yes.
Q. Over week ends?-A. Yes.
Q. You call that residing?-A. That is residing. I was not domiciled there, but I resided there.
And this gentleman again swore that he could not name one place in Canada where he had resided a single day 'before his enlistment.
Now I come to Lieutenant H. L. Phillips. We find his evidence at page 193:
Q. You voted at the poll presided over by Mr. Corbett?-A. Yes.
Q. You answered questions Nos 6, 7 and 8 by saying "I cannot say"?-A. Yes.
Q. And question No. 9 you answered "Cham-bly-Yerchi'res" ?-A. Yes.
Q. You were sworn?-A. I do not remember the swearing.
Q. You do not know?-A. I do not know.
Q. Do you remember that these answer were required under the law to be given under oath? -A. I did not know very much about that. I only voted once before in my life.
Q. Giving the word "residence" its natural meaning and not any artificial meaning, such as a man going for a week end as the guest of a friend, but confining it to its ordinary sense, you have always been a resident in Canada?- A. Since 1911.
By the Commissioner:
Q. I suppose you knew some places in which you had lived in Canada between 1911 and the time you enlisted?-A. Oh, yes, practically all in Toronto.
Q. Why did you not say Toronto in answer to the question instead of saying " I cannot say"?-A. (No answer).
Q. You had a house there and knew the number of it?-A. Of course that changed a little.
Q. But you, lived in Toronto?-A. Yes, it was continuous.
Here is another question the Commissioner put to the witness:
Q. Seeing that you have just admitted that you lived for twelve months in Toronto before enlistment, how do you pretend now that you were justified in saying "I cannot say" in answer to question No. 6?-A. That is the one which has the word in electoral district?
Q. Electoral district or place.
By the Commissi onner:
Q. There is nothing about electoral district in question No. 6. It is place or places in Canada where you last cohtinously resided during the last four months of the twelve months immediately preceding your appointment enlistment or calling ^u^xin active service. It seems to me you	been a little more
specific. At the samWitiie there may have been some reason why you answered as you did. If there is any reason, you had better make a statement in regard to it now. A. The only thing I can say is that I wanted to place my vote in Chambly-VerchSres for Mr. Rainville.
The next witness I wish to refer to is Lieut. R. N. Pettigrew. His evidence will be found at page 205:
Q. You answered "I cannot say" to questions 6v 7 and 8 and "Chambly-VerehSres" to question 9?-A. Yes.
Q. You gave those answers?-A. Yes
Q. And you were sworn?-A. I remember being sworn, yes.
Q. You think the word "residence" in its ordinary sense, and not speaking of week end visits to friends your residence is in Canada?- A. Yes, I have lived in Canada all my life.
Q. Were you born in Canada?-A. Yes.
Q. Where?-A. Glen Morris, Ontario.
At page 210 he repeats the same answer. There is another man-one of the eleven men who were still in Canada when the inquiry was taken-who swore that he could not name one place where he had lived in

Canada, although he was born in this country and had lived here all his life.
The next witness I wish to refer to is that of Major R. W. Powell, at pages 21 and 219:
Q. You voted at that election?-A. I believe so, yes.
Q. You answered questions 6, 7 and 8 "I cannot say " and question 9 " Chambly-Ver-chferes"?-A. Yes.
Q. As a matter of fact you have always been a resident of Canada prior to the war?-
Q. Until you enlisted? A. Yes. .
Q. You were bom in Canada? A. Yes.
Q. Where? A. I was born in Ottawa.
Q. Was your home in Ottawa up to the time of the outbreak of the war? A. My parents lived there.
Lieut. Edwin T. Adney, page 233:
Q. I see by the envelope prepared by Deputy Presiding Officer Corbett that you answered "I cannot say" to question No. 6, "I cannot say" to question No. 7, and apparently gave no answer to question No. 8, and answered question No. 9 " Chambly-VerchSres " ?-Is that correct? A.. I stated I desired to have my vote placed at Chambly-VerchSres and I intended to say that I could not answer question No. 6. I am not sure of the manner in which I did so, that is, whether I said ''I cannot say" or "I do not know" or what the exact wording was.

To continue:
Q. Your fundamental reason was that anything whatever could be done to win the election? A. In that respect I might be permitted to quote Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's judgment on that point. He says that the safety of the country is the supreme law against which no other law can prevail.
Lieut. Adney is purporting to quote Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's judgment. Now, Sir, you will undoubtedly he perplexed, and I am sure you will wonder, how the Commissioner could say in his report, as was reiterated with pride yesterday by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) in his no-answer speech, that my charges

were unfounded. Let us examine the logic of the report of this most favoured commissioner. He begins by relating the incidents which brought about the granting of the commission-the speech I made in the House, the accusation, and so forth-and proceeds to state the number of sittings. He then recites sections 6, 7 and 8 of the Military Voters' Act, 1917, and gives a dissertation on the word " residence." I may read what he says:
The officers whose conduct is impugned were almost all civil engineers and in civil life before their enlistment in the Engineers' Training Depot or their enrolment in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. Their work did not permit them to be in any one place permanently or for any fixed time and they had to move from place to place as duty called them. Such of them as were married men were frequently away from home. Those who were not engineers were also on the move at brief intervals, as their oecupa-tions required them to travel more or less About half of the officers of the Engineers' Training Depot who voted at the general election had left for service overseas before Mr. Archambault had made his charges of perjury in the House of Commons, and are still absent from Canada. All the remaining officers were brought before me and subjected to exhaustive cross-examination by able and skilful counsel selected by Mr. Archambault. Several of the officers who appeared had never voted before, and none of them knew much about electoral districts. They were not politicians or political workers. They answered, "I cannot say," or words equivalent thereto, to questions Nos. 6 and 7, and several of them gave similar answers to question No. 8. Question No. 6 is not simply an inquiry as to where the military voter resided at a fixed and definite date, but it is complicated by the word "continuously," which must mean constantly and uninterruptedly and by reference to the period of "four months of the twelve months immediately preceding appointment, enlistment or enrolment or calling out on active service." The question is rather indefinite, as an officer's appointment, enlistment, enrolment and calling out on active service in some cases were on different dates.
I may point out at this juncture, the fact that the statute does not use the words "and calling out on active service." The statute says, "enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service." It is alternative or optional, which makes it a much easier matter. But the Commissioner in his report does not use the word which appears in the statute; he uses the word " and."
It was so in the case of Colonel Melville.
Then the Commissioner gives the definition of the word "residence." He says:
The place of a man's residence, or where he resides, is not always easy to determine. Laymen, lawyers and even judges are liable to confound it with "domicile;" but residence and domicile are two distinct things. A man's home, or the home of his parents if he is unmarried, may be his "residence" but it often

is' not; it is usually his "domicile." It is not the residence of an engineer who is following his profession, or a salesman on the road at a place from which he is unable to return to his home in order to sleep there. An oft-quoted definition of the word "residence" is the place where a person abides, eats and sleeps. A person's residence to-day may not be his residence next week or next month, and within a given period of time he may have no continuous or uninterrupted residence. Some of the officers swore they did not know the meaning of "residence," or what was meant in these questions by the place where they resided. Question No. 7 contains an inquiry as to the electoral district in which the voter resided. As the time referred to in question No. 6 is not definite, the time in No. 8 is necessarily so, and reference to the electoral district or place within Canada where he had "resided" is of a character liable to lead to confusion and uncertainty. The right of soldiers as such to vote was new in Canada.
Observe, Mr. Speaker, all these preliminary explanations.
The right of soldiers as such to vote was new in Canada.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext: It was new everywhere.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it was new everywhere, and I believe he is right; for I do not think that England gave any vote to the Canadian soldiers who were in the English army, nor do I think the French Government gave any vote to Canadian soldiers who were in the French army during the French election. The report continues:
And it was abundantly proved in the inquiry that there was a widespread conviction amongst not only military voters but civilians that every military voter had a right to apply his or her vote wherever he or she saw fit. And all the officers whi were examined swore that they believe they answered truthfully to the best of their knowledge and belief and that they had the right to specify Chambly-Yerch6res as the electoral district where they wished to have their vote applied. These officers are charged with having committed perjury in their answers to the foregoing questions.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that the Commissioner admits that the officers gave the answer, " I cannot say," and that he admits the fact that their residence was in Canada. He says:
These officers are charged with having committed perjury in their answers to the foregoing questions. Perjury by a witness as part of his evidence in a judicial proceeding is defined by section 170.
And then the Commissioner gives a definition of the word perjury. Further on he
says:
The officers here each and all testify to their belief in the truth of their answers as they understood the questions.
And evidently they understood the questions, Mr. Speaker.
That is to say, every one of the officers was asked by the Commissioner at the end of his evidence: Do you believe you spoke the truth in this evidence; do you believe that you acted right? Naturally they answered, " yes." What accused before a criminal court, if asked by the judge if he was guilty or not guilty, but would answer: "I am not guilty?" What court would acquit an accused person for the simple reason that the accused himself said that he was not guilty, and in face of the proof that he was guilty? The Commissioner goes on to say:
Few words have been the subject of judicial consideration more frequently than the word "resides" and its derivative "residence", which has many different meanings varying according to circumstances between a transient presence for purposes purely temporary and a fixity and permanence of abode equivalent to domicile.
Then there are some authorities cited to show that " residence," " domicile " and " home '' are the hardest things for a man to define when he is called to the box as a witness. The Commissioner says:
The officers who were examined before me gave their evidence in a straightforward manner and their conduct and demeanour while under examination, and the reasons which they gave for their answers established their good faith and they honestly believed that they had a right to answer questions 6, 7, and 8 as they did. The envelopes show that Colonel Melville, Lieutenant Trow, Lieutenant Adney and Lieutenant Armer did not answer question No. 8.
Here is the conclusion of the 'Commissioner regarding these officers:
That disposes of the charges of perjury against these officers.
These officers were bound to answer the first question, No. 6, whether they had resided in Canada for four months before their enlistment and the fact that they did not answer question No. 8, if they were wrong in answering question No. 6 the way they did, does not absolve them from the accusation of perjury. Nevertheless, the Commissioner says:
That disposes of the charge of perjury against these officers. In my opinion these charges are unfounded. It was proved to my satisfaction-
I wish you to notice these words " my satisfaction."
It was proved to my satisfaction that Colonel Melville was not sworn by the deputy presiding officer when he polled his vote.
The Commissioner declares that it was proved to his satisfaction that Colonel Melville was not sworn. But, this proves that Colonel Melville violated the law-violated the Military Voters' Act-because according to the Military Voters' Act, every sol-

dier who wants to vote must be sworn. Because, Colonel Melville was not sworn the Commissioner is satisfied and happy. He goes on to say:
In view of the answers given to questions 6, 7, and 8 the officers had the right to apply their votes to Chambly and VerchSres.
Nobody denies that. By answering questions 6, 7, and 8 the way they did, by not answering truthfully to these questions, by stating that they could not name a place in Canada where they had resided before their enlistment, surely they were entitled to answer question 8 by saying " Chambly-Vercheree" or any other county. But what we are arraigning them for is that they did not answer questions 6, 7, and 8 truthfully. They had all resided in Canada, they had all had a previous residence in Canada and in answering this question by " I cannot say" they perjured themselves. The Commissioner goes on:
Mr. Rainville the Government candidate in the electoral district was known to some of the officers, but not to all of them from having taken one meal the date of which is not proved, at the officers' mess. There were no speeches and no votes asked for on that occasion and the suggestion that something improper occurred between the officers and Mr. Rainville is absolutely unfounded.
I was precluded from bringing in evidence regarding this banquet and regarding the speeches made at it. I was precluded from bringing in any evidence other than evidence relating to the charge of perjury and subornation of perjury. When Colonel Melville made the statement that there were no speeches and no banquet, the Crown Prosecutor proposed to produce evidence to show that there was a banquet, to show that there were suggestions made by officers as to voting and to show that there were incitements to perjury, "the Commissioner ruled that, according to the Order in Council and the instructions of the Minister of Justice that the investigation should be judicially conducted, he could not go beyond the question of perjury or subornation of perjury and that he could not accept proof of the banquet.or of the suggestions made by officers. Nevertheless the Commissioner states that there were no speeches, no votes asked on that occasion and that the suggestion that something improper occurred between the officers and Mr. Rainville is absolutely unfounded. The Commissioner allowed proof on one side but he prevented me from bringing evidence on the other side. Then he goes on to state that these
[iMr. Archambault.]
charges are 'absolutely unfounded. He proceeds:
The officers and soldiers at St. Johns were strong supporters of the Union Government. From patriotic motives they wished to see the Government returned.
Is it proper for a Commissioner to mention such facts or to mention them in that way?
Mr. Rainville's public record as a supporter of the Government and his stand in favour of conscription and of adequate reinforcements for the Canadian army strongly appealed to the military voters and a considerable number of them, but not all who answered "I cannot say" questions 6, 7 and S desired to have their votes applied to Chambly and Verchcres as they honestly believed they had a right to do.
Then the Commissioner goes on to deal with the accusation of subornation of perjury.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext: Are those the Commissioner's words "from patriotic motives"?

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
This Commissioner's judgment was that "from patriotic motives they wished to see the Government returned".
These officers were also accused of subornation of perjury by having induced certain military voters, being non-commissioned officers and men of the engineers' training depot to commit perjury by falsely representing themselves upon oath to be unable to specify or state in what place or places, or electoral district in Canada, they had resided at any time preceding their appointment, enlistment, or enrolment or calling out on active service for the purpose of having their votes applied to the electoral district of Chambly-VercMres.
And he goes on:
The evidence clearly establishes that there was no canvassing for votes on the part of any officers. The men published a regimental newspaper called Knots and Lashings. Lieutenant Knight was the editor. It is a weekly newspaper published every Saturday, and in the edition of the 15th December, 1917, there were several articles of a partisan character-
I should say so-
-but. in no way different from the usual political information to be found in party newspapers during an election campaign.
I have read these special articles, Mr. Speaker. I have read an extract from the paper in which the soldiers were told not to vote in constituencies where they came from, but to apply their vote in the constituency where they were needed, and the Commissioner not only admits this but he approves of this paper Knots and Lashings inducing the men to perjure themselves, and says it was nothing else blit an ordinary political campaign.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext: Patriotic motives.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
On 17th December, 1917, election day, an extra of Knots and Lashing's was issued in which appeared among other matter a "specimen envelope showing how questions may be answered." The answer to questions 6, 7, and 8, is " I cannot say " and to question 9,
Chambly and VerchSres."
The fact that the paper was published for the men in the barracks, the Commissioner, himself has admitted in his judgment. Now he goes on and says:
Any military voter who was a British subject and had not resided in Canada would have a right to give the answers suggested in the printed specimen envelope.
Certainly, we have no objection to that. This is why the Military Voters' Act was passed in order to give British subjects who had no residence in Canada the right to vote at a Canadian election.
The applications for enlistment of 191 noncommissioned officers and men in the Engineers Training Depot were examined with the result that 299 gave Canadian addresses and 1'<2 gave their residence as being outside of Canada. If the latter never resided in Canada, and there is no presumption that they had-
There is no proof either that they had nottheir right to answer "I cannot say" to questions 6, 7 and 8 and to select "Chambly-Verchdres" for their vote, is undoubted.
That is true that over 147 men that voted never resided in Canada. Now here is one peculiar interpretation:
Every voter who did not understand the import of questions 6, 7 and 8, or who was honestly unable to give the information asked for, would also be entitled to answer them in the manner suggested in the specimen envelope. There is the further circumstance that the prevailing impression in military circles was that the questions could be answered in the manner suggested.
Who circulated that impression, Mr. Speaker? It was circulated by the newspaper that was published in the barracks. That newspaper was sent to the Minister of Militia, as stated in this evidence; and the fact that 17,000 men, as I will show later on, voted the same way in other places and answered the same question in the same manner, " I cannot say," shows there was a big organization and system created to use the votes of the soldiers for political purposes.
The men read the Montreal papers and were greatly interested in the result of the election. Mr. Rainville's public career and his stand on the important question before the country met with their approval. Ten of the men and noncommissioned officers were brought before the Commission and subjected to a thorough examination as to where they had resided, and why they answered "I cannot say" to questions 6, 7, and 8, and chose Chambly-VerchSres a's the place they wished to have their vote applied. These ten men were practically all that remained at St. Johns of the rank and' file that were there at the time of the election and who had voted. Their evidence does not show that they were influenced by anything that appeared in Knots and Lashings.
Mr. Speaker, practically every one of them swore that it was Knots and Lashings that influenced their vote.
They gave what appeared to me to be good, valid and sufficient reasons for the answers which they gave to the questions and of their choice of Chambly-VerchSres. . . . There were no improper inducements, representations, suggestions or other misconduct by the officers', or any of them, to influence any non-commissioned officer or man to commit perjury by giving false answers to the questions on the envelope, and the non-commissioned officers and men who appeared and were examined did not, in my opinion, commit perjury in connection with their questions. The charges of perjury and subornation of perjury are unfounded.
Now I wish to make a few further observations, but I will not add an iota or remark to this most extraordinary document of partisanship for fear I might spoil the lesson which it conveys and destroy one of the most vivid, typical and historical monuments of the administration of justice under the Unionist Government. But, Sir,

That is news to me. It is a new function to attribute to the Minister of Justice that he is charged with the administration of justice. The administration of justice, so far as it is a matter to be dealt with by governments, is absolutely in the hands of the provincial governments. But when taking as his basis the action of a man who is a judge, although he may have been a commissioner, the hon. gentleman chooses to condemn the administration of justice. He may seek by one means or another to avoid the conclusion, but I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the conclusion is unavoidable. There is no connection between what this commissioner did and the administration of justice, except it be in the fact that this commissioner was a Judge of the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec; and that being so, I submit that the commentary of the hon. gentleman is a reflec-

tion upon Mr. Justice Maclennan in his office as an administrator of justice-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Government has nothing to do with the administration of justice, why is my hon. friend called the Minister of Justice?

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.

speechtext:
I am not in a position to determine why those who chose the title to be attached to the minister holding the position which I do adopted that title. But the hon. gentleman must know that there is a statute defining what are the duties of the Minister of Justice, and he may go through that and he will not find that the Parliament which enacted that statute undertook to take over to itself the function which the British North America Act assigned to the provinces, and to assign to a minister in a Government of the Dominion any share in the administration of justice. The hon. gentleman will not take me as an authority, but I may say that I heard my predecessor, whom he will accept as an authority, the Minister of Justice in the Government in which my hon. friend was the distinguished Minister of Finance-I heard him, standing in his place in this House, say in substance precisely what I have said, and not waiting for the question which the hon. gentleman put, he himself undertook to say that he was at a loss to understand why the designation of "Minister of Justice" had been attached to the office, and that it was misleading. I am in receipt of numinous letters-as he said himself he was-wriUon to me on the strength of that title and on the assumption that I administer justice. I have to explain to the writers of those letters, as I have tried to explain to the hon. gentleman to-night, that it is quite an unjustified conclusion to draw from the title itself-which, I admit may be a misleading title-that the Minister of Justice is charged with the administration of justice. As I have said, the statute is there for all hon. gentlemen to read, and they will see that in substance the Minister of Justice is the legal member of this Government, and, as such, the legal adviser of this Government and of the different departments of the Government; but his nearest approach to taking part in the administration of justice is that in his hands is the nomination, to be submitted to Council of the judges to be appointed. And the

function of this Government goes no further than the appointment of the judges. To the provinces belongs the administration of justice; to this Government belongs the function of the appointment of those men who shall sit in the Provincial Courts.

With reference to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) concerning the ruling given by the Chairman in this House the other day, I must put him right to this extent: The ruling was given concerning Mr. O'Connor, a member of the Board of Commerce, appointed by this Government and removable by the Governor in Council for
cause. He was not and is not a judge of the Superior Court, and the ruling had nothing to do with Mr. Justice Robson, who is the Chairman of the Board of Commerce. Hon. members will find if they look up the statute creating the Board of Commerce that when a judge is appointed Chief Commissioner of the Board he shall not be removed at any time by the Governor in Council except upon address of the Senate and -House of Commons. The ruling does not apply here. I have paid great attention to the remarks made by hon. members on both sides of the House, but I have not found anything which to my mind sets aside the rulings which I find in May's Parliamentary Practice. At page 224, I read:
A question reflecting on the action in Court of the Judicial Commissioner of the Irish Land Commission, was by the Speaker's direction not allowed.
At page 296, I read:
Reflections against judges generally are equally out of order.
And on the same page:
The Speaker has ruled out of order language disrespectful to persons administering justice.
It is very difficult to separate in a -Commissioner the personality of the judge from that of the Commissioner. The conduct and character of a judge certainly cannot be attacked by a member of the House of Commons, except by pursuing the constitutional course of moving an address to the Crown. As I pointed out before, I allowed the hon. member to read the findings of Mr. Justice Maclennan, sitting as Commissioner upon the inquiry. His remarks have been placed upon Hansard and are before the House and the country for the judgment of the people of Canada, but when the hon. member reflects upon the conduct, character and motives of Mr. Justice Maclennan, and comments unfavourably upon the administration of justice in this country, be it under this or any other Government, he is exceeding his rights under the rules of the House.
The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) referred to a ruling given in this House in 1917 when the right hon. -Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for whose knowledge of the rules- of the House I have much respect, rose to a point of order. On that occasion Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. The hori. gentleman (Mr. Rogers) is speaking to a question of privilege. I submit to you. Sir, that it is not in order for him to impugn the character of the Commissioner. He can dispute the Commissioner's conclusions, if he wants to, but he has no right to impugn the character of the Commissioner.

The ruling given at that time is as follows, Mr. Speaker being in the Chair:
Speaking without having had opportunity to consult the rules. X am inclined to think the point of order is well taken.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. If I am not allowed to discuss the motives of the judge or Commissioner I shall certainly be allowed, I think, to read some of his remarks in the evidence. I had not intended to proceed in that way, but I shall do so now, as under your ruling I have no right to discuss his motives. I should like to direct the attention of the House to the change of attitude of the judge, shown by his remarks, at a certain point during the in-

quiry. The inquiry started on the 12th of September, and from the 12th to the 18th of that month the Commissioner seems to have been very severe towards the men coming up before him. On the 18th there was a change of attitude, and in order to explain this change I must refer you, Mr. Speaker, to Hansard of last year, where it is stated that on the 18th of September the Commissoner was made permanent Chairman of the Labour Disputes Board.
At page 183 of the evidence, after Major Keefer had stated the different residences he had in Canada, the Crown Prosecutor was about to examine him in further detail when the commissioner said: "I think we have gone sufficiently into that, Mr. Geoffrion." He was satisfied with the residence at that time. At page 198 the commissioner said in connection with the answer of Lieut. Philips :
On page 200 in the examination of Lieut. Philips the attorney for the defence objected to a question, saying: "As to residence, I think the witness has already answered," and the Commissioner intervened: "Then let him answer again." He seemed at that time to be very anxious to obtain the truth in order to make his report. At page 202 the Commissioner said again to Lieut. Philips:
Seeing' that you have just admitted that you lived for twelve months in Toronto before enlistment, how do you pretend now that you were justified in saying "I cannot say" in answer to question No. 6?'' At page 203 the Commissioner said to Lieutenant Philips '. "It seems to me you could have been a little more specific." At page 208 he again stopped the Crown Prosecutor from further examination of the witness in regard to residenoe, saying: "X think that is sufficient for the question of residence, Mr. Geoffrion."

Is it your contention that from the time you were 21 years of age you did not reside any-

where continuously for four months?-A. Yes, that is correct.
The Commissioner:	Of course none of those

I have nothing else to add regarding this change of attitude on the part of the Commissioner, but I may cite a Latin dictum which is very appropriate to the occasion: " Sine conscientia, gubernatores, cibis, ves-timentis, auro et honoribus, suos implent abjectos servos."

In his evidence Lieutenant Knight also stated that the law was framed by the Government in order to win the election and to get that kind of a vote. I am sorry to detain the House so long but I believe that I have a duty to perform to the country. The examination of Lieutenant Knight proceeds at page 303:
Q. Do you know whence the desire to vote in Charribly-Verchdres arose?-A. I do not.
Q. How did Chambly-Verchdres come to be chosen?-A. I could not say.
Q. Why did you choose it yourself?-A. Well I met Mr. Rainville. As a matter of fact, I think most of us wished to have one Union representative at least in Quebec. That was our main desire.
Q. And you thought of Mr. Rainville as the chosen one?-A. Yes, he had a chance.
Q. You met him?-A. Yes.
Q. Did you think he had more chance than others?-A. Looking at the question of numbers-yes. It would have been useless for instance to put any votes in St. Johns1-As a mathematical proposition, he had a fairly good chance.
Q. Surely you cannot say that your soldiers all went through that process of reasoning? You would not pretend they are sufficiently well' versed in politics to do that?-A. They were not versed in politics at all. They got some information from somewhere and the number of Knots and Lashings helped a little. They did what they wished to do-plumped their votes in one district so as to do some good.	-
Q. Were they not advised or was it not suggested to them in the barracks by you, or through your knowledge, that they should answer in that way?-A. I emphatically deny that there was any canvassing at all done by the officers or by any men amongst the men. The men were not met at all by anybody to my knowledge. I think in Knots and Lashings is probably the only indication that there was any suggestion made as to where they should put their votes.
The only indication is given in Knots and Lashings which was not only produced but distribution of which was proved and which proof I have placed before the House to-day.
By the Commissioner:
Q. Did you "honestly think you were entitled to publish that specimen, envelope?-A. I understood the Act was drawn up-and I have a very good authority for saying this-I will not quote the authority-I understood that the Act was drawn up...
By Mr. Geoffrion (interrupting) :
Q. Tou will have to give us the authority if you quote it.-A. Pardon me, let me have a go. I understood that the Act'was so drawn up that you could easily drive a carriage and pair through it, and those questions were more or less modelled so that you could skip them conscientiously.
That is what Lieutenant Knight says. That is what the Government will not ad-

mit now but that is what everybody in the country believed. Everybody believed that this Act was so framed as to give the soldiers' vote to certain constituencies where it was needed for certain members as is shown in the telegram which is the subject of this resolution.
Now, Sir, I believe that I have really done my share of the work. I believe also that I have brought forward facts sufficient to show that the affair at St. Johns was, as the Minister of Justice stated, " judiciously investigated," and that the charges are not, as the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and the Commissioner said utterly unfounded. Therefore, I would like to include in this inquiry an investigation into the iSt. Johns vote, in order to remove from the minds of the people of Canada the strong impression that the safeguard which they have had in the courts of the country has been abolished and destroyed by the Government, and in order to restore the sanctity of the vote. Let us have a full inquiry and if heads are bound to fall, whether of friend or foe, let them fall for the rejuvenation of honesty which has been assailed in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the many friends of the genial member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) will be glad to see that his health is in the excellent state that he has shown it to be in to-night. He has held the attention of the House, more or less, for the last four hours in an endeavour to make out a case. Now I would not like to say anything uncomplimentary about my hon. friend, and I could not say that he had a good case without being uncomplimentary to him. Had he possessed a strong ease, my hon. friend has sufficient ability to have presented the strength of that case in much less than four hours. The weakness of the hon. gentleman's case is shown by the length of time which he has spent in picking out shreds and patches from the evidence taken by Mr. Justice Maclennan. I have heard that it is a custom or rule amongst lawyers-not having the privilege of being a member of that learned profession I am not able to speak as to its truth-that when a lawyer gets the worst of it in a case it has always been regarded as his time-honoured privilege to go down to the nearest tavern and abuse the judge who gave the decision against him. Hon. gentlemen who belong to the legal profession will know whether or not there ever was such a custom. Of course my hon. friend could not follow that course

in the province of Ontario. He probably availed himself of that privilege in the province of Quebec after the decision was given by Mr. Justice Maclennan, but as to that I could not say. But he has certainly availed himself of the privilege of abusing the judge here in language as strong as the rules of this House will permit, because that judge saw fit to give -a decision against him.

subtopic: ALLEGED MANIPULATION OF SOLDIER VOTES.
subsubtopic: DEBATE RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend finds his vigour boiling over and cannot repress it,' let him avail himself of some future occasion to introduce a resolution of impeachment which will give him a further opportunity tq spend another half or three-quarters of a day in airing his eloquence in this House. It is not an unknown thing of course for lawyers, when they get the worst of a case, to spend some time in abusing the opposing counsel or even casting reflections upon the judge who rendered a verdict against them. My hon. friend has succeeded in convincing every one that he made a very great mistake when he made charges in the first place, and that he rushed in where angels fear to tread, in making charges. Having rushed in rather hurriedly in the making of those charges he naturally had the decision given against him, and now he is advertising to the House and to the country that he feels very sore indeed because of that decision. My hon. friend, in the course of his remarks, has stated that some 491 soldiers voted, or presented themselves to vote, at the poll in question. The returns of the general election show that .there were only 137 votes polled in that constituency all told-ten for my hon. friend nnd 127 for his opponent. The difference between f37 and 491 is 354 soldier votes which must have been discarded. My hon. friend laboured for hours, citing case after case, to show that men came forward who were under a misapprehension with regard to the .law, thinking they had a right to vote in this constituency when the evidence went to 38
show that they had resided in different parts of Canada. My hon. friend furnishes figures to show that the votes were not recorded; .that 354 of these votes were discarded because the voters had no residence, and he charges conspiracy. A conspiracy by whom? Might I ask, Mr. Speaker, in that regard this pertinent question:	who was likely
to benefit by the polling of those votes? Was it my hon. friend who only received ten as against his opponent's 127? If those ,354 votes had not been discarded, who was most likely to have obtained them, my hon. .friend or his opponent? His opponent unquestionably, Mr. Speaker, was the one most likely to have obtained those votes. Then who conspired to deprive his opponent, the Government candidate,, of votes? Was it ,the Government that conspired to deprive .the Government candidate of his votes, or .was there misrepresentation, as was stated by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. (Meighen) in discussing this matter-a distinct and definite propaganda of misrepresentation to mislead voters and to try and get them to place their votes in constituencies where the parties responsible knew those votes would be discarded and could .not be counted.
In regard to the charge that there was a conspiracy to rob soldiers of their vote, what do the facts show? That because of the propaganda of this man Preston, and others who were backing him up, some fifty thousand odd of these soldier votes were discarded. That was because the soldiers were misled by a definite propaganda intended to mislead them. Now what was the reason for that? Because hon. gentlemen opposite, Laurier candidates in the Dominion of Canada in 1917, knew perfectly well that they stood a mighty poor show of getting very many of the soldier votes. There is where your conspiracy comes in, and that conspiracy worked out definitely to the advantage of hon. gentlemen opposite. May I be permitted to call attention to this fact: my hon. friend in the four hours during which he spoke was dealing with what? He was dealing with the vote here in Canada. But the telegram which is the subject of debate to-day has reference to the overseas vote. My hon. friend's share of the soldier vote in Canada was practically the same as his share of the soldier vote polled overseas. However, before I leave this matter, I wish to quote for the benefit of the House, and to place on Hansard, a few words from the judgment of Mr. Justice Maclennan, who investigated the charges made by the hon member (Mr. Archam-bault) who has just taken his seat.



Mr. Justice Maclennan dealing with this matter, states in his report as follows:
This investigation was in consequence of representations-[DOT]
The hon. judge is very kind in using ithe word "representations." He might have prefixed another syllable there, I think.
-made by Mr. Joseph Arehambault, member of Parliament, for the electoral district of Chambly and Vercheres, to the House of Commons on 22nd May, 1918, alleging that certain military officers at the Barracks of the Engineers' Training Depot in St. Johns in the Province of Quebec, on 17th December, 1917, and previously thereto in connection with the general election held on that date, committed perjury and were guilty of other nyseonduct whereby certain military voters, being members of said Engineers' Training Depot, were alleged to have been induced to commit perjury by falsely representing themselves upon oath to be unable to specify, or state in what place, or places, or electoral districts in Canada they had resided at any time, preceding their appointment, enlistment, or enrolment, or calling out on active service, for the purpose of having their votes applied to the electoral district of Chambly and VercMres pursuant to the Military Voters Act 1917.
That is what the Judge was called upon to investigate. I am not going to again place on Hansard many of the statements which have been quoted by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Arehambault), but I want to quote this passage. The hon. Judge says:
About one-half of the officers of the Engineers'
Training Depot who voted at the general election had left on service overseas before Mr. Arehambault had made his charges of perjury in the House of Commons and are still absent from Canada. All the remaining officers were brought before me and subjected to an exhaustive cross-examination by able and skilful Counsel selected by Mr. Arehambault. Several of the officers who appeared had never voted before and none of them knew much about electoral districts. They were not politicians or political workers.
The right of soldiers as such to vote was new in Canada, and it was abundantly proved in the inquiry that there was a widespread conviction among not only military voters but civilians that every military voter had a right to apply his, or her vote wherever he or she saw fit.
Why, Mr. Speaker, is there any doubt in regard to that? Is there any doubt in the mind of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Mo<lloy) in regard to that? Did not that hon. gentleman write to his leader the late Bight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier asking him to get for him some of the soldiers' votes for his constituency? Was there anything wrong in that action, of the hon. member? Not at all. But there was a misapprehension on his part as to the soldier vote-a misapprehension which was not confined to soldiers alone but was

pretty general throughout the country. That misapprehension, Mr.. Speaker, I maintain was deliberately added to for party purposes by hon. gentlemen opposite-[DOT] or at least by the party supporting the hon. gentlemen opposite-who did everything in their power through the instrumentality of one of the greatest political crooks who ever lived in the Dominion of Canada, W. T. R. Preston, to deceive the soldier electors for the purpose of destroying their ballots so they would not be counted, as he and the party he represented knew perfectly well they would be counted, if they went as the soldiers wanted them to go. But, Sir, Mr. Justice Maclennan makes this comment on the officers who testified before him:
The officers who were examined before me gave their evidence in a straightforward manner, and their conduct and demeanour while under cross examination and the reasons they gave for their answers established their good faith and that they honestly believed they had the right to answer questions 6, 7, and 8 as they did. That disposes of the charge of perjury against the officers. In my opinion these charges are unfounded.
Let me add to that, Sir, this further statement at the conclusion of the judge's report:
There is a further circumstance that the prevailing impression in military circles was that the questions could be answered in the manner suggested.. .The men read the Montreal papers and were greatly interested in the result of the election, Mr. Rainville's public career and his stand on the important question before the country met with their approval.. . . There were no improper inducements, representations, suggestions or other misconduct by the officers or any of them to influence any non-commissioned officer or man to commit perjury by giving false answers to the questions on the envelopes, and the non-commissioned officers and men who appeared and were examined did not, in my opinion, commit perjury in connection with their answers. The charges of perjury and subornation of perjury are unfounded.
That is the judgment of Mr. Justice Maclennan, Mr. Speaker. But it is not as my hon. friend (Mr. Arehambault) would like it to be. My hon. friend picks passages here and there from the evidence and asks this House to pass upon his garbled scraps and condemn a judge who came to his conclusions on all the evidence, not on those extracts quoted by my hon. friend.
Now, there is one further remark of my hon. friend to which I wish to refer, because it elicited some rounds of applause from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. He said:
Many of the members of this House were elected by this soldier vote.

That called forth a vigorous "hear, hear" from many hon. gentlemen, on the other side of the House. There has been, Mr. Speaker a deliberate and persistent attempt on the part of the leader of the Opposition and his followers to get the people of this country to believe that this Government is in power and that many hon. members are sitting in this House because of the manipulation of the soldier vote. I want the attention of the House, Sir, while I refute that absolutely. I challenge any hon. gentleman opposite, from the leader of the Opposition to his most brilliant supporter, to question the figures which I am now going to give or to refute my argument based on those figures.
In the first place, referring to the province of Ontario, there are 82 seats for the Dominion House. I hold in my hand the general elections returns for 1917, which give the civil vote for each candidate and the military vote divided, showing those who voted in Canada, in the United Kingdom, and on the continent of Europe. To what extent were those 82 seats influenced by the soldier vote? All but four oj the members elected from the province of Ontario were elected, by the civilian vote alone by enormous majorities, and of the 4 elected with the help of soldier votes 3 were Conservative-Unionists and 1 was a Liberal-Unionist. Is it unreasonable, Mr. Speaker, for me to argue thus:	That we
might fairly assume that a candidate would get as large a proportion of the overseas vote as he did of the vote at home? Is it unfair to argue that a man who received 75 per cent of the vote polled here in Canada would likely receive 75 per cent of the soldier vote overseas? If that is a fair proposition, then we will allow to each of these four candidates the same proportion of the vote polled overseas as that which he received of the soldier vote polled in Canada, and we will hand to their opponents all the soldier votes polled overseas over and above that proportion. This done, each of these four candidates still has a seat in this House, and has it by handsome majority. More than that, each could afford to give to his opponent several hundred soldier votes, and still hold his seat in this House. Where, then, is there, so far as Ontario is concerned, the slightest evidence of any manipulation of the soldier vote?
I come next to the province of Quebec, which is represented in the House of Commons by sixty-five members. By the way, may I advert in this connection to a refer-
38i
ence made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Blondin)? He said that the Postmaster General ran in two constituencies in Quebec, and insinuated that the Government, by manipulating these votes, diverted votes to that hon. gentleman in order to elect him. Well, if there was any intention of doing anything of that kind it was foolish for the Postmaster General to run in two constituencies, and thus divide up the soldier vote; he might better have run. in one constituency only and had all the soldier votes coming to him go to that one place. But I may inform the hon. member for Brome that the Postmaster General, though defeated in that election in Quebec, polled nearly three times as many civilian votes as did the member for Brome. Further, of the 122 candidates in the sixty-five constituencies in the province of Quebec, only twenty candidates polled a larger civil vote than did the Postmaster General. So that although he did not get enough votes to elect him to this House, the vote which he did receive showed that he had in very large measure the confidence of the people. But if there was any conspiracy to elect the Postmaster General, why were those who were handling the thing so remiss that they did not see to it that several thousand votes were thrown to the Postmaster General to make sure of his election? Why was it not done? You have only to look through these election returns. The figures given in respect of the various constituencies carry with them a refutation of the charge or insinuation which has been made by the hon. member.
There is not a single member of this House from the province of Quebec whose seat could have been influenced in any way by the soldier vote. Every member from Quebec holds his seat in this House absolutely regardless of the soldier vote. Every member from the province of Quebec could have given his whole soldier vote to his opponent and still have held his seat in this House. In the face of these facts, how can hon. gentlemen argue that there was manipulation of the soldier vote so far as the province of Quebec is concerned?

Who appointed Preston?
Mr. EDWARDS-:' This man Preston was appointed by the leader of the Opposition at that time, the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Inasmuch as this man Preston has had quite a lot to say about the soldier vote overseas, may I be permitted to say one or two words about W. T. R. Preston? In the first place, I think it would be well for the members of this House to know who this man Preston is and who he was. He was organizer for the Liberal party in the province of Ontario from 1883 to 1893. He was defeated when he ran as a candidate in Durham for this House in 1885. He was appointed librarian of the Ontario Legislature in 1893. About that time a man named H. H. Cook testified that this man Preston had demanded from him $10,000 as the price of a senatorship. He not only made that statement, but he took his oath that such a demand had been made upon him by Preston. In 1896 Preston ran as a -candidate for the Hou-se of Commons in West Toronto. The people of West Toronto knew him as well as they knew him in Durham and he was defeated there. He resigned the librarianship to take charge of the campaign machine in the provnce of Ontario and from the time he took charge of the campaign machine it went from bad to worse in the way of corruption and scandals of all kinds, until the province of Ontario became disgraced in the eyes of the world.
He took a very active part in the election of a man by the name of Macnish in West Elgin in January, 1899. Mr. Macnish resigned because of the corruption which was disclosed on that occasion. Let me tell you one or two things that were done in that election. Preston was handling the gang in West Elgin.

speechtext:
The machine.
Mr. EDWARDS He was hugging the machine and he had with him the Pritchards, the Cap Sullivans, the Lewises and a lot -more of those fellows of unsavoury reputation. On the -Sunday before the election, Preston put on his Sunday air, went to the Sunday school and talked to the children. I presume he had on a regulation long coat, probably a silk hat, and he perhaps looked as pious as the leader of the Opposition (does sometimes-. He quoted Scripture, spoke to the children, told them to be good, not to do anything wrong, and there were tears in his voice. Then he said: " Now children, there is,one hymn I want you to sing; I like it very much; I want you to sing it for me to-day as a special favour." "What is the name of the hymn, sir?" "There is sunshine in my soul." And so he got them to sing the hymn "There is sunshine in my soul." That was on Sunday afternoon. On Sunday evening he met the gang; they got the machine together in an upper room of the hotel and laid their plans for defeating the wishes of the electors of West Elgin, by switching and spoiling ballots and defrauding the electors of their right of making a choice at the polls. The election was held and after the election, Preston, not happening to be in the riding that evening, telegraphed from

Toronto to Mr. Mannish, the Liberal candidate in West Elgin, as follows:
Heartiest congratulations, sorry to the bot-of my heart I cannot he with you to-night."
I suppose if he had been there he would have asked them to sing "There is sunshine in my soul."
To be supported by such a noble army oi workers should make you the proudest man in Ontario. Shake hands with the boys for me, and hug the members of the much-abused threshing machine for ' Auld Hang Syne.'
That telegram showed the intimate relations existing between Preston and Mac-nish. A day or two after Preston sent that telegram he received one from Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Sir Wilfrid sent for him. He said: "Mr. Preston, you have made a nice job of it, but you have not been getting enough money; we are going to send you to England as our Commissioner of Immigration at a salary of $3,000 a year." That was the reward for the good work which he had done. Shortly after that charges were made against Mr. Macnish, his election was protested, and he finally resigned his seat, couching his reasons in the following letter:
Messrs Crothers & Price,
Barristers, St. Thomas. Ont.
Hear Sirs :-
We beg to advise you that Mr. Macnish has discussed at length with his solicitors the charges contained in the petition which has been filed against his return as member of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario for West Elgin, and that they have to a considerable extent investigated the charges contained therein and other matters which have come to their knowledge in connection with the election. And the subscribers hereto make the following statements and admission respecting the same:
1.	That a large number of persons were specially sent into the constituency by men working on behalf of the liberal party for the express purpose of taking part on Mr. Macnish's behalf on the election held Januray 12, 1899, and we believe that fraudulent and corrupt means were used by some such persons to secure his election.
2.	That several of the said persons illegally and without authority acted as deputy returning officers at the said election, and in at least three cases so acted in the names of reputable local men, having under assumed names, been introduced to the returning officer by local agents of Mr. Macnish.
3.	That in many polling subdivisions of the riding there were grave irregularities connected with the return of the ballot boxes and their contents, the voting, and the counting of the ballots thereat.
4.	That there were large numbers of persons brought into the riding for the express purpose of personating legitimate voters, and assisted by some of Mr. Macnish's local supporters, such persons did personate qualified voters in voting for Mr. Macnish.
5.	That the declared number of votes for Mr. Macnish largely exceeded the number of bona-fide votes cast for him.

6.	That a large number of votes cast for Mr. Macdiarmid were in some nefarious and corrupt manner manipulated whereby the result of the election was rendered doubtful, and that in this connection the voting at Shedden and Middlemarch, and in several divisions in St. Thomas, where said persons acted as deputy returning officers, merits special mention.
7.	That there are good reasons to believe that there are many specific and well-authenticated cases where agents of Mr. Naenish concealed at their homes some of these strangers, who there paid large sums of money to electors to induce them to vote for him.
8.	That Mr. Naenish will forthwith deliver to the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly his resignation as a member thereof for the said electoral district.
I call attention to this statement:
And the subscribers hereto make the following statements and admissions respecting the same.
Who are the subscribers to this document? Donald Macnish, Liberal candidate, and A. B. Aylesworth, at one time Minister of Justice in the Laurier Government. Those are the men whose names arc signed to that confession of rascality of the worst kind, to that confession of all sorts of corruption. Those are the men, I say, who subscribed to that confession on the part of Macnish which this man Preston was connected with as he was connected with very many other shady transactions, and I will give you one or two more of them. It was Preston who, as organizer of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario, brought in this gang of pluggers, ballot-switchers, ballot-spoilers and markers. He is the man who was behind the cruise of the "Minnie M.", the nefarious work of Cap. Sullivan; he is the man who was behind the self-confessed ballot-switcher Pritchard, and others of his ilk. This man, Preston, was the individual who organized this machine, and he was rewarded for his work by being appointed to a $3,000 position as emigration officer over in England.
Now let us see what he did when he got there. No sooner had he got to England than he started his dirty work, his crooked work, over there. His hand was seen in connection with the North Atlantic Trading Company, for which his son-in-law was the .solicitor; and a certain Leopold Lazarus -a man of Hebrew extraction I would judge by his name, and about as crooked as they make them-was one of the agents for the company and had a room just across the hall from the office occupied by Mr. W.
T. R. Preston, emigration agent for the Dominion of Canada. Well, Sir, let me give you a letter which will indicate to some degree at least, but only to a small degree, what an unscrupulous rascal this

man W. T. R. Preston was, and I believe is. This is a letter, dated 18th October, 1901, and it is addressed to Mr. Thomas Southworth. The letter was written by Mr. W. T. R. Preston on his own printed paper and it reads as follows:
W. T. R. Preston,
Emigration Department.
IT Victoria Street,
London S.W.
October IS, 1901.
My dear Southworth,-
I have your letter of a late date on emigration to Ontario. You incidentally say in the letter that you are opposed to indiscriminate emigration. Well, in that respect you agree with everybody else. I do not know any one who suggests, or who would propose, that there should be indiscriminate emigration to that province. Whatever is done must be done carefully and any who are sent out must be well-selected emigrants. But don't run away with the idea that only well-to-do people, or those with money, are going to emigrate. If you are going to keep up a population in the old parts of the province, you must be satisfied with sober, energetic and industrious emigrants. I know all you people are terribly afraid of the foreign element. Upon that point I don't agree with you and have no hesitation in saying that a good class of foreigners scattered about the old parts of Ontario will do very much *more towards preserving a proper agricultural population than those from England, for instance. Politically speaking, I believe the introduction of a hundred families or so into some of those close ridings with the connections which could be had and maintained here would easily preserve for us many doubtful seats in that province. I know the anxiety or nervousness of the minister upon this question. Confidentially, I may tell you I fear it bears some slight resemblance to one of courage. You know enough about politics to know that courage always beats. However, as we don't agree upon that phase of the question we won't discuss it.
I have heard from the Wallaceburg people in answer to my letter of the middle of last month and I' am now trying to meet their wishes among the beet growers of Belgium. I will be over there in the course of a week or ten days and will then write to you as also to them upon the outlook there.
Yours very truly,

Now the signature on that is not typewritten. It is written with pen and ink, it is written on the paper of the Emigration Office where Preston had his office-there is no doubt about that. The leader of the Opposition in his remarks on 'the motion before the House spoke about fingermarks and earmarks and so on. Let him produce the telegram to which he refers, so that we may look at the fingermarks and the earmarks; let us see if he can produce this telegram with authentic marks on it as to its origin and parentage.
Mr. Speaker, why have I placed these matters before you and before the House.''
I have done so because I want to ask one question, and it is this: Knowing as we do know, and admitting as we must admit, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier knew the history of this W. T. R. Preston as he knew his alphabet; knowing that this W. T. R. Preston was the man who was connected with the switching of ballots, with the West Elgin election and with very many other elections which were protested in -the province of Ontario and with which his connection could not be doubted; knowing that he was the man who made a demand upon a certain gentleman for $10,000 as the price of a senatorship; knowing that he was the man connected with the North Atlantic Trading company and several organizations which were bleeding or robbing this country to the extent of thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars on the emigrants that were brought out here; knowing all this-knowing his connection and his loose, crooked connection with the politics of this country, the question I ask is: Why was that man selected as the agent of the Laurier party over in England? There is only one reason why he was selected. If this Government was guilty of the charge which has been levelled and of the insinuations that have been made__against it, that there was a conspiracy to'manipulate the votes overseas, may I tell you, Sir, that it was fully aware of the record, the reputation and the ability for crookedness of W. T. R. Preston, and if it wanted to manipulate votes and wanted somebody crooked to handle those votes, it knew where to get the best man for that kind of work in the Dominion of Canada, or on the continent of North America-W. T. R., Preston. I repeat that if the Government wanted to manipulate votes and wished for a past master in crookedness to do it, and to divert the soldier votes, it knew that W. T. R. Preston was the man to apply to for that purpose. It did not wish to manipulate the soldier votes and it did not apply to or get Mr. W. T. R. Preston to do it . What reason was there for the leader of the Opposition to select W. T. R. Preston for that job? Was it because of his record for integrity, was it because of his record for political purity that he was selected for that position? Is the Laurier party so lacking in men of integrity and honour and credibility that they have to select a man of the stamp of W. T. R. Preston to represent their candidates over in the United Kingdom? Why was it done? It was done in my judgment, Sir, because they knew that the
