speechtext:
sentiment of the soldiers was opposed to a leader and a party which had refused to back them up in their fight in Flanders. The Laurier Party said: "The man who is most likely to deceive those soldiers, to devise a plan whereby their votes will not be counted as they want ithem to be counted, is W. T. E. Preston. We will send that prince of political crooks over to England to represent the Laurier candidates." And yet the leader of the Opposition gets up here and professes a righteous indignation because of an alleged telegram which is vouched for by whom? By W. T. E. Preston. And the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) boasts that his ethical training makes him look with holy horror upon a request that a certain number of votes should be sent here or there. Well, well, the member for Brome shocked, the member whose ethical training is along the lines of political morality! When have we ever heard from the member for Brome or from the hon. leader of the Opposition, or from the honourable member from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) or from the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Eobb) or from a whole lot more that I would name if they were in their seat3-whoever heard of their having spasms over the crooked acts of the party they have supported for years? Did they stand aghast at the Sawdust Wharf transaction, at the Saskatchewan land deals,-at the selling of timber limits,-at the bogus ballot box affair down in Frontenac and Hastings Counties? Did they shed any tears over that last scandal? No, they did not express any honor, nor was the hon. George Graham tried or reproved for his part in it. Those bogus boxes were made at Watertown, and on a Sunday afternoon when the principals were going over to see how the work was progressing they went out of their way to visit Brockville and closet themselves with the Hon. George Graham,-the man who aspired to be the leader of the Liberal parity-to talk over the situation. Many of the ballots were printed in his newspaper office. That came out in the trial of Eiley, who served a year in Belleville jail for his share in the work. When have these hon. gentlemen, who now pose as political purists, ever denounced that sort of thing on their side of the House? I have yet to hear the first one.
We have a record here which is as long as a telegraph pole, if any one wanted to take time to read it, of attempt after attempt being made during the fifteen years the Laurier Government was in power to

investigate this, that and the other scandal, this act of corruption and that act of cor-rupion, but all attempts were voted down every time. I can give a list of nine or ten just off-hand. For instance, there was the request made on 13th April, 1899, on the motion of E. F. Clarke, to investigate the Yukon scandal. On June 27th 1899, Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper asked for the appointment of two judges to investigate the Yukon scandal. But he did more than that-and I commend this particularly to the attention of the hon. leader of the Opposition, who speaks of never getting behind a bush. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper said: "Appoint those judges to investigate the Yukon scandal, and if I cannot prove my charges to the hilt I will resign my seat in this House and place myself in a position that I will never run for or attempt to hold any public office as long as I live." That was a different attitude from the way my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition seeks shelter. He takes care that he gets behind something that will serve his purpose . to protect him from any harm. Then on 30th May, 1906, we asked for a committee to inquire into the management of public lands-that was refused. In 1909, another committee was asked to be appointed to investigate dredging scandals-that was refused. In 1910, Mr. Lennox,-now Judge Lennox-asked for a committee of seven to be appointed to go into the Lumsden charges -that was refused. Evidently, to use an expression which I heard the late 'Sir Wilfrid Laurier use in this House, " to the pure all things are pure," and he did not see any wrong in all those scandals, or if he did he was too clever or too shrewd to permit any investigation. Then we had a demand on March 26, 1907, for a special committee to investigate matters " affecting the honour of a ministef "-that was a motion growing out of the celebrated " Wine, women and graft " charge. I specially commend that to a certain hon. gentleman opposite. There we had an hon. minister directly involved. The charges were made, but the committee was refused -the party then dominant would not allow any investigation. Then on April 16, 1907, the present Prime Minister (Sir Eobert Borden) moved for the appointment of a committee to investigate election frauds in the constituencies of Brockville and West Huron as disclosed in the confessions of some of the hirelings of this man Preston -James Farr, Pritchett and others. These hon. gentlemen who were then supporting the Laurier party, and who are very much

concerned about the votes going the right way now-did they show any concern at that time? No, none whatever. They were quite sure that no investigation was needed. There was undoubted evidence of political frauds as shown by the confessions of various men taking part in the elections, and yet every attempt to secure an investigation was refused.
Now, Sir, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster) said in answer to a question that the officers over there had no right to canvass any soldier for his vote. Well, that -certainly is a funny doctrine. Where was the wrong, supposing a request was made for a certain number of votes to be applied to a certain constituency? Both sides had the same opportunity.
Is there anything wrong with my going to my friend John Jones and saying: John, I wish you to go out to the fifth concession, see the people there, tell them I am the better candidate of the two, that I am supporting the Government, and try to induce them to poll their votes for me- is there anything wrong about that? Every member of this House does it; every member of this House places his case before the electors and tries to induce them to vote for him. Any member of the House, had he the opportunity of going overseas, would have gone to the soldiers and tried to influence them to vote for him. And why should he not do it? W. T. R. Preston, who handled the campaign for the Liberals over there, had that opportunity and he certainly made use of it-by sending out advertisements and lies by the hour. And he did not stop at one lie, or two, or half a dozen. If he thought that by telling lies he could influence the soldier vote, that would not stop W. T. R. Preston. That is why he was sent over there-because he did not scruple to lie or to use any other means he could to influence votes. But he found out, as did those on the other side of the House, that the Laurier platform was very unpopular with the soldiers-and naturally so; therefore the only thing for them to do was to organize some kind of scheme whereby they could make many of the soldiers believe that they had a right to vote anywhere they saw fit. This scheme they organized and followed out to the extent of practically disfranchising fifty or sixty thousand voters by deceiving them in regard to their franchise. An hon. member asks me if Preston has been banned from the party. Oh no, W. T. R. Preston will not be banned from that party. He is the prime mover,
the man who is back of this whole thing. That is what I am trying to emphasize, Mr. Speaker. It was W. T. R. Preston who first made use of the expression used by the leader of the Opposition to-night-it did not originate with the leader of the Opposition -about officers sending soldiers to the front if they did not vote as they were directed to vote. How were the officers to know how these men voted? Did you ever hear such nonsense in your life? The soldier goes into the poll and marks his ballot. He is all alone when he marks that ballot; he puts an X opposite the name of the Government candidate or the Opposition candidate, as he sees fit. Nobody sees him mark the ballot; he puts it in the envelope and, if he is one of these voters at large, he designates the constituency in which he wants his vote to be applied. The point I make is that no returning officer or military officer could hold a club over that soldier's head and say:	If you do not vote so-and-so I will
send you up to the firing line, where, in all probability, you will be killed. The soldier went in there and marked his ballot behind a curtain, nobody saw him mark it; he marked it as he saw fit. How is the returning officer to know whether he voted for the Government candidate or against the Government candidate?
Earlier in the course of my remarks I quoted from the speech delivered by the leader of the Opposition and asked him to state explicitly what he meant by certain words he used. In explaining his words he emphatically and explicitly charged certain generals, colonels and others overseas with having intimated to the soldiers that if they did not vote for the Government candidates they would be sent to the front, where they would be likely to lose their lives. Now, a statement of that kind, coming from the hon. gentleman who is leader of the Opposition, even though only temporarily, calls for a little bit more, I think. The leader of the Opposition accompanied the assertion to which I have referred with an emphatic declaration that he was not the kind of man who would hide behind the bush in anything that he had to say. I ask him now to give me the name of one general, one colonel, one major, one officer, one man of any kind over there, who made such a statement as that? Now we will see whether the hon. member will hide behind the bush or not. He does not reply; he is hiding, all right-and it is a mighty small bush, too.

speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, what do you think of an hon. member of this House who charges that an officer threatened to send his men up to the firing line, where they would in all probability be killed, if they did not vote as he wanted them to vote; and who sits there in silence and refuses to name the man to whom he refers? I do not know what you think, Mr. Speaker; I am not a mind reader. But I credit you, Sir, with being a mind reader, and I believe that you can guess what I think. Perhaps .it will be a whole lot safer to let you guess than for me to attempt to say what I think and at the same time to keep within the rules of Parliament.
Well, what is the object of all this? I would apologize to the House for speaking at half-past twelve were it not for the fact that we have all listened very patiently to an hon. member "who spoke for four hours. What is the object of this motion that has been put forward by the leader of the Opposition? Mr. Speaker, the object was stated very clearly and explicitly this afternoon by the member for Bed Deer (Mr. M. Clark). I give it as my solemn belief and conviction that not an hon. member on the other side -not even the leader of the Opposition, who moved, this motion; not even the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), who sits beside him; not even the humblest back-bencher-believes for a moment the insinuation which has been cast upon the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon and yesterday. I do not believe that any hon. member opposite is convinced that the Minister of the Interior was mixed up in any dishonourable act or in any act that could reflect in the slightest degree on his honour as a man, as a member of this House, or as a minister of the Crown. I repeat, then, what is the object of all this? The object is, as the member for Bed Deer said, to play the game of politics; that is the object, and that is the only object. It was started at a political convention by one of the most unscrupulous political shysters that this country has ever produced.
Following it up, if you want to get at the parentage of that alleged telegram, I believe W. T. B. Preston had something to do with it. There is no doubt about that. Does anybody in this House believe that the statement made by a man with the record of W. T. B. Preston is going to weigh with this House or the people of this country for one single fraction of a second, when he imputes anything dishonourable to a man of the standing of the Minister of the Interior? Not for a moment.

As the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) said, hon. gentlemen opposite have made a great mistake in bringing this matter before the House, and they realized that shortly after the matter was brought up. I am quite sure they realized it because they took up all the time they could in a short afternoon. Then the suggestion came from that hon. gentleman who never gets behind a bush-he is an awfully good fellow to himself, isn't he?-when the Minister of the Interior was about to answer, that the debate be adjourned until the next day. " Oh, yes,'' he says, " only let my statement go out to the country with a few hours' start, and you cannot catch up to it. Let my statement get to the public now, and you defer your answer for twenty-four hours until to-morrow or the next day, and then things will be all right." That was the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman who never gets behind a bush. Well, if that was not getting behind a bush, it was getting in the direction of the bush pretty fast. The next indication we had of their superabundant courage was when the Minister of the Interior had spoken about twenty minutes or half an hour and six o'clock came. Then the courageous member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)' jumps up and calls the Speaker's attention to the fact that it is six o'clock, Wednesday, and no evening session. The medicine was coming to them faster than they could take it comfortably, and they wanted to get away. Then this afternoon we had the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) sticking most courageously to his guns and reading out extracts from the judgment of Mr. Justice Maclennan, occupying four hours of the time of this House, for what purpose? For the purpose, I am inclined to think, of preventing discussion on this matter. Perhaps I am wrong in that. I do not want to do the hon. member an injustice, but I certainly think I have some grounds for coming to that conclusion.
Well, we have given consideration to this matter, and what does it all amount to? An alleged charge based upon an alleged telegram which the leader of the Opposition cannot produce, and a statement made by some person overseas who says when he made the statement that he was a scoundrel or was doing what was wrong. Then we have that great and glorious and saintly man, W. T. B. Preston, to back up these charges. Mr. Speaker, it will require more than the sanctimonious air of the leader of the Opposition and his assumed

indignation at an alleged telegram which he is afraid to carry on his person, because he does not like to carry stolen property, or the vociferous declamation of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) or the long-winded side-tracking of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheras .(Mr. Ar-chambault) for hon. gentlemen opposite to make out their case.
I am content to leave it there. I rose for the purpose of endeavouring to show, what I think cannot be refuted, that the result of the election was not influenced in any way by the soldier vote, and I have demonstrated that province by province. I also wanted to show the company hon. gentlemen were keeping when they were making these charges. I wanted to show the record of W. T. R. Preston, the kind of man they *were relying on and applauding at their Liberal convention, when he was mouthing charges of this kind against a man whose shoe latchet he is not worthy to unloose. I am satisfied to leave the whole matter to the judgment of the country, and I am well satisfied also as to what the soldiers will say as to the remark of the hon. leader of the Opposition, a remark which I say he should never have made, a charge which I say is unworthy of any man in this House, implying, as it does, crime of the worst possible kind on the part of gallant men who were risking their lives for the people of this country. Certainly a charge of that kind should not be made unless the leader of the Opposition gets up and names the man who had been guilty of making a threat of that kind, for otherwise he leaves all these officers and gentlemen under that imputation.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 12.45 a.m.
Friday, September 26, 1919.

The House met at Three o'clock.

From the little county of Brome^probably the smallest agricultural community in Canada-many of its youth bravely went to the front, but through death, wounds and other wastage, *at i the time the election was held there were not enlisted in the Canadian army or otherwise capable of casting soldiers' votes from that county more than three hundred men. speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty, the House again went into Committee on Bill No. 4, to amend the Interpretation Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-application of Act to Orders in Council and regulations:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill remained in the Committee the other day in order that the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) might have an opportunity of satisfying himself as to whetner its enactment would in any way produce the effect of continuing in force or reviving Orders in Council that may have been heretofore passed, more especially Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act.
I ventured the opinion that the Bill would not produce that effect and since the matter was up before I have had it carefully gone through by the Deputy Minister of Justice, who advises me that there are no provisions in the Interpretation Act which, by being made applicable to the Orders in Council, would produce the results apprehended.

The difliculty I have is altogether in relation to the provisions of section 19 of the Interpretation Act. As I understand it, under the War Measures Act, when the war ceases those Orders in Council are repealed and disappear as if they never existed, and no proceeding can be instituted under them or anything at all done by virtue of them once they have lapsed. I have some idea that parts of this section 19 of the Interpretation Act, when applied to an Order in Council, would have the same effect upon it as it would upon a statute. I had better read the section:
Where any Act or enactment is repealed, or where any regulation is revoked, then, unless the contrary intention appears, such repeal or revocation shall not, save as in this section otherwise provided,

(a)	revive any Act, enactment, regulation or thing not in force or existing at the time at which the repeal or revocation takes effect; or,
(h) affect the previous operation of any Aot, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked, or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; cr,
(c)	affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred under the Act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked; or,
(d)	affect any offence committed against any Act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked, or any penalty or forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect thereof; or
It appears to me that if it is found that any offence has been committed against a repealed Order in Council,' which offence has not been tried or punished, even if the Order in Council of itself has been repealed by the operation of the law, this keeps it alive for the purpose of enabling proceedings to be instituted to collect a fine or enforce punishment:
(e)	affect any investigation, legal proceeding or remedy in respect of any such privilege, obligation, liability, penalty, forfeiture or punishment as aforesaid:
and any such investigation, legal proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty, forfeiture or punishment may be imposed, as if the Act or regulation had not been repealed or revoked.
These are the considerations which I wish to bring before the minister. If he is satisfied that it does not keep alive such an Order in Council, that is entirely a matter for himself and the Department of Justice, but I would suppose the provisions of this Bill keep alive, for the purpose of collecting a fine or enforcing punishment, an Order in Council, notwithstanding that the War Measures Act has been repealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not before me the section of the War Measures Act but, speaking from memory, the provisions of that Act in regard to the effect of the revocation of regulations passed under it is in the sense of the provision of this particular section 19, ifamely, that the revocation of an Order in Council would leave standing the position of everybody as it existed at the revocation and if, for instance, a man had committed an offence which rendered 'him liable then to a penalty or punishment, that revocation would not operate to relieve that man; it would operate for the future.
It would operate for the future, the law being no longer in force, so that no man could commit any offence under , it; but speaking from memory I think a provision in the War Measures Act itself saves that situation. That is to say that when orders made under it are revoked they are revoked for the future, but it maintains the .situa-

tion of everybody as it existed at that time and leaves the parties who have violated those orders, where the offence is completed, liable to the punishment to which they already had rendered themselves liable before the revocation of the law. If it be necessary to make application of this section for the purpose of obtaining that result, it seems to me that that is a result that ought to be obtained so that a man who has violated any of these regulations, many of which were applicable only in war time, should not escape scot free from the consequences of that offence which he has committed, merely by reason of the fact that the war having ended that law ceases to be operative and is not being applicable under the existing conditions. An opposite interpretation would create a situation which would be, I think, manifestly unfair and unjust-a situation where, as between two violators of a law absolutely in force at the time of the violation, the one that managed to escape until the war ended would go scot free, whereas the other, who was apprehended while the war was still on, might be subjected to very serious punishment. I hardly think it would be suggested that a consequence of that kind would be just as between people all of whom, while that law was in force, were equally affected and equally bound to obey it, and equally subject to be punished if they failed to obey it. The provision of the War Measures Act on the subject of the revocation of orders and regulations under it is found in subsection 2 of section 6. It provides:,
All orders and regulations made under this section shall have the force of law, and shall be enforced in such manner and by such courts, officers, and authorities, as the Governor in Council may prescribe, and may be varied, extended or revoked by any subsequent order or regulation; but if any order or regulation is varied, extended or revoked, neither the previous operation thereof, nor anything duly done thereunder shall be affected thereby, nor shall any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing, or incurred thereunder toe affected by such variation, extension, or revocation.
It seems to me that while this is not in the actual words of the section of the Interpretation Act, it is very nearly so. The provision of subsection of section 19 of the Interpretation Act declares that the repeal or revocation shall not have the effect ,of reviving:
Any Act, enactment, regulation or thing not in force or existing at the time at which the repeal or revocation takes effect;
I understand no exception is taken to that proceeding.

-or, (b) affect the previous operation of any Act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked, or anything duly done or suffered thereunder.
Now the provision of the War Measures Act is that neither the previous operation thereof-that is the previous operation of the revoked order under the War Measures Act-nor anything duly done thereunder shall be affected thereby nor shall any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing, or incurred thereunder be affected by such variation which is, I think, substantially the same provision as in subsections (b) and (c) of section 19 of the Interpretation Act. Subsection (c) is almost in the same words. The revocation shall not:
Affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred under the Act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked; or,
Then subsection (d):
Affect any offence committed against any Act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked, or any penalty or forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect thereof; or,
And then subsection (e):
Affect any investigation, legal proceeding-

and so on. Those I think are simply
in substance the same as the provisions already contained in the War Measures Act as to the effect of orders made under it or their subsequent revocation. If they were not so, I would submit that it would be proper to make that provision. That is not reviving or continuing the law in operation, hut it is leaving everybody in the same position in which they were at the date of the revocation.
The Act itself says that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Act itself says that, that is what I am pointing out. If that be a good rule of interpretation for a statute, and Parliament has determined that it is, it seems to us good rules of interpretation for the interpretation of statutes and for the interpretation of Orders in Council. As I said the other day, we have found that it was of great practical advantage to have settled rules of interpretation. In the absence of these rules we found the necessity arises very frequently in the case of each particular Order in Council of inserting clauses to define the precise meaning of certain terms that might be used in the Order in Council; and in our opinion we were not following a very bad example in following the example of

Parliament in its determination of how its enactments should be interpreted when we adopted the provisions governing that interpretation and applied them simply to such rules, regulations and orders as the Governor in Council is authorized to make. The statutes have general application; they have no special application to the orders made under the War Measures Act.

This discussion would possibly not have taken place at all were it not for the fact that during last session this same point was debated in the absence of the minister. An Order in Council was passed enabling a commissioner, I think Mr. Pringle, to deal with difficulties between the pulp-producing companies of this country and the newspaper people, and in the absence of the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance introduced a Bill for the purpose of continuing the power that was vested in the commissioner under the Order in Council, otherwise the Order in Council would have lapsed by reason of peace. I took the point then that there was no necessity for that Act, because the provisions which the minister read enabled proceedings, once begun, to continue to the end whether the order lapsed or not. The Minister of Finance, himself a lawyer, agreed with me, but he said that the solicitor in charge of the business and the Department of Justice did not agree with him, they holding the view that the Order in Council of itself was not enough and that there would have to be a statute. The minister will And that Act in last year's statute. Therefore if that interpretation was correct, I do not want to see any laws kept alive to punish people if it was not the intention of the War Measures Act to keep such laws alive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not desire in virtue of this enactment to alter the law on that subject, whatever it may be. What we had in mind was the interpretation of the particular statute of last year, and of course I am not in a position to determine between the different opinions on that statute. It may have been thought that it was more important to make that absolutely clear which might perhaps without the statute have been the law. But in any event it does seem to me quite clear that there is no substantial modification made in the effect of provisions under the War Measures Act by simply subjecting those provisions to the interpretation clauses, including this one which applies to statutes generally; and, as I
read the War Measures Act, the effect would be the same. But more than that, I think if there be a difference between them that in this Bill these interpretation rules are made to apply only in so far as they are not inconsistent. The section is:
Every provision of the Interpretation Act ehall extend and apply to every order and regulation heretofore or hereafter passed by the Governor in Council in the execution of any powers delegated by statute, except in so far as any such provision is inconsistent with the intent or object of such order or regulation, or would give to any word, expression or clause thereof an interpretation repugnant to the subject matter or the context, or is in any such order or regulation declared not applicable thereto.
There is no exception as to the legal provision; I was under the impression there was some exception. But I think the provisions are substantially the same. I think if there be any difference it would produce the effect which, I take it, was intended by the War Measures Act, and which in any event, in order to be just to everybody concerned, ought to be so.

Mr. Chairman, we have from time to time had debates of this House referred to before the courts to justify the interpretation of an Act, and I have heard instances where the remarks of the gentlemen introducing Bills had been quoted to justify a certain interpretation, but the judges <amd the lawyers would not hear of it. Now we have had the Minister of Justice and the leader of the Opposition, both gentlemen who adorned the bench in days gone by, talking a long time on this Bill. This may be a very far-reaching Bill- I have not caught the full scope of it yet- but if there is any doubt in it it should be dispelled. There must be a purpose in passing this Bill. Whatever may be the purpose it should be enunciateu, and whatever the language of the Bill it should be clear and concise. Surely there is no need for all this discussion on such a short Bill if the foundation be absolutely clear and nothing hidden. Language is made sometimes to conceal one's ideas. I think in our statutes we should use language that is absolutely clear so that a child may read as he runs. I do not know how this would apply to the War Measures Act, or to the Military Service Act, or anything of that kind, but I would like the language to be clear and the meaning made explicit right now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose is precisely to make a clear-cut rule by which Orders in Council may be interpreted, and we find those clear-cut rules in a statute laying



down the principles by which tows are to be interpreted. Now, we want the same rules that Parliament decided ought to be applied to the interpretation of the laws enacted by Parliament to be applied to Orders in Council. The purpose is to make for clearness and for uniformity of interpretation so thai * we may not be in a position where it may be contended that whereas a certain expression in a statute must, under this Act, be held to mean a certain thing, the same expression in an Order in Council might be open to the suggestion that it meant something else. The purpose is precisely to ma*.e for clearness of understanding of these Orders in Council and for uniformity of interpretation.

Mr. Chairman, is there any particular case the minister could give to the House which has suggested this legislation, where the terms of an Order in Council were subject- to an interpretation which did not conform to the interpretation which should be given if we used the Interpretation Act? I see the section reads:
Every provision of the Interpretation Act shall extend and apply to every order and regulation heretofore or hereafter passed by the Governor in Council.
Now, there may have been conditions heretofore different from those which now exist, and by passing this Bill we submit the interpretation of those Orders in Council, passed a long -while ago, to this particular legislation. I think that is what my friend from Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) had, in mind.
Yes.

We are binding the courts to give a decision which might be other than what would be given if the Bill were not passed. I would like to know from the minister what was the date of the Order in Council under which the question arose which brought to his mind this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot recollect that it was in view of any particular Order m Council. What called attention to it was that in the carrying out of the War Measures Act the number of Orders in Council became very considerably multiplied, and it was found a great inconvenience to have to insert an Interpretation Act in each order.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was a very unhandy way to have to embody the clauses of the Interpretation Act in each Order in Council in order to make them apply. It seemed

therefore much more desirable that we should once for all enact that the rules of interpretation laid down by law for statutes should apply to Orders in Council; and we did enact, under the War Measures Act, an Order in Council to that effect. Now that Order ,in Council, in common wlith others under the War Measures Act, is about to come to the end of its effect. Our experience: of the value of such a rule led us to believe that it ought to be continued, and therefore we submit to this House that what are good rules to interpret its statutes must surely be good rules to interpret Orders in Council.

I admit that. But the
word " heretofore '' does not merely cover Orders in Council passed during the war, but Orders in Council passed ever since Confederation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there can ,be no
doubt about it. I do not think we have had for a great many years any material alterations in the Interpretation Act; the rules therein .contained represent the wisdom of Parliament upon the subject of interpretation. They have been consecrated by the respect that has been accorded to them in all these years and by their application by the courts,, and it did seem to us that we could not set to work to-day to make a better system of rules of interpretation. It is, after all, Parliament exercising its authority over these Orders in Council ,in the same way that it has exercised authority over statutes; it is making what we did subject to interpretation in the way that Parliament thinks laws .ought to be interpreted. -As those Orders in Council were given the effect of law, I should think it would commend itself to the judgment of Parliament that upon a question of determining their precise meaning they should he interpreted in the same way as all other laws are interpreted-laws of .the past as well as the laws of the future.

There is doubtless good reason for the enactment of such a section as that which,is before the committee. But how is it going to work out if the Interpretation Act of to-day is different from the Interpretation Act of yesterday? Is there not a danger that, a result which is not intended may be brought about?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not,in a position to say that there has been no amendment of the Interpretation, Act or how -many years we would have to go back to find any amendment ; but It must be a very considerable, time since there was was any su-bstan-

tial modification. When the Interpretation Act was passed it was made applicable to then existing legislation as well as to future legislation. The very first section of it is:
Every provision of this Act shall extend and apply to every Act of the Parliament of Canada, now or hereafter passed.
Sir SAM,HUGHES:	Are there any exceptions in the Interpretation Act as there are in this section of the Bill which we are now considering?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The exceptions in this Act are the exceptions made when the interpretation of the Interpretation Act would be inconsistent with the very context of the Order in Council itself. The purpose of the Interpretation Act is not to determine that things which, on their face, clearly mean one	thing are	to	mean	another;the	purpose of	the Act	is to
give an interpretation to any expression which, on the face of either an Act of Parliament or an Order in Council, is not clearly defined, and which might have one meaning or another. The law says that when an expression is used in that way it shall mean a certain thing, and we are. applying that to Orders in Council. The wording of section 29 of the Interpretation Act is: " Unless the context otherwise requires," and of section 30: " In every Act, unless the contrary intention appears." The *words used in this Bill are:
Except in so far as any such provision is inconsistent with the intent or object of such order or regulation, or would give to any word, expression or clause thereof an interpretation repugnant to the subject matter or the context, or is in any such order or regulation declared not applicable thereto.
In other words, these rules are to apply except when, on the face of the Order itself, it appears that the intention was different from that which the application of these rules would give to it, or unless the Order in Council itself says that such and such an expression shall have a different meaning.
If the intent or the object of such order or regulation runs counter to the provisions of the Interpretation Act, then the Interpretation Act shall not apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is right. If Parliament, in passing an Act, or the Governor in Council in passing an Order in Council, indicates that it is not intended to say the thing which the Interpretation Act would make the Act or Order say, then what is intended is made perfectly clear and the Interpretation Act is overruled. The Interpreta-
39i
tion Act is not intended to restrict the power of Parliament to legislate or the power that the Governor in Council may have under Orders in Council. It is simply intended, where nothing to the contrary appears-in other words, where no different definition of intention appears-to apply certain rules as to how the interpretation shall be made. [DOT]
The intent or object of such order or regulation is to be determined, not by the debates in the House, but by a reading of the statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
By a reading of the
statute.

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the Dominion By-Elections Act, 1919.
He said: This Bill became necessary by reason of what was, I think an oversight when the By-Elections Act, 1919, was passed during the spring session of the House. It is well known that the Dominion franchise is, in principle, based upon the Franchise Acts which exist in the various provinces throughout the country. The Dominion qualification, as set out in section 10 of the Dominion Elections Act, is as follows :

In a country ais great as Canada, and with such wonderful differences in geography and social conditions, it is extremely difficult for a person living in one part of the country to utter words of conviction in regard to social problems that prevail thousands of miles away. It is to be noted that in the enumeration of the courts to 'which applicants may apply for naturalization, the long-established Court of General Sessions of the Peace of Ontario has been omitted. I suppose for the last fifty or sixty years in Ontario nearly all applications for naturalization have been made .to the Court of General Sessions of the Peace. The clerk of that court is the clerk of the peace, but he is not the clerk t)f the county court. The clerk of the peace in practically all the country districts is the Crown attorney, who has for many years been in the habit of receiving and dealing with these applications. I do not think it was the intention to deprive him of that function or of the simple fee that usually accompanies such applications. On the other ,liand, the 'County 'Court is enumerated in the Act, but the clerk of that court has not been in the habit of receiving applications for naturalization. This proposed legislation, therefore, is simply to .include in the enumeration of the courts in Ontario the Court of General Sessions of the Peace.

I have no objection to
including the Court of General Sessions of the Peace for Ontario, but I wish,to point out that we have similar courts in Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec city.

speechtext:
They sit and hold the
court of King's Bench, of course, but the office of their court is a civil court; the clerk of their court is a clerk of the civil court; the whole matter is handled by a court of civil jurisdiction. I do not think that the quantity of work that is entailed can be very excessive. As to finding a man always at his post, if I am not mistaken, the procedure is- not one under which an applicant presents himself there one day and says: Now I want to be heard about my naturalization.
Notice has to be given.

I quite agree with my hon. friend that we should not, for the pleasure of adding the name of the province of Quebec, alter the Bill. My only point was that I thought that, speaking for the district of Montreal, the judges of the Superior Court and Circuit Court are so busy that proper distribution of the work should be made. My hon. friend may imagine what it means for a judge in Montreal during the term, sitting in a case of importance, to have to adjourn that case or to postpone the hearing of witnesses in order to look after this purely ministerial work. If my hon. friend finds something in my suggestion, I would ask him to think of it, because they have all the officers of the Crown at the Court of Sessions of the Peace, and with the small fee given, I am quite sure that they would see that those cases are channelled towards the sessions of the Peace, thus relieving the judges of the Superior 'Court in Montreal who are already overtaxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In Montreal, the judges of the Superior Court are not, I understand, troubled with these applications, which are made to the Circuit Court. There was a time when I used to hear a great deal of complaint about the overwork of the Circuit Court, but-I do not know whether the salve that was applied, which was not in the direction of taking away jurisdiction, but rather in that of conferring remuneration, had anything to do with the matter or not,-I have not, for quite some time, heard any complaint or .suggestion that the judges of the Circuit Court are at present overworked, and they have carried on that work as I have said, from time immemorial. I shall, however, be very glad to make inquiry into the situation.
Montreal is a special place; it is the only district in the province where there are circuit judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think it can be said that in our rural districts generally the judges of the Superior Court who also hold the Circuit Court are overburdened with work. I understand that the work in the district which the hon. gentleman has in mind has very much increased of recent years, but taking the average rural district where the judge of the Superior Court holds the Circuit Court, I think we would all agree that they can hardly be described as being overworked.
There is also to be considered
5 p.m. the fact that I am not sure that in most of the rural districts you will find a court answering to the name of Court of Sessions. That is doubtful, although I do not want to speak positively. Most of that work is done by stipendiary magistrates. Before we proceed to make the change, the conditions should be looked into, and I will make inquiries.

Since the Minister of
Justice (Mr. Doherty) has spoken about the district I have in mind, I am going to name it. I have in mind the district of Three Rivers. My hon. friend laughs. He knows that the district of Three Rivers is just undergoing a period of development unique in the Dominion of Canada, and it is the place where applications for naturalization are being made every day by Americans and Norwegians, who are manufacturing pulp and paper. We are getting more applications for naturalization in that district than in any other district that I know of just now, with the exception, perhaps, of the West, into which farmers are flocking. We have a Court of General Sessions of the Peace which has time to look into the applications, pass upon them and issue certificates. Since the minister is going to take this question into consideration, I make a special plea for Three Rivers on that ground, and I think my plea ought to be granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will certainly look into it, and I want to make it clear that my laughing did not imply any reflection on Three Rivers, but was because my hon. friend thought it necessary to tell me what district he had in mind. I understand, with the devotion to his duties which characterizes him, he always has Three Rivers in mind.
